## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## (Volume II)
## 68. Explanation of the Indriyaparopariyattañāṇa Niddesa

In the Indriyaparopariyattañāṇa Niddesa, although the word "Tathāgatassa" (of the Tathāgata) does not appear explicitly in the Mātikā-uddesa (the summary table of contents), it is already considered as taught as "Tathāgatassa" because it is stated (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi) that "the six knowledges are not shared with the disciples."

Therefore, the term "Tathāgata," which is established by way of meaning in the summary known as the Mātikā, is included in the Niddesa (detailed exposition). "He sees beings" means they are called "beings" (satta) because of their state of being attached (laggatā) to the aggregates of form (rūpa) and so forth by way of desire and lust (chandarāga). He sees and observes those beings with the eye of wisdom known as the Knowledge of the Degree of Maturity of the Faculties (Indriyaparopariyattañāṇa).

"Apparajakkha" (those with little dust) means those in whose wisdom-eye there is little dust of lust and so forth; thus they are called "apparajakkha." Or, those for whom the dust of lust and so forth is little; thus they are called "apparajakkha." (He sees) those persons with little dust.

"Mahārajakkha" (those with much dust) means those in whose wisdom-eye there is much dust of lust and so forth; thus they are called "mahārajakkha." Or, those for whom the dust of lust and so forth is much; thus they are called "mahārajakkha."

"Tikkhindriya, Mudindriya": "Tikkhindriya" means those whose faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā) and so forth are keen. "Mudindriya" means those whose faculties such as faith and so forth are dull.

"Svākāra, Dvākāra": "Svākāra" means those who have good portions or aspects (ākāra) of faith and so forth. "Dvākāra" means those who have loathsome and blameworthy portions or aspects of faith and so forth.

"Suviññāpaya, Duviññāpaya": "Suviññāpaya" means those who can note the reason or cause taught and are easy to make understand. Those who are the opposite of that are "duviññāpaya."
2:
Some people see both the next world and faults such as lust as fear. In the exposition of this term "appekacca" (some), it does not refer only to the next world; because they are accustomed to seeing great fear in the world of the aggregates (khandha) and so forth, as well as in faults such as lust, the meaning should be taken as "paralokavajjabhayadassāvī" (those who see fear in the next world and in faults). Some people are those who do not see fear in the next world and in faults. It is called "loka" (world) because of its nature of crumbling and disintegrating. It is called "vajja" (fault) in the sense of that which should be avoided. By this much, the detailed exposition (niddesa) of the summary (uddesa) is completed.

Again, wishing to further explain the detailed exposition, he said "apparajakkha, mahārajakkha," and so forth. In that passage, one who has faith, characterized as placing confidence in the Three Jewels, is called "saddho" (the faithful). That person endowed with faith is "apparajakkha" (with little dust) because the dust of lack of faith (assaddhiya) and the remaining unwholesome dust rooted in lack of faith are little. One who has no faith is called "assaddho" (the faithless). That person is "mahārajakkha" (with much dust) because the aforementioned dusts are great.

One who has exerted energy is called "āraddhaviriyo." That person is "apparajakkha" because the dust of laziness (kosajja) and the remaining unwholesome dust rooted in laziness are little. One who sinks down in a loathsome manner due to deficient energy is called "kusīda" (the lazy). That person is "mahārajakkha" because the aforementioned dusts are great.

One who has mindfulness established by approaching the object is called "upaṭṭhitasati." That person is "apparajakkha" because the dust of forgetfulness (muṭṭhassacca) and the remaining unwholesome dust rooted in forgetfulness are little. One whose mindfulness is confused and lost is called "muṭṭhassati." That person is "mahārajakkha" because the aforementioned dusts are great.

One who is well-established in the object through absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) is called "samāhita" (the concentrated). That person is "apparajakkha" because the dust of restlessness (uddhacca) and the remaining unwholesome dust rooted in restlessness are little. One who is not concentrated is "asamāhita." That person is "mahārajakkha" because the aforementioned dusts are great.

One who has wisdom that perceives the arising and passing away is called "paññavā" (the wise). That person is "apparajakkha" because the dust of delusion (moha) and the remaining unwholesome dust rooted in delusion are little. One who has bad wisdom, being confused due to delusion, is called "duppañño" (the unwise). That person is "mahārajakkha" because the aforementioned dusts are great.

A faithful person is one with keen faculties (tikkhindriya). He is called "faithful" because strong faith arises frequently; because of that very faculty of faith (saddhindriya), he is called "one with keen faculties." A faithless person is one with dull faculties (mudindriya). Frequently...
3: One is called faithless (assaddha) because of the repeated arising of faithlessness (assaddhiya). One is called of weak faculties (mudindriya) because of the intermittent arising of the weak faculty of faith (saddhindriya). The same method applies to the remaining individuals. A person with faith has a good state (svākāra) because of that very faith. A person without faith has a bad state (durākāra) because of that very faithlessness. The same applies to the remaining individuals. One is called 'easy to instruct' (suviññāpaya) because they can be easily made to understand. One is called 'difficult to instruct' (duviññāpaya) because they are hard to make understand. Regarding the phrase 'seeing the danger of faults in the next world' (paralokavajjabhayadassāvī), since faith and other qualities are extremely pure only for one endowed with wisdom, such a person sees the danger of faults in the next life through wisdom associated with those extremely pure faith and other qualities, or through wisdom conditioned by those pure qualities. Therefore, those endowed with the four qualities starting with faith are also called 'those who see the danger of faults in the next world.' Now, to show the 'world' (loka) and 'fault' (vajja) mentioned in the phrase 'paralokavajjabhayadassāvī,' the text says 'loko' and so forth. Therein, the aggregates themselves are called the 'world' (khandha-loka) in the sense of perishing. The same method applies to the other two types of worlds. The 'world of unfortunate existence' (vipatti-bhava-loka) refers to the woeful planes (apāya). Since that woeful world is an undesirable result and a distorted gain, it is called 'vipatti' (misfortune); since it comes to be, it is called 'bhava' (existence); since misfortune itself is the existence, it is called 'vipatti-bhava'; and since the misfortune-existence is the world, it is called 'vipatti-bhava-loka.' The 'world of the origin of misfortune' (vipatti-sambhava-loka) refers to the kamma that leads to the woeful planes. Since the result arises from that kamma, it is called 'sambhava' (origin); since it is the cause of ruin, it is called 'vipatti-sambhava'; and since the origin of misfortune is the world, it is called 'vipatti-sambhava-loka.' The 'world of fortunate existence' (sampatti-bhava-loka) refers to the happy planes (sugati). Since that happy world is a desirable result and a good gain, it is called 'sampatti' (fortune); since it comes to be, it is called 'bhava'; since fortune itself is the existence, it is called 'sampatti-bhava'; and since the fortune-existence is the world, it is called 'sampatti-bhava-loka.' The 'world of the origin of fortune' (sampatti-sambhava-loka) refers to the wholesome kamma that leads to the happy planes. Since the result arises from that kamma, it is called 'sambhava'; since it is the cause of fulfillment, it is called 'sampatti-sambhava'; and since the origin of fortune is the world, it is called 'sampatti-sambhava-loka.' The phrases 'eko loko' (one world) and so forth have the same meanings as stated below. The neuter term 'vajja' (fault) is used because it is not specifically designated by name. Defilements (kilesa) refer to greed (rāga) and so forth. Misconduct (ducarita) refers to killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth. Volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) refer to meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth. They are called 'kamma leading to existence' (bhavagāmikamma) because they lead to existence through their power of producing results. Among volitional formations, only those kammas that produce results are intended. The word 'iti' indicates the various types mentioned. The perception of intense fear in this world and in these faults is called 'tibbābhayasaññā.' With the word 'tibba' (intense), the meaning of 'para' in the word 'paraloka' is explained. With the word 'bhayakaññā,' the meaning of 'bhaya' (fear/danger) is explained. Both the world and faults are called 'danger' (bhaya) because they are the causes of the danger of results, and because they occur together with dangers such as birth (jāti). The perception of danger that arises thus is based on those respective worlds and faults. For example, just as an intense perception of fear arises regarding an enemy who has raised a sword to strike, similarly, the intense perception of fear is directed toward the world and faults. The phrase 'by these fifty aspects' means that within each of the ten groups of five (pañcaka), such as the group of five regarding those with little dust in their eyes (apparajakkha-pañcaka), there are five aspects; thus, the Buddha knows the five faculties such as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) as if seeing them with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). 'Ājānāti' means knowing through all aspects and boundaries. 'Paṭivijjhati' means...
4:
In the aforementioned world and in the fault, "tibba bhayasaññā" means an intense perception of fear. By the word "tibba," the meaning of the other world (paraloka) is intended. "Bhayasaññā" is the meaning of the word fear (bhaya). Both the world, such as the aggregates, and the fault, such as lust, are called fear (bhaya) because they are the causes of fears like [karmic] results, and because they occur together with fears like birth (jāti). The perception of that as fear is "bhayasaññā." "Paccupaṭṭhitā hoti" means it stands close to and depends on that world or fault. For example, just as an intense perception of fear arises when seeing an enemy who has raised a sword to strike, so too does an intense perception of fear arise regarding the world and the fault.

"By these fifty aspects" means that among the ten groups of five, starting with the group of five regarding those with little dust in their eyes (apparajakkha-pañcaka), there are five aspects in each, thus making fifty aspects. "These five faculties" refers to the five faculties starting with the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). "He knows (jānāti)" means the Buddha knows through wisdom. "He sees (passati)" means he makes it as if seen with the divine eye. "He understands (aññāti)" means he knows through all aspects and limits. "He penetrates (paṭivijjhati)" means he pierces through with wisdom by way of seeing completely without leaving any part behind.

## ဣန္ဒြိယပရောပရိယတ္တဉာဏနိဒ္ဒေသဝဏ္ဏနာ နိဋ္ဌိတာ။

## ၆၉။ အာသယာနုသယဉာဏနိဒ္ဒေသဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the exposition of the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa), the exposition is set forth in five ways, starting with "Here, the Tathāgata..." Among those five, "inclination" (āsaya) and "latent tendency" (anusaya) have the meanings already mentioned. "Carita" (conduct) refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed in the past. "Adhimutti" (resolve) refers to the releasing (inclining) of the mental continuum toward wholesome or unwholesome states in the present life. "Bhabbābhabba" refers to beings who are capable [of realization] and those who are incapable. They are called "bhabba" (capable) because they are born through the noble birth (ariya-jāti). Here, the present tense is used to indicate the near future. Or they are called "bhabba" because they will be born through the noble birth; it means they are a vessel (bhājana) for the supramundane states. Those beings who are endowed with the supporting condition (upanissaya) suitable for penetrating the Noble Path are called "bhabba." Those opposite to what has been said are "abhabba."

"What is the inclination of beings?" and so forth is the detailed explanation (paṭiniddesa) of the exposition. Therein, "eternal (sassata)" means the view that it is permanent and eternal. "World (loka)" refers to the self (attabhāva). In this view, they think that only the body (sarīra) perishes, but as for the self, it is the same self in this life and in the next. They call it "world" because they assume the self sees by itself. "Non-eternal (asassata)" means impermanence. They think the self perishes along with the body. "Finite (antavā)" means having produced jhāna in a limited kasina, they regard the mind with that limited kasina object as a finite self. "Infinite (anantavā)" means having produced jhāna in an immeasurably vast kasina, they regard the jhāna mind with that vast kasina object as an infinite self. "The soul (jīva) is the same as the body (sarīra)" means the view that the self and the body are one and the same. "Jīva" refers to the self. Here, the masculine gender is changed to the neuter. "Sarīra" refers to the collection of the five aggregates in the sense of a heap. "The soul is one thing, the body is another" means the view that the self is one thing and the collection of the five aggregates is another. "The being (tathāgata) exists after death" means that although the five aggregates perish in this life, the being still exists after death and does not perish. Here, the name "tathāgata" is said to be a name for beings. Some say "tathāgata" refers to an Arahant. Those who hold this view see the fault of the destruction of the noble ones' virtues in the view "does not exist after death," and thus they hold the view "exists after death." "The being does not exist after death" means the view that the five aggregates also perish in this life, and the being also ceases and perishes after death, not arising again. Those who hold this view see the fault in the eternalist view of "exists after death" and in the lack of benefit in developing the path, and thus they hold the view "does not exist after death."
5:
They think the self is finite. 'Anantavā' means without end; having produced jhāna in a vast kasiṇa, they think that the mind which has that vast kasiṇa as its object is the infinite self. 'The soul (jīva) is the same as the body (sarīra)' means that the soul and the body are one and the same. 'Jīva' refers to the self (atta); it is used in the neuter form 'jīvaṃ' due to a change in gender. 'Sarīra' refers to the group of five aggregates in the sense of a heap. 'The soul is one thing, the body is another' means the soul is one thing and the group of five aggregates is another. 'The being exists after death' means the aggregates perish right here in this life, but the being exists after death, persists, and does not perish. Here, they say the word 'Tathāgata' is a designation for a being. Some, however, say 'Tathāgata' means an Arahant. Those who hold the view 'the being exists after death' take this position because they see a fault in the side of 'does not exist'. 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death' means the aggregates perish right here, and the Tathāgata also does not exist after death, but is cut off and perishes. These people take this position because they see a fault in the side of 'exists'. Those who hold the view 'he both exists and does not exist' see a fault in taking only one side and thus take both sides. Those who hold the view 'he neither exists nor does not exist' see that both faults apply to taking both sides, and thus adopt the 'eel-wriggling' (amarāvikkhepa) view, saying 'it is not that he exists, and it is not that he does not exist; it is not that he neither exists nor does not exist.'

In this context, the method of the Commentary is: the divisions of views are stated in ten modes, starting with 'The world is eternal.' Among them, 'The world is eternal' is the view occurring by way of taking the five aggregates as the world and holding 'This world is permanent, stable, and eternal.' 'Non-eternal' is the view occurring by way of annihilationism, holding that very world to be 'cut off and perishing.' 'Finite' is the view occurring by way of holding 'The world is finite' by one who has attained a limited kasiṇa, entering into attainment (samāpatti) in a kasiṇa the size of a winnowing tray or a saucer, taking the mental and material phenomena occurring within that attainment as 'the world' and as 'finite' due to the limitation of the kasiṇa. That view can be either eternalism or annihilationism. For one who has attained a vast kasiṇa, entering into attainment in that kasiṇa, taking the mental and material phenomena within the attainment as 'the world' and as 'infinite' due to the extent of the kasiṇa, it is the view occurring by way of holding 'The world is infinite.' That view also can be either eternalism or annihilationism. 'The soul is the same as the body' is the view occurring by way of annihilationism because the body, which is of a perishable nature, is taken as the 'soul,' holding 'When the body perishes, the soul also perishes.' In the second phrase, because a soul other than the body is taken, holding 'Even though the body perishes, the soul does not perish but is eternal'...
6:
"...this is the view occurring by way of eternalism. Among the views such as 'The Tathāgata exists,' for one who holds 'The being called Tathāgata exists after death,' it is the first eternalist view. For one who holds 'He does not exist,' it is the second annihilationist view. For one who holds 'He both exists and does not exist,' it is the third partial-eternalist view. For one who holds 'He neither exists nor does not exist,' it is the fourth eel-wriggling view.

The word 'iti' indicates the basis of the aforementioned various views. Beings are either dependent on the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi) or dependent on the view of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi). Eternalism is called 'bhava'; the view arising by the power of eternalism is 'bhava-diṭṭhi.' Thus, 'bhava' means the view [of eternalism]. Annihilationism is called 'vibhava'; the view arising by the power of annihilationism is 'vibhava-diṭṭhi.' Thus, 'vibhava' means the view [of annihilationism]. The aforementioned ten kinds of views are of only two types: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Beings are always dependent on, resorting to, and clinging to one or the other of these two views.

'Not approaching these two extremes'—in this phrase, the word 'vā' has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), as in passages like 'either by fire, or by water, or by mutual dissension.' It means not approaching, not clinging to, and abandoning the two sides formed by the power of eternalism and annihilationism as described. It can also have the sense of alternative (vikkapa), as in 'anulomikā vā khanti.' 'In specific conditionality (idappaccayatā) and dependently arisen phenomena' means: the causes of these [factors] such as aging and death are 'idappaccaya' (this-condition); the term 'idappaccaya' itself is 'idappaccayatā' (specific conditionality), or the collection of these conditions is 'idappaccayatā.' Its characteristics should be sought from grammatical treatises. Those phenomena that arise together and rightly depending on their respective conditions are 'dependently arisen' (paṭiccasamuppanna). [The patience occurring] in that specific conditionality and in those dependently arisen phenomena.

'Anulomikā' means 'conformable' because it conforms to the supramundane states. 'Khanti' means knowledge (insight knowledge). Knowledge is called 'khanti' (patience/acceptance) because it examines and takes pleasure in [the three characteristics]. 'Is obtained' means it is attained by beings. Through the 'khanti' (insight) occurring in specific conditionality (the cause), there is no approaching the view of annihilationism. This is because, since the phenomena produced by causes exist in dependence on the harmony of conditions, by seeing the non-interruption of causes, one sees the non-interruption of results. Through the 'khanti' occurring in dependently arisen phenomena (the results), there is no approaching the view of eternalism. This is because one sees the arising of ever-new phenomena produced by causes within the harmony of conditions. Thus, the right vision (sammādassana) that arises as 'neither annihilationism nor eternalism' by seeing the law of dependent origination (cause) and dependently arisen phenomena (result) without approaching these two extremes should be understood as 'conformable patience' (anulomikā khanti). In this way..."
7:
Right view is said to be the opposite of both those [views, i.e., eternalism and annihilationism]. "Knowledge in accordance with reality" (yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ) refers to the things that should be known (neyyadhamma) according to their true nature. The knowledge that arises regarding those knowable things is also called "knowledge in accordance with reality" by way of metaphorical designation, applying the name of the object to the subject. In this context, this "knowledge in accordance with reality" is intended as insight knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa) culminating in the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa). However, below, by the phrase "knowledge and vision in accordance with reality" (yathābhūtañāṇadassana), the knowledge of the appearance as terror (bhayatūpaṭṭhānañāṇa) is meant. The connection [of the words] is that "beings have obtained knowledge in accordance with reality."

Now, having shown the continuity of beings permeated by wrong view through such words as "The world is eternal" (sassato loko), and the continuity of beings permeated by right view through such words as "But these [two extremes]..." (ete vā pana), [the text] shows the continuity of beings permeated by the remaining unwholesome states and the remaining wholesome states through such words as "Only those indulging in sensual pleasures..." (kāmaṃ sevantanyevā). In this regard, the construction should be understood as: "The Tathāgata knows only the person who indulges in sensual pleasures." "Indulging" (sevantaṃ) means one who indulges by way of frequent practice. One is called "valuing sensual pleasures" (kāmagaruko) because one regards the defilement of sensual pleasure as important due to past indulgence. Similarly, one is called "having an inclination for sensual pleasures" (kāmāsayā) because sensual pleasure exists in one's inclination or continuity. One is called "intent on sensual pleasures" (kāmādhimutto) because one is absorbed in and attached to sensual pleasures by way of the continuity of the mind. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Terms like "renunciation" (nekkhamma) have the meanings already stated. It should be understood that by the three states starting with "sensual pleasure" (kāma), the remaining unwholesome states are included; and by the three states starting with "renunciation" (nekkhamma), the remaining wholesome states are included. By saying "This is the inclination of beings," it shows only the continuity [of the mind] described in three ways.

In this matter, the method of the Commentary is: "Thus they depend on the view of becoming" (iti bhavadiṭṭhisannissitā) means they depend on the eternalist view. For here, the eternalist view is called "the view of becoming" (bhavadiṭṭhi), and the annihilationist view is called "the view of non-becoming" (vibhavadiṭṭhi). Since all views are encompassed by the eternalist and annihilationist views, all beings who hold views depend on these two views. This has also been said [in the Saṃyutta Nikāya]: "Kaccāna, this world [of beings] mostly depends on two things: existence (atthitā) and non-existence (natthitā)." Here, "existence" is the eternalist view, and "non-existence" is the annihilationist view. This is the inclination of worldlings (puthujjana) who are dependent on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Now, to show the inclination of pure beings who are dependent on the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), it is said: "But without approaching these two extremes..." (ete vā pana ubho ante anupagamma). In that phrase, "but these" (ete vā pana) refers to those very [extremes]. "Both extremes" (ubho ante) refers to the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism. "Without approaching" (anupagamma) means without clinging or adhering to them. "In things that are dependently arisen through specific conditionality" (idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu) means both in specific conditionality (idappaccayatā) and in dependently arisen states (paṭiccasamuppannadhamma). "Conformity-patience" (anulomikā khanti) is insight knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa). "Knowledge in accordance with reality" (yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ) is path knowledge (maggañāṇa). The meaning is this: whatever insight wisdom is obtained regarding the law of dependent origination and dependently arisen states without clinging to those two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism, and whatever path knowledge is obtained beyond that insight—this insight knowledge and path knowledge are the inclination of beings.
8:
Whatever insight wisdom is obtained regarding the law of dependent origination and dependently arisen states without clinging to those two extremes of eternalism and annihilationism, and whatever path knowledge is obtained beyond that insight—this insight knowledge and path knowledge are the inclination (āsaya) of beings. This means that this is the inclination of all beings, both those dependent on the round (vaṭṭa) and those dependent on the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), and this is their dwelling place (vasanaṭṭhāna). This is the consistent method of the Commentaries of the great teachers.

However, a sophist (vitaṇḍavādī) says: "The Path proceeds by destroying the dwelling (āsaya); why do you say the Path is a dwelling (vāsa)?" That sophist should be asked: "Are you a reciter (bhāṇaka) of the Ariyavāsa Sutta or not?" If he says, "I am not," he should be told, "Because you are not a reciter, you do not know." If he says, "I am a reciter," he should be told, "Produce that Sutta." If he can produce it, that is good. If he cannot, one should produce it oneself: "Monks, there are these ten dwellings of the noble ones (ariyavāsā) in which the noble ones have dwelt, are dwelling, or will dwell." This Sutta shows that the Path is a dwelling (vāsa). Therefore, what I have said is well-spoken. The Blessed One, knowing this inclination of beings, knows it even at the moment when these views or these insight and path knowledges have not yet arisen. That is why it was said: "He knows even the one who indulges in the desired sensual pleasures," and so on.

In the description of underlying tendencies (anusayaniddesa), for what reason are they called "underlying tendencies" (anusaya)? Because of the sense of "lying along with" (anusayana). What is this sense of "lying along with"? It is the sense of not being abandoned (appahīnaṭṭha). These states are called "underlying tendencies" because they lie along in the continuity of this or that being in the sense of not being abandoned. "They lie along" (anusenti) means they arise upon obtaining a suitable cause.

If it is argued: "The sense of 'lying along' is merely the state of not being abandoned; it is not appropriate to say that this state of not being abandoned 'arises,' therefore underlying tendencies do not arise." To this, the following reply is given: "Underlying tendency" does not mean merely the state of not being abandoned. Rather, a defilement that has gained strength (thāmagata) because it has not been abandoned is called an underlying tendency. That [underlying tendency] is associated with the mind, has an object, and because it exists with its conditions, it has a cause; it is exclusively unwholesome, and it can be past, future, or present. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that it arises. The evidence for this is: in this very Treatise on Realization (Abhisamayakathā) of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, after asking the question, "Does one abandon present defilements?", it is stated, "One abandons the underlying tendency that has gained strength," because of the existence of the present nature of underlying tendencies. In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the word-analysis of delusion (moha), it is stated: "The underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the shackle of ignorance, delusion, the unwholesome root... this is the delusion that exists at that time," thus stating the arising of delusion together with the unwholesome mind.
9:
In the Kathāvatthu, all views stating that "latent tendencies (anusayas) are indeterminate (abyākata), latent tendencies are causeless (ahetuka), latent tendencies are dissociated from the mind (cittavippayutta)" are refuted and abolished. In the Anusaya Yamaka, within the Uppajjanavāra (Chapter on Arising) which is one of the seven Mahāvāras, it is stated: "To whom the latent tendency to sensual lust arises, to him the latent tendency to aversion arises," and so forth (Yam. II, 300). Therefore, it should be understood that the statement "What is called anusaya is said to 'lie latent' (anusenti) because it arises upon obtaining a suitable cause" is consistent with this scriptural authority. The statement "It is associated with the mind, it has an object," etc., is also well-spoken. It should be concluded here that what is called anusaya is an unwholesome state (akusaladhamma) produced by causes and associated with the mind.

In terms such as kāmarāgānusaya, it is called kāmarāgānusaya because it is both sensual lust (kāmarāga) and a latent tendency (anusaya) in the sense of not yet being abandoned by the Path (magga). The same method applies to the remaining terms. Here, kāmarāgānusaya is the greed (lobha) that arises in greed-rooted consciousness by way of conascence (sahajāta) and by way of object (ārammaṇa), and arises only by way of object in the remaining pleasant sensuous-sphere states (kāmāvacaradhamma). Paṭighānusaya is the hatred (dosa) that arises in consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassa) by way of conascence and by way of object, and arises only by way of object in the remaining unpleasant sensuous-sphere states. Mānānusaya is the conceit (māna) that arises in greed-rooted consciousness dissociated from wrong view by way of conascence and by way of object, and arises only by way of object in the sensuous-sphere states remaining after painful feeling, and in the fine-material (rūpāvacara) and immaterial (arūpāvacara) states. Diṭṭhānusaya arises in the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view. Vicikicchānusaya arises in consciousness accompanied by doubt. Avijjānusaya arises in the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness by way of conascence and by way of object. These three (diṭṭhi, vicikicchā, and moha) are themselves the wrong view, doubt, and delusion that arise only by way of object in the remaining states of the three planes (tebhūmaka). Although bhavarāgānusaya arises in the four types of consciousness dissociated from wrong view, it is not mentioned by way of conascence; rather, it is mentioned as the greed that arises only by way of object in the fine-material and immaterial states.

Now, wishing to show the location where the aforementioned latent tendencies lie latent, the text says "Yaṃ loke," etc. In that Pali, "yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ" means that which has a lovable nature or lovable characteristic in this world. "Sātarūpaṃ" means that which has an agreeable nature, which is the proximate cause of greed, an agreeable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa). That the kāmarāgānusaya of beings lies latent in this agreeable object means...
10:
In this agreeable object, the latent tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) lies latent in beings because it has not yet been abandoned (by the Path). By the words "lovely nature, agreeable nature," only sensuous-sphere states (kāmāvacaradhamma) are intended here. Just as for a person submerged in water, there is only water below, above, and all around, similarly, the arising of lust in an agreeable object is a constantly practiced habit of beings. Likewise, the arising of aversion (paṭigha) occurs in a disagreeable object. "Thus in these two states" means thus in these two types of states: agreeable objects and disagreeable objects. "Ignorance follows along (avijjā anupatitā)" means that being associated with sensual lust and aversion, ignorance follows along or accompanies them by way of taking them as objects. There is also a reading where the words are separated. "Having the same basis as that ignorance" means standing together by way of having the same basis due to being conascent with that ignorance. "Conceit, wrong view, and doubt" refer to the nine types of conceit, sixty-two types of wrong view, and doubt with eight bases. It should be read as: conceit having the same basis as that ignorance, wrong view having the same basis as that ignorance, and doubt having the same basis as that ignorance. "Should be seen (daṭṭhabbā)" means should be viewed or understood. The three states are combined and expressed in the plural. It should be understood here that bhavarāgānusaya is included within kāmarāgānusaya itself.

In the Caritaniddesa (Description of Conduct), thirteen types of volition (cetanā) are called meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra). Twelve types of volition are called demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra). Four types of volition are called imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). Among those states, the sensuous-sphere state is called parittabhūmaka (of the limited plane). The remaining fine-material and immaterial states are called mahābhūmaka (of the great plane). Alternatively, among these three formations, whichever formation has small results is called parittabhūmaka, and whichever has great results is called mahābhūmaka.

In the Adhimuttiniddesa (Description of Disposition), "there are (santi)" means they exist or are found. "Those of low disposition (hīnādhimuttikā)" means those with base inclinations. "Those of superior disposition (paṇītādhimuttikā)" means those with good inclinations. "They associate (sevanti)" means they rely on or cling to. "They resort to (bhajanti)" means they approach. "They frequent (payirupāsanti)" means they approach again and again. For if the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous, but the pupils and fellow-residents are virtuous, those pupils do not approach even their own teachers and preceptors, but approach only those monks who are similar and suitable to themselves. Even if the teachers and preceptors are suitable monks, but the others (pupils) are unsuitable, they also do not approach their teachers and preceptors, but approach only those of low disposition who are similar to themselves. To show that such approaching happens not only now, but also in the past and future, the text says "in the past time also (atītampiddhānaṃ)," etc. There, "in the past time also" means in the past time; or the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga).
11:
The remaining words have an obvious meaning. Indeed, what determines that those of immoral nature associate only with the immoral, those of virtuous nature associate only with the virtuous, those of poor wisdom associate only with those of poor wisdom, and those of great wisdom associate only with the wise? It is the element of disposition (ajjhāsayadhātu) that determines it.

In the exposition of the capable and the incapable (bhabba-abhabba-niddesa), the incapable persons are mentioned first in order to mention the persons to be rejected first and the persons to be accepted later, thus following an inverted order of the brief exposition (uddesa). However, in the brief exposition, the word 'bhabba' is placed first according to the grammatical rule of dvanda compounds where the word with fewer syllables is placed first. 'By the obstruction of kamma' (kammāvaraṇena) refers to the fivefold kamma with immediate result (ānantariya-kamma). 'Are endowed with' (samannāgatā) means they are possessed of (those kammas). 'By the obstruction of defilement' (kilesāvaraṇena) refers to fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). These two are called 'obstructions' (āvaraṇa) because they obstruct the path to heaven and the Noble Path. Actions such as violating a bhikkhunī are also included within the obstruction of kamma. 'By the obstruction of result' (vipākāvaraṇena) refers to rootless rebirth (ahetuka-paṭisandhi). Since those with double-rooted rebirth (duhetuka) also lack the penetration of the Noble Path, double-rooted rebirth should also be understood as an obstruction of result. 'Those without faith' (assaddhā) means those lacking faith in the Buddha and so forth. 'Those without desire' (acchandikā) means those lacking the wholesome desire to act (kattukamyatā-kusala-chanda). The people of Uttarakuru fall into the category of those without wholesome desire. 'Those without wisdom' (duppaññā) means those lacking bhavaṅga-wisdom. Even if one is complete in bhavaṅga-wisdom, if their bhavaṅga cannot serve as a basis for the supramundane, they are also called 'unwise' (duppañña). 'Incapable of entering the certainty of rightness among wholesome states' means they are incapable of entering the Noble Path, which is called the certainty of rightness (sammatta-niyāma) among wholesome states. The Noble Path is called 'rightness' (sammatta) because of its unerring nature; it is called 'certainty' (niyāma) because it gives results immediately or because of its own unshakable nature. They are incapable of entering or penetrating that. Phrases such as 'because of the absence of the obstruction of kamma' should be understood as the reverse of what has been stated.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Dispositions and Latent Tendencies is finished.

## 70. The Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Twin Miracle

In the exposition of the knowledge of the Twin Miracle, the phrase 'unshared with disciples' (asādhāraṇaṃ sāvakchi) was not mentioned in the other five unshared knowledges because there was no room due to other words, but it should be understood that it is mentioned here because there are no other words. 'From the upper part of the body' means from the body above the navel. 'A mass of fire proceeds' means that after emerging from the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) having the fire kasina as its object, one reflects, 'Let a flame of fire rise from the upper part of the body,' performs the preliminary work, and immediately after, through the direct knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa)...
12:
...when one resolves, 'Let a flame of fire rise from the upper part of the body,' simultaneously with the resolution, a flame of fire rises from the upper part of the body. That flame is called a 'khandha' (mass) in this context in the sense of a heap. 'Heṭṭhimakāyato' means from the body below the navel. 'A stream of water proceeds' means that after emerging from the basic jhāna having the water kasina as its object, one reflects, 'Let a stream of water rise from the lower part of the body,' performs the preliminary work, and immediately after, through the direct knowledge, when one resolves, 'Let a stream of water rise from the lower part of the body,' simultaneously with the resolution, a stream of water rises from the lower part of the body. It is said that in both parts of the body, it proceeds without interruption. Between the resolution of direct knowledge and the subsequent reflection, two bhavaṅga-moments occur. For that very reason, the mass of fire and the stream of water proceed in pairs, and the interval between them is not perceived. For others (besides the Buddha), there is no such brief duration of bhavaṅga.

'Puratthimakāyato' means from the front side. 'Pacchimakāyato' means from the back side. 'Dakkhiṇa-akkhito vāma-akkhito' (from the right eye, from the left eye) and so on are merely compound terms and nothing else. The reading 'dakkhiṇa-nāsikāsotato vāma-nāsikāsotato' (from the right nostril, from the left nostril) is excellent. Some also read it by making the vowels short (rassa). In the term 'aṃsakūṭato' (from the shoulder-top), it is called 'kūṭa' because it is like a peak in the sense of being elevated; the shoulder itself is the peak, thus 'aṃsakūṭa'. 'Aṅgulaṅgulehi' means from each finger. 'Aṅgulantarikāhi' means from the intervals between the fingers. The repetition of the words 'a mass of fire proceeds from each hair, a stream of water proceeds from each hair' in both instances means that because all hairs are included, the mass of fire and the stream of water proceed in pairs from every single hair. The same method applies to the phrase 'from each hair-pore a mass of fire proceeds, from each hair-pore a stream of water proceeds'. In some books, it is written: 'A mass of fire proceeds from each hair. A stream of water proceeds from each hair-pore, a mass of fire proceeds from each hair-pore, a stream of water proceeds from each hair.' That is also suitable. However, the former reading is better as it illustrates the extreme subtlety of the miracle.

Now, what is the connection of the phrase 'channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ' (of the six colors)? Below, many parts of the body have been mentioned with 'from the upper part of the body' and so forth. Therefore, by the connection of the sentence that it proceeds in relation to the parts of the body, and by the context of the Twin Miracle, of the six colors...
13:
It means that the rays of the six colors, which are parts of the body, arise in pairs. Because of the connection with the genitive case (sāmivacana), the remaining word 'rasmiyo' (rays) is necessarily desired. 'Nīlānaṃ' refers to those having the color of the flax flower (umāpuppha). 'Pītakānaṃ' refers to those having the color of the kaṇikāra flower. 'Lohitakānaṃ' refers to those having the color of the indagopaka insect. 'Odātānaṃ' refers to those having the color of the morning star (osadhitārakā). 'Mañjiṭṭhānaṃ' refers to those having a slightly red (crimson) color. 'Pabhassarānaṃ' refers to those having a naturally luminous and sparkling appearance. Although the brilliant color (pabhassara-vaṇṇa) does not exist separately, whatever rays among the five colors mentioned are intensely radiant, those very rays are called 'pabhassara' (brilliant).

This is indeed true: when the Blessed One performs the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), by the power of the Twin Miracle Knowledge alone, blue rays emanate from the hair, the beard, and the blue portions of the eyes. By the power of those rays, the sky becomes like one scattered with collyrium powder, like one covered with flax flowers and blue lotus petals, like a waving ruby fan, and like a spread dark cloth (mecakapaṭa). From the skin and the yellow portions of the eyes, yellow rays emanate. By the power of those rays, the directions shine as if being sprinkled with liquid gold, as if gold sheets were spread out, and as if scattered with saffron powder and kaṇikāra flowers. From the flesh, the blood, and the red portions of the eyes, red rays emanate. By the power of those rays, the directions shine as if dyed with powder from China (cinapiṭṭha) [or vermilion], as if being sprinkled with well-boiled lac, as if wrapped in red blankets, and as if scattered with jayasumana and pālibhaddaka flowers. From the bones, the teeth, and the white portions of the eyes, white rays emanate. By the power of those rays, the directions shine as if sprinkled with milk from silver pots, like spread silver canopies, like waving silver fans, and as if covered with flowers such as kunda, kumuda, sinduvāra, sumana, and mallikā. From the palms, the soles, and the slightly red (crimson) portions, crimson rays emanate. By the power of those rays, the directions shine as if wrapped in coral nets and as if scattered with red kuravaka flowers. From the uṇṇā hair, the nails, and other brilliant portions, brilliant rays emanate. By the power of those rays, the directions shine as if filled with clusters of morning stars and as if filled with layers of lightning.

The passage beginning with 'Bhagavā caṅkamati' (The Blessed One walks) is stated to show that the performance of various postures by the Blessed One and the created Buddhas (nimmita) occurs only through the Twin Miracle. The postures of those created Buddhas occur only in pairs. If the created Buddhas are many, why is the singular form 'nimmito' used? In the case of the created Buddhas...
14:
The singular number is used to show the state of various postures (such as standing, sitting, and reclining) of each individual created Buddha. Indeed, if the plural "nimmitānaṃ" were used, all the created Buddhas would appear as if they were in a single posture at one time. However, when the singular "nimmito" is used, it is understood that among the created Buddhas, each one possesses various postures. Therefore, the singular designation is made.

Even the Elder Cūḷapanthaka could create a thousand monks in various postures. How much more, then, would the Blessed One not create many created Buddhas during the Twin Miracle? Setting aside the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, for other disciples, the creation of various forms in various postures through a single act of advertence (āvajjana) is not possible. Indeed, forms created without specific determination of various postures and so forth are exactly like the possessor of psychic power. Whatever action the possessor of psychic power performs—whether in standing, sitting, and so forth, or in speaking, remaining silent, and so forth—those created forms perform that very same action. The act of making them different from one another and performing various actions is accomplished by individually adverting and resolving: "Let this many created forms be of such a nature; let this many forms perform such an action." But for the Tathāgata, the creation of various kinds is accomplished through only a single act of advertence and resolution. In the same way, it should be understood regarding the creation of masses of fire and streams of water, and the creation of various colors (that they occur through a single advertence).

In that Pali, "The Buddha walks to and fro" means walking to and fro in the air or on the ground. "Nimmito" refers to the form of the Buddha created by psychic power. The Pali terms such as "He stands" also refer to being in the air or on the ground. "Kappeti" means he performs. In places such as "The Buddha stands," the same method applies.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Twin Miracle is finished.

## 71. Explanation of the Exposition of the Knowledge of Great Compassion

In the Exposition of the Knowledge of Great Compassion, "by many modes" means by the eighty-nine modes that will now be mentioned. "Those who see" refers to the Buddhas who look with the eye of knowledge and the Buddha-eye. "Descends" (okkāmati) means he goes down or enters. "Aflame" (āditto) means set on fire in the sense of causing burning, because it is associated with the oppression by the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa). Because it was said, "Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering," it should be understood that "aflame" is first mentioned by way of the characteristic of suffering, because all conditioned things (saṅkhata) are oppressed by the characteristic of suffering, and because this is the root of compassion. The state of being aflame with lust (rāga) and so forth will be mentioned later. Alternatively, "aflame" means being aflame with lust and so forth. Later, however, it is mentioned again with regard to the meaning, "There is no one else who can extinguish it for him."
15:
It burns only with lust and so forth. To speak specifically, it should be understood that above, it is preached again by way of desiring the meanings of 'extinguished,' as there is no one other than the Buddha who can extinguish the fire of lust and so forth.

'Loka-sannivāsa' (the world of beings) means: the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā) are called 'loka' (world) because of the sense of breaking up and perishing. In these five aggregates, beings always dwell by the power of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi); therefore, it is called 'sannivāsa' (dwelling). Since the world itself is the dwelling, it is called 'loka-sannivāsa.' Based on the continuity of the aggregates that have reached suffering, the collective of beings is also called 'loka-sannivāsa' because of the existence of the designation 'beings' and because of its association with the world of beings. That collective of beings also exists only together with the five aggregates.

'Uyyutta' means being constantly exerted in many duties, having performed engagement and effort; it means having concern and diligence in constant duties. Alternatively, it is called 'uyyutta' because it is associated with impact or striking. 'Payāta' refers to a being who has begun to go toward death by way of non-stop movement, like river water flowing from a mountain peak. 'Kummagga-ppaṭipanna' refers to one who has entered a loathsome wrong path. However, above, it is preached with distinction using various terms such as 'vipathapakkhanda' (gone astray).

'Upanīyati' means being led or carried toward death by the power of old age (jarā). Old age is preached as 'the decline of life.' 'Addhuva' means not permanent; it does not remain the same at all times. Because it is impermanent, it is led toward death; thus, this word 'addhuva' is the statement of cause for the preceding word 'upanīyati.' By this statement, the suffering of old age (jarā-dukkha) along with its cause is preached. Seeing that suffering of old age, even wise people who are free from the ruin of old age go forth into homelessness.

'Atāṇa' means being devoid of someone capable of guarding or protecting; it means having no protection. 'Anabhissara' means being devoid of someone capable of comforting by approaching and speaking, or it means having no companion. Because one is 'anabhissara,' therefore one is 'atāṇa'; thus, this statement is the statement of cause for the preceding term. By this statement, the suffering of separation from the loved (piyavippayoga-dukkha) along with its cause is preached. Seeing that suffering of separation from the loved, even wise people who are free from the ruin of relatives go forth into homelessness.

'Assaka' means being devoid of one's own property. 'All must be abandoned and gone' means the world of beings must go, abandoning everything marked as one's own property. Because all must be abandoned and gone, therefore it is called 'assaka'; thus, this statement is the statement of cause for the preceding term. By this statement, the suffering of death (maraṇa-dukkha) along with its cause is preached. Seeing that suffering of death, even wise people who are free from the ruin of wealth go forth into homelessness.

In other suttas like the Subha Sutta, it is preached: 'Young man, beings are the owners of their kamma (kammassakā).' However, in this Paṭisambhidāmagga and the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, it is preached: 'The world has no owner of its own (assako loko).' If it is asked how these two statements are consistent: 'The world has no owner' is preached with reference to property that must be abandoned and gone. Kamma, however, cannot be abandoned and gone. Therefore, it is preached: 'Beings are the owners of their kamma.' In the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta itself, it is preached: 'But you will go according to your kamma.'

'Ūna' means devoid of fullness. 'Atitta' means insatiable even if one desires greatly. This statement is the statement of cause for the state of being deficient. 'Taṇhā-dāsa' means being a slave to craving because one must follow the will of craving. This statement is the statement of cause for the state of being insatiable. By this statement, the affliction of craving is pointed out, and the suffering of disease (byādhi-dukkha) along with its cause is preached. Seeing that suffering of disease, even wise people who are free from the ruin of illness go forth into homelessness.

'Atāṇa' is so called because there is no protection even by children and so forth; it means there is no one to protect, or it means having happiness that cannot be obtained. 'Aleṇa' means not fit for shelter, and not performing the function of a hiding place for those who come for shelter. 'Asaraṇa' means not one who removes or destroys the danger of those who seek refuge. 'Asaraṇībhūta' means 'asaraṇa' because it does not exist by itself even before arising; it means that as soon as it arises, it is not a refuge.

'Uddhata' means because of the arising of the mental factor of restlessness (uddhacca) in all unwholesome states, and because of the abundance of unwholesome states in the continuity of beings...
16:
Inability to be satisfied. This statement explains the cause of the state of being incomplete. 'Slave to craving' means being a slave to craving because of following the will of craving. This statement explains the cause of the state of being unable to be satisfied. By pointing out the disease of desire in this way, the suffering of illness along with its cause is taught. Seeing that suffering of illness, wise people who are free from the ruin caused by illness (those who are healthy and strong) also go forth into the Buddha's Dispensation.

Having no refuge means having no refuge because even children and others cannot protect, having no one to guard, or having no obtainable safety. Having no shelter means being unworthy of being relied upon or resorted to, and being unable to perform the function of a shelter even for those who have resorted to it. Having no protection means being unable to remove the fear of those who rely on one, or being unable to destroy that fear. Being one who is not a protection means having no protection because of the absence of a self even from the moment of initial arising; it means being one who is not a protection at the very moment of arising.

Agitation means the arising of restlessness (uddhacca) in all unwholesome states, and because of the abundance of unwholesome arisings in the continuity of beings, the world endowed with the unwholesome is agitated by that restlessness. Being unpeaceful means being unpeaceful and trembling like a startled deer due to association with restlessness, which has the characteristic of lack of tranquility. In the four places such as 'The world is led away by old age and death' and the place 'The world is agitated,' in these five places, the word 'world' (loka) appears, while in the remaining places, 'the world of beings' (lokasannivāsa) appears. In both ways, it is just the world.

Being with darts means existing together with the darts such as lust (rāga), which are called 'darts' because they cause pain, prick within, and are difficult to remove. Being struck means that while animals and others are sometimes struck by others, this world is always struck (pierced) by itself. 'With many darts' refers to the seven darts taught as: 'the seven darts—the dart of lust, the dart of hatred, the dart of delusion, the dart of conceit, the dart of views, the dart of defilements, and the dart of misconduct.'

The remover of the darts of that world of beings is the person who extracts those darts from the continuity of beings. 'Other than me' means setting me (the Buddha) aside. The disciples of the Blessed One also remove the darts, but since those disciples remove them only by the word of the Blessed One, the Blessed One alone is called the remover.

Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance means that ignorance itself is the darkness of ignorance because it acts like a blind person by concealing the vision of the nature of things. That darkness itself is called an envelopment (āvaraṇa) for this world because it prevents the understanding of the nature of things. Being cast into the cage of defilements means that defilements themselves are called a cage because they block and obstruct the path to wholesome states. One is cast or fallen into the cage of defilements that arises from ignorance. One who shows the light means...
17:
One who has the habit of showing the light of wisdom, or the meaning is the shower of the light of wisdom. 'Gone to ignorance' (avijjāgata) means entering into the delusion that is ignorance. It is not merely the envelopment by ignorance, but rather, like one who has entered a thicket, it is the distinction from the previous meaning that one has entered inside the shell (egg) of ignorance.

Terms such as 'become as an egg' (aṇḍabhūta) are also distinctions. 'Become as an egg' means being born within an eggshell. Just as some beings born within an eggshell are called 'egg-born,' so too this world is called 'become as an egg' because it is born within the eggshell of ignorance. 'Enwrapped' (pariyonaddha) means being completely enwrapped, bound, and entwined by that eggshell of ignorance.

'Tangled like a weaver's thread' (tantākulakajāta) means being confused like a loom's thread. For example, a weaver's thread that is poorly kept and bitten by rats becomes tangled here and there, making it difficult to align end with end or root with root, saying 'this is the end, this is the root.' In the same way, beings have slipped and become very confused in the law of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and they are unable to make the law of Dependent Origination straight. In that example, it might be possible to straighten the tangled thread through human effort, but with the exception of the two types—the Bodhisatta and the prospective Paccekabuddha—there is no other being who is able to straighten the law of Dependent Origination by their own nature.

Furthermore, just as a tangled thread, when soaked in rice-scum and struck with a comb, becomes a mass of knots (kulakajāta) here and there, so too this world of beings, having slipped regarding causes and being unable to straighten the causes, becomes a mass of knots and bound by tangles through the power of the sixty-two views. Indeed, all beings who rely on wrong views are simply unable to straighten the causes such as ignorance.

'Become like a matted ball of thread' (kulagaṇṭhikajāta) means becoming like a ball of thread soaked in rice-scum by weavers. The thread-ball soaked in rice-scum by weavers is called 'kulagaṇṭhika.' Some teachers also say, 'Kula is a female bird, and it refers to her nest.' Just as both of those are tangled and difficult to align end with end or root with root, this should be understood by applying the same method mentioned previously for the term 'tantākulakajāta.'

'Become like muñja and pabbajja grass' (muñjapabbajabhūta) means becoming like muñja grass and pabbajja grass. It means being born similar to muñja and pabbajja grass. When a rope made by pounding those grasses becomes old and falls somewhere, and one picks it up, it is difficult to align end with end or root with root of those grasses, saying 'this is the end, this is the root.' Even though it might be possible to straighten that rotting grass rope through human effort...
18:
To make straight: except for the two types of Bodhisattas—the Bodhisatta who will become a Buddha and the Bodhisatta who will become a Paccekabuddha—no other being is able to make straight the mode of conditions (Paccayākāra/Paṭiccasamuppāda) by their own nature. Thus, this world, being unable to make straight the mode of conditions, becomes entangled by the power of the sixty-two types of wrong views and cannot transcend Saṃsāra, which consists of the states of deprivation (Apāya), the bad destination (Duggati), and perdition (Vinipāta).

Among those (Apāya, etc.), 'Apāya' refers to hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), and the host of asuras. All these are called 'Apāya' because of the absence of 'aya', which means growth or prosperity. Similarly, it is called 'Duggati' because it is a destination of suffering. It is called 'Vinipāta' because it is a state of ruin, having fallen away from the mass of happiness. As for the other, Saṃsāra:

"The continuous and uninterrupted
Proceeding of the aggregates,
And of the elements and bases,
Is called Saṃsāra."

One cannot transcend or overcome that entire Saṃsāra. Indeed, taking up death and rebirth repeatedly—from death to rebirth and from rebirth to death—one merely revolves in the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a boat tossed by the wind in the great ocean, or like an ox yoked to a machine.

'Avijjāvisadosasallitta' means: ignorance (avijjā) itself is called 'the poison of ignorance' because it destroys the life of merit by generating demerit. That very poison of ignorance is 'the fault of the poison of ignorance' because it corrupts the mental continuity. Being intensely smeared or anointed with that poison of ignorance, which consists of latent tendencies, obsessions, and misconduct, one is 'avijjāvisadosasallitta'.

'Kilesakalalībhūta' means: the defilements (kilesa) rooted in ignorance and so forth are themselves called 'mire' (kalala) in the sense of sinking. To be in such a state, having the mire of defilements, is the meaning.

'Rāgadosamohajaṭājaṭita' means: lust, hatred, and delusion—known as greed, aversion, and ignorance—repeatedly arise in sense objects such as forms through the power of 'below and above'. Because they interweave, they are called a 'tangle' (jaṭā), like the network of branches in a bamboo thicket. One is entangled by that tangle of lust, hatred, and delusion. Just as bamboo plants and the like are entangled by bamboo thickets, so too this world is entangled, enveloped, and bound by that tangle of dhammas. This is the meaning.

'Jaṭaṃ vijaṭetā' means: the one who well cuts through and shatters this tangle that stands enveloping the world of the three realms.

'Taṇhāsaṅghāṭapaṭimukka' means: craving (taṇhā) itself is called the 'joinery of craving' (taṇhāsaṅghāṭa) in the sense of being joined by continuous occurrence. One who has entered into or is caught within that joinery of craving is 'taṇhāsaṅghāṭapaṭimukka'. By the net of craving...
19:
'Otthaṭo' means: according to the method mentioned before, craving itself is called a 'net' (jāla) in the sense of interweaving; it means being covered and enveloped from all sides by that net of craving. 'Taṇhāsotena vuyhati' means: craving itself is called a 'stream' (sota) in the sense of pulling one along in Saṃsāra; it means being pulled along (carried away) by that stream of craving. 'Taṇhāsaṃyojanena saṃyutto' means: craving itself is called a 'fetter' (saṃyojana) because it binds the world to the round of suffering; it means being joined and bound by that fetter of craving. 'Taṇhānusayena anusaṭo' means: craving itself is called an 'underlying tendency' (anusaya) in the sense of repeatedly lying latent; that underlying tendency of craving follows along and gains strength. 'Taṇhāsantāpena santappati' means: craving itself is called 'fever' (santāpa) because it causes the world to burn both at the time of its occurrence and at the time of its result; it means being tormented by that fever of craving. 'Taṇhāpariဠāhena pariḍayhati' means: craving that has become powerful is called 'great heat' (mahāpariဠāha) in the sense of burning from all sides both at the time of its occurrence and at the time of its result; it means being scorched from all sides by that heat of craving. The 'joinery of views' (diṭṭhisaṅghāṭa) and so forth should be applied in this same manner.

'Anugato' means entered into. 'Anusaṭo' means followed after. 'Abhibhūto' means oppressed. 'Abbhāhato' means struck down violently in front. 'Dukkhe patiṭṭhito' means established (clinging) in the mass of the five aggregates of suffering through the perversion of [perceiving] happiness (sukhavipallāsa).

'Taṇhāya uḍḍito' means suspended by craving. The eye-consciousness is threaded by the rope of craving and suspended on the wall-peg (nāgadanta) of forms; the ear-consciousness and others are also threaded by the rope of craving and suspended on the wall-pegs of sounds and so forth. The world of beings endowed with those eyes, ears, etc., is also called 'suspended'. 'Jarāpākāraparikkhitto' means enclosed by the wall of old age (jarā), which is like a wall in the sense of being insurmountable. 'Maccupāsena parikkhitto' means bound by the snare of death (maraṇa), which is like a snare in the sense of being difficult to escape. 'Mahābandhanabaddho' means bound by great bonds because they are firm and difficult to cut. 'Rāgabandhanena' means lust (rāga) itself binds and does not allow one to move away from Saṃsāra (to go to Nibbāna), thus it is called the 'bond of lust'. One is bound by that bond of lust. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. 'Kilesabandhanena' means by the bond of the remaining defilements apart from those already mentioned (lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views). 'Duccaritabandhanena' means by the three types of misconduct. Good conduct (sucarita), however, is the cause for liberation from bonds and is itself liberation from bonds. Therefore, good conduct should not be taken [as a bond in this context].
20:
"Bandhanaṃ mocetā" means one who is able to release that person's bonds. There is also a variant reading "Bandhanā mocetā," which means one who can release that person from bonds. "Mahāsambādhappaṭipanno" means one who has reached the thicket of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, defilements, and misconduct, known as the 'great confinement' (mahāsambādha) because it oppresses and prevents the arising of wholesome states. "Okāsaṃ dassetā" means one who can show the opportunity and place of mundane and supramundane concentration and wisdom. "Mahāpalibodhena palibuddho" means being obstructed by a great hindrance (nīvaraṇa) or being smeared by a great smearing substance. Hindrances (palibodha) are the seven states beginning with lust. Some teachers say, "Craving and wrong view are hindrances." "Palibodhaṃ chetā" means one who can cut those hindrances. "Mahāpapāte" means falling into the precipice of the five destinations or the precipice of birth, aging, and death. All these are called 'precipices' (papāta) in the sense of being difficult to cross. "Papātā uddhatā" means one who is lifted out and rescued from that precipice. "Mahākantārappaṭipanno" means one who has entered the wilderness (kantāra) of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. All these are called 'wilderness' (kantāra) in the sense of being difficult to pass through; [he is] one who can enable one to cross that wilderness. There is also a reading "Kantārā tāretā." "Mahāsaṃsārappaṭipanno" means one who has entered the uninterrupted continuity of the aggregates. "Saṃsāraṃ mocetā" means one who can release from Saṃsāra. There is also a reading "Saṃsāraṃ mocetā." "Mahāvidugge" means in the difficult pass of Saṃsāra. Saṃsāra itself is called a 'difficult pass' (vidugga) in the sense of being hard to travel through. "Samparivattati" means wandering around intensely. "Mahāpalipe" means in the great mire of sensual pleasures. Sensuality is called 'mire' (palipa) in the sense of being a place where one sinks. "Palipanno" means one who is stuck. There is also a reading "Mahāpalipapalipanno."

"Abbhāhato" means one who is severely struck by all calamities. "Rāgagginā" means lust and so on are called 'fire' in the sense of burning repeatedly; it is the state of being burned by that fire of lust. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Unnītako" means one who is led away poorly; it means one who is seized by birth and led to calamities such as aging. Here, the letter "ka" should be understood in the sense of compassion (anukampā). "Haññati niccamatāṇo" means being constantly oppressed while lacking a protector. "Pattadaṇḍo" means one who has received punishment and authority from kings and others. "Takkaro" means a thief. "Vajjabandhanabaddho" means one who is bound by the bonds of faults such as lust. "Āghātanapaccupaṭṭhito" means one who is standing at the place of the execution block of death. [He is] someone who releases another from bonds. There is also a reading "Koci bandhanaṃ mocetā." "Anātho" means one who is helpless because there is no lord or master over him, or because he himself is not a master; or it means one without a refuge. "Paramakāpaṇyappatto" means one who has reached a state of extreme misery and destitution because of the inability to prevent aging and so on. "Tāyetā" means one who can protect. There is also a reading "Tāyitā."
21:
...is good. "Dukkhābhitunno" means one who is severely pierced, severely afflicted, and severely shaken by many sufferings such as the suffering of birth. "Cirarattaṃ pīḷito" means one who is oppressed and struck by sufferings for a long duration of time. "Gadhito" means one who is greedy through craving, or bound by the bodily tie of covetousness. "Niccaṃ pipāsito" means thirst (pipāsā) is the desire to drink or eat; that thirst is craving itself, and it means one who is constantly thirsty with the thirst of craving. "Andho" means one who is blind due to the absence of wisdom, which is called the 'eye' (cakkhu) in the sense of seeing objects. Indeed, only wisdom sees the nature of things. "Acakkhuko" means that blindness did not occur later, but it refers to being naturally without eyes, thus specifying that very blindness. "Hatanetto" means one who has destroyed eyes precisely because of the absence of wisdom, which is called the 'eye' (netta) in the sense of leading beings. It is called 'netta' because it leads the individual existence (attabhāva) as if showing what is even and uneven. Wisdom leads to a happy destination (sugati) or to Nibbāna. Intending to show that such a being has no leader to take them to a happy destination or Nibbāna because the eye of wisdom is destroyed, it is said "Apariṇāyako." It means one who has no eyes. It also means that there is no other leader for that being. "Vipathappakkhando" means a 'wrong path' (vipatha) is a path that is perverted or uneven; one who has rushed into or entered that wrong path is called "Vipathappakkhando." It means one who has entered wrong view, known as the 'wrong path' (micchāpatha). "Añjasāparaddho" means one who has failed or erred on the straight path of the Middle Way (the Eightfold Path). "Ariyapathaṃ ānetā" refers to the absence of someone who would lead or bring one to the Noble Eightfold Path. "Mahoghappakkhando" means those states which exist and sink or submerge one in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) are called 'floods' (ogha). They are called 'great floods' (mahogha) because they are greater than natural floods. Those floods are fourfold: the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. One who has rushed into or entered those great floods is called "Mahoghappakkhando." Or it means one who has rushed into the great flood known as Saṃsāra.

Now, the method of increasing by one (Ekuttarikanaya) will be explained. In that method, "dvīhi diṭṭhigatehi" means by the two views of eternalism and annihilationism. In that phrase, the view itself is "diṭṭhigata," similar to terms like "gūthagata" (excrement) or "muttagata" (urine). Or it is "diṭṭhigata" because it is merely the occurrence of a view due to the absence of anything to be truly known. Also, it is "diṭṭhigata" because this vision is included within the sixty-two views. For even the sixty-two or sixty-three views are only two: the eternalist view and the annihilationist view. Therefore, wishing to include all views concisely, it is said "dvīhi diṭṭhigatehi." "Pariyuṭṭhito" means one who has reached obsession, one who has reached manifestation (samudācāra); it means one who has reached the state of obstructing and overwhelming the practice of wholesome states by not allowing them to arise.
22: The meaning is reaching the state of taking up wholesome states. Thus the Blessed One also said: 'Monks, some devas and humans, overwhelmed by two kinds of views, hold back; some overreach; but those with vision see.' (Itivuttaka, 49). ## 'By the three types of misconduct' means by the three types of bodily misconduct, the four types of verbal misconduct, and the three types of mental misconduct. 'One who practices perversely' means one who practices wrongly, one who has wrong conduct. 'One yoked with the bonds (yogas)' means one who is joined with or possessed of those states called bonds, because they yoke one to the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) or because of the meaning of 'danger' (or 'destruction'). 'One yoked by the four bonds' means one who is yoked to the round of rebirth by these four bonds—the bond of sensual desire (kāmayoga), the bond of existence (bhavayoga), the bond of views (diṭṭhiyoga), and the bond of ignorance (avijjāyoga)—like an ox yoked to a cart. Lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is called the bond of sensual desire. Strong lust for fine-material existence and immaterial existence, attachment to meditative absorptions (jhāna), lust accompanied by the eternalist view, and longing by the power of existence is called the bond of existence. The sixty-two views are called the bond of views. Ignorance regarding the eight instances is called the bond of ignorance. These same four are called 'floods' (oghas) when they are powerful, and 'bonds' (yogas) when they are weak. ## 'By the four ties (ganthas)' means for whoever these ties exist, they are called ties because they bind that person to the round of rebirth by way of death and rebirth. These ties are of four kinds: the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha), the bodily tie of ill will (byāpāda-kāyagantha), the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa-kāyagantha), and the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence that 'This is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha). It is called covetousness (abhijjhā) because one covets by means of this craving, or it covets by itself, or it is just the act of coveting; it is simply greed (lobha). It is called a 'bodily tie' (kāyagantha) because it binds the mental body (nāmakāya) to the round of rebirth by way of death and rebirth. It is called ill will (byāpāda) because the mind reaches a state of putrefaction due to that anger, or because it destroys disciplinary conduct, perfection of appearance, prosperity, happiness, and so on. The wrong adherence that 'purification comes through the habits, purification through the observances, purification through the habits and observances' of recluses and brahmins outside of this Dispensation is called adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa). Rejecting even the words spoken by the Omniscient Buddha and adhering in such a way as 'The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is empty' is called dogmatic insistence that 'This is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesa). The meaning is one who is tied or bound by these four ties. ## 'By the four kinds of clinging (upādānas)' means they are called clinging because they take up intensely or grasp firmly. These kinds of clinging are of four types: clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna), clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna), and clinging to a doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). It is called clinging to sensual pleasures because it intensely clings to the five strands of sensual pleasure known as objective sensuality (vatthukāma). That state is both sensuality...
23: ...because it intensely clings to sensual pleasure, and because it is subjective sensuality (kilesakāma) and clings intensely, it is called clinging to sensual pleasures. It is called clinging to views because it is a view and clings intensely; it is also called clinging to views because it clings intensely to a view. In views such as 'The self and the world are eternal,' a subsequent view clings to a preceding view by the power of making that view firm. It is called clinging to rules and observances because it clings to the practices of cattle; it is also called clinging to rules and observances because it is the practice of cattle and clings intensely. In fact, the bovine virtue (gosīla), bovine observance (govata), and so on, are themselves clingings because of the orientation that 'purification from defilements comes by practicing in this way.' It is called 'doctrine' (vāda) because one speaks by means of this view; it is called 'clinging' (upādāna) because one clings by means of this view. What do they speak of or cling to? They speak of and cling to the self (attabhāva). It is called clinging to a doctrine of self because it is the cause for speaking of and clinging to the self. Or, it is called clinging to a doctrine of self because it clings to the mere speech of 'self' by means of this view as being the self. Excluding these two views called clinging to rules and observances and clinging to a doctrine of self, all remaining views are also called clinging to views. One is intensely grasped by those four kinds of clinging. Alternatively, there is a variant reading 'upādiyati,' meaning the world intensely takes up various objects by means of clingings. ## 'Ascended to the five destinations (gatis)': it is called a destination (gati) because it is reached due to the causes of good and bad deeds; it refers to the five aggregates along with the physical space (okāsaloka). One has intensely ascended to these five destinations—hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the human realm, and the deva realm—by way of entering them. ## 'By the five strands of sensual pleasure' means by the five groups of objective sensuality known as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. ## 'Is dyed' (rajjati) means that because of unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), lust arises, and thus the world of beings is made to be dyed or intensely infatuated by those five strands of sensual pleasure. ## 'By the five hindrances' means they are called hindrances (nīvaraṇas) because they envelop and obstruct the mind. They are the five hindrances known as sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill will (byāpāda), sloth and torpor (thīna-middha), restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), and doubt (vicikicchā). ## 'Overspread' (otthaṭo) means covered from above. ## 'By the six roots of contention' means by the six causes of disputes. The Blessed One said: 'Monks, there are these six roots of contention. What six? Here, monks, a monk is angry and resentful. Monks, that monk who is angry and resentful lives without respect and deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and he does not fulfill the training. Monks, that monk who lives without respect and deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and does not fulfill the training, creates contention in the Saṅgha. That contention is for the harm of many, for the unhappiness of many, for the multitude's...'
