24: It is for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans. Monks, if you should see such a root of dispute either internally or externally, then, monks, you should make an effort to abandon that evil root of dispute. Monks, if you should not see such a root of dispute either internally or externally, then, monks, you should practice so that that evil root of dispute does not arise in the future. By doing so, that evil root of dispute is abandoned. By doing so, that evil root of dispute does not arise in the future.## Monks, furthermore, a monk is one who disparages others' virtues and is domineering. He is envious and miserly. He is crafty and fraudulent. He has evil wishes and wrong views. He is one who misinterprets and adheres to his own views, holding on tightly and relinquishing with difficulty. Monks, whatever monk misinterprets and adheres to his own views, holding on tightly and relinquishing with difficulty, that monk lacks respect even for the Teacher... (it is said) 'it does not arise in the future.'## In that text, 'angry' (kodhana) means one endowed with anger characterized by being furious. 'Malicious' (upanāhī) means one endowed with malice characterized by not relinquishing enmity. Regarding 'for the detriment and suffering of gods and humans'—how does the dispute between two monks lead to the detriment and suffering of gods and humans? Just as in the Kosambaka chapter, when two monks fall into a dispute, their resident pupils (antevāsika) in that monastery also dispute. The community of bhikkhunīs who receive their instruction also disputes. Then, their lay supporters also dispute. At that time, the guardian deities of humans divide into two groups. The guardian deities of the speakers of Dhamma (dhammavādī) become speakers of Dhamma; the guardian deities of the speakers of non-Dhamma (adhammavādī) become speakers of non-Dhamma. Then, the earth-dwelling deities (bhumaṭṭha devatā) who are friends of the guardian deities also divide. In this way, successively up to the Brahma realm, excluding the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka), all gods and humans divide into two groups. However, the speakers of non-Dhamma are more numerous than the speakers of Dhamma. Therefore, thinking that whatever is held by the majority is the truth, many people abandon the true Dhamma and take up non-Dhamma. Living with non-Dhamma as their priority, they are reborn in the planes of misery (apāya). Thus, the dispute between two monks leads to the detriment and suffering of gods and humans.
25: 'Internally' (ajjhattaṃ vā) means in your internal assembly. 'Externally' (bahiddhā vā) means in the assembly of others. 'Disparaging' (makkhi) means one endowed with disparagement characterized by smearing the virtues of others. 'Domineering' (paḷāsī) means one endowed with domineering characterized by rivalry. 'Envious' (issukī) means one endowed with envy characterized by being jealous of the honor and offerings of others. 'Miserly' (maccharī) means one endowed with the five types of stinginess, such as stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsamacchariya). 'Crafty' (saṭho) means one associated with deceitful actions. 'Fraudulent' (māyāvī) means one who conceals the evil he has committed. 'Of evil wishes' (pāpiccho) means an immoral person who wishes to make known virtues he does not possess. 'Of wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhi) means a person who is a nihilist (natthikavādī), one who denies cause (ahetukavādī), or one who denies the efficacy of action (akiriyavādī). 'Adhering to one's own views' (sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī) means one who misinterprets only his own view. 'Holding on tightly' (ādhānaggāhī) means one who has a firm grasp. 'Relinquishing with difficulty' (duppaṭinissaggī) means one who is unable to let go of the view he has taken up. In the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga, however, it is taught individually as primary factors: 'Among those states, what are the six roots of dispute? They are anger, disparaging, envy, craftiness, evil wishes, and misinterpreting one's own views; these are the six roots of dispute.'## 'By the six groups of craving' (chahi taṇhākāyehi) means by the six cravings taught as craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental objects. In that context, since each craving has many objects and arises repeatedly even in a single object, they are numerous; therefore, the word 'kāya' meaning 'group' is joined to say 'groups of craving' (taṇhākāya). Even though it is called 'groups of craving,' it is just craving. 'Lusts' (rajjati) means he himself lusts after the object, becoming intensely attached.## 'By the six types of views' (chahi diṭṭhigatehi) means by the views taught in the Sabbāsava Sutta. In that sutta, it is taught thus:## 'To one who attends unwisely in this way, one of the six views arises. The view "I have a self" arises in him as true and stable. The view "I have no self" arises in him as true and stable. The view "I perceive self with self" arises in him as true and stable. The view "I perceive non-self with self" arises in him as true and stable. The view "I perceive self with non-self" arises in him as true and stable. Or else, he has such a view: "This self of mine that speaks..."'
26: That self experiences the results of various good and bad deeds; indeed, this self of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain just so as long as eternity. Among these views, 'I have a self' is the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) because it grasps the existence of one's self at all times. 'By way of truth, by way of stability' means truly and firmly; it means 'this nature is true' in an extremely firm manner. 'I have no self' is the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) because it grasps the destruction of an existing being in various states of existence. Alternatively, the former is the eternalist view because it grasps existence in all three periods of time; if one grasps that it exists only in the present, it is the annihilationist view. The latter is also the annihilationist view because it grasps non-existence in the past and future, like those of wrong views who hold that 'offerings end in ashes.' If one grasps non-existence only in the past, it is the eternalist view, like those who hold the view of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppanna). 'With self I perceive self' means taking the five aggregates as self, headed by the aggregate of perception (saññā-kkhandha), and perceiving the remaining aggregates through perception; thus it occurs as 'with this self (perception), I perceive this self (the remaining aggregates).' 'With self I perceive non-self' means taking only the aggregate of perception as self and the remaining four aggregates as non-self, and perceiving those aggregates through perception. 'With non-self I perceive self' means taking the aggregate of perception as non-self and the remaining four aggregates as self, and perceiving those aggregates through perception. All these are merely eternalist and annihilationist views. The views such as 'it speaks, it experiences' are modes of clinging belonging only to the eternalist view. Among them, it is called 'vada' (speaker) because it speaks; it means the doer of verbal action. It is called 'vedeyya' (experiencer) because it knows and experiences. What does it experience? It experiences the result of various good and bad deeds. 'There and there' (tatra tatra) means in those various origins (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness, abodes, and groups of beings, or in objects. 'Permanent' (nicca) means being free from arising and passing away. 'Stable' (dhuva) means being a firm essence. 'Eternal' (sassata) means existing for all time. 'Not subject to change' (avipariṇāmadhamma) means having the nature of not abandoning its original state; it does not reach various states like a chameleon. 'As long as eternity' (sassatisama): the moon, sun, ocean, great earth, and mountains are called 'eternal' (sassati) in worldly parlance. 'Sassatisama' means equal to those eternal things. For one who grasps that 'as long as those eternal things remain, it will remain just so,' such a view arises.
27: In the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga, however, it is stated: 'In various lives, for a long time, one experiences the result of good and bad deeds. That self was not not-born in the past, and it will not not-exist in the future; it is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.' Thus, six views arise for the person with wrong view by way of truth and stability. In that text, 'that self was not not-born in the past' means that because that self does not have the nature of being born, it is not 'born' in the sense of a new beginning; it simply exists always. For that very reason, it did not not-exist in the past, and it will not not-exist in the future. For whatever is born is said to have existed at a point of birth, and whatever will be born is said will exist. Alternatively, 'it was not not-born in the past' means that because it exists always, it never did not exist in the past, and it never will not exist in the future. The meaning of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) has already been stated. 'By the seven fetters' refers to the fetters taught in the Book of the Sevens (Sattaka Nipāta). For it is said there: 'Monks, there are these seven fetters. Which seven? The fetter of attachment (anunaya), the fetter of aversion (paṭigha), the fetter of view (diṭṭhi), the fetter of doubt (vicikicchā), the fetter of conceit (māna), the fetter of lust for existence (bhavarāga), and the fetter of ignorance (avijjā). These, monks, are the seven fetters.' Among them, the 'fetter of attachment' (anunaya-saṃyojana) is the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāga). All these are called 'fetters' (saṃyojana) in the sense of binding. 'By the seven conceits' refers to the conceits taught in the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga. For it is said there: 'Conceit (māna), superiority conceit (atimāna), arrogant conceit (mānātimāna), inferiority conceit (omāna), overestimation (adhimāna), the conceit "I am" (asmimāna), and wrong conceit (micchāmāna).' Among those conceits, 'māna' is the elation based on birth and so forth, without considering the person through the power of 'better' and so forth. 'Atimāna' is the elation of disparaging others by way of birth and so forth, thinking 'there is no one equal to me.' 'Mānātimāna' is the conceit that arises thinking 'this person was equal to me before, but now I am superior and this person is inferior.' 'Omāna' is the conceit that occurs by lowering oneself by way of birth and so forth, thinking 'I am inferior.' 'Adhimāna' is the conceit of thinking one has attained the Four Noble Truths when one has not yet attained them. This overestimation (adhimāna) occurs to one who has pure virtue, is diligent in the meditation subject, has defined mentality-materiality, and has crossed over doubt by grasping the conditions...
28:
For a worldling who, having applied the three characteristics, contemplates conditioned formations and possesses initiated insight, [overestimation] arises; it does not arise for others. *Asmimāna* (the conceit 'I am') is the conceit that arises as 'I am' regarding the five aggregates such as the form aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*). It means the conceit that arises through the view such as 'the form aggregate is indeed I.' *Micchāmāna* (wrong conceit) is the conceit that arises through bad skills such as the art of [training] elephants and horses.

The meaning of the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) has been stated. *Samparivattati* means that because of the causal worldly conditions, one changes greatly through compliance with the four things such as gain, and through opposition to the four things such as loss; it means one abandons their natural state. The meaning of the eight factors of wrongness (*micchatta*) has also been stated. *Niyyāto* means one has gone into or is overwhelmed.

It means [overwhelmed] by the eight faults of a person (*purisadosa*) taught with the similes of the floorboards in the Aṭṭhakanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and without similes in the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga. In that Aṅguttara text, it is taught thus:

'What are the eight faults of a person? In this Dispensation, monks accuse a monk of an offense (*āpatti*). That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, pretends to be forgetful, saying "I do not remember, I do not remember," and thus tries to release himself from the offense. This is the first *purisadosa* (fault of a person).

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, retorts and insults the accuser, saying "What is the use of the words of an ignorant and unskilled person like you? Do you think someone like you should speak to me?" This is the second *purisadosa*.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, counter-accuses the accuser, saying "You too have committed such-and-named offense; you should first atone for that offense yourself." This is the third *purisadosa*.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, evades by answering with irrelevant matters, leads the conversation away, and manifests anger, malice, and dissatisfaction. This is the fourth *purisadosa*.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, speaks while waving his arms in the midst of the Saṅgha. This is the fifth *purisadosa*.'
29:
'Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, without regarding the accusation, without regarding the Saṅgha, and without regarding the accuser, departs for wherever he wishes while still having the offense. This is the sixth *purisadosa*.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, says "I have neither fallen into an offense, nor have I not fallen into an offense," and by remaining silent in that way, he harasses the Saṅgha. This is the seventh *purisadosa*.

Furthermore, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, says thus: "Venerable sirs, why do you strive so excessively against me? Right now, I shall renounce the training and return to the lower life (lay life)." That monk, having renounced the training and returned to the lower life, says again: "Venerable sirs, now indeed, may you be satisfied." This is the eighth *purisadosa*. These are the eight faults of a person.' (Vibhaṅga 957, Aṅguttara 8.14).

Among those [eight *purisadosa*], *purisadosā* means the faults of persons. They are called 'faults' (*dosa*) because they corrupt the continuum of persons. *Na sarāmi na sarāmi* means 'I do not remember, I do not recognize the place where I committed this act,' and thus, by pretending forgetfulness, he releases himself from the accusation. *Codakaṃyeva paṭippharati* means he becomes oppositional and insults [the accuser], standing in a state of retorting. *Kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ* means 'What is the use of the words of one like you who is ignorant and unskilled in the Vinaya? You, the accuser, know neither the basis (*vatthu*), nor the offense (*āpatti*), nor the accusation (*codanā*).' Thus he shows. 'Do you, who know nothing at all like this, think you should speak to another?' Thus he overwhelms and oppresses. *Paccāropeti* means he counter-accuses by saying words such as 'You too are [guilty].' *Paṭikarohi* means 'Confess the offense that requires confession (*desanāgāminī*); atone for the offense that requires rehabilitation (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*); only after standing in such purity shall you accuse another.' Thus he shows. *Aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati* means he conceals one reason or word with another reason or word. When it is said 'You have fallen into an offense,' he says 'Who fell? What offense? Why? How? To whom are you speaking? What are you saying?' 'Have you seen any such matter?' thus...
30:
When it is said, "I do not hear," he brings his ear close. How does he deflect the speech to the outside? When asked, "Have you committed such-and-such an offense?" he says, "I have gone to Pāṭaliputta." When told again, "We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta," he says again, "I have gone to Rājagaha." When told, "Go to Rājagaha or to a brahmin's house, (but) you have committed an offense," he deflects the speech to the outside by saying such things as, "In that Rājagaha, I obtained pork."

"Kopa" means the state of being angry; "dosa" means the state of being corrupted (malicious). Both of these are just names for anger. "Appaccaya" means the manner of being dissatisfied; it is a name for distress (domanassa). "Pātukaroti" means he makes manifest, he shows. "Bāhāvikkhepakaṃ bhaṇati" means he speaks the words of those who have no shame, waving his arms again and again. "Anādiyitvā" means not taking with a respectful manner, but disregarding; the meaning is being without respect. "Viheseti" means he harasses, he oppresses. "Atibāḷhaṃ" means very firmly, excessively. "Mayi byāဝဋာ" means they have reached the state of exertion towards me. "Hīnāyāvattitvā" means returning to the low state of a layman; the meaning is becoming a layman. "Attamanā hotha" means be of happy mind; he speaks with the intention, "May you obtain the requisites that I should obtain, may you live in the place where I should live, I have made a comfortable living for you." "Dussati" means he becomes corrupted (or he destroys).

"Navahi āghātavatthūhi" (by nine grounds for resentment) is taught only by way of arising in beings. As it was said:

"Monks, there are these nine grounds for resentment. Which nine? One harbors resentment thinking, 'He did me harm'; one harbors resentment thinking, 'He is doing me harm'; one harbors resentment thinking, 'He will do me harm.' One harbors resentment thinking, 'He did harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me; he is doing harm...; he will do harm...' One harbors resentment thinking, 'He did good to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me; he is doing good...; he will do good...' Monks, these are the nine grounds for resentment" (as taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

In that Pāḷi, "āghātavatthūni" means the causes of resentment. Here, "āghāta" is just anger; that anger itself is called "āghātavatthu" because it is the ground for further anger. "Āghātaṃ bandhati" means he binds, shows, or produces anger. "He did not do me good, he is not doing, he will not do. He did not do good to one who is dear and pleasing to me, he is not doing, he will not do. He did not do harm to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me, he is not doing..."
31:
The other nine grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu) taught in the Niddesa (in the Mahāniddesa, Vibhaṅga, and Dhammasaṅgaṇī) starting with "He will not do [harm/good]..." are also included within these nine grounds for resentment. Āghātito means "impacted" (ghaṭṭito).

What are the nine types of conceit (navavidhamāna)? The conceit "I am superior to one who is superior," the conceit "I am equal to one who is superior," the conceit "I am inferior to one who is superior." The conceit "I am superior to one who is equal," the conceit "I am equal to one who is equal," the conceit "I am inferior to one who is equal." The conceit "I am superior to one who is inferior," the conceit "I am equal to one who is inferior," and the conceit "I am inferior to one who is inferior." These are the nine types of conceit.

Among these, the conceit "I am superior to one who is superior" arises in kings and monks. A king thinks, "Who is equal to me in terms of country, wealth, or vehicles?" and thus forms this conceit. A monk also thinks, "Who is equal to me in terms of virtue (sīla), ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and so on?" and thus forms this conceit.

The conceit "I am equal to one who is superior" also arises in them. A king thinks, "In what way am I different from other kings in terms of country, wealth, or vehicles?" and thus forms this conceit. A monk also thinks, "In what way am I different from another monk in terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so on?" and thus forms this conceit.

The conceit "I am inferior to one who is superior" also arises in them. A king whose country, wealth, or vehicles are not very abundant thinks, "I have only the mere name of 'king'; how can I truly be called a king?" and thus forms this conceit. A monk with few gains and little honor thinks, "I am called a Dhamma-preacher, one of great learning (bahussuta), or a Great Elder (mahatthera) only in speech; how can I, who have no gains or honor, truly be called a Dhamma-preacher, one of great learning, or a Great Elder?" and thus forms this conceit.

Conceits such as "I am superior to one who is equal" arise in ministers and others. A minister or a regional ruler thinks, "Who is another royal official equal to me in terms of wealth, carriages, or vehicles?" or "In what way am I different from others?" or "I have only the name of 'minister'; I do not even have enough for food and clothing; how can I truly be called a minister?" and thus forms this conceit.
32:
Conceit and other such states as 'I am superior' arise in inferior persons such as slaves and the like. A slave might develop this conceit by thinking, 'Is there any other slave like me from either my mother's or my father's side? Others became slaves for the sake of food because they were unable to make a living, but I am superior as I have descended from a lineage of slaves.' Or he might think, 'Since I have descended from a lineage of slaves and am a slave of pure descent from both parents, how am I different from a slave of such-and-such a name?' Or he might think, 'I have become a slave for the sake of food, but from my parents' side, I have no status of a slave; how can I be called a real slave?' Just like a slave, those such as Pukkusas and Caṇḍālas also develop this conceit.

Among these types of conceit, only the conceit that arises in a superior person as 'I am superior' is called true conceit (yāthāvamāna); the other two are false conceits (ayāthāvamāna). Similarly, only the conceit that arises in an equal person as 'I am equal' and in an inferior person as 'I am inferior' is called true conceit; the other two are false conceits. Among these, true conceits are to be abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga), while false conceits are to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga).

Those states rooted in craving (taṇhā) have already been mentioned. Regarding the term 'is attached' (rajjati), it does not mean being attached only by lust (rāga). In fact, because seeking (pariyesana) and other such activities rooted in craving can occur, it means one is attached to, associated with, and bound by all unwholesome states rooted in craving.

In the phrase 'by the ten bases of defilement' (kilesavatthu), what are the ten bases of defilement? They are: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), conceit (māna), wrong view (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), sloth (thina), restlessness (uddhacca), shamelessness (ahirika), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa). These are the ten bases of defilement.

Among these ten, the defilements themselves are called the bases of defilement. Alternatively, they are called bases (vatthu) because beings whose taints are not yet exhausted dwell in greed and so forth; since they are both defilements and the bases for beings who dwell in them, they are called bases of defilement. Furthermore, because defilements that arise through the force of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) and so forth also dwell therein, they are called bases of defilement as the bases for defilements. One is attached by that state, or it itself is attached, or it is merely the act of attaching; therefore, it is called greed (lobha). One is corrupted by that state, or it itself is corrupted, or it is merely the act of corrupting; therefore, it is called hatred (dosa). One is bewildered by that state, or it itself is bewildered, or it is merely the act of being bewildered; therefore, it is called delusion (moha). It is called conceit (māna) because one imagines [himself]. Wrong view (diṭṭhi) and the others have the meanings already stated. It is called shamelessness (ahirika) because one is not ashamed; the state of such a person who is not ashamed is ahirika.
33:
One is called anottappī because he does not fear [wrongdoing]; the state of such a person who does not fear is fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa). Among those two states, shamelessness (ahirika) has the characteristic of not loathing bodily misconduct and so forth. Fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa) has the characteristic of not fearing (or being bold towards) those very same acts of bodily misconduct and so forth. The term 'kiliissati' means being oppressed or tormented.

'By the ten grounds for resentment' (āghātavatthu) refers to the nine grounds previously mentioned and the ground for resentment described as 'resentment arises even in inappropriate places.' Resentment can arise even in inappropriate places such as against a tree stump or a thorn, without specifically reflecting on the reasons for resentment like 'he has done me harm' and so forth.

'By the ten unwholesome courses of action' (akusala-kammapatha)—what are the ten? They are: killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), taking what is not given (adinnādāna), sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra), false speech (musāvāda), slandering speech (pisuṇā vācā), harsh speech (pharusā vācā), frivolous chatter (samphappalāpa), covetousness (abhijjhā), ill-will (byāpāda), and wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). These are the ten unwholesome courses of action. These states are unwholesome actions and also the paths leading to the miserable realms (duggati); therefore, they are called unwholesome courses of action. 'Samannāgata' means being endowed with or possessed of.

'By the ten fetters' (saṃyojana)—what are the ten? They are: the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāga-saṃyojana), the fetter of aversion (paṭigha-saṃyojana), the fetter of conceit (māna-saṃyojana), the fetter of wrong view (diṭṭhi-saṃyojana), the fetter of doubt (vicikicchā-saṃyojana), the fetter of clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa-saṃyojana), the fetter of lust for existence (bhavarāga-saṃyojana), the fetter of envy (issā-saṃyojana), the fetter of stinginess (macchariya-saṃyojana), and the fetter of ignorance (avijjā-saṃyojana). These are the ten fetters. The states of wrongness (micchatta) have already been mentioned.

What is the 'wrong view with ten bases' (dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi)? It is the view that: there is no fruit in giving, there is no fruit in sacrifice, there is no fruit in offerings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds, there is no this world, there is no other world, there is no fruit in serving one's mother, there is no fruit in serving one's father, there are no spontaneously born beings (opapātika), and there are no recluses and brahmins in the world who have practiced well and rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through higher knowledge, make them known. This is the wrong view with ten bases.

In this context, 'dasavatthukā' means having ten bases because this wrong view possesses ten grounds. 'There is no giving' means one knows that giving exists and that it is possible to give something to someone, but one holds the view that there is no fruit or result of that giving. 'There is no sacrifice' means a great sacrifice is called 'yiṭṭha'; one knows that such a sacrifice can be made, but holds the view that there is no fruit or result of that sacrifice. 'Huta' refers to hospitality, offerings brought to guests, or acts performed for the sake of auspiciousness. One knows that such acts can be performed, but regarding the [fruit] of that huta...
34:
However, one holds the view that there is no fruit or result [of giving]. In this context, 'well-done and ill-done' means: the ten wholesome courses of action are called 'well-done deeds,' and the ten unwholesome courses of action are called 'ill-done deeds.' One knows the existence of these wholesome and unwholesome deeds. However, one holds the view that there is no fruit or result. 'There is no this world' means: one staying in the next world holds the view that this present world does not exist. 'There is no next world' means: one staying in this present world holds the view that the next world does not exist. 'There is no mother, there is no father' means: one knows the existence of parents. However, one holds the view that there is no fruit or result from the cause of serving those parents. 'There are no spontaneously born beings' means: one holds the view that there are no beings who pass away and are reborn. 'There are no those who have practiced rightly' means: one holds the view that there are no righteous recluses and brahmins in the world who have practiced the path in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma. 'Those who, having known this world... proclaim it' means: one holds the view that there is no Omniscient Buddha who is capable of proclaiming this present world and the next world, having known them by himself through his own distinguished knowledge.

Antaggāhikā-diṭṭhi (extremist view) is so called because it takes up one extreme part, such as 'the world is eternal.' Or, taking up one extreme is called 'antaggāha,' and because of having that taking up of an extreme, it is called 'antaggāhikā.' With that extremist view. That extremist view has already been mentioned.

By the one hundred and eight types of craving-proliferations: one hundred with eight extra is one hundred and eight. It is called 'pappañca' because it causes one to stay for a long time in saṃsāra. Craving itself is a proliferation, thus 'craving-proliferation' (taṇhā-pappañca). Because of the multiplicity of cravings due to the diversity of objects and repeated occurrences, the plural form is used, and a hundred of craving-proliferations is called 'taṇhā-pappañca-sata.' Therefore, although it should be said in the singular as 'taṇhā-pappañca-satena,' it is expressed in the plural as 'taṇhā-pappañca-satehi' by way of grammatical variation (vacana-vipallāsa). It should be understood as 'by a hundred craving-proliferations reckoned as one hundred and eight.' It should be known that the eight are treated as negligible and only the hundred is taken. In the Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga, however, they appear as 'cravings-maneuvers' (taṇhā-vicaritāni). As it is said:
'18 craving-maneuvers based on the internal five aggregates,
18 craving-maneuvers based on the external five aggregates,
combining and condensing these two, there are 36 craving-maneuvers.
Thus, 36 past craving-maneuvers,
36 future craving-maneuvers,
36 present craving-maneuvers (totaling 108).'
35:
Combining and condensing those craving-maneuvers, there are one hundred and eight craving-maneuvers.

In this context, the craving-proliferations themselves are called by the name 'craving-maneuvers' (taṇhā-vicarita). It means the occurrences of craving or the activities of craving. 'Based on the internal' means based on the five aggregates within one's own continuity. Here, the word 'internal' (ajjhattika) is in the genitive case with the meaning of the accusative. Its detail should be understood according to the method stated in the Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga. This is another method: based on the object of forms, there are three cravings: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Similarly, with the six objects such as sounds, etc., there are eighteen cravings. There are eighteen with internal objects and eighteen with external objects, making thirty-six. Those thirty-six themselves, being thirty-six with past objects, thirty-six with future objects, and thirty-six with present objects, become one hundred and eight craving-maneuvers. 'Pappañcita' means caused to stay for a long time (clinging) in the object or in saṃsāra.

Regarding the sixty-two views: 'What are the sixty-two views spoken of by the Blessed One in the Brahmajāla Sutta Exposition? They are: four doctrines of Eternalism, four doctrines of Partial-Eternalism, four doctrines of Finite and Infinite (Extensionism), four doctrines of Eel-wriggling, two doctrines of Fortuitous Origination, sixteen doctrines of Percipient-after-death, eight doctrines of Non-percipient-after-death, eight doctrines of Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient-after-death, seven doctrines of Annihilationism, and five doctrines of Nibbāna-in-this-life. These are the sixty-two views spoken of by the Blessed One in the Brahmajāla Sutta Exposition.' The detail here should be understood according to the method stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta.

'I also have crossed over' means I, the Buddha, have crossed over the four floods or the ocean of saṃsāra. 'I am liberated' means liberated from the bonds such as lust. 'I am tamed' means one who has no companion [of defilements] and is without the agitation of defilements. 'I am calmed' means one with a cooled heart. 'I have found relief' means having the relief obtained by seeing Nibbāna. 'I am extinguished' means extinguished by the extinction of defilements. 'I am capable' means I am one who is able. The word 'kho' is a particle in the sense of 'certainly.' In the phrase 'to also extinguish others,' the word 'others also' should be connected with previous words such as 'to also cross others over,' etc.

## The Commentary on the Exposition of the Great Compassion Knowledge is finished.
36:
## 72-73. Explanation of the Exposition of Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññutañāṇaniddesavaṇṇanā)

In the Exposition of Omniscient Knowledge, the question "What is the Tathāgata's Omniscient Knowledge?" is asked. Because it has the same scope as that Omniscient Knowledge, Unobstructed Knowledge (Anāvaraṇañāṇa) is explained extensively along with it. In truth, Unobstructed Knowledge is not separate from Omniscient Knowledge in essence. This single knowledge is described in two ways based on the distinction of its functions, just like the faith-faculty (saddhindriya) and the faith-power (saddhābala).

Omniscient Knowledge itself is called "Unobstructed Knowledge" because no dhamma or person can obstruct it, as it is free from any hindrance. This is because all knowable dhammas are connected to the adverting of the mind-door (manodvārāvajjanā). Persons other than the Buddha cannot know even if they advert. Some teachers say: "It is called Omniscient Knowledge because it can take all things as objects like mind-consciousness. That same knowledge is called Unobstructed Knowledge because it is unimpeded in its objects like Indra's thunderbolt (vajira). Omniscient Knowledge is the negation of being a gradual omniscient (anupubbasabbaññū). Unobstructed Knowledge is the negation of being a simultaneous omniscient (sakiṃsabbaññū). The Blessed One is called 'Omniscient' (Sabbaññū) due to the attainment of Omniscient Knowledge, but he is not a 'gradual omniscient'. He is also called 'Omniscient' due to the attainment of Unobstructed Knowledge, but he is not a 'simultaneous omniscient'."

In the passage "He knows all conditioned and unconditioned things without remainder," the word "Sabba" (all) refers to the exhaustive inclusion of all dhammas by way of their classes (jāti). "Anavasesa" (without remainder) refers to the exhaustive inclusion of each individual dhamma by way of all its aspects. The phrase "Conditioned and Unconditioned" (saṅkhata and asaṅkhata) shows the two-fold division. The conditioned is one division, and the unconditioned is another division. That which is produced by the combination of causes is called "conditioned"; this refers to the five aggregates. Similarly, that which is not produced by the combination of causes is called "unconditioned"; this refers to Nibbāna.

He knows conditioned dhammas without remainder through aspects such as impermanence, suffering, and non-self. He knows unconditioned dhammas without remainder through aspects such as voidness (suññata), signlessness (animitta), and desirelessness (appaṇihita). It is called "without remainder" because there is no remainder left of those conditioned and unconditioned dhammas. It refers to conditioned dhammas (the five aggregates) and unconditioned dhammas (Nibbāna). Concepts (paññatti), which have many divisions, also fall into the side of the unconditioned because they are not produced by causes. Indeed, Omniscient Knowledge knows all concepts in their many divisions. Alternatively, the word "Sabba" means the grasping of all dhammas. "Anavasesa" means the grasping of the entire range. Since Omniscient Knowledge has no attachment or obstruction in those conditioned and unconditioned dhammas that are known without remainder, it is called Unobstructed Knowledge. This is the meaning.
37:
Now, to show the various divisions of objects, the text says "Atītaṃ" (past) and so forth. By the words "Atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ," the division by way of time is shown. By the words "Cakkhuñceva rūpā ca" (the eye and forms), the division by way of bases and objects is shown. The phrase "Thus all that" refers to the exhaustive inclusion of those eyes and forms. The same method applies to the remaining terms. The word "Yāvatā" (as far as) means exhaustive inclusion. The word "Aniccaṭṭhaṃ" (the meaning of impermanence) and so forth are shown by way of the division of common characteristics. "Aniccaṭṭhaṃ" is simply the aspect of impermanence. Alternatively, it is a word where the accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative. This method applies to such words. The word "Rūpassa" (of form) and so forth are shown by way of the division of aggregates. The words "of the eye... of aging and death" should be connected according to the method of elision (peyyāla) mentioned below. In the words "Abhiññāya" (having known directly) and so forth, these are the same knowledges mentioned below. "Abhiññaṭṭhaṃ" is the nature of direct knowledge. This method applies to such words. "Khandhānaṃ khandhaṭṭhaṃ" (the aggregate-meaning of the aggregates) and so forth should be understood according to the method mentioned below. The words "Kusale dhamme" (wholesome states) and so forth are the division by way of the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-tika). "Kāmāvacare dhamme" (sense-sphere states) and so forth are by way of the four planes (bhūmi). In both cases, the plural reading "sabbē jānāti" is better. However, because it falls into the singular flow, it is written in the singular in the texts. The words "Dukkhassa" (of suffering) and so forth are the division of objects of the fourteen Buddha-knowledges. If it is asked why Omniscient Knowledge is not mentioned after the four knowledges such as "knowledge of the degrees of faculties," it is because the knowledge being described is itself Omniscient Knowledge. When Omniscient Knowledge is being described by the division of its objects, that knowledge itself should not be mentioned (as an object), yet Omniscient Knowledge is indeed the object of Omniscient Knowledge.

Furthermore, wishing to show the domain of Omniscient Knowledge according to the method taught in the Kālakarāma Sutta and others, the text says "Yāvatā sadevakassa lokassa" (as far as the world with its devas). In that passage, "Sadevaka" means with devas; "Samāraka" means with Māra; "Sabrahmaka" means with Brahmā; "Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā" means with recluses and brahmins; "Sadevamanussāya pajāya" means with the generation of devas and humans. It is called "Pajā" (generation) because it is born; this is a synonym for the world of beings (sattaloka). Among those terms, by the word "Sadevaka," the five sense-sphere deva realms are taken; by the word "Samāraka," the sixth sense-sphere deva realm is taken; by the word "Sabrahmaka," the Brahmā realms such as Brahmakāyika are taken; by the word "Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇi," both the recluses and brahmins who are enemies of the Dispensation and those who have calmed and expelled evil are taken; by the word "Pajā," the world of beings is taken; and by the word "Sadevamanussa," conventional devas and the rest of humanity are taken. Thus, it should be understood that in this context, the world of locations (okāsaloka) is taken by three terms, and the world of beings (sattaloka) is taken by two terms.
38:
In another way—by the inclusion of 'sadevaka' (with the devas), the world of the formless sphere (arūpāvacara) is taken. By the inclusion of 'samāraka' (with Māra), the six heavens of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) are taken. By the inclusion of 'sabrahmaka' (with Brahmā), the world of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) is taken. By the inclusion of 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇādi' (with recluses and brahmins, etc.), it refers to the human world along with the conventional devas (kings), or the remaining world of beings, by virtue of the fourfold assembly. Furthermore, here, by the word 'sadevaka', he establishes the fact that he knows the seen (diṭṭha) and so forth of the entire world in its highest limit. Then, to dispel the doubt of those who might think, 'Māra has great power, he is the lord of the six heavens of the sense sphere, he can make others follow his will; does the Buddha know even his seen and so forth?', he said 'samārakassa'. To dispel the doubt of those who might think, 'Brahmā has great power, he can spread light through a thousand world systems with one finger, and from two fingers up to ten fingers, he can spread light through ten thousand world systems, and he also experiences the incomparable bliss of meditative attainments; does the Buddha know even his seen and so forth?', he said 'sabrahmakassa'. Then, to dispel the doubt of those who might think, 'There are many recluses and brahmins who are enemies of the Dispensation; does he know even their seen and so forth?', he said 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya'.

Thus, having shown his knowledge of the seen and so forth of superior beings, he then shows his knowledge of the seen and so forth of the rest of the world of beings, based on the conventional devas and the remaining humans, by way of the highest limit. This is the sequence of connection here. Ancient teachers, however, say: 'sadevakassa' means the rest of the world along with the devas. 'samārakassa' means the rest of the world along with Māra. 'sabrahmakassa' means the rest of the world along with the Brahmās. Thus, having included all beings in the three planes of existence in three terms by three modes, he then said 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya' to include them exhaustively by two modes. In this way, by these five terms, the three planes of existence are exhaustively included in various modes.

'Diṭṭha' (seen) is the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana). 'Suta' (heard) is the base of sounds (saddāyatana). 'Muta' (sensed) refers to the base of smells (gandhāyatana), the base of tastes (rasāyatana), and the base of tangibles (phoṭṭhabbāyatana), because they are to be apprehended by reaching (the sense organ). 'Viññāta' (cognized) is the mental object (dhammārammaṇa) such as pleasure and pain. 'Patta' (attained) is an object obtained whether sought or unsought. 'Pariyesita' (sought) is an object sought whether obtained or not. 'Anuvicaritaṃ manasā' (pondered by the mind) is an object thought about by the mind. By the words 'He knows everything,' he shows this meaning: In the immeasurable world systems, whatever visible form—such as blue or yellow—appears at the eye-door of this world with its devas, the Buddha’s omniscience knows all of that. 'This being, at this moment, having seen such a visible form, has become happy, or sad, or neutral'—in this way, the Buddha’s omniscience knows each object. Likewise, in the immeasurable world systems, whatever sound—such as the sound of a drum or a tabour—appears at the ear-door of this world with its devas; whatever smell—such as the smell of roots or bark—appears at the nose-door; whatever taste—such as the taste of roots or stems—appears at the tongue-door...
39:
In this world with its devas, the visible form such as 'blue, yellow' etc., comes into the range of the eye-door. That the Tathāgata’s omniscience knows all this: 'This being, at this moment, having seen this particular visible form, has become glad, or sad, or indifferent.' Likewise, in the immeasurable world systems, the sound such as 'drum-sound, tabour-sound' etc., comes into the range of the ear-door of this world with its devas; the smell such as 'root-smell, bark-smell' etc., comes into the range of the nose-door; the taste such as 'root-taste, trunk-taste' etc., comes into the range of the tongue-door; the tangible object consisting of the earth element, fire element, and air element, such as 'rough, soft' etc., comes into the range of the body-door. That the Tathāgata’s omniscience knows all this: 'This being, at this moment, having touched this particular tangible object, has become glad, or sad, or indifferent.' Likewise, in the immeasurable world systems, the mental object consisting of pleasure, pain, etc., comes into the range of the mind-door of this world with its devas. That the Tathāgata’s omniscience knows all this: 'This being, at this moment, having cognized this particular mental object, has become glad, or sad, or indifferent. For this mass of people, there are things sought but not obtained, and things sought and obtained. There are things unsought and not obtained, and things unsought but obtained. Through the Tathāgata’s omniscience, there is nothing that is 'not obtained' (not known).

Again, in another way, to establish the state of omniscience, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Na tassa...'. In that verse, 'Na tassa addiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñci' means: for that Tathāgata, in this world of the three planes, or in this present time, there is nothing whatsoever, even the slightest, that is unseen by the eye of wisdom; it is not that it is not manifest. 'Atthi' (is) is a verb in the present tense. By this, he shows the state of knowing all phenomena occurring in the present time. Here, the letter 'da' is doubled for the sake of ease in the metrical composition of the verse. In the phrase 'atho aviññātaṃ', the word 'atho' is an indeclinable (nipāta). 'Aviññātaṃ' means there was no phenomenon whatsoever unknown in the past; the verb 'nāhosi' (was not) is the elided portion of the text. If the word 'atthi' is taken as an indeclinable, it is suitable even without the elided text. In this way, [he shows] the state of knowing all phenomena occurring in the past...
40:
[In this way, the state of being known of all things that occurred in the past] is shown. "Ajānitabba" means that there will not be, or there is not, any phenomenon (dhamma) that is unknown in the future. In this way, the state of being known of all things that occur in the future is shown. Alternatively, in this word "ajānitabba," the letter "a" merely qualifies the action of knowing. In the phrase "sabbaṃ abhiññāsi yadatthi neyyaṃ," the Blessed One has fully known and penetrated with his superior omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) whatever knowable (neyya) phenomena exist, whether belonging to the three periods of time or being beyond time. Here, because the word "atthi" (exists) includes objects belonging to the three periods of time and objects beyond time, the word "atthi" should be understood as an indeclinable (avyaya). Because of that omniscient knowledge, the Blessed One is called "Samantacakkhu" (the All-Seeing Eye). He is called "Samantacakkhu" because he possesses the eye of knowledge that functions everywhere in all directions, without remainder, in terms of both time and space (okāsa). For the reasons mentioned, the Blessed One is called "Samantacakkhu" and "Sabbaññū" (the Omniscient One). In this verse, omniscient knowledge is established through a teaching based on a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).

Furthermore, wishing to show omniscient knowledge by way of the objects of the Buddha's knowledges, he said: "Samantacakkhu; in what sense is he called Samantacakkhu?" and so on. In that verse, regarding the term "Samantacakkhu," the meaning is: "In what sense is that Samantacakkhu so called?" Its meaning will be explained by the words "As far as the suffering nature of suffering," and so forth. Omniscient knowledge itself is called "Samantacakkhu." As it is said, "Omniscient knowledge is called Samantacakkhu," once the meaning of omniscient knowledge is stated, the meaning of Samantacakkhu is also stated. "Buddha-ñāṇāni" refers to the knowledges belonging only to the Buddha. Knowledges such as the knowledge of suffering occur in their entirety only to the Blessed One, whereas for others, they occur only in part. The statement "knowledges shared with disciples" (sāvaka-sādhāraṇa) is made with reference to their existence in part. "Sabbo ñāto" means everything is known by knowledge. By the negative statement "There is no unknown aspect of suffering," the previously mentioned meaning is clarified. "Sabbo diṭṭho" means not merely known, but made as if seen with the eye (i.e., it is clear). "Sabbo vidito" means not merely seen, but clearly understood. "Sabbo sacchikato" means not merely understood, but realized through the attainment of knowledge regarding that object. "Sabbo phassito" means not merely realized, but touched (experienced) by way of repeated practice (samudācāra) as desired. Alternatively, it is known (ñāta) by way of individual essence (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa); seen (diṭṭha) by way of general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa); understood (vidita) by way of function (rasa); and realized (sacchikata).
41:
(He realizes) by way of manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna). He touches by way of proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Or otherwise, he knows by way of the arising of knowledge (ñāṇa). He sees by way of the arising of the eye (cakkhu). He understands by way of the arising of wisdom (paññā). He realizes by way of the arising of clear vision (vijjā). He touches by way of the arising of light (āloka).

In this manner, the detailed explanation should be understood: "Whatever the suffering nature of suffering is, all has been seen; there is no suffering nature that has not been seen," and so forth; and "Whatever in the world with its devas... has been wandered over by the mind, all is known; there is nothing unknown," and so forth.

The verse mentioned earlier is stated again by way of conclusion. For when that conclusion is made, the conclusion of the knowledge is also indeed completed.

## The Explanation of the Sabbaññutañāṇa Niddesa is finished.
## In the Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā named Saddhammappakāsinī,
## The Explanation of the Ñāṇakathā is finished.

## 2. Diṭṭhikathā
## 1. Explanation of the Assādadiṭṭhi Niddesa

Now, the sequential explanation of the Diṭṭhikathā (Discourse on Views), which was taught immediately after the Ñāṇakathā, has arrived. This Diṭṭhikathā is taught immediately after the Ñāṇakathā because it is easy to clear the stain of wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) for a person who has practiced knowledge in the Ñāṇakathā and has well-attained right view (sammā-diṭṭhi), and because right view becomes very pure.

In that Diṭṭhikathā, the question beginning with "What is view?" is the inquiry (pucchā). The answer to the question asked, beginning with "What is view? Adherence and misapprehension is view," is the response (vissajjanā). The detailed exposition of the response given, beginning with "How is adherence and misapprehension view?" is the elaboration (vitthāraniddesa). The comparison with the Diṭṭhi Sutta, beginning with "All those views are views of gratification (assādadiṭṭhi)," is the correlation (saṃsandanā). Thus, there are these four sections.

Among those four, in the section of the inquiry, first, the question "What is view?" is an inquiry into the phenomenon (dhamma-pucchā) or an inquiry into the nature (sabhāva-pucchā). The question "How many are the bases of view?" is an inquiry into the root (hetu-pucchā) or an inquiry into the condition (paccaya-pucchā); the meaning is "How many are the causes of views?"

The question "How many are the obsessions of view (diṭṭhi-pariyuṭṭhāna)?" is an inquiry into the occurrence (samudācāra-pucchā) or an inquiry into the alteration (vikāra-pucchā). This is because views themselves arise by way of occurrence, enveloping and obstructing the mind.
42:
Now, following the Ñāṇakathā (Treatise on Knowledge), the explanation of the terms in the Diṭṭhikathā (Treatise on Views) has arrived in due order. Indeed, for a person who is practiced in knowledge or who has properly attained Sammādiṭṭhi (Right View), the cleansing of the stain of Micchādiṭṭhi (Wrong View) is very easy to perform. Sammādiṭṭhi is also exceedingly pure. Therefore, the Diṭṭhikathā is taught immediately after the Ñāṇakathā. In that Diṭṭhikathā, the statement beginning with "What is view?" is the question (pucchā). The statement beginning with "Adherence and misapprehension is view" is the answer (vissajjanā) to the question asked. The statement beginning with "How is adherence and misapprehension?" is the detailed exposition (vitthāraniddesa) of the answer. The statement beginning with "All views are views of gratification (assādadiṭṭhi)" is the comparison and collation (saṃsandanā) with the Suttas that teach about views. Thus, there are four sections (pariccheda). Among these four, in the section of questions, first, the question "What is view?" is a question regarding the nature (sabhāvapucchā) of view. The question "How many are the bases of views?" is a question regarding the cause (hetupucchā/paccayapucchā). Its meaning is "How many are the causes of views?". The question "How many are the obsessions of views (diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhāna)?" is a question regarding constant occurrence (samudācārapucchā/vikārapucchā).

Views themselves manifest as obsessions because they envelop through constant occurrence. Therefore, they are called diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhāna. The question "How many views are there?" is a question regarding the number (saṅkhāpucchā/gaṇanapucchā) of views. "How many are the misapprehensions of views (diṭṭhābhinivesa)?" is a question regarding the variety of views by way of the variety of bases (vatthu) and the variety of objects (ārammaṇa). Views themselves are called "diṭṭhiparāmāsa" because they wrongly adhere to and misapprehend those various bases and objects. The question "What is the eradication of the bases of views (diṭṭhiṭṭhānasamugghāta)?" is a question regarding the opposite of views and the method of abandonment (pahānūpāya). The aggregates (khandha) and so forth, which are the causes of views, no longer become the causes of those views because of the total eradication of views. Therefore, those causal aggregates are also said to be totally eradicated. Thus, because the causal aggregates of views are well and truly destroyed (abandoned) by this (the Path of Stream-entry), it is called "diṭṭhiṭṭhānasamugghāta."

Now, the six answers to those six questions, beginning with "What is view?", will be shown. Among those six, the statement "What is view?" is the question regarding the meaning to be answered, and "Adherence and misapprehension is view" is the answer. That wrong mental orientation is called "abhinivesa" (adherence) because it firmly stands and strongly grasps the five aggregates, which are impermanent by nature, by way of permanence and so forth. It is called "parāmāsa" (misapprehension) because, having bypassed the mode of impermanence, it occurs by way of permanence and so forth, and wrongly grasps. Alternatively, it is called "parāmāsa" because it grasps a view such as permanence as the supreme truth. Because it is both a firm grasping (abhinivesa) and a misapprehending (parāmāsa), it is called "abhinivesaparāmāsa." In this way, the nature of view is answered by way of its function as a type of clinging. "Tīṇi sataṃ" means three hundred. (In this case, there is a grammatical shift from plural to singular). Without directly repeating the question "What is the eradication of the bases of views?", the answer is given as "The Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) is the eradication of the bases of views."

Now, the detailed exposition beginning with "How is adherence and misapprehension?" will be stated. Therein, the word "rūpaṃ" is in the accusative case (object). It is connected as "misapprehending the aggregate of form." Here, "form" (rūpa) refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) which is an object of clinging, and the form of the kasina. It should be understood by applying each: the view that misapprehends "This is mine" is a view; the view that misapprehends "This I am" is a view; and the view that misapprehends "This is my self" is a view. The word "etaṃ" is a general term applicable to all three genders. For that reason, the neuter singular is used as "This (etaṃ) is mine regarding feeling (vedanā), this (etaṃ) is mine regarding mental formations (saṅkhāra)." However, the word "eso" is used in the masculine singular in consideration of the word "attā" (self) which follows. "This is mine" is a view rooted in the imagining of craving (taṇhā-maññanā). "This I am" is a view rooted in the imagining of conceit (māna-maññanā). "This is my self" is simply the imagining of view (diṭṭhi-maññanā). Some teachers, however, say that "This is mine" is the notion of mine-making (mammaṃkārakappanā), "This I am" is the notion of I-making (ahaṃkārakappanā), and "This is my...
43:
Self is the adherence to a self conceived through the notions of 'I-making' (ahaṃkāra) and 'mine-making' (mamaṃkāra). Likewise, in due order, it is the adherence to a self based on craving, the exaltation of conceit, and the adherence to a self based on craving and exalted by conceit. It is the adherence to a self caused by not seeing the characteristic of suffering in formations, not seeing the characteristic of impermanence in formations, and not seeing the three characteristics of formations. It is the adherence to a self of one who has fallen into the perversion of taking the painful and the foul as pleasant and beautiful, the adherence to a self of one who has fallen into the perversion of taking the impermanent as permanent, and the adherence to a self of one who has fallen into the fourfold perversions. It is the adherence to a self of one who depends on the conceptions regarding the modes of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the conceptions regarding the future attainment of the divine eye, and the conceptions regarding the past, the future, and the phenomena arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination. It is the adherence to a self of one who follows the past with delight, expects the future with delight, and is led away by craving and views regarding present phenomena. It is the view caused by ignorance regarding the past, the view caused by ignorance regarding the future, and the adherence to a self caused by ignorance regarding the past, the future, and the phenomena arisen through specific conditionality and dependent origination—thus they explain the meaning of these three statements.

Herein, views first have the five aggregates as their object. Thereafter, views are stated having as their objects the six internal and external bases, the six classes of consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, volition, craving, thought, and evaluation, the elements, the ten kasinas, and the thirty-two parts of the body. Among the thirty-two parts, where individual adherence is not appropriate, it should be understood that it is treated as if there were individual adherence by way of adherence to the whole body. Thereafter, the application is made by way of the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the nineteen faculties. Indeed, the three purely supramundane faculties are not applied. For there are no views that have supramundane states as their object. In all cases, among phenomena that are a mix of mundane and supramundane, the supramundane should be excluded and only the mundane should be taken. Materiality not connected with the faculties (anindriyabaddha-rūpa) should also not be taken, as it is not a cause for view. Thereafter, the application is made by way of the three realms, the nine types of existence, the jhānas, the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), the attainments (samāpatti), and the factors of dependent origination. Regarding the separate taking of birth, aging, and death, the explanation is the same as the method already stated. All these terms from materiality to aging and death amount to one hundred and ninety-eight.

Regarding the statement that the aggregates are also bases for views: because the five aggregates are the objects for the twenty types of personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), and because it was said, 'Monks, whatever recluses or brahmins see a self, they all see it only in the five aggregates of clinging, or in one of them,' the five aggregates of clinging are the causes of views. Regarding the statement that ignorance is also a base for views: because views arise in those who are like the blind due to ignorance, and because it was said in response to the question, 'Venerable sir, regarding the view that appears in the six teachers who are not fully enlightened, that they are indeed fully enlightened—venerable sir, depending on what does that view appear?': 'Puṇṇa, depending on the inferior element of ignorance, inferior perception and inferior view arise,' therefore ignorance is a cause of views. Regarding the statement that contact is also a base for views: because views arise in one who is touched by that contact, and because it was said, 'Monks, those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, who hold views about the past, assert various doctrinal statements concerning the past; that view also has contact as its condition,' therefore contact is a cause of views. Regarding the statement that perception is also a base for views: by taking only the mode...
44:
"Bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins regard the self, they all regard it in the five aggregates of clinging, or in one of them" (Saᅃyutta Nikāya). Because of this, the five aggregates of clinging are a cause for wrong views.

Ignorance (avijjā) is also a standing-point for wrong view. Because wrong view arises for those who are blinded by ignorance, and because it was said: "Venerable sir, this view 'In those who are not perfectly enlightened, they are perfectly enlightened' exists. Venerable sir, depending on what does this view appear?" "Kaccāna, this element of ignorance is great. Kaccāna, depending on the low element of ignorance, there arises low perception and low view" (Saᅃyutta Nikāya). Thus, ignorance is a cause for wrong views.

Contact (phassa) is also a standing-point for wrong view. Because wrong view arises for one touched by that contact, and because it was said: "Bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, who hold views about the past, who assert various speculative propositions concerning the past—that too is conditioned by contact" (Dĩgha Nikāya). Thus, contact is a cause for wrong views.

Perception (saā) is also a standing-point for wrong view. Because it is a cause for grasping what is not in accordance with reality by grasping a mere mode, and because it was said: "O Sage of broad wisdom, there are those three views and those sixty views that are based on the assertions of recluses, which are dependent on names and perceptions and are points of entry; having removed them, you have crossed the darkness of the flood" (Sutta Nipāta). Also, because it was said: "For the categories of conceptual proliferation (papaca) have perception as their source" (Sutta Nipāta, Mahāniddesa). Thus, perception is a cause for wrong views.

Initial thought (vitakka) is also a standing-point for wrong view. Because wrong view arises through thinking about modes, and because it was said: "Indeed, the truths are not many and various, except for perception, which are permanent in the world. Having devised reasoning among views, they speak of a duality: 'truth and falsehood'" (Sutta Nipāta). Thus, initial thought is a cause for wrong views.

Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) is also a standing-point for wrong view. Because unwise attention is the uncommon cause of unwholesome states, and because it was said: "For one who attends unwisely in this way, one of the six views arises" (Majjhima Nikāya). Thus, unwise attention is a cause for wrong views...
45:
In explaining the cause, an evil friend (pāpamitta) is also called the basis (cause) of wrong view (diṭṭhi). Because wrong view arises by following the example (diṭṭhānugati) of an evil friend, and because of the words spoken in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: “Monks, I do not see any other single external factor that leads to such great harm as this, monks, namely evil friendship (pāpamittatā)” (A. I. 110), an evil friend is the root cause of wrong views. The voice of another (paratoghosa) is also called the basis (cause) of wrong view. Because wrong view arises by hearing a poorly taught Dhamma, and because of the words: “Monks, there are these two causes, two conditions for the arising of wrong view. Which two? The voice of another and improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra)” (A. II. 126), the speech of one with wrong views, which is connected to wrong views, is the root cause of wrong views.

Now, the teacher, wishing to explain the meaning of the term “diṭṭhiṭṭhāna” (basis of wrong view), says: “The aggregates (khandhā) are the cause, the aggregates are the condition,” and so forth. It means that only the aggregates are the generative cause (janaka-hetu) and the supporting condition (upatthambhaka-paccaya) for wrong views. “Samuṭṭhānaṭṭhena” means that because they arise from these things such as the aggregates, they are called “samuṭṭhāna” (origin/cause). By the sense of being the cause of origin, it means being the cause of wrong view.

Now, wishing to show the classification of wrong view by way of specific functions, he says: “What are the eighteen obsessions of wrong view (diṭṭhi-pariyuṭṭhāna)?” and so forth. In that text, the term “yā diṭṭhi” (which wrong view) is the root term connected with the eighteen terms to be mentioned. It should be connected with all terms as: “Whatever wrong view there is, that itself is called 'diṭṭhigata' (resorting to wrong view),” and so on. It is called “diṭṭhi” in the sense of seeing incorrectly. That same incorrect seeing is called “diṭṭhigata” because it is included within the sixty-two types of wrong views. This meaning has also been stated below. It is also called “diṭṭhigata” because it has reached one of the two extremes. That same wrong view is called “diṭṭhigahana” (thicket of views) in the sense of being difficult to overcome, like a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, or a thicket of mountains. It is called “diṭṭhikantāra” (wilderness of views) in the sense of being repulsive and accompanied by danger, like a wilderness of thieves, a wilderness of wild beasts, a waterless wilderness, or a wilderness of famine. In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, it appears as “diṭṭhikantāro” using its own [masculine] gender. It is called “diṭṭhivisūka” (contortion of views) in the sense of piercing right view and in the sense of being contrary to it. Indeed, when wrong view arises, it both pierces and opposes right view. In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, it appears as “diṭṭhivisūkāyikaṃ.” It is called “diṭṭhivipphandita” (vacillation of views) because it is the distortion and trembling of view, sometimes grasping the eternalist view and sometimes the annihilationist view. Indeed, one who resorts to wrong views cannot remain in a single position, but sometimes reflects on eternalism and sometimes on annihilationism. It is called “diṭṭhisaṃyojana” (fetter of views) because wrong view itself binds one to harm. It is called “salla” (dart/thorn) because wrong view itself stabs within and is difficult to extract. ...
46:
View itself is called the dart of view because it is like a dart. View itself is called the confinement of view because it causes confinement in the sense of being oppressive. View itself is called the impediment of view because it is an impediment in the sense of obstructing the Path. View itself is called the bond of view because it is a bond in the sense of being difficult to escape. View itself is called the precipice of view because it is like a precipice in the sense of being difficult to emerge from. View itself is called the underlying tendency of view because it is an underlying tendency in the sense of having gained strength. View itself is called the torment of view because it torments oneself. View itself is called the fever of view because it repeatedly burns oneself. View itself is called the tie of view because it ties together the mass of defilements. View itself is called the clinging of view because it clings strongly. View itself is called the adherence of view because it adheres with the thought, 'This is the truth,' and so on. View itself is called the misapprehension of view because it misapprehends as 'This is superior,' or because it misapprehends wrongly.

Now, the Elder, wishing to show the sixteen views by way of groups, says: 'What are the sixteen views?' and so on. Therein, the view regarding gratification, known as pleasure and joy, is called the view of gratification (assādadiṭṭhi). The view that follows along with the self (or conforms to the grasping of a self) is called the view following the self (attānudiṭṭhi). The view that is perverted because it occurs as 'There is no fruit of giving' is called wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). The view occurring in the existing five aggregates is called identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). In this term 'sakkāyadiṭṭhi,' 'kāya' means the collection of the five aggregates. Because it has the 'existing body' (sakkāya), which is the collection of the five aggregates, as its basis, it is called sakkāyavatthukā. The view occurring as 'It is eternal' is called the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi). The view occurring as 'It is annihilated' is called the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). Because it grasps an extreme such as eternalism, or because it has the characteristic of grasping an extreme, it is called the view of grasping an extreme (antaggāhikā). The view following the prior end, known as the past, is called the view following the prior end (pubbantānudiṭṭhi). The view following the latter end, known as the future, is called the view following the latter end (aparantānudiṭṭhi). Because it binds to that which is not beneficial, it is called the fettering view (saṃyojanikā). The view that arises in connection with the conceit 'I,' which arises through the mode of 'I' as the root of the view, is called the view connected with the conceit 'I.' Similarly, the view connected with the conceit 'mine,' which arises through the mode of 'mine' as the root of the view, is called the view connected with the conceit 'mine.' Speaking of one's own five aggregates as 'self' is called the doctrine of self (attavāda); the view connected with that doctrine of self is called the view connected with the doctrine of self. Speaking of one's own five aggregates as 'the world' is called the doctrine of the world (lokavāda); the view connected with that doctrine of the world is called the view connected with the doctrine of the world. The eternalist view is called existence (bhava); the view arising by the power of the eternalist view is called the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi). The annihilationist view is called non-existence (vibhava); the view arising by the power of the annihilationist view is called the view of non-existence (vibhavadiṭṭhi).

127-128. Now, the Elder, wishing to show the three hundred adherences of view, asks: 'What are the three hundred adherences of view?' and without answering those three hundred directly yet, wishing to answer them only by explaining each adherence separately, [begins] with the view of gratification...
47: By asking about the number of modes of attachment for the sixteen views in the manner beginning with "In how many modes does attachment occur?", and then answering the number of modes of attachment for those sixteen views as "In the view of gratification (assādadiṭṭhi), attachment occurs through thirty-five modes," the Elder, wishing to explain those numbers in detail, said: "In the view of gratification, in what thirty-five modes does attachment occur?" and so forth. In that passage, "dependent on form" (rūpaṃ paṭicca) means dependent on the aggregate of form. "Pleasure (sukha) and joy (somanassa) arise" refers to the arising of pleasure and joy associated with lust and connected to the household life, based on the perfection of form (rūpasampatti) such as "This body of mine is of such a nature." Pleasure and joy are as defined previously. In the phrase "That itself is the gratification (assāda) of form," it refers to the gratification that arises depending on form. Indeed, that pleasure is enjoyed and relished by the power of craving; therefore, it is called gratification. "Attachment and misapprehension are the view" means that the misapprehension and attachment to that gratification occur as "It is eternal," or "It will be annihilated," or "It makes the self (attā), whether eternal or being annihilated, happy." Therefore, in the phrase "Whatever view and whatever gratification," although gratification is not the nature of the view itself, because that view cannot exist without gratification, both are presented together. "Assādadiṭṭhi" means the view that occurs regarding gratification.## Now, the Elder, wishing to condemn wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) and the person with wrong view by comparing them with various suttas, said: "The view of gratification is a wrong view," and so forth. In that passage, "failure of view" (diṭṭhivipatti) is the failure or perversion of view known as wrong view, which destroys right view. "One who has failed in view" (diṭṭhivipanna) means one for whom right view has failed or disappeared; it means a person of failed view. Alternatively, one who is ruined by wrong view is called "diṭṭhivipanna." Such a person should not be associated with by visiting, should not be befriended in the heart, and should not be attended upon by approaching and sitting near. "For what reason is that so?" is a question about the reason why such association and so forth should not be done. "Because his view is evil" is the answer giving the reason. The meaning is that because that person's view is evil, one should not associate with him. "Lust for view" refers to the lust that arises regarding a view, taking one's own view as the object, such as "My view is excellent." "One stained by lust for view" refers to one who is stained by that lust for view, like a cloth stained with dye. It is "not of great fruit" in terms of the resultant fruit (vipākaphala). It is "not of great benefit" in terms of the consequential fruit (nissandaphala).## "To the purisa-individual" means to the individual known as a purisa. In worldly usage, the body is called "puri"; because one sleeps (dwells) in that body, one is called "purisa." Hell is called "puṃ"...
48: Hell is called 'puṃ'; because one goes to that hell, one is called 'puggala'. In truth, most beings, after passing away from a happy destination, are reborn only in a miserable destination. For what reason is that so? Why is there no great fruit? The meaning is that because that person's view is evil, there is no great fruit. There are only two destinations among the five destinations. If the view is perverted (such as practicing the cow-duty, etc.), one reaches hell. If one practices (the cow-duty, etc.) to perfection, one is reborn in the animal realm.## Bodily action (kāyakamma) refers to bodily deeds such as bearing one's own characteristic marks, undertaking practices, bowing, rising to greet, and saluting with joined palms. Verbal action (vacīkamma) refers to verbal deeds such as learning, reciting, preaching, and exhorting others to undertake one's own doctrine. Mental action (manokamma) refers to mental deeds associated with thoughts of this world, thoughts of the next world, and thoughts of what is done and what is not done. It also includes bodily, verbal, and mental actions involved in giving, receiving, and consuming for a person who holds the view that there are living beings in grass, wood, grain, and seeds. 'Yathādiṭṭhi' means in accordance with that view. 'Samatta' means complete. 'Samādinna' means undertaken or grasped.## In the Commentary, however, it is said that bodily action is of three types: bodily action established in accordance with the view, bodily action co-nascent with the view, and bodily action conforming to the view. Among these three, the bodily action known as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct performed while holding the view that "There is no evil resulting from killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct; there is no coming of evil," is called 'bodily action established in accordance with the view'. The bodily action that arises together with that view and that vision is called 'bodily action co-nascent with the view'. That same bodily action, when it is completed, undertaken, and wrongly misapprehended, is called 'bodily action conforming to the view'. The same method applies to verbal and mental actions. Here, for one with wrong view who tells lies, slanders, speaks harshly, talks frivolously, is covetous, and has a mind of ill-will, the connection should be made as: "There is no evil resulting from that cause; there is no coming of evil." The meaning explained through the methods of bearing characteristic marks, learning, and thinking about the world is very excellent.## Among volition and so forth, volition co-nascent with the view is called 'volition' (cetanā). Aspiration co-nascent with the view is called 'aspiration' (patthanā). The fixing of the mind on an object by the power of volition and aspiration is called 'resolution' (paṇidhi). The states such as contact (phassa) and so forth, which are associated with that volition and so forth and are included in the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), are called 'formations' (saṅkhāra).
49:
States included in the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) are called formations (saṅkhāras). By terms such as 'undesirable' (aniṭṭha), only suffering (dukkha) is meant. This is because suffering is not sought by beings who desire happiness; therefore, it is called undesirable (aniṭṭha). Because it is not loved, it is called unpleasant (akanta). Because it does not cause the mind to grow and does not spread in the mind, it is called disagreeable (amanāpa). Because it is bad in the future, it is called harmful (ahita). Because it oppresses, it is called suffering (dukkha).

'For what reason does this happen?' asks for what reason it leads to such suffering, starting from being undesirable. Now, the reason for this is stated as 'because his view is evil.' This means because that person's view is evil and inferior, he arrives at such suffering. 'Placed in moist soil' refers to planting something like a neem seed in ground moistened with water. 'Essence of earth, essence of water' refers to the excellence of the earth and the excellence of the water in those respective places where the seed is sown.

For not all the earth and all the water in the place where the seed is sown cause the seed to bear fruit; only the part that touches the seed causes it to bear fruit.
