Therefore, only that part which is the cause for nourishing the seed should be known as the essence of earth and the essence of water. The word 'rasa' (essence/taste) denotes the fulfillment of a function (kicca-sampatti). Thus, the commentators said, 'It is called rasa in the sense of fulfillment of function.' In the world, when one says 'a musician with rasa,' it is understood as a well-accomplished musician.

'Takes up' means to grasp. When the seed obtains that part of the earth which is the cause for its nourishment, it is said to 'take up' the potency of that earth. 'All that' refers to all those essences. 'Because of bitterness' means that although those essences of earth and water are not bitter themselves, depending on the bitter seed, they lead to the bitterness of the neem tree and its fruits. The term 'because of pungency' (kaṭukattāya) is a synonym for the previously mentioned 'because of bitterness' (tittakattāya).

Just as in the verse from the Jātaka: 'This mango tree was formerly endowed with color, scent, and taste; receiving the same care, why does this mango tree have bitter fruit?'—here too, 'pungency' should be understood as 'bitterness' in the sense of being disliked. 'Because of being unenjoyable' means because of being not sweet. There is also a variant reading 'asāduttāya,' which also means the state of being unenjoyable. 'Sādu' means sweet. 'Its seed' refers to the seed of that neem tree and so on. 'In the same way' means in this very manner.

Since gratification (assāda) has pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) as its peak, the disadvantage (ādīnava) of wrong view is shown by way of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Again, to show the disadvantage of view by way of eighteen divisions, it says 'gratification-view, wrong view' and so on. The meaning of those words is as already stated. The connection of the mind overwhelmed by these eighteen modes is called 'yoke' (saññoga), showing that it is only because of view that one is bound in saṃsāra.
50:
However, there are fetters that are views, and there are fetters that are not views. Therefore, wishing to show that distinction, He said 'Atthi saññojanāni ceva' and so on. In that text, because there are places where the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāga-saṃyojana) is referred to as the fetter of attraction (anunaya-saṃyojana), it is called 'anunaya-saṃyojana'. It should be understood that this is said in reference to greed (lobha) that has arisen but not yet reached the state of sensual lust. In the sections based on the remaining aggregates, bases, and so on, the meaning should be understood in this same way. Because gratification (assāda) is limited to feeling (vedanā), the teaching is given ending with feeling. Perception (saññā) and so on are not taken. 'By these thirty-five modes' means by way of the objects of gratification that arise depending on these thirty-five bases: the five aggregates, and the five sets of six such as the internal bases.

## The Explanation of the Description of Gratification-View is Finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Description of Self-View

In the description of self-view, 'an uninstructed worldling' (assutavā puthujjana) should be understood as one who lacks scripture (āgama) and attainment (adhigama). For one who, due to being devoid of learning, questioning, and discernment regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, truths, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, and so on, lacks the scripture (āgama) that prohibits self-view. Because he has not yet attained the paths and fruits that are to be reached through practice, he also lacks attainment (adhigama). Such a person should be known as 'uninstructed' (assutavā) because of the absence of scripture and attainment. 'Suta' (learning/hearing) refers to the scripture of the Buddha's word (buddhavacana-āgama) and also to attainment (adhigama), which is called 'suta' by way of metaphorical usage of the cause for the effect, as it is the fruit of hearing. One who possesses that learning is called 'learned' (sutavā); one who does not possess it is 'uninstructed' (assutavā). That uninstructed worldling (puthujjana) is so called because:

He is a worldling (puthujjana) due to many reasons such as generating [defilements],
He is a worldling because he is included among the many folk (puthu-jana).

He is a worldling due to reasons such as generating many various defilements and so on. As it is said: 'They are worldlings because they generate many defilements; they are worldlings because they have many unabandoned identity views; they are worldlings because they look up to the faces of many teachers; they are worldlings because they have not emerged from all destinations (gati); they are worldlings because they construct many various volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra); they are worldlings because they are carried away by many various floods (ogha).'
51:
They are called worldlings (puthujjana) because they are tormented by various and manifold afflictions. They are called worldlings because they are burned by various and manifold fevers. They are called worldlings because they have reached the state of being attached, greedy, tied, infatuated, immersed, submerged, clinging, and entangled in the five cords of sensual pleasure. They are called worldlings because they are heavily obstructed, specifically obstructed, blocked, shut in, covered, and overturned by the five hindrances (Mahāni. 94). Alternatively, they are called worldlings because they are included among the many people who have exceeded the count [of those to be saved], who have turned their backs on the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and who habitually practice base dhammas. Or, this person is called a worldling because they stand apart and are distinct from the Noble Ones who are endowed with qualities such as virtue (sīla) and learning (suta). Thus, by these two words 'uninstructed worldling' (assutavā puthujjana)—

The Buddha, the kinsman of the Sun, taught:
One is the blind worldling,
And one is the virtuous worldling.

Among the two types of worldlings mentioned in this verse, it should be understood that the 'blind worldling' (andha-puthujjana) is meant here.

In the phrases such as 'ariyānaṃ adassāvī' (one who does not see the Noble Ones), they are called 'Noble Ones' (ariya) because they are far from defilements, because they do not proceed in misfortune (anaya), because they proceed in welfare (aya), and because they are to be resorted to by the world including the devas; these include Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha. Or, in this context, only the Buddhas are called Noble Ones. As it was said: 'Monks, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is called a Noble One' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1098).

In the word 'sappurisā' (true persons), however, Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Tathāgata should be understood as 'true persons'. They are called true persons (sappurisa) because they are excellent men due to their association with supramundane qualities. Or, all of these are referred to by both terms. For Buddhas are both Noble Ones and True Persons; so too are Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddha. As it was said:

'That wise one who is indeed grateful and appreciative,
Who has good friends and is firm in devotion,
Who respectfully performs the duties for one in distress,
Such a one is called a true person' (Jā. 2.17.78).

Here, by the phrase 'kataññū katavedī dhīro', the Paccekabuddha is meant. By the phrase 'kalyāṇamitto daḷhabhatti ca', the disciple of the Buddha is meant. By the phrase 'dukkhitassa sakkacca karoti kiccaṃ', the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) is meant.

Now, one who does not habitually see those Noble Ones, and does not properly practice seeing them, is to be understood as 'one who does not see the Noble Ones' (ariyānaṃ adassāvī). Such a person is of two kinds: one who does not see with the eye and one who does not see with wisdom. Here, the one who does not see with wisdom is intended. Even if one sees the Noble Ones with the physical eye or the divine eye, it is as if they do not see, because those eyes grasp only the appearance and do not have the state of being a Noble One as their object. Dogs, jackals, and so on also see the Noble Ones with their eyes, but they are not 'seers of the Noble Ones'. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not true seeing; only seeing with wisdom is true seeing. Thus it was said: 'Vakkali, what is the use to you of seeing this foul body of mine? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me.' Therefore, even if one sees with the eye, if one does not see with wisdom the characteristics such as impermanence seen by the Noble Ones, if one does not attain the Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones, and if one does not know or see the qualities that make one a Noble One or the state of being a Noble One...
52:
One who does not habitually see the Noble Ones and does not properly practice seeing them is to be understood as 'one who does not see the Noble Ones'. This 'one who does not see the Noble Ones' is of two kinds: one who does not see with the eye and one who does not see with wisdom. Of these two, the one who does not see with wisdom is intended here. Indeed, even if the Noble Ones are seen with the physical eye or the divine eye, they are as if unseen, because those eyes grasp only the appearance and not the state of being a Noble One, which is the domain [of wisdom]. Even dogs, jackals, and so on see the Noble Ones with the eye, but they are not seers of the Noble Ones. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not seeing; only seeing with wisdom is seeing.

As it was said: 'Vakkali, what is the use to you of seeing this foul body? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.87). Therefore, even if seeing with the eye, if one does not see with wisdom the characteristics such as impermanence seen by the Noble Ones, does not attain the Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones, and because of not seeing the qualities that make one a Noble One and the state of being a Noble One, one should be understood as 'one who does not see the Noble Ones'.

'Unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones' (ariyadhammassa akovido) means being unskillful in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so on. In the phrase 'untrained in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones' (ariyadhamme avinīto)—

Discipline (Vinaya) is of two kinds;
Each of these is fivefold.
Due to the absence of that,
This person is called 'untrained'.

Indeed, this discipline is of two kinds: the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandoning (pahāna-vinaya). In these two kinds of discipline, each discipline is divided into five. The discipline of restraint is fivefold: restraint by virtue (sīla-saṃvara), restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), restraint by wisdom (ñāṇa-saṃvara), restraint by patience (khanti-saṃvara), and restraint by energy (vīriya-saṃvara). The discipline of abandoning is also fivefold: abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandoning by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna), and abandoning by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna).

Among those five, 'He is endowed, fully endowed, with this restraint of the Pātimokkha' (Vibh. 511)—this restraint is called restraint by virtue (sīla-saṃvara). 'He guards the eye-faculty, he practices restraint in the eye-faculty' (Dī. Ni. 1.213, Ma. Ni. 1.295, Saṃ. Ni. 4.239, A. Ni. 3.16)—this restraint is called restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara).

'Ajita, whatever streams [of craving etc.] there are in the world, mindfulness is the means to block those streams; I speak of the restraint of those streams, they are shut off by wisdom'—this restraint is called restraint by wisdom (ñāṇa-saṃvara).
53:
This is restraint through wisdom (ñāṇasaṃvara). 'He is one who endures cold and heat'—this is restraint through patience (khantisaṃvara). 'He does not tolerate (endure) an arisen sensual thought'—this is restraint through energy (vīriyasaṃvara). All these restraints are also called 'restraint' (saṃvara) because they restrain bodily misconduct and so forth that should be restrained and disciplined, and they are called 'discipline' (vinaya) because they discipline. Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of restraint is fivefold.

Similarly, in the insight knowledges such as the discernment of mentality and materiality, because they are opposites, there is the abandonment of various harmful states by each insight knowledge, just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp. Specifically: the abandonment of the view of self (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) by the discernment of mentality and materiality (nāmarūpavavatthāna); the abandonment of the view of no-cause and the view of wrong-cause by the comprehension of conditions (paccayapariggaha); the abandonment of doubt by the overcoming of doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa); the abandonment of the grasping of 'I' and 'mine' by the comprehension of groups (kalāpasammasana); the abandonment of the perception of the path in what is not the path by the discernment of path and non-path (maggāmagga-vavatthāna); the abandonment of the view of annihilation by the observation of arising (udayadassana); the abandonment of the view of eternalism by the observation of passing away (vayadassana); the abandonment of the perception of fearlessness in the fearful aggregates by the observation of fear (bhayadassana); the abandonment of the perception of gratification by the observation of danger (ādīnavadassana); the abandonment of the perception of delight by the observation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā); the abandonment of the lack of desire for liberation by the knowledge of the desire for liberation (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa); the abandonment of the lack of equanimity by the knowledge of equanimity (upekkhāñāṇa); the abandonment of being contrary to dependent origination and Nibbāna by the knowledge of conformity (anulomañāṇa); and the abandonment of grasping the signs of formations by the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhūñāṇa). This is called abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna).

The abandonment of the hindrances and other states by means of concentration, categorized as access concentration and absorption concentration, which prevents their occurrence—like removing moss from the surface of the water by striking it with a pot—is called abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna). The abandonment of the group of defilements associated with the origin [of suffering], which is described in such ways as 'for the abandonment of views,' etc., in the mental continuum of one who possesses the respective path because the four noble paths have been developed, such that they never occur again, is called abandonment by eradication (samucchedapahāna). The tranquilization of defilements at the moment of fruition is called abandonment by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhipahāna). Nibbāna, which is the relinquishment of all conditioned things because it is the escape from all conditioned things, is called abandonment by escape (nissaraṇapahāna). All these types of abandonment are called 'abandonment' (pahāna) in the sense of giving up, and 'discipline' (vinaya) in the sense of disciplining. Therefore, they are called 'discipline of abandonment' (pahānavinaya). Alternatively, they are called 'discipline of abandonment' because the respective discipline arises for the person who possesses the respective abandonment. Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of abandonment is also fivefold.
54:
Thus, this discipline, which is twofold in brief and tenfold in detail, does not exist for this uninstructed worldling because his restraint is broken and because the things to be abandoned have not yet been abandoned. Because of this absence, he is called 'untrained' (avinīta). In the same way, this should be understood regarding the phrases: 'one who does not see the virtuous,' 'one who is unskilled in the Dhamma of the virtuous,' and 'one who is untrained in the Dhamma of the virtuous.' This is because all these terms do not differ in meaning.

As it is said: 'Those who are Noble Ones, they are the virtuous. Those who are virtuous, they are the Noble Ones. That which is the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, that is the Dhamma of the virtuous. That which is the Dhamma of the virtuous, that is the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. Those which are the disciplines of the Noble Ones, they are the disciplines of the virtuous. Those which are the disciplines of the virtuous, they are the disciplines of the Noble Ones. Whether called Noble One or virtuous person, Dhamma of the Noble Ones or Dhamma of the virtuous, discipline of the Noble Ones or discipline of the virtuous—all these have the same nature, the same meaning, are equal, have equal parts, and are of that very nature.'

Why did the Elder, after asking 'In how many twenty modes does the adherence to the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi) occur?', point out the worldling by saying 'Here, an uninstructed worldling...' without first answering that question? It should be understood that he first pointed out the worldling in order to clarify the meaning of that view of self through a person-centered teaching (puggalādhiṭṭhāna desanā).

Having thus pointed out the worldling, now wishing to show the summary of adherence, he said: 'He regards form as self,' and so forth. In that context, 'regards form as self' means regarding the aggregate of form and the kasina form as 'self' through the observation of [wrong] view. In the detailed explanation, however, adherence to this aggregate of form is obvious because it is the domain of the five aggregates; therefore, without stating the aggregate of form directly, it should be understood that only the kasina form is referred to generally as 'form.' 'Or self as possessing form' means taking a mental state (arūpa) as 'self' and regarding that self as possessing form. 'Or form as in self' means taking a mental state as 'self' and regarding form as being in that self. 'Or self as in form' means taking a mental state as 'self' and regarding that self as being in form.

Among those four, by the statement 'regards form as self,' only pure form is spoken of as 'self.' In the three modes—'self as possessing form,' 'form in self,' and 'self in form'—and in the four places 'regards feeling as self,' 'perception,' 'formations,' and 'consciousness as self,' in these seven places, mental states (arūpa) are spoken of as 'self.' In this manner, for the remaining four aggregates, three modes each, such as 'self as possessing feeling,' 'feeling in self,' 'self in feeling'...
55:
By way of the three modes, the self is spoken of in twelve instances as a mixture of form and the formless. These twenty views also obstruct the Path, but they do not obstruct heaven; they are to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry.

Now, wishing to point out that fact, the teacher said "Kathaṃ rūpaṃ" and so forth. In that Pali, 'earth kasina' refers to the earth kasina itself, known as the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) produced depending on the earth mandala, by way of pervading the whole. "Ahaṃ" (I) refers to taking hold of oneself. "Attaṃ" (self) is indeed oneself. "Adwayaṃ" (non-dual) means only one. "Telappadīpassa" means of an oil lamp. "Jhāyato" means burning or flaming. The phrase "the flame is such, the color is such" and so forth is said because color cannot exist apart from the flame. Combining both the view and the object, it means the self-view (attānudiṭṭhi) which has form as its basis.

Water kasina and so forth are just kasina signs produced depending on water and so on. Although the limited-space kasina (paricchinnākāsa-kasiṇa) is an object of fine-material jhana, it should be understood that it is not taken here because, if called 'space kasina', it would be confused with the space of the removal of the kasina (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa), which is the object of immaterial jhana. Since this is the section on form, the consciousness kasina (viññāṇa-kasiṇa) should not be taken at all. "In this Dispensation, some person regards feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as self" is said by way of taking the four immaterial aggregates together without distinguishing them. Because that person is unable to distinguish mind and mental factors separately, he takes them all together as "self". In the phrase "possesses form by means of this form", both the physical body and the kasina form can be obtained. "Chāyāsampanno" refers to a tree endowed with shade, having dense foliage. In the word "tamenaṃ", the particle "ena" is merely a suffix, or it means "tam etaṃ". "Chāyāvā" means a tree with a manifest shade. Even if one does not take "form is self", it is called a view based on form because the view arises without letting go of form.

"Regard form in self" means because the physical body and kasina form depend on the mind, one regards that form in that self, which is the collection of immaterial aggregates. "This scent" refers to the scent that is smelled. "In this flower" is said because the scent exists depending on the flower.

"Regard self in form" means wherever form goes, the mind also goes. Therefore, taking the mind that depends on form, one regards that self, which is the collection of immaterial aggregates, in that form. Because form is gross, the example of a casket, which is a gross container, is given.
56:
In this Dispensation, some person, although not taking each feeling individually with a view in such passages as "feeling born of eye-contact", by taking "feeling" as a single group, all feelings—pleasant, painful, and neutral—are included; thus, it should be understood that they are taken individually and presented accordingly. Indeed, that person, because feeling is manifest by way of experiencing, takes feeling itself as "self". "Regard perception, formations, consciousness, and form as self" means regarding the immaterial states such as perception together with form as "self". Indeed, a worldling is like a madman; however things appear in the mind, so he takes them.

In such passages as "perception born of eye-contact", one takes perception as "self" because perception is manifest by way of recognizing. The rest should be understood in the same manner as said for feeling.

In such passages as "volition born of eye-contact", among the states included in the aggregate of formations, volition alone is mentioned because it is primary and manifest. By mentioning volition, the other mental factors are also mentioned. That person takes volition as "self" because it is manifest by way of being a mental factor. The rest is in the same manner as already said.

In such passages as "eye-consciousness", one takes the mind as "self" because the mind is manifest by way of cognizing. Here too, the rest is in the same manner as already said.

## The explanation of the description of self-view is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Description of Wrong View

Wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) has the same meaning as already stated below. This, however, is another method: "Natthi dinnaṃ" (There is no gift) means the denial of the fruit of giving because of having the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). In the phrase "Natthi yiṭṭhaṃ", "yiṭṭha" refers to a small sacrifice. "Huta" refers to a great sacrifice. He denies the fruit of both. "There is no fruit or result of good and bad actions" means that since the fruit of giving has been denied, he denies the fruit of meritorious actions such as virtue and the fruit of evil actions such as killing. "There is no this world" means there is no world resulting from actions done in a previous life. "There is no other world" means there is no other world that will result from actions done in this life. "There is no mother, there is no father" means denying the fruit of actions done towards those mothers and fathers. "There are no spontaneously reborn beings" means denying rebirth caused by kamma. "There are no ascetics and brahmins in the world... who make it known" means denying the path of practice for attaining direct knowledge to see this world and the next. In this description Pali, however, "Natthi dinnaṃ" is the object. It means that the gift, which is spoken of as having no fruit as "natthi dinnaṃ", is the object and basis of that wrong view.
57:
The meaning is that saying 'there is no gift' is a wrong and perverted view.

## End of the Explanation of the Description of Wrong View.

## 4. Explanation of the Description of the View of Self-Identity
It should be understood that the view of self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is indeed the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi), and it is taught as 'sakkāyadiṭṭhi' to show the synonymous terms found in other teachings.

## End of the Explanation of the Description of the View of Self-Identity.

## 5. Explanation of the Description of the View of Eternalism
The term 'sakkāyavatthukāya sassatadiṭṭhiyā' is a kammadhāraya compound. At the end of the fifteen statements beginning with 'or the self possessing form' (rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ), the word 'samanupassati' (regards) should be connected, or that is the reading. This is because the meaning cannot be connected in any other way. Thus, only one description, 'regards the self as possessing form', is shown, and the remaining fourteen descriptions are abbreviated.

## End of the Explanation of the Description of the View of Eternalism.

## 6. Explanation of the Description of the View of Annihilationism
In the view of annihilationism based on the self-identity basis, only one description, 'regards form as self' (rūpaṃ attato samanupassati), is shown, and the remaining four descriptions are abbreviated.

## End of the Explanation of the Description of the View of Annihilationism.

## 7. Explanation of the Description of the View of Finitude
In the view of finitude (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi), the first turn is the questioning of the mode. The second turn is the grasping of the mode. The third turn is the answering of the mode.

In that context, 'world' (loka) means the self. Regarding the 'end' (anta), among the mutually opposing eternalist and annihilationist ends, the eternalist end is grasped in the eternalist view, and the annihilationist end is grasped in the annihilationist view. 'A small space' (parittaṃ okāsaṃ) refers to a small place the size of a tray or a bowl. 'Pervades by making it blue' (nīlakato pharati) means taking the color blue as the object. 'This world' (ayaṃ loko) is said in reference to the self. 'Bounded' (parivaṭumo) means having a boundary all around. 'Perceiving the end' (antasaññī) means having the perception of being finite. Since that world, which is the self, has an end, it should be taken as 'end' (anto). 'That which it pervades' (yaṃ pharati) refers to the kasina-form that is pervaded. That kasina-form is both the object and the 'world' (loka) in the sense of being looked upon. 'That by which it pervades' (yena pharati) refers to the mind by which it pervades. In the phrase 'that is both the self and the world' (so attā ceva loko ca), the masculine gender is used in consideration of the self (attā); it means that mind is both the self and the world in the sense of looking. 'Finite' (antavā) means having an end. 'Pervades by means of space' (okāsakato pharati) means by means of the light kasina...
58:
By means of the light kasina, the fire kasina, or the white kasina, it pervades as light. Since only the five colored kasinas starting with blue are taken, it should be understood that there is no adherence to the self by means of the earth, water, or air kasinas.

'A vast space' (vipulaṃ okāsaṃ) refers to a large place by means of a kasina circle the size of a threshing floor, etc. 'Infinite' (anantavā) means infinite by way of development. 'Boundless' (apariyanto) means boundless by way of development. 'Perceiving the infinite' (anantasaññī) means having the perception of being infinite. 'That soul' (taṃ jīvaṃ) means that is the soul. Here, the gender is changed to masculine. 'Soul' (jīva) is also the self (attā). The five aggregates starting with form are called 'body' (sarīra) because they are rounded all around. 'The soul is not the body' (jīvaṃ na sarīraṃ) means the soul, called the self, is not the body, called the aggregate of form. The same applies to the aggregates of feeling, etc. 'Tathāgata' means a being (satta). Some teachers say it means an Arahant. 'After death' (paraṃ maraṇā) means the time after dying, in the next world. 'Form has the nature of death in this very place' (rūpaṃ idheva maraṇadhammaṃ) means taking the five aggregates by making the prominent aggregate the head for one who grasps 'self', and it means that the aggregate of form has the nature of perishing in this very world. The same applies to the remaining aggregates.

It means after the breaking up of the body, called the group of five aggregates. This statement explains the meaning of the term 'after death' (paraṃ maraṇā). In the words beginning with 'hotipi', 'hoti' is the root word. In all four words, the word 'api' has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya). 'Stands' (tiṭṭhati) means it stands because of being eternal, meaning it does not pass away. Or, it should be understood that the word 'tiṭṭhati' is said to show a specific meaning of the word 'hoti'. 'Arises' (uppajjati) means arising by way of entering the womb in egg-born and womb-born births, and 'is produced' (nibbattati) means arising by way of moisture-born and spontaneous births; thus the connection of meaning should be understood. 'Is cut off' (ucchijjati) means being cut off by way of the absence of continuity. 'Perishes' (vinassati) means perishing by way of dissolution. 'Does not exist after death' (na hoti paraṃ maraṇā) is an explanation of the meaning of the preceding words, meaning it does not exist after passing away.

'Exists and does not exist' (hoti ca na ca hoti) is the view of some partial-eternalists (ekaccasassatavādī), meaning it exists in one way and does not exist in another way. It means it exists as a soul, but does not exist because of the absence of the previous soul. 'Neither exists nor does not exist' (neva hoti na na hoti) is the view of the eel-wrigglers (amarāvikkhepika), meaning it is neither 'it exists' nor 'it does not exist'. Out of fear of being blamed, fear of lying, or due to dullness and confusion, they merely reject the previously mentioned ways. 'By these fifty modes' means by means of the fifty modes according to the ten groups of five mentioned.

## End of the Explanation of the Description of the View of Finitude.
59:
## 8. Commentary on the Description of Views Related to the Past

Among the views based on the past and the future, they are called Eternalists (Sassatavāda) because they say 'it is eternal.' Alternatively, it is called a 'doctrine' (vāda) because one speaks by means of that view; this is a synonym for wrong view. The doctrine 'it is eternal' is also called eternal (sassata) because it is associated with the eternalist view; those who hold this eternalist doctrine are called Eternalists.

Similarly, the doctrine that 'some things are eternal' is called Partial-eternalism (Ekaccasassatavāda); those who hold that view are called Partial-eternalists (Ekaccasassatikas).

Likewise, the doctrine that occurs as 'it is finite, it is infinite, it is both finite and infinite, it is neither finite nor infinite' is called Finitism and Infinitism (Antānantavāda); those who hold that view are called Finitists and Infinitists (Antānantikas).

It is called 'Amarā' because it does not die. What is this 'Amarā'? It is the view and the speech of a person with wrong view that is without limit, in the manner of 'it is not thus for me,' and so on. Various tossings are called 'vikkhepa' (vacillation); vacillation by means of the view or speech called 'Amarā' is 'Amarāvikkhepa' (Eel-wriggling); those who hold that view are called Eel-wrigglers (Amarāvikkhepikas). Alternatively—'Amarā' is a type of fish; just as that fish, running through the water by way of surfacing and diving, etc., cannot be caught, so too this doctrine runs here and there and does not reach a firm grasp; thus it is called 'Amarāvikkhepa'; those who hold that view are called Eel-wrigglers.

The vision that 'the self and the world arise without a cause' is called Fortuitous Origination (Adhiccasamuppanna); those who hold that view are called Fortuitous Originists (Adhiccasamuppannikas).

## The Commentary on the Description of Views Related to the Past is Finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Description of Views Related to the Future

They are called Proponents of Percipiency (Saññīvāda) because they say 'there is perception.' They are called Proponents of Non-percipiency (Asaññīvāda) because they say 'there is no perception.' They are called Proponents of Neither-percipiency-nor-non-percipiency (Nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda) because they say 'it is neither percipient nor non-percipient.' Alternatively, the doctrine that occurs as 'there is perception' is called Saññīvāda; those who have that doctrine are Saññīvāda; likewise for Asaññīvāda and Nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda.

They are called Annihilationists (Ucchedavāda) because they say 'it is cut off.'

'Present life' (diṭṭhadhamma) refers to the immediate individual existence (attabhāva); it is a synonym for the individual existence obtained in various births. Nibbāna in the present life is 'Diṭṭhadhammanibbāna,' meaning the subsiding of suffering in this very individual existence; they are called Proponents of Nibbāna in the Present Life (Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda) because they say so. If this meaning were to be expanded, the entire Brahmajāla Sutta along with its commentary would have to be told. Since doing so would be too extensive, it is not expanded. Those who desire that meaning should take it by looking at the Brahmajāla Sutta.

## The Commentary on the Description of Views Related to the Future is Finished.
60:
## 10-12. Saññojanikādiditthiniddesavaṇṇanā
Since views connected with fetters (saññojanikā diṭṭhi) are common to all views, the meaning common to all views is explained by their nature as fetters for all views. These are the same as the obsessions of views (diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhāna) mentioned below.

Among views bound by conceit (mānavinibandha), the misinterpretation and obsession (abhinivesaparāmāsa) such as "The eye is I" is an obsession preceded by conceit. In truth, view (diṭṭhi) is not associated with conceit (māna). For that reason, it is called "bound by conceit" (mānavinibandha), meaning a view connected with or rooted in conceit.

In the phrase "The eye is mine," the same method applies. Here, it should be understood that in the place where "mamā" should be said, "mamaṃ" occurs as a nasal augment (anunāsikāgama). In the view connected with the conceit of "I," forms (rūpa) and so on are only internal (ajjhattika). Excluding the kasina-form, one does not grasp external bases as "I." However, in the view connected with the conceit of "mine," one can grasp external bases as "mine." Because painful feeling (dukkha vedanā) is undesirable, it does not become a basis for conceit (mānavatthu); therefore, the six feelings and the six contacts (phassa) which are their root causes are not included. It should be understood that perception (saññā) and so on are not included here because the text is interrupted.

## End of Saññojanikādiditthiniddesavaṇṇanā.

## 13. Attavādapaṭisaṃyuttadiṭṭhiniddesavaṇṇanā
Views connected with the doctrine of self are just the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi). Because they are connected with the doctrine of self, they are again called "connected with the doctrine of self" (attavādapaṭisaṃyutta).

## End of Attavādapaṭisaṃyuttadiṭṭhiniddesavaṇṇanā.

## 14. Lokavādapaṭisaṃyuttadiṭṭhiniddesavaṇṇanā
"Self and the world" means that the self is the same as the world in the sense of being perceived (ālokanaṭṭhena). "Eternal" (sassata) is the view of eternalists. "Non-eternal" (asassata) is the view of annihilationists. "Both eternal and non-eternal" is the view of partial-eternalists (ekaccasassatika). "Neither eternal nor non-eternal" is the view of eel-wrigglers (amarāvikkhepika). "Finite" (antavā) is the view of those who attain limited kasinas, logicians (takkika), Nigaṇṭhas, and Ājīvakas. Alternatively, annihilationists say, "A being has a beginning through birth and an end through death." Fortuitous-originationists (adhiccasamuppannika) say, "A being has a beginning through birth." "Infinite" (anantavā) is the view of those who attain immeasurable kasinas. Eternalists say, "There is no beginning or end, therefore it is infinite." Fortuitous-originationists say, "It is infinite in terms of the end."
61:
"The world is finite and infinite" is the view of those who have a kasiṇa object that is expanded horizontally but not vertically (upwards and downwards). "The world is neither finite nor infinite" is the view of those who hold the Amarāvikkhepa (eel-wriggling) view.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Views Connected to Doctrines of the World is Finished.

## 15-16. Explanation of the Exposition of the View of Existence and the View of Non-existence

Since the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi) and the view of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi) do not exist as distinct obsessions from the views mentioned above, they are not presented as separate expositions. Instead, they are described through the modes of "receding (oḷīyana)" and "overrunning (atidhāvana)" based on those aforementioned views, without posing a question. It was said: "The obsession with receding is the view of existence; the obsession with overrunning is the view of non-existence." In this context, the obsession with receding, as taught in the words "when the Dhamma is being taught for the cessation of existence, the mind does not leap forward," refers to the obsession of shrinking back from Nibbāna due to the perception of permanence (sassata-saññā). The obsession with overrunning, as taught in the words "some, being troubled, ashamed, and disgusted by existence, delight in non-existence (vibhava)," refers to the obsession of overstepping the path leading to cessation (nirodhagāminī paṭipadā) due to the perception of annihilation (uccheda-saññā).

Now, to show the connection of these views of existence and non-existence with all other views, the phrase beginning with "Assādadiṭṭhiyā" was stated. In that context, because those with the view of gratification (assāda-diṭṭhi) hold that "there is no fault in sensual pleasures" by relying on either eternalism or annihilationism, it is said that the thirty-five modes of the view of gratification can be either views of existence or views of non-existence. This means that each individual view can become a view of existence through the grasp of eternalism, or a view of non-existence through the grasp of annihilationism. In the view of self (attānudiṭṭhi), regarding the five points—seeing form as self, feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness as self—because the self is taken as not different from (identical to) form etc., it is held that when those aggregates are annihilated, the self is also annihilated; thus, they are called the five views of non-existence. In the remaining fifteen points, because the self is taken as different from form etc., it is held that even when those aggregates are annihilated, "the self is eternal"; thus, they are called the fifteen views of existence.

In wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), because it proceeds by way of annihilation, all of them are only views of non-existence. Regarding the views of the finite and infinite (antavānantavā-diṭṭhi), those who have attained jhāna with a limited or immeasurable object, when they see beings passing away from the fine-material realm (rūpa-dhātu) and being reborn elsewhere with the divine eye, they do not see the view of existence but grasp the view of non-existence. Therefore, in those views, there can be the view of existence, ... can be ...
62:
...are called views of non-existence. In the phrase "it both is and is not," "it is" is the view of existence, and "it is not" is the view of non-existence. In the phrase "it neither is nor is not," "it neither is" is the view of non-existence, and "it is not not" is the view of existence. Therefore, regarding that extremist view (antaggāhika-diṭṭhi), it was said "it can be."

In the views about the past (pubbantānudiṭṭhi), those who hold partial eternalism describe both what is eternal and what is not eternal. Therefore, that partial eternalism (ekaccasassata-diṭṭhi) is both a view of existence and a view of non-existence. The four types of people who hold views of the finite and infinite describe the self as finite or infinite. Therefore, that view of the finite and infinite (anantita-diṭṭhi) is similar to the view of self and is both a view of existence and a view of non-existence. The four types of eel-wrigglers (amarāvikkhepika) resort to verbal shuffling based on either the view of existence or the view of non-existence. The remaining views (the 4 eternalist views and 2 fortuitous origin views) are only views of existence. Therefore, referring to those various views, it was said "it can be." In the views about the future (aparantānudiṭṭhi), the seven doctrines of annihilation are views of non-existence; the remaining thirty-two views about the future are views of existence. Therefore, referring to those various views, it was said "it can be." In the fetter-forming view (saññojanika-diṭṭhi), it was said "it can be" by way of all views. In the view connected with the conceit "I am," because the eye etc. are grasped as "I," it is held that when the eye etc. perish, the self perishes; thus, all those are called views of non-existence. Just as in the view of self, in the view connected with the conceit "mine," because the self is different from the sense bases (āyatana) like the eye etc., it is held that even when those sense bases perish, the self does not perish; thus, all those are called views of existence. In the view connected with doctrines of the world, because it is stated in the manner "the self and the world are eternal" etc., the views of existence and non-existence are quite clear. By this much of the discourse, the sixteen views beginning with the view of gratification and ending with the view of non-existence, and the three hundred points of adherence to views (diṭṭhābhinivesa), have been explained. The view of self (attānudiṭṭhi), the identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), and the view connected with the doctrine of self (attavāda-paṭisamyutta-diṭṭhi) are identical in meaning but are stated in three ways according to the method of exposition. The fetter-forming view (saññojanika-diṭṭhi), however, encompasses all views according to the difference in circumstances.

Now, all those views will be compared with one another in another way, such as the view of gratification, as appropriate. In that passage "all those views," it refers to all the aforementioned views without exception. They are called views of gratification (assāda-diṭṭhi) because they are enamored with the lust for views and because they rely on the gratification of craving. They are called views of self (attānudiṭṭhi) because they follow the craving that is affectionate toward the self. They are called wrong views (micchā-diṭṭhi) because they have a perverted vision. They are called identity views (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) because they have the five aggregates as their basis. They are called extremist views (antaggāhika-diṭṭhi) because they grasp one of the extremes. They are called fetter-forming views (saññojanika-diṭṭhi) because they bind one to what is harmful. Because they are connected with the doctrine of self...
63:
These seven views associated with the theory of self (attavāda) encompass all views; however, the remaining nine views do not encompass all views.

Now, in order to show that all those views previously mentioned in detail are summarized into only two views and that beings rely on these two views, he spoke the verse beginning with "Bhavañca diṭṭhiṃ". Indeed, all those views are either the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi) or the view of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi). In this context, "Bhavañca diṭṭhiṃ vibhavañca diṭṭhiṃ", the word "ca" (and) serves to collect the views themselves, not the reliance (nissaya). This is because a single individual cannot simultaneously rely on both the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Therefore, it was stated (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga): "Thus, beings are either those who rely on the view of existence or those who rely on the view of non-existence."

"Takkikā" refers to those who speak by way of reasoning (takka), hence they are called reasoners. Because those of wrong views lack the wisdom of penetrating the nature of reality, they proceed solely by reasoning. Even those who have attained jhāna or higher powers (abhiññā) are still considered "takkikā" if they grasp a view through reasoning. "Nissitāse" means "nissitā" (relying on/clinging to). It is either a single word, or the "se" is merely a particle (nipāta).

The phrase "They have no knowledge of cessation" is a statement of the reason for relying on views. Since they lack the knowledge that realizes Nibbāna—the cessation of the personality view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi)—it means they rely on these two views. In the phrase "Na hi atthi ñāṇaṃ", the word "hi" is a particle indicating the cause. "Where this world has a distorted perception" means that in Nibbāna, which is the bliss of cessation, this world together with its devas has the distorted perception of "suffering"; the connection is that they have no knowledge of that cessation. Regarding the state of having the distorted perception of "suffering", this discourse (verse) is spoken:

"Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, touches, and all mental objects,
Which are desirable, lovely, and pleasing, as far as they are said to exist.
To the world including the devas, these are considered happiness,
But where these cease, that is considered suffering by them.

The Noble Ones see the cessation of the person-pack (sakkāya) as happiness;
This view is contrary to that of the whole world who see it (as suffering).
What others call happiness, the Noble Ones call suffering;
What others call suffering, the Noble Ones know as happiness.

See the Dhamma (Nibbāna) which is difficult to understand; the ignorant are greatly confused herein.
For those who are veiled (by ignorance), it is darkness; for those who do not see, it is blind gloom."
64:
"But for the virtuous who see, it is revealed like light.
Though it is near, they do not understand it—the fools unskilled in the Dhamma.
By those overcome by lust for existence (bhava-rāga), following the stream of existence,
And fallen into the realm of Māra, this Dhamma is not easily understood.

Who else but the Noble Ones are worthy to understand the state,
By fully knowing which state, the taintless ones attain Parinibbāna?"

Now, wishing to show through a Sutta how all views are contained within the two types—the view of existence and the view of non-existence—and to show Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) which completely uproots views, he cited the Sutta beginning with "Dvīhi bhikkhave". In that Sutta, the word "devā" also refers to Brahmas. "Olīyanti" means they shrink back. "Atidhāvanti" means they overshoot and go beyond. "Cakkhumanto" refers to those with wisdom. The word "ca" is used in the sense of an extra particle. They are called "bhava-rāmā" because existence (bhava) is their place of delight and enjoyment. "Bhava-ratā" means they greatly delight in existence. "Bhava-samuditā" means they are satisfied with existence. "Desiyamāne" refers to when the Dhamma is being taught by either the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. "Na pakkhandati" means they do not enter into the teaching or the cessation of existence. "Na pasīdati" means they do not attain clarity or confidence in it. "Na santiṭṭhati" means they do not settle or stand firm in it. "Nādhimuccati" means they do not become resolved or firmly convinced of it. By this much, the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) is stated.

"Aṭṭīyamānā" means reaching the state of being troubled by suffering. "Harāyamānā" means reaching the state of being ashamed. "Jigucchamānā" means reaching the state of loathing. "Vibhavaṃ abhinandanti" means they rejoice by relying on the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi), or it means they long for annihilation. "Kira" is a particle used in the sense of hearsay. "Bho" is a form of address (ālapana). "Santāṃ" means peaceful (extinguished). "Paṇītaṃ" means sublime because of the absence of suffering, or it means sublime because it has reached the foremost state. "Yāthāvaṃ" means according to its true nature. By this much, the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) is stated.

"Idha" means in this Dispensation (sāsana). "Bhūtaṃ" refers to the suffering comprised of the five aggregates that have arisen from causes. "Bhūtato passati" means seeing that "this 'become' is suffering". "Nibbidāya" means for the sake of disenchantment (for the purpose of vipassanā). "Virāgāya" means for the sake of dispassion (for the purpose of the Noble Path). "Nirodhāya" means for the sake of cessation (for the purpose of Nibbāna). "Paṭipanno hoti" means he is practicing the practice appropriate for that Nibbāna. "Evaṃ passanti" means they see in this manner with mundane knowledge in the preliminary stage, and with supramundane knowledge at the time of penetration. By this much, Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) is stated.
65:
Now, with two verses, he shows the benefits of that right view (sammādiṭṭhi). In those verses, 'yo bhūtaṃ bhūtato disvā' (who, having seen the truth as truth) means having understood the Truth of Suffering, which is the five aggregates, through the penetration of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya). 'Bhūtassa ca atikkamaṃ' (and the transcendence of the truth) means having realized the Truth of Cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyābhisamaya). 'Yathābhūte adhimuccati' (is resolved on reality) means that by the power of the penetration of path-development (maggabhāvanābhisamaya), one is resolved on Cessation, which is Nibbāna, as it truly is, thinking: 'This Nibbāna is peaceful, this Nibbāna is sublime.' 'Bhavataṇhā parikkhayā' (through the destruction of craving for existence) means by way of abandoning the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca).

In this context, although there is no sequential realization of the four truths at different times (as they are not realized separately but simultaneously), it should be understood that the preceding verbal form 'disvā' (having seen) is spoken by way of conventional usage (vohāra) together with the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) that occurs before the Path. Indeed, one does not first see and then later become resolved. The penetration of the four truths occurs only simultaneously. Alternatively, even in a simultaneous moment, there is no fault because there can be preceding terms.

'Sa ve' means that Arahant indeed. 'Bhūtapariññāto' means one who has fully understood suffering. 'Vītatāṇho' means one who is free from craving. 'Bhavābhave' means in small and large existences. Indeed, since the letter 'a' can also occur in the sense of increase (vuddhi), 'abhava' means a great existence. However, that state of being small or large should be understood by way of comparison. Alternatively, 'bhava' refers to the view of eternalism (sassata), and 'abhava' refers to the view of annihilationism (uccheda). In both these views, one is free from craving because of the absence of lust associated with views. 'Bhūtassa vibhavā' means due to the cutting off of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). 'Nāgacchati punabbhavaṃ' (does not come to renewed existence) refers to the Parinibbāna of the Arahant.

The words beginning with 'tayo puggalā' (three persons) are spoken for the purpose of censuring those with wrong view and praising those with right view. In that passage, those whose view has reached a corrupted state are called 'vipannadiṭṭhi' (one failed in view). Those whose view has reached an excellent state are called 'sampannadiṭṭhi' (one accomplished in view). A view is called 'tittha' (a ford/sect); one is called a 'titthiya' (sectarian) because of practicing that view or because that view belongs to them. This refers to one who has gone forth outside this Dispensation. 'Titthiyasāvaka' (a disciple of sectarians) refers to a layperson who follows the views of those sectarians. 'Yo ca micchādiṭṭhiko' (and who is a person of wrong view) refers to a person who, without falling into those two categories, holds a wrong view by way of any particular view.

'Tathāgata' refers to the Fully Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha). The Paccekabuddha is also included in this term 'Tathāgata'. 'Tathāgatasāvaka' (a disciple of the Tathāgata) refers to those who have reached the Paths and the Fruits. 'Yo ca sammādiṭṭhiko' (and who is a person of right view) refers to a person who, being distinct from both the Tathāgata and the Tathāgata's disciple, possesses right view by way of mundane right view (lokiya-sammādiṭṭhi).

In the verses, 'kodhana' (angry) refers to one who is frequently angry. 'Upanāhī' (resentful) refers to one who has the nature of nourishing that very anger and binding it as a grudge. 'Pāpamakkhī' (evil disparager) refers to one who has the base quality of disparaging others' virtues. 'Māyāvī' (deceitful) refers to one who conceals the evil they have committed. 'Vasala' (outcaste) refers to one of low birth. 'Visuddho' (pure) refers to one who is especially pure through the purity of knowledge and vision.
66:
One is especially purified by the purification of knowledge and vision. "One who has reached purity" (suddhatāṃ gato) means one who has reached the state of purity known as Path and Fruition (magga-phala). "The wise" (medhāvī) means one who possesses wisdom. By this verse, only the one endowed with supramundane right view (lokuttara-sammādiṭṭhi) is praised.

By using the terms "those with wrong views" and "those with right views" (vipannadiṭṭhiyo, sampannadiṭṭhiyo), the Buddha spoke by setting aside the designation of "person" (puggala) and wishing to blame or praise only the Dhamma itself, unmixed with the person. "This is mine" (etaṃ mama) is a view occurring by the power of craving-obsession (taṇhā-maññana). "This I am" (esohamasmi) is a view rooted in conceit-obsession (māna-maññana). "This is my self" (eso me attā) is simply view-obsession (diṭṭhi-maññana).

Through the passages beginning with "etaṃ mama," the classification, enumeration, and temporal inclusion of the three types of wrong views are asked and answered. In that context, "What view?" (kā diṭṭhi) means which specific view among the many views. "Followed by which end?" (katamantānuggahitā) means which of the two periods called the former end and the latter end is it followed by or bound to? Because a person who wrongly misapprehends "This is mine" does so by referring to a past object, thinking, "This was mine, it was mine in this way, it was mine for this long," it is therefore a view following the former end (pubbantānudiṭṭhi). Those views are also followed by the former end. Because a person who misapprehends "This I am" does so by grasping for a future result, thinking, "By this virtue, or practice, or austerity, or holy life, I will be such a person and will be purified," it is therefore a view following the latter end (aparantānudiṭṭhi). Those views are also followed by the latter end. Because a person who misapprehends "This is my self" does so by grasping the continuity of the aggregates in the past and future, thinking, "This is my self," and misapprehends by the power of identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), it is therefore identity view. Those views are followed by both the former end and the latter end.

Since the sixty-two views are headed by identity view, and the sixty-two views are eradicated only by the eradication of identity view, they are called "the sixty-two views headed by identity view." It means that the sixty-two views occur with identity view as the root or through the door of identity view. The reading "sakkāyadiṭṭhippamukhāni" is better. It means those for which identity view is the head or beginning. What are they? They are the sixty-two views.

In the question "What view?", the answer is the twenty-fold view of self (attānudiṭṭhi) and the twenty-fold identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). In the question "How many views are there?", the answer is the sixty-two views headed by identity view. That same identity view is called "This is my self"...
67:
By the common meaning of the word "self" (attā), it is called "view of self" (attānudiṭṭhi). When that view of self is mentioned, the view associated with the doctrine of self (attavāda) is also mentioned.

The citation of the Sutta beginning with "Whosoever, monks..." is made for the purpose of classifying and showing the person of right view (sampannadiṭṭhi-puggala) in connection with the Sotāpanna. In that Sutta, "reached the conclusion" (niṭṭhaṃ gatā) means those who have reached the decision through the power of Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) that "The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One," meaning they are free from doubt (nibbe-matika). Although the reading "niṭṭhāgatā" is a compound word, the meaning is the same. "Endowed with view" (diṭṭhisampannā) means those who have reached the excellence of view. "Finality here" (idha niṭṭhā) means attaining Parinibbāna in this sense-sphere (kāmadhātu). "Finality after leaving here" (idha vihāya niṭṭhā) means attaining Parinibbāna in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) of the Brahma world after leaving this sense-sphere existence.

"Seven-times-at-most" (sattakkhattuparama) refers to one whose rebirth and acquisition of existence is limited to seven times at most; one who does not take an eighth existence beyond those seven. This refers to the sattakkhattuparama Sotāpanna. "From family to family" (kolaṃkola) means one who goes from family to family. It means that from the time of realizing the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), there is no rebirth in low families, but one is reborn only in families of great wealth. This refers to the kolaṃkola Sotāpanna.

In the term "one-seeded" (ekabījī), the seed of the aggregates (khandha-bīja) is spoken of. A Sotāpanna who has only one seed of aggregates, meaning one more acquisition of existence, is called "one-seeded." This refers to the ekabījī Sotāpanna.

These names are only the names given to them by the Blessed One. The Blessed One designated their names, saying, "One who has reached this much is called a sattakkhattuparama, this much a kolaṃkola, and this much an ekabījī." The Blessed One, knowing that "this person will go this far, and that person will go that far," gave them those respective names.

A Sotāpanna with dull wisdom (mudupañña) who takes seven more existences is called a sattakkhattuparama; one with medium wisdom (majjhimapañña) who takes up to six more existences is called a kolaṃkola; and one with sharp wisdom (tikkhapañña) who takes only one more existence is called an ekabījī. Their levels of wisdom—dull, medium, or sharp—are determined by prior causes. All three types of Sotāpannas are spoken of in terms of the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava); however, in the fine-material and immaterial existences (rūpa-arūpa bhava), they may take many more rebirths.

"Once-returner" (sakadāgāmī) means one who returns to the sense-sphere existence only once by the power of rebirth. This refers to the sakadāgāmī person. "An Arahant in this very life" (diṭṭheva dhamme arahā) means one who becomes an Arahant in this present existence. There is also a reading "arahant." "Finality here" (idha niṭṭhā) is spoken of only with reference to the five types of persons who wander in the sense-sphere existence.
68:
It is spoken with reference only to those wandering in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava). Noble ones (ariyas) who are born in the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) and immaterial existence (arūpabhava), however, are not born again in the sense-sphere existence, but attain Parinibbāna right there.

'Antarāparinibbāyissa' means one who attains Parinibbāna through the extinguishing of defilements within the middle of the lifespan; thus, they are called an 'Antarāparinibbāyī' (one who attains Nibbāna in the interval). That Antarāparinibbāyī Anāgāmī is of three types: one who attains Parinibbāna immediately after rebirth, one who attains Parinibbāna before reaching the middle of the lifespan, and one who attains Parinibbāna after reaching the middle of the lifespan. (The text) is spoken with reference to that Antarāparinibbāyī Anāgāmī. 'Upahaccaparinibbāyissa' refers to an Anāgāmī who attains Parinibbāna through the extinguishing of defilements after passing the middle of the lifespan or when nearing death. 'Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyissa' refers to an Anāgāmī whose nature is to attain Parinibbāna through the extinguishing of defilements with slight effort (without making excessive effort). 'Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyissa' refers to an Anāgāmī whose nature is to attain Parinibbāna through the extinguishing of defilements only after making excessive effort with difficulty and toil.

'Uddhaṃsotassa akaniṭṭhagāmino' means one is called 'Uddhaṃsota' (one who flows upwards) because of having a nature that leads upwards, or because the stream of craving or the stream of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) is directed upwards. Alternatively, one is called 'Uddhaṃsota' because the stream of the Path (magga) is directed upwards, as it is to be attained by going to higher realms. One is called 'Akaniṭṭhagāmī' because of going to the Akaniṭṭha realm. (The text) is spoken with reference to that Uddhaṃsota Akaniṭṭhagāmī Anāgāmī.

This Anāgāmī is of four types: the person who, starting from the Aviha realm, purifies the four Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) and then goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm to attain Parinibbāna; this person is called an 'Uddhaṃsota Akaniṭṭhagāmī'. The person who purifies the lower three Pure Abodes and attains Parinibbāna while staying in the Sudassī realm; this person is called an 'Uddhaṃsota' but not an 'Akaniṭṭhagāmī'. The person who goes directly from this sense-sphere to the Akaniṭṭha realm and attains Parinibbāna; this person is called an 'Akaniṭṭhagāmī' but not an 'Uddhaṃsota'. The person who attains Parinibbāna in whichever of the four lower Brahma realms they are born; this person is called 'neither an Uddhaṃsota nor an Akaniṭṭhagāmī'.

These five types of Anāgāmīs are spoken of based on the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). However, because Anāgāmīs have not yet abandoned attachment to fine-material existence (rūparāga) and attachment to immaterial existence (arūparāga), they may also be born in the remaining fine-material and immaterial realms if they so desire. But those born in the Pure Abodes are never born in other realms again. 'Aveccappasannā' refers to those who, having known and understood by the power of the Noble Path, are confident with unshakeable devotion. 'Sotāpannā' refers to those who have entered the stream, which is the Noble Path. By this word 'Sotāpanna', all persons established in the Noble Fruits (phalattha) are included.

## The Explanation of the Description of Views on Existence and Non-existence is finished.
## In the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga named Saddhammappakāsinī,
## The Explanation of the Discourse on Views is finished.
69:
## 3. Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing
## 1. Explanation of the Section on Counting
Now, the explanation of the new meaning of the Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing (Ānāpānassatikathā), spoken immediately after the Discourse on Views (Diṭṭhikathā), has arrived. This Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing is spoken after the Discourse on Views because, for one whose mind is well-purified by cleansing the stain of wrong view after clearly seeing the danger of views in the Discourse on Views, the development of concentration (samādhibhāvanā) is easy for the realization of things as they truly are. Alternatively, among all developments of concentration, this development of concentration is the most principal because all All-Knowing Bodhisattas, with minds concentrated by this very mindfulness of breathing at the foot of the Bodhi tree, realized things as they truly are; therefore, it is spoken immediately after the Discourse on Views. In that Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing, the statement "For one who develops mindfulness of breathing concentration with sixteen objects, more than two hundred knowledges arise" is the Brief Exposition of the Count of Knowledge (Ñāṇagaṇanuddesa). The statement beginning with "Eight knowledges regarding obstacles" is the Detailed Exposition of the Count of Knowledge (Ñāṇagaṇananiddesa). The same applies to "What are the eight knowledges regarding obstacles?" and so on. The passage ending with "These twenty-one knowledges in the bliss of liberation" is the detailed exposition of all knowledges. At the end, the statement beginning with "For one who develops mindfulness of breathing concentration with sixteen objects" is the conclusion. In this way, the divisions of the Pali text should first be understood.

In that Section on Counting (Gaṇanavāra) of the Brief Exposition, first, "with sixteen objects" (soḷasavatthukaṃ) refers to: the tetrad of contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā-catukka) consisting of "long, short, experiencing the whole body, calming the bodily formation"; the tetrad of contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā-catukka) consisting of "experiencing rapture, experiencing bliss, experiencing the mental formation, calming the mental formation"; the tetrad of contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā-catukka) consisting of "experiencing the mind, gladdening the mind, concentrating the mind, liberating the mind"; and the tetrad of contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā-catukka) consisting of "contemplating impermanence, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment". Because there are sixteen bases or objects for this mindfulness of breathing concentration by way of these four tetrads, it is called "soḷasavatthuka". That mindfulness of breathing concentration with sixteen objects is "soḷasavatthukaṃ". In this compound, the case-ending is elided by the power of the compound (samāsa). "Āna" is the air entering inside. "Apāna" is the air exiting outside. Some teachers say the opposite. It is called "apāna" because it is away (apeta) from the in-breath (āna). In the Niddesa, however, the letter "na" is made long as "āpāna". Mindfulness regarding that in-breathing and out-breathing is "ānāpānassati". This is a designation for the mindfulness that grasps the out-breath and in-breath. With mindfulness of breathing...
70:
Concentration associated with mindfulness of breathing, or concentration in mindfulness of breathing, is called ānāpānassatisamādhi. "Bhāvayato" means for one who develops the state leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). "Samadhikāni" means they exist with an excess; the meaning is 'surplus' (sātirekāni). The letter 'ma' here is merely for euphonic junction (sandhi). Some teachers say "saṃadhikāni". If so, it would imply that only two hundred knowledges are in excess, which is not appropriate. This is because these knowledges are two hundred with twenty in excess (220).

"Paripanthe ñāṇāni" refers to knowledges that arise by taking obstacles (such as sensual desire, etc.) as objects. Similarly, knowledges regarding helpful factors (upakāra) and knowledges regarding defilements (upakkilesa) are the same. "Vodāne ñāṇāni": it is called vodāna (purification) because the mind becomes pure through that knowledge. What is that? It is knowledge itself. Although it should be said "vodānañāṇāni", it is stated as "vodāne ñāṇāni" as in "sutamaye ñāṇaṃ", etc. One is called "satokārī" because they act while being mindful and clearly comprehending; these are the knowledges of that satokārī person. "Nibbidāñāṇāni" are knowledges characterized by disenchantment. "Nibbidānulomañāṇāni" are knowledges that conform to disenchantment (nibbidā/vipassanā). There is also a variant reading "nibbidānulomiñāṇāni", meaning those knowledges possess conformity to disenchantment. "Nibbidāpaṭippassaddhiñāṇāni" are knowledges regarding the tranquillization of disenchantment. "Vimuttisukhe ñāṇāni" are knowledges associated with the bliss of liberation.

With the words "katamāni aṭṭha", etc., knowledges regarding obstacles and helpful factors are shown together because they are pairs of opposites and counterparts. Sensual desire (kāmacchanda), renunciation (nekkhamma), etc., have the meanings already mentioned below. In the word "upakāraṃ", the neuter gender is used due to gender transformation (liṅgavipallāsa). "Sabbepi akusalā dhammā" refers to all remaining unwholesome states. Similarly, "sabbepi nibbedhabhāgiyā kusalā dhammā" is the same. In the phrase "paripantho upakāraṃ", the singular is used in consideration of each individual state. Here, by asking about knowledges of obstacles and helpful factors and answering only their objects, those knowledges are considered answered; thus, the knowledges having those objects are shown in conclusion. The same method applies to knowledges regarding defilements, etc.

## The Explanation of the Section on Counting is finished.
71:
## 2. Explanation of the Exposition of the Sixteen Knowledges

"Soḷasahi ākārehi" means by the sixteen groups of knowledge mentioned by way of both the side of obstacles and the side of helpful factors. "Uducitaṃ cittaṃ samuducitaṃ" means, in the access stage (upacārabhūmi), the mind is cultivated upwards, well-cultivated upwards, repeatedly practiced upwards, and well-practiced upwards. There is also a reading "udujitaṃ cittaṃ samudujitaṃ". "Udujita" means a mind conquered for the sake of reaching a higher state, or conquered by knowledges that lead to a higher state. "Samudujita" means a mind conquered evenly for the sake of reaching a higher state, or by knowledges that lead to a higher state. Here, the word "samā" has the meaning of rejecting unevenness. In this reading, there are two prefixes each: "u" and "du". There is also a reading "urūjitaṃ cittaṃ sammārūjitaṃ". Here too, the meaning is 'conquered'. Some say "urū" and "arū" are merely particles (nipāta). In the Commentary on the Simile of the Lute (Vīṇopama Sutta), the meaning is given as "tajjitaṃ sutajjitaṃ", but that meaning is not appropriate here. "Ekatte santiṭṭhati" means that in the access stage, because there is no distraction toward various objects, it stands in a single object. "Nīvaraṇā" in the phrase "niyyānāvaraṇaṭṭhena nīvaraṇā" refers to dissatisfaction (arati) and all unwholesome states, called hindrances because of their sense of obstructing. "Niyyānāvaraṇaṭṭhena" means in the sense of obstructing the arrival at the Path, which is the way out. There is also a reading "niyyānawāraṇaṭṭhena", meaning in the sense of rejecting the ways out. "Nekkhammaṃ ariyānaṃ niyyānaṃ": Renunciation (jhāna) is called the deliverance of the Noble Ones by way of metonymy of the fruit (phalūpacāra) because it is the cause of the Noble Path, which is known as the deliverance of the Noble Ones. Because of that renunciation which is the cause, the Noble Ones depart at the moment of the Path. Some teachers say "deliverance (niyyāna) is the Path". Since the access stage is intended here, and since at the moment of the Path, the perception of light (ālokasaññā) and all wholesome states are absent, that statement is not appropriate. "Nivutattā" means because of being covered. "Nappajānāti" is stated by way of the person.

"Visuddhacittassa" refers to a person with a purified mind only in the access stage. "Khaṇikasamodhānā" means the succession of defilements (upakkilesa) which are momentary because they arise in every thought-moment. Therefore, defilements arising due to the conjunction of moments arise by way of a momentary continuity, a momentary succession, and not by way of a single thought-moment.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Sixteen Knowledges is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Exposition of Knowledge of Defilements

In the first sextet:

154. In the first sextet, "assāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ" means: for the incoming breath (inhalation), the tip of the nose or the upper lip is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the navel is the end. The mind of that yogi who follows the beginning, middle, and end of that inhalation with mindfulness, because it reaches various locations, falls into distraction regarding the internal objects of the nose-tip, heart, and navel. That mind, being distracted by internal objects, cannot stand in a single object and is thus called an obstacle (paripantha) to concentration. "Passāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ" means: for the outgoing breath (exhalation), the navel is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the tip of the nose or the upper lip or the external space is the end. Here, the construction of the meaning should be understood in the same way as already stated. "Assāsapaṭikaṅkhanā nikantitanhācariyā" means noting 'this meditation subject is connected with the breath of the nose' and...
72:
The corruptions (upakkilesa) occur according to the sequence of the three moments. Because they arise according to the sequence of moments, these corruptions occur by the power of the sequence of moments. It means they do not arise by the power of a single mind-moment. The commentary explaining the sixteen knowledges is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Knowledge of Corruptions

## The First Hexad

In the first hexad, "the beginning, middle, and end of inhalation" means: for the air entering inside, the tip of the nose or the sign of the mouth is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the navel is the end. For the yogi who follows the beginning, middle, and end of that inhalation with mindfulness, the mind reaches a state of internal distraction due to following the different locations. That mind, having reached internal distraction, is a hindrance to concentration (samādhi) because it does not remain steady in a single object. "The beginning, middle, and end of exhalation" means: for the air going outside, the navel is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the tip of the nose, the sign of the mouth, or the outer space is the end. Here, the construction of the meaning should be understood in the same manner as already stated. "Longing for inhalation is the practice of craving which is delight" means: having noted that "this meditation subject depends on the nasal air," the very longing, characterized as the desire for coarse inhalation, is the occurrence of craving. When craving occurs, it is a hindrance to concentration because the mind cannot remain steady in a single object. "Longing for exhalation is delight" means: the delight characterized as the longing for exhalation which is preceded by inhalation. The remaining words should be connected in the same manner as already stated. "For one who is oppressed by inhalation" means: for one who makes the inhalation too long or too short, because of the existence of physical and mental fatigue rooted in inhalation, it refers to the person who is struck and oppressed by that inhalation. "Stupefaction upon obtaining exhalation" means: because of being oppressed by inhalation, one who perceives exhalation as pleasant and longs for it, experiences attachment when that exhalation is obtained. The same method applies to attachment rooted in exhalation.

In the verse compositions stated to further explain the meaning already mentioned, "following" means the mental factor that follows. "Mindfulness" (sati) refers to the weak mindfulness that is the cause of internal and external distraction. Because the mind is distracted by this inhalation, it is called "distraction" (vikkhepa). What is that distraction? It is the inhalation itself. "Internal distraction" is the inhalation that causes distraction toward an internal object. Desiring it is "desiring internal distraction." It means desiring the inhalation that causes internal distraction by the power of improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra). In this same way, the longing for external distraction should also be understood. "By which" means by which corruptions. "For one who is distracted" means for one who is being distracted or brought to a state of distraction. "The mind is not liberated" means the mind neither stays fixed on the object of inhalation and exhalation, nor is it liberated from opposing states (paccanīka dhamma). It should be connected as: the mind is not liberated and falls into the conviction of others. "Those not knowing liberation (vimokkha)" means that yogi or another person does not know the two kinds of liberation: the liberation of entering and fixing upon the object, and the liberation from opposing states. "By the faith of others" means by the reasons of others or being worthy of the conviction of others. Because of the absence of one's own direct knowledge (paccakkha-ñāṇa), the term "parapattiyā" is used in the place where "parapaccayikā" (dependent on others) would be. Other explanations are also according to the meaning already stated.

## The Second Hexad

In the second hexad, "sign" (nimitta) is the point of contact of the inhalation and exhalation. Indeed, for a person with a long nose, the inhalation and exhalation occur by striking the tip of the nose. For a person with a short nose, they occur by striking the upper lip. If this yogi contemplates only that sign of contact, for that yogi who contemplates only the sign, the mind wavers during inhalation and cannot be steady; this is a danger. Because that mind is not steady, concentration cannot exist, and thus that wavering is a hindrance to concentration. If one contemplates only the inhalation, the mind of that yogi who so contemplates is carried away into distraction by the power of entering inside along with the inhalation. At the tip of the nose which is the sign...
73:
Those who do not know the liberation of being resolved on the object (ārammaṇādhimutti-vimokkha) and the liberation of being freed from opposites (paccanīkavimutti-vimokkha) in this way must follow the lead of others (parapattiyā). "Parapattiyā" means believing due to external causes without having direct knowledge for oneself. Although the term "parapattiyā" is used where the meaning is "parappaccayikā" (relying on others), the meaning is the same.

## Second Hexad
In the second hexad (dutiyacchakka), "sign" (nimitta) refers to the point of contact for the in-breaths and out-breaths. For a person with a long nose, the in-breaths and out-breaths occur striking the nostril; for a person with a short nose, they strike the upper lip. If this yogi reflects only on that sign, the mind of that person reflecting on the sign wavers regarding the in-breath and does not remain steady. When the mind is not steady, there is no concentration, so that wavering is an obstacle (paripantha) to concentration. If one reflects only on the in-breath, the mind brings about distraction by way of entering inside and does not remain on the sign; therefore, it wavers at the sign. In this same way, the application should be made to the remaining points. In the verses, "vikkhippate" means it is distracted or brought to a state of distraction.

## Third Hexad
