In the third hexad (tatiyacchakka), "mind following the past" (atītānudhāvanaṃ cittaṃ) is the mind that follows the in-breath or out-breath that has already passed the point of contact. "Fallen into distraction" (vikkhepānupatitaṃ) is the mind that follows along with distraction or itself falls into distraction. "Mind anticipating the future" (anāgatapaṭikaṅkhanaṃ cittaṃ) is the mind that expects or longs for the in-breath or out-breath that has not yet reached the point of contact. "Wavered" (vikampitaṃ) is the mind that wavers due to that distraction of not being steady. "Sluggish" (līnaṃ) is the mind that is shrunken due to excessively lax energy (vīriya) and so on. "Fallen into indolence" (kosajjānupatitaṃ) is the mind that follows the state of laziness. "Over-exerted" (atipaggahitaṃ) is the mind that is excessively uplifted due to over-strenuous energy and so on. "Fallen into restlessness" (uddhaccānupatitaṃ) is the mind that follows distraction. "Inclined" (abhinataṃ) is the mind that is strongly leaning towards or attached to objects of enjoyment. "Averse" (apanataṃ) is the mind that is repelled by or turning away from objects lacking enjoyment. "Fallen into lust" (rāgānupatitaṃ) here means that lust follows the joy and happiness arising while attending to the sign of in-breaths and out-breaths, or it follows past objects of laughter, talk, and play. "Fallen into ill-will" (byāpādānupatitaṃ) here means that ill-will follows by way of the displeasure arising in a mind that lacks enjoyment during attention, or it follows past objects of resentment that were habitually practiced. In the verses, "na samādhiyati" means there is no concentration. "Higher mind" (adhicitta) is the superior concentration (samādhi) described with the mind as the head.
74:
Having pointed out the eighteen defilements (upakkilesa) through these three sextets, he now says "assāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ" (the beginning, middle, and end of the breath) and so forth, wishing to show the danger by establishing the fact that these defilements are obstacles to concentration. In that passage, "kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti" (both the body and the mind become agitated) means that the material body (rūpa-kāya) becomes agitated through the power of the material forms produced by the distracted mind, and the mind also becomes agitated through the power of the continuity of distraction; both become disturbed by great agitation and are distressed. They are shaken by an agitation slightly weaker than that great agitation. They are stirred by an agitation even weaker than that. It means that whether the agitation is strong, medium, or weak, it exists; it is impossible for there to be no agitation. "Cittaṃ vikampitattā" means because of the state of the mind being wavered. In the verses, "paripuṇṇā abhāvitā" means when it is not developed in a complete manner. "Iñjito" means shaken. "Phandito" means slightly shaken. Because there is no interval (it is close) to the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) mentioned below, the phrase "imehi ca pana nīvaraṇehi" (and by these hindrances) was used to indicate extreme proximity. However, in this conclusion, because there is an interval (it is distant) from the hindrances, the phrase "tehi ca pana nīvaraṇehi" (and by those hindrances) was used to indicate a distant reference.

## The Explanation of the Knowledge of Defilements is Finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Knowledge of Purification

"Vodāne ñāṇāni" means the pure knowledges. "Taṃ vivajjayitvā" (having avoided that) should be connected as: having avoided that mind which was previously mentioned as running after the past and falling into distraction. "Ekaṭṭhāne samādahati" (concentrates in one place) means he places or establishes the mind evenly at the point of contact of the in-breaths and out-breaths (the tip of the nose or the upper lip). "Tattheva adhimoceti" (resolves right there) means he resolves and fixes the mind right at that aforementioned point of contact; he makes it stay permanently. "Paggaṇhitvā" (having uplifted) means having uplifted it by developing the enlightenment factors of investigation-of-states and rapture. "Viniggaṇhitvā" (having restrained) means having restrained it by developing the enlightenment factors of tranquillity, concentration, and equanimity. Some also say, "having uplifted it with the faculties of mindfulness and energy, and having restrained it with the faculties of mindfulness and concentration." "Sampajāno hutvā" (being clearly comprehending) means [knowing] through the meditation on foulness and so forth. "Puna sampajāno hutvā" (again being clearly comprehending) means [knowing] through the meditation on loving-kindness and so forth. It should be connected as: he abandons that lust by which [the mind] was followed, and that ill-will by which it was followed. One who clearly knows that "the mind is of such a nature" [abandons them] with the opposite of that lust and ill-will...
75:
It means one abandons lust (rāga) or abandons ill-will (byāpāda). 'Pari-suddha' means the absence of the defilement of impurities. 'Pariyodāta' means being radiant or extremely pure. 'Ekattagataṃ hoti' means, for a person who has reached various distinguished states, reaching those respective states of oneness.

The question 'What are those states of oneness?' is asked by grouping the states of oneness together, whether appropriate or not in this context. 'Dānūpasaggupaṭṭhānekattaṃ': 'Dānūpasagga' refers to the relinquishing of gifts (dāna-vatthu) or the volition (cetanā) that causes relinquishment. Establishing oneself by taking that volition as an object is called 'dānūpasaggupaṭṭhāna'. That very object is called oneness (ekatta). Or, the concentration (ekaggatā) arising because of that object is called 'dānūpasaggupaṭṭhānekattaṃ'. The reading 'Dānavossaggupaṭṭhānekattaṃ' is better; the meaning is the same. By presenting the term in this way, the concentration of the recollection of generosity (cāgānussati-samādhi) is taught. Although taught by presenting the term in this way, they say it is mentioned here because this concentration of the recollection of generosity serves as a decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for the other three states of oneness.

Indeed, the great laywoman Visākhā also once addressed the Buddha thus: 'Venerable Sir, in this Dispensation, monks who have completed the rains retreat in various regions will come to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One. They will approach the Blessed One and ask, "Venerable Sir, a monk named so-and-so has passed away; what is his destination and what is his future state?" The Blessed One will explain that he was established in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or Arahantship. Then I will approach those monks and ask, "Venerable Sirs, has that venerable one ever been to Sāvatthī before?" If they reply, "That monk has been to Sāvatthī before," I will come to this conclusion without doubt: "Surely, this venerable one has used the rain-cloth, the food for guests, the food for those departing, the food for the sick, the food for those attending the sick, the medicine for the sick, or the permanent supply of congee donated by me." Recalling that use of my gifts, joy (pāmojja) will arise in me; in one who is joyful, rapture (pīti) will arise; in one whose mind is rapturous, the body (mentality-materiality) will become tranquil; one whose body is tranquil will experience happiness (sukha); the mind of one who is happy will become concentrated (samādhi). That will be for me the development of the faculties (indriya-bhāvanā), the development of the powers (bala-bhāvanā), and the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga-bhāvanā).'

Alternatively, among the four states of oneness, it should be understood that the first is taught by way of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), the second by way of absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), the third by way of insight (vipassanā), and the fourth by way of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala). The object of serenity is called the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta). Because dissolution (bhaṅga) itself is the characteristic, it is called the characteristic of passing away (vaya-lakkhaṇa). Cessation is Nibbāna. The remaining points should be understood by applying them to these three states of oneness in the same manner as previously stated.
76:
## 
'Cāgādhimuttānaṃ' means those who are intent on giving (dāna). 'Adhicitta' refers to absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) which is the basis for insight (vipassanā). 'Vipassakānaṃ' refers to those who are contemplating formations (saṅkhāra) through the three contemplations (anupassanā)—impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta)—starting from the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā). 'Ariyapuggalānaṃ' refers to the eight noble persons. The three types of oneness (ekatta) starting from the second are appropriate by way of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) and by way of the remaining meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). 'Catūhi ṭhānehi' means by four reasons. By way of concentration (samādhi), insight (vipassanā), path (magga), and fruition (phala), the summary terms (uddesa-pada) are: "The mind that has reached oneness enters into the purification of the way (paṭipadā-visuddhi), is augmented by equanimity (upekkhā), and is gladdened by knowledge (ñāṇa)."

The terms starting with "What is the beginning of the first jhāna?" are the explanatory terms (niddesa-pada) presented by way of questions because of the desire to expand upon those summary terms. In that context, 'paṭipadāvisuddhippakhanda' means: the way (paṭipadā) itself is purification (visuddhi) because it cleanses the defilements of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa); it refers to the [change-of-lineage mind, gotrabhū] that has entered into that purification of the way. 'Upekkhā-nubrūhita' means augmented or increased by specific-neutrality equanimity (tatramajjhattūpekkhā). 'Ñāṇena ca sampahamsita' means gladdened, purified, and cleansed by the knowledge that brings about purity. Some teachers explain that 'paṭipadā-visuddhi' is access concentration (upacāra) along with its prerequisites (such as making a kasina) up to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū); 'upekkhā-nubrūhanā' is absorption (appanā); and 'sampahamsanā' is reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā).

However, because it is said, "The mind that has reached oneness enters into the purification of the way," etc., one should understand: paṭipadā-visuddhi by way of the means of arrival (āgamana) within the absorption itself; upekkhā-nubrūhanā by way of the function of specific-neutrality equanimity; and sampahamsanā by way of the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge that brings about purity through the non-overstepping of mental states, etc.

How? At the time when the absorption-impulsion (appanā-javana) arises, the group of defilements called hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are obstacles to that jhāna; the mind is purified from them. Being purified and free from obstructions (āvaraṇa), it reaches the middle sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta), which is absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). The "middle sign of serenity" is simply absorption concentration that occurs evenly [without wavering or distraction]. The preceding mind, immediately before that absorption, reaching that state by way of the evolution of a single continuity, is said to "reach the middle sign of serenity." Having reached it in this way, by attaining that state, it is said to "enter" into that absorption concentration. Thus, first, paṭipadā-visuddhi should be understood by way of the [change-of-lineage mind] which accomplishes the characteristic present in the preceding mind and is the means of arrival at the very moment of the arising of the first jhāna. For the jhāna-mind thus purified, since there is nothing further to be purified, the person who no longer exerts effort in purifying is said to "look on with equanimity" (ajjhupekkhati) at the purified mind. By reaching the state of serenity, the person who no longer exerts effort in further undertaking is said to "look on with equanimity" at the mind that has reached serenity. Because of having reached serenity, having abandoned association with defilements and standing in oneness, the person who no longer exerts effort in establishing oneness is said to "look on with equanimity" at the establishment of oneness. In this way, upekkhā-nubrūhanā should be understood by way of the function of specific-neutrality equanimity.
77:
In this way, the states called concentration and wisdom, which are coupled together and arise in that steady mind nurtured by equanimity, occur without overstepping one another. The faculties such as faith and so forth, being free from various defilements, occur with a single function through the taste of liberation. It brings forth energy that is appropriate to that state of non-overstepping and having a single function. There is also the repetition (āsevanā) occurring at that moment. All these aspects are accomplished because, through knowledge, one sees the respective disadvantages and advantages in defilement and purification, and thus they are gladdened, cleansed, and purified. Therefore, it is said that gladdening (sampahaṃsanā) should be understood by way of the accomplishment of the function of knowledge that purifies by achieving the state of non-overstepping of the dhammas and so forth.

Among those (nurturing equanimity and gladdening), knowledge becomes manifest by the power of equanimity. As it is said in the Pali: 'He looks on with equanimity at the mind thus exerted; by the power of equanimity, by the power of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant. By the power of equanimity, the mind is liberated from various defilements; by the power of liberation, by the power of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom becomes predominant. Because they are liberated, those states have a single function; in the sense of having a single function, it is called development (bhāvanā).' Therefore, gladdening, which is the function of knowledge, is called the conclusion (pariyosāna).

The words beginning with 'evaṃ tivattagataṃ' (thus gone to the threefold state) are words of praise for that very mind of absorption (appanā). Therein, 'evaṃ tivattagataṃ' means having reached the threefold state by way of the purity of the way (entering absorption), the nurturing of equanimity (upekkhānubrūhanā), and the gladdening of knowledge (ñāṇasampahaṃsanā), according to the method already mentioned. 'Vitakkasampannaṃ' (endowed with initial thought) means having reached a good state through initial thought because of being free from the disturbance of defilements. 'Cittassa adhiṭṭhānasampannaṃ' (endowed with the mind's resolve) means being endowed with resolve, which is the continuous occurrence of the mind on that very object. Just as the occurrence of jhāna in the mastery of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī) is called resolve, here too, the 'resolve of the mind' can also mean one-pointedness of mind (citt'ekaggatā). This is because, through that one-pointedness, the mind stays fixed on a single object and does not wander. However, since 'samādhisampannaṃ' (endowed with concentration) is mentioned separately, it should be taken as previously explained. Alternatively, since concentration is included in the jhāna factors, 'cittassa adhiṭṭhānasampannaṃ' is stated by way of the five jhāna factors, and 'samādhisampannaṃ' is stated by way of the five faculties (indriya). In the second jhāna and so forth, by discarding the factors that are not obtainable and by way of the factors that are obtainable, it is stated as 'pītisampannaṃ' (endowed with rapture) and so on.

In the eighteen great insights (mahā-vipassanā) such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), initial thought and so forth are fully present, because those insights are sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) states. Since there is no absorption (appanā) in those insights, purity of the way and so forth should be associated by way of momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi). In the four paths (magga), because initial thought and so forth are obtained by way of association with the first jhāna, it is said that initial thought and so forth are fully present by way of the obtainable factors. In the paths of the second jhāna and so forth, it should be understood that initial thought and so forth are diminished just as in the mundane jhānas. With this sequence of words, the thirteen types of purification knowledge (vodāna-ñāṇa) have been explained in detail. How are they explained? They are: the six types of knowledge associated with placing the mind well in a single place (the tip of the nose), attending well to it, abandoning sloth, abandoning restlessness, abandoning lust, and abandoning ill-will; the four types of knowledge associated with the four states of singleness (ekatta); and the three types of knowledge associated with the purity of the way, the nurturing of equanimity, and gladdening. Thus, the thirteen types of knowledge are explained. Although they are connected with these thirteen types of knowledge, because of the desire to show the completion of those inhalations and exhalations by the power of developing mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), these types of knowledge are not concluded, but rather, putting forward an inquiry (codanā) by the method beginning with 'the sign, the inhalation, and the exhalation'...
78:
In the paths, because initial thought (vitakka) and so on are obtainable by way of the first jhāna, vitakka and the other factors are stated in full only by way of the obtainable factors. However, in the paths of the second jhāna and so on, vitakka and the others decrease just as they do in the mundane jhānas. By this sequence of words, the thirteen knowledges of purification (vodānañāṇa) have been explained in detail.

How are they explained? There are six knowledges associated with: concentrating the mind well in a single place, resolving right there, abandoning sloth (kosajja), abandoning restlessness (uddhacca), abandoning lust (rāga), and abandoning ill-will (byāpāda). There are four knowledges associated with the four unities (ekatta). There are three knowledges associated with equanimity of purification of progress (paṭipadāvisuddhi-upekkhā), strengthening (anubrūhanā), and gladdening (sampahaṃsanā). Thus, these thirteen knowledges are explained.

Although they are connected with these thirteen knowledges, wishing to show their production by way of the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati-samādhi), the Teacher did not conclude those knowledges yet. Instead, he first presented the method of developing ānāpānassati-samādhi preceded by questioning in the manner of "the sign (nimitta), the in-breath (assāsa), and the out-breath (passāsa)," and finally concluded by showing those knowledges. In that text, the meaning of the word "nimitta" has already been stated. "Anārammaṇām-ekacittassa" means not being an object of a single mind. Here, the letter "ma" is inserted for euphonic junction (sandhi). There is also a reading "anārammaṇam-ekacittassa," meaning they do not become the object of a single mind. "Tayo dhamme" refers to the three things, beginning with the sign. "Bhāvanā" refers to the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.

The question "Kathaṃ" (How?) is an inquiry made with the desire to explain the meaning of the response verse stated after the initial questioning verse (codanāgāthā). "Na cime" is "na ca ime." There is also a reading "na came," which is the same word-splitting. The word "kathaṃ" should be understood as connected with the remaining five terms, such as "How are they not unknown?" and "How does the mind not fall into distraction?"

"Padhānañca paññāyati" means the energy (viriya) exerted in the development of ānāpānassati-samādhi is evident. Because one strives with that energy, energy is called "padhāna" (exertion). "Payogañca sādheti" means the meditator (yogī) accomplishes the jhāna that suppresses the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Because jhāna is applied to suppress the hindrances, it is called "payoga" (application). "Visesam-adhigacchati" means one attains the path (magga) that abandons the fetters (saṃyojana). The path is called "visesa" (distinction) because it is the benefit of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā). Since the path is the foremost distinction, the conjunction "ca" (and) was not used to connect it.

Now, wishing to establish the questioned matter with a simile, he said "seyyathāpi rukkho" (just as a tree) and so on. The meaning of that passage is: For example, a log that has been planed with an adze (vāsī) for the purpose of being split with a saw (kakaca) is placed on a level piece of ground, made ready for the task, so that it remains motionless at the time of splitting. "Kakacena" means with a hand-saw. "Āgate" means...
79:
(Regarding the saw teeth) that have touched the log and come towards one's side. 'Gate' means (the saw teeth) that have touched the log and gone to the other side. The word 'vā' has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya). 'Na aviditā honti' (they are not unknown) means that just as a man watching the point where the saw teeth touch the log knows all the saw teeth because of their coming and going, even before they arrive at his position and before they depart.

'Padhāna' (exertion) is the energy (viriya) used in cutting the log. 'Payoga' (effort/application) is the action (kiriya) of cutting the log. The phrase 'visesamadhigacchati' (attains distinction) is not present in the simile. 'Upanibandhanā nimitta' (the sign for binding) refers to the tip of the nose or the sign of the mouth (the upper lip), which is the cause for mindfulness that binds. Because the mind is bound to the object by this mindfulness, mindfulness is called 'upanibandhanā'. 'At the tip of the nose' means a person with a long nose (should attend) at the tip of the nose. 'At the sign of the mouth' means a person with a short nose (should attend) at the upper lip. The upper lip is called 'mukhanimitta' (the sign of the mouth) because it is the cause for mindfulness placed at the mouth (face).

'Āgate' (having come) refers to the incoming breath (assāsa) entering from the point of contact. 'Gate' (having gone) refers to the outgoing breath (passāsa) going out from the point of contact. 'Na aviditā honti' means that because there is no coming and going of the breaths before they reach the point of contact, all those breaths are clearly known. 'Kammaniyaṃ hoti' (becomes wieldy) means that through which energy both the body and mind become wieldy and fit for the work of meditation (bhāvanā). Calling this energy 'padhāna' is an instance of naming the cause by its effect.

'Upakkilesā pahīyanti' (defilements are abandoned) means the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). 'Vitakkā vūpasammanti' (thoughts are stilled) means the calming of unstable thoughts that wander among various objects. The jhāna by which defilements are abandoned and thoughts are stilled is called 'payoga' (preliminary work/application). The masculine pronoun 'ayaṃ' is used in reference to the word 'payoga'. 'Saṃyojanā pahīyanti' (fetters are abandoned) means the abandoning of the fetters to be destroyed by the respective paths (magga) through the abandoning by destruction (samuccheda-pahāna). 'Anusayā byantīhonti' (underlying tendencies are eliminated) means that because the abandoned underlying tendencies are of a nature not to arise again, their extremes of arising (uppāda) or passing away (bhaṅga) are cut off. Since the underlying tendencies that were not previously eliminated are now gone, it is said 'byantīhonti' (they are eliminated/come to an end). The abandoning of underlying tendencies is mentioned to show that the abandoning of fetters occurs only through the abandoning of underlying tendencies and not otherwise. The path by which fetters are abandoned and underlying tendencies are eliminated is called 'visesa' (distinction).

Since the Noble Path (ariya-magga) is also shown in the fourth tetrad, it is the Noble Path that is spoken of here. Although it is obvious without being stated that a single mind cannot take two objects simultaneously, without discarding that point, the conclusion is made: "These three things are not the objects of a single mind."

Now, wishing to praise the practitioner (yogāvacara) who achieves success in that meditation, he spoke the verse beginning with "Ānāpānassati yassa" and gave its detailed exposition (niddesa). In that verse (the meaning is): For whichever yogi mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing is perfected, well-developed, and practiced in due order as taught by the Blessed One, that practitioner illuminates this world of formations (the world of the aggregates) like the moon freed from a cloud. In the detailed explanation of the verse, the phrase "no passāso no assāso" is a special statement made by way of negating the previously mentioned meaning. Mindfulness is called 'sati' because it stays fixed on the in-breath due to the state of non-forgetfulness. Similarly, it is called 'sati' because it stays fixed on the out-breath. Mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing to this extent is called 'ānāpānassati'.

Now, wishing to point out the person mentioned in the verse solely by the power of mindfulness, he said "Yo assasati ... tiṭṭhati" and so on. Whichever person produces the in-breath, that person's mindfulness stays fixed on the in-breath. Whichever person produces the out-breath, that person's mindfulness stays fixed on the out-breath. 'Paripuṇṇā' (perfected) means in the sequence of jhāna, vipassanā, and magga...
80:
For whoever mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) is well-developed, fulfilled, and practiced in due order, just as taught by the Blessed One, that person illuminates this world. How? Like the moon freed from clouds. Just as the moon, freed from clouds and such, illuminates this world of space (okāsaloka), so too does that practitioner (yogāvacara) illuminate this world of formations (saṅkhāraloka) such as the aggregates (khandha); thus should the connection in the verse be understood. In the detailed explanation of the phrase "Abbhā muttova candimā" (Like the moon freed from clouds), since mist and so forth are also mentioned, it should be understood that the word "ādi" (and so forth) is elided here.

In the detailed explanation of the verse, the words "no passāso no assāso" (no out-breath, no in-breath) express the same meaning previously mentioned, but distinguished by way of negation. "Establishment is mindfulness" (upaṭṭhānaṃ sati) means that because of non-forgetfulness, the state of standing close to the in-breath is called mindfulness. The same applies to the out-breath. By this much, the meaning of mindfulness occurring in the out-breaths and in-breaths is stated as "ānāpānasati."

Now, wishing to point out the person referred to as "yassa" (to whom) by the power of mindfulness alone, it is said: "For one who breathes in, mindfulness is established; for one who breathes out, mindfulness is established." This means: for one who breathes in, their mindfulness stands close to the in-breath; for one who breathes out, their mindfulness stands close to the out-breath. "Fulfilled" (paripuṇṇā) means fulfillment through the attainment of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) in the sequence of jhana, insight (vipassanā), and the Path (magga). Referring to those very states of jhana, insight, and the Path, it is said "by way of the sense of being grasped," and so forth. Because those states are grasped by this yogi, they are called "pariggaha" (grasping); they are fulfilled by way of that sense of being grasped. In that Path of Arahantship, because all consciousness and mental factors (citta-cetasika) are mutually accompanied, they are fulfilled by way of the sense of accompaniment (parivāra). They are fulfilled by way of the sense of fulfillment through the completion of development (bhāvanā).

The words "four developments" (catasso bhāvanā) and so forth are stated by the power of the meaning of the word "well-developed" (subhāvitā). The four developments have already been mentioned below. "Made into a vehicle" (yānikatā) means made like a well-yoked vehicle. "Made into a foundation" (vatthukatā) means made like a foundation in the sense of a basis. "Persisted in" (anuṭṭhitā) means well-established. "Consolidated" (paricitā) means developed and accumulated from all sides. "Well undertaken" (susamāraddhā) means well and thoroughly initiated, well performed. "Wherever one desires" (yattha yattha ākaṅkhati) means in whichever jhanas or in whichever insights one wishes. "There, there" (tattha tattha) means in those respective jhanas and insights. "Attained to mastery" (vasippatto) means having reached the state of mastery and the state of abundance. "Attained to power" (balappatto) means having reached the power of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). "Attained to self-confidence" (vesārajjappatto) means having reached the state of confidence and the state of proficiency. "Those states" (te dhammā) refers to the states of serenity and insight. "Dependent on advertence" (āvajjanapaṭibaddhā) means they are dependent on advertence; just upon advertence, they [reach] association with that person's continuity or with knowledge...
81:
It means they are connected with desire. It implies that by mere wishing, they reach conjunction in the manner already stated. Here, the term 'manasikāra' (attention) is used to explain the meaning as a synonym for 'āvajjanā' (advertence), and 'cittuppāda' (thought-arising) as a synonym for desire. Therefore, it is said 'yānikatā' (made into a vehicle). Because they are made so, these qualities of serenity and insight are said to be made like a well-hitched vehicle.

'In whichever object' (yasmiṃ yasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ) means in each of the sixteen objects called mindfulness of breathing. 'Svādhiṭṭhitaṃ' means well-established. 'Supaṭṭhitā' means well-placed. Since the well-conjoined mind and mindfulness perform their respective functions together, these two states—mind and mindfulness—are shown by connecting them in forward and reverse order. Therefore, it is said 'vatthukatā' (made a foundation). Because they have become thus, it means they have been made into a foundation. 'Whithersoever he directs the mind' (yena yena cittaṃ abhiniharati) means withdrawing the mind from its previous object and inclining it toward a specific distinction in meditation. 'There mindfulness revolves around' (tena tena sati anuparivattati) means that in that very distinction of meditation, mindfulness becomes compliant, turns away from its previous object, and proceeds. Here, the terms 'yena' and 'tena' should be understood in the locative sense, as in the passage 'yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami' (where the Blessed One was, there he approached). Therefore, it is said 'anuṭṭhitā' (well-pursued). Because of doing so, it means the mind and mindfulness remain following that particular meditation. Since mindfulness is the principal factor in the practice of mindfulness of breathing, it should be understood that it is conjoined with mindfulness in the terms 'vatthukatā' and 'anuṭṭhitā'.

Because only fulfilled states are thoroughly practiced, developed, and have obtained repetition (āsevana), the three meanings stated for the word 'fulfilled' (paripuṇṇā) are also stated for the word 'practiced' (paricitā), and a fourth specific meaning is also given. In that fourth meaning, 'comprehending with mindfulness' (satiyā pariggaṇhanto) refers to a meditator who comprehends and develops the in-breaths and out-breaths, which are to be comprehended either by mindfulness conjoined with insight or by mindfulness occurring in the preliminary stage of the Path. 'He conquers evil unwholesome states' (jināti pāpake akusale dhamme) means he conquers or overcomes the low defilements by way of abandoning by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna). This teaching is a person-centered discourse (puggulādhiṭṭhāna). Indeed, when the states (Dhamma) conquer, the person endowed with those states is also said to conquer. And those states, without abandoning mindfulness, are called 'conquered' (jitā) because they have begun to conquer at the moment of their own occurrence, just as it is said 'he has eaten' of one who has begun to eat. The specific characteristic here should be understood according to the rules of grammar. Even so, although it should be said 'parijitā' (thoroughly conquered), the letter 'j' is changed to 'c', and it is stated as 'paricitā'. This is like the word 'Sugato' (Well-gone), used because the Buddha has good speech, where the letter 'd' is changed to 't'. In explaining these various meanings, the word 'paricitā' is an agentive formation (kattu-sādhana). The three terms previously mentioned—'yānikatā', 'vatthukatā', and 'anuṭṭhitā'—are objective formations (kamma-sādhana). 'Four are well-undertaken' (cattāro susamāraddhā) means the tasks of well-undertaken effort are four. Here, it should be understood that the word 'meaning' (attha) is elided. The meanings of the word 'susamāraddhā' are also stated here as 'well-undertaken'. Or else, it should be understood that there are four because the well-undertaken states of serenity and insight are distinguished by four kinds of meanings. Because only well-developed states are well-undertaken states. Therefore, the three meanings of development (bhāvanā) are also stated in the analysis of this term 'undertaken' (samāraddhā). When the fourth meaning, development by repetition (āsevana-bhāvanā), is also stated in the three previous types of development...
82: It is said, "Paricitā." Just as in the alternative meaning of "Sugata," where it is said, "The Blessed One has good speech," the letter 'd' is changed to 't' by the rule of Nirutti (linguistics), so it should be understood here as well. In this variation of meaning, the word "paricitā" is in the active sense (kattu-sādhana), while the preceding three words are in the passive sense (kamma-sādhana).## "Cattāro susamāraddhā" means "four well-undertaken matters" (cattāro susamāraddhatthā); it should be understood that the word 'attha' is elided. The meanings of the word "susamāraddhā" are also stated here as "susamāraddhā." Or they should be understood as "well-undertaken dhammas." It is said "four" according to the fourfold division of meaning, not according to the division of dhammas. Because only well-developed dhammas are called well-undertaken, and no others, the three meanings of development (bhāvanā) are also stated here. The meaning of repetition (āsevana) is already included by stating the three previous developments. Therefore, without directly stating the meaning of repetition, the meaning of well-uprooting its opposite defilements is stated. Through the total destruction of the opposites, the completion of the undertaking is known. Thus, the meaning of energy (vīriya) that has reached its peak is stated. In that fourth meaning, "tappaccanīkānaṃ" refers to the defilements which are the opposites of jhāna, vipassanā, and magga. "Kilesānaṃ" refers to sensual desire (kāmacchanda) etc., and self-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) etc., associated with the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) etc. "Susamūhatattā" means being well-uprooted or destroyed through the abandonments of suppression (vikkhambhana), substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), and eradication (samuccheda). In some palm-leaf manuscripts, they write "susamugghātattā," but that reading is not good.Again, to show another variation of the meaning of the word "susamāraddhā," he said "susamaṃ" etc. In that text, "tattha jātā" means arisen in that specific development that has reached its peak. "Anavajjā" means free from the fault of defilements because of not becoming an object for defilements. "Kusalā" means wholesome by way of their nature (jāti). "Bodhipakkhiyā" means belonging to the side of the Noble Path, which receives the name "Bodhi" because of the sense of awakening. "Belonging to the side" means standing in the state of being helpful. Those Bodhipakkhiya dhammas are the 37 factors: the 4 foundations of mindfulness, the 4 right efforts, the 4 bases of power, the 5 faculties, the 5 powers, the 7 factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. "Idaṃ samaṃ" means this group of dhammas at the moment of the path is called "sama" (calm/peaceful) because it calms or destroys defilements through eradication (samuccheda). "Nirodho nibbānaṃ": it is called "nirodha" (cessation) because it is the cessation of suffering; it is called "nibbāna" because of the absence of craving (taṇhā) known as "vāna" (binding). "Idaṃ susamaṃ" means this Nibbāna is called "susama" (well-calmed) because it is free from the unevenness of all conditioned things. "Ñātaṃ" means the "sama" dhamma known as Bodhipakkhiya...
83: ...is "known" (ñātaṃ) because it is known by path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) without delusion; the "well-calmed" (susama) known as Nibbāna is "known" by path-knowledge through taking it as an object. Both of these are "seen" (diṭṭhaṃ) as if seen with the eye of that path-knowledge. "Vidita" (known/realized) means that these two are obtained by bringing them into existence in one's own continuity (the 'sama' dhammas) and by making it an object (the 'susama' dhamma). It means realized and touched by wisdom, just like "ñātaṃ." The words "not shrinking (asallīna), not confused (asammūṭṭhā), not agitated (asāraddho), one-pointed (ekagga)" clarify the meanings of the preceding words. Therein, "āraddha" means initiated or undertaken (paṭṭhapita). "Asallīna" means not shrunken (asaṅkucita). "Upaṭṭhitā" means standing near or established (upagantvā ṭhitā). "Asammūṭṭhā" means not lost or unconfused (avinaṭṭhā). "Passaddho" means calmed (nibbuto). "Asāraddho" means without fever or unagitated (niddaratho). "Samāhita" means well-placed or concentrated (samaṃ ṭhapitaṃ). "Ekagga" means undistracted (avikkhittaṃ)."Cattāro susamāraddhā" etc., is the primary meaning of the entire term "susamāraddha." "Atthi samaṃ" etc., is the meaning of the word "susama," and "ñātaṃ" etc., are the alternative meanings (vikkappattha) of the word "āraddha." Here is the correlation of the word meanings: although it should be said "samā ca susamā ca samasusamā," it is stated only as "susamā" by retaining one of the similar parts (ekasesa), just as "nāma and rūpa" are called "nāmarūpa." "Idaṃ samaṃ, idaṃ susamaṃ" are stated in the neuter gender without depending on others. Since "ñāta" is also called "diṭṭha," and "diṭṭha" and "āraddha" are identical in meaning, and since "vidita," "sacchikata," and "phassita" are synonyms of "ñāta," by saying "ñāta," the meaning of "āraddha" is intended."Energy is undertaken, not shrinking" (āraddhaṃ hoti vīriyaṃ asallīnaṃ) is the direct meaning (ujukattha) of the word "āraddha." "Mindfulness is established" (upaṭṭhitā sati) etc., are stated to show the dhammas that are helpful to the associated energy, not to show the meaning of the word "āraddha." By the first meaning, it is "susamāraddhā" because it is well-undertaken; by this meaning, it is "susamāraddhā" because the "susama" dhammas are undertaken; thus it is called "susamāraddhā" by the rule of ekasesa. Taking this meaning, it is said, "Therefore it is called susamāraddhā.""Anupubbaṃ" means in order (yathānukkamena); it means according to (anu) what preceded (pubbaṃ pubbaṃ). "Dīghaṃ" (long) is by way of the long out-breaths and in-breaths. "Purimā purimā" refers to the preceding mindfulness. By this phrase, the meaning of the word "pubba" is stated. "Pacchimā pacchimā" refers to the succeeding mindfulness. By this phrase, the meaning of the word "anu" is stated. By both, the meaning is that the preceding and succeeding mindfulnesses are developed (paricitā). Since the sixteen subjects will be explained in detail above, here it is summarized by showing only the final term, "contemplating relinquishment" (paṭṭinissaggānupassī). For one who has reached the peak of development, all...
84:
Because mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) is practiced repeatedly as desired, it is also said to be continuously cultivated. Therefore, it is said: "They are both practiced with one another and continuously cultivated."

'Yathattha' refers to meanings that have the nature of truth. 'Attadamathattha' refers to the meaning of the quelling of one's own perverted indulgence at the moment of the Path of Arahatship. 'Samathattha' refers to the meaning of tranquility (cooling). 'Parinibbāpanattha' refers to the meaning of extinguishment through the total cooling of defilements. 'Abhiññattha' refers to the meaning of knowledge through the power of all phenomena. 'Pariññattha' and so forth are understood through the power of the function of the Path-knowledge. 'Saccābhisamayattha' is understood through the power of seeing the four truths with a single penetration. 'Nirodhe patiṭṭhāpakattha' is understood through the power of making [cessation] the object.

Even though the word 'Buddho' is not explicitly present, the word 'Buddhena' refers to that Buddha; desiring to point out that Buddha, it is said 'Buddho'. 'Sayambhū' means becoming [enlightened] by oneself without any guidance. 'Anācariyaka' is an explanation of the meaning of the term 'Sayambhū'. Indeed, one who penetrates the Truths without a teacher is called 'Sayambhū'. The phrase 'In things not heard before' and so forth expresses the state of being without a teacher. 'Ananussutesu' means not having heard from a teacher. 'Sāmaṃ' means by oneself. 'Abhisambujjhi' means he has fully and rightly penetrated. 'Attained omniscience therein' means he attained the state of omniscience regarding those four Truths. Just as those who penetrate the Truths are omniscient, it is said thus because of his penetration of the Truths. There is also a variant reading 'Sabbaññutaṃ patto'. 'Mastery over the powers' means he attained sovereignty over the ten powers of a Tathāgata. One who is of such a nature is called 'Buddha'. In that context, the Buddha is a special being designated based on the continuity of aggregates (khandha-santāna) permeated by the attainment of the unsurpassed liberation, which is caused by the unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena; or he is designated based on the awakening to the Truths, which is the proximate cause of omniscience. By this much, the explanation of 'Buddha' by way of meaning is completed.

Now, desiring to explain by way of phrasing (byañjanato), it is said 'Buddho, in what sense is he Buddha?' and so forth. Therein, just as in the world one who knows is called 'avagata' (understood), so he is 'Buddha' because he has known the Truths. Just as the wind that dries leaves is called 'paṇṇasusa', so he is 'Buddha' because he makes the generation of beings know. 'Buddha through omniscience' means he is called 'Buddha' because of the wisdom (buddhi) capable of knowing all phenomena. 'Buddha through all-seeing' means he is called 'Buddha' because all phenomena have been seen by his eye of knowledge.
85:
'Buddha through not being led by others' (ananya-neyyatā) means he is called 'Buddha' because he is not to be awakened by another, but is awakened by himself. 'Buddha through blossoming' (visavitā) means he is called 'Buddha' in the sense of blossoming like a lotus, because of the blossoming of various special qualities. By the six figurative descriptions such as 'Buddha as one whose taints are destroyed' (khīṇāsava-saṅkhāta), he is called 'Buddha' because he has awakened from the sleep of all defilements, like a man who has awakened from sleep by abandoning the states that cause the mind to shrink.

Because the terms 'saṅkhā' and 'saṅkhāta' are identical in meaning, the word 'saṅkhātena' should be understood as 'by way of a group' (koṭṭhāsa). He is said to be 'one designated as free from smearing' (nirupalepa-saṅkhātena) because of the absence of the smearing of craving and the smearing of views. Because all defilements along with their residual impressions (vāsana) have been abandoned, he is distinguished by the word 'ekanta' (absolute/total) and described as 'absolutely free from lust' (ekanta-vītarāga) and so forth. 'Absolutely free from defilements' (ekanta-nikkileso) means he is free from all defilements, including the remnants of lust, hatred, and delusion. In the phrase 'gone to the one-way path' (ekāyana-maggaṃ gato), 'Buddha' is used because roots meaning 'to go' also mean 'to know', and roots meaning 'to know' also mean 'to go'; therefore, he is called 'Buddha' because he has gone to (or known) the one-way path. In this term 'ekāyana-magga':

'Magga, pantha, patha, pajja, añjasa, vaṭuma, ayana,
nāvā, uttara-setu, kulla, bhisi, saṅkama.'

Among these many names for the path, it is called by the name 'ayana'. Therefore, it is a path that is a single way, not a two-forked road. Alternatively, it is the 'ekāyana-magga' because it is a path to be traveled by one alone. 'By one' (ekena) means with a secluded mind, having abandoned the company of a group. 'To be traveled' (ayitabba) means to be practiced. Or, it is 'ayana' because they go by means of this; the meaning is that they go from saṃsāra to Nibbāna. It is 'ekāyana' because it is the path of the Excellent Ones. 'Eka' refers to the Excellent Ones, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas who are the most excellent of all beings. Thus, 'ekāyana-magga' means the path that is the way of the Fully Enlightened Buddhas. Or, it is 'ayana' because it goes, meaning it proceeds. It is 'ekāyana-magga' because it is a path proceeding in only one [dispensation]; the meaning is that it is a path proceeding only in the Buddha's dispensation and not elsewhere. Furthermore, it is 'ekāyana' because it goes to one [goal]. Although in the preliminary stage it proceeds by way of various methods of meditation, in the later stage it goes only to the single Nibbāna. Therefore, 'ekāyana-magga' means the path leading to the single Nibbāna. He is 'Buddha' because he alone has fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; the meaning is that he is not a Buddha because of being awakened by others, but he is called 'Buddha' because he himself has fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. He is 'Buddha' because of the destruction of non-intelligence (abuddhi) and the acquisition of intelligence (buddhi). Intelligence...
86:
The word 'Buddha' is merely a synonym for the word 'Bodha'. In this context, just as a cloth is called 'blue cloth' or 'red cloth' due to its connection with the qualities of blueness or redness, it is stated [in the Commentary] that he is called 'Buddha' due to his connection with the qualities of a Buddha.

Furthermore, it is stated to show that the name 'Buddha' is not a name [given by parents, etc.], but a designation that follows the intrinsic meaning (quality). In that passage, *mittā* means companions. *Amaccā* means attendants (servants). *Ñātī* means paternal relatives. *Sālohitā* means maternal relatives. *Samaṇā* means those who have gone forth. *Brāhmaṇā* means those who habitually say 'bho bho' or those who have calmed and removed evil. *Devatā* means deities such as Sakka and the Brahmas.

*Vimokkhantika* means: *Vimokkha* is the Path of Arahatship (*arahattamagga*). The end (*anta*) of *vimokkha* is the Fruit of Arahatship (*arahattaphala*). A name occurring at that end of liberation (Fruit of Arahatship) is called *Vimokkhantika*. Indeed, the state of omniscience is accomplished by the Path of Arahatship and is perfected upon the arising of the Fruit of Arahatship. Therefore, the state of omniscience occurs at the end of liberation. The name based on that cause (*nemittika*) is also a name occurring at the end of liberation. Thus it is said: 'This name Buddha is the name of the Blessed Buddhas occurring at the end of liberation.'

'Along with the attainment of omniscient knowledge at the foot of the Bodhi tree' means along with the attainment of omniscient knowledge at the moment of the Fruit of Arahatship as mentioned, at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree. 'Realized designation' (*sacchikā paññatti*) means a designation born from the realization of the Fruit of Arahatship or from the realization of all phenomena. 'Yadidaṃ buddho' refers to this designation 'Buddha'. This is an explanation of the meaning of 'Buddha' by way of syllables (verbal definition).

The verse 'Yathā buddhena desitā' (As taught by the Buddha) should be compared with the meaning stated in the Word-Analysis (*Padabhājanīya*) as follows: Mindfulness of breathing is taught by the Blessed One in such a manner. The ten meanings encompassed by the word *yathā* are also as taught by the Blessed One. It should be understood that the word *yathā* in the sense of 'manner' (as taught in such a way) and the word *yathā* in the sense of 'nature' (intrinsic state) are combined into the single term 'yathā' by the method of *sarūpekasesa* (retaining one of two identical forms). In the Word-Analysis, however, the singular 'desito' is used by way of connecting each of those meanings of *yathā* individually.

Because it is stated, 'Whether he be a householder or a renunciant,' the initial word 'yassa' also means 'of whichever householder or renunciant.' The meaning of 'loka' (world) has already been stated. 'Pabhāseti' means making one's own knowledge manifest.
87:
The meaning is: 'Abhisambuddhattā' is due to the state of having penetrated [the truth] even with the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*). 'Obhāseti' means illuminating the world of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*). 'Bhāseti' means making the world of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) bright. 'Pabhāseti' means making the world of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) bright in various ways.

Noble knowledge (*ariyañāṇa*) refers to the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship. 'Mahikā mutta' means freed from frost. 'Mahikā' refers to frost (*nīhāra*). There is also a variant reading 'mahiyā mutta'. 'Dhūmarajā mutta' means freed from smoke and dust. 'Rāhugaheṇā vippamutta' is stated with the two prefixes 'vi' and 'pa' for emphasis because the Asura Rāhu is a proximate defilement of the moon. 'Bhāsate' means shining because of having its own radiance. 'Tapate' means glowing because of its own brilliance. 'Virocate' means being beautiful because of its sparkling nature.

'Evamevaṃ' means 'just so, just so'. This is because, just as the moon, while itself shining, glowing, and being beautiful, illuminates this world of space (*okāsaloka*), so too the monk, while shining, glowing, and being beautiful through wisdom, illuminates this world of the aggregates, etc., through wisdom. Therefore, in both cases, 'bhāsate' is used instead of 'bhāseti'. By saying this, the causal meaning is also included.

If it is asked why the simile of the moon was taken instead of the sun, which has a much clearer light? It should be understood that the simile of the moon, endowed with peaceful qualities, is appropriate for a monk who is peaceful due to the subsiding of the fever of all defilements. Thus, having praised the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) who accomplishes the success of the development of mindfulness of breathing, he concludes by showing those knowledges: 'These are the thirteen knowledges of purification.'

## The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Purification is Finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Description of the Knowledge of Acting Mindfully

In the table of contents (*mātikā*) of the Description of the Knowledge of Acting Mindfully, 'a monk in this dispensation' means a monk in this Teaching (*sāsanā*). Here, the word 'idha' (here) points to the Dispensation which is the support for the person who produces the concentration of mindfulness of breathing in every way, and it excludes such a state in other teachings. For it is said: 'Monks, only here is there a recluse... other systems of thought are empty of recluses.'

'Whether gone to the forest, or gone to the root of a tree, or gone to an empty hut'—this indicates his selection of a dwelling (*senāsana*) suitable for the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing.
88:
The mind of this monk, which has long been wandering among objects such as forms, does not wish to ascend to the object of mindfulness of breathing concentration; it is like a carriage harnessed to a rogue bull that runs only off the path. Therefore, for example, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a rogue calf that has grown up drinking all the milk from a rogue cow, would take it away from the cow and tie it with a rope to a large post planted in a suitable place. Then that calf, struggling here and there and unable to run away, would sit or lie down right by that post. 

In the same way, this monk, wishing to tame his coarse mind which has grown up by enjoying the taste of objects such as forms for a long time, should leave those objects and enter a forest, the foot of a tree, or a secluded place, and tie it with the rope of mindfulness to the post of inhalation and exhalation. When tied thus, even if that monk's mind struggles here and there, unable to find its previously accustomed objects and unable to break the rope of mindfulness and run away, it sits and lies down right at the object of inhalation and exhalation by the power of access concentration and absorption concentration. 

Therefore, the ancient teachers said: 
'Just as a man here would tie a calf to be tamed to a post, 
So should one tie one's own mind firmly to the object with mindfulness.' 

Thus, that lodging becomes suitable for his meditation. Or else, because this Anāpānasati meditation is the pinnacle among the various subjects of meditation and is the proximate cause for the attainment of the special distinction and the dwelling in happiness in the present life for all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha, it is not easy to develop without abandoning a village-bordering monastery crowded with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, and so on; for sound is a thorn to jhāna. However, in a forest far from a village, it is easy for a practitioner to grasp this meditation subject, produce the four jhānas of Anāpānasati, and using that very jhāna as a basis, contemplate the formations (saṅkhāra) to reach the highest fruit, Arahatship. Therefore, the Blessed One, pointing out the suitable lodging for that monk, said 'gone to the forest' and so on; likewise, the Elder [Sāriputta] said so. 

The Blessed One is like an expert in the science of building sites (vatthuvijjā). Just as a site-expert, seeing a ground suitable for a city and having well-investigated it, advises 'Build a city here,' and when the city is safely completed, receives great honor from the royal family; in the same way, the Blessed One, having investigated the lodging suitable for the practitioner, advises 'Meditation should be practiced here.' Because of that advice, the practitioner practicing meditation in that place...
89:
...when he reaches Arahatship in due course, he [the Buddha] receives great honor, with the thought: 'Truly, that Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One.' This monk, however, is called 'one like a leopard.' Just as a great leopard king, relying on a grass thicket, a forest thicket, or a mountain thicket in the forest, hides and catches animals such as wild buffaloes, elks, and pigs; in the same way, this monk practicing meditation in places such as the forest should be known as one who catches (attains) the paths of Stream-entry, Once-returning, Non-returning, and Arahatship, as well as the Noble Fruits, in due order.

Therefore, the ancient teachers said: 
'Just as a leopard catches animals by hiding, 
So too this son of the Buddha, diligent in yoga and practicing insight, 
Having entered the forest, catches the supreme fruit.'

Therefore, wishing to show the forest lodging as the suitable ground for the speed of his effort, he said 'gone to the forest' and so on.

In those words, 'gone to the forest' means gone to a forest that has the characteristics mentioned above and possesses the bliss of seclusion. 'Gone to the foot of a tree' means gone to the vicinity of a tree. 'Gone to an empty hut' means gone to a secluded place. Here, excluding the forest and the foot of a tree, one who goes to the remaining seven types of lodgings can also be called 'one who has gone to an empty hut.' For there are nine types of lodgings. As it is said [in the Vibhaṅga]: 'He frequents a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a mountain cave, a cemetery, a woodland, the open air, a heap of straw.'

Thus, having pointed out the lodging suitable for the three seasons, suitable for his temperament, and suitable for the development of Anāpānasati meditation, [the Buddha] said 'he sits,' wishing to point out a calm posture that is on the side of non-sluggishness and non-agitation. Then, wishing to show the firmness in his sitting, the capacity for the occurrence of inhalation and exhalation, and the means of grasping the object, he said 'having folded his legs cross-wise' and so on. In those words, 'cross-wise' (pallaṅka) means a sitting position with the thighs locked all around. 'Having folded' means having bound. 'Setting the body erect' means keeping the upper body straight, placing the eighteen vertebrae end to end. For the skin, flesh, and sinews of one sitting thus do not become bent. Then, the pains that would arise moment by moment due to their being bent do not arise. When those pains do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not fall away, and it reaches growth and increase.
90:
"Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā" means establishing (setting up) mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). "Mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out" means that the monk, having sat down in this manner and having established mindfulness in this way, without abandoning that mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject, breathes in only in conjunction with mindfulness and breathes out only in conjunction with mindfulness; it means he is one who acts with constant mindfulness.

Now, to show the modes by which he acts with constant mindfulness, the phrase beginning with "Dīghaṃ vā assasanto" (Breathing in long) is stated. In that passage, "Dīghaṃ vā assasanto" refers to the practitioner who produces a long inhalation. The same applies to the short inhalation. The length or shortness of these inhalations and exhalations should be understood by way of duration (time). For at times, humans breathe in and out for a long duration, like elephants, snakes, and so on. At other times, they breathe in and out for a short duration, like dogs, rabbits, and so on. In another sense, inhalations and exhalations that are extremely subtle (pulverized) cannot be called long or short. Therefore, inhalations and exhalations that enter and exit over a long period are to be understood as "long," and those that enter and exit over a short period are to be understood as "short." In this regard, this monk, while producing long inhalations and exhalations through the nine modes mentioned above, knows, "I breathe in long, I breathe out long." He knows similarly in the case of the short breath.

For the monk who knows in this way, it is said:
"Long and short inhalations, and likewise exhalations;
These four aspects occur only at the tip of the monk's nose."

It should be understood that for that practitioner, the development of the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna bhāvanā) is accomplished through one of these nine modes. "He trains, thinking: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains, thinking: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body'" means he trains by making known and making clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire body of the inhalation. He trains by making known and making clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire body of the exhalation. Thus making it known and making it clear, he breathes in and breathes out with a mind associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta-citta). Therefore, it is said, "He trains, thinking: 'I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out.'"

To explain in detail: for one monk, the beginning of the entire body of the inhalation or exhalation, which is subtle and diffused, is clear, but the middle and the end are not clear. That monk is able only to grasp the beginning and becomes exhausted at the middle and the end. For another monk, the middle is clear, but the beginning and the end are not clear. That monk is able only to grasp the middle and becomes exhausted at the beginning and the end. For another monk, the end is clear, but the beginning and the middle are not clear. That monk is able only to grasp the end and becomes exhausted at the beginning and the middle. For yet another monk, the beginning, middle, and end—the whole—is clear. That monk is able to grasp the whole and does not become exhausted anywhere. To show that one should be a monk of this latter kind, the phrase beginning with "Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī" is stated. In that passage, "sikkhati" (he trains) means he strives and exerts himself by making it clear in this way. The restraint (saṃvara) that such a person possesses is called the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) in this mindfulness of breathing. The concentration that such a person possesses, the wisdom...
91:
It is said, "he trains." This is because for one monk, the beginning of the body of inhalation or the body of exhalation, which is subtle and diffused, is clear, but the middle and the end are not clear. That monk is able only to grasp the beginning and becomes exhausted at the middle and the end. For another monk, the middle is clear, but the beginning and the end are not clear. That monk is able only to grasp the middle and becomes exhausted at the beginning and the end. For another monk, the end is clear, but the beginning and the middle are not clear. That monk is able only to grasp the end and becomes exhausted at the beginning and the middle. For yet another monk, the beginning, middle, and end—all—are clear. That monk is able to grasp all of them and does not become exhausted in any part. To show that one should be a monk of such a nature, the words beginning with "Experiencing the whole body..." are stated.

In that passage, "sikkhati" (he trains) means he strives and exerts himself by making it clear in this way. The restraint (saṃvara) of a person of such a nature is called the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) in this context. The concentration (samādhi) of a person of such a nature is called the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā). The wisdom (paññā) of a person of such a nature is called the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). He trains in, pursues, develops, and frequently practices these three trainings on that object along with that mindfulness and that attention (manasikāra); this is how the meaning should be understood here. In that passage, because in the previous method there was only the mere act of breathing in and breathing out with nothing else to be done, and because from this point onwards, effort must be made in the arising of knowledge and so on, therefore, in that previous passage, the Pali was stated by way of the present tense as "He knows: 'I breathe in,' he knows: 'I breathe out.'" But from this point onwards, to show the mode of the arising of knowledge and so on which is to be performed, the Pali is presented by way of the future tense in the manner of "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in," and so forth.

"Calming the bodily formation... pe... he trains" means that while calming, further calming, ceasing, and especially quieting the bodily formation known as the coarse inhalation and exhalation, he trains, thinking: "I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out."

In this regard, coarseness, subtlety, and calming should be understood as follows: For this monk, in the period before he has grasped the meditation subject, both the body and the mind are coarse along with distress (sadaratha). While the coarseness of the body and mind has not yet been calmed, the inhalations and exhalations are also coarse; they occur with great strength, and the nose being insufficient, he remains breathing in and out through the mouth.
92: When both the body and the mind are grasped, they become calm and particularly tranquil. When they have become tranquil, the in-breaths and out-breaths occur subtly, reaching a state where one must reflect, "Do they still exist, or do they exist no more?" For example, a man who has been running, or has come down from a mountain, or has lowered a heavy burden from his head, has coarse in-breaths and out-breaths while standing. Breathing through the nose is not enough, so he stands breathing through his mouth as well. But when he has dispelled that fatigue, bathed and drunk, and lies down in the cool shade with a wet cloth on his chest, his in-breaths and out-breaths become subtle, reaching a state where one must reflect, "Do they still exist, or do they exist no more?" In the same way, for this monk, in the period before grasping the breaths... (it should be understood in detail thus). This is because, in the period before grasping, he did not have the advertence, the bringing to mind, and the attention: "I shall calm the coarse bodily formations." But in the period of grasping, he has such attention. Therefore, the bodily formation is subtler in the period of grasping than in the period before grasping. Hence, the ancient teachers said: "When the body and mind are agitated, the bodily formation occurs excessively. When the body is not agitated, it occurs subtly." Although coarse at the beginning of grasping, it is subtle at the access to the first jhāna. Although coarse at that access to the first jhāna, it is subtle in the first jhāna. Although coarse in the first jhāna and at the access to the second jhāna, it is subtle in the second jhāna. Although coarse in the second jhāna and at the access to the third jhāna, it is subtle in the third jhāna. Although coarse in the third jhāna and at the access to the fourth jhāna, it is extremely subtle in the fourth jhāna, even reaching the state of non-occurrence. This is the opinion of the Dīghabhāṇakas and the Saṃyuttabhāṇakas. The Majjhimabhāṇakas, however, desire it to be even subtler at the access to each higher jhāna than in the preceding lower jhāna, saying: "It is coarse in the first jhāna and subtle at the access to the second jhāna." According to the opinion of all teachers, the bodily formation occurring in the period before grasping is calmed in the period of grasping. The bodily formation occurring in the period of grasping is calmed at the access to the first jhāna... and so on, and the bodily formation occurring at the access to the fourth jhāna is calmed in the fourth jhāna. This is the method in the way of Samatha.
93:
In Vipassanā, the bodily formation (in-breath and out-breath) that occurs when [mind-and-matter] have not yet been grasped is coarse; it is subtle when the great elements (mahābhūta) are grasped. That bodily formation which is subtle when the great elements are grasped is coarse compared to the bodily formation occurring when derived matter (upādārūpa) is grasped; it is subtle when derived matter is grasped. That bodily formation which is subtle when derived matter is grasped is coarse compared to when all matter is grasped; it is subtle when all matter is grasped. That bodily formation which is subtle when all matter is grasped is coarse compared to when the immaterial (nāma) is grasped; it is subtle when the immaterial is grasped. That bodily formation which is subtle when the immaterial is grasped is coarse compared to when both matter and the immaterial are grasped; it is subtle when both matter and the immaterial are grasped. That bodily formation which is subtle when both matter and the immaterial are grasped is coarse compared to when the causes are grasped; it is subtle when the causes are grasped. That bodily formation which is subtle when the causes are grasped is coarse compared to when mind-and-matter together with their causes are seen; it is subtle when mind-and-matter together with their causes are seen. That bodily formation which is subtle when mind-and-matter together with their causes are seen is coarse compared to Vipassanā that takes the three characteristics as its object; it is subtle when Vipassanā takes the three characteristics as its object. That bodily formation which is subtle when Vipassanā takes the three characteristics as its object is coarse in weak Vipassanā; it is subtle in strong Vipassanā. In that Vipassanā, just as in the method previously stated, the subsiding of each preceding bodily formation by the succeeding one should be understood. Thus, in this Vipassanā, the state of being coarse, the state of being subtle, and the subsiding should be understood. This is the sequential explanation of the terms of the first tetrad taught by way of contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) in this mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati).

Since in this discourse on mindfulness of breathing, only this first tetrad is taught by way of the meditation subject for a beginner (ādikammika), while the other three tetrads are taught by way of contemplation of feelings, mind, and mental objects for one who has attained jhāna in this [first tetrad], therefore, a clansman (kulaputta) who is a beginner, wishing to develop this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing and reach Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) through insight having the four jhānas of mindfulness of breathing as its proximate cause, should perform all duties such as purification of virtue in the manner stated in the Visuddhimagga. Then, he should learn the meditation subject with the five-fold connection from a teacher endowed with the seven qualities. Here, the five connections are: learning (uggaha), questioning (paripucchā), appearance (upaṭṭhāna), absorption (appanā), and characteristic (lakkhaṇa). Among these, learning (uggaha) means the learning of the meditation subject. Questioning (paripucchā) means the discussion and questioning about the meditation subject. Appearance (upaṭṭhāna) means the appearance of the meditation subject (the counterpart sign). Absorption (appanā) means the completion or development of the meditation subject. Characteristic (lakkhaṇa) means the characteristic of the meditation subject; it means noting the nature of the meditation subject as 'this meditation subject has such a characteristic.'

A person learning the meditation subject with the five-fold connection in this way does not weary himself nor trouble the teacher. Therefore, having had a little instruction and having recited it for a long time, and having thus learned the meditation subject with the five-fold connection, he should avoid dwellings with the eighteen faults and live in a lodging endowed with the five qualities. Having cut off minor impediments, finished his meal, and dispelled the drowsiness following the meal, he should sit comfortably and gladden his heart by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem. Then, without omitting even a single word of the meditation subject learned from the teacher, he should attend to the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing. Here, this is the sequence of attention: counting (gaṇanā), following (anubandhanā), touching (phusanā), fixing (ṭhapanā), observing (sallakkhaṇā), turning away (vivaṭṭanā), purification (pārisuddhi), and reviewing (paṭipassanā). Among these eight, counting (gaṇanā) is just counting. Following (anubandhanā) is following after [the breath]. Touching (phusanā) is the place of contact (the tip of the nose or the upper lip). Fixing (ṭhapanā) is absorption (appanā). Observing (sallakkhaṇā) is insight (vipassanā). Turning away (vivaṭṭanā) is the Path (magga). Purification (pārisuddhi) is the Fruition (phala). Reviewing (paṭipassanā) is reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā). Among these sequences of attention, a beginner should first attend to this meditation subject by way of counting (gaṇanā). In counting, one should not count less than five, nor more than ten, and there should be no interruption in between. For if one counts less than five, the mind becomes agitated like a herd of cattle shut in a narrow pen.
94:
This meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-kammaṭṭhāna) should be attended to without omitting even a single word or phrase learned from the teacher. In this regard, the method of attention is as follows:

"Counting (gaṇanā), following (anubandhanā),
Touching (phusanā), fixing (ṭhapanā), noting (sallakkhaṇā),
Turning away (vivaṭṭanā), purification (pārisuddhi),
And reviewing them (paṭipassanā)."

Among these eight, counting (gaṇanā) is just counting. Following (anubandhanā) is following after. Touching (phusanā) is the place of contact. Fixing (ṭhapanā) is absorption (appanā). Noting (sallakkhaṇā) is insight (vipassanā). Turning away (vivaṭṭanā) is the path (magga). Purification (pārisuddhi) is fruition (phala). Reviewing them (paṭipassanā) is reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā).

Among these methods of attention, this clansman (kulaputta) who is a beginner should first attend to this meditation by counting. When counting, one should not stop below five, nor go beyond ten, and should not show a break in between. For one who counts below five, the mind becomes agitated in a narrow space, like a herd of cattle shut in a narrow pen. For one who counts beyond ten, the mind tends to rely only on the number. For one who shows a break in between, the mind wavers, thinking, "Has my meditation reached the peak or not?" Therefore, one should count while avoiding these faults.

When counting, one should first count with slow counting, like the counting of a grain measurer. A grain measurer, having filled the measure, says "one" and pours it out; when filling it again, if he sees any rubbish and removes it, he says "one, one." The same method applies to "two, two" and so on. In the same way, this yogi should take the breath that becomes clear among the in-breaths and out-breaths and count, starting with "one, one" up to "ten, ten," noting whatever arises. To the yogi who counts in this way, the out-breaths and in-breaths become clear.

Then, that yogi should give up the slow counting like a grain measurer and count with fast counting, like the counting of a cowherd. A skilled cowherd, taking pebbles and the like in his pocket and holding a rope and a stick in his hand, goes to the cow pen early in the morning, strikes the cows on their backs, and sitting on the top of the gatepost, counts each cow as it reaches the gate, saying "one, two," and dropping a pebble each time. The herd of cattle, having stayed miserably in a narrow place throughout the three watches of the night, comes out rushing and huddling together when they exit. That cowherd counts rapidly, "three, four, five, ten." In the same way, for that yogi, according to the previous method...
95:
For one who counts, the in-breaths and out-breaths become clear and move back and forth rapidly and repeatedly. Then, that yogi, knowing "they move back and forth repeatedly," without following the air inside or outside, should take only what reaches the nostrils and count rapidly: "one, two, three, four, five; one, two, three, four, five, six; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven... eight, nine, ten." For in the meditation connected with counting, the mind becomes one-pointed by the power of counting alone, like a boat held in a swift current by the support of a pole.

To the yogi who counts rapidly in this way, the meditation appears as if it proceeds without interruption. Then, knowing "it proceeds without interruption," without following the air inside or outside, one should count with speed as before. For one who sends the mind inside along with the incoming air, the interior becomes as if struck by wind or as if filled with fat. For one who sends the mind outside along with the outgoing air, the mind becomes distracted by the many objects outside. Meditation is successful only for one who develops it by placing mindfulness at the place of contact. Therefore, it is said, "Without following the air inside or outside, one should count with speed as before."

How long should one count? One should count as long as mindfulness stands firm on the object of in-breaths and out-breaths without counting. Counting is only for the purpose of cutting off wandering thoughts that spread outside and establishing mindfulness on the object of in-breaths and out-breaths.

After attending by counting in this way, one should attend by following (anubandhanā). Following means stopping the counting and following the in-breaths and out-breaths continuously with mindfulness. That following is not by way of following the beginning, middle, and end. The faults of following the beginning, middle, and end, and following after them, have already been stated before.

Therefore, one attending by following should not attend by way of beginning, middle, and end, but rather by way of touching (phusanā) and fixing (ṭhapanā). There is no separate attention by way of touching and fixing as there is with counting and following. One who counts only at the place of contact attends by both counting and touching. Stopping the counting there and following them with mindfulness, and fixing the mind by way of absorption (appanā), one attends by way of following, touching, and fixing...
96:
It is said, "he pays attention." This meaning should be understood through the similes of the lame man and the gatekeeper mentioned in the Commentaries, and the simile of the saw mentioned in this very Pali text.

Among these, this is the simile of the lame man—For example, a lame man, having swung a swing for a mother and child playing with it, sits right there at the foot of the swing-post. He sees both ends and the middle of the swing-plank as it successively comes and goes, yet he does not need to strive to see those two ends and the middle. In the same way, the monk, standing by the power of mindfulness at the foot of the post of binding—the tip of the nose or the upper lip—swings the swing of in-breaths and out-breaths. Staying right there at that sign with mindfulness, he follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breaths and out-breaths as they successively come and go at the point of contact, and he watches, fixing his mind (citta) only at that point of contact. He does not need to strive to see that beginning, middle, and end. This is the simile of the lame man.

This is the simile of the gatekeeper—For example, a gatekeeper does not examine people inside or outside the city, asking, "Who are you? Where have you come from? Where are you going? What is in your hand?" Those people are not the gatekeeper's concern. Indeed, he only examines each person as they arrive at the gate. In the same way, for this monk, the air that has entered inside and the air that has gone outside are not his concern; it should be understood that only the air as it arrives at the nostrils is his concern. This is the simile of the gatekeeper.
