As for the simile of the saw, it has already been taught in this Pali text by the method beginning with "the sign, the in-breath, the out-breath." Here, however, it should be understood that for that practitioner, merely not paying attention to the coming and going [of the breath] is beneficial.

For someone paying attention to this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), the sign (nimitta) appears before long, and the fixing (ṭhapanā) called absorption (appanā), adorned with the remaining jhana factors, is accomplished. For another, however, from the time of paying attention by way of counting (gaṇanā)—just as when a person with an agitated body sits on a couch or a chair, the couch or chair sags and creaks, and the bedspread becomes wrinkled; but when a person with a non-agitated body sits, the couch or chair neither sags nor creaks, and the bedspread does not wrinkle, being like a couch filled with cotton...
97:
Why is that? Because a non-agitated body is light. In the same way, from the time of paying attention by way of counting (gaṇanā), as the physical distress is calmed through the successive cessation of gross in-breaths and out-breaths, both the body and the mind become light. It is as if the body has reached a state of floating in the air.

When the gross in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased for that person, the mind occurs with the sign of subtle in-breaths and out-breaths as its object. When those subtle ones also cease, the mind continues to occur with a sign of in-breaths and out-breaths that are successively subtler and subtler than that. This meaning should be understood by the simile of the bronze gong to be mentioned later.

Unlike other meditation subjects which become clearer and clearer at higher stages, this mindfulness of breathing is not like that. This meditation subject, for one who develops it further and further, becomes subtle and does not even appear [clearly]. When the meditation subject does not appear in this way, that monk should not get up from his seat, thinking, "I will ask the teacher," or "Now my meditation subject is lost." For one who goes after breaking the posture, the meditation subject becomes something entirely new. Therefore, it should be brought back from the point of contact while sitting just as he was.

This is the method for bringing it back—That monk, knowing the state of the meditation subject's non-appearance, should reflect as follows: "Where do these in-breaths and out-breaths exist, and where do they not exist? For whom do they exist, and for whom do they not exist?" Then, while reflecting thus, he understands: "These in-breaths and out-breaths do not exist for one inside the mother's womb, they do not exist for those submerged in water, likewise they do not exist for unconscious beings (asaññasatta), for the dead, for those who have attained the fourth jhana, for those existing in the fine-material and immaterial realms, and for those who have attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)." Then he should admonish himself thus: "O wise one, you are not one in the mother's womb, nor submerged in water, nor an unconscious being, nor dead, nor one who has attained the fourth jhana, nor one existing in the fine-material or immaterial realms, nor one who has attained the attainment of cessation. You certainly have in-breaths and out-breaths; it is only because of the dullness of your wisdom that you are unable to perceive them." Then, he should establish his mind at the natural point of contact and proceed with paying attention. For these in-breaths and out-breaths occur by striking the nostril for a long-nosed person, and the upper lip for a short-nosed person. Therefore, he should establish the sign [thinking], "They strike this particular place." Regarding this matter, the Blessed One said: "Monks, I do not say that the development of mindfulness of breathing is for one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension." Although all meditation subjects occur only for one who is mindful and has clear comprehension...
98:
Every meditation subject succeeds only for a person who is mindful and possesses clear comprehension. However, for one who attends to a meditation subject other than this Ānāpānassati, it also becomes clear. This Ānāpānassati meditation subject is profound and involves a profound development. It is the ground for the attention only of Great Beings (Mahāpurisa) such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddha. It is neither inferior, nor is it a meditation subject cultivated by inferior beings. In whatever manner it is attended to, in that very manner it becomes peaceful and subtle. Therefore, strong mindfulness and wisdom are required in this Ānāpānassati.

Indeed, just as when sewing fine cloth, a fine needle is required, and even finer than that, a tool to pierce the eye of the needle; even so, when developing this meditation subject which is like fine cloth, mindfulness which is like the needle and strong wisdom associated with that mindfulness which is like the tool to pierce the eye of the needle are required. A monk endowed with such mindfulness and wisdom should not search for those in-breaths and out-breaths anywhere other than the place they normally touch.

For example, a farmer, after plowing the field, releases the oxen and lets them head towards the grazing ground while he rests in the shade to relax. Then those oxen might enter the forest with speed. A skilled farmer, wishing to catch them and yoke them again, does not wander in the forest following their tracks. Instead, taking a rope and a goad, he goes directly to the watering hole where the oxen descend and waits there, either sitting or lying down. Then, after the oxen have grazed all day, they descend to the watering hole, bathe, drink, and emerge. Seeing them standing there, he binds them with the rope, prods them with the goad, brings them back, yokes them, and performs his work again. In the same way, that monk should not search for those in-breaths and out-breaths anywhere other than the place they normally touch. Holding the rope of mindfulness and the goad of wisdom, he should fix his mind on the place of normal contact and maintain his attention. To the monk who attends in this way, those in-breaths and out-breaths will soon appear, just as the oxen appear at the watering hole. Then, binding them with the rope of mindfulness and yoking them at that very place, he should repeatedly apply himself to the meditation subject, prodding with the goad of wisdom. To him who applies himself in this way, the sign (nimitta) soon appears. That sign, however, is not the same for everyone. Some teachers say that to some it appears producing a pleasant touch like a tuft of wool, or a tuft of cotton, or a draft of air.
99:
The following is the decision in the Commentaries: This sign appears to some like the color of a star, like a gem, or like a pearl. To some, it has a rough touch and appears like a cotton seed or like a wooden peg made of heartwood. To some, it appears like a long sash, like a garland of flowers, or like a crest of smoke. To some, it appears like a spread-out spider's web, like a film of clouds, like a lotus flower, like a chariot wheel, like the orb of the moon, or like the orb of the sun.

To make the appearance of the sign clear: while many monks were sitting together after reciting a Sutta, one monk asked, "How does this Sutta appear to you?" One said, "To me, it appears like a great river flowing from a mountain top." Another said, "To me, it appears like a forest range." Another said, "To me, it appears like a great tree with cool shade, full of branches and laden with fruit." To those monks, that single Sutta appeared differently because of the diversity of their perception (saññā). Similarly, it should be understood that this single meditation subject appears differently because of the diversity of perception. For this sign is born of perception, has perception as its source, and originates from perception; therefore, it should be understood that it appears differently due to the diversity of perception.

When the sign has appeared in this way, the monk should go to his teacher and report, "Venerable sir, an object of such a nature has appeared to me." The teacher should say, "Friend, this is the sign; O good man, attend to this meditation subject again and again." Then, he should fix his mind on the sign itself. From this point onwards, development (bhāvanā) occurs by way of fixing (ṭhapanā). As the ancients said:

"The wise one, fixing the mind on the sign,
And developing various aspects,
Binds his own mind to the in-breaths and out-breaths."

From the moment the sign appears to him, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are suppressed, the defilements (kilesa) subside, and the mind is concentrated with access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). Then, he should not attend to that sign by way of its color, nor should he contemplate it by way of its characteristics. Rather, just as a queen consort carefully protects the embryo of a Universal Monarch, or a farmer protects the ripening ear of hill rice, he should carefully protect it by avoiding the seven unsuitable (asappāya) things such as the dwelling place and by following the seven suitable (sappāya) things. Having protected it in this way, and causing it to grow and flourish by way of repeated attention, he should fulfill the ten kinds of skill in absorption (appanā-kosalla) and balance his energy. To him who thus strives...
100:
For that yogi who strives according to the sequence stated in the Visuddhimagga, the fourfold and fivefold jhanas arise in that counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta). Having attained these fourfold and fivefold jhanas, that bhikkhu, desiring to reach the fruit by developing the meditation subject through the power of insight and the path, first masters that very jhana in five ways. Then, having defined mind and matter (nāmarūpa), he begins insight (vipassanā).

How does he begin? That bhikkhu, having emerged from the attainment, sees that the cause of the in-breaths and out-breaths is the physical body (karajakāya) and the mind. Just as when a blacksmith's bellows are being blown, the air moves depending on the bellows and the appropriate effort of the man blowing them, even so, the in-breaths and out-breaths occur depending on the body and the mind. Thereafter, he defines the in-breaths, out-breaths, and the body as "matter" (rūpa), and the mind and the states associated with that mind as "mind" (nāma).

Having thus defined mind and matter, he searches for the cause of that mind and matter. While searching, he sees that cause and, by contemplating the occurrence of mind and matter in the three periods of time, he overcomes doubt. Having overcome doubt, by the power of the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa), he applies the three characteristics: "impermanent, suffering, and non-self." Then, abandoning the ten imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa) such as illumination (obhāsa) that arise in the early stage of the insight into arising and passing away (udayabbaya-nupassanā), he defines the knowledge of insight into arising and passing away, which is free from imperfections, as "the path." Thereafter, abandoning arising (udaya) and reaching the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅga), and by continuously contemplating dissolution, he becomes weary of, detached from, and liberated from all formations (saṅkhāra) that appear as fearful. Progressing in order, he reaches the four Noble Paths and, established in the fruit of Arahatship, he reaches the end of the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). He thus becomes the supreme recipient of offerings in the world including the devas. To this extent, the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati-samādhi-bhāvanā), beginning with counting and ending with insight, is completed. This is the explanation of the first tetrad in all its aspects.

In the remaining three tetrads, however, since there is no separate method for developing the meditation subject, their meaning should be understood in this way through the method of explaining the terms in sequence. "Pītipaṭisaṃvedī" (experiencing rapture) means that he trains, thinking, "I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out," while making rapture clear and evident. In this context, rapture is made evident in two ways: by way of the object and by way of non-delusion.

How is rapture made evident by way of the object? He enters the two jhanas accompanied by rapture. For him, at the moment of attainment, rapture is made evident by way of the object through the acquisition of the jhana, because the object is clearly experienced.
101:
How is rapture clearly known through non-delusion? Having entered the two jhanas accompanied by rapture (the first and second jhanas) and having emerged from them, he reviews the rapture associated with the jhana in terms of its destruction and passing away. For him, at the moment of insight, rapture is clearly known through non-delusion by penetrating the characteristics. In this same way, the remaining terms should also be understood according to their meaning. Here, there is this distinction: happiness (sukha) is clearly known through the power of three jhanas (first, second, and third). Mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra) should be understood as being clearly known through the power of all four jhanas. Mental formations refer to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha). "Tranquillizing the mental formation" means tranquillizing and ceasing the gross mental formations. This matter should be understood in detail according to the method stated for the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra). Furthermore, in this tetrad, in the term "pīti" (rapture), feeling is spoken of with rapture as the head; but in the term "sukha" (happiness), feeling is spoken of by its own nature. In the two terms regarding mental formations, according to the word of the Buddha, "Perception and feeling are mental; these states are bound to the mind, they are mental formations," it refers to feeling associated with perception. Thus, it should be understood that this tetrad is spoken of by way of the contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā).

In the third tetrad also, the mind is to be understood as being clearly known through the power of the four jhanas. "Gladdening the mind" (abhippamodayaṃ cittaṃ) means he trains, thinking, "I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out," while gladdening, rejoicing, cheering, and exhilarating the mind. In that context, gladdening occurs in two ways: by the power of concentration (samādhi) and by the power of insight (vipassanā).

How is it by the power of concentration? He enters the two jhanas accompanied by rapture. At the moment of attainment, he gladdens and rejoices the mind with the associated rapture. How is it by the power of insight? Having entered the two jhanas accompanied by rapture and having emerged from them, he reviews the rapture associated with the jhana in terms of its destruction and passing away. Thus, at the moment of insight, he gladdens and rejoices the mind by making the rapture associated with the jhana the object. A person who trains in this way is said to "train, thinking, 'I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out,' while gladdening the mind."

"Steadying the mind" (samādahaṃ cittaṃ) means placing and establishing the mind evenly on the object by the power of the first jhana and so forth. Or else, for one who has entered those jhanas and emerged, and who reviews the mind associated with the jhana in terms of its destruction and passing away, momentary one-pointedness of mind (khaṇika-cittekaggatā) arises at the moment of insight through the penetration of the characteristics. Since he places and establishes the mind evenly on the object by the power of that arisen momentary one-pointedness of mind, he is said to "train, thinking, 'I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out,' while steadying the mind."
102:
"Liberating the mind" means liberating the mind from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by means of the first jhāna, especially liberating it; from initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) by the second jhāna; from rapture (pīti) by the third jhāna; and from pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha) by the fourth jhāna, especially liberating it (one breathes in and out). Or else, having entered those jhānas and emerged from them, one contemplates the mind associated with the jhāna in terms of its exhaustion and fall. At the moment of insight (vipassanā), that person liberates the mind from the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā); from the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā); from the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā); from delight (nandi) through the contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā); from lust through the contemplation of fading away (virāgānupassanā); from origination through the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā); and from grasping (ādāna) through the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā), especially liberating it, one breathes in and breathes out. Therefore, it is said: "He trains, 'I shall breathe in liberating the mind; I shall breathe out liberating the mind.'" Thus, it should be understood that this fourth tetrad (catukka) is taught by way of the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā).

In the fourth tetrad (catuttha-catukka), regarding the term "contemplating impermanence" (aniccānupassī), first, impermanence (anicca) should be known, the nature of impermanence (aniccata) should be known, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) should be known, and the one contemplating impermanence (aniccānupassī) should be known. Therein, "impermanence" refers to the five aggregates. Why? Because they have the nature of arising, falling away, and change (uppāda, vaya, aññathatta). "The nature of impermanence" is the arising, falling away, and change of those very aggregates. Or it means non-existence after having been, or the destruction of the arisen aggregates by way of momentary dissolution (khaṇabhanga) without remaining in that same state. "Contemplation of impermanence" is the repeated contemplation of materiality and so on as "impermanent" by way of that nature of impermanence. "One contemplating impermanence" is the person endowed with that contemplation. Therefore, it should be understood that such a person, while breathing in and out, trains in this Dispensation: "Contemplating impermanence, I shall breathe in; contemplating impermanence, I shall breathe out."

Regarding the term "contemplating fading away" (virāgānupassī), there are two kinds of fading away: fading away as destruction (khaya-virāga) and absolute fading away (accanta-virāga). Therein, "fading away as destruction" is the momentary dissolution (khaṇabhanga) of formations (sankhāra). "Absolute fading away" is Nibbāna. "Contemplation of fading away" is the insight (vipassanā) and the path (magga) that occur by way of seeing both of these. Being endowed with these two kinds of contemplation, while breathing in and out, one trains: "Contemplating fading away, I shall breathe in; contemplating fading away, I shall breathe out." The same method applies to the term "contemplating cessation" (nirodhānupassī).

Regarding the term "contemplating relinquishment" (paṭinissaggānupassī), there are also two kinds of relinquishment: relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga). Relinquishment itself is the contemplation, hence it is called "contemplation of relinquishment"; this is a designation for insight and the path. Insight gives up the defilements along with the aggregates and volitional formations by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga). By seeing the fault in formations, [it enters into] the opposite of those formations...
103:
Because it enters into Nibbāna by way of being inclined towards Nibbāna, it is called "relinquishment as giving up" (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) and "relinquishment as entering into" (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga). The path gives up the defilements along with the aggregates and volitional formations by way of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna); it also enters into Nibbāna by making it the object. Therefore, it is called relinquishment as giving up and relinquishment as entering into. Both insight and the path are called "contemplation" (anupassanā) because of the repeated viewing of the preceding knowledges. Being endowed with these two kinds of contemplation of relinquishment, while breathing in and out, one trains: "Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe in; contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe out."

Herein, "contemplating impermanence" is taught by way of tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā). "Contemplating fading away" is taught by way of insight that is stronger than that, capable of becoming dispassionate towards formations. "Contemplating cessation" is taught by way of insight that is even stronger, capable of making defilements cease. "Contemplating relinquishment" is taught by way of extremely sharp insight that is in close proximity to the path. Where the path is also attained, that path is indeed undivided. Thus, this tetrad is taught by way of pure insight (suddha-vipassanā), whereas the preceding three tetrads were taught by way of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā).

## The Explanation of the Matrix of Mindfulness of Breathing is finished.

Now, in order to analyze the established matrix in due order, the section beginning with "Idha means in this view (idhāti imissā diṭṭhiyā)" is commenced. Therein, by the ten terms beginning with "in this view," only the Dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha, known as the three trainings (sikkhā), is spoken of. That Dispensation is called "view" (diṭṭhi) because it was seen by the Blessed One; "patience" (khanti) because of His approval; "relish" (ruci) because of His liking; "taking up" (ādāya) because of His taking it up; "Dhamma" because of its intrinsic nature; "Vinaya" because it is to be trained in; "Dhamma-Vinaya" because of both; "teaching" (pāvacana) because it is taught in various ways; "holy life" (brahmacariya) because it is the best conduct; and "Teacher's Instruction" (satthu-sāsana) because it provides instruction.

Therefore, in the terms beginning with "in this view," the meaning should be understood as: in this Dispensation seen by the Buddha, in this Dispensation approved by the Buddha, in this Dispensation liked by the Buddha, in this Dispensation taken up by the Buddha, in this Dhamma of the Buddha, in this Vinaya of the Buddha, in this Dhamma-Vinaya of the Buddha, in this teaching of the Buddha, in this holy life of the Buddha, and in this Teacher's Instruction of the Buddha. Alternatively, this entire teaching known as the three trainings is called "view" because it was seen by the Blessed One, because it is a condition for right view, and because it is preceded by right view. It is called "patience" because it is approved by the Blessed One. It is called "relish" because it is liked. It is called "taking up" because...
104:
It is called *ādāyo* (by way of taking). It is called 'Dhamma' because it bears (upholds) the person who practices it (within their own continuum) so that they do not fall into the four woeful states. That Dhamma (or the Dispensation) itself is called 'Vinaya' because it disciplines the side of defilement. Because that teaching is both Dhamma and Vinaya, it is called 'Dhamma-Vinaya'. Or, it is called 'Dhamma-Vinaya' because this (collection of the three trainings) disciplines unwholesome states by means of wholesome states. Therefore, it was said: "Gotamī, you should know of certain qualities: 'These qualities lead to dispassion, not to passion...' Gotamī, you should definitely bear in mind: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction'" (A.Ni. 8.53, Cūḷava. 406). Or, it is called 'Dhamma-Vinaya' because it disciplines by means of the Dhamma, not by means of sticks and so forth. This was also said:

"Some discipline with sticks, with hooks, and with whips;
But the Elephant [Nālāgiri] was disciplined by the Great Sage without stick or weapon."
(Ma.Ni. 2.352, Cūḷava. 342).

Likewise, "For the wise who are led by the Dhamma, what envy could there be?" (Mahāva. 63). Or, it is called 'Dhamma-Vinaya' because it is the means of disciplining for the sake of Nibbāna (or the Fruit of Arahantship). Indeed, this discipline is for the purpose of attaining the faultless Dhamma of Nibbāna, not for the purpose of worldly gains or the pleasures of existence. Therefore, the Blessed One said in detail: "Monks, this holy life is not lived for the sake of deceiving (tricking) people..." (Itivu. 35, A.Ni. 4.25). The Elder Puṇṇa also said: "Friend [Sāriputta], the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging" (Ma.Ni. 1.259). Or, it is called 'Vinaya' because it leads to pure Nibbāna. It is called 'Dhamma-Vinaya' because it leads from the states of Saṃsāra or states such as sorrow to pure Nibbāna. Or, it is called 'Dhamma-Vinaya' because it is the discipline of the Dhamma, not that of the sectarians. Indeed, the Blessed One is the Dhamma personified; this discipline belongs only to that Blessed One. Or, because only the Dhammas (phenomena) are to be known with higher knowledge, fully understood, abandoned, developed, and realized; therefore, this is a discipline regarding Dhammas, not regarding beings or souls, hence 'Dhamma-Vinaya'. It is called 'Pavacana' because it is the preeminent speech compared to the words of others due to its richness in meaning and phrasing; 'Pavacana' itself is 'Pāvacana'. It is 'Brahmacariya' (the holy life) because it is a conduct superior to all other conducts. It is 'Satthusāsana' (the Teacher's instruction) because it is the instruction of the Blessed One who is the Teacher of gods and men; or it is 'Satthusāsana' because the instruction itself acts as the Teacher. For it was said: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya I have taught and prescribed shall be your teacher after I am gone" (Dī.Ni. 2.216); thus, the Dhamma-Vinaya itself is called the Teacher. In this way, the meaning of these terms should be understood. Furthermore, because only in this Dispensation does there exist a monk who brings about concentration through mindfulness of breathing in all its aspects, and not elsewhere, it should be understood that the restriction was made in various places as 'in this [Dispensation]' and 'herein'. This is the explanation of the meaning of the matrix term 'Idha' (Herein).
105:
By the phrase beginning with "puthujjanakalyāṇako," the literal definition of the word 'Bhikkhu' is not given; rather, only the specific Bhikkhu intended in this context is shown. Therein, a 'noble worldling' (*puthujjana-kalyāṇaka*) is one who is a worldling because defilements are not yet eradicated, and noble because of being endowed with practice such as virtue (*sīla*); 'puthujjana-kalyāṇa' is the same as 'puthujjana-kalyāṇaka'. A 'trainee' (*sekha*) is one who trains in higher virtue and so forth; he is either a Stream-enterer, a Once-returner, or a Non-returner. One of 'unshakable nature' (*akuppadhamma*) is an Arahant, because he possesses the Dhamma of the Fruit of Arahantship which is without decay and cannot be shaken. Indeed, even that Arahant develops this concentration through mindfulness of breathing.

In the explanation of 'forest' (*arañña*), according to the Vinaya method, it first appears as: "Excepting the village and its precincts, the remainder is the forest" (Pārā. 92). According to the Suttanta method, referring to a forest-dwelling monk, it appears as: "A forest lodging is one at least five hundred bow-lengths away" (Pāci. 573). However, both the Vinaya and Suttanta methods are figurative (*pariyāya*) teachings, whereas the Abhidhamma is the non-figurative (*nippariyāya*) teaching. Therefore, to show the forest by the Abhidhamma method, it is said: "Having gone out beyond the threshold (*indakhīla*)"; this means having gone outside the threshold. There is also a variant reading "nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlaṃ," which means having passed the gate-threshold and being outside. Here, 'indakhīla' refers to the threshold (gate-pillar) of either a village or a city.

In the explanation of 'the foot of a tree' (*rukkhamūla*), since the foot of a tree is well-known, its definition is not given, but the phrase beginning with "yatttha" (where) is stated. Therein, "yattha" means at whichever tree-foot. It is called "āsana" (seat) because one sits there. "Paññatta" means prepared (laid out). The words beginning with "mañco vā" (or a couch) are terms describing the varieties of seats. Indeed, a couch is also mentioned among seats here because it is a place for sitting. That couch is one of the four types: *masāraka*, *bundikābaddha*, *kuḷīrapādaka*, or *āhaccapādaka*. A chair (*pīṭha*) is likewise one of those same types. "Bhisī" (bolster/cushion) is one of the following: a wool-bolster, a cloth-bolster, a bark-bolster, a grass-bolster, or a leaf-bolster. "Taṭṭikā" (mat) is a mat made by weaving palm leaves and so forth. "Cammakhaṇḍa" (skin-rug) is any piece of hide suitable for sitting. "Tiṇasanthara" (grass-mat) and so forth are mats made by bunching together grass and such. Therein, "tattha" means at that tree-foot. By the words beginning with "caṅkamati vā" (or walks), the suitability of the tree-foot for the exercise of the four postures is stated. By all the words beginning with "yattha," the dense shade of the tree-foot and its seclusion from people are expressed. "Kenaci" means with any group of companions. Wishing to expand on that group by analyzing it, he said: "either with laypeople or with monastics." "Anākiṇṇa" means uncrowded, not cramped. Around that lodging, for a distance of a *gāvuta* or half a *yojana*, there are mountain ranges or forest thickets...
106:
If a place is thick with rivers and no one can approach it at an improper time, this monastery, even if nearby, is called 'uncluttered' (anakiṇṇā). If a monastery is half a league or a league away, it is called 'uncluttered' simply because of its distance.

'Vihāra' refers to any remaining dwelling other than an aḍḍhayoga and so on. 'Aḍḍhayoga' is a house with a curved roof like a garuda's wing. 'Pāsāda' is a long mansion made by taking two gables. 'Hammiya' is a pinnacled mansion situated on an upper open-air level. 'Guhā' refers to brick caves, stone caves, wooden caves, or earth caves, as stated in the Khandhaka Commentary. However, in the Vibhaṅga Commentary, 'vihāra' is a dwelling with a walkway around it, showing places for the night and day only within. 'Guhā' is an earth cave suitable for obtaining light day and night. These two, mountain caves or earth caves, are specifically mentioned.

In the Matika, the present tense 'nisīdati' (he sits) is used by way of the characteristic common to all three times. But in this exposition (niddesa), the past participle 'nisinno' (seated) is used to show the completion of the act of sitting, because the practice of meditation arises for one who has already sat down. Since the body of one who sits keeping the body straight is upright, the Buddha said 'ujuka' (upright) and so forth, intending to show only the desired meaning without being overly concerned with the literal syllables. In that text, 'thito supaṇihito' means it remains upright because it has been placed upright; it does not mean it stays that way by itself.

'Pariggahaṭṭha' means the sense of being embraced. What is embraced? The liberation (niyyāna). What is liberation? Concentration on mindfulness of breathing itself is liberation, up to the path of arahantship. Therefore, it is called 'niyyānaṭṭha'; by the power of the word 'mukha' in the sense of 'chief', it means the sense of leading out from saṃsāra. 'Upaṭṭhānaṭṭha' is simply the sense of the nature of mindfulness. By all these words, the meaning is 'having established mindfulness which has liberation embraced'. Some teachers, however, explain: 'Pariggahaṭṭha is the sense of being embraced by mindfulness; niyyānaṭṭha is the sense of being the door for the entry and exit of the in-breaths and out-breaths.' It means 'having established mindfulness which has the door of exit and entry of the embraced in-breaths and out-breaths'.

'By thirty-two modes' is said by way of completely exhausting the in-breaths and out-breaths obtained in those various stages in due order. 'By the power of a long in-breath' means by the power of the in-breath called 'long' (dīgha) in the Matika. The same applies to the remaining terms. 'Ekaggatā' means the state of one-pointedness. 'Avikkhepa' means non-distraction. 'Ekaggatā' is the state of one-pointedness.
107:
Indeed, it is called 'avikkhepa' (non-distraction) because the mind does not wander among various objects. 'Pajānato' means for one who knows by way of non-delusion, or for one who experiences. Or it means for one who knows by way of making it an object, thinking, "Non-distraction has been attained by me." 'Tāya satiyā' means by that established mindfulness. 'Tena ñāṇena' means by that knowledge of non-distraction. In the phrase 'sato kārī hoti', since only mindfulness associated with knowledge is intended as 'mindfulness', it is said: "He is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and wisdom." Therefore, by the word 'sato' (mindful) alone, knowledge is also included.

'Addhānasaṅkhāte' means in the time called 'long' (dīgha). Indeed, a long path is called 'addhāna'. This time is also called 'addhāna' like a long path because of its length. Although "he breathes in" and "he breathes out" are spoken of separately for the in-breath and out-breath, they are spoken of again in combination as "he breathes in and breathes out" to show the continuous occurrence of meditation. 'Chando uppajjati' means zeal arises for the further increase of meditation. 'Sukhumataraṃ' (more subtle) is said because of the nature of calming. 'Pāmojjaṃ uppajjati' means joy arises due to the fulfillment of meditation. 'Assāsapassāsāpi cittaṃ vivaṭṭati' means when the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) arises depending on the in-breaths and out-breaths, the mind turns away (reverts) from the natural in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Upekkhā saṇṭhāti' means because there is no longer a need for effort to establish the mind again upon reaching access concentration or attainment concentration in that counterpart sign, it is called the well-establishment of equanimity-in-the-middle (tatramajjhattūpekkhā). In the phrase 'navahākārehi' (by nine modes), there are three modes spoken of as "he breathes in and breathes out" in the period before zeal arises from the start of meditation, three modes in the period after zeal arises but before joy arises, and three modes after joy arises; thus there are nine modes. 'Kāyo' (body) refers to the extremely subtle in-breaths and out-breaths in the sense of a group (samūha). The sign that arises depending on the natural in-breaths and out-breaths also receives the name 'in-breath and out-breath'. 'Upaṭṭhānaṃ sati' means mindfulness is called 'upaṭṭhāna' because it stands having approached that object. 'Anupassanā ñāṇaṃ' means the knowledge of contemplating the sign-body (nimittakāya) by way of serenity (samatha), and contemplating the mental body (nāmakāya) and material body (rūpakāya) by way of insight (vipassanā). 'Kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ' means that body is called 'upaṭṭhāna' because mindfulness stands having approached that group of in-breaths and out-breaths. 'No sati' means that body is not what is called mindfulness. 'Tāya satiyā' means by that mindfulness just mentioned. 'Tena ñāṇena' means...
108:
He contemplates with the knowledge just mentioned. "He contemplates that body" means that, following the body (the counterpart sign, the mental body, and the material body) as previously described through the power of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), he contemplates it either with knowledge associated with absorption (jhāna) or with insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa).

Although terms such as "body" (kāya) are not present in the Matrix (mātikā), because this first tetrad is taught by way of the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), the exposition (niddesa) of the term "body" is now made with reference to the phrase "the development of the foundation of mindfulness in the contemplation of the body in the body." "Contemplating the body in the body" means contemplating each specific body within the manifold body (the collection of inhalations and exhalations). Alternatively, it means contemplating only the body in the body, and not contemplating other phenomena. In the body, which is of the nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness, one does not contemplate it as permanent, pleasant, self, or beautiful; rather, one contemplates the body only as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Alternatively, it means contemplating only that body itself, without contemplating anything that might be grasped as "I," "mine," "woman," or "man" in the body. The same method applies to the three types to be mentioned above, such as "contemplating feelings in feelings." Mindfulness itself is called a "foundation of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna) because it is established (by approaching the object). The foundation of mindfulness associated with the contemplation of the body is called "the foundation of mindfulness in the contemplation of the body." The development of that foundation of mindfulness in the contemplation of the body is called "the development of the foundation of mindfulness in the contemplation of the body."

"That body" is spoken of as if it had already been shown, because the mental body (nāmakāya) and the material body (rūpakāya), which have not yet been shown below, are also included by the word "body." Contemplations such as impermanence are attainable only in the mental and material bodies, not in the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta). The meanings of "contemplation" (anupassanā) and "development" (bhāvanā) are just as previously stated. The phrase beginning with "by way of a long inhalation and exhalation" is spoken to show the benefits of the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). The abundance of mindfulness and the abundance of knowledge are the benefits of that mindfulness of breathing. In that context, "for one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind" is spoken with reference to the mental stability that occurs during the time of insight (vipassanā) for one who has attained absorption (jhāna). "Feelings are known" refers to feelings that are known by observing their arising in a general sense. "They arise clearly" means they arise clearly through [the observation of] their exhaustion, fall, and voidness. "They reach cessation clearly" means they reach destruction and breaking up clearly by observing their fall in a general sense. The same method applies to perception (saññā) and thought (vitakka). When these three are taught, the remaining material phenomena are also said to be taught. If it is asked, "Why are only these three taught?" it is because they are difficult to grasp. Among feelings, pleasant and painful feelings are clear. Equanimous feeling, however, is subtle and difficult to grasp, and thus not very clear. To that person, even that equanimous feeling becomes clear. Because perception grasps only the appearance...
109:
Because perception (saññā) grasps only the appearance, it cannot grasp the nature of things like impermanence as they truly are. Furthermore, because that perception is associated with insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) which grasps individual and general characteristics, it is very unclear. Yet, even that perception becomes clear to that person. Thought (vitakka) is difficult to grasp separately from knowledge because it resembles knowledge. It is true that thought resembles knowledge. As the Blessed One said: "Friend Visākha, whatever right view there is and whatever right intention there is, these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom." Even that thought becomes clear to that person. When these states that are difficult to grasp have been mentioned, it should be understood that the remaining material phenomena (rūpadhamma) have also been mentioned. In the exposition of these terms, having asked, "How do feelings that are known arise?" and without answering that question directly, by answering only regarding the clarity of the arising of feelings, it is meant that the clarity of feelings has been answered; thus, he said, "How is the arising of feelings known?" and so on. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Terms such as "the origination of ignorance" (avijjā-samudaya) and "the cessation of ignorance" (avijjā-nirodha) have the same meanings as stated below. In this same way, perception and thought should also be understood. However, in the section on thought (vitakka-vāra), instead of saying "the origination of contact" (phassa-samudaya) and "the cessation of contact" (phassa-nirodha), he said "the origination of perception" (saññā-samudaya) and "the cessation of perception" (saññā-nirodha). Why? Because thought has perception as its root. For was it not said: "Dependent on the diversity of perceptions, there arises the diversity of intentions"?

In the Pali passages such as "for one who attends [to it] as impermanence," in each respective section, the respective phenomenon should be applied in the manner of "for one who attends to feeling as impermanent," and so on. Feeling associated with insight (vipassanā) is unable to perform the function of insight and thus cannot be of assistance to insight knowledge. For that very reason, it is not included among the states partaking of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma). The function of perception associated with insight is also not clear; therefore, that perception certainly does not assist insight knowledge. Without thought (vitakka), the function of insight cannot exist. Only insight that has thought as its companion can perform its own function. The commentators said: "Wisdom, by its own nature, cannot determine the object as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; it can only determine it when thought strikes it again and again." How is this? It is like a goldsmith who, placing a coin on his hand and wishing to look at all its sides, is unable to turn it over with just the surface of his eyes, but is able to look at it from here and there by turning it over and over with his finger joints. In the same way, wisdom, by its own nature...
110:
Wisdom, by its own nature, is not able to decide upon an object through the aspect of impermanence and so forth. However, it is able to decide only upon the object that is given, having been taken up again and again by initial application (vitakka), which has the characteristic of directing [the mind] onto [the object] and the function of striking and thrashing, as if striking or turning [the object] over (Visuddhimagga 2, 568).

Therefore, because feeling (vedanā) and perception (saññā) are not helpful for insight, they are indicated in the singular as 'vedanāya saññāya' in various places, merely to show their characteristics. It is appropriate to say that 'vitakkānaṃ' is indicated in the plural in various places to show that just as there are many divisions of insight, there are just as many divisions of initial application.

Again, the statement beginning with 'dīghaṃ assāsapassāsavasena' is made to show the accomplishment of the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) and the fruit of that development. In that text, 'samodhāneti' means it places [the mind] on the object, or establishes it on the object. Even if there is no active effort to place it on the object, it is said to 'place' it simply because of the fulfillment of the development. 'Gocara' (domain) refers to the object of formations (saṅkhāra) at the moment of insight, and the object of Nibbāna at the moments of Path and Fruition. 'Samattha' means 'equal meaning' or it is called 'samattha' because it is the meaning of the four equal [factors]. In the remaining terms, the method is the same. 'Maggaṃ samodhāneti' refers only to the object of Nibbāna at the moment of Path and Fruition. 'Ayaṃ puggalo' (this person) refers to the practitioner (yogāvacara) who is devoted to the development of mindfulness of breathing. 'Imasmiṃ ārammaṇေ' (in this object) refers to the conditioned object known as the mental body (nāmakāya) and physical body (rūpakāya), which are included by the term 'kāya', and likewise to the object of Nibbāna in the Path. By the words beginning with 'yaṃ tassa', it is stated that the words 'ārammaṇa' (object) and 'gocara' (domain) have the same meaning. 'Tassa' means 'of that person'. 'Pajānāti' (he understands) means the person understands through wisdom. 'Ārammaṇassa upaṭṭhānaṃ' (the establishment of the object) is mindfulness established near the object of formations at the moment of insight, and near the object of Nibbāna at the moments of Path and Fruition. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object, just like 'attendance on the king' (rañño upaṭṭhānaṃ). 'Avikkhepa' (non-distraction) is concentration (samādhi). 'Adhiṭṭhāna' (foundation) is the aforementioned object of formations and the object of Nibbāna. Because the mind stays firm on that object, it is called 'adhiṭṭhāna'. 'Vodāna' (purification) is knowledge (ñāṇa). Because the mind is purified by that knowledge, it is called 'vodāna'. Concentration belonging to the side of sluggishness is 'equal' (sama) because it has reached the state of non-sluggishness; knowledge belonging to the side of agitation is 'equal' (sama) because it has reached the state of non-agitation. By that concentration and knowledge, at the moments of insight, Path, and Fruition...
111:
The state of being yoked together (yuganaddha) of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) is being taught. Mindfulness (sati), however, is beneficial in all circumstances and is called 'equal' (sama) because it assists in the equality of both serenity and insight. The object is also called 'equal' because it is the foundation for the equality of the three 'equal' factors: mindfulness, concentration, and knowledge.

'Anavajjaṭṭha' (the sense of blamelessness) is the blameless nature of insight. 'Nikkilesaṭṭha' (the sense of being without defilements) is the defilement-free nature of the Path. There is also a variant reading 'nikkilesaṭṭha'. 'Vodānaṭṭha' (the sense of purification) is the extremely pure nature of Fruition. 'Paramaṭṭha' (the supreme sense) is the nature of Nibbāna, which is superior to all dhammas.

'Paṭivijjhati' (he penetrates) means he penetrates and knows that particular nature without delusion. Here too, by the words 'ārammaṇassa upaṭṭhānaṃ' and so forth, right penetration (paṭivedha) is taught. Since the penetration of the sense of purification (vodānaṭṭha) is taught right here, the senses of blamelessness, freedom from defilements, and the supreme, which have the same characteristic as that sense of purification, are already taught by way of the 'Method of Characteristics' (lakkhaṇa-hāra). As it is said:

'When one dhamma is mentioned, all those dhammas that have the same characteristic are also mentioned; that method is called the Method of Characteristics.' (Netti. 4, 5 Niddesavāra).

In this context, 'anavajjaṭṭha' and 'nikkilesaṭṭha' are called 'samattha' because they are the benefit (attha) of the 'equal' dhamma known as non-distraction (avikkhepa). 'Vodānaṭṭha' is called 'samattha' because, with reference to the purification of the path of insight, the 'equal' dhamma itself is the meaning (attha). With reference to the purification of Fruition, it is called 'samattha' because it is the benefit of the 'equal' dhamma known as the purification of the Path. 'Paramaṭṭha' is called 'samattha' either because the 'equal' dhamma itself is the meaning, or because Nibbāna is the benefit, it is the benefit of all 'equal' dhammas. Having made the aforementioned various 'equal' (sama) and 'benefit' (samattha) terms into a single remainder of the same form (ekadesa-sarūpeka-sesa), it is stated: 'he penetrates the equal benefit' (samatthañca paṭivijjhati).

Faculties (indriya), powers (bala), and factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are obtained at the moments of insight, Path, and Fruition. The Path and the three purifications (visuddhi) are obtained only at the moments of Path and Fruition. Deliverance (vimokkha), clear vision (vijjā), and the knowledge of destruction (khaya-ñāṇa) are obtained only at the moment of the Path. Liberation (vimutti) and the knowledge of non-arising (anuppāda-ñāṇa) are obtained only at the moment of Fruition. The remaining dhammas are obtained at the moment of insight as well. In the section on dhammas (dhamma-vāra), in the passage 'he combines these dhammas in this object', Nibbāna should be excluded and the remaining dhammas should be understood as they apply. This teaching is given by way of generality (yebhuyya). The meanings not yet explained here are only those already explained below. Although the way of exit (niyyāna) is shown here by way of each tetrad, because each individual part included in a tetrad is also a supporting condition (upanissaya) for the way of exit, the way of exit is shown by way of each individual part. For there is no way of exit without each individual part.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Long In-breath and Out-breath is Finished.

In the description of the short [breath] (rassaniddesa), 'ittara-saṅkhāta' means occurring in a brief period of time. The remaining meanings should be understood according to the method already stated.
112: ## Explanation of Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī Among mental phenomena, because feeling (vedanā) is coarse and easy to understand, the Buddha first taught feeling, which experiences pleasant and unpleasant objects. Then, he taught perception (saññā), which takes the mode of the object of feeling, as in "whatever one feels, that one perceives." Then, he taught volition (cetanā), which constructs by the power of perception. Then, he taught contact (phassa) according to the teaching: "one who is touched feels, one who is touched perceives, one who is touched wills." Then, he taught attention (manasikāra), which has the characteristic common to all consciousness. By volition and so on, the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is taught. When these three aggregates are thus taught, the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), which is their support, is also already taught. "Nāmañca" refers to the aforementioned mental phenomena. The phrase "nāmakāyañca" is taught to exclude those phenomena because Nibbāna is also included under the name "nāma," and because supramundane states are not the objects of insight (vipassanā). By the word "kāya" (group/body), Nibbāna is excluded. This is because Nibbāna is free from being a group (rāsi). Mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra), which are taught as "perception and feeling are mental factors; these states are bound to the mind and are mental formations," are also meant to be included here under the term "nāmakāya." They are called "mahābhūta" (Great Essentials) because of their great manifestation, because they are like a great magician (bhūta), because they are nurtured by many states, because of their great transformation, and because of their great existence. These Great Essentials are four: earth (pathavī), water (āpo), fire (tejo), and air (vāyo). In the phrase "catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ," the genitive case expresses the meaning of the accusative. It means matter that arises depending on the four Great Essentials without leaving them. That derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is of twenty-four kinds: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, form, sound, smell, taste, femininity, masculinity, life faculty, heart-base, nutriment, bodily intimation, vocal intimation, space element, lightness of matter, softness, wieldiness, growth, continuity, decay, and impermanence. "Assāsa" and "passāsa" are simply the natural in-breath and out-breath. The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) that arises depending on the in-breath and out-breath also receives the same name, just like the earth kasiṇa and so forth. Because it resembles matter, it also receives the name "rūpa" (form/matter), as in sentences such as "he sees external forms." "Nimittañca upanibandhanā" refers to the place of contact of the in-breath and out-breath (the tip of the nose), which is the cause for binding mindfulness. Bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra), which are taught as "in-breaths and out-breaths are bodily; these states are bound to the body and are bodily formations," are also meant to be included here under the term "rūpakāya."
113: "Those bodies are penetrated" means that at the moment of Jhana, the bodies which are the signs of in-breaths and out-breaths are penetrated by way of being the object. At the moment of insight (vipassanā), the remaining material and mental bodies are penetrated by way of being the object. At the moment of the path (magga), they are penetrated by way of non-delusion. Aiming also at the insight and path that arise for a yogi who has attained Jhana through the power of in-breaths and out-breaths, it is said: "by the power of long in-breaths and out-breaths," and so forth. The terms "he knows while reflecting" and so forth have the meanings already stated in the Discourse on Virtue (Sīlakathā). Including those bodies of the aforementioned nature within, it is said: "experiencing the whole body." In the passages beginning with "experiencing the whole body by way of the sense of restraint of in-breaths and out-breaths," restraint itself in the Jhana, insight, and path that arise because of the in-breaths and out-breaths mentioned as "experiencing the whole body" is called purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) in the sense of restraint. Non-distraction itself is called purification of mind (cittavisuddhi) in the sense of non-distraction. Wisdom itself is called purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) in the sense of seeing. It should be understood that even if there is no mental factor of abstinence (virati) in Jhana and insight, the mere absence of unwholesome states is called restraint (saṃvara). In the explanation of "calming" and so forth, "bodily" means existing in the physical body (rūpakāya). "Bound to the body" means connected to the body, depending on the body; they exist when the body exists and do not exist when it does not. For that very reason, because those in-breaths and out-breaths are conditioned by the body, they are called "bodily formations" (kāyasaṅkhāra). "Calming" means making peaceful, making subside. By the word "calming" itself, the calming of the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths is accomplished. "Ceasing" means making them cease by not letting the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths arise. "Quieting" means bringing the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths to a state of quietude by way of turning them into a single continuity. "He trains" is connected as "he trains, thinking 'I shall breathe in'" according to the context; or it means he trains in the three trainings (sikkhā). Now, to show the calming of the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths, he says "by whatever nature" and so forth. There, "by whatever nature" means of whatever kind. "Ānamanā" is bending backward. "Vinamanā" is bending to both sides (left and right). "Sannamanā" is the thorough bending of one who bends in all directions. "Paṇamanā" is bending forward. "Iñjanā" is shaking. "Phandanā" is slight movement. "Pakampanā" is violent shaking. The connection should be made as: "calming the bodily formations of such nature by which there is bending backward... violent shaking of the body," and "calming that bending backward... violent shaking of the body." This is because when the bodily formations (in-breaths and out-breaths) are calmed, the bending backward and so forth of the body are also calmed. "By whatever nature of bodily formations..."
114:
It should be understood through the connection of the meanings that he calms the bodily formation which is of such a nature that it does not cause the bending, etc., of the physical body, and that it is calm and subtle; and that he calms that which is the non-occurrence of bending, etc., of the physical body, which is calm and subtle. The term 'santaṃ sukhumaṃ' (calm and subtle) is an adverbial neuter (bhāvanapuṃsakavacana). In the phrase 'iti kira', the word 'iti' is used in the sense of 'eva' (thus), and the word 'kira' is used in the sense of 'yadi' (if). An objection is raised by an objector: 'If it is so, does he train himself thinking, "I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out," while calming even the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths?'

Alternatively, since 'kira' is the word of an objector, it is also appropriate in the senses of disbelief, intolerance, and that which is not personally witnessed. The meaning is: 'I do not believe, I cannot tolerate, it is not evident to me that one trains in the calming of such subtle in-breaths and out-breaths.' 'Evaṃ sante' means: 'when there is such calming of the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths.' 'There is no arising of the perception of the wind' means there is no arising of the consciousness (or the meditative consciousness) that perceives the wind of the in-breath and out-breath. The meaning is that there is no arising of the meditative consciousness which has that in-breath and out-breath as its object, and the meditation on that object does not occur. 'There is no arising of the in-breaths and out-breaths' means that because the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased due to the meditation, their arising and occurrence do not take place.

'There is no arising of the mindfulness of breathing' means that because of the very absence of the in-breaths and out-breaths, there is no occurrence of the mindfulness associated with the meditative consciousness that has those in-breaths and out-breaths as its object. For that very reason, there is also no development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing associated with that mindfulness. In the phrase 'na ca naṃ taṃ', the words 'ca naṃ' are merely particles, as in the passages such as 'bhikkhu ca naṃ' (Pārājika 273). It should be understood in connection that the wise neither enter into nor emerge from that aforementioned attainment of mindfulness of breathing. In the words answering the side of the objection, 'iti kira' is to be understood in the same way. Here, the word 'kira' should be understood in the sense of 'eva' (only). 'Evaṃ sante' means: 'only when there is such calming.'

'How is it like?' is a question asking for a simile: 'In what manner is that aforementioned procedure?' Now, with the words 'seyyathāpi', he shows that simile. 'Kaṃse' means in a vessel made of bronze. 'Nimittaṃ' means the intense characteristic of the sounds [vibrations] coming from that bronze vessel. The word 'nimittaṃ' is in the accusative case (upayogavacana) used in the sense of the genitive (sāmī), meaning 'of the sign' (nimittassa). And the sign of the sound is not other than the sound itself. 'Suggahitattā' means because of being well-learned. There is also a reading 'sugahitattā', meaning well...
115:
...because of being [well] taken. 'Sumanasikatattā' means because of being well-attended to. 'Supadhāritattā' means because of being well-upheld in the mind. 'Because of having the subtle sign of sound as an object' means that at that time, because the subtle sounds have ceased, for one who has not repeatedly grasped the sign of the sound, even though it is not an object, the consciousness occurs by making the extremely subtle sign of sound its object, because of the state of having the extremely subtle sign of sound as its object. Or, the meaning is: because of the state of having the extremely subtle sign of sound as its object. In this same manner, the meaning should also be understood in the case of absorption (appanā).

In the passages beginning with 'passambhayaṃ', the in-breaths and out-breaths mentioned as 'passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ' (calming the bodily formation) are called 'kāya' (body); or, the connection should be understood that in this phrase 'passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ', the in-breaths and out-breaths are called 'kāya'. Although the bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra) become calm due to the purity of meditation, when the yogi has the advertence, 'I shall calm the gross bodily formation,' they become exceedingly calm due to that very care. Even the subtle (in-breath and out-breath) which is not manifest becomes easy to bring [to mind].

The 'eight insight knowledges' (anupassanāñāṇa) are: in the four bases mentioned as 'long, short, experiencing the whole body, calming the bodily formation,' there are four by way of the in-breath and four by way of the out-breath, making eight insight knowledges. The 'eight mindfulnesses of establishment' (upaṭṭhānānussati) are: in the four bases mentioned in the manner of 'mindfulness is established in one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by way of a long in-breath' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.170), there are four by way of the in-breath and four by way of the out-breath, making eight mindfulnesses of establishment. There is also a reading 'aṭṭha cupaṭṭhānānussatiyo'. The 'four bases from the Suttas' are the four bases by way of the first tetrad, because they were taught by the Blessed One in the Ānāpānassati Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 3.144, etc.).

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the First Tetrad is Finished.

In the exposition of 'experiencing rapture' (pītipaṭisambhedī) of the second tetrad, in the phrase 'rapture and gladness arise,' 'pīti' (rapture) is the primary term. 'Pāmojja' (gladness) is the term explaining its meaning; the meaning is the state of one who is gladdened. That which receives such names as 'pīti' and 'pāmojja' in the passages beginning with 'yā pīti pāmojjaṃ' is called 'pīti'. Therein, 'pīti' is the term for its intrinsic nature. The state of one who is gladdened is 'pāmojja'. The manner of rejoicing is 'āmodanā'. The manner of rejoicing intensely is 'pamodanā'. Or, just as the mixing together of medicines, oils, or hot and cold water is called 'modanā', so also this rapture is called 'modanā' because it joins together the associated states. By the power of the prefix 'ā', the word 'modanā' is adorned to become 'āmodanā' and 'pamodanā'. It is called 'hāsa' (mirth) because it gladdens the person associated with it (or the associated states). It is called 'pahāsa' (intense mirth) because it gladdens intensely. These names 'hāsa' and 'pahāsa' are names for mirth and intense mirth. It is called 'vitti' (satisfaction) because it pleases. That name 'vitti' is also a name for wealth. In truth, this rapture is called 'vitti' because it is a cause for joy (somanassa) and because it is like wealth. Just as gladness arises for a wealthy person depending on his wealth, so also gladness arises for one who has rapture depending on that rapture. Therefore, it is called 'vitti'. This name 'vitti' is the name for rapture well-established in the nature of pleasing. Because the body and mind of a person who has rapture are uplifted, he is called 'udagga' (uplifted). The state of an uplifted person is 'odagya'. The state of one's own mind is 'attamanatā'. The mind of one who has no delight is not his own mind, because it has suffering as its proximate cause. (The mind) of one who has delight...
116:
Just as the making into one of medicines, oils, or hot and cold waters is called 'modanā' (rejoicing/mixing), so too, this is called 'modanā' because of the making into one of these states. By decorating the word with prefixes, it is called 'āmodanā' and 'pamodanā'. It is called 'hāsa' (mirth) because it gladdens; it is called 'pahāsa' (intense mirth) because it gladdens in various ways. This is a designation for the modes of mirth. It is called 'vitti' (joy) because it delights; this is also a name for wealth (dhana). However, this rapture (pīti) is called 'vitti' because it is a cause for joy and resembles wealth. Just as a wealthy person experiences joy depending on wealth, so too, one who has rapture experiences joy depending on rapture. Therefore, it is called 'vitti'. This is a name for rapture because it is well-established in the nature of delight. A person possessing rapture is called 'udagga' (exultant) because of the upliftment and great upliftment of body and mind; the state of an exultant person is 'odajja' (exultation). The state of having one's own mind is 'attamanatā' (delight). The mind of one who is not pleased is not called 'one's own mind' because it has suffering as its proximate cause; the mind of one who is pleased is called 'one's own mind' because it has happiness as its proximate cause. Thus, the state of having one's own mind is 'attamanatā', meaning the state of being one's own mind. Since that 'attamanatā' is not the state of any other thing but is a mental factor (cetasika) which is a state of the mind itself, it is called 'the attamanatā of the mind'. The remaining points here and above and below should be understood by applying the method already mentioned.

In the explanation of 'experiencing happiness' (sukha-paṭisaṃvedī), the phrase 'two kinds of happiness' (dve sukhāni) is said to show the grounds for serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Bodily happiness (kāyika-sukha) is the ground for insight, while mental happiness (cetasika-sukha) is the ground for both serenity and insight. 'Kāyika' (bodily) means associated with the body, because it cannot arise without the sensitive body (kāya-pasāda). 'Cetasika' (mental) means associated with the mind, because it is associated with the mind inseparably. Therein, by the word 'kāyika', mental happiness is excluded; by the word 'sukha', bodily pain is excluded. Similarly, by the word 'cetasika', bodily happiness is excluded; by the word 'sukha', mental pain is excluded. 'Sāta' (pleasant) means a sweet or very sweet nature. 'Sukha' (happiness) means only happiness and not suffering. 'Kāyasamphassaja' (born of bodily contact) means produced in bodily contact. 'Sātaṃ sukhaṃ vedayitaṃ' (pleasant and happy feeling) means a pleasant feeling and not an unpleasant feeling; a happy feeling and not a painful feeling. The three words that follow are stated in the feminine gender. A pleasant feeling (vedanā) and not an unpleasant one; a happy feeling and not a painful one—this is the meaning here. The explanation of mental happiness should be applied by the method of opposites already mentioned. 'Te sukhā' is a change of gender; it means 'tāni sukhāni'.
117:
The remaining terms in this second tetrad should be understood in the same way as mentioned in the first tetrad below. The four Suttanta bases should be understood by way of the second tetrad.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Second Tetrad is Finished.

In the exposition of the third tetrad, 'citta' (mind) is the primary term. 'Viññāṇa' (consciousness) is the term that shows the meaning. The phrase 'yaṃ cittaṃ' (that mind) and so on should be applied and understood according to the method mentioned in the exposition of rapture (pīti). Among those terms, it is called 'citta' because it is variegated (citta). It is called 'mana' (intellect/mind) because it knows the object as if measuring (minamāna) it. 'Mānasa' is also the mind itself.

'The snare (of lust) that moves in the sky, which is made of mind (mānasa), moves about.'

In this Pali passage, however, the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) are called 'mānasa'.

'O Blessed One, why does your disciple, who delights in the Dispensation, a trainee (sekha) who has not yet reached the mental state (mānasa) of Arahatship, pass away while being famous among the people?'

In this place, Arahatship is called 'mānasa'. But in this (exposition of the mind), 'mana' itself is 'mānasa'. This word is expanded by way of syllables (grammar).

'Hadaya' (heart) is the mind itself. In the Pali passage, 'I will scatter your mind or split your heart (hadaya),' the chest is called 'hadaya'. In the Pali passage, 'Knowing another's mind with one's own mind, it is as if he were carving,' the mind is called 'hadaya'. In the Pali passage, 'kidneys, heart (hadaya),' the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) is called 'hadaya'. But here, the mind itself is called 'hadaya' because of its internal meaning.

That mind itself is called 'paṇḍara' (luminous/white) because of its purity. This name is said in reference to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). As the Blessed One said: 'Monks, this mind is luminous (pabhassara), but it is defiled by adventitious defilements.' Because it emerges from that bhavaṅga mind, even an unwholesome mind is called 'paṇḍara', just as a river flowing from the Ganges is called the Ganges, and a river flowing from the Godhāvarī is called the Godhāvarī. Alternatively, the mind, which has the characteristic of cognizing an object, is not itself a defilement because of defilements; it is pure by nature. It is only called 'defiled' when there is a connection with adventitious defilements. For that reason also, it is appropriate to call it 'paṇḍara'.

In the phrase 'mano manāyatanaṃ', the inclusion of the word 'mano' is for the purpose of showing that the mind itself is the base (āyatana). By that word 'mano', this is shown: 'This mind-base (manāyatana) is not a base for the mind like a temple is a base for a deity; rather, the mind itself is the base, thus it is the mind-base.'
118:
The meaning of āyatana has already been stated below. It is called 'mana' because it knows; 'it knows' is the meaning. However, the teachers of the Commentaries say: it is called 'mana' because it knows the object as if measuring with a vessel or weighing with a great scale. That very mana is called 'indriya' (faculty) because it exercises lordship over the associated states in the characteristic of knowing the object; because mana itself is a faculty, it is called 'manindriya' (mind-faculty).

It is called 'viññāṇa' because it knows specifically. Because consciousness itself is a group, it is called 'viññāṇakkhandha' (the aggregate of consciousness). The term 'khandha' (aggregate) is used for a part by way of metaphorical attribution of the whole's name to its part. In the sense of a heap, a single consciousness is a part of the aggregate of consciousness. Therefore, just as in the world a person who cuts a part of a tree is said to 'cut the tree,' so too, a single consciousness, which is a part of the aggregate of consciousness, is called 'viññāṇakkhandha' by attributing the name of the whole to the part. Furthermore, the sense of a heap is not the only meaning of khandha; the sense of a portion (koṭṭhāsa) is also the meaning of khandha. Therefore, by way of the sense of a portion, the meaning 'portion of consciousness' should also be understood. 'Tajjā manoviññāṇadhātu' refers to the mind-consciousness element that is appropriate for those associated states such as contact (phassa) and so on. In this term, the single mind itself is called by three names: 'mana' in the sense of measuring, 'viññāṇa' in the sense of knowing, and 'dhātu' (element) in the sense of its own nature or in the sense of being non-substantial (not a being).

'Abhippamoda' means excessive joy.

In the description of concentration (samādhi), it is called 'ṭhiti' (steadfastness) because it stands on the object in an unmoving manner. The two subsequent terms are expanded by the power of prefixes (upasagga). Alternatively, it is called 'saṇṭhiti' (steadiness) because it stands by collecting the associated states together on the object. It is called 'avaṭṭhiti' (fixity) because it stands by entering into and descending into the object. In the wholesome side, four states descend into the object: faith (saddhā), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). For this very reason, faith is called 'okappanā' (conviction), mindfulness is called 'apilāpanatā' (non-superficiality), concentration is called 'avaṭṭhiti' (fixity), and wisdom is called 'pariyogāhanā' (penetration). On the unwholesome side, however, three states descend into the object: craving (taṇhā), wrong view (diṭṭhi), and ignorance (avijjā). For this very reason, they are called 'ogha' (floods). It is called 'avisāhāra' (non-distraction) because it is the opposite of the distraction that occurs by the power of restlessness (uddhacca) and doubt (vicikicchā); 'non-distraction' is the meaning. The mind that occurs only by the power of restlessness and doubt is called distracted; this concentration is called 'avikkhepa' (non-wavering) because it has no such distraction. The mind is called distracted only by the power of restlessness and doubt; it is carried here and there; this concentration is called 'avisāhaṭamānasatā' (non-scatteredness of mind) because it is the state of a mind that is not distracted.
119:
Tranquillity (samatha) is of three kinds: tranquillity of mind (cittasamatha), settling of legal processes (adhikaraṇasamatha), and tranquillity of all formations (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha). Among these three, one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā) in the eight attainments is called tranquillity of mind. Indeed, depending on that one-pointedness of mind, the movement and wavering of the mind are stilled and calmed; therefore, that concentration is called 'cittasamatha.' The sevenfold Vinaya, starting with sammukhāvinaya, is called settling of legal processes. Indeed, depending on those seven kinds of samatha, various legal processes (adhikaraṇa) are stilled and calmed; therefore, those seven kinds of samatha are called 'adhikaraṇasamatha.' Furthermore, because all formations are stilled and calmed depending on Nibbāna, that Nibbāna is called 'sabbasaṅkhārasamatha.' In this context, tranquillity of mind is intended. It is called the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) because it exercises lordship in the characteristic of steadiness. It is called the power of concentration (samādhibala) because it is unshakeable by restlessness (uddhacca). Right concentration (sammā-samādhi) is concentration as it really is, concentration that leads out (niyyānika), and wholesome concentration.

179. By the words 'liberating the mind from lust' and so forth, liberation from the ten grounds of defilement (kilesavatthu) is stated. In this text starting with 'from lust,' it should be understood that by taking sloth (thina), torpor (middha) is also taken; by taking restlessness (uddhacca), remorse (kukkucca) is also taken. This is because they have the nature of occurring together in other texts. By teaching liberation from the grounds of defilement, liberation from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth by means of the first jhāna and so forth, and liberation from the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) and so forth by means of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and so forth, are also stated. In this ellipsis (peyyāla), 'How does one repeatedly contemplate that mind?', the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth by means of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth is also stated. The four Suttanta topics should be understood by way of the third tetrad.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Third Tetrad is Finished.

180. In the description of the fourth tetrad, because of the saying 'In what is not specified, the neuter gender is used,' and because it is not specifically pointed out which state is impermanent, the question is asked in the neuter singular: 'What is impermanent?' 'Uppādavayaṭṭhena' means by way of the nature called arising and passing away, or by the nature of arising and passing away. In this context, the five aggregates are the individual characteristic (sabhāvalakkhaṇa); the arising and passing away of the five aggregates is the characteristic of change (vikāralakkhaṇa). By this characteristic of arising and passing away, it is called 'impermanent' (anicca) because it does not exist after having come to be. Therefore, even though it is said in the Commentary, 'Impermanence by way of the characteristic of the conditioned is the arising, passing away, and alteration of those very states,' it is also said, 'or non-existence after having come to be.' By these words of the teacher of the Commentary, it is stated that the mode of non-existence after having come to be is the characteristic of impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇa). It is stated by way of ellipsis: 'For one who sees the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, these are the characteristics of wisdom.' 'Dhammā' refers to the states mentioned above, such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) and so forth.
120:
In the explanation of 'one who contemplates fading away' (virāgānupassī), 'having seen the danger in form' means having seen the danger in the aggregate of form through the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, which are taught later, starting from the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa).

'Fading away of form' (rūpa-virāga) refers to Nibbāna. For, depending on Nibbāna, the aggregate of form fades away; it ceases by reaching the state of not arising again. Therefore, Nibbāna is called 'fading away of form'.

'One in whom desire has arisen' means one who has the desire for the Dhamma that has arisen through the power of hearing (anussava) from the virtuous.

'One who is committed through faith' means one who has entered into and decided upon that very Nibbāna through faith.

'And his mind is well-established' means it should be understood through the connection of meaning that the yogi's mind is well-established and well-fixed in the dissolution of form, known as 'fading away as destruction' (khaya-virāga), by way of the object, and in the fading away of form, known as 'absolute fading away' (accanta-virāga), which is Nibbāna, by way of hearing.

In 'one who contemplates fading away in form', 'fading away as destruction'—the destruction of the aggregate of form—is expressed as 'fading away in form' using the locative case in the sense of a natural support (pakati-ādhāra). 'Absolute fading away'—the final cessation of the aggregate of form—is expressed as 'fading away in form' using the locative case in the sense of a cause (nimittattha). One who habitually contemplates those two kinds of fading away by way of the object and by way of inclination (ajjhāsaya) is called 'one who contemplates fading away in form' (rūpe virāgānupassī). This same method applies to the aggregates of feeling and so forth. This same method should also be understood in the explanation of the term 'one who contemplates cessation' (nirodhānupassī).

However, here, the phrase 'by how many modes' and so forth is a distinction. In that context, by seeing the danger and cessation of the factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) such as ignorance and so forth, the danger and cessation of form and so forth are also shown. This is because form and so forth do not transcend the factors of dependent origination. By this specific statement, the excellence of the contemplation of cessation over the contemplation of fading away is stated.

In that contemplation of cessation, 'by way of the sense of impermanence' means by way of the sense of destruction, or by way of the sense of non-existence after having been.
