'By way of the sense of suffering' means by way of the sense of danger, or by way of the sense of constant oppression. 'By way of the sense of non-self' means by way of the sense of being coreless, or by way of the sense of not following one's will. 'By way of the sense of burning' means by way of the sense of being burnt by the defilements. 'By way of the sense of change' means by way of the sense of twofold transformation through aging and dissolution.

'By the cessation of the source' (nidāna) means by the absence of the root cause (āsava). 'Ceases' means it no longer occurs. 'By the cessation of the origin' (samudaya) means by the absence of the proximate cause. Just as unsuitable food (asappāya-bhojana) is called the 'source' (nidāna) as the root cause of a disease, the root cause is called nidāna. Just as wind, bile, and phlegm are called the 'origin' (samudaya) as the proximate causes of a disease, the proximate cause is called samudaya. For, that which definitely gives the result is called nidāna. Moreover, that from which the result well-arises is called samudaya.

'By the cessation of birth' (jāti) means by the non-arising of the root cause. 'By the cessation of production' (pabhava) means by the non-arising of the proximate cause. Since this suffering begins and arises because of birth, it is appropriate to call birth itself 'production' (pabhava). 'By the cessation of the cause' (hetu) means by the absence of the generative cause (janaka-paccaya). 'By the cessation of the condition' (paccaya) means by the absence of the supportive cause (upatthambhaka-paccaya). For, the root cause and the proximate cause are indeed the generative cause and the supportive cause.
121:
At the moment of sharp insight, 'cessation by substitution' (tadanga-nirodha) is meant; at the moment of the path, 'cessation by uprooting' (samuccheda-nirodha) is meant. 'By the arising of knowledge' (ñāṇuppādena) means by the arising of either sharp insight knowledge or path knowledge. 'By the appearance of cessation' (nirodhupaṭṭhānena) means, at the moment of insight, by the appearance of the cessation as destruction (khaya-nirodha) through direct perception, and by the appearance of Nibbāna, known as cessation, through the power of hearing; and at the moment of the path, by the appearance of Nibbāna through direct perception. By these terms (arising of knowledge and appearance of cessation), only the determination of the object and the subject (the one who perceives the object) is made, and thus cessation by substitution and cessation by uprooting are also stated.

In the explanation of the term 'one who contemplates relinquishment' (paṭinissaggānupassī), 'he relinquishes form' (rūpaṃ pariccajati) means he abandons the aggregate of form because of the lack of desire for it, having seen its danger. 'Relinquishment as giving up' (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) means it is called relinquishment in the sense of giving up completely. By this, the sense of 'giving up' (pariccāga) of the word 'relinquishment' (paṭinissagga) is stated; therefore, it means the abandoning of defilements. Here, insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā) abandons defilements by way of substitution (tadanga), while the path abandons them by way of uprooting (samuccheda).

'The mind enters into Nibbāna, which is the cessation of form' means insight leading to emergence enters into it by way of being inclined towards it, while the path enters into it by making it the object. 'Relinquishment as entering into' (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga) means it is called relinquishment in the sense of entering into. By this, the sense of 'entering into' (pakkhandana) of the word 'relinquishment' (paṭinissagga) is stated; therefore, it means the entering of the insight mind and path mind into Nibbāna. The four subjects from the Suttas should be understood by way of the fourth tetrad. In this tetrad, what should be said regarding aging and death should be understood in the same way as stated below.

In the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), 'contemplation of the body in the body' (kāye kāyānupassanā) and 'contemplation of the mind in the mind' (citte cittānupassanā) are designated in the singular number by way of the common worldly usage of the body and mind as single entities. 'Contemplation of feelings in feelings' (vedanāsu vedanānupassanā) and 'contemplation of mental objects in mental objects' (dhammesu dhammānupassanā) are designated in the plural number by way of the common worldly usage of feelings and mental objects as being diverse.

## The explanation of the description of the fourth tetrad is finished.

## The explanation of the description of the knowledge of one who acts with mindfulness (satokāri-ñāṇa) is also finished.

## 6. Explanation of the description of the six groups of knowledge

Now, among the knowledges shown by the six groups, in the description of the twenty-four knowledges of concentration (catuvīsati-samādhi-ñāṇa), first, by way of the three tetrads starting with the contemplation of the body, among the twelve subjects, in each subject, there is one concentration by way of exhalation (assāsa) and one concentration by way of inhalation (passāsa)...
122:
## 6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Six Groups of Knowledge

Regarding "two concentrations each," there are twenty-four concentrations across the twelve bases. At the moment of jhāna, the knowledges associated with those concentrations occur by way of the twenty-four concentrations.

In the exposition of the seventy-two types of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), "long inhalation" occurs because of the inhalation called "long." What does this mean? Having attained jhāna which has long inhalation as its cause, at the moment of contemplating with insight with a concentrated mind, it is called insight (vipassanā) because of the sense of contemplating repeatedly as impermanent (aniccato anupassanā). This method applies to subsequent parts as well. In those same twelve bases, there are six contemplations for each base—three by way of inhalation and three by way of exhalation—resulting in seventy-two contemplations across the twelve bases. These seventy-two contemplations are themselves knowledges by way of the seventy-two types of insight.

In the exposition of the Knowledge of Revulsion (nibbidā-ñāṇa), "breathing out while contemplating impermanence" means one who breathes out and in while contemplating impermanence. This phrase "breathing out" (assasanti) should be understood in the sense of cause. "Knows and sees as it really is" refers to the Knowledge of Revulsion. From the Knowledge of Comprehension (kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa) up to the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa), one knows the true nature of formations (saṅkhāra) through the insight knowledge that has arisen, and sees with that very eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu) just as one sees with the physical eye. Therefore, it is called Knowledge of Revulsion, meaning the knowledge that is weary of formations. Since knowledges such as Appearance as Fear (bhayatūpaṭṭhāna) and Desire for Deliverance (muñcitukamyatā) will appear separately later, in this exposition of Knowledge of Revulsion, only the aforementioned insight knowledges are to be understood as knowledges of revulsion.

In the exposition of the Knowledge of Conformity to Revulsion (nibbidā-anuloma-ñāṇa), "breathing out while contemplating impermanence" refers to the person who breathes out while contemplating impermanence. The nominative case is used here in the sense of the possessive. By the phrase "wisdom in the appearance as fear," the Knowledge of Appearance as Fear, the Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger (ādīnavānupassanā), and the Knowledge of Contemplation of Revulsion (nibbidānupassanā) are taught, because these three share the same characteristic. These three knowledges are called Knowledge of Conformity to Revulsion because they are in accordance with and do not oppose the previously mentioned knowledges of revulsion.

In the exposition of the Knowledge of Tranquillization of Revulsion (nibbidā-paṭippassaddhi-ñāṇa), "breathing out while contemplating impermanence" is the same as in the preceding exposition. By the phrase "wisdom of reflective staying" (paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā paññā), the Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance, the Knowledge of Reflective Contemplation (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā), and the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) are mentioned, because these three share the same characteristic. By the phrase "reflective staying," Conformity Knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) and Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) are also included.
123:
The Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations and Conformity Knowledge are also called Knowledges of Tranquillization of Revulsion because they have reached the peak of revulsion and have abandoned the effort (byāpāra) to produce revulsion, thus completing the task of revulsion. As for Path Knowledge, it is very appropriate to call it Knowledge of Tranquillization of Revulsion because it arises at the end of the tranquillization of revulsion. Unlike in the Knowledges of Conformity to Revulsion, not taking the initial Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance but taking the two final knowledges (Knowledge of Reflective Contemplation and Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations) as "reflective staying" is for the purpose of including Path Knowledge. If "Desire for Deliverance" were said, it would only include Conformity Knowledge and would not include Path Knowledge. This is because Path Knowledge is not called Desire for Deliverance; rather, it is called "staying" (santiṭṭhanā) because it stays well in the completion of the task.

In the Commentary, it is also said, "Touching is absorption (appanā)." This Path Knowledge is called "staying" because it is an absorption that enters and stays in Nibbāna; thus, by the word "staying," Path Knowledge is also included. The Knowledges of Conformity to Revulsion are also essentially knowledges of revulsion; therefore, they are included under the knowledges of revulsion, and only the term "nibbidā" is used in "Knowledges of Tranquillization of Revulsion," not "nibbidā-anuloma." In these three expositions of the groups of eight knowledges, by way of the fourth tetrad of Contemplation of Dhamma, for the four bases mentioned, there are two knowledges each—one by way of inhalation and one by way of exhalation—resulting in eight knowledges for the four bases.

In the exposition of the Knowledge of the Bliss of Liberation (vimuttisukha-ñāṇa), after showing abandoning by the word "pahīnattā," the author says "samucchinnattā" (because of being cut off) to show that this abandoning is abandoning by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna). Knowledge in the bliss of liberation refers to the knowledge associated with the bliss of liberation of the Fruit (phala) and the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) that has the bliss of liberation of the Fruit as its object. To show that by abandoning the defilements which are the basis of underlying tendencies (anusaya), the abandoning of the bases of outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna) and misconduct (duccarita) occurs, the abandoning of underlying tendencies is mentioned again. With reference to the twenty-one types of Fruit Knowledge, the count of knowledge is made by the count of abandoned defilements; and with reference to Reviewing Knowledge, the count of Fruit Reviewing Knowledge is made by the count of reviewing abandoned defilements.

## The explanation of the Exposition of the Six Groups of Knowledge is finished.
## In the Saddhammappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga,
## the explanation of the Discussion on Mindfulness of Breathing is finished.
124:
## 4. Indriyakathā
## 1. Paṭhamasuttantaniddesavaṇṇanā

Now, the explanation of the meanings not yet discussed in the Indriyakathā (Discourse on the Faculties), which is taught immediately after the Ānāpānassatikathā (Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing), has arrived. It should be understood that this Indriyakathā is taught immediately after the Ānāpānassatikathā to show the method of purifying the faculties and so forth, which are supportive of the development of mindfulness of breathing; for without the faculties that support it, the development of mindfulness of breathing cannot occur. Desiring to explain the meaning of that Suttanta teaching—which he himself (the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta) had heard directly from the Blessed One and whose intention he had understood—by making that teaching the foremost, he first said, "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard), and so forth.

Among those words beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," the word "evaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta). The words beginning with "me" are nouns (nāma). In the word "viharati," "vi" is a prefix (upasagga) and "harati" is a verb (ākhyāta); in this way, the division of words should be understood.

As for the meaning, the word "evaṃ" is seen in the senses of simile, instruction, censure, praise, manner, assent, illustration (nidassana), and emphasis (avadhāraṇa). Here, however, the wise use the word "evaṃ" in the senses of manner (ākāra), illustration (nidassana), and emphasis (avadhāraṇa).

Among these, the word "evaṃ" in the sense of manner reveals this meaning: Who is capable of knowing in every aspect the word of the Blessed One—which is subtle through various methods, which arises according to the diverse inclinations of beings, which is endowed with meaning and phrasing, which possesses various miracles, which is profound in Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration, and which reaches the ear-path of all beings according to their respective languages? Indeed, even while generating the desire to hear with all one's power, the intended meaning of "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is: "I too have heard it in one such manner."

In the sense of illustration (nidassana), he exempts himself by saying, "I am not self-enlightened (Sayam-bhū), nor was this realized by me alone," and points to the entire sutta to be spoken hereafter, saying, "I too have heard it thus."

In the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), the Elder Sāriputta shows his own power of mindfulness and power of wisdom in accordance with the way the Blessed One praised him, saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who possess great wisdom, this Sāriputta is foremost" (A. Ni. 1.188-189); and "Monks, I do not [see] another..."
125:
"...I do not see even a single person, monks, who so rightly keeps the matchless Wheel of Dhamma in motion as set in motion by the Tathāgata, as does Sāriputta. Sāriputta, monks, rightly keeps the matchless Wheel of Dhamma in motion as set in motion by the Tathāgata" (A. Ni. 1.187). By such methods, showing his own power of retention in accordance with the praise bestowed by the Blessed One, he generates in beings the desire to hear, implying: "Thus have I heard; and that which was noted is exactly like this, neither less nor more in terms of meaning or phrasing; it is just so, not otherwise."

The word "me" is seen in the senses of the instrumental (karana), the dative (sampadāna), and the genitive (sāmī). Here, however, it is appropriate in both senses: "It was heard by me" and "My hearing."

This word "sutaṃ," whether with a prefix or without, is seen in the senses of famous, going, wet, accumulated, and that which is cognizable by the ear-consciousness. It is also seen in the sense of an object perceived through the ear-door. Here, its meaning is "that which was noted through the ear-door" or "the act of noting." If the word "me" is taken in the sense of "by me," it is appropriate as: "Thus was it noted by me through the ear-door." If taken in the sense of "my," it is appropriate as: "Thus was my noting through the ear-door."

Furthermore, by saying "Thus have I heard," he does not claim the Dhamma as his own creation but reveals what was previously heard, saying: "I received this sutta from the presence of the Blessed One—who is confident through the fourfold intrepidity, who possesses the ten powers, who stands in the place of the noble, who roars the lion's roar, who is the supreme of all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, the Turner of the excellent Wheel of True Dhamma, the Fully Enlightened One. Therefore, one should not have doubt or hesitation regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the word, or the phrasing of this sutta." Thus, he destroys lack of faith in this Dhamma and generates the fulfillment of faith. Therefore, it is said:

"The disciple of Gotama, saying 'Thus have I heard,'
Destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Dispensation."

"Ekaṃ" is the designation defining the number. "Samayaṃ" is the designation of the defined time. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" (On one occasion) is an indefinite indication. Therein, the word "samaya" is seen in the senses of concourse, moment, time, group, cause, view, attainment, abandonment, and penetration.
126:
In this context, the meaning of the word 'samaya' should be understood as 'time' (kāla). By this word 'samaya' meaning time, the phrase 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ' (at one time) indicates one among the various divisions of time such as year, season, month, fortnight, night, day, morning, noon, evening, the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, and moments (muhutta).

In this Sutta Piṭaka, although the Elder (Ānanda), through his wisdom, well knew and well distinguished which sutta was taught in which year, season, month, fortnight, part of the night, or part of the day among these times such as years and seasons, if he were to teach the meaning of the time in detail as 'Thus have I heard, in such a year, in such a season, in such a month, in such a fortnight, in such a part of the night, or in such a part of the day,' it would not be easy to memorize, learn, or recite, and there would be too much to say. Therefore, combining all those meanings of year, month, season, etc., into a single term, he said 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ'.

Alternatively, there are many occasions (samaya) of the Blessed One which are very famous among devas and humans, consisting of various divisions of time, such as: the occasion of descending into the womb, the occasion of birth, the occasion of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the occasion of the Great Renunciation, the occasion of practicing austerities, the occasion of the victory over Mara, the occasion of attaining Supreme Enlightenment, the occasion of dwelling in the bliss of the present life, the occasion of teaching, and the occasion of Parinibbāna. Among these occasions, 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ' indicates one occasion known as the occasion of teaching (desanā-samaya). Furthermore, among the occasions of performing the functions of wisdom and compassion, it refers to the occasion of performing the function of compassion; among the occasions of practicing for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, it refers to the occasion of practicing for the benefit of others; among the two duties (karaṇīya) to be performed for the assembled audience, it refers to the occasion of Dhamma talk; and among the occasions of teaching and practice, it refers to the occasion of teaching. Thus, 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ' is said with reference to one of these indefinite occasions.

In the phrase 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ', the sense of continuous duration (accanta-saṃyoga) is also appropriate. This is because for however long the Blessed One taught this sutta or any other sutta, he continuously (accanta) dwelt in the abiding of compassion (karuṇā-vihāra) during that time. Therefore, to illustrate that meaning, it should be understood that the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) is used here.

Hence, it is said:
'Depending on various meanings, the word samaya is expressed
In other places in the locative and instrumental cases;
But here, it is expressed in the accusative case.'

The ancient teachers, however, explain that 'tasmiṃ samaye' (locative), 'tena samayena' (instrumental), or 'taṃ samayaṃ' (accusative) are merely differences in linguistic expression, and in all cases, the meaning is locative (ādhāra-attha).
127:
Therefore, even when it is said 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ', the meaning should be understood as 'ekasmiṃ samaye' (at one occasion).

'Bhagavā' means a venerable person (garu). In the world, a venerable person is called 'Bhagavā'. This Blessed One is also the venerable one of all beings because of His excellence in all qualities; therefore, He should be known as 'Bhagavā'. The ancient teachers also said:
'The word Bhagavā is the most noble; the word Bhagavā is the most excellent.
He is endowed with the qualities of being venerable and worthy of respect;
Therefore, He is called Bhagavā.'

Furthermore:
'Because He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), has broken defilements (bhaggavā), is endowed with the six glories (bhagehi yutto),
Has analyzed the Dhamma (vibhaktavā), has partaken (bhattavā), and has vomited out craving for existences (vanta-gamana),
He is therefore called Bhagavā.'
By virtue of this verse, the meaning of the word 'Bhagavā' should be understood in detail. That detail has already been explained in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati-niddesa).

By this much, in this context, the word 'Evaṃ' indicates the perfection of the teaching (desanā-sampatti); 'Me sutaṃ' indicates the perfection of the disciple (sāvaka-sampatti); 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ' indicates the perfection of time (kāla-sampatti); and 'Bhagavā' indicates the perfection of the teacher (desaka-sampatti).

In the word 'Sāvatthiyaṃ', the city that was the dwelling place of the sage named Savattha is called Sāvatthī, just as in the cases of Kākandī and Mākandī; so say the grammarians first. The teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), however, say: Sāvatthī is so called because everything (sabbaṃ atthi) that humans use and enjoy is found there. Also, when groups of merchants met and were asked, 'What goods are there?' they replied, 'Everything is there' (sabbaṃ atthi); based on this statement, it is called Sāvatthī.
'At all times, all requirements are gathered in Sāvatthī;
Therefore, because of everything, it is called Sāvatthī.'

In that city of Sāvatthī (Sāvatthiyaṃ) is the locative case (sattami) used in the sense of proximity (samīpa). The word 'viharati' (dwells) generally indicates being endowed with one of the abidings: the abiding in postures (iriyāpatha), the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra), the Brahma abiding (brahma-vihāra), or the noble abiding (ariya-vihāra). Here, however, it indicates being engaged in one of the postures such as standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. Therefore, whether the Blessed One is standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, He should be understood simply as 'viharati' (He dwells). For the Blessed One carries on and maintains the physical body (attabhāva) without it falling, by interrupting the discomfort of one posture with another posture; therefore, it is said 'viharati'.
128:
In the phrase "Jetavane," he is called "Jeta" because he conquers his own enemies. Alternatively, he is called "Jeta" because he was born when the King [of Kosala] conquered his enemies. Or, he is called "Jeta" because that name was given to the prince for the sake of auspiciousness. It is called "vana" (forest) because it causes affection to arise. This means that through its own perfection, it inspires devotion in beings and causes love for itself to arise. Alternatively, it is called "vana" because it "entreats." It is as if it entreats living beings, saying, "Come here and enjoy me," by means of the fragrance of various flowers, the songs of birds such as intoxicated cuckoos, and the branches, twigs, shoots, buds, and leaves moving in the gentle breeze. Because it is the forest (garden) of Prince Jeta, it is called "Jetavana." Indeed, that garden was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner; therefore, it is called "Jetavana." "In that Jetavana" [is the meaning]. There are two kinds of forests (vana): those that are planted and those that are self-grown. This Jetavana, as well as Veḷuvana and others, are planted forests, while Andhavana, Mahāvana, and others are self-grown forests.

In the phrase "Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme," that householder was named "Sudatta" by his parents. However, because he was endowed with all desirable things, was free from stinginess, and possessed virtues such as compassion, he constantly gave alms-food (piṇḍa) to the helpless (anātha); thus, he became known as "Anāthapiṇḍika." An "ārāma" is so called because living beings, and especially those who have gone forth (monks), come there and delight (ramanti). This means that they come from various places and delight there, dwelling without weariness, because of the beauty of its flowers, fruits, and so on, and because it is endowed with the five qualities of a resting place, such as being neither too far nor too near. Alternatively, it is called "ārāma" because, due to the aforementioned perfections, it draws in even those who have gone elsewhere and causes them to delight. That monastery was purchased by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from the hand of Prince Jeta by covering the ground with eighteen koṭis of gold. He then spent eighteen koṭis to have dwellings (senāsana) constructed, and eighteen koṭis to complete the monastery dedication ceremony. Thus, having sacrificed fifty-four koṭis of gold, it was dedicated to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha; therefore, it is called "Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo" (Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery). "In that monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika" [is the meaning].

Here, the mention of "Jetavane" is the proclamation of the former owner, and "Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme" is the proclamation of the latter owner. What is the purpose of proclaiming both? It is to provide an example (diṭṭhānugati) for those who desire to perform merit. In that Jetavana, the eighteen koṭis of gold received from the sale of the land for the construction of the gatehouse and pinnacled buildings, as well as the trees worth many koṭis, constitute the donation of Prince Jeta. The fifty-four koṭis of gold...
129:
It means “in the park of Anāthapiṇḍika.” By praising these individuals in this way, Venerable Sāriputta shows that those who desire merit perform such meritorious deeds, and he encourages others who desire merit to follow their example.

In this regard, it might be argued: “If the Blessed One is staying in Sāvatthī, it should not be said ‘in Jeta’s Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.’ If he is staying in that monastery, it should not be said ‘in Sāvatthī.’ For it is impossible to stay in both places at the same time.” However, it should not be viewed in that way. Did we not say that this is the “locative case in the sense of proximity” (samīpatthe bhumma-vacana)? Therefore, just as herds of cattle grazing near the Ganges or Yamunā rivers are said to be “grazing in the Ganges” or “grazing in the Yamunā,” so too here, the Blessed One, who is staying in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park near Sāvatthī, is said to be “staying in Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.” The mention of Sāvatthī is to indicate his alms-resort village (gocara-gāma), while the remaining words are to indicate a dwelling place suitable for monastics.

Among those words, by mentioning Sāvatthī, Venerable Sāriputta shows the Blessed One’s favor toward lay devotees, and by mentioning Jeta’s Grove and so on, he shows the favor toward monastics. Similarly, by the former phrase, he shows the avoidance of the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) through the acceptance of the four requisites; and by the latter phrase, he shows the means of avoiding the practice of sensual indulgence (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) through the renunciation of sensual objects. Alternatively, by the former, he shows the devotion to teaching the Dhamma, and by the latter, the inclination toward seclusion (viveka). By the former, he shows the approach [to beings] through compassion (karuṇā), and by the latter, the withdrawal [from defilements] through wisdom (paññā). By the former, he shows the intention to fulfill the welfare and happiness of beings, and by the latter, the state of being unstained while performing the welfare and happiness of others. By the former, he shows the pleasant dwelling due to not abandoning righteous happiness, and by the latter, the pleasant dwelling due to the practice of higher human states (uttarimanussadhamma). By the former, he shows the great benefit to humans, and by the latter, to devas. By the former, he shows being born and raised in the world, and by the latter, being unstained by worldly conditions. By the former, in accordance with the words, “Monks, there is one person who, when arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. Who is that one person? It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,” he illustrates the purpose for which the Blessed One arose; and by the latter, he illustrates the dwelling suitable to the place where he arose. For the Blessed One was born first in the Lumbinī Grove and secondly at the Bodhimaṇḍa—both being forest areas where mundane and supramundane states arose—and thus he shows his dwelling in the forest itself. In this and other ways, the explanation of the meaning here should be understood.
130:
The word "tatra" indicates the place and time. This is because it signifies "at that time" when he was dwelling, and "in that Jeta Grove" where he was dwelling. Alternatively, it indicates the place and time suitable for preaching. For the Blessed One does not preach the Dhamma in an unsuitable place or time. The statement "Bāhiya, it is not yet the time [to preach the Dhamma]," etc., serves as evidence here. The word "kho" is a particle used merely as an expletive (filler), in the sense of emphasis, or in the sense of the initial time. The word "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One) indicates that he is the Teacher who is the object of the world's reverence. The word "bhikkhū" (monks) refers to persons suitable for listening to the Dhamma. Furthermore, the etymological meaning (vacanattha) should be understood here in such ways as: "He is a bhikkhu because he begs," or "He is a bhikkhu because he has undertaken the practice of going for alms."

"Āmantesi" means he addressed, he spoke to, or he informed; this is the meaning here. In other contexts, it may also mean to inform or to summon. "Bhikkhavo" (O monks) indicates the manner of addressing. By this word "Bhikkhavo," which is established through the connection with qualities such as the habit of begging, the nature of begging, and the excellence in begging, he manifests the livelihood of seeking alms practiced by both the lowly and the noble, thereby suppressing both arrogance and despondency. With this word "Bhikkhavo," and with speech preceded by a gaze from a heart and eyes made serene by the diffusion of great compassion, he makes them face him. By that very speech which indicates the desire to speak, he generates in them the desire to listen. By that very word in the sense of addressing, he urges them to listen well and to pay proper attention. For the fulfillment of the Sasana depends on listening well and paying proper attention.

If it is asked, "Why did he address only the monks when other devas and humans were present?"—it is because they are the eldest, the most excellent, the nearest, the ones constantly in attendance, and the proper vessels [for the Dhamma]. Although the Buddha's Dhamma teaching is common to all assemblies, among the assembly, the monks are the eldest because they were the first to arise. They are the most excellent because, starting with the renunciation of the home life, they follow the Teacher's conduct and are the recipients of the entire Sasana. They are the nearest because they sit closest to the Teacher among those seated there. They are constantly in attendance because they move in the vicinity of the Teacher. And they alone are the proper vessels for the Dhamma teaching because they practice according to the instruction.

In this regard, there might be a question: "Why does the Blessed One, when preaching the Dhamma, first address the monks instead of preaching the Dhamma directly?" It is for the purpose of generating mindfulness. For the monks in the assembly might be sitting there thinking of other things, with distracted minds, reflecting on the Dhamma, or meditating on a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). If the Dhamma were preached without addressing them, they would be unable to discern, "What is the source of this teaching? What is its cause? On what occasion was it preached?" and thus they might fall into distraction or grasp it wrongly.
131:
(The monks) might take it wrongly. Therefore, to arouse mindfulness in those monks, the Blessed One first addresses them and then preaches the Dhamma after having addressed them.

The word "Bhadante" is a term of respect, or it is a way of giving a response to the Teacher. Alternatively, in this context, the Blessed One addresses those monks by saying "Bhikkhave," and those monks respond to the Blessed One by saying "Bhadante." Similarly, the Blessed One speaks first saying "Bhikkhave," and those monks respond saying "Bhadante." By saying "Bhikkhave," He causes them to give a response; they give the response by saying "Bhadante." "Those monks" refers to the monks whom the Blessed One addressed. "They responded to the Blessed One" means they heard the Blessed One's address, they listened attentively, they acknowledged, and they accepted it. "The Blessed One said this" means the Blessed One spoke this entire sutta that is now being preached.

By this much sequence of words, the Venerable Sāriputta spoke the introduction (nidāna), adorned with the time, place, speaker, and assembly, so that this sutta—which is endowed with meaning and phrasing and indicates the depth of the Buddhas' knowledge of teaching—might be easily entered. It is like a landing place (tittha) with a beautiful staircase made of pure stone slabs for easy descent into a lotus pond of clear, sweet water shimmering with red and blue lotuses, and a white ground covered with sand like a scattered net of pearls. It is like a staircase shimmering with the light of gems, bound with golden creepers and having smooth, soft steps made of ivory, for easy ascent to a magnificent palace that rises up as if wishing to touch the path of the stars, surrounded by well-proportioned walls and ornate railings. It is like a great gateway with wide, well-set door-leaves, brilliantly illuminated by the radiance of gold, silver, gems, pearls, and coral, for easy entrance into a great house (or palace) beautified by the splendor of vast sovereignty and wealth, where the household people move about with sweet voices of talk and laughter mixed with the tinkling of golden bracelets and anklets. Thus, the explanation of the meaning of that introduction is completed.

In the sutta, the word "five" is a delimitation of number. The phrase "these faculties" is a demonstration of the delimited phenomena. The meaning of "faculty" (indriya) has been stated below.

Now, having shown this sutta, wishing to show the method of developing the purification of the faculties mentioned in this sutta, their state of being developed, and their subsiding (paṭippassaddhi), he said "These five faculties," and so on. Therein, "are purified" means they reach purification. "In one who is faithless" means in one devoid of faith in the Three Jewels. "In one who is faithful" means in one endowed with faith in the Three Jewels.
132:
"Sevato" means associating by way of the mind. "Bhajato" means approaching. "Payirupāsato" means sitting near and attending respectfully. "Pasādanīye suttante" means suttas connected with the virtues of the Three Jewels that arouse confidence. "Kusīte": they are called "kusīda" because they sink down in a contemptible manner; the word "kusīda" itself becomes "kusīta." It refers to those lazy persons. "Sammappadhāne" means suttas connected with the energy that accomplishes the fourfold task of Right Effort. "Muṭṭhassatī" refers to those who are forgetful or devoid of mindfulness. "Satipaṭṭhāne" means suttas that primarily present the foundations of mindfulness. "Jhāna-vimokkhe" means suttas that primarily present the fourth jhāna, the eight liberations, and the three types of liberation. "Duppaññe" refers to those who lack wisdom, or those whose wisdom is corrupted due to the absence of true wisdom; they are called "duppaññā." It refers to those of little wisdom. "Gambhīra-ñāṇa-cariyaṃ" means suttas connected with the Four Truths, Dependent Origination, etc., or suttas similar to a discourse on knowledge. "Suttantakkhandhe" means the sections of the suttas.

In the words beginning with "assaddhiyaṃ," "assaddhiyaṃ" means the state of being faithless. One who sees the danger in faithlessness and abandons faithlessness develops the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). One who sees the benefits in the faculty of faith and develops the faculty of faith abandons faithlessness. This same method applies to the remaining terms. "Kosajjaṃ" means laziness. "Pamādaṃ" means the absence of mindfulness. "Uddhaccaṃ" means the state of being restless; "vikkhepa" (distraction) has the same meaning. "Pahīnattā" (because of being abandoned) is because they have been abandoned through the perfection of jhāna by way of absorption (appanā). "Suppahīnattā" (because of being well-abandoned) is because they have been well-abandoned through the perfection of insight by way of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā). The phrase "bhāvitaṃ hoti subhāvitaṃ" (is developed, is well-developed) should be applied in the same manner as already stated. Indeed, because of being abandoned by way of the opposites through insight, it is appropriate to say "well-abandoned" (suppahīnattā). For that very reason, it is called "well-developed" (subhāvitaṃ), but not so in the case of jhāna. This is because the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā) is through the abandoning of things to be abandoned, and the abandoning of things to be abandoned is fulfilled through the fulfillment of development; therefore, they are presented as a pair.

In the section on subsiding (paṭippassaddhivāra), "bhāvitāni ceva honti subhāvitāni ca" refers to the state of the already developed faculties being well-developed. "Paṭippassaddhāni ca suppaṭippassaddhāni ca" refers to the state of the already subsided faculties being well-subsided. The state of being developed and the state of being subsided should be understood by way of the accomplishment of the Path-function at the moment of Fruition (phala). "Samuccheda-visuddhi" (purifications by cutting off) are the Path-purifications themselves. "Paṭippassaddhi-visuddhi" (purifications by subsiding) are the Fruition-purifications themselves.

Now, in order to show the faculties with such stated methods by connecting them with the performing person, he said "Kati nnaṃ puggalānaṃ," and so on. Therein, "savane na buddho" (awakened by hearing) means one who knows or has understood the Four Truths by hearing a Dhamma discourse from a Fully Enlightened Buddha.
133:
This statement explains the state of having developed faculties (bhāvitindriya). The reason is that through the power of the realization of development (bhāvanābhisamaya), which is the Path, one becomes a person with developed faculties at the moment of the Fruit (phala) because the Path was being developed. Although all eight noble persons (ariya) are disciples of the Blessed One, the term 'khīṇāsava' (one whose taints are destroyed) is used specifically to point out the one established in the Fruit of Arahantship. Only such an Arahant is called 'bhāvitindriya' because of the completion of all tasks of the Path. However, the remaining learners (sekha) are also called 'bhāvitindriya' in a figurative sense (pariyāyena) because of the completion of their respective Path tasks. For this very reason, it is said regarding the four moments of the Fruit: "The five faculties are both developed and well-developed." Nevertheless, since those learners still have to develop their faculties for the sake of the higher Paths, they are not called 'bhāvitindriya' in the literal sense (nippariyāyena). 'Sayam bhūtaṭṭhena' refers to the Blessed One (or Paccekabuddha) who has arisen by a noble birth through himself alone, without a teacher. He is called 'Sayam-bhū' (Self-become) at the moment of the Fruit due to the accomplishment of development. Thus, he is 'bhāvitindriya' in the sense of having become so by himself. 'Appameyyaṭṭhena' means in the sense of being immeasurable because of being endowed with infinite virtues. The Blessed One is called 'Appameyya' (Immeasurable) at the moment of the Fruit due to the accomplishment of development. Because he is called immeasurable, he is also called 'bhāvitindriya'.

## The Explanation of the First Suttanta Niddesa is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Second Suttanta Niddesa

Setting forth another Sutta again, wishing to show the classification of faculties, He showed the Sutta beginning with "Monks, these are the five faculties." In that Sutta, the phrase "Ye hi keci" (whoever) expresses the sense of including everything without exception. The particle "hi" is used merely as a filler (padapūraṇa). "Samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā" (ascetics or brahmins) is spoken according to worldly usage. "Samudaya" means the cause. "Atthangama" means the cessation of the faculties that have arisen, or the non-arising of those that have not yet arisen. "Assāda" means the benefit of gratification. "Āဒီနဝ" (Ādīnava) means the fault or danger. "Nissaraṇa" means the escape. "Yathābhūtaṃ" means according to the true nature. "Samaṇesu" refers to those who have stilled evil. "Samaṇasamatā" refers to those who are not considered ascetics by Me (the Buddha). When "sammatā" is spoken in the present tense, according to grammatical rules, the word "me" is in the genitive case (sāmivacana). "Brāhmaဏေသူ" (Brāhmaṇesu) refers to those who have put away evil. "Sāmaññattha" means the benefit of the state of an ascetic. "Brahmaññattha" means the benefit of the state of a brahmin. Both terms refer only to the Fruit of Arahantship. Alternatively, "sāmaññattha" refers to the three lower Fruits, and "brahmaññattha" refers to the Fruit of Arahantship. "Sāmañña" and "brahmañña" are names for the Noble Path itself. "Diṭṭheva dhamme" means in this very life. "Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā" means having realized by oneself through higher knowledge. "Upasampajja" means having attained or having accomplished.
134:
## Suttanta Niddesa

In the Suttanta Niddesa, first the number of divisions of the origin (samudaya) of the faculties, etc., is asked, and then the number of divisions is answered. In that answer, "asītisata" means one hundred and eighty (180). It should be construed as "by the modes called one hundred and eighty" by the wise.

Again, in showing the enumeration preceded by the question on the number of divisions, "adhimokkhatthāya" means for the sake of conviction or faith. "Āvajjanāya samudaya" means the arising of the mind-door advertence consciousness. "Saddhindriyassa samudaya" means the cause of the faculty of faith. For one who practices with the thought "I will arouse faith," the advertence that occurs in the preliminary stage is the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for the faculty of faith. The advertence of the javana associated with the faculty of faith is the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) for the first javana, and the strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for the second javana and so on. "Adhimokkhavasena" means by the power of resolution (adhimokkha) associated with desire (chanda). "Chandassa samudaya" means the arising of the desire for the Dhamma (dhammachanda), which is a 'yevāpanaka' (miscellaneous) state associated with resolution, arising due to the condition of the preliminary advertence. That desire is a condition for the faculty of faith by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). At the time when desire is predominant, it is also a predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya). That same desire is a condition for the second javana by way of proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), decisive support (anantarūpanissaya), repetition (āsevana), absence (natthi), and disappearance (vigata).

In this same way, attention (manasikāra) should also be construed. However, here 'manasikāra' refers only to the 'yevāpanaka' attention characterized by remembering (sāraṇa). It does not have the nature of a predominance condition. It should be understood that among the associated states, only these two (desire and attention) are taken because they are powerful conditions. "Saddhindriyassa vasena" means by the power of the faculty of faith that has reached the state of a faculty through the expansion of development. "Ekattupaṭṭhāna" means firm establishment in a single object without wavering, which is a condition for the faculty of faith in higher and higher stages.

In the same way as described for the faculty of faith, the remaining faculties should also be understood. Thus, as there are four origins for each faculty, there are twenty (20) origins for the five faculties. Again, among the four origins, by associating the five faculties with each origin, twenty origins are spoken of. It is said that the first twenty should be understood by way of different paths, and the second twenty by way of a single path. Thus, there are forty modes.

The section on cessation (atthangama) should also be understood in this same way. That cessation is: the cessation of attainment (paṭilābha-atthangama), which is the non-attainment of faculties not yet obtained by one who does not strive in the development of faculties; the cessation of loss of what was attained (paṭiladdhaparihāni-atthangama) for one who falls away from the development of faculties; and the cessation through subsiding (paṭippassaddhi-atthangama) for one who has reached the Fruit. "Ekatta-anupaṭṭhāna" means non-establishment in a single object.
135:
## A. Explanation of the Exposition on Gratification
In the exposition on gratification, "the non-occurrence of lack of faith" (assaddhiyassa anupaṭṭhānaṃ) means the non-occurrence of lack of faith (assaddhiya) due to avoiding faithless persons, associating with faithful persons, reflecting on suttas that inspire confidence, and frequently applying wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) to those inspiring subjects. Regarding "the non-occurrence of the fever of lack of faith" (assaddhiyapariḷāhassa anupaṭṭhānaṃ), when talk concerning faith is given to a faithless person, suffering and displeasure arise. This occurrence is called the "fever of lack of faith" (assaddhiya-pariḷāha). "Confidence in the practice of resolution" (adhimokkhasacariyāya vesārajjaṃ) refers to the state of being courageous in the arising of faith that has reached mastery, either through the power of the Triple Gem—the cause of faith—or through the power of meditation (bhāvanā). "Attainment of peaceful abidings" (santo ca vihārādhigamo) refers to the acquisition of either serenity (samatha) or insight (vipassanā). In the phrase "happiness and joy" (sukhaṃ somanassaṃ), the word "joy" (somanassa) is used here to show the nature of mental happiness. For one whose body is touched by the sublime material form arising from the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), physical happiness (kāyika sukha) is also certainly obtained. Because happiness and joy are the primary gratifications (assāda), it is specifically stated, "This is the gratification of the faculty of faith." In this same manner, the gratifications of the remaining faculties should also be understood by application.

## B. Explanation of the Exposition on Danger
In the exposition on danger, "in the sense of impermanence" (aniccaṭṭhena) refers to the impermanent nature of the faculty of faith. It means that this sense of impermanence is the danger (ādīnava) of the faculty of faith. The same method applies to the other two [characteristics] (suffering and non-self). It should be understood that these [aspects of] origin (samudaya), passing away (atthaṅgama), gratification (assāda), and danger (ādīnava) pertain only to the mundane (lokiya) faculties.

## C. Explanation of the Exposition on Escape
In the exposition on escape, regarding the terms beginning with "in the sense of resolution" (adhimokkhaṭṭhena), twenty-five escapes (nissaraṇa) for the five faculties are shown by way of Path and Fruition (magga-phala), taking five for each faculty. Therein, "from the acquisition of a more sublime faculty of faith" (tato paṇītatara-saddhindriyassa paṭilābhā) means by way of acquiring a faculty of faith at the moment of the Path that is more sublime than the faculty of faith occurring at the moment of insight (vipassanā). "It has escaped from the previous faculty of faith" (purimatara-saddhindriyā nissaṭaṃ hoti) means that at that moment of the Path, the faculty of faith has emerged from the previous faculty of faith occurring at the moment of insight. In this same manner, the faculty of faith at the moment of Fruition, as well as the remaining faculties in both instances (Path and Fruition), should be applied.
136:
In the preliminary stage, "by the five faculties" means: eight escapes by way of the eight attainments (samāpatti) such as the first jhāna, through the five faculties in the access (upacāra) to the first jhāna; eighteen escapes by way of the eighteen great insights (mahāvipassanā) such as the contemplation of impermanence; and eight supramundane escapes by way of the Path of Stream-entry and so on. Thus, thirty-four escapes are shown by way of meditative attainment, great insight, Path, and Fruition, through the transcendence of each preceding one. However, the thirty-seven escapes beginning with "the five faculties in renunciation" (nekkhamme pañcindriyāni) are shown by way of the abandonment of opposites (paṭipakkha). Among those thirty-seven, the seven escapes in the seven [factors] such as renunciation are stated by way of the plane of access (upacārabhūmi); however, Fruitions are not mentioned because they do not involve the abandonment of opposites.

"Co-arising with view" (diṭṭhekaṭṭhehi) means they are called so because they stand together with [wrong] view in a single person up until the Path of Stream-entry. It means "by those co-arising with view." "By the coarse" (oḷārikehi) refers to coarse sensual lust and ill-will. "By the subtle" (aṇusahagatehi) refers only to subtle sensual lust and ill-will. "By all defilements" (sabbakilesehi) refers to lust for form and so on. When those [lust for form, etc.] are abandoned, all defilements are abandoned; therefore, it is said "by all defilements." Terms whose meanings are not stated here have the same meanings as stated below. Regarding "the five faculties in each case for all Arahants" (khīṇāsavānaṃ), in the previously mentioned instances such as "in the sense of resolution," the five faculties of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciple-Arahants have escaped from the respective defilements as appropriate in each instance. In this section, the methods first mentioned are stated by way of Arahants as appropriate.

How do these escapes become one hundred and eighty? It is said: twenty-five are stated by way of Path and Fruition, thirty-four are stated by way of transcendence, and thirty-seven are stated by way of opposites; thus, in the first round, there are ninety-six escapes in total. In the second round, when twelve are removed from these same [ninety-six] by way of Arahants, they become eighty-four. Thus, the previous ninety-six and these eighty-four together make one hundred and eighty. Which twelve are to be removed for Arahants? Among those stated by way of transcendence, the eight escapes stated by way of Path and Fruition; and among those stated by way of opposites, the four stated by way of the Path—these twelve are to be removed. If it is asked why the escapes stated by way of the Fruition of Arahantship should be removed: because they are already obtained by way of Path and Fruition in the twenty-five escapes stated at the very beginning for all objects. The escapes by way of the Fruition of Arahantship have already been stated.

Specifically, higher noble persons (ariyas) cannot enter lower fruition attainments. Therefore, the three lower Fruitions are not obtainable by Arahants. However, meditative attainments, great insight, and the seven factors such as renunciation are obtainable by Arahants by way of functional (kiriya) consciousness. These five faculties have indeed escaped from the opposite defilements because the opposite defilements were already stilled in the Path together with insight that occurs prior to the Fruition of Arahantship. Thus, the conclusion should be understood.

## II. Explanation of the Exposition on the Second Suttanta
137:
Higher noble persons do not usually enter lower fruition attainments (phala-samāpatti). Therefore, Arahants do not obtain the three lower fruits. However, they can obtain meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti), insight (vipassanā), renunciation (nekkhamma), and so forth, by way of functional consciousness (kiriya-citta). These five faculties are also already liberated from opposing states, as those opposing states were calmed previously.

## The Explanation of the Second Suttanta Exposition is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Third Suttanta Exposition

Setting forth another Suttanta, the Teacher said, "Monks, these five faculties..." and so forth, wishing to show the arrangement of the faculties. In that text, regarding "sotāpattiyangesu" (in the factors of stream-entry), the "sota" (stream) is the Noble Eightfold Path. Reaching that stream abundantly is "sotāpatti" (stream-entry). The constituents (causes) of stream-entry are "sotāpatti-anga" (factors of stream-entry). This means the factors to be obtained beforehand in order to become a stream-enterer. Association with superior persons (sappurisa-saṃseva), hearing the true Dhamma (saddhamma-savana), wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra), and practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti)—these are the four factors of stream-entry. The remaining terms have been explained previously. This Suttanta is spoken to show the predominance of these faculties in their respective domains.

For example, when four sons of wealthy merchants and a king (five in total), as companions, go down to the street saying, "Let us play at the festival of the stars," and they arrive at the house of one merchant's son, the other four remain silent. Only the host merchant's son gives orders in the house, saying, "Give these people food and snacks; give these people perfumes, flowers, and ornaments." When they arrive at the houses of the second, third, and fourth merchant's sons, the host alone gives orders in the same manner. Finally, when they arrive at the king's house, although the king is the ruler everywhere, at this time he gives orders only in his own house, saying, "Give these people food and snacks; give these people perfumes, flowers, and ornaments."

In the same way, although the five faculties such as faith (saddhā) and so forth arise in a single object like companions going down to the street together, just as the host alone gives orders while the other four remain silent in the first merchant's son's house, when reaching the factors of the path of stream-entry, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), characterized by conviction (adhimokkha), is the chief and the precursor. The remaining four faculties follow the lead of that faith. Just as the host alone gives orders in the second merchant's son's house, when reaching the right strivings (sammappadhāna), the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya), characterized by exertion (paggaha), is the chief and the precursor. The remaining four faculties follow the lead of that energy. Just as the host alone gives orders in the third merchant's son's house, when reaching the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), characterized by establishing (upaṭṭhāna), is the chief and the precursor. The remaining four faculties follow the lead of that mindfulness. Just as the host alone gives orders in the fourth merchant's son's house, when reaching the meditative absorptions (jhāna), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), characterized by non-distraction (avikkhepa)...
138:
...gives orders. In this way, when reaching the factors of the path of stream-entry, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), characterized by conviction, is the chief and the precursor; the remaining faculties follow that faith.

Just as the other four remain silent in the second merchant's son's house and only the host gives orders, in this way, when reaching the right strivings (sammappadhāna), the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya), characterized by exertion, is the chief and the precursor; the remaining faculties follow that energy.

Just as the other four remain silent in the third merchant's son's house and only the host gives orders, in this way, when reaching the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), characterized by presence [in the object], is the chief and the precursor; the remaining faculties follow that mindfulness.

Just as the other four remain silent in the fourth merchant's son's house and only the host gives orders, in this way, when reaching the meditative absorptions (jhāna), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), characterized by non-distraction, is the chief and the precursor; the remaining faculties follow that concentration.

Finally, just as the other four remain silent when arriving at the king's house and only the king gives orders, in this way, when reaching the Noble Truths (ariya-sacca), the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), characterized by understanding (pajānana), is the chief and the precursor; the remaining faculties follow that wisdom.

## (a) Explanation of the Classification and Enumeration

In the exposition of classification and enumeration, which is preceded by questions on the divisions of the Suttanta, "association with superior persons" (sappurisa-saṃseva) means properly associating with good people. "By way of the sense of predominance of conviction" (adhimokkhādhipateyyaṭṭhena) means in the sense of being the predominant factor among the remaining faculties through what is called conviction (adhimokkha); it means in the sense of being the precursor to the remaining faculties. "Hearing the true Dhamma" (saddhamma-savana) means listening to the Dhamma of the virtuous, or the Dhamma that is beautiful, which is the True Dhamma. "Wise attention" (yoniso-manasikāra) means attention by way of skillful means. In the term "practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma" (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti), the Dhamma that follows the nine supramundane states is called "dhammānudhamma"; the practice of that dhammānudhamma, known as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, is "dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti." The same method applies to the right strivings and so forth.

## (b) Explanation of the Section on Conduct

In the section on conduct (cariyāvāra), the meaning should be understood in this same way. Specifically, the first section is spoken by way of the time of the arising (uppādana) of the faculties, whereas the section on conduct is spoken by way of the time of cultivation (āsevana) and the time of fulfillment (pāripūri) of the faculties that have already arisen. The terms conduct (cariyā), nature (pakati), and abundance (ussannatā) are identical in meaning.
139:
## Commentary on the Exposition of Conduct and Abiding

Now, wishing to explain the arrangement of the faculties in another way through the exposition of conduct (cāra) and abiding (vihāra), specifically in connection with conduct (cariyā), [the Teacher] points to the summary (uddesa) beginning with "Conduct and abiding" and then speaks the detailed exposition (niddesa) of that summary. In that summary, first, the connection of the summary should be understood thus: in whatever manner wise fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) would place faith in deep matters regarding one who practices and abides with faith and so on—thinking, "Indeed, this venerable one has attained or will attain [jhāna, etc.]"—in that same manner, the conduct (cāra) and abiding (vihāra) of one endowed with faculties are appropriately known and penetrated by wise fellow practitioners. In the summary and detailed exposition, cāra is indeed cariyā. The two terms cāra and cariyā are identical in meaning. Therefore, in the detailed exposition of the term "cāra", it is spoken as "cariyā". "Conduct of postures" (iriyāpathacariyā) means the occurrence or proceeding of postures. The same method applies to the remaining types of conduct. "Conduct of sense bases" (āyatanacariyā) is the occurrence of mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding the sense bases. "Attainment" (patti) refers to the fruits (phala). Because those fruits are reached, they are called "attainments". The welfare of the world of beings in this life and the next is called "benefit for the world" (lokattha); this is the distinction among the three types of conduct.

Now, wishing to show the ground (bhūmi) of those types of conduct, he says "in the four postures" and so on. "In the foundations of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhānesu) means in the foundations of mindfulness as objects. Although they are not different from mindfulness, in the teaching of the foundations of mindfulness, they are spoken of as if they were different by way of conventional usage. "In the Noble Truths" (ariyasaccesu) is spoken by way of the individual grasping of the truths through mundane knowledge of the four truths occurring prior to the path. "In the Noble Paths" and "in the fruits of recluseship" are also spoken merely by way of conventional usage. "In a portion" (padese) means in a part of the conduct for the benefit of the world. For only the Buddhas perform conduct for the benefit of the world completely and without remainder. Again, wishing to show those same types of conduct by way of the person who performs them, he says "of those endowed with resolution" (paṇidhisampannānaṃ) and so on. Therein, "endowed with resolution" refers to those who are endowed with the protection of postures due to the tranquility of postures, whose postures are unshakable, and who are endowed with tranquil postures suitable for the state of a monk. "Those with guarded doors in the faculties" (indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ) refers to those whose doors are guarded by way of each individual door occurring in its respective object among the six faculties such as the eye. Here, "door" refers to the eye and so on by way of the door of arising. "Those who abide in heedfulness" (appamādavihārīnaṃ) refers to those who habitually abide in heedfulness regarding virtue and so on. "Those devoted to the higher mind" (adhicittamanuyuttānaṃ) refers to those devoted to concentration, known as the higher mind, as a basis for insight. "Those endowed with wisdom" (buddhisampannānaṃ) refers to those endowed with knowledge occurring from the delimitation of mind and matter up to change-of-lineage (gotrabhū).
140:
(Those endowed with wisdom) are those endowed with knowledge occurring from the delimitation of mind and matter up to change-of-lineage. "Of those who have practiced rightly" (sammāpaṭipannānaṃ) refers to those practicing at the moment of the four paths. "Of those who have attained the fruits" (adhigataphalānaṃ) refers to those who possess the fruits attained at the moment of the four fruits.

"Resolving" (adhimuccanto) means one who exercises resolution (adhimokkha). "He conducts himself with faith" (saddhāya carati) means he proceeds by the power of faith. "Exerting" (paggaṇhanto) means one who strives with the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna). "Establishing" (upaṭṭhāpento) means one who establishes the object with mindfulness. "Making non-distraction" (avikkhepaṃ karonto) means one who does not allow distraction by the power of concentration. "Understanding" (pajānanto) means one who knows in various ways through the wisdom that understands the four truths. "Cognizing" (vijānanto) means one who specially cognizes the object through the adverting consciousness (āvajjana-viññāṇa) which precedes the impulsion (javana) associated with the faculties. "By the conduct of consciousness" (viññāṇacariyāya) means by the power of adverting consciousness. "Of one who has practiced thus" (evaṃ paṭipannassa) refers to the person who practices the occurrence of the faculties together with impulsion. "Wholesome states sustain" (kusalā dhammā āyāpenti) means wholesome states occurring by way of serenity and insight greatly sustain or proceed; this is the meaning. "By the conduct of sense bases" (āyatanacariyāya) means by the conduct of great effort (yatana), the conduct of exertion (ghaṭana), and the conduct of proceeding (pavattana) of wholesome states. "He attains distinction" (visesamadhigacchati) means he attains a distinguished state by the power of the abandonments of suppression (vikkhambhana), substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), extirpation (samuccheda), and tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi). "Conduct of vision" (dassanacariya) and so on have the meanings already stated.

In the words "He abides with faith" (saddhāya viharati) and so on, the abiding in postures of a person endowed with faith and so on should be understood. "Known" (anubuddho) refers to what is known by inferential wisdom (anumāna-paññā). "Penetrated" (paṭividdho) refers to what is penetrated by direct realization (paccakkha-paññā). Since the conduct (cāra) and abiding (vihāra) are also known by inference and penetrated by direct realization when the meanings of resolution and so on are known by inference and penetrated by direct realization, therefore, the meanings of resolution and so on are also shown in the context of knowing (anubodha) and penetration (paṭivedha).

In the words "Thus conducting himself with faith" (evaṃ saddhāya carantaṃ) and so on, the teacher, pointing out the variety already mentioned by the word "thus" (evaṃ), indicates the meaning of the word "as" (yathā). In the terms "wise" (viññū) and so on: they are called "wise" because they know according to reality. They are called "prudent" (vibhāvī) because they clarify or make plain the reality already known. Wisdom is called "medhā" because it strikes or harms the defilements like a thunderbolt strikes a mountain, or because of the sense of quickly grasping and retaining; those who possess this wisdom are called "sagacious" (medhāvī). They are called "learned" (paṇḍitā) because they move or proceed by the movement of knowledge. They are called "endowed with wisdom" (buddhisampannā) because they are possessed of the perfection of wisdom. They are called "fellow practitioners" (sabrahmacārino) because they practice the noble practice (brahmacariya), the supreme path, together. A "single act" (ekaṃ kammaṃ) refers to the fourfold Vinaya acts such as the act of notification (apalokana-kamma) being performed together. Similarly, the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha is a "single recitation" (ekuddeso). They are "equal in training" (samasikkhā) because they have the same training; the state of being so is "equality in training" (samasikkhatā). It is also read as "samasikkhātā". Those monks who have the same Vinaya acts, the same recitation of the Pātimokkha, and the state of equality in training are called "fellow practitioners" (sabrahmacārī).
141:
In the place where it should be said as "jhānāni", the change of gender (from neuter to masculine) is made as "jhānā". Deliverances (vimokkha) refer to the three or eight deliverances. Concentration (samādhi) refers to the three types of concentration: with initial application and sustained application (savitakka-savicāra), without initial application but with sustained application only (avitakka-vicāramatta), and without both initial and sustained application (avitakka-avicāra). Attainments (samāpatti) refer to the attainments of emptiness (suññata), the signless (animitta), and the undirected (appaṇihita). Direct knowledges (abhiññā) refer to the six direct knowledges.

Because there is only one part (aṃsa) and no second part, it is called "ekaṃsa" (certainty); the expression of that certain meaning is called "ekaṃsavacana" (certain speech). This method should also be applied to the remaining terms. Specifically, because it occurs equally (samam) or from all sides (samantā), it is called "saṃsaya" (doubt); because there is no doubt in this word, it is called "nissaṃsaya" (without doubt). Because one cannot decide on a single meaning and thus doubts another meaning, it is called "kaṅkhā" (doubt); because there is no doubt in this meaning, it is called "nikkaṅkho" (without doubt). The state of being twofold is called "dvejjhaṃ" (duality); because there is no duality in this meaning, it is called "advejjho" (without duality). Because it wavers in two ways, it is called "dveḷhakaṃ" (wavering); because there is no wavering in two ways in this meaning, it is called "adveḷhako" (without wavering). Speech made by way of necessity or rule (niyama) is called "niyogavacana" (definite speech). Some also read it as "niyyogavacana". Speech that expresses an unfailing meaning that leads out of saṃsāra is called "apaṇṇakavacana" (unfailing speech). "Avatthāpanavacana" means decisive speech (nicchayavacana). All these terms are synonyms for the absence of indecision (vicikicchā). Speech spoken because the desired meaning is clearly present is called "piyavacana" (pleasant speech). Likewise, it is also "garuvacana" (respectful speech). Because it occurs with respect (gārava) and esteem (garubhāva), it is called "sagārava" (with respect). "Patissaya" means relying on another with respect. "Patissava" means listening to the words of others with a humble demeanor. Both of these are names for treating another as a superior. Because it occurs with respect, it is called "sagārava". Because it occurs with deference (patissaya) or obedience (patissava), it is called "sappatissaya". Instead of saying "sappatissava", the letter 'ya' or 'va' is elided, and it is said as "sappatissa". Superior or distinct speech is called "adhivacana"; the superior speech that is both respectful and deferential is called "sagārava-sappatissādhivacana". In both cases, this is stated repeatedly by way of synonyms, variations, and distinctions. It should be understood that one has already attained or will attain the jhānas and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Third Suttanta is Finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Description of the Fourth Suttanta

Basing on the first sutta again, the faculties (indriya) are described in another way. In that description, (to the question) "In how many ways and for what reason should they be seen?", in how many...
142:
...ways they should be seen. By the question "For what reason should they be seen?", he asks about the aspects to be seen and the sense to be seen. "They should be seen in six ways and for that reason" means they should be seen through six aspects, and they should be seen precisely by that sense characterized by the six aspects. "In the sense of sovereignty" (ādhipateyyaṭṭhena) means in the sense of being a lord/master. "In the sense of purifying the beginning" (ādivisodhanaṭṭhena) means in the sense of purifying virtue (sīla), which is the beginning of wholesome states. "In the sense of predominance" (adhimattaṭṭha) means in the sense of being powerful. Indeed, a powerful faculty is called "adhimatta" because it has an exceeding measure or proportion. "In the sense of foundation" (adhiṭṭhānaṭṭha) means in the sense of a standing place. "In the sense of consuming" (pariyādānaṭṭha) means in the sense of exhausting (defilements). "In the sense of establishing" (patiṭṭhāpakaṭṭha) means in the sense of making firm.

## A. Explanation of the Description of the Sense of Sovereignty

In the description of the sense of sovereignty, the statement about abandoning the opposite of each individual faculty, such as "for one who abandons faithlessness" (assaddhiyaṃ pajahato), is spoken to accomplish the state of sovereignty in achieving the task of abandoning its respective opposite, such as faithlessness, even in a single moment. It is stated that the remaining four faculties are simply associated with that dominant faculty. Alternatively, it should be understood that in different moments, each single faculty is made the leader, and in abandoning its respective opposite, that particular faculty is made the chief while the remaining faculties are made to follow it. However, the statement beginning with "for one who abandons sensual desire" (kāmacchandaṃ pajahato) is spoken solely by way of a single moment.

## B. Explanation of the Description of the Sense of Purifying the Beginning

In the description of the sense of purifying the beginning, "purification of virtue in the sense of restraint from faithlessness" (assaddhiya-saṃvaraṭṭhena sīlavisuddhi) is called purification of virtue because it purifies the taints of virtue by way of the sense of preventing faithlessness and the sense of abstinence. "Purifying the beginning of the faculty of faith" means purifying virtue, which is the beginning by way of being a strong support (upanissaya) for the faculty of faith. In this same way, the faculties which have the restraint of sensual desire and so forth as their root should also be understood.

## C. Explanation of the Description of the Sense of Predominance

In the description of the sense of predominance, "desire arises for the development of the faculty of faith" (saddhindriyassa bhāvanāya chando uppajjati) means that for a person with faith, after hearing a teaching connected with faith or after seeing the gratification (assāda) in the development of the faculty of faith, a blameless desire for the Dhamma (dhammacchanda) arises regarding the faculty of faith. "Gladness arises" (pāmojjaṃ uppajjati) means that because desire has arisen, weak rapture arises. "Rapture arises" (pīti uppajjati) means that because of being glad, strong rapture arises. "Tranquility arises" (passaddhi uppajjati) means that because of being satisfied by rapture, tranquility of body and mind arises. "Happiness arises" (sukhaṃ uppajjati) means mental happiness based on the mind because of the tranquil body and mind...
143:
It arises. 'Illumination arises' means that the light of knowledge arises because of being suffused with happiness. 'Spiritual urgency arises' means that spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arises regarding the occurrence of formations because the faults of formations are known through the light of knowledge. 'Having caused spiritual urgency, he concentrates the mind' means that having produced spiritual urgency, he makes the insight-mind concentrated by that very spiritual urgency. 'He exerts well' means that he exerts well by freeing the mind from sluggishness and agitation. 'He looks on with equanimity well' means that because energy has arisen in balance with other faculties, he no longer makes an effort to balance energy again, but looks on with equanimity well by way of specific neutrality (tatramajjhattūpekkhā). 'By way of equanimity' means by way of specific neutrality, which has the characteristic of balanced proceeding. 'From various defilements' means from defilements of various natures which are the opposites of insight (vipassanā). 'By way of liberation' means by way of being liberated from various defilements starting from the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā). 'Because of being liberated' means because of being liberated from various defilements.

'Those states' refers to states such as desire (chanda) and so on. 'They have a single taste' means they have a single taste through the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa). 'By way of development' means by way of development that has a single taste. 'They turn away to a more sublime object' means that because of that development, states such as desire and so on turn away from the object of formations and proceed towards the object of Nibbāna, which is more sublime, by means of change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) known as the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā). 'By way of turning away' means by way of turning away from the object of formations at the moment of the arising of change-of-lineage. 'Because of having turned away, he relinquishes from that' means that the person possessed of the path, because of having turned away by way of emerging from both at the very moment of the arising of the path, relinquishes both defilements and aggregates for that reason. 'Because of having relinquished, they cease from that' means that because of having relinquished defilements and aggregates at the very moment of the arising of the path, defilements and aggregates cease by way of the cessation of non-arising. In the phrase 'because of having relinquished,' the past tense is used for what will happen in the future. The cessation of aggregates is mentioned because when defilements cease, the cessation of aggregates is certain. 'By way of cessation' means by way of the aforementioned cessation.

Desiring to show the two kinds of relinquishment (vossagga) at the moment of the arising of that path, he said 'two kinds of relinquishment by way of cessation,' and so on. Both kinds of relinquishment have the same meaning as stated below. In the passages such as 'Desire arises to abandon lack of faith,' the detailed meaning should be understood in this same way. This same method applies to the sections based on the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) and so on. The explanation of the meaning of establishing (adhiṭṭhānaṭṭha-niddesa) should also be understood in detail in this same way. Only the word 'he establishes' (adhiṭṭhāti) is special here, and it means 'he stands firm' (patiṭṭhāti).
144:
## D-E. Commentary on the Explanation of the Meaning of Exhaustion and Establishing

202-203. In the explanation of the meaning of exhaustion (pariyādānaṭṭha-niddesa), 'pariyādiyati' means it exhausts or consumes. In the explanation of the meaning of establishing (patiṭṭhāpakaṭṭha-niddesa), 'the person with faith establishes the faculty of faith in resolution (adhimokkha)' means that the person endowed with faith, being resolved that "all formations are impermanent, suffering, and non-self," establishes the faculty of faith in resolution. By showing this special individual, the special development of the faculties is explained. 'He establishes the faculty of faith of the faithful one in resolution' means that the faculty of faith of the person endowed with faith establishes that very faith. Likewise, 'he establishes the resolving person in resolution.' By this special development of the faculties, the special individual is explained. In this same way, 'one who exerts the mind establishes it in exertion (paggaha),' 'one who makes mindfulness present establishes it in presence (upaṭṭhāna),' 'one who concentrates the mind establishes it in non-distraction (avikkhepa),' and 'one who sees as impermanent, suffering, and non-self establishes it in seeing (dassana)'—thus the application should be understood in the remaining cases as well.
