'Yogāvacara' (practitioner) means one who practices (avacarati) in the practice (yoga) of tranquility (samatha) or the practice of insight (vipassanā). 'Avacarati' means he enters and practices.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Sutta Explanation is Finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Combination of Faculties

Now, desiring to show the combination of the faculties of one developing concentration and one developing insight, he first said 'A worldling (puthujjana) developing concentration,' and so on, to point out the divisions of skill in presence (upaṭṭhāna-kosalla). In that phrase, 'a worldling developing concentration' means developing concentration that leads to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). However, for the trainee (sekha) and the one free from lust (arahant), supramundane concentration is also attained. 'Because of having adverted' (āvajjitattā) means because of having adverted to the object-sign (nimitta) such as a kasiṇa, or it means having the sign produced in that object after performing the preliminary work (parikamma) of a kasiṇa and so on. 'Skilled in the presence of the object' (ārammaṇūpaṭṭhāna-kusala) means one who is skilled in making that very produced sign appear clearly. 'Skilled in the presence of the sign of tranquility' (samathanimittūpaṭṭhāna-kusala) means one who is skilled in making the sign of mental tranquility appear by way of developing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity when the mind is agitated due to over-exerted energy and so on. 'Skilled in the presence of the sign of exertion' (paggahanimittūpaṭṭhāna-kusala) means one who is skilled in making the sign of mental exertion appear by way of developing the enlightenment factors of investigation of states, energy, and joy when the mind is sluggish due to overly lax energy and so on.
145:
Skill in the appearance of non-distraction (avikkhepūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means proficiency in the appearance of concentration associated with a mind that is neither distracted nor sluggish. Skill in the appearance of illumination (obhāsūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means proficiency in the appearance of the light of knowledge by alarming the mind through reflection on the eight grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu) when the mind is joyless due to weak intellectual application. The eight grounds for urgency are: the four of birth, aging, sickness, and death; the suffering of the states of woe as the fifth; suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the past; suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the future; and suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present. Skill in the appearance of gladdening (sampahaṃsanūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means proficiency in the appearance of gladdening by making the mind clear through recollection of the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha when the mind is joyless because the bliss of peace has not yet been attained. Skill in the appearance of equanimity (upekkhūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means proficiency in the appearance of equanimity by making the mind free from concerns such as suppression or encouragement when the mind is free from faults like distraction. A trainee (sekha) is so called because he is still training in the three trainings. Skill in the appearance of singleness (ekattūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means proficiency in the appearance of a single object (ekatta) such as renunciation (nekkhamma) because of having abandoned identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and so forth.

One free from lust (vītarāga) refers to an Arahant who is called 'vītarāga' because lust has been entirely abandoned. Skill in the appearance of knowledge (ñāṇūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means that the Arahant, being free from delusion regarding phenomena, is proficient in the appearance of non-deluded knowledge in various instances. Skill in the appearance of liberation (vimuttūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means proficiency in the appearance of the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. By 'liberation' (vimutti), the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship is intended, as it is the state of being liberated from all defilements.

Regarding the appearance and non-appearance in the development of insight (vipassanābhāvanā), the terms 'as impermanent' (aniccato) etc., and 'as permanent' (niccato) etc., should be understood in the same way as stated in the Sīlakathā. According to the Pali text, however, in the terms 'āyūhanānupaṭṭhānakusalo, vipariṇāmūpaṭṭhānakusalo, animittūpaṭṭhānakusalo, nimittānupaṭṭhānakusalo, appaṇihitūpaṭṭhānakusalo, paṇidhi-anupaṭṭhānakusalo, abhinivesānupaṭṭhānakusalo', the compound words should be analyzed using the genitive case (sāmivacana). In the remaining terms, the text is presented using the ablative case (nissakkavacana).

In the term 'skill in the appearance of the void' (suññatūpaṭṭhānakusalo), the words should be analyzed either as 'suññato upaṭṭhānakusalo' (skill in appearance from the void) or 'suññatāya upaṭṭhānakusalo' (skill in the appearance of voidness). Because these eight—insight into revulsion (nibbidānupassanā), insight into dispassion (virāgānupassanā), insight into cessation (nirodhānupassanā), insight into relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā), insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (adhipaññādhammavipassanā), knowledge and vision according to reality (yathābhūtañāṇadassana), insight into reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā), and insight into turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā)—...
146:
The great insights (mahāvipassanā) are distinguished by their own specific nature, not by a specific object. Therefore, for these eight great insights, phrases such as 'is skilled in the appearance by way of revulsion (nibbidā)' are not appropriate, unlike phrases such as 'is skilled in the appearance by way of impermanence (anicca)'. For this reason, these eight are not formulated [in that manner]. Insight into danger (ādīnavānupassanā), however, is formulated through this pair of expressions: 'is skilled in the appearance as void, is skilled in the non-appearance of misinterpretation (abhinivesa)'. In terms of meaning, this is equivalent to saying 'is skilled in the appearance by way of danger, is skilled in the non-appearance of misinterpretation of the clinging-place (ālaya)'; thus, it is not formulated by its own name. In this way, it should be understood that among the eighteen great insights, these nine—the previous eight and this insight into danger—are not formulated, while the other nine are formulated.

'Skill in the appearance of knowledge' (ñāṇūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means that a trainee (sekha) is proficient in the appearance of knowledge in the development of insight because of the absence of the imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa). However, in the development of concentration (samādhibhāvanā), it is not said that one is skilled in the appearance of knowledge because attachment (nikanti) may still exist.

'Skill in the appearance of dissociation' (visaṃyogūpaṭṭhānakusalo) means one who is proficient in the appearance of dissociation (visaṃyoga), which is taught in four ways: dissociation from the yoke of sensual desire, dissociation from the yoke of existence, dissociation from the yoke of views, and dissociation from the yoke of ignorance. 'Skill in the non-appearance of yokes' (saṃyogānupaṭṭhānakusalo) means one who is proficient in the non-appearance of the yokes (saṃyoga), taught in four ways as the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance. 'Skill in the appearance of cessation' (nirodhūpaṭṭhānakusalo) refers only to an Arahant (khīṇāsava) who, by the power of an Arahant's strength, has a mind that is inclined toward Nibbāna, sloped toward Nibbāna, directed toward Nibbāna, stands in seclusion, delights in renunciation, and is entirely free from those states that are the basis for taints; thus, he is proficient in the appearance of Nibbāna, which is called cessation (nirodha).

In terms such as 'skill in the appearance of the object' (ārammaṇūpaṭṭhānakusala), 'skill' (kusala) refers to knowledge (ñāṇa). Knowledge is also called 'kusala' because of its association with a skilled person, just as phenomena are called 'wise' (paṇḍitā dhammā) because of their association with a wise person. Therefore, it means 'by way of proficiency' (kosalla).

Now, although the statement beginning with 'by way of sixty-four modes' was taught in the Ñāṇakathā, it is brought here and taught because it is connected to the Indriyakathā. That statement should be understood in the same way as previously explained.
147:
Furthermore, wishing to speak about the arrangement of the faculties in connection with the knowledge of omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa), he said the words beginning with "Na tassa addiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñci" (There is nothing here unseen by him). In that statement, 'Samantacakkhu' (the all-seeing eye) refers to the knowledge of omniscience. By the words beginning with "Paññindriyassa vasena," he shows the inseparable association of the five faculties. By the five sets of four (catukka) based on each individual faculty, beginning with "Saddahanto paggaṇhāti," he shows the state of having a common function (ekarasa) and the state of being mutually dependent conditions (aññamaññapaccaya) either at the time of practicing strong insight (vipassanā) or at the moment of the path (magga). By the five sets of four based on each individual faculty, beginning with "Saddahitattā paggahitaṃ," he shows the state of having a common function and the state of being mutually dependent conditions either at the time of the arising of the faculties or at the time of the fruit (phala).

Furthermore, wishing to speak about the arrangement of the faculties in connection with the Buddha-eye (Buddhacakkhu), he said the words beginning with "Yaṃ Buddhacakkhu." In that statement, 'Buddhacakkhu' refers to the knowledge of the degrees of faculties (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa) and the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusayañāṇa). "Buddhañāṇaṃ" also refers to these two types of knowledge; the remaining meaning is exactly as stated below.

## The Explanation of the Combination of Faculties (Indriyasamodhana-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
## Within the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga named Saddhammappakāsinī,
## The Explanation of the Discourse on Faculties (Indriyakathā-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
## 5. Discourse on Liberation (Vimokkhakathā)
## 1. Explanation of the Summary of Liberation (Vimokkhuddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Now, the explanation of the new meanings in the Discourse on Liberation (Vimokkhakathā), which was taught immediately after the Discourse on Faculties, has arrived in due order. This Discourse on Liberation was taught immediately after the Discourse on Faculties because liberation (vimokkha) occurs for a person devoted to the development of the faculties. In teaching that Discourse on Liberation, the Venerable Sāriputta taught it by taking the Sutta teachings heard in the presence of the Blessed One as the starting point.

In that Discourse on Liberation, first, among the words in the Sutta such as "Suññato vimokkho" (void liberation), the Noble Path (ariya magga) that arises by taking Nibbāna as the object through the aspect of being void of greed, hatred, and delusion is called 'void liberation'. That Noble Path is called 'void' (suññata) because it arises from the void element (Nibbāna), and it is called 'liberation' (vimokkha) because it is liberated from the defilements. In this same manner, the path that arises by taking Nibbāna as the object through the aspect of being signless is to be understood as 'signless' (animitta), and the path that arises by taking Nibbāna as the object through the aspect of being undirected is to be understood as 'undirected' (appaṇihita).
148:
A certain person contemplates formations (saṅkhāra) as impermanent (anicca) from the very beginning. However, since the emergence of the path (maggavuṭṭhāna) cannot occur merely by contemplating as impermanent, one must also contemplate as suffering (dukkha) and as non-self (anatta); therefore, he contemplates them as suffering and non-self as well. For such a practitioner, if the emergence of the path occurs while contemplating as impermanent, this person is said to have emerged through impermanence, having firmly entered into impermanence. If the emergence of the path occurs while contemplating as suffering or non-self, this person is said to have emerged through suffering or non-self, having firmly entered into impermanence. This same principle applies to those who emerge after having firmly entered into suffering or non-self. In this context, there are three types: one who enters through impermanence, one through suffering, and one through non-self. If the emergence occurs through impermanence, all three types of persons are those with a preponderance of resolution (adhimokkha); they obtain the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), they are liberated through signless liberation (animittavimokkha), they are faith-followers (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the first path, and they are faith-liberated (saddhāvimutta) in the seven instances. If the emergence occurs through suffering, all three types of persons are those with a preponderance of tranquility (passaddhi); they obtain the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), they are liberated through undirected liberation (appaṇihitavimokkha), and they are body-witnesses (kāyasakkhī) in all places. Among them, one who uses an immaterial absorption (arūpajjhāna) as a basis becomes a both-ways-liberated person (ubhatobhāgavimutta) in the highest fruit of Arahantship. If the emergence occurs through non-self, all three types of persons are those with a preponderance of knowledge (veda); they obtain the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), they are liberated through void liberation (suññatavimokkha), they are dhamma-followers (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the first path, they are attained-to-view (diṭṭhippatta) in the six instances, and they are wisdom-liberated (paññāvimutta) in the highest fruit of Arahantship.

Furthermore, the path receives its name through five reasons: by its own nature (sarasa), by the opposite (paccanīka), by its quality (guṇa), by the object (ārammaṇa), or by the arrival (āgamana). If the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa) emerges after contemplating formations as impermanent, one is liberated through signless liberation. If it emerges after contemplating as suffering, one is liberated through undirected liberation. If it emerges after contemplating as non-self, one is liberated through void liberation. This is the name received by its own nature. It is called 'signless' (animitta) because, through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), it breaks down the compact mass of formations and arrives after abandoning the sign of permanence, the sign of stability, and the sign of eternity. It is called 'undirected' (appaṇihita) because, through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), it abandons the perception of pleasure and arrives after drying up longing and desire. It is called 'void' (suññata) because, through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), it abandons the perception of self, being, and person, and sees formations as void. This is the name received by the opposite. It is called 'void' because it is void of greed and so on. Because of the [abandoning] of the signs of forms and so on...
149:
It is called *animitta* (signless) because of the absence of signs such as lust (*rāga*), and it is called *appaṇihita* (undirected) because of the absence of desires such as lust. This is the name of that path based on its own qualities (*saguṇa*). Because that path takes Nibbāna—which is void of lust, etc., free from the signs of lust, etc., and free from the desires of lust, etc.—as its object, it is also called *suññata* (void), *animitta*, and *appaṇihita*. This is its name based on its object (*ārammaṇa*).

Arrival (*āgamana*) is of two kinds: arrival through insight (*vipassanā*) and arrival through the path (*magga*). Between these two, arrival through insight is obtained in the path, and arrival through the path is obtained in the fruit (*phala*). Contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*) is called *suññatā*. The path arising through *suññatā-vipassanā* is called *suññata*. The fruit of the *suññata* path is *suññata*. Contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) is called *animitta*. The path arising through *animitta-vipassanā* is called *animitta*. This name is not found in the Abhidhamma method, but it is found in the Sutta method. In that Sutta method, teachers say that change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*), having Nibbāna called *animitta* as its object and being named *animitta* itself, stands in the position of the means of arrival and gives its name to the path. Therefore, the path is called *animitta*. It is very appropriate to call the fruit *animitta* through arrival by the path. Contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*) is called *appaṇihitā* because it dries up desire for formations (*saṅkhāra*). The path arising through *appaṇihita-vipassanā* is called *appaṇihita*. The fruit of the *appaṇihita* path is *appaṇihita*. Thus, insight gives its name to the path, and the path gives its name to the fruit. This is the name based on arrival (*āgamana*). Thus, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) determines the specific liberation (*vimokkha*).

Having pointed out the three liberations of great importance taught by the Blessed One, and wishing to point out other liberations by way of their description, he said: 'Furthermore, there are sixty-eight liberations,' and so on. In that text, 'furthermore' (*api ca*) indicates another method. How do they become sixty-eight? Are they not seventy-five? True, according to the literal text, they are seventy-five. However, because the three liberations taught by the Blessed One are set aside and other liberations are described, and because these three are included within those others, these three should not be counted. The three liberations such as internal liberation (*ajjhatta-vimokkha*) are also not counted because they are included within the fourfold detailed explanation. In the phrase 'directed liberation (*paṇihita-vimokkha*) and undirected liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*)', the undirected liberation is not counted because it has the same name as the one previously mentioned. Thus, when these seven are removed, the remaining liberations are sixty-eight. If so, why are the three such as the void liberation mentioned again? They are mentioned to include them in the summary and to provide a detailed description of them as well. As for the three such as internal emergence (*ajjhatta-vuṭṭhāna*), without distinction...
150:
...they are shown by way of the original group. It should be understood that the undirected liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*) is mentioned again by way of being the opposite of the directed liberation (*paṇihita-vimokkha*).

Among the terms such as internal emergence (*ajjhatta-vuṭṭhāna*), it is called *ajjhatta-vuṭṭhāna* because it emerges from one's own continuity. They are called *anuloma* because they act in conformity. The absence of the tranquillization of internal emergence is called *ajjhatta-vuṭṭhāna-paṭippassaddhi*. 'Possessing form' (*rūpī*) means the fine-material sphere jhāna (*rūpāvacara-jhāna*) produced in one's own hair, etc., is called *rūpa*; because that person possesses that jhāna, he is called *rūpī*. 'He sees forms' (*rūပါနိ ပဿတိ*) means he sees external forms such as the blue kasina with the eye of jhāna. By this, the attainment of jhāna in kasinas based on internal and external objects is shown. 'Internally perceiving formlessness' (*ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī*) means not having the perception of form internally; it means a person who has not produced fine-material sphere jhāna in his own hair, etc. By this, it is shown that the jhāna is attained only externally after performing the preliminary work externally. 'Resolved only on the beautiful' (*subhanteva adhimutto*) means the attention is directed only to the object as 'it is beautiful'. In that regard, although there is no such attention as 'it is beautiful' within the absorption (*appanā*), because one who dwells pervading the object of a being's concept with a non-repulsive aspect is said to be 'resolved only on the beautiful', this summary was made.

It is called temporal liberation (*samaya-vimokkha*) because the nature of liberation by suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*) exists only at the time of each absorption. That same liberation is called *sāmayika* because it is associated only with the time of absorption by way of performing its own function. There is also a reading *sāmāyika*. It is called *kuppa* (shakeable) because it can be destroyed. It is called *lokika* (mundane) because it is associated with the world, not having transcended the world. There is also a reading *lokiya*. It is called *lokuttara* (supramundane) because it is transcending or has transcended the world. It is called *sāsava* (with taints) because it is with taints by way of making them an object. It is called *anāsava* (without taints) because there are no taints in this liberation, either by way of making them an object or by way of association. It is called *sāmisa* (carnal) because it is with the material thing (*āmisa*) known as form (*rūpa*). It is called *nirāmisa-nirāmisatara* (more non-carnal than non-carnal) because it is more excellent than the non-carnal due to the abandoning of both material and immaterial states in every way. *Paṇihita* (directed) is the liberation desired by way of craving. It is called *saññutta* (yoked) because it is associated with fetters by way of making them an object. *Ekatta-vimokkha* (liberation of oneness) is the liberation that has a single nature because it is not overwhelmed by defilements. *Saññā-vimokkha* (liberation of perception) is insight knowledge itself, because it is liberated from perverted perception. That same insight knowledge is called *ñāṇa-vimokkha* (liberation of knowledge) because the knowledge itself is the liberation by way of being liberated from delusion. *Sītisiyā-vimokkha* (liberation of coolness) is insight knowledge itself because of its coolness...
151:
Insight knowledge itself, which arises as the liberation (vimokkha) with the thought, "May the cooling of the fires of defilements occur for me," is called Sītisiyāvimokkha. There is also a reading as "Sītisikāvimokkha"; they explain the meaning of that Pali as "the liberation that arises for the sake of cooling in the mental continuum that brings about cooling." Absorption (jhāna) itself, which is divided into access (upacāra) and fixed concentration (appanā), as well as mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara), is called Jhānavimokkha. "Anupādā cittassa vimokkha" refers to the liberation of the insight mind without clinging and without forming views. The remaining terms should be understood in the manner already stated.

## The Explanation of the Brief Exposition of Liberations is finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Detailed Exposition of Liberations

In the detailed exposition of the brief summary beginning with "Katamo," the phrase "thus he repeatedly reflects" means investigating and reflecting, or observing closely with wisdom, or observing thoroughly from all sides. "Suññamidaṃ" means this group of the five aggregates is empty. Empty of what? It is empty of a self (atta) or of what belongs to a self (attaniya). In that passage, "of a self" means it is empty of a self because the self imagined by foolish people does not exist. "Of what belongs to a self" means it is also empty of what belongs to that self imagined by foolish people. Only because there is no self, there is no "what belongs to a self." What is called "belonging to a self" would be either permanent (nicca) or pleasant (sukha). Both of these things belonging to a self, called permanent and pleasant, are not found in the five aggregates. By rejecting the nature of permanence, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is taught; by rejecting the nature of pleasure, the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) is taught. By the Pali phrase "suñamidaṃ attena vā," only the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) is taught. "So" refers to that monk who practices insight through these three contemplations. "Abhinivesaṃ na karoti" means not making an adherence (abhinivesa)—that is, a wrong view—clinging to a self, by the power of the contemplation of non-self.

"Nimittaṃ na karoti" means not making a sign of permanence by the power of the contemplation of impermanence. "Paṇidhiṃ na karoti" means not making a desire (paṇidhi) by the power of the contemplation of suffering. These three liberations are obtained figuratively at the moment of insight by the power of abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna). In the literal sense, however, they are obtained only at the moment of the Path by the power of abandonment by destruction (samucchedapahāna). The four fine-material sphere absorptions (rūpāvacara jhāna) are called internal-emergence liberations (ajjhattavuṭṭhāna vimokkha) because they emerge from hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth within one's own continuum. The four immaterial attainments (arūpasamāpatti) are called external-emergence liberations (bahiddhāvuṭṭhāna vimokkha) because they emerge from objects such as kasinas. In this context, objects such as kasinas are also taught as "external" (bahiddhā), like the six external sense bases. Both these internal-emergence liberations and external-emergence liberations are called liberations by suppression (vikkhambhanavimokkha). Emergence from both (dubhatovuṭṭhāna), which refers to the four Paths, is called liberation by destruction (samucchedavimokkha).

By the passages beginning with "nīvaraṇehi vuṭṭhāti," the internal-emergence is taught in its own nature (sarūpa). By the passages beginning with "rūpasaññāya," because the transcending of objects such as kasinas is evident...
152:
Without teaching the transcending of those objects such as kasinas, he teaches only the transcending of perceptions of form (rūpasaññā) and so forth as taught in the Suttas. "Sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsa" is a compound word (samāsa), and it should be analyzed by breaking it into "from personality view, from doubt, and from adherence to rules and rituals." Alternatively, this analyzed reading itself is the original text.

By the passages beginning with "vitakko ca," the access levels (upacāra) of the fine-material sphere absorptions and the immaterial attainments are taught. By the passages beginning with "aniccānupassanā," the insight (vipassanā) that precedes the four Paths is taught. "Paṭilābho vā" is called attainment (paṭilābha) because it is an attainment that is pervasive and widespread through the reaching of the five kinds of mastery (vasībhāva). Indeed, through the reaching of mastery, all preliminary efforts (payoga) for the fine-material sphere absorptions and all preliminary efforts for the immaterial attainments are stilled; therefore, that attainment is called "liberation by tranquilization" (paṭippassaddhivimokkha). The meaning that the resultant (vipāka) is the tranquilization of the fine-material sphere absorptions and the immaterial attainments is quite straightforward. Some teachers, however, say: "Because the efforts of the access level are stilled, the attainment of absorption and attainment occurs; therefore, the attainment of absorption and attainment is called 'liberation by tranquilization'."

"Ajjhatta" refers to states occurring based on one's own individual existence (attabhāva). "Paccatta" refers to states occurring dependent on one's own individual existence. Both these terms point only to what is internal (ajjhatta) related to oneself. "Nīlanimitta" is the blue sign (blue kasina) itself. "Nīlasaññaṃ paṭilabhati" means obtaining the perception of "blue" in that blue sign. "Suggahitaṃ karoti" means one grasps it well at the stage of preliminary meditation (parikamma-bhāvanā). "Sūpadhāritaṃ upadhāreti" means one reflects on it after having well noted it at the stage of access meditation (upacāra-bhāvanā). "Svāvatthitaṃ avatthāpeti" means one makes a firm determination at the stage of fixed concentration (appanā-bhāvanā). There is also a reading as "vavatthāpeti." One who performs the preliminary work on the blue kasina internally does so on the hair, or the bile, or the pupils of the eyes. "Bahiddhā nīlanimitte" refers to any kind of blue kasina among external blue flowers, blue clothes, or blue minerals. "Cittaṃ upasaṃharati" means directing the mind. The same method applies to yellow (pīta) and so forth.

"Āsevati" means associating with that very perception from the beginning. "Bhāveti" means developing it. "Bahulīkaroti" means doing it repeatedly. "Rūpaṃ" refers to the form that is the blue sign. "Rūpasaññī": the perception that arises in that form is called perception of form (rūpasaññā); because one has that perception of form, one is called "percipient of form" (rūpasaññī). One who performs the preliminary work on the yellow sign and so forth internally does so on the fat, or the skin, or the yellow part of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on the red kasina (lohitakasina) does so on the flesh, or the blood, or the tongue, or the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, or the red part of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on the white kasina (odātakasina) does so on the bones, or the teeth, or the nails, or the white part of the eyes. "Ajjhattaṃ arūpaṃ" means that there is no kasina-form sign in one's own internal continuum.
153:
"Mettāsahagatena" means (a mind) endowed with loving-kindness through the power of the first, second, and third jhānas. "Cetasā" means with the mind. The phrase "ekaṃ disaṃ" (one direction) is spoken in the sense of pervading beings included in that direction, taking as an object the beings first grasped in one particular direction. "Pharitvā" means having touched (the object) and taken it as an object. "Viharati" means he maintains the postures of dwelling supported by the Brahma-vihāra jhāna. "Tathā dutiyaṃ" means just as he dwells pervading one direction such as the East, etc., likewise he dwells pervading the second, third, or fourth direction immediately following that. "Iti uddhaṃ" means in this same way, he pervades the upward direction. "Adho tiriyaṃ" means he dwells pervading the downward and across (intermediate) directions in the same manner. In that context, "adho" refers to the downward direction, and "tiriyaṃ" refers to the intermediate directions (anudisā). Thus, in all directions, just as a horse is made to run around inside a stable, one should understand that the mind accompanied by loving-kindness is sent forward and sent all around. By this much, the pervading of loving-kindness by way of limitation (odhiso), having grasped each direction individually, is shown. However, the words beginning with "sabbadhī" are spoken to show the pervading of loving-kindness without limitation (anodhiso). In that context, "sabbadhī" means in all places. "Sabbattatāya" means treating all beings—distinguished as low, middle, high, friends, enemies, and neutral—as oneself (attasamatā), without making the distinction "this is another being." Alternatively, "sabbattatāya" means the entire mind becoming loving-kindness without being distracted outward even slightly. "Sabbāvantaṃ" means associated with all beings. There is also a variant reading "sabbavantaṃ." "Lokaṃ" refers to the world of beings (sattaloka).

Because of the desire to show synonymous expressions such as "vipulena," the word "mettāsahagatena" is spoken again here. Or else, because the word "tathā" or the word "iti" is not used here as it was in the limited pervading of loving-kindness, "mettāsahagatena cetasā" is spoken again. Or else, it is spoken by way of conclusion. In the word "vipulena," its expansiveness should be understood by way of its pervading (all beings). By way of its plane (bhūmi), that loving-kindness is "mahaggata" (exalted). Indeed, that exalted state has reached greatness because of its ability to suppress defilements, its expansive fruits, and its long-lasting continuity. Or, it is called "mahaggata" because it is attained by great persons possessed of noble desire, energy, mind, and wisdom. It is "appamāṇa" (immeasurable) by way of mastery and by way of taking immeasurable beings as objects. It is "averaṃ" (free from enmity) because of the abandonment of the opposing enmity called ill-will (byāpāda). It is "abyāpajjhaṃ" because of the abandonment of mental distress (domanassa), which means being free from suffering. "Appaṭikūlā honti" means they appear to the monk's mind without being repulsive. In the remaining Brahma-vihāras also, it should be applied by way of compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā) according to the method already mentioned. In compassion, it is "averaṃ" because of the abandonment of the opposing enmity called cruelty (vihesā). In appreciative joy, it is because of the abandonment of the opposing enmity called boredom (arati).
154:
"Accompanied by equanimity" (upekkhāsahagatena) means with a mind endowed with equanimity through the power of the fourth jhāna. It is "without enmity" (averaṃ) because of the abandoning of the danger which is lust (rāga). It is "without ill-will" (abyāpajjaṃ) because of the abandoning of household-based joy (gehasita somanassa). For all unwholesome states, being associated with the fever of defilements, are indeed "with ill-will" (sabyāpajja). This is the distinction between these (compassion, etc.).

"In every way" (sabbaso) means in all modes, or all without exception. "Of the perceptions of form" (rūpasaññānaṃ) refers to the fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara jhāna) which are spoken of by taking perception as the head, as well as their objects. Indeed, the fine-material sphere jhāna is also called "form" (rūpa) in such passages as "Possessing form, he sees forms" (Paṭis. I. 209; Dhs. 248). Its object is also called "form" in such passages as "He sees forms externally, beautiful or ugly" (Dhs. 223). Therefore, in this context, the perception occurring in the fine-material sphere jhāna is called "perception of form" (rūpasaññā); thus it is a name for the fine-material sphere jhāna spoken of by taking perception as the head. That which has form as its perception is "rūpasaññaṃ"; this means "form" is its name. In this way, it should also be understood as the name for the objects of those fine-material sphere jhānas, such as the earth kasiṇa and so on. "By the surmounting" (samatikkamā) means through fading away and through cessation. What is meant? It means that through the fading away and cessation, in every way or without exception, of the fifteen perceptions of form known as jhānas by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional states, and of the nine perceptions of form known as objects by way of the earth kasiṇa and so on—and because of the cause of fading away and the cause of cessation—one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). Indeed, it is not possible for one who has not in every way surmounted the perceptions of form to enter and dwell in this sphere.

Because these attainments are to be reached by surmounting the object, unlike the first jhāna and so on which are reached in a single object. And for one who is not dispassionate towards the object, the surmounting of perception does not occur. Therefore, it should be understood that this explanation of the meaning is also made by way of surmounting the object.

"With the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction" (paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā): perception arising from the impact of the sense bases such as the eye and the objects such as forms is called "perception of sensory reaction" (paṭighasaññā). This is a name for the perceptions of form and so on. By the "disappearance" (atthaṅgamā)—meaning the abandoning, the non-arising, the making non-existent—in every way of all ten perceptions of sensory reaction, namely, the five wholesome resultants and the five unwholesome resultants. Granted, these perceptions of sensory reaction do not exist even for one who has attained the first jhāna and so on. For at that time, the mind does not proceed by way of the five sense doors. Even though they do not exist, just as pleasure and pain which were abandoned elsewhere are mentioned in the fourth jhāna, and just as self-view and so on which were abandoned in lower paths are mentioned in the third path, so too these perceptions of sensory reaction are mentioned here by way of praising this jhāna in order to generate effort for this jhāna...
155:
In this sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), the teaching regarding (the surpassing of) perceptions of resistance (paṭighasaññā) should be understood. Alternatively, although those perceptions of resistance do not exist for one who has attained a fine-material sphere jhāna (rūpāvacara jhāna), it is not because they have been fully abandoned. This is because fine-material sphere meditation (rūpāvacara bhāvanā) does not lead to detachment from form (rūpavirāga), and the occurrence of those perceptions of resistance is related only to form. However, this (immaterial) meditation does lead to detachment from form. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that those perceptions of resistance are abandoned in this sphere of infinite space. Not only is it appropriate to say so, but it should also be definitely maintained that they are thus abandoned. Indeed, it is because those perceptions of resistance were not yet abandoned prior to this immaterial jhāna that the Blessed One said: "Sound is a thorn to one who has attained the first jhāna" (A. Ni. 10.72). But in this immaterial jhāna, because they have been abandoned, the imperturbability (āneñjatā) and peaceful liberation (santavimokkhatā) of the immaterial attainments are spoken of.

"Non-attention to perceptions of diversity" (nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā) refers either to perceptions occurring in diverse objects or to perceptions that are diverse in nature. Because these perceptions occur in objects of diverse natures, such as the distinctions of visible forms, sounds, etc., and because these forty-four perceptions—namely, 8 sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, 12 unwholesome perceptions, 11 sense-sphere wholesome resultant perceptions, 2 unwholesome resultant perceptions, and 11 sense-sphere functional perceptions—are diverse, having different natures and being dissimilar to one another, they are called "perceptions of diversity" (nānattasaññā). Non-attention to all those perceptions of diversity in every way means non-adverting to them and not producing them in the mind. It means that because one does not advert to them, does not produce them in the mind, does not attend to them, and does not review them, this is said. Furthermore, since the previously mentioned perceptions of form (rūpasaññā) and perceptions of resistance (paṭighasaññā) do not exist even in the rebirth-process produced by this sphere of infinite space jhāna, what need is there to mention their absence at the time of dwelling in the attainment of this jhāna in that life? Therefore, by both "surpassing" (samatikkama) and "disappearance" (atthangama), their mere non-existence is meant. However, among the perceptions of diversity, twenty-seven perceptions—namely, 8 sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, 9 functional perceptions, and 10 unwholesome perceptions—still exist in the rebirth-process produced by this jhāna. Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "non-attention" (amanasikārā) is used regarding those perceptions. Even in that life, one who dwells in the attainment of this jhāna does so only by not attending to those perceptions. If one were to attend to those perceptions, one would not be in the attainment. In brief, by the phrase "through the surpassing of perceptions of form" (rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā), the abandoning of all fine-material sphere states (rūpāvacara dhamma) is stated. By the phrase "through the disappearance of perceptions of resistance and non-attention to perceptions of diversity" (paṭighasaññānaṃ atthangamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā), it should be understood that the abandoning of and non-attention to all sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consciousness and mental factors are stated.
156:
In the phrase "Infinite is space" (ananto ākāso), because space is a mere concept (paññatti), no end in terms of arising (uppāda) or end in terms of falling away (vaya) is evident in that concept of space; therefore, it is called infinite (ananta). It is also called infinite by way of infinite pervasion. For that yogi does not pervade it partially, but pervades it entirely. "Space" (ākāsa) refers to the space resulting from the removal of the kasina (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa). The terms such as "sphere of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatana) have the meanings already mentioned. "Attaining and dwelling" (upasampajja viharati) means that having reached and produced that jhāna, one dwells with a posture suitable for it. That jhāna itself is called an attainment (samāpatti) because it is to be attained.

In the phrase "surpassing the sphere of infinite space" (ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma), according to the method previously mentioned, both the jhāna is called the sphere of infinite space and the object is called the sphere of infinite space. The object is also called the sphere of infinite space according to the method previously mentioned: it is infinite space (ākāsānañca), and because it is the object of the first immaterial jhāna, it is a base (āyatana) in the sense of an abode (adhiṭṭhāna), like the "abode of the devas" (devāyatana). Thus, it is the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). Likewise, it is infinite space, and because it is the cause for the arising of that jhāna, it is a base (āyatana) in the sense of a place of origin (sañjātidesa), like the expression "Kamboja is the place of origin (āyatana) of horses." Thus, it is also called the sphere of infinite space. It should be understood that because one must attain and dwell in this sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) only after surpassing both this jhāna and its object by way of non-occurrence and non-attention, this was said by taking both together as "surpassing the sphere of infinite space."

"Infinite is consciousness" (anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ) means that one attends to that very consciousness which occurred pervading the infinite space as "infinite is consciousness." Or, it is infinite by way of attention. For that yogi, when attending to that consciousness which has space as its object without remainder, is said to be attending to infinite consciousness.

In the phrase "surpassing the sphere of infinite consciousness" (viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma), here too, according to the method previously mentioned, both the jhāna is called the sphere of infinite consciousness and the object is called the sphere of infinite consciousness. The object is also called the sphere of infinite consciousness according to the method previously mentioned: it is infinite consciousness (viññāṇañca), and because it is the object of the second immaterial jhāna, it is a base (āyatana) in the sense of an abode (adhiṭṭhāna). Thus, it is the sphere of infinite consciousness. Likewise, it is infinite consciousness, and because it is the cause for the arising of that same jhāna, it is a base (āyatana) in the sense of a place of origin (sañjātidesa). Thus, it is also called the sphere of infinite consciousness. It should be understood that because one must attain and dwell in this sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) only after surpassing both this jhāna and its object by way of non-occurrence and non-attention, this was said by taking both together as "surpassing the sphere of infinite consciousness." "There is nothing" (natthi kiñci) means that one attends to it in this way: "nothing, nothing," "void, void," "secluded, secluded."
157:
"Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkammā": In this phrase also, according to the method already mentioned, the jhāna is called "ākiñcaññāyatana" and the object is also called "ākiñcaññāyatana." For the object is "ākiñcaññāyatana" because it is "nothingness" (ākiñcañña) and is also a "sphere" (āyatana) in the sense of being a foundation, as it is the object of the third formless jhāna. Furthermore, it is "ākiñcaññāyatana" because it is "nothingness" and is also a "sphere" in the sense of being a place of origin, as it is the cause for the arising of that jhāna. Thus, having transcended both this jhāna and the object by not bringing them into existence and by not attending to them, one must enter and dwell in this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana); therefore, taking both together, it should be understood as "ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkammā." The discussion on the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha) has been mentioned below.

The seven deliverances (vimokkha) beginning with "rūpī rūပါနိ passati" (one possessing form sees forms) are called deliverances in the sense of being well-freed from opposing states and in the sense of being well-freed by way of delight in the object. The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), however, is called deliverance in the sense of being free from mind and mental factors. It is called "samayavimokkha" (occasional deliverance) because one is freed at the time of being in the attainment and not freed at the time of having emerged from the attainment. The Noble Paths are "asamayavimokkha" (non-occasional deliverance) because they are absolutely freed by way of deliverance through eradication (samucchedavimutti); the Fruits of Recluseship (sāmaññaphala) are so because they are absolutely freed by way of deliverance through tranquilization (paṭippassaddhivimutti); and Nibbāna is so because it is absolutely freed by way of deliverance through escape (nissaraṇavimutti). Likewise, there are occasional (sāmayika) and non-occasional (asāmayika) deliverances.

It is called "kuppa" (shakeable) because it can decline due to negligence. It is called "akuppa" (unshakeable) because it does not decline in that way. It is called "lokiya" (mundane) because it occurs in the world. The Noble Paths are called "lokuttara" (supramundane) because they transcend the world; the Fruits of Recluseship and Nibbāna are called "lokuttara" because they have transcended the world. They are called "anāsava" (taintless) because the taints (āsava) cannot take the supramundane Dhamma as an object, just as flies do not dare to land on a glowing iron ball that is intensely hot. "Rūpappaṭisaññutta" refers to the fine-material jhānas (rūpajjhāna). "Arūpappaṭisaññutta" refers to the formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti). That which is taken as an object by craving is "paṇihita" (directed). That which is not taken as an object is "appaṇihita" (undirected). The Paths and Fruits are called "ekattavimokkha" (deliverance of oneness) because they have a single object and a single finality (Nibbāna). Nibbāna is called "ekattavimokkha" because it is peerless (without a second). It is called "nānattavimokkha" (deliverance of diversity) because of the diversity of objects and the diversity of results.

"Siyā" means "might be"; it means "there might be ten" or "there might be one." This word "siyā" is an indicative statement (vidhi), not a question. "By way of basis" (vatthu-vasena) means there are ten by way of the ten bases such as the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā), etc. "By way of method" (pariyāyena) means...
158:
...it is one by way of the method of liberation. Regarding "might be" (siyā), it asks: "How might it be?" or "In what way is that which is prescribed as 'might be' possible?" "Knowledge of contemplation of impermanence" (aniccānupassanāñāṇaṃ) is a compound word. There is also a reading as "aniccānupassanā-ñāṇaṃ." The same applies to the remaining terms. "From the perception of permanence" (niccato saññāya) means from the perception that occurs as permanent, meaning the perception that occurs as "permanent." This same method applies to the perceptions of pleasure (sukha), self (atta), and sign (nimitta). "From the sign" (nimittato) means from the sign of permanence. "From the perception of delight" (nandiyā saññāya) means from the perception that occurs by way of delight, meaning the perception associated with delight (craving). This same method applies to the perceptions of lust (rāga), origin (samudaya), grasping (ādāna), directing (paṇidhi), and adherence (abhinivesa).

In fact, these three—contemplation of destruction (khaya), vanishing (vaya), and change (vipariṇāma)—are specific types of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) which serve as powerful conditions for the strengthening of the contemplation of impermanence and others. For through the vision of dissolution, the contemplation of impermanence becomes powerful. When the contemplation of impermanence has become powerful, the contemplations of suffering and non-self also become powerful, according to the saying: "What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self." Therefore, when the contemplation of impermanence and others are taught, those three (destruction, vanishing, change) are also already taught. Since contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā) is already taught by the statement "one is freed from the perception of adherence (abhinivesa)," it means one is freed from the perception of adherence to core (sāra), delusion (sammoha), attachment (ālaya), bondage (saññoga), and insistence (abhinivesa). And because of the absence of adherence, it is already taught that one is freed from the perception of non-reflection (appaṭisaṅkhā) from the perception. Therefore, it should be understood that the five contemplations such as the contemplation of higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā) are not taught separately. Thus, it should be understood that among the eighteen great insights (mahā-vipassanā), these eight contemplations are not mentioned, and only ten contemplations are taught.

"Contemplation of impermanence is knowledge of things as they really are" (aniccānupassanā yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ): Contemplation of impermanence itself is the knowledge of things as they really are. Both words are in the nominative case (paccattavacana). By the term "knowledge of things as they really are," the meaning of knowledge is stated. The same applies to the rest. "From ignorance which is delusion" (sammohā aññāṇā) means from the ignorance that is of the nature of delusion. By the word "is freed" (muccati), the meaning of liberation (vimokkha) is stated.

"Contemplation of impermanence is the unsurpassed knowledge of the state of coolness" (aniccānupassanā anuttaraṃ sītibhāvañāṇaṃ): Here, it is "unsurpassed" (anuttara) in the sense of being excellent because it exists only in the Dispensation, or it is "unsurpassed" because it is a condition for the unsurpassed (Path, Fruit, Nibbāna). The state of coolness itself is the knowledge, hence "knowledge of the state of coolness" (sītibhāvañāṇa). It is that unsurpassed knowledge of the state of coolness known as contemplation of impermanence. "Monks, a monk endowed with six things..."
159:
“He is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness (anuttara sītibhāva)” (A. Ni. 6.85). In this Pali passage, Nibbāna is called the unsurpassed state of coolness. In this [Paṭisambhidāmagga], however, insight (vipassanā) is intended by the unsurpassed state of coolness. In the passage, “He is freed from the burning, the intense heat, and the distress that arise from [the view of] permanence,” the defilements that arise from the assumption of “permanence” are called “burning” (santāpa) because they cause burning in both this world and the next; “intense heat” (paridāha) because they burn all around; and “distress” (daratha) because of their nature of heat.

The terms starting with jhāna, such as “He meditates on renunciation (nekkhamma),” have the meanings already stated below. In this context, renunciation and the eight attainments are indeed factors leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya).

“The liberation of the mind without clinging” refers here only to insight (vipassanā). However, in the Pali passage, “There is that liberation of the mind without clinging [Nibbāna]; discourse [on the Vinaya] is for the sake of that Nibbāna; consultation is for the sake of that Nibbāna” (Pari. 366, A. Ni. 3.68), Nibbāna is called “the liberation of the mind without clinging.” “Katihu pādānehi” means “from how many clingings [is one freed]?” “Katamā ekupādānā” means “from which single clinging [is one freed]?” “Idaṃ ekupādānā” means “[is freed] from this single [clinging to sensual pleasure].” The word “idaṃ” (this) may also be a word that refers back to the knowledge mentioned previously. Regarding the liberation from clinging, it should be understood as follows: Because in the beginning, one contemplates the arising and passing away of formations (saṅkhāra) repeatedly and develops insight through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā); later, one contemplates only the dissolution (bhaṅga) of formations and develops insight through the signless contemplation (animittānupassanā). Indeed, the signless contemplation is a specific form of the contemplation of impermanence. By seeing the arising and passing away of formations and by seeing their dissolution, the absence of self (emptiness of self) becomes clear. Through such contemplation, there is the abandoning of the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna) and the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). Due to the abandonment of the clinging to views, the view (wrong view) that “the self is purified by the practices of cows, goats, etc.” no longer exists, and thus there is the abandoning of the clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna). Because one directly sees the absence of self through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), and because the contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā) is a specific form of the contemplation of non-self, these four knowledges [aniccā, animittā, anattā, suññatā] are liberated from the three clingings starting with the clinging to views. It is not stated that the four knowledges starting with the contemplation of impermanence are liberated from the clinging to sensual pleasure, because only the four knowledges starting with the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) are directly opposed to craving (taṇhā). For, in the beginning, for one who sees “formations are suffering” through the contemplation of suffering, and later for one who sees “formations are suffering” through the desireless contemplation (appaṇihitānupassanā), the longing (patthanā) for formations is abandoned. Indeed, the desireless contemplation is a specific form of the contemplation of suffering. For one who is weary through the contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā) toward formations, and for one who is dispassionate through the contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā), the longing for formations is abandoned. Therefore, these four knowledges [dukkhā, appaṇihitā, nibbidā, virāgā] are liberated from the clinging to sensual pleasure (kāmupādāna). Because defilements are ceased through the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā), and because defilements are relinquished through the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā), these two knowledges are liberated from all four clingings.
160:
For one who is dispassionate through the contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā), the longing for formations (saṅkhāras) is abandoned; therefore, these four knowledges are liberated from the clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna). Because one causes defilements to cease through the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā) and relinquishes defilements through the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā), these two knowledges are liberated from the four types of clinging. Thus, the sixty-eight liberations (vimokkha) have been explained by way of difference in nature and difference in mode.

Now, wishing to show the causes of the three liberations (vimokkha-mukha) that were briefly mentioned at the beginning, and to show the distinction of faculties and the distinction of individuals preceded by liberation, he said the words beginning with "Tīṇi kho panimāni." In that passage, "vimokkha-mukhāni" refers to the insights (vipassanā) that are the causes of the three liberations. "They lead to the emergence from the world" (lokaniyyānāya saṃvattanti) means they lead to the exit from the three worlds (the sense world, the fine-material world, and the immaterial world).

"By contemplating all formations as delimited and circumscribed" (sabbasaṅkhāre paricchedaparivaṭumato samanupassanatāya) means that emergence from the world occurs because of contemplating all formations uniformly, both by delimiting them through the power of arising and passing away, and by circumscribing them through the power of passing away; this should be understood as the completion of the text. Contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) delimits that formations do not exist before the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa); and when searching for the destination of those formations, it contemplates them as circumscribed (parivaṭumato) or as having an end-limit, seeing that they do not go elsewhere after the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa), but vanish right at that moment of dissolution. All formations are delimited at the preceding end by arising and at the subsequent end by dissolution.

"By the mind's leaping into the signless element" (animittāya ca dhātuyā cittasampakkhandanatāya) means that emergence from the world occurs because the mind enters the Nibbāna-element called "signless" (animitta), due to its appearing in the mode of signlessness and because of the mind's inclination toward Nibbāna even at the moment of insight. "By the stirring of the mind" (manosamuttejanatāya) means because of the occurrence of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in the mind. Through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), the mind reaches a state of urgency regarding formations.

"And into the desireless element" (appaṇihitāya ca dhātuyā) means emergence from the world occurs because of the mind's entry into the Nibbāna-element called "desireless" (appaṇihita), due to its appearing in the mode of desirelessness and because of the mind's inclination toward Nibbāna even at the moment of insight. "All phenomena" (sabbadhamme) is stated instead of "all formations" (sabbasaṅkhāre) because, although Nibbāna is not an object of insight contemplation, the nature of non-self (anatta) is evident in it.

"By contemplating as other" (parato samanupassanatāya) means emergence from the world occurs because of contemplating uniformly as non-self, such as "not I, not mine," due to the fact that things are dependent on causes and thus not subject to one's will or control. "And into the void element" (suññatāya ca dhātuyā) means that emergence from the world occurs because the mind enters the Nibbāna-element called "void" (suññata), due to its appearing in the mode of voidness and because of the mind's inclination toward Nibbāna even at the moment of insight.

Thus, these three statements were spoken by way of the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. For this very reason, immediately after those gateways to liberation, he spoke the words beginning with "aniccatō manasikarōtō" (when attending as impermanent). In that passage, "khayato" means by way of exhaustion. "Bhayato" means by way of being fearful. "Suññato" means by way of being devoid of self.
161:
"Abundance of resolution" (adhimokkha-bahula) means that for a person practicing with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), believing that "conditioned things break up by way of momentary dissolution," upon seeing the momentary dissolution directly, a mind abundant in faith arises toward the Blessed One, thinking, "The Blessed One indeed spoke the truth." Alternatively, by seeing the impermanence of present partial formations and resolving that "all formations—past, future, and present—are thus impermanent," a mind abundant in resolution arises. "Abundance of tranquility" (passaddhi-bahula) means that through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), by abandoning the longing (paṇidhi) that causes mental agitation, a mind abundant in tranquility arises due to the absence of mental distress. Alternatively, because the contemplation of suffering generates spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and for one who is stirred, by striving wisely, a mind abundant in tranquility arises due to the absence of distraction. "Abundance of knowledge" (veda-bahula) means that through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), for one who sees the profound characteristic of non-self unseen by those outside the Dispensation (titthiyas), a mind abundant in wisdom arises. Alternatively, for one who rejoices, thinking, "I have seen the characteristic of non-self unseen by the world including the devas," a mind abundant in joy and satisfaction arises.

"One abundant in resolution obtains the faculty of faith" (adhimokkhabahulo saddhindriyaṃ paṭilabhati) means that in the preliminary stage, when resolution occurs abundantly, it is called the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) upon the fulfillment of meditation; he is said to obtain that faculty of faith. "One abundant in tranquility obtains the faculty of concentration" (passaddhibahulo samādhindriyaṃ paṭilabhati) means that for one abundant in tranquility in the preliminary stage, according to the teaching, "One with a tranquil body experiences happiness; the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) arises based on tranquility upon the fulfillment of meditation; he is said to obtain that faculty of concentration. "One abundant in knowledge obtains the faculty of wisdom" (vedabahulo paññindriyaṃ paṭilabhati) means that in the preliminary stage, when knowledge (veda) occurs abundantly, it is called the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) upon the fulfillment of meditation; he is said to obtain that faculty of wisdom.

"There is predominance" (ādhipateyyaṃ hoti) means that although the four factors such as desire (chanda) etc., arise as predominant, there is predominance or primacy by way of accomplishing its own task of liberation (vimokkha). The word "bhāvanāya" is in the locative case, or it means for the sake of developing further and further. "They are its followers" (tadanvayā honti) means they follow that faculty of faith; they arise following that faculty of faith. "They are conascence conditions" (sahajātapaccayā honti) means that the states currently arising also assist by way of arising together, just as a lamp assists light. "They are mutuality conditions" (aññamaññapaccayā honti) means they assist by way of mutual production and support, just as a tripod of sticks supports each other. "They are dependence conditions" (nissayapaccayā honti) means they assist by way of being a foundation and a support, just as the earth is to trees or a cloth is to a painting. "They are association conditions" (sampayuttapaccayā honti) means they assist by way of being associated, characterized by having the same physical base, the same object, the same arising, and the same cessation.
162:
"At the time of penetration" (paṭivedha-kāle) means at the moment of the Path (magga-kkhaṇa), when penetrating the Truths. "The faculty of wisdom becomes predominant" (paññindriyaṃ ādhipateyyaṃ hoti) means that at the moment of the Path, taking Nibbāna as the object, the faculty of wisdom alone is the chief, both by way of performing the task of seeing the Four Noble Truths and by way of performing the task of abandoning the defilements. "For penetration" (paṭivedhāya) means for the sake of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. "Of a single taste" (ekarasa) means they have a common function by way of the taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa). "In the sense of seeing" (dassanaṭṭhena) means in the sense of seeing the Four Noble Truths. The statement "even while penetrating thus, one develops; even while developing, one penetrates" is said to show that at the moment of the Path, the state of development (bhāvanā) and the state of penetration (paṭivedha) exist simultaneously. Because the faculty of wisdom is predominant even at the moment of insight through the contemplation of non-self, the word "api" (even/also) is used in "paṭivedha-kālepi."

The passage beginning with "For one who attends to [formations] as impermanent, which faculty is predominant?" is said to show the distinction of individuals through the distinction of faculties. In that text, "adhimattaṃ" means predominant or excessive. In that moment of the Path, the predominance of the faculty of faith, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom should be understood through the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa). Although "Saddhā-vimutta" (one liberated by faith) is mentioned here without distinction, because it is distinguished later, it refers to the Saddhā-vimutta individual in the seven stages, excluding the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), namely the three higher paths and the four fruits. It also means that one becomes a Saddhā-vimutta because the faculty of faith is predominant; it does not mean that one is a Saddhā-vimutta in all paths and fruits whenever the faculty of faith is predominant. They say that because the faculty of faith is predominant at the moment of the path of stream-entry, one is called a Saddhā-vimutta even if the faculties of concentration and wisdom are predominant in the remaining path-moments. "He becomes a body-witness" (kāya-sakkhī hoti) means he is called a body-witness in all eight stages (four paths and four fruits). "He becomes one attained to vision" (diṭṭhi-ppatto hoti) should be understood in the same manner as explained for the Saddhā-vimutta.

"Liberated while believing" (saddahanto vimutto) means he is a Saddhā-vimutta; because the faculty of faith is predominant, one who believes at the moment of the path of stream-entry is liberated from defilements at the four moments of fruition, and is thus called a Saddhā-vimutta. The state of being a Saddhā-vimutta at the moments of the three higher paths will be explained presently. However, the state of being a faith-follower (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the path of stream-entry will be explained later. "Realized through contact" (phuṭṭhattā sacchikato) means he is a body-witness (kāya-sakkhī); if he is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka), he is a body-witness because he realizes Nibbāna through touching the contact of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna); if he is an obtainer of fine-material or immaterial jhānas, he is a body-witness because he realizes Nibbāna through touching the contact of those jhānas. It means he is a witness to the contact of jhāna as described and to Nibbāna with the mental body (nāma-kāya). "Attained through seeing" (diṭṭhattā patto) means he is one attained to vision (diṭṭhi-ppatto); because he first sees Nibbāna with the faculty of wisdom associated with the moment of the path of stream-entry, and later reaches Nibbāna by way of the fruit of stream-entry etc., he is called one attained to vision. By the faculty of wisdom known as...
163:
It means reaching Nibbāna through wisdom associated with the path of Stream-entry, which is called the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). The state of being a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the path of Stream-entry will be explained later. Because of the predominance of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), one who is being liberated from defilements while having faith at the moments of the path of Once-returning, the path of Non-returning, and the path of Arahantship is called one freed by faith (saddhāvimutta). In this context, although the liberation is yet to happen, the term 'freed' (vimutta) is used based on the sense of a completed action in the future.

'Meditative contact' (jhānaphassa) refers to the three types of meditative contact: sensual, fine-material, and immaterial spheres. The terms beginning with 'jhānaphassa' and 'dukkhā saṅkhārā' are stated specifically to distinguish the two types of individuals mentioned earlier. Terms like 'ñātaṃ hoti' have the meanings already stated below. In this context, it is the teachers' intention that a person who has attained jhāna emerges from the insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), which is conducive to the faculty of concentration, and attains the paths and fruits.

'Siyā' means 'they might be' or 'should be'. This word 'siyā' is merely a word expressing a rule or injunction (vidhi). The 'three individuals' refers to the three types of persons described by the determination of insight and the determination of faculties. 'By the power of the object' (vatthuvasena) means by the power of the mode that is the cause of a particular faculty in the three contemplations. 'By way of method' (pariyāyena) means by that very cause. What is shown by this section (vāra)? It is intended to show that, generally, the predominance of a particular faculty in a particular contemplation was stated below, and sometimes, even in all three contemplations, only one faculty might be predominant. Alternatively, because all three contemplations are clearly present at the moment of insight in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga-vipassanā), the names such as saddhāvimutta occur at the moments of the path and fruit in consideration of the predominance of the respective faculties in those preliminary insights. Only when stated thus, the determination of the predominance of faculties and the determination of individuals made below in the insight leading to emergence and above in the moments of the path and fruit will be well-established and unshakable. In the subsequent section, the word 'siyā' relates only to the word 'aññoyeva'. Here too, the determination is the same as stated below.

Now, to analyze and show the special individuals by the power of the paths and fruits, the text says: 'One who attends [to things] as impermanent... attains the path of Stream-entry' and so on. In that text, one is a faith-follower (saddhānusārī) because one follows after faith, or because one follows after Nibbāna through faith. 'Sacchikata' means 'realized' or 'made manifest'. 'Arahatta' refers to the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). One is a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) because one follows after the Dhamma known as wisdom, or because one follows after Nibbāna through that Dhamma.
164:
Again, wishing to explain the distinction of individuals through the distinction of the three faculties by other methods, the text says: 'Ye hi keci' and so on. In that text, 'have been developed' (bhāvitā vā) means they were developed in the past. 'Are being developed' (bhāventi vā) means they are being developed in the present. 'Will be developed' (bhāvissanti vā) means they will be developed in the future. The words beginning with 'have been attained' (adhigatā vā) end with the word 'iti' in each case and are stated to explain the meaning of the preceding words. 'Have been touched' (phassitā vā) means they have been touched by knowledge. 'Have attained mastery' (vasippattā) means they have reached the state of being a master. 'Have reached the end' (pāramippattā) means they have reached the conclusion (vosāna). 'Have reached confidence' (vesārajjappattā) means they have reached the state of being confident. In all instances, individuals such as the saddhāvimutta should be understood only in the moments (of path and fruit) stated below; however, the factors such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are to be understood only at the moment of the path. The 'eight liberations' (aṭṭha vimokkha) beginning with 'one possessing form sees forms' are attained only by reaching the path of discrimination (paṭisambhidāmagga).

The 'three trainings' (tisso sikkhā) are the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā); they are practiced upon reaching the path. The words beginning with 'they fully understand suffering' (dukkhaṃ parijānanti) occur only at the moment of the path. 'One penetrates the penetration of full understanding' (pariññā-paṭivedhaṃ paṭivijjhati) means one penetrates by means of the penetration of full understanding (the path-knowledge that fully understands the truth of suffering), or it is called 'penetration of full understanding' because it is the truth of suffering that should be penetrated by full understanding (pariññā). The remaining terms should be understood in the same way. The terms such as 'penetration of direct knowledge' (abhiññā-paṭivedha) are stated to distinguish them from terms like 'all dhammas' (sabba-dhamma). The 'penetration of realization' (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha) should be understood as being accomplished at the moment of the path by the power of the completion of the path-knowledge, which is the cause for the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) Nibbāna. Thus, five types of noble persons (ariya-puggala) are indicated here; the two types, the one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) and the one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta), are not indicated here. However, in another text (the Visuddhimagga), it is said: 'The person who, attending [to things] as suffering, has much tranquility (passaddhi) and attains the faculty of concentration, is called a body-witness (kāyasakkhī) in all instances. But having reached the immaterial jhānas and then the highest fruit, he is called one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta). The person who, attending [to things] as non-self, has much wisdom and attains the faculty of wisdom, is a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the path of Stream-entry, one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta) in the six stages, and one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta) at the highest fruit.' In this text, those individuals are included within the body-witness (kāyasakkhī) and one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta). In terms of meaning, one is liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) because one is liberated by both the immaterial jhāna and the noble path. One is liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta) because one is liberated while knowing distinctly. With this much, the distinctions of faculties and individuals have been indicated.

223-226. Now, wishing to show the distinction of liberations and the distinction of individuals preceded by liberation, the text says: 'One who attends [to things] as impermanent' and so on. In that text, 'two liberations' (dve vimokkhā) refers to the desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha) and the emptiness liberation (suññata-vimokkha). For the path that has acquired the name 'signless liberation' (animitta-vimokkha) by way of proceeding through the contemplation of impermanence, [is the path of] the desires (paṇidhi) of greed, hatred, and delusion...
165:
Because of the absence of the longings (aspirations) known as lust, hatred, and delusion, and by virtue of its own quality, Nibbāna—which has acquired the name 'desireless' (appaṇihita) because of the absence of those longings—is taken as an object. Thus, it also receives the name 'desireless liberation' (appaṇihita-vimokkha) by way of the object. Similarly, because of being void of lust, hatred, and delusion, and by virtue of its own quality, Nibbāna—which has acquired the name 'void' (suññata) because of being void of lust and so on—is taken as an object. Thus, it also receives the name 'void liberation' (suññata-vimokkha) by way of the object. Therefore, these two liberations are said to follow the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha). Among the eight path factors which are not different from the signless path, it should be understood that they also occur by way of each path factor through conascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya) and so forth.

Again, the two liberations are the void liberation and the signless liberation. The path which has acquired the name 'desireless liberation' by virtue of reaching the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), because of the absence of signs of form (rūpa-nimitta) etc., signs of lust (rāga-nimitta) etc., and signs of permanence (nicca-nimitta) etc., and by virtue of its own quality, takes Nibbāna—called 'signless' (animitta) because of the absence of those signs—as an object. Thus, it also receives the name 'signless liberation' (animitta-vimokkha) by way of the object. The rest should be applied in the same manner as previously stated. Again, the two liberations are the signless liberation and the desireless liberation. The application here is exactly as previously stated.

Regarding the phrase 'paṭivedhakāle' (at the time of penetration), it is spoken according to the previously stated order of the faculties (indriya). Excluding the path-moment (magga-kkhaṇa), there is no such thing as liberation at the moment of insight (vipassanā-kkhaṇa). The path-liberation mentioned first is specifically shown by the word 'paṭivedhakāle'. Although the two sections (vāra) beginning with 'The person who is liberated by faith (saddhā-vimutta)' and the section beginning with 'One who attends [to formations] as impermanent attains the path of stream-entry' are presented in brief, they should be understood in detail by applying them by way of liberation. The section beginning with 'Those who [attain] renunciation (nekkhamma)...' should also be understood in the same manner as previously stated. By this much, the distinctions of individuals regarding liberation have been shown.

Again, wishing to point out the doors to liberation (vimokkha-mukha) and the liberations in various ways, it is said: 'One who attends [to formations] as impermanent...'. Therein, 'yathābhūtaṃ' means according to the actual nature. 'Jānāti' means one knows with knowledge. 'Passati' means one sees with that same knowledge as if with the eye. 'Tadanvayena' means by following that knowledge; the meaning is by knowing in accordance with what has been seen by that direct knowledge. 'Kankhā pahīyati' (doubt is abandoned) means that by the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), doubt regarding permanence and impermanence is abandoned; by the other contemplations, the other doubts are abandoned. 'Nimittaṃ' (the sign) means that because the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) has been abandoned by the dissection of the compactness of continuity, one knows the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta), which is the object, as it really is. Therefore, because of knowing thus as it really is, that knowledge is called 'right seeing' (sammā-dassana).
166:
It is called 'right seeing' (sammā-dassana). Regarding the occurrence (pavatta): having removed the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā) in formations that are of the nature of suffering, and by abandoning the perception of pleasure, craving—known as longing (paṇidhi)—is abandoned. Thus, one knows the occurrence of resultants (vipāka-pavatta), though commonly regarded as pleasure, as it really is.
