In saying that one knows the sign (nimitta) and the occurrence (pavatta), because of the abandoning of the perception of self (atta-saññā) in both ways through the knowledge that analyzes the mass and compactness by attending to various elements, one knows the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta) and the occurrence of resultants as they really are. The triad of knowledges beginning with 'And that which is knowledge as it really is' has just been explained; it is nothing else. 'Appears as fear' (bhayato upaṭṭhāti) means that because of seeing the absence of permanence, pleasure, and self, those respective states appear as fear in due order. Among the nine insight knowledges (vipassanā-ñāṇa) known as the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi)—namely, knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa), knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa), knowledge of appearance as fear (bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa), knowledge of contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa), knowledge of contemplation of dispassion (nibbidānupassanā-ñāṇa), knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa), knowledge of contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa), knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa), and conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa)—only three knowledges which are identical in meaning but differ in phase in connection with the appearance as fear are meant here, not the remaining six.

Again, among the three contemplations, in order to show the identity in meaning of the contemplation of voidness (suññatānupassanā) with the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) which stands at the end and is mentioned immediately after, it is said: 'That which is contemplation of non-self and that which is contemplation of voidness...'. For these two knowledges are one in essence, but differ only in phase. Just as these are, so too contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and contemplation of the signless (animittānupassanā) are essentially one knowledge; and contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) and contemplation of the desireless (appaṇihitānupassanā) are essentially one knowledge. They differ merely in phase. When the identity in meaning of the contemplation of non-self and the contemplation of voidness is stated, the identity in meaning of each of those pairs of knowledges is already stated because they have the same characteristic. 'Knowledge arises by reflecting on the sign' means that having known by way of the characteristic of impermanence that 'the sign of formations is unstable and temporary,' knowledge arises. In reality, it is not that one knows first and then knowledge arises later; however, in terms of conventional usage, it is spoken of in this way, like the passage: 'Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises.' Experts in grammar also accept this usage even for simultaneous events, as in the example: 'Upon reaching the sun, darkness disappears.' Or it should be understood that it is stated this way by taking the preceding and succeeding as one by the method of unity (ekatta-naya). By this method, the meaning in the other two phrases should also be understood. The identity in meaning of the three knowledges beginning with the desire for deliverance is exactly as the method stated below.
167: "The mind emerges from the sign" means that because of seeing the fault in the sign of formations (saṅkhāranimitta), the mind does not cling to that sign of formations, and thus it is said to emerge from the sign of formations. "The mind enters into the signless" means that the mind enters into Nibbāna, which is called signless (animitta) as it is the opposite of the sign of formations, because of the mind's inclination towards that Nibbāna. The meaning in the remaining two contemplations (anupassanā) should also be understood in this way. By saying "In cessation, in the Nibbāna element" in this contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), it is also said in the two preceding contemplations. There is also a reading "nirodhe" (in cessation). "Wisdom in turning away from emergence externally" refers to the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) because of its connection with emergence (vuṭṭhāna, or insight leading to emergence). "Change-of-lineage states" (gotrabhū dhammā) refers to the change-of-lineage knowledge itself. Otherwise, having the same meaning would not be appropriate. Alternatively, it should be understood that the plural is used as in "unconditioned states (asaṅkhatā dhammā), uncaused states (appaccayā dhammā)," or by way of the four paths. Since liberation (vimokkha) is the path, and the path emerges from both (defilements and formations), therefore, in connection with that liberation, it is said "the wisdom in turning away from emergence from both," and so on. Furthermore, wishing to show the single-moment method of the various liberations occurring at different moments, he said "In how many ways," and so on. In that text, "in the sense of predominance" (ādhipateyyaṭṭhena) means in the sense of being the chief. "In the sense of foundation" (adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena) means in the sense of establishment. "In the sense of directing" (abhinīhāraṭṭhena) means in the sense of leading out from the course of insight. "In the sense of leading out" (niyyānaṭṭhena) means in the sense of attaining Nibbāna. "When one attends as impermanent" occurs only at the moment of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā). "Signless liberation" occurs only at the moment of the path. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Establishes the mind" means it stands making the mind predominant; it means it causes the mind to be established. "Directs the mind" means it leads the mind out from the course of insight. "Leads out to Nibbāna, the cessation" means it approaches Nibbāna called cessation. Thus, by the diversity of modes, the state of having different moments is shown in four ways. Regarding the state of having a single moment, "in the sense of gathering together" (samodhānaṭṭhena) means in the sense of meeting in one place. "In the sense of attainment" (adhigamanaṭṭhena) means in the sense of gaining. "In the sense of acquisition" (paṭilābhaṭṭhena) means in the sense of reaching. "In the sense of penetration" (paṭivedhaṭṭhena) means in the sense of penetrating with knowledge. "In the sense of realization" (sacchikiriyaṭṭhena) means in the sense of making manifest. "In the sense of touching" (phassanaṭṭhena) means in the sense of touching with the touch of knowledge. "In the sense of clear realization" (abhisamayaṭṭhena) means in the sense of coming together face to face. Here, "in the sense of gathering together" is the primary term; the remaining terms are synonyms for attainment. Therefore, the answer for all of them is given together. "Liberated from the sign" means liberated from the sign of permanence. By this, the meaning of liberation is stated. "From which it is liberated" means from which sign of permanence it is liberated. "Therein one does not desire" means in that...
168: ...sign, one does not make an aspiration. "Wherein one does not desire" means in which sign one does not desire. "Empty of that" means empty of that sign. "By which it is empty" means by which sign it is empty. "Signless by that sign"—by this, the meaning of signless (animitta) is stated. "Liberated from desire" means liberated from craving (taṇhā). The reading "paṇidhi muccati" also has the sense of the ablative (departure). By this, the meaning of liberation is stated. "Wherein one does not desire" means in which suffering (dukkha) one does not desire. "Empty of that suffering" means empty of that suffering. "By which it is empty" means by which sign of suffering it is empty. "By which sign" means by which sign of suffering. "One does not desire in that"—by this, the meaning of the desireless (appaṇihita) is stated. "Liberated from adherence" (abhinivesa)—by this, the meaning of liberation is stated. "By which it is empty" means by which sign of adherence it is empty. "By which sign" means by which sign of adherence. "Wherein one does not desire, it is empty of that sign" means one does not desire in that sign of adherence, and it is empty of that sign of adherence. By this, the meaning of voidness (suññata) is stated. Furthermore, wishing to point out the eight liberations and so on, he said "There is liberation," and so on. In that text, "from adherence as permanent" and so on should be understood according to the method stated in the liberation of perception (saññā-vimokkha). "From all adherences" means from the adherences of the types already mentioned. Thus, by way of liberation from adherence, they are called "voidness liberations." Those same liberations are called "signless liberations" by way of liberation from the sign of permanence, etc., and "desireless liberations" by way of liberation from aspirations such as "it is permanent," etc. Here, in "paṇidhi muccati," the ablative sense should be understood everywhere. There is also a reading "paṇidhiyā muccati." The Pali "liberated from all aspirations" is the evidence here. Thus, the three contemplations are called liberations figuratively, both because they are liberations by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimokkha) and because they are the cause for liberation by uprooting (samuccheda-vimokkha). In that text, "which have arisen" means that although there is insight-liberation in the immediate [preceding state], since this discourse concerns path-liberation, it means "arisen in that path-liberation." "Blameless wholesome states" are wholesome states free from faults such as greed (rāga). There is also a reading with a sentence break. "Factors of enlightenment" (bodhipakkhiya-dhammā) means the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven...
169:
The seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and so forth, are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma). "This is the door (mukha)" means that this group of factors of enlightenment, as previously described, is called "mukha" because it serves as a door for entering Nibbāna by way of being an object. "Of those dhammas" means of those factors of enlightenment. "This is the door to liberation (vimokkhamukha)" means that among the five kinds of liberation—suppression (vikkhambhana), substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), eradication (samuccheda), tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi), and escape (nissaraṇa)—Nibbāna is only the liberation of escape. Because it is said, "Monks, whatever dhammas there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, detachment (virāga) is said to be the foremost of them," it is called "mukha" in the sense of being noble. Therefore, because it is both liberation and a door, it is called "vimokkhamukha". This meaning is expressed through the compound (kammadhāraya-samāsa) "vimokkhamukha", meaning it is both liberation and a door. In the phrase "vimokkhañca", a change of gender (from masculine to neuter) is made.

The three unwholesome roots are greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha). The three types of misconduct are bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. "All unwholesome dhammas" refers to all unwholesome dhammas associated with the unwholesome roots and those associated or dissociated with misconduct, excluding things like cultivated displeasure (domanassa) and so forth. Wholesome roots and good conduct should be understood as the opposites of the aforementioned unwholesome ones. "All wholesome dhammas" refers to all wholesome dhammas, whether associated or dissociated in the same manner, which serve as a strong decisive support (upanissaya) for liberation. The Discussion on Liberation from the Round (vivaṭṭakatha) has been mentioned below. However, in this context, other types of liberation from the round are also mentioned in connection with the liberation from the round that is vimokkha.

Repetition (āsevanā) means associating from the beginning. Development (bhāvanā) means the growth of that same association. Frequent practice (bahulīkamma) means doing it repeatedly to achieve mastery (vasībhāva). In the case of the Path, however, repetition and so forth should be understood as the accomplishment of the task in a single moment. Phrases such as "attainment or result" (paṭilābho vā vipāko vā) have the same meanings as mentioned below.

## The Explanation of the Description of Liberation is finished.
## The Explanation of the Discussion on Liberation in the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga, named Saddhammappakāsinī, is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Discussion on Destinations (Gatikathā)

Now, in order to show the fulfillment of causes (hetusampatti) which is the cause for the arising of that liberation, the explanation of the unprecedented meanings in the Discussion on Destinations (Gatikathā) is given. For, according to the statement "There is no meditative absorption (jhāna) for one without wisdom," even jhāna cannot arise for one with a rebirth associated with only two roots (duhetuka-paṭisandhi)...
170:
What is liberation? In that Discussion on Destinations, "by success in destination" (gatisampattiyā) means the success of the destination known as human or deva, among the five destinations known as hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), humans, and devas. By this term "success in destination", the three previous failures in destination (gativipatti)—hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts—are excluded. Success in destination is called "gatisampatti", meaning a happy state of existence (sugati). "Destination" (gati) also refers to the aggregates (khandha) along with their respective planes. Among the five destinations, by taking the realm of hungry ghosts, the host of asuras is also included. "Devas" refers to the six heavens of the sense sphere and the Brahmas. By the term "deva", the deva-asuras are also included.

"Associated with knowledge" (ñāṇasampayutte) means at the moment of rebirth-linking associated with knowledge. It should be understood that even that moment is called "associated with knowledge" by way of its association with consciousness associated with knowledge. "How many roots" means how many among the roots of non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha). "Arising" (upapatti) means being born or coming into existence.

Since those born in poor families can also have a rebirth with three roots (tihetuka), the first question is asked with reference to them. And since, for the most part, those of great merit are born in the three types of great wealthy families (mahāsāla), three questions arise based on those three families. The Pali text is concise. They are called "mahāsāla" because they have large houses; it means those with large houses and great wealth. Alternatively, it should be said "mahāsāra" because they have great essence (wealth), but by changing the letter "r" to "l", it is called "mahāsāla". "Khattiya-mahāsāla" means great wealthy families of the warrior caste, or those who are great wealthy ones among the warriors. The same method applies to the others. Among them, a Khattiya-mahāsāla is one who has at least one hundred crores of wealth buried in the ground and from whose house twenty ambaṇas of coins are taken out for daily expenses. A Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla is one who has at least eighty crores of wealth buried and from whose house ten ambaṇas are taken out for daily expenses. A Gahapati-mahāsāla is one who has at least forty crores of wealth buried and from whose house five ambaṇas are taken out for daily expenses.

For the Brahmas of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, "associated with knowledge" is not specifically mentioned because they invariably have a rebirth with three roots. However, since there are individuals with two roots or no roots (ahetuka) among humans, and since there are those with two roots among the devas of the sense sphere, the term "associated with knowledge" is used for the remaining devas and humans. Here, the devas of the sense sphere are called "deva" because they play and enjoy the five cords of sensual pleasure and shine with the radiance of their bodies. The Brahmas of the fine-material sphere delight in the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna)...
171:
Devas delight by sporting in the five strands of sensual pleasure and shine with the radiance of their bodies. The Brahmas of the formless realm (arūpāvacara) delight by sporting in meditative absorption (jhāna) and shine with the radiance of wisdom. Therefore, they are called Devas.

Regarding the phrase 'at the moment of the javana of wholesome kamma' (kusalakammassa javanakkhane): this refers to the time occurring at the seventh javana moment by way of repeated occurrence in the javana-process (javana-vīthi) of a triple-rooted sense-sphere wholesome kamma (tihetuka-kāmāvacara-kusala-kamma) which produces a triple-rooted rebirth-linking (tihetuka-paṭisandhi) in this realm from a past life. The three wholesome roots are the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha), the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa), and the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha). Regarding 'to the volition (cetanā) arisen at that moment': this refers to the wholesome volition arisen at that very moment mentioned. Regarding 'they are conascent conditions' (sahajāta-paccayā honti): they are helpful by way of arising together. Therefore, it is said, 'because of being conascent conditions.' The statement 'formations (saṅkhārā) arise due to the condition of wholesome roots' is taught according to the method of single-moment dependent origination (ekacittakkhaṇika-paṭiccasamuppāda). By using the plural term 'formations,' it should be understood that all mental factors (cetasika) included in the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) at that javana moment are taken. By the word 'pi' (also), it implies that wholesome roots also arise due to the condition of formations.

Regarding 'at the moment of attachment' (nikantikkhane): this occurs at the moment of attachment arising either towards the kamma that has appeared to give its result, or towards the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) or the sign of destination (gati-nimitta) manifested by that kamma. Attachment (nikanti) means desire or longing. For a person near death, because the mind is agitated by delusion, attachment (relishing) can arise even for the flames of the Avīci hell; what need is there to mention other signs? The two roots are the unwholesome root of greed (lobha) and the unwholesome root of delusion (moha). Attachment to existence (bhava-nikanti), however, arises for all beings by taking their own continuity of aggregates as an object, just after emerging from the life-continuum process (bhavaṅga-vīthi) that occurs immediately after rebirth-linking. This attachment to existence is intended in the teaching: 'If for someone in a certain realm unwholesome states have never arisen, have wholesome states never arisen for him there? Yes (āmanta),' and so on. The volition arisen at that moment refers to unwholesome volition.

Regarding 'at the moment of rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhikkhane): this occurs at the moment of rebirth-linking obtained through that kamma. The three roots are the indeterminate root of non-greed, the indeterminate root of non-hatred, and the indeterminate root of non-delusion. The volition arisen at that moment refers to resultant indeterminate (vipākābyākata) volition. In the phrase 'consciousness also arises due to the condition of mentality-materiality,' here, at that moment of rebirth-linking, the three resultant roots and the remaining mental factors are called 'mentality' (nāma), and the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) is called 'materiality' (rūpa).
172:
Due to the aforementioned condition of mentality-materiality, rebirth-consciousness also arises. In the phrase 'mentality-materiality also arises due to the condition of consciousness' (viññāṇappaccayāpi nāmarūpaṃ), 'mentality' is of the same kind as previously described (the mental factors remaining from the resultant roots). As for 'materiality,' since it refers here to the rebirth of a human being with roots, for womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) beings, there are thirty types of matter: the heart-decad (vatthu-dasaka), the body-decad (kāya-dasaka), and the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka). For moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings with complete sense-bases, there are seventy types of matter: the eye-decad (cakkhu-dasaka), the ear-decad (sota-dasaka), the nose-decad (ghāna-dasaka), and the tongue-decad (jivhā-dasaka) [along with the previous three]. That aforementioned mentality-materiality arises at the moment of rebirth-linking due to the condition of rebirth-consciousness.

In the phrase 'five aggregates' (pañcakkhandhā), the matter obtained at the moment of rebirth-linking along with the rebirth-linking consciousness is the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). The co-arisen feeling is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); the remaining mental factors are the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); and the rebirth-linking consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). Regarding 'they arise by way of conascent condition' (sahajāta-paccayā honti): the four mental aggregates are helpful to one another by way of conascent condition. In the aggregate of matter, the four great essentials (mahābhūta) are helpful to one another by way of conascent condition. The mental aggregates and the heart-base are also helpful to one another by way of conascent condition. The great essentials are also helpful to derived matter (upādā-rūpa) by way of conascent condition. Regarding 'they arise by way of mutuality condition' (aññamañña-paccayā honti): they are helpful to one another by way of producing and supporting. The four mental aggregates are helpful to one another by way of mutuality condition, and the four great essentials are helpful to one another by way of mutuality condition. Regarding 'they arise by way of dependence condition' (nissaya-paccayā honti): they are helpful by way of being a foundation and a support. The way the four mental aggregates are helpful to one another by way of dependence condition should be understood in detail just like the conascent condition. Regarding 'they arise by way of dissociation condition' (vippayutta-paccayā honti): they are helpful by way of being dissociated, not reaching the state of having a common base, etc. The mental aggregates are helpful to rebirth-linking matter by way of dissociation condition. The heart-base is helpful to the mental aggregates by way of dissociation condition. In this phrase 'five aggregates,' it is spoken according to what is applicable.

In the phrase 'four great essentials' (cattāro mahābhūtā), the three conditions have already been mentioned. Regarding 'three vital formations' (tayo jīvitasaṅkhārā): these are life (āyu), heat (usmā), and consciousness (viññāṇa). 'Life' refers to the physical life-faculty and the mental life-faculty. 'Heat' refers to the fire element (tejo-dhātu). 'Consciousness' refers to rebirth-consciousness. These are called vital formations because they successively form and maintain the formation of life. Regarding 'they arise by way of conascent condition': the mental life-faculty and rebirth-consciousness are mutual conascent conditions for the associated aggregates and the heart-base. The fire element is a mutual conascent condition for the other three great essentials, but it is only a conascent condition for derived matter.
173:
The material life faculty (rūpajīvitindriya) should be understood as assisting conascent material phenomena by way of conascence condition (sahajātapaccaya) in a figurative sense. Regarding the pair of conditions, namely mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccaya) and dependence condition (nissayapaccaya), the immaterial life faculty (arūpajīvitindriya) and rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhivinnāṇa) assist the associated aggregates (sampayuttakhandhā) by way of mutuality condition and mutuality-dependence condition, which should be understood by applying the method already stated. 'Assisting by way of dissociation condition (vippayuttapaccaya)' means the immaterial life faculty and rebirth-linking consciousness assist rebirth-linking material phenomena by way of dissociation condition. However, it is not appropriate for the material life faculty to assist (rebirth-linking material phenomena) by way of mutuality, dependence, and dissociation conditions. Therefore, 'three life-formations' (jīvitasaṅkhāra) is stated according to what is obtainable. Both mind (nāma) and matter (rūpa) should be applied in the sense of having the four conditions, such as conascence, as previously stated. '14 phenomena' refers to the five aggregates, four great elements (mahābhūta), three life-formations, and mind and matter; thus, there are 14 phenomena by way of counting. Above these 14 and for others such as the rootless (ahetuka), the state of assisting by way of conascence and so on is just as previously stated. 'Assisting by way of association condition (sampayuttapaccaya)' means assisting by way of the nature of association, characterized by having a single base, a single object, arising together, and ceasing together.

The five faculties (indriya) are the faith faculty (saddhindriya) and so on. 'Mind' here refers to the three aggregates of feeling and so on. 'Consciousness' refers to rebirth-linking consciousness. Again, '14 phenomena' refers to the four aggregates, five faculties, three roots (hetu), mind, and consciousness; thus, there are 14 phenomena by way of counting. '28 phenomena' refers to the previous 14 and these 14 combined. Since matter is included here, association condition is excluded and dissociation condition is stated.

Thus, having shown the various types of conditions for the respective resultant phenomena existing at the moment of rebirth-linking, and wishing to conclude the roots previously shown, he said: 'Rebirth occurs due to these eight roots.' There are three wholesome roots at the moment of accumulating kamma, two unwholesome roots at the moment of attachment, and three indeterminate (abyākata) roots at the moment of rebirth-linking; thus, there are eight roots. Among these eight, the three wholesome roots and two unwholesome roots assist the phenomena occurring at the moment of rebirth-linking in this life by way of decisive support condition (upanissayapaccaya). The three indeterminate roots assist by way of root condition and conascence condition as appropriate. In the remaining sections, the method is the same.

In the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), because there is no matter, it is said: 'Consciousness arises because of mind, and mind arises because of consciousness.' The section of 14 mixed with matter is also omitted. Because that section is omitted, the section of '28 phenomena' is also not obtained.
174:
Now, after showing the triple-rooted rebirth (tihetukapaṭisandhi) which is the cause for the three liberations (vimokkha), and wishing to show the distinction of double-rooted rebirth (duhetukapaṭisandhi) in connection with that, he said 'Gatisampattiyā ñāṇavippayutte' and so on. 'At the moment of impulsion (javana) of wholesome kamma' refers to the occurrence at the moment of impulsion, according to the method already stated, of the double-rooted wholesome kamma that produces rebirth in this life from a past existence. 'Two roots' refers to non-greed (alobha) and non-hatred (adosa), which are wholesome roots, because it is disconnected from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta). The two indeterminate roots are also non-greed and non-hatred.

'Four faculties' refers to the four faculties such as the faith faculty, excluding the wisdom faculty (paññindriya). 'Twelve phenomena' refers to twelve because the wisdom faculty and the non-delusion root (amoha) are diminished. Because those two are diminished, there are twenty-six. 'Of the six roots' refers to the six roots: two wholesome roots, two unwholesome roots, and two resultant (vipāka) roots. The fine-material and immaterial sphere phenomena are not taken here because they are exclusively triple-rooted. The remaining meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the first section. In this section, since only double-rooted kamma is mentioned for double-rooted rebirth, it means that double-rooted rebirth cannot occur through triple-rooted kamma.

Therefore, in the commentary to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the view of Elder Tipiṭaka Mahādhammarakkhita states: 'Through triple-rooted kamma, rebirth is only triple-rooted; it cannot be double-rooted or rootless. Through double-rooted kamma, it is double-rooted or rootless; it cannot be triple-rooted.' This statement agrees with this Pali text. However, in the views of Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga and Elder Mahādatta of Moravāpī, it is stated: 'Through triple-rooted kamma, rebirth can be triple-rooted or double-rooted, but not rootless. Through double-rooted kamma, it can be double-rooted or rootless, but not triple-rooted.' This statement seems to contradict this Pali text. It should be understood that because this discussion focuses on the topic of roots, rootless rebirth is not mentioned.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Destinations is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Discourse on Kamma

Now, wishing to show the kamma which is the cause of that attainment of roots (hetusampatti), I shall state the new explanation of the meaning in the Discourse on Kamma (Kammakathā). Therein, among the terms 'There was kamma, there was kamma-result' (ahosi kammaṃ ahosi kammavipāko) and so on, 'There was kamma... result' is said taking the resultant effect that has already ripened in past lives for kamma performed in past lives. It is also said 'There was kamma... result' taking the result that has not yet ripened in past lives due to the incompleteness of conditions for that same past kamma—specifically kamma to be experienced in this life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīyakamma) or kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīyakamma); or taking the result that has not yet ripened of the kamma called 'to be experienced in this life', 'to be experienced in the next life', or 'to be experienced in subsequent lives' (aparāpariyavedanīyakamma) for a person who attained Parinibbāna in a past life. It is also said 'There was kamma... result' taking the result in the present life of past kamma that has not yet ripened. It is also said 'There was kamma... result' taking the result that will no longer ripen for a person whose time for the ripening of kamma has passed, or for a person who is currently attaining Parinibbāna in the present life. It is also said 'There was kamma... result' taking the result that will ripen in a future life due to the completeness of conditions for past kamma which, though fit to give result, has not yet ripened.
175:
Taking the result that has already ripened in past lives, it is said: "Kamma was, the result of kamma was." Taking the non-ripening in past lives of that same past kamma—whether it be kamma to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) or kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya)—due to the deficiency of conditions, and taking the non-ripening of kamma to be experienced in the present, next, or subsequent lives for one who has already attained parinibbāna in the past, it is said: "Kamma was, the result of kamma was not." Taking the result that is ripening in the present life because of the fulfillment of conditions for that same past kamma which has not yet produced its result, it is said: "Kamma was, the result of kamma is." Taking the non-ripening of results for that same past kamma because the time for its ripening has passed, or for one who is attaining parinibbāna in the present life, it is said: "Kamma was, the result of kamma is not." Taking the result that will ripen in a future life because of the fulfillment of conditions for that same past kamma which is worthy of ripening but has not yet ripened, it is said: "Kamma was, the result of kamma will be." Taking the non-ripening of results for that same past kamma because the time for its ripening has passed, or for one who will attain parinibbāna in a future life, it is said: "Kamma was, the result of kamma will not be." Thus, past kamma is shown in six ways according to the existence or non-existence of results in the past, present, and future.

Taking the result ripening in this very life for kamma to be experienced in the present life performed in the present life, it is said: "Kamma is, the result of kamma is." Taking the non-ripening of results in this life for that same present kamma due to the deficiency of conditions, or the non-ripening of results in this life for one who attains parinibbāna in this very life, it is said: "Kamma is, the result of kamma is not." Taking the result that will ripen in a future life for that same present kamma—whether it be kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya) or kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya)—it is said: "Kamma is, the result of kamma will be." Taking the non-ripening of results in a future life for that same present kamma due to the deficiency of conditions for kamma to be experienced in the next life, or the non-ripening of results for kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives for one who will attain parinibbāna in a future life, it is said: "Kamma is, the result of kamma will not be." Thus, present kamma is shown in four ways according to the existence or non-existence of results in the present and future.

Taking the result that will ripen in a future life for kamma to be performed in a future life, it is said: "Kamma will be, the result of kamma will be." For that same kamma...
176:
Taking the non-ripening of results for kamma to be performed in the future due to the deficiency of conditions, or the non-ripening of results for one who will attain parinibbāna in a future life, it is said: "Kamma will be, the result of kamma will not be." Thus, future kamma is shown in two ways according to the existence or non-existence of results in the future. When all these are combined, kamma is shown in twelve ways.

Standing at this point, the three sets of four kammas are brought forth and explained. Indeed, when these sets of four kammas are explained, this meaning will become much clearer. Indeed, kamma is of four types: kamma to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya), kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya), kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya), and lapsed kamma (ahosikamma). Among these, in a single process of impulsion (javana-vīthi), the volition (cetanā) in the first impulsion—whether wholesome or unwholesome—is called kamma to be experienced in the present life. It gives its result in this very existence. If it is unable to do so, it is called lapsed kamma (ahosikamma) by way of these three aspects: "Kamma was, the result of kamma was not; the result of kamma will not be; the result of kamma is not." The volition in the seventh impulsion, which accomplishes the result, is called kamma to be experienced in the next life. It gives its result in the immediately following existence. If it is unable to do so, it is called lapsed kamma in the same manner as mentioned before. The volitions in the five impulsions between these two are called kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives. It gives its result in the future whenever it gains an opportunity. As long as the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) continues, it never becomes lapsed kamma.

Another set of four kammas consists of: weighty kamma (garukamma), habitual kamma (bahulakamma), death-proximate kamma (āsannakamma), and reserve kamma (kaṭattākamma). Among these, whether wholesome or unwholesome, between weighty and non-weighty kamma, that which is weighty—such as matricide (mātughātaka) etc., or sublime kamma (mahaggata)—ripens first. Similarly, between frequent and infrequent kamma, that which is habitual—whether it be virtue or immorality—ripens first. Death-proximate kamma is kamma remembered or performed at the time of death. Indeed, whatever kamma one is able to remember or perform at the point of death, one is reborn by that very kamma. Kamma that is distinct from these three and has been frequently practiced is called reserve kamma (kaṭattākamma). In the absence of those three, this reserve kamma draws one to rebirth.

Another set of four kammas consists of: productive kamma (janakakamma), supportive kamma (upatthambhakakamma), obstructive kamma (upapīḷakakamma), and destructive kamma (upaghātakakamma). Among these, productive kamma can be either wholesome or unwholesome. It [produces results] at the time of rebirth and during the course of existence...
177:
Janaka-kamma produces the result (vipāka) of mind and matter. Upatthambhaka-kamma, however, cannot produce the result itself; it supports and prolongs the pleasure or pain that arises in the result produced by the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) given by another kamma. Upapīḷaka-kamma oppresses and afflicts the pleasure or pain that arises in the result produced by the rebirth-linking given by another kamma, preventing it from lasting long. Upaghātaka-kamma, whether wholesome or unwholesome, destroys another weaker kamma, prevents its result, and creates an opportunity for its own result to manifest. When kamma thus creates an opportunity, that result is said to have arisen.

Thus, the true realization of the distinction between these twelve types of kamma and their results is clear only to the Buddhas' Knowledge of Kamma and its Result (Kammavipāka-ñāṇa), which is an exclusive knowledge (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa) not shared with the disciples. A practitioner of insight (vipassanā), however, should know the distinction of kamma and its result partially. Therefore, this distinction of kamma has been explained by way of a mere indication.

Having thus taught the first turn (vāra) by way of pure kamma, the Teacher taught ten other turns through ten methods, dividing that same kamma into two, such as the wholesome and unwholesome pairs. Among those turns, it is called wholesome (kusala) in the sense of being free from illness, and unwholesome (akusala) in the sense of being ill. This dyad is spoken of by way of its nature (jāti). Only the unwholesome is called blameworthy (sāvazza) because it is associated with faults such as greed; the wholesome is blameless (anavazza) because of the absence of those faults. The unwholesome is called dark (kaṇha) because it is impure or because it is the cause of a dark birth; the wholesome is called bright (sukka) because it is pure or because it is the cause of a bright birth. The wholesome is called 'resulting in happiness' (sukhudraya) because it increases happiness; the unwholesome is called 'resulting in suffering' (dukkhudraya) because it increases suffering. The wholesome is called 'having a happy result' (sukhavipāka) because it has a happy fruit; the unwholesome is called 'having a painful result' (dukkhavipāka) because it has a painful fruit. In this way, the different aspects of these states should be understood.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Kamma is Finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Discourse on Perversions (Vipallāsa)

Now, wishing to show the perversions (vipallāsa) which are the causes of that kamma, the explanation of the meanings not yet explained in the Discourse on Perversions, which is preceded by the Suttanta, will be given. In the Suttanta, 'perversion of perception' (saññā-vipallāsa) means 'distorted perception' because of the state of having a perverted meaning or a perverted manner of perception. The same method applies to the other two perversions. When the function of the mind in noting and knowing is weak, the unwholesome perception devoid of wrong view becomes the perversion of perception when its own function is strong. Of the unwholesome mind devoid of wrong view...
178:
...when its own function of thinking about the object is strong, it is the perversion of thought (citta-vipallāsa). In a mind associated with wrong view, it is the perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa). Therefore, the perversion of perception is the weakest of all; the perversion of thought is stronger than that; and the perversion of view is the strongest of all. Indeed, perception is like a child who has not yet matured in intelligence (unable to distinguish gold and silver) seeing a coin, because it grasps only the mere appearance of the object. Thought is like a traveler seeing a coin, because it can also lead to the penetration of specific and general characteristics. View is like a blacksmith grasping iron with a large pair of tongs, because it reflects and misinterprets by way of another manner.

'Perversion of perception as permanent in the impermanent' means the perception that arises by grasping 'this is permanent' regarding the object of the five aggregates which are impermanent (anicca). In this same way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. 'No perversion of perception, no perversion of thought, no perversion of view' refers to the correct grasp because of the absence of the twelve perverted grasps regarding the four objects.

In the verses, 'self in what is non-self' (anattani ca attāti) means those who have such a perception of 'self' in the five aggregates which are non-self (anatta). 'Destroyed by wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhihatā) means they are not only possessed of such perception, but are also destroyed by wrong view that arises just like the perception. 'With scattered minds' (khittacittā) means they are possessed of a mind that is scattered and wandering, arising just like perception and view. 'Bereft of perception' (visaññino) is a mere way of teaching, meaning they have perverted perception, thought, and view. Alternatively, since view is preceded by perception, the perversion of perception is first mentioned with four terms. Then, the perversion of view is mentioned with 'destroyed by wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhihatā), and the perversion of thought with 'with scattered minds' (khittacittā). 'Bereft of perception' (visaññino) means they have reached delusion (moha), being devoid of natural perception due to the three perverted grasps, as in the passage: 'Fainted by the power of poison, he became bereft of perception (visaññī).' 'They are yoked to the bonds of Māra' means those people or beings are yoked to the four bonds of Māra, such as the bond of sensual desire. 'Not finding security from the bonds' means they do not reach Nibbāna, which is security from the four bonds or calamities. 'Beings travel through saṃsāra' means those very individuals wander in the round of rebirths. Why? Because they go to birth and death; therefore, they wander in saṃsāra.

'Buddhas' refers to the All-knowing Buddhas who have realized the Four Noble Truths. The plural is used because it applies to all three times. 'In the world' means in the world of locations (okāsaloka). 'Light-makers' (pabhaṅkarā) means those who create the light of wisdom for the world of beings. 'They reveal this Dhamma' means they illuminate the Dhamma that abandons perversions. 'Leading to the subsiding of suffering' means the Dhamma that leads towards Nibbāna, the subsiding of suffering. 'Having heard their [teaching]' means having heard the Dhamma of those Buddhas. 'Wise' (sappaññā) means those wise individuals who are capable of liberation. 'Regained their own mind' means having regained their own insight-mind which is free from perversion. The word is analyzed as 'paṭi-aladdhū'. Alternatively, it means 'they obtained' (paṭilabhiṃsu).
179:
"Paṭialaddhun" is a word-splitting. "Aniccato dakkhuṃ" means they saw only by way of impermanence. "Anattani anattā" means they saw the non-self in the five aggregates which are non-self. Or, they saw that in the object of the five aggregates, which are non-self, there is no self as imagined by the sectarians. "Sammādiṭṭhisamādānā" refers to those who have taken up right view. "Sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ upaccaguṃ" means they have completely transcended the entire suffering of the round of rebirth.

In the question regarding abandoned and unabandoned perversions (vipallāsa), "diṭṭhisampannassa" refers to a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). The perception of pleasure in suffering and the thought [of pleasure in suffering] occur because the turbidity of delusion has not yet been abandoned; thus, a mere perverted perception or a mere perverted thought occurs. It still occurs even for a Non-returner (anāgāmī); how then could it not occur for a Stream-enterer? These two—the perversion of perception and the perversion of thought that perceive pleasure in suffering—are abandoned only by an Arahant. The perception of beauty in the foul and the thought [of beauty in the foul] still occur for a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī); how then could they not occur for a Stream-enterer? It is stated in the Commentary that these two are abandoned only by a Non-returner. Therefore, it should be understood that these two perversions are mentioned with reference to Stream-enterers and Once-returners. It should be understood that because a Non-returner has abandoned sensual lust (kāmarāga), they have abandoned the perversions of perception and thought that perceive beauty in the foul.

By the words beginning with "dvīsu vatthūsu," the abandoned and unabandoned perversions are shown in conclusion. Therein, regarding the two objects—perceiving permanence in the impermanent and perceiving self in the non-self—six perversions are abandoned. Regarding the two objects—perceiving pleasure in suffering and perceiving beauty in the foul—two perversions of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa) are abandoned. In some books, "two" is written first and "six" is written later. "Catūsu vatthūsu" is said by combining the four objects together. "Aṭṭha" (eight) means six in two objects and two in two objects, totaling eight. "Cattāro" (four) means there are two each—perversion of perception and perversion of thought—in the objects of suffering and the foul, thus making four. In some books, even in places where "cha dvīsu" is mentioned, it is written in this same manner.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Perversions is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Discourse on the Path

Now, I shall explain the meaning of the Discourse on the Path (Magga-kathā), which was spoken to show the Noble Path that abandons those three perversions. In that Discourse on the Path, in what sense is the Path called 'Path'? The meaning is: for what reason is the thing called 'Path' in the Buddha's Dispensation known as 'Path'? In the teachings beginning with "for the abandoning of wrong view"...
180:
Among the ten methods, the first and subsequent ones are taught by way of being the direct opposites of each respective path factor. It is called "Path" (Magga) because of the sense of the practice to perform various tasks, and it is called "Cause" (Hetu) because of the sense of bringing about [the result]. Therefore, the sense of practice and the sense of bringing about the result of the Path are taught. For in such passages as "This is the path, this is the practice," the practice is the path. In passages such as "The sense of deliverance of the path is the sense of cause," the state that brings about [the result] is the cause. Thus, by these two words—"Path" and "Cause"—the answer to the question "In what sense is the path called 'Path'?" is given.

"For the support of conascent states" means supporting the mental states (arūpadhamma) that are conascent with itself through the power of conascent, mutuality, and support conditions, etc. "For the exhaustion of defilements" means for the ending of the remaining defilements other than the [already mentioned] wrong view, which are to be abandoned by each respective path. In the phrase "for the purification of the beginning of penetration," according to the word, "What is the beginning of wholesome states? It is well-purified virtue and straight view," virtue and view are the beginning of the penetration of the Truths. And that beginning is purified at the moment of the initial path (the moment of the Path of Stream-entry). Therefore, it is said, "for the purification of the beginning of penetration."

"For the establishment of the mind" means for the establishing of the associated mind in its own function. "For the cleansing of the mind" means for the state of purity of the mind. "For the attainment of distinction" means for the acquisition of a distinction superior to the mundane. "For higher penetration" means for the sake of penetrating states higher than the mundane. "For the realization of the Truths" means for the single realization of the four Truths, for the simultaneous penetration by way of the fulfillment of the function. "For establishing in cessation" means for the sake of establishing the mind or the person in Nibbāna.

At the moment of the Path of Once-returning, etc., the eight path factors are combined, and the abandoning of the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path is taught. The reason for speaking thus has already been stated below. Because the thorough purification of the beginning and the thorough cleansing of the mind also occur through the higher paths, those words are also spoken. "Dassanamagga" (Path of Seeing) and the words following it until the end teach the meaning of the path by way of the characteristics of that state. All those words have the same meanings as taught in the Description of the Higher Knowledges (Abhiññeyya-niddesa). Thus, here, the mundane and supramundane paths are indicated as applicable. By the phrase "Path in the sense of cause," the Eightfold Path is indicated. And because it is the path in the primary sense (nippariyāya), it is not called "Path" again. Words such as "Faculties in the sense of predominance" are spoken by way of the meaning of faculties, etc., not by way of the meaning of the path. Here, "Truths" refers to the knowledges of the truths (sacca-ñāṇa). All those states are the path in the sense of the practice leading to Nibbāna. What is taught at the end is that Nibbāna is called "Path" because it is sought by virtuous people who are oppressed by the suffering of the round of rebirth and desire liberation from suffering. This should be understood thus.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Path is finished.

Now, with the desire to show the essence (maṇḍapeyya) of that path, the explanation of the meaning of the Discussion on the Essence (Maṇḍapeyya-kathā), beginning with the words of the Blessed One, will be given. In that Discussion on the Essence, "Maṇḍapeyya" is like calling complete, stainless, and clear ghee "the essence of ghee"; it is called "Maṇḍa" (essence) because of its particularly clear meaning, and "Peyya" because of the sense of being worthy to be drunk.
181:
Nibbāna, however, should be understood as being called 'Magga' (the Path) because it is sought after and searched for by virtuous people who, being oppressed by the suffering of Saṃsāra, desire liberation from suffering.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Path is Finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Discourse on the Essence to be Drunk (Maṇḍapeyya-kathā)

Now, I shall provide the explanation of the meanings not yet mentioned in the Maṇḍapeyya-kathā, which begins with a portion of the words of the Blessed One, intended to show the nature of that Path as an essence to be drunk (maṇḍapeyya). In that Maṇḍapeyya-kathā, 'maṇḍapeyya' is so called because, just as complete, stainless, and clear ghee is called 'the essence of ghee' (sappimanda), it is called 'maṇḍa' (essence) in the sense of being exceptionally clear, and 'peyya' (to be drunk) in the sense of being fit for drinking. Indeed, although liquor may be clear, it is not fit to be drunk, for those who drink it fall down in the middle of the road, lose consciousness, and even lose possession of their own clothes and belongings. However, this Holy Life of the Dispensation (sāsana-brahmacariya) of mine, which is comprised of the three trainings, is 'maṇḍa' because it is complete, stainless, and exceptionally clear; and it is 'peyya' because it brings about welfare and happiness. Thus, it is shown by the name 'maṇḍapeyya'.

It is called 'maṇḍapeyya' because the clear 'maṇḍa' and the drinkable 'peyya' exist in this Dispensation. What is that? It is the Holy Life of the Dispensation (sāsana-brahmacariya) itself. Why are the three trainings called 'brahmacariya'? Nibbāna is called 'Brahma' in the sense of being noble/excellent. The three trainings are called 'brahmacariya' because they proceed for the sake of Nibbāna and because they are a practice for the sake of the noble goal. The 'sāsana-brahmacariya' is also these same three trainings.

'The Teacher is present' (satthā sammukhībhūta)—this statement is the reason here. Since the Teacher is present, drink this essence (maṇḍa) by exerting effort. For those who drink an external medicinal essence in the absence of a physician, there is doubt, as they do not know the dosage or the effects of its rising or falling. But in the presence of a physician, they drink without doubt, thinking, 'The physician will know.' In the same way, our Teacher, the Lord of Dhamma, is present; therefore, drink with effort—thus He encourages the drinking of the essence. He is called 'Satthā' (the Teacher) because He instructs accordingly regarding the welfare of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method of description beginning with 'Satthā bhagavā satthavāho' (The Teacher, the Blessed One, the Caravan-leader). He is called 'sammukhībhūta' because He has become manifest (literally, 'become a face that is seen').

In the description of Maṇḍapeyya, 'tidhattamaṇḍa' means the state of having three parts is 'tidhatta'. The essence that exists in three parts is 'tidhattamaṇḍa', meaning the essence in three ways. The phrase 'while the Teacher is present' is said to show the triad of essences complete in every aspect. Even after the Parinibbāna...
182:
However, even after the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna, the three essences continue to exist in part. For that very reason, in the detailed description, it should be understood that He did not say 'while the Teacher is present,' but instead said, 'What is the essence of teaching (desanā-maṇḍa)?' and so on.

'Desanā-maṇḍa' means the Dhamma teaching itself is the essence. 'Paṭiggaha-maṇḍa' means the recipient of the teaching is the essence. 'Brahmacariya-maṇḍa' means the Holy Life of the Path is the essence.

'Ācikkhanā' (proclaiming) means telling by way of names, such as 'these are the names of the Truths,' etc., which are to be taught. 'Desanā' (exposition) means showing. 'Paññāpanā' (making known) means making others understand, or placing it before the eye of knowledge. Indeed, one who prepares a seat is said to 'prepare the seat' (paññāpeti). 'Paṭṭhapanā' (establishing) means making known, or setting in motion, or placing before the eye of knowledge. 'Vivaraṇā' (unveiling) means making open; it means showing by opening up. 'Vibhajanā' (analyzing) means the act of dividing; it means showing by way of analysis. 'Uttānīkamma' (making clear) means making the meaning evident.

Alternatively, 'ācikkhanā' is the root term for the six terms beginning with 'desanā'. The six terms beginning with 'desanā' are spoken to explain the meaning of that root term. Among those six, 'desanā' is the initial teaching by way of a brief outline (uddesa) for the sake of those of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū). Indeed, those of quick understanding penetrate what is spoken briefly and what is spoken first. 'Paññāpanā' is the making known by way of a detailed explanation (niddesa) of what was first summarized, for the sake of those who understand through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), in order to satisfy their minds and sharpen their wisdom. 'Paṭṭhapanā' is the making known to those same people by way of a further detailed explanation (paṭiniddesa) with even more extensive words. 'Vivaraṇā' is the unveiling by speaking repeatedly even what has been explained in detail. 'Vibhajanā' is the analysis by making divisions even of what has been spoken repeatedly. 'Uttānīkamma' is the making clear by even more extensive words of what has been unveiled, and by using illustrations for what has been analyzed. This teaching also leads to the penetration of the Dhamma by those who are to be led (neyya).

By the words 'and whoever others,' beings such as the Vinipātika spirit Piyankarāmātā and others are included. 'Viññātāro' (those who understand) are those who realize the supramundane Dhamma by way of penetration. These people, such as monks and others, are called 'paṭiggaha' (recipients) because they receive the Dhamma teaching by way of penetration. The meanings of 'ayam eva' and so on are the same as those stated in the description of the first knowledge. The Noble Path is called 'brahmacariya' because it converges with Nibbāna and because it is a practice for the sake of the noble goal.

Now, by means of 'adhimokkha-maṇḍa' and so on, He shows the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and path factors (maggaṅga) existing at that moment of the Path, by applying them to the arrangement of the Maṇḍapeyya.
183:
In that (explanation of Maṇḍapeyya), 'adhimokkha-maṇḍa' refers to the essence (maṇḍa) known as decision (adhimokkha). 'Kasata' (dregs) refers to turbidity that is devoid of clarity. 'Chaddetvā' (having discarded) means having abandoned by way of cutting off (samuccheda). In the statement, "He drinks the essence of decision of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya); therefore, it is called Maṇḍapeyya," although the faculty of faith and the essence of decision are not different, they are spoken of as if they were distinct by way of conventional usage. For example, in the world, although the grindstone and the body of the grindstone are not different, it is said, "the body of the grindstone." Similarly, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pāḷi, in such terms as 'phusitatta' (the state of being touched), the state is spoken of as if it were distinct from the phenomenon (dhamma) of contact (phassa), though they are not different. Also, in the Commentary, in such phrases as 'phusanalakkhaṇo phasso' (contact has the characteristic of touching), the characteristic is spoken of as if it were distinct from the phenomenon, though they are not different. This (Maṇḍapeyya) should be understood in the same way. Regarding the word "drinks," it refers to the person endowed with those qualities. Because that person drinks that essence, that person is the drinker; and because that essence is to be drunk by that person, it is called 'Maṇḍapeyya.' Although it should be said as 'Maṇḍapeyyo' (masculine), it is used as 'Maṇḍapeyyaṃ' by way of gender transformation (neuter). The meaning of the remaining terms should be understood in this same manner.

Regarding the terms not yet explained: 'Parilāha' (fever) is the heat of defilements which is the opposite of zest (pīti), which has the characteristic of pleasing. 'Duṭṭhulla' (grossness) is the state of coarseness and unrest caused by defilements, which is the opposite of tranquility (passaddhi). 'Appaṭisaṅkhā' (lack of reflection) is the state of being unable to carry the mind evenly due to defilements, which is the opposite of reflection (upekkhā).

Furthermore, wishing to show the method of Maṇḍapeyya in another way, the text says "Atthi maṇḍo" and so on. In that Pāḷi, "tattha" means in that faculty of faith (saddhindriya). In the terms such as 'attharasa,' the decision (entering into the object) of the faculty of faith is 'attha'; the faculty of faith itself is 'dhamma'; that same faith, because it is liberated from various defilements, is 'vimutti' (liberation). The fulfillment of that attha is 'attharasa.' The fulfillment of that dhamma is 'dhammarasa.' The fulfillment of that vimutti is 'vimuttirasa.' Alternatively, the delight (rati) from obtaining the attha is 'attharasa'; the delight from obtaining the dhamma is 'dhammarasa'; and the delight from obtaining the vimutti is 'vimuttirasa.' 'Rati' (delight) refers to the zest (pīti) associated with those states or having those states as its object. In this way, the meaning of the remaining terms should be understood. According to this method, the meaning is that the essence which is to be drunk (delightful) is 'Maṇḍapeyya.'

Thus, after showing Maṇḍapeyya by way of the sequence of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) such as the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and path factors (maggaṅga), and then wishing to show the essence of the holy life (brahmacariya-maṇḍa) which stands at the end, the teacher presents the path factors, factors of enlightenment, powers, and faculties in reverse order, making the Path (magga) the precursor because of its primacy.
184:
(The Elder) showed (the path factors, factors of enlightenment, powers, and faculties). In the sense of predominance (ādhipateyyaṭṭha), the statement "the faculties are the essence (maṇḍa)" and so on, refers to the mundane and supramundane essences as appropriate. This should be understood according to the method mentioned below. In the statement, "Because of their nature of being true, the Truths (sacca) are the essence (maṇḍa)," it should be understood that since the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) and the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) do not possess the nature of an essence (in the sense of a refined core), only the knowledges of the truths (sacca-ñāṇa) are referred to as "Truths," as in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta (M. Ni. 1.300).

## The explanation of the Maṇḍapeyya-kathā
## in the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga named Saddhammapakāsinī is finished.
## The explanation of the Mahāvagga (Great Chapter) is also finished.
185:
## (2) Yuganaddha Vagga

## 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Yoked

Now, I shall explain the previously unstated meaning of the Discourse on the Yoked (Yuganaddha-kathā), which is preceded by a Sutta and was spoken to show the quality of being yoked (tranquillity and insight) of the Noble Path, which possesses the quality of being like a choice drink (maṇḍapeyya). Since the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) attained Parinibbāna while the King of Dhamma (the Buddha) was still alive, in the very year of the King of Dhamma's Parinibbāna, it should be understood that this Sutta, taught by the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Venerable Ānanda) while the King of Dhamma was still alive, was heard directly from that Venerable Ānanda, and thus it was said, "Thus have I heard" (Evaṃ me sutaṃ), and so on.

In that text, "āyasmā" is an endearing term, a term of respect, a term accompanied by reverence and deference; it means "one who has life" (long-lived). "Ānanda" is the name of that Elder. Indeed, as soon as he was born, he caused great joy and delight in his family. Therefore, it should be understood that he was named "Ānanda." "Kosambiyaṃ" means in the city of that name. In various places such as the parks and lotus ponds of that city, Kosamba trees (Schleichera oleosa) were abundant; therefore, it came to be known as "Kosambī." Some say it was because it was established not far from the hermitage of the seer named Kusamba.

"Ghositārāme" means in the park-monastery built by the banker Ghosita. In the city of Kosambī, there were three bankers: Ghosita the banker, Kukkuṭa the banker, and Pāvārika the banker. These three, having heard that "a Buddha has arisen in the world," had five hundred carts each loaded with offerings, went to Sāvatthī, set up camp near the Jetavana monastery, went to the Teacher, paid homage, performed their duties, and sat down. Having heard the Teacher's Dhamma desanā, they were established in the fruit of Stream-entry. They invited the Teacher and gave a great offering (mahādāna) for about half a month to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Prostrating at the Teacher's feet, they requested the Blessed One to visit their own region. When the Blessed One said, "Householders, the Tathāgatas delight in secluded places," they understood, "The Blessed One has given us his consent." Being exceedingly joyful, they paid homage to the Ten-Powered One and departed. Along the way, at every league (yojana), they had monasteries built for the Blessed One to stay in. Gradually reaching Kosambī, they sacrificed much wealth in their respective parks and had monasteries built for the Blessed One. Among those monasteries in Kosambī, the one built by the banker Ghosita is called Ghositārāme.
186:
(Those householders) had monasteries built. In that city of Kosambī, the monastery built by the householder Ghosita was named Ghositārāma; the monastery built by the householder Kukkuṭa was named Kukkuṭārāma; the monastery built by the householder Pāvārika in the mango grove was named Pāvārikambavana. With reference to that monastery, it is said: "in the monastery built by the householder Ghosita."

In the phrase "Friends, monks" (Āvuso bhikkhave), the Blessed Buddhas, when addressing disciples, say "Monks" (Bhikkhave). However, the disciples, thinking "Let us not be like the Buddhas," first say "Friends" (Āvuso) and then say "Monks" (Bhikkhave). When addressed by the Buddhas, the Saṅgha of monks responds with "Venerable Sir" (Bhante); when addressed by disciples, they respond with "Friend" (Āvuso).

The phrase "Whoever" (Yo hi koci) is an indefinite expression. By this, all such monks are included without exception. "In my presence" (Mama santike) means near me, Ānanda. "Arahattappattaṃ" means one's own attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. It is a word formed in the neuter gender expressing the state. Alternatively, the words should be split as "arahattaṃ pattaṃ," meaning the fruit of Arahantship attained by oneself. Or, the remaining text should be understood as "arahattappattaṃ attānaṃ" (oneself who has attained the fruit of Arahantship).

"By the four paths" (Catūhi maggehi) refers to the four paths of practice (paṭipadāmagga) to be mentioned later, not the Noble Paths (ariyamagga). Because "by the four paths" is stated separately, it should be understood that for some Arahants, the first Noble Path (the path of stream-entry) is a path preceded by the distraction of the Dhamma (dhammuddhaccapubbaṅgama); for one, the Noble Path is preceded by tranquility (samathapubbaṅgama); for one, it is preceded by insight (vipassanāpubbaṅgama); for one, it is preceded by the yoked pair (yuganaddhapubbaṅgama). Thus, there are four paths of practice. "By any one of these paths" means that by one of these four paths of practice, one declares the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.

Indeed, for a dry-vision Arahant (sukkhavipassaka), having reached the path of stream-entry preceded by the distraction of the Dhamma, and reaching the remaining three paths through pure insight alone, the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship is called a path preceded by the distraction of the Dhamma. Whether reaching the state of distraction of the Dhamma (vipassanūpakkilesa) or not, for an Arahant who attains the four paths by way of each of the three paths of practice such as those preceded by tranquility, the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship is preceded by each of the remaining paths of practice. Therefore, it is said: "By any one of these paths."

"Develops insight preceded by tranquility" (Samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāveti) means one develops insight by making tranquility the precursor or forerunner; it means first producing (absorption) concentration and afterwards developing insight. "The path arises" (Maggo sañjāyati) means the first supramundane path is produced. In the passages such as "He [follows] that path," there is no such thing as repetition (āsevana) etc. for a supramundane path that lasts only a single mind-moment. However, one who produces the second path and so forth is said to "cultivate (āsevati)..."
187:
...is said to "cultivate, develop, and make much of." "Fetters are abandoned, underlying tendencies are eliminated" means that all fetters are abandoned and underlying tendencies are eliminated in succession up to the path of Arahantship. "Underlying tendencies are eliminated" means they are removed so as not to arise again.

Furthermore, there is another reason. "Develops tranquility preceded by insight" (Vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāveti) means one develops tranquility by making insight the precursor or forerunner; it means first producing insight and afterwards developing concentration. "Develops the yoked pair" (Yuganaddhaṃ bhāveti) means one develops by making (tranquility and insight) a yoked pair. Here, in this development of the yoked pair, it is not possible to enter an attainment with that very mind and contemplate formations with that same mind. Rather, this person enters attainments for as long as he enters them, and contemplates formations for as long as he contemplates them. For as long as he contemplates formations, for that long he enters attainments. How? He enters the first jhāna; emerging from it, he contemplates formations. Having contemplated formations, he enters the second jhāna; emerging from it, he contemplates formations. Having contemplated formations, [he enters] the third jhāna... up to... he enters the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; emerging from it, he contemplates formations. This is called developing tranquility and insight as a yoked pair.

"The mind is seized by the distraction of the Dhamma" (Dhammuddhaccaviggahitaṃ mānasaṃ hoti) — in this passage, for insight-practitioners with weak wisdom, because it is an object of defilement, the arising of a mind accompanied by agitation (uddhacca) by way of wavering among the ten things called imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa) such as light (obhāsa) is called "distraction of the Dhamma" (dhammuddhacca). A mind that is wrongly seized or brought into conflict by that distraction of the Dhamma is called "a mind seized by the distraction of the Dhamma" (dhammuddhaccaviggahitaṃ mānasaṃ). Or, it means the mind is wrongly seized by the arising of craving, conceit, and wrong view rooted in that distraction of the Dhamma as the cause. There is also a reading "dhammuddhaccaviggahita-mānasaṃ." By the passage "Friends, there is such an occasion," it shows the time when, by defining what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmagga-vavatthāna), one wards off that distraction of the Dhamma and again enters the course of insight. "That mind" (Yaṃ taṃ cittaṃ) refers to the mind that occurs having entered that course of insight at that time. "Stands only internally" (Ajjhattameva santiṭṭhati) means having descended back into the course of insight, it stands or is established in the object called the internal sphere (gocarajjhatta) at that time. "Settles down" (Sannisīdati) means it settles well by way of occurrence in that very object. "Becomes unified" (Ekodhi hoti) means it becomes one-pointed. "Becomes concentrated" (Samādhiyati) means it is well-placed, meaning it is firmly established.

## This is the Commentary on the Sutta.
188:
## 1. Explanation of the Suttanta Niddesa

In that explanation of the Suttanta Niddesa, "the states arisen in that (concentration)" refers to the mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) that have arisen in that concentration. By the words "in the sense of contemplating as impermanent," etc., he shows the divisions of insight (vipassanā). "Right view is the path" means the path known as right view. This is because each of the eight path factors is also called a "path." "He pursues" is by means of the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). "He develops" is by producing the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga). "He cultivates" is by producing the paths of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) and arahantship (arahatta-magga). Although these three differ in terms of stages, because they are similar in aspects such as advertence (āvajjana), etc., the same explanation was given.

In the ellipsis (peyyāla) between the perception of light (ālokasaññā) and the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā), non-distraction (avikkhepa), etc., as well as the jhānas, attainments (samāpatti), kasiṇas, recollections (anussati), foulness (asubha), and "long breath" (dīghaṃ assāsa), etc., are mentioned in brief because they have already been explained in the Explanation of Knowledge of Concentration of Immediate Succession (Paṭis. I. 80-81). In that explanation, "by power of non-distraction" should be understood as the power of non-distraction of the preliminary stage (of concentration). However, in the tetrad taught by way of pure insight (suddha-vipassanā), such as "contemplating impermanence by power of out-breath," etc., at the time of tender insight, strong insight preceded by concentration associated with insight should be understood.

In the section where insight is the precursor, he first teaches insight without limiting the object by saying "by way of impermanence," etc., and later teaches by limiting the object by saying "form is impermanent," etc. In that context, "arisen" refers to the state of mental states and mental factors that have arisen in that insight. In this context of "vossaggārammaṇatā" (the state of having relinquishment as an object), "vossagga" is Nibbāna. Nibbāna is called "vossagga" because it is the relinquishing and abandoning of conditioned things (saṅkhata). Insight and the states associated with that insight are based on Nibbāna and have Nibbāna as their object because they are established in Nibbāna by the power of the inclination (ajjhāsaya) that leans towards Nibbāna. For even a base (patiṭṭhā) is called an "object" (ārammaṇa) because it is taken as an object; thus, it is said to have Nibbāna as its object precisely because it is established in Nibbāna. In other scriptures (Pāḷi) as well, a base is called an "object." As it was said: "Monks, for example, if a man were to approach a reed-house or a grass-house that was dry, withered, and over a year old, with a burning grass torch from the eastern direction, the fire would find an opening, the fire would find a base (ārammaṇa)" (SN 4.243), etc. Therefore, because of the reason of being based on Nibbāna through the state of having Nibbāna as the object of those states arisen in that insight, there is non-distraction (avikkhepa) known as one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā), which is divided into access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā).
189:
That concentration refers to the concentration conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) produced after insight. Therefore it is said, "Thus, first insight, then serenity."

In the Explanation of the Coupled Way (Yuganaddha-niddesa), the sequence of coupling mentioned below in the Suttanta explanation is clear through the method of the first two explanations (serenity-led and insight-led). However, the sequence of coupling at the moment of the path (magga-khaṇa) is not clear. Therefore, without speaking of the coupling that is not certain in the preliminary stage, and wishing to show only the coupling that is certainly obtained at the moment of the path, he said "by sixteen modes," etc. Among those seventeen modes such as "ārammaṇaṭṭhena," etc., the term "yuganaddha" mentioned at the end is omitted because it has the same meaning as the root term, and it is said "by sixteen" by way of the remaining sixteen modes.

"Ārammaṇaṭṭhena" means in the sense of taking an object, or by the power of the object. The remaining terms should be understood in the same way. "Gocaraṭṭhena" means in the sense of a place to be frequented, even though it has the nature of taking an object. "Pahānaṭṭhena" means in the sense of abandoning. "Pariccāgaṭṭhena" means in the sense of relinquishing by not taking back again, even though it has the nature of abandoning. "Vuṭṭhānaṭṭhena" means in the sense of emerging. "Vivaṭṭanaṭṭhena" means in the sense of turning away without returning, even though it has the nature of emerging. "Santaṭṭhena" means in the sense of being peaceful. "Paṇီtaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of being sublime, even though it has the nature of being peaceful, or in the sense of being so excellent that one cannot be satisfied. "Vimuttaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of being liberated from bonds. "Anāsavaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of being free from taints (āsava) that arise by taking an object, even though it has the nature of being liberated from bonds. "Taraṇaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of floating without sinking into the object, or in the sense of crossing over. "Animittaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of being free from the signs of conditioned things (saṅkhāra-nimitta). "Appaṇihitaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of being free from desire. "Suññataဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of being free from misinterpretation. "Ekarasaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of having a single function. "Anativattanaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of not overstepping one another. "Yuganaddhaဋ္ဌေန" means in the sense of being coupled.

"To one who abandons restlessness, to one who abandons ignorance" is said by way of abandoning the opposing states for that respective yogi. Here, "cessation" (nirodha) refers to Nibbāna itself. "They do not overstep each other" means that if serenity were to overstep insight, the mind would lead to laziness (kosajja) because serenity is on the side of slackness. If insight were to overstep serenity, the mind would lead to restlessness (uddhacca) because insight is on the side of distraction. Therefore, serenity, by not overstepping insight, does not cause a fall into laziness. Insight, by not overstepping serenity, does not cause a fall into restlessness. Serenity evenly...
190:
Samatha occurring in harmony with Vipassanā protects Vipassanā from falling into restlessness (uddhacca). Vipassanā occurring in harmony with Samatha also protects Samatha from falling into sloth (kosajja). Thus, these two, Samatha and Vipassanā, have a common function by way of the function of not overstepping each other; by occurring in harmony, they achieve the goal without overstepping each other. Their state of being yoked together (yuganaddhatta) at the moment of the Path occurs only because they were yoked together at the moment of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā).

Because the functions of the Path are described as performing abandoning, relinquishing, emerging (from defilements), and turning away (from Saṃsāra), in order to show the entire function of the Path, the defilements and aggregates associated with restlessness (uddhacca) as well as the defilements and aggregates associated with ignorance (avijjā) are pointed out. Since the remaining meanings are not described by way of the Path's function, only restlessness and ignorance are pointed out for the purpose of showing merely the opposing states. "Vivaṭṭato" refers to a person who does not turn back (to Saṃsāra).

"Concentration is liberated from the taint of sensual desire" is said because concentration is the opposite of sensual desire (kāmacchanda). "Rāga-virāgā" is so called because that liberation of mind (ceto-vimutti) has the fading away (virāga) or transcending of lust (rāga).
