Alternatively, it can be the ablative case meaning "from the fading away of lust." The term "avijjā-virāgā" is similar. "Ceto-vimutti" is concentration associated with the Path. "Paññā-vimutti" is wisdom associated with the Path. "Tarato" refers to one who is crossing over. "Sabba-paṇidhīhi" means by way of longings such as lust, hatred, and delusion, or by all longings. Thus, after answering in fourteen ways, without separately analyzing the meanings of "single flavor" (ekarasaṭṭha) and "not overstepping" (anatiwattanattha), it is said "by these sixteen ways." Why? Because at the end of each of those fourteen ways, it is pointed out that "they become of a single flavor, they are yoked together, they do not overstep each other," so those two ways are already pointed out. Therefore, it is said "by sixteen." As for the meaning of being yoked together (yuganaddhaṭṭha), it is indeed not mentioned even in the summary (uddesa).

## 2. Commentary on the Explanation of the Section on Restlessness regarding the Dhamma

In the section on restlessness regarding the Dhamma, "light arises for one contemplating as impermanent" means for one established in the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), who repeatedly contemplates formations with the three contemplations (impermanence, suffering, non-self). When the insight knowledges reach maturity, for one whose mind is purified by the abandoning of defilements through the substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), at the moment of contemplating as impermanent, suffering, or non-self, light (obhāsa) naturally arises by the power of insight knowledge. Thus, first, the arising of light for one contemplating as impermanent is described. An unskilled practitioner of insight, when that light arises, thinks: "Indeed, such light has never arisen for me before; surely I have reached the Path, the Fruit..."
191:
"...reached," he mistakenly takes what is not the Path for the "Path," and what is not the Fruit for the "Fruit." For one who thus mistakenly takes what is not the Path for the "Path" and what is not the Fruit for the "Fruit," the course of insight (vipassanā-vīthi) goes astray. He either abandons his course of insight and falls into distraction, or he remains perceiving that very light through the lenses of craving, views, and conceit. That light arises for some monks illuminating only the area of their seat; for some, the interior of the room; for some, even the exterior of the room; for some, the entire monastery; for some, a quarter-league (gāvuta), half a league, one league, two leagues, and so on... for some, creating a single mass of light from the surface of the earth up to the Akanittha Brahma realm. For the Blessed One, however, it arose illuminating the ten-thousandfold world system. This light arises illuminating various places even in darkness characterized by four factors.

"The light is the Dhamma" means he adverts to the light; he attends to that light thinking, "This light is the Dhamma of the Path" or "the Dhamma of the Fruit." "Distraction therefrom is restlessness" means the distraction that arises from that light or from the act of adverting to it as "the Dhamma" is called "restlessness" (uddhacca). "A mind gripped by that restlessness" means a mind disturbed by that restlessness arising in such a way, or a practitioner of insight whose mind is disturbed by the arising of defilements rooted in that restlessness as a cause. Because he has departed from the course of insight and stands in distraction or in the defilements rooted in that restlessness, he does not know formations as they really are as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Therefore, the phrase "one whose mind is gripped by restlessness regarding the Dhamma" (dhammuddhacca-viggahita-mānasa) should be applied. "That time occurs" means if investigation (upaparikkha) arises even for a yogi whose mind is thus defiled by way of enjoyment, he understands thus: "Insight has formations as its object; the Path and Fruit have Nibbāna as their object. These minds have formations as their object. Therefore, this light is not the Path; only the contemplation of rise and fall is the mundane path leading to Nibbāna." Having thus distinguished the Path from what is not the Path, and having avoided that distraction, he stands in the contemplation of rise and fall and clearly contemplates formations as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. For one who investigates thus, "that time occurs." However, one who does not see thus becomes a person of overestimation (adhimānika), thinking "I have reached the Path and Fruit."

"That mind" means that insight-mind. "Only internally" means in the very internal sphere (gocarajjhatta) which is the object of the contemplation of impermanence. "Knowledge arises" means for that practitioner who is weighing and investigating material and mental phenomena, insight knowledge arises with an unswerving momentum, sharp, courageous, and extremely pure, like the thunderbolt (vajira) hurled by the King of Devas. At that time, for that practitioner, the five types of joy—minor joy (khuddikā-pīti), momentary joy (khaṇikā-pīti), showering joy (okkantikā-pīti), uplifting joy (ubbegā-pīti), and pervading joy (pharaṇā-pīti)—arise associated with insight, pervading the entire body. At that time, for that practitioner, there is no fever of body or mind, no heaviness, no coarseness, no unwieldiness, no sickness, and no crookedness. On the contrary, his body and mind are tranquil, light, malleable, wieldy, proficient, extremely pure, and upright. Having a body and mind uplifted by these states such as tranquility (passaddhi), he then experiences a delight called "superhuman" (amānusī) which transcends the sensual pleasures of humans. With reference to such experience, it was said: "One who has entered a secluded place..." and so on. Entering a secluded monastery (or insight) and attending to the meditation subject, with a mind peaceful due to the subsiding of defilements...
192:
Vipassanā insight arises, which is unremitting, sharp, courageous, and exceedingly pure.

"Rapture (pīti) arises" means that at that time, fivefold rapture associated with insight arises, pervading the entire body: minor rapture (khuddikā pīti), momentary rapture (khaṇikā pīti), showering rapture (okkantikā pīti), uplifting rapture (ubbegā pīti), and pervading rapture (pharaṇā pīti).

"Tranquillity (passaddhi) arises" means that at that time, there is no longer distress, heaviness, coarseness, unreadiness, sickness, or crookedness in the body and mind of that person. Instead, the body and mind become tranquil, light, malleable, ready for work, proficient, exceedingly pure, and straight. That person, with body and mind supported by this tranquillity and so on, experiences a superhuman delight at that time. With reference to this, it was said:

"For the bhikkhu who has entered an empty house, with a peaceful mind, there is a superhuman delight as he rightly discerns the Dhamma.
Whenever he contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, he attains rapture and joy; for those who know, that is the Deathless (Nibbāna)." (Dhammapada 373-374)

In this way, for that person, the tranquillity (passaddhi) of both body and mind associated with insight arises, accompanied by lightness and so on, fulfilling this superhuman delight.

"Happiness (sukha) arises" means that at that time, happiness associated with insight arises, drenching and suffusing the entire body of that person.

"Resolution (adhimokkha) arises" means that at that time, faith (saddhā) associated with insight arises, which is the nature of extreme clarity of the mind and mental factors.

"Exertion (paggaha) arises" means that at that time, energy (vīriya) associated with insight arises, which is well-exerted, neither too lax nor too strained.

"Establishment (upaṭṭhāna) arises" means that at that time, mindfulness (sati) associated with insight arises, which is well-established, well-founded, firm like a well-planted pillar, and immovable like the king of mountains. Whatever object that person adverts to, brings to mind, or reviews, that object appears clearly in his mindfulness, as if rushing or leaping into it, just as the next world appears to one with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu).

"Equanimity (upekkhā)" refers to both equanimity of insight (vipassanūpekkhā) and equanimity of advertence (āvajjannūpekkhā). At that time, equanimity of insight, which is neutral towards all formations (saṅkhāra), arises strongly, as does equanimity of advertence at the mind-door. For that person adverting to various objects, that equanimity of advertence is courageous and sharp, like Indra's thunderbolt (vajira) or like a heated iron needle piercing through a leaf-bundle.
193:
It proceeds thus. This has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Among these, teachers say that equanimity of insight (vipassanūpekkhā) is "equanimity as neutrality (tatramajjhattūpekkhā) associated with insight." If it were taken as insight-knowledge, there would be the fault of repetition (punaruttidosa) because it was already mentioned that "insight-knowledge arises." In the description of the third jhāna, it is also stated: "Equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) and equanimity of insight (vipassanūpekkhā) are one in meaning. It is wisdom itself, divided into two according to function." Therefore, by stating it as equanimity as neutrality associated with insight, the fault of repetition is avoided, and it accords with the description of the third jhāna. Furthermore, among the five faculties, the faculties of wisdom, faith, energy, and mindfulness are mentioned as "knowledge, resolution, exertion, and establishment," but the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is not directly mentioned. Since the faculty of concentration must also be mentioned by way of the pair-yoking (yuganaddha) of serenity and insight, it should be understood that concentration which proceeds evenly is called "equanimity" because it abandons the effort of further re-establishing the associated states upon the object.

"Attachment (nikanti) arises" means that a subtle and peaceful form of attachment arises, which creates a longing for the insight adorned with light (obhāsa) and so on. It is difficult to even perceive this attachment as a defilement. Just as with light, when any one of these (knowledge, rapture, etc.) arises, the practitioner thinks: "Indeed, such knowledge has never arisen in me before; such rapture, tranquillity, happiness, resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and attachment have never arisen before. Surely I have reached the Path, I have reached the Fruition." Thus, he takes what is not the Path to be "the Path," and what is not the Fruition to be "the Fruition." For him who takes the non-path as "the Path" and the non-fruition as "the Fruition," the course of insight is diverted. He abandons his original meditation subject and sits enjoying only that attachment. Here, light (obhāsa) and so on are called "imperfections" (upakkilesa) because they are the objects/bases of imperfections, not because they are unwholesome. Attachment (nikanti), however, is both an imperfection and an object of imperfection. These are ten by way of object, but they become thirty by way of grasping (gāha). How? If one thinks, "Light has arisen in me," there is grasping by way of wrong view (diṭṭhi). If one thinks, "How wonderful this light is," there is grasping by way of conceit (māna). If one enjoys the light, there is grasping by way of craving (taṇhā). Thus, in the case of light, there are three types of grasping: view, conceit, and craving. The same applies to the remaining states, and thus there are thirty imperfections by way of grasping. (This should be understood in the same way) when one brings to mind by way of suffering (dukkha) and non-self (anatta).
194:
When attending [to things] as suffering, or when attending as non-self, the meaning should be understood in this same way. Indeed, among these three contemplations (anupassanā), the occurrence of the defilements of insight (vipassanupakkilesa) for each individual insight through the power of each contemplation should be understood; it is not understood as occurring in only one contemplation.

Having thus shown the ten defilements through the power of insight without distinguishing between the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so on among the three contemplations, [the teacher] speaks the words beginning with "rūpaṃ aniccato manasikaroto" (when attending to form as impermanent) wishing to show them again by way of distinction. In that text, "jarāmaraṇaṃ aniccato upaṭṭhānaṃ" means the appearance of old age and death as impermanent.

Because an unskilled and unwise practitioner is shaken by illumination (obhāsa) and so on through the power of the thirty defilements mentioned previously, and regards any one of them as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self," therefore, wishing to show that meaning, [the teacher] spoke the two verses beginning with "obhāse ceva ñāṇe ca" (in illumination and in knowledge). In those verses, "vikampati" means that the practitioner is shaken and trembles in various ways through the power of various defilements regarding objects such as illumination. "Yehi cittaṃ pavedhati" means that the mind trembles in various ways through the power of various defilements because of causes such as tranquility (passaddhi) and happiness (sukha). Therefore, the connection should be understood as: the practitioner is shaken in tranquility and in happiness. "Upekkhāvajjanāya ceva" means that one is shaken in the adverting called equanimity, and also in the equanimity of adverting (āvajjanupekkhā). In the Visuddhimagga, however, it is stated as "upekkhāvajjanāyañca." "Upekkhāya ca" means that one is shaken in the equanimity which is the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) mentioned below, and also in attachment (nikanti).

## Commentary on the Explanation of Restlessness regarding the Dhamma

In this verse, because the two types of equanimity—equanimity of adverting and equanimity of concentration—are referred to, the meaning in the place where it is taught below as "upekkhā uppajjati" (equanimity arises) is also stated by way of both adverting and the faculty of concentration. Also, in the contemplations of impermanence and so on, because of the suitability of each individual equanimity of adverting, it means that each contemplation is developed repeatedly as "impermanent, impermanent," "suffering, suffering," and "non-self, non-self."

Because a skilled, wise practitioner, who is proficient in the Pāḷi texts and endowed with wisdom, when illumination and so on arise, distinguishes and contemplates that light with wisdom thus: "This illumination has arisen in me; however, this illumination is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of the nature of wasting away, of the nature of vanishing, of the nature of fading away, and of the nature of cessation." Or otherwise, when such light arises, that practitioner thinks: "If illumination were the self, it would be proper to take it as 'self.' However, this illumination which is taken as 'self' is only non-self." Thus, seeing it as non-self because of the sense of being ungovernable, he removes wrong view (diṭṭhi). If illumination...
195:
If (that illumination) were of a permanent nature, it would be proper to take it as "permanent." However, this illumination is taken as "permanent" while being impermanent. Therefore, this practitioner, seeing it as impermanent because of its non-existence after having come to be, removes pride (māna). If illumination were of the nature of happiness, it would be proper to take it as "happiness." However, this illumination is taken as "happiness" while being suffering. Therefore, this practitioner, seeing it as suffering because of the oppression of arising and falling, exhausts attachment (nikanti). As one contemplates regarding illumination, so it is with the remaining states.

Having contemplated thus, he repeatedly regards illumination as "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." From knowledge... (and so on) up to attachment, he repeatedly regards them as "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." One who regards them thus is not shaken and does not tremble in illumination and so on. Therefore, wishing to show that meaning, [the teacher] spoke the verse beginning with "imāni dasa ṭhānāni" (these ten states). In that verse, "dasa ṭhānāni" refers to the ten states such as illumination. "Paññā yassa pariccitā" means [the ten states] that have been practiced, repeatedly touched, and cultivated by the insight-wisdom of a practitioner who is free from defilements. "Dhammuddhaccakusalo hoti" means that the practitioner who has the ten states practiced with wisdom becomes skilled through the penetration of the true nature of the aforementioned restlessness regarding the Dhamma. "Na ca sammohaṃ gacchati" means that due to being skilled in restlessness regarding the Dhamma, he does not fall into great delusion, by way of removing craving (taṇhā), pride (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi).

Now, wishing to clarify the same procedure mentioned previously by another method, [the teacher] spoke the verse beginning with "vikkhipati ceva kilissati ca" (he is distracted and defiled). In that verse, a practitioner with dull wisdom (mandapañña) reaches both distraction and the occurrence of the remaining defilements regarding illumination and so on. A practitioner with medium wisdom (majjhimapañña) reaches only distraction, not the occurrence of the remaining defilements; such a person is one with over-estimation (adhimānika) [thinking he has reached the path]. A practitioner with sharp wisdom (tikkhapañña), even though reaching distraction, abandons that over-estimation and strives in insight. A practitioner with very sharp wisdom (atitikkhapañña) reaches neither distraction nor the occurrence of the remaining defilements. "Vikkhippati ceva" means that among those four types of persons, the one with dull wisdom reaches the distraction called restlessness regarding the Dhamma. "Kilissati ca" means he is defiled by the defilements of craving, pride, and wrong view; he is distressed and oppressed. "Cavati cittabhāvanā" means that the insight-meditation of that person with dull wisdom falls away and declines, because of delighting and staying only in the defilements, and because the defilements are not suppressed by the opposing insight. "Vikkhipati na kilissati" means the person with medium wisdom is distracted by distraction but not defiled by the defilements. "Bhāvana parihāyati" means that for the person with medium wisdom, because of his over-estimation, there is no striving in insight, and thus insight declines.
196: It means it does not occur. 'Distracted but not defiled' means that even a person with sharp wisdom, though distracted due to agitation (uddhacca), is not defiled by defilements (kilesa). 'Meditation does not decline' means that for such a person with sharp wisdom, although there is distraction, by abandoning the distraction caused by overestimation (adhimāna) and because of the presence of the undertaking of insight (vipassanā), insight meditation does not decline but continues to occur. 'The mind is not distracted, not defiled' means that the mind of a person with extremely sharp wisdom is not distracted by agitation, nor is it defiled by defilements. 'Mental development does not waver' means that the insight mental development of that person does not waver; because of the absence of distraction and defilements, it remains established in its proper place. In the passage beginning with 'By these four grounds,' the meaning should be understood in connection with the fact that the practitioner (yogāvacara) of great wisdom, possessing the fourth wholesome state which is free from the arising of distraction and defilements, and whose mind is the opposite of the mind's contraction and distraction in the ten grounds such as light (obhāsa), knows in various ways that the minds of the three practitioners, such as those with dull wisdom, are such and such, through these four grounds which are the causes or instruments just mentioned. Herein, 'contraction' (saṅkhepa) should be understood as the sluggish state of the mind due to the arising of distraction and defilements. 'Distraction' (vikkhepa) should be understood as the agitated state of the mind through the distraction mentioned in the two places 'distracted but not defiled.' ## The Commentary on the Yuganaddha-kathā is finished. ## 2. Commentary on the Sacca-kathā Now, the commentary on the new meanings in the Sacca-kathā (Discourse on Truth), which is preceded by the Suttanta and taught with the desire to show the meaning of truth, the distinction of the penetration of truth, and the arrangement of the characteristics of truth by means of the Noble Path which has the quality of yoking (yuganaddha). In that Suttanta, first, 'tathāni' means things that are real by virtue of their true nature. Indeed, only those phenomena that exist according to their true nature are called truths (sacca) because of their meaning of truth. The meaning of truth was stated in the commentary on the first knowledge description (paṭhama-ñāṇa-niddesa). 'Avitathāni' means things that are free from distortion in the stated nature. Indeed, truths do not become non-truths. 'Anaññathāni' means things that are free from other natures. Indeed, non-truths do not become truths. 'Monks, this is suffering; monks, this is real' means...
198:
At the moment of the Path, one penetrates the unity of the nature of reality (tathaṭṭha) and so forth with a single Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). How is it penetrated? When the unity of the nature of reality and so forth of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) is penetrated, the unity of the nature of reality and so forth of the remaining truths is also penetrated. For example, in the preliminary stage, for one who stands having well-defined the diversity and unity of the five aggregates, when emerging from the Path (or insight) as impermanent, suffering, or non-self, if one aggregate is seen as impermanent and so forth, the remaining aggregates are also seen as impermanent and so forth; in the same way, it should be understood in this case. The meaning of suffering in 'suffering' is called tathaṭṭha (the meaning of reality). The fourfold meaning of the Truth of Suffering, such as the meaning of oppression (pīḷanaṭṭha), is called tathaṭṭha because it is real by its own nature. The same method applies to the remaining truths. That same fourfold meaning is called the meaning of non-self (anattaṭṭha) because of the absence of a self. It is called the meaning of truth (saccaṭṭha) because it is non-deceptive in the stated nature. It should be understood that it is called the meaning of penetration (paṭivedhaṭṭha) because it is to be penetrated at the moment of the Path.

The statement beginning with 'Yaṃ aniccaṃ' (What is impermanent) is shown by making the common characteristic (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) the precursor. In that Pali, when it is said, 'What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is impermanent,' the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin, and the Truth of the Path are taken. For those three truths are indeed impermanent, and because they are impermanent, they are suffering. When it is said, 'What is impermanent and suffering, that is non-self,' those same three truths are taken. When it is said, 'What is impermanent, suffering, and non-self,' the Truth of Cessation is also included along with those three. For all four truths are indeed non-self. 'Taṃ tathaṃ' means that those four truths are real by nature. 'Taṃ saccaṃ' means that those same four truths are non-deceptive in their true nature. In the words beginning with 'by nine aspects,' according to the word of the Buddha, 'Monks, all should be known by direct knowledge (abhiññeyya),' it is shown by the meaning of direct knowledge (abhiññaṭṭha), and by the specific meanings of the meaning of full understanding (pariññaṭṭha) for suffering, the meaning of abandoning (pahānaṭṭha) for the origin, the meaning of development (bhāvanaṭṭha) for the path, and the meaning of realization (sacchikiriyaṭṭha) for cessation. In this context, it should be understood that it is shown by the meaning of full understanding because there is the presence of known-understanding (ñāta-pariññā) in all four truths; by the meaning of abandoning because there is the presence of abandoning through the vision of the four truths; by the meaning of development because there is the presence of development of the four truths; and by the meaning of realization because there is the presence of realization of the four truths. In the words beginning with 'by nine aspects as the nature of reality,' the application should be made according to the method previously stated.

In the words beginning with 'by twelve aspects,' the nature of reality and so forth have the meanings already stated in the Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā). In the exposition (niddesa) of these things, the application should be understood according to the method already stated.

In the words beginning with 'How many characteristics of the truths are there,' the six characteristics to be spoken of later are divided into two by way of the conditioned and the unconditioned, and thus he said, 'two characteristics.'
199:
Among those two characteristics, the characteristic of the conditioned and the characteristic of the unconditioned are as follows: "Monks, these three are the conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. Arising (uppāda) is manifest, vanishing (vaya) is manifest, and alteration of what is present (ṭhitassa aññathatta) is manifest. Monks, these three are the unconditioned characteristics of the unconditioned. Arising is not manifest, vanishing is not manifest, and alteration of what is present is not manifest." Thus, as spoken (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya), there is the characteristic of the conditioned as conditioned and the characteristic of the unconditioned as unconditioned. However, the conditioned is not the characteristic, and the characteristic is not the conditioned. It is not possible to make known the characteristic without the conditioned, nor the conditioned without the characteristic. But the conditioned becomes manifest only through the characteristic.

Again, wishing to show those same two characteristics in detail, he said, "six characteristics." The characteristics of the conditioned truths refer to the characteristics of the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin, and the Truth of the Path. For those truths are called conditioned (saṅkhata) because they are constructed by combining causes. 'Uppāda' means birth (jāti). 'Paññāyati' means it is known (it is manifest). 'Vaya' means dissolution (bhaṅga). 'Alteration of what is present' means aging (jarā), which is the change into another state of things that have reached the phase of presence (ṭhiti). Because the three conditioned truths are produced (nipphanna), arising, vanishing, and alteration are spoken of. However, because the arising, aging, and dissolution of those very truths are not themselves produced (anipphanna), it should not be said that they have arising, vanishing, and alteration. It should also not be said that arising, vanishing, and alteration are not manifest because they depend on the conditioned. Rather, they should be called conditioned (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa) because they are the modes of change of the conditioned. Some teachers say that the arising, aging, and dissolution of the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin are included within the truths, but the arising, aging, and dissolution of the Truth of the Path are not included within the truth.

In that regard, it is stated in the Commentary to the Khandhakavagga: "At the moment of arising of conditioned things, the conditioned thing, the characteristic of arising, and its moment called the time of arising are manifest. When arising has passed, the conditioned thing, the characteristic of aging, and its moment called the time of aging are manifest. At the moment of dissolution, the conditioned thing, aging, the characteristic of dissolution, and its moment called the time of vanishing are manifest." The unconditioned truth refers to the Truth of Cessation (Nibbāna). For that Truth of Cessation is called unconditioned because it is not constructed by the coming together of causes, but is produced by itself. 'Of what is present' (ṭhitassa) means established because it is permanent, not because it has reached the phase of presence (ṭhī-khaṇa). Again, wishing to show those same two characteristics in detail, he said, "twelve characteristics."

In the phrases such as 'Among the four truths, how many are wholesome (kusala),' 'indeterminate' (abyākata) refers to the indeterminate of Nibbāna (nibbāna-abyākata) among the four types of indeterminate: resultant indeterminate (vipāka-abyākata), functional indeterminate (kiriya-abyākata), material indeterminate (rūpa-abyākata), and Nibbāna indeterminate. For all four are called indeterminate because they are not determined by the characteristics of wholesome or unwholesome. 'It may be wholesome' refers to the occurrence by way of the wholesome of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
200:
"It may be wholesome" means it occurs by way of wholesome states of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere. "It may be unwholesome" means it occurs by way of the remaining unwholesome states, excluding craving (taṇhā). "It may be indeterminate" means it occurs by way of the resultant (vipāka) and functional (kiriya) states of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere, as well as by way of material forms (rūpa). In the phrases such as "the three truths are included," it means they are counted. "By way of the basis (vatthu)" means it occurs by way of the bases known as unwholesome, wholesome, indeterminate, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

"That truth of suffering which is unwholesome" refers to the unwholesome states excluding craving. "Two truths are included in one truth in the sense of being unwholesome" means these two truths—the truth of suffering and the truth of the origin—are included in one unwholesome truth in the sense of being unwholesome; this is the meaning of "unwholesome truth." "One truth is included by two truths" means one unwholesome truth is included by the two truths of suffering and the origin.

"That truth of suffering which is wholesome" refers to the wholesome states occurring in the three planes of existence. These two truths—the truth of suffering and the truth of the path—are included in one wholesome truth in the sense of being wholesome; it is called the "wholesome truth." "One wholesome truth is included by the two truths of suffering and the path."

"That truth of suffering which is indeterminate" refers to the resultant and functional states in the three planes, and material forms. These two truths—the truth of suffering and the truth of cessation—are included in one indeterminate truth in the sense of being indeterminate; it is called the "indeterminate truth." "One indeterminate truth is included by the two truths of suffering and cessation."

"Three truths are included in one truth" means the truths of the origin, the path, and cessation are included in one truth of suffering which is unwholesome, wholesome, and indeterminate. "One truth is included by three truths" means one truth of suffering is respectively included by the three truths of the origin, the path, and cessation, which are unwholesome, wholesome, and indeterminate.

Some teachers, however, explain: "The truth of suffering and the truth of the origin are included by the truth of the origin in the sense of being unwholesome. The truth of suffering and the truth of the path are included by the truth of the path in the sense of being wholesome, but not in the sense of seeing [Nibbāna]. The truth of suffering and the truth of cessation are included by the truth of cessation in the sense of being indeterminate, but not in the sense of being unconditioned (asaṅkhata)."

## 2. Commentary on the Second Suttanta Text

Again, wishing to point out the penetration of the truths by way of another Suttanta, he presented the Suttanta beginning with "Formerly, monks, in my case..." In that Suttanta, "Formerly, monks, before my enlightenment (sambodha)" means, monks, in the time before my enlightenment, that is, before the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). "Before I had attained full enlightenment (anabhisambuddhassa)" means before having penetrated all phenomena (dhamma). "While I was still a Bodhisatta" means while being a Bodhisatta. "This occurred to me" means this reflection occurred while sitting on the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka). "Gratification (assāda)" is so called because it is enjoyed. "Danger (ādīnava)" means fault. "Escape (nissaraṇa)" means the departure from the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
201:
It is called "happiness (sukha)" because it causes happiness; it means that for whomsoever happiness arises, it makes that person happy. One who has a beautiful mind due to association with joy (pīti) and mental pleasure (somanassa) is called "one of good mind (sumana)"; the state of being such a "sumana" is "mental pleasure (somanassa)." It is simply happiness (sukha) distinguished by its association with joy. "Impermanent (anicca)" means not lasting. "Suffering (dukkha)" is so called because it is the basis of suffering and because it is the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā). "Subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma)" means having the nature of turning around by way of aging and breaking, without following one's will. By this, the state of non-self (anatta) is stated. "The removal of desire and lust (chandarāgavinaya)" is the restraint of lust known as desire; it is not the lust for color (vaṇṇarāga). "The abandoning of desire and lust (chandarāgappahāna)" is the abandoning of that very desire and lust.

In the words beginning with "As long as (yāvakīvañca)," the meaning should be understood in connection as follows: "As long as I did not penetrate with superior knowledge these five aggregates of clinging... according to reality, I did not claim to have fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the unsurpassed state of omniscience." "Kīvañca" is merely a particle. "Yato" means "because" or "when." "Atha" means "then," after having known thus. "The knowledge and vision arose in me" means the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) known as "vision" (dassana) because it performs the function of seeing, arose in me. "Unshakable (akuppā)" means unable to be provoked or moved. "Liberation (vimutti)" is the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship. By this reviewing of the fruit, the reviewing of the path and Nibbāna is also stated. "This is the last birth" means this is the final occurrence of the aggregates. "Now there is no more renewed existence" means there is no further arising (rebirth) now. By this, the reviewing of the abandoned defilements is stated. For an Arahant, there is no reviewing of remaining defilements.

## 3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Second Suttanta

In the sequence of applying the knowledge of penetrating the truths, "This is the gratification of form" is the penetration by abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha). Having known in the preliminary stage, "This is the gratification of the aggregate of form associated with craving," it is the penetration of the truth of the origin known as the abandoning of the origin at the moment of the path. "The truth of the origin" refers to the knowledge that penetrates the truth of the origin. The knowledge that takes the noble truths as its object is also called "truth," as in the passage: "Whatever wholesome states there are, all those are included in the four noble truths." "This is the danger of form" is the penetration by full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha). Having known in the preliminary stage, "This is the danger of the aggregate of form," it is the penetration of the truth of suffering known as the full understanding of suffering at the moment of the path. "The truth of suffering" refers to the knowledge that penetrates the truth of suffering. "This is the escape from form" is the penetration by realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha). Having known in the preliminary stage, "This is the [escape from] the aggregate of form..."
202:
Knowing “This is the escape (Nibbāna) from the aggregate of form,” the penetration of the Truth of Cessation is the realization of the Truth of Cessation at the moment of the Path. The “Truth of Cessation” refers to the knowledge of the penetration of the Truth of Cessation which takes the Truth of Cessation as its object. In the phrase “In these three places, that which...”, it should be understood as referring to the Right View and Right Intention that arise by way of penetration into these three truths already mentioned: the Truth of the Origin, the Truth of Suffering, and the Truth of Cessation. “Penetration by development” (bhāvanā-paṭivedha) is the penetration of the Truth of the Path, which is the development of the Path. The “Truth of the Path” refers to the knowledge that penetrates the Truth of the Path.

Furthermore, wishing to show the four truths and the penetration of the truths by another method, he said: “By how many aspects is it called truth?” and so forth. In that context, while all the omniscient Bodhisattas were sitting upon the Throne of Enlightenment, they searched for the Truth of the Origin, such as birth, which is the cause of the Truth of Suffering, such as aging and death, asking, “Why does this exist?” While searching in this way, the Bodhisattas defined and grasped that the Truth of the Origin, such as birth, is the “cause” of the Truth of Suffering, such as aging and death. Therefore, because that searching and grasping are the searching for and grasping of the truths, they are designated as “Truth” in the sense of searching and in the sense of grasping. This procedure is also obtained by the Paccekabuddhas in their grasping of conditions; for the disciples (sāvakas), however, it is obtained in the grasping of conditions by way of tradition (anussava).

“The sense of penetration” (paṭivedhaṭṭha) refers to the sense of penetrating simultaneously at the moment of the Path those truths that were thus searched for and grasped in the preceding stage.

In the terms “kiṃnidānaṃ” and so forth, all terms such as nidāna are synonyms for “cause.” A cause is called “nidāna” because it brings forth the effect, as if saying, “Come, take this effect.” It is called “samudaya” because the effect arises from it; “jāti” because it is born; and “pabhava” because it originates. The meaning of the compound here is: “What is its source (nidāna)?” thus it is kiṃnidānaṃ. “What is its origin (samudaya)?” thus it is kiṃsamudayaṃ. “What is its birth (jāti)?” thus it is kiṃjātikaṃ. “What is its source (pabhava)?” thus it is kiṃpabhavaṃ. Since the birth (jāti) of that Truth of Suffering, namely aging and death, is—in the sense already mentioned—the source, the origin, the birth, and the cause, he said “jātinidānaṃ” and so forth. “Aging and death” is the Truth of Suffering. “The origin of aging and death” is the Truth of the Origin, which is the cause of that aging and death. “The cessation of aging and death” is the Truth of Cessation. “The practice leading to the cessation of aging and death” is the Truth of the Path. The meaning should be understood in this same way for all terms.

“Understanding cessation” (nirodhappajananā) means understanding the Truth of Cessation by making it an object. The statement “Birth may be the Truth of Suffering, or it may be the Truth of the Origin” means it is known as such in the sense of being caused by existence (bhava).

## 3. Explanation of the Discussion on the Factors of Enlightenment

17. Now, wishing to show the distinction of the Factors of Enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) which is accomplished through the penetration of the truths, I shall explain the meaning not yet mentioned in the Bojjhaṅgakathā, which is preceded by the Sutta. In that Bojjhaṅgakathā, first, in the Sutta, they are called “bojjhaṅga” because they are the parts (aṅga) of the omniscient knowledge (bodhi), or because they are the causes for the noble disciple (bodhi). To explain in detail, the noble disciple understands (bujjhati), or awakens, or realizes by the harmony of those states called mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, which arise at the moment of the supramundane path and are the opposites of many dangers such as sloth and torpor, restlessness, defilements, volitional formations, sensual happiness, self-mortification, the view of annihilation, and the view of eternity; for that reason, they are called “bojjhaṅga.” “He understands (bujjhati)” means waking up from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, penetrating the four Noble Truths, or realizing Nibbāna itself. It is as he said: “Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment... he awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.”
203:
It is the Truth of Suffering; it is the Truth of the Origin by way of being the cause of aging and death. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. In the statement “Ignorance may be the Truth of Suffering,” it means [it is the Truth of the Origin] by way of being the cause of ignorance due to the origin of the taints (āsava).

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Truths is Finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Discussion on the Factors of Enlightenment

Now, the Elder, wishing to show the distinction of the Factors of Enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) which is accomplished through the penetration of the truths, will explain the meaning not yet mentioned in the Bojjhaṅgakathā, which is preceded by the Sutta. In that Bojjhaṅgakathā, first, in the Sutta, they are called “bojjhaṅga” because they are the parts or limbs of enlightenment (bodhi, i.e., omniscient knowledge), or because they are the causes for enlightenment (bodhi, i.e., the noble disciple).

What is meant is this: when the harmony of those states such as mindfulness and so forth arises at the moment of the supramundane path, the noble disciple understands by that harmony of states called mindfulness, investigation of states, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, which are the opposites of many dangers such as sloth and torpor, restlessness, defilements, volitional formations, sensual happiness, self-mortification, and the adherence to annihilation and eternity; therefore, it is called “bodhi.” “He understands” means waking up from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or penetrating the four truths, or realizing Nibbāna.

It is as he said: “Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, he awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.” Because they are the parts of that enlightenment (bodhi) which is called the harmony of states, they are called “bojjhaṅga,” like the factors of jhāna (jhānaṅga) or the factors of the path (maggaṅga). Because the noble disciple is called “bodhi” since he understands by this harmony of states of the aforementioned kinds, they are also called “bojjhaṅga” because they are the limbs or causes of that enlightenment (the noble disciple), like the components of an army (senaṅga) or the parts of a chariot (rathaṅga). Therefore, the teachers of the Commentaries said: “The factors of the person who understands are the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).” The meaning of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness and so forth has been stated in the Abhiññeyyaniddesa.

In the Bojjhaṅgatthaniddesa, “bodhāya saṃvattanti” means they lead to understanding. For whose understanding do they lead? It means they lead to the understanding of the person who has completed his task for the purpose of reviewing Nibbāna through the path and fruit; or they lead to the awakening from the sleep of defilements by the path, and to the state of having awakened by the fruit. Even in powerful insight (vipassanā), the factors of enlightenment lead to the understanding of Nibbāna...
204:
They become. Therefore, this powerful insight (vipassanā) has a shared meaning with the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas) associated with the path of insight and the fruition of insight. Indeed, the factors of enlightenment established in the three stages—insight, path, and fruition—conduce to the penetration of Nibbāna. By the phrase "conduce to enlightenment" (bodhāya saṃvattanti), it is meant that they are called factors of enlightenment because they are the components (or causes) of the insight, path, and fruition (or the realization of Nibbāna).

In the Exposition of Things to be Known (Abhiññeyya-niddesa), the place of arising through association of the factors of enlightenment, which are described by the five groups of four beginning with "they awaken" (bujjhanti), has been stated. Furthermore, the word "bujjhanti" is an agentive designation (kattu-niddesa) indicating the seven factors of enlightenment as the agents, to show their capability in performing their respective functions. The term "in the sense of awakening" (bujjhanathena) is an abstract designation (bhāva-niddesa) to show the absence of any agent other than the seven factors of enlightenment, even though the capability to perform their functions exists. "They enlighten" (bodhenti) is a causal agentive designation (hetukattu-niddesa) indicating the seven factors of enlightenment as the causal agents, because they urge the practitioners (yogīs) who awaken through the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment. "In the sense of enlightening" (bodhanathena) is an abstract designation (bhāva-niddesa) indicating the causal agent in the same manner as previously mentioned. By these terms such as "they awaken," it is meant that they are called factors of enlightenment because they are the components (or causes) of insight, path, and fruition (or the realization of Nibbāna).

"In the sense of being on the side of enlightenment" (bodhipakkhiyaṭṭhena) means they exist on the side of the practitioner who has acquired the name "Bodhi" in the sense of knowing. This exposition beginning with "bodhipakkhiya" shows the state of these requisites of enlightenment as being beneficial to the practitioner. By these terms such as "bodhipakkhiya," it is meant that they are called factors of enlightenment because they are the components of the practitioner named Bodhi.

In the group of six (chakka) beginning with "in the sense of obtaining wisdom" (buddhilabhanaṭṭhena), the term "buddhilabhanaṭṭhena" means the sense of the practitioner reaching the noble path and fruition through the wisdom of insight. "In the sense of planting" (ropanaṭṭhena) means the state of establishing beings in the path and fruition. "In the sense of bringing to completion" (pāpanaṭṭhena) means the sense of completing what has already been established. The teachers say that when these factors of enlightenment associated with insight are distinguished by the three prefixes "pati," "abhi," and "saṃ," they are called factors of enlightenment associated with the path and fruition. It should be understood that all factors of enlightenment described through the conventional usage of Dhamma are called factors of enlightenment because they are the causes (or components) of the path and fruition.

## Explanation of the Tenfold Group Beginning with Root-Root
18. In the tenfold group (dasaka) where the term "root" is the primary word, beginning with "in the sense of being a root" (mūlaṭṭhena), the term "mūlaṭṭhena" means that in insight, path, and fruition, the preceding factors of enlightenment are the root-origin for the succeeding factors of enlightenment, for the co-nascent (sahajāta) states, and for each other. "In the sense of root-conduct" (mūlacariyaṭṭhena) means conduct or occurrence as a root is called root-conduct; it means the sense of occurring as a root. "In the sense of root-grasping" (mūlapariggahaṭṭhena) means that those very factors of enlightenment associated with insight, path, and fruition are called "grasping" (pariggaha) because they are grasped for the sake of arising from the beginning; since the seven factors of enlightenment which are roots are themselves what is grasped, they are called "root-grasping." It is in the sense of being a root that is grasped.

Those very factors of enlightenment also exist in the sense of being an entourage (parivāraṭṭha) by way of accompanying each other; in the sense of fulfillment (paripūraṇaṭṭha) by way of the perfection of cultivation (bhāvanā); and in the sense of maturation (paripākaṭṭha) by way of reaching the end (or the noble fruition). Those seven factors of enlightenment are called "roots" and also "analytical knowledges" (paṭisambhidā) because they are divided into six types; thus they are called "root-analytical knowledges" (mūlapaṭisambhidā). It is in the sense of being both a root and an analytical knowledge. "In the sense of bringing to the root-analytical knowledge" (mūlapaṭisambhidāpāpanaṭṭhena) means that for the practitioner devoted to the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, to that factor of enlightenment called root-analytical knowledge...
205:
...because of the sense of reaching it, and because of the sense of mastery (vasībhāva) in that root-analytical knowledge for that practitioner. In other such conventional usages regarding persons (puggala-vohāra), it should be understood that they are called factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas) because they are the causes of enlightenment. In such concluding statements as "also for those who have attained mastery in the root-analytical knowledge," the factors of enlightenment associated with fruition should be understood. There is also a reading "vasībhāvaṃ pattānaṃ."

## The Tenfold Group of Root-Root is Finished.

In the remaining nine tenfold groups such as the one rooted in cause (hetu-mūlaka), the meaning of the common terms should be understood in this same manner. As for the uncommon terms, the aforementioned factors of enlightenment are called "causes" (hetu) because they produce the aforementioned states. They are called "conditions" (paccaya) because they are supportive. Those very states are called "purity" (visuddhi) because they are the purity of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), of uprooting (samuccheda), and of tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi). They are called "blameless" (anavajja) because they are free from faults. They are called "renunciation" (nekkhamma) because of the statement "all wholesome states are renunciation." They are called "liberation" (vimutti) by way of liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti) and so on, because they are liberated from defilements. The factors of enlightenment of the path and fruition are called "taintless" (anāsava) because they are free from the taints (āsavas) which are their objects. The three types of factors of enlightenment are called "seclusion" (viveka) by way of seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-viveka) and so on, because they are empty of defilements. The factors of enlightenment of the path of insight are called "relinquishment" (vossagga) because of relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-vossagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga). The factors of enlightenment of fruition are called "relinquishment" (vossagga) because of relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga).

The nine tenfold groups described by way of each individual term, such as "they know the sense of the root," should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. However, the term "vasībhāvappattānaṃ" is not applied here because it does not express the present tense. Terms such as "the sense of grasping" (pariggahaṭṭha) have already been explained in the Exposition of Things to be Known (Abhiññeyya-niddesa).

Furthermore, the Elder Sāriputta, wishing to show the method of the factors of enlightenment by way of the exposition of the Sutta he himself taught, first introduced the Sutta by stating the origin (nidāna) beginning with "At one time" (ekaṃ samayaṃ). Because it was a Sutta taught by himself, he did not say "Thus have I heard" (evaṃ me sutaṃ) in this context; instead, to show the clarity of the speaker, he spoke of himself as if he were another, saying "Venerable Sāriputta" (āyasmā sāriputto). Such usage is employed in the world and in treatises. "In the morning time" (pubbaṇhasamayaṃ) means throughout the whole morning. The accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). In the remaining two terms, the method is the same. "The enlightenment factor of mindfulness" (satisambojjhaṅgo) means...
206:
"May the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arise in me"—thus it occurs to me. "May the immeasurable (appamāṇa) enlightenment factor of mindfulness arise in me"—thus it occurs to me. "May the well-undertaken (susumāraddha) enlightenment factor of mindfulness arise in me" means: may the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that is thoroughly fulfilled arise in me—thus it occurs to me. "Remaining" means persisting by way of occurrence in the object that is Nibbāna. "Falls away" means departing from the object that is Nibbāna. The same method applies to the remaining enlightenment factors.

"To the king's great minister" means either to the king's chief minister or to a minister endowed with a great measure of wealth and possessions. "Of various colors" means cloths dyed with various dyes; here, although the genitive case (sāmivacana) expressing possession is used, it should be understood as "with cloths of various colors." "Cloth chest" means a casket for storing cloths. "Pair of cloths" means a pair of garments. "For the purpose of clothing" means for the purpose of dressing. In this Sutta, the enlightenment factors associated with fruition (phalabojjhaṅga) of the Venerable Sāriputta are discussed. For when the Elder enters the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) making the enlightenment factor of mindfulness the head, the remaining enlightenment factors follow in the wake of that mindfulness. When he makes any other factor, such as the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya), the head, the rest also follow in its wake. Thus, the Elder spoke this Sutta wishing to show his mastery (vasībhāva) in the attainment of fruition.

## Explanation of the Introduction to the Sutta
"How does the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arise?" means: for one entering the attainment of fruition making mindfulness the head, while other enlightenment factors are present, when the thought "this enlightenment factor of mindfulness occurs in this way" arises, in what way does that mindfulness become the leader? This is the meaning. "As long as cessation appears" means for as long a time as Nibbāna is manifest as an object. "As much flame" means a flame of such a measure. "How does the immeasurable (appamāṇa) enlightenment factor of mindfulness arise?" means: while the immeasurable (or mundane) enlightenment factor of mindfulness is present, when it occurs making mindfulness the head, "this immeasurable enlightenment factor of mindfulness occurs in this way," for what reason does that immeasurable mindfulness become the leader? This is the meaning. "Bound by measure" means the defilements, the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna), and the volitional formations leading to rebirth (ponobbhavika-saṅkhāra) are called "bound by measure." According to the teaching, "Lust is a maker of measure, hatred is a maker of measure, delusion is a maker of measure," for the person in whom lust and so on arise, it is called "measure" (pamāṇa) because it makes a measure such as "this person has this much quality." Because they are connected to that measure of lust and so on, defilements and others are called "bound by measure" (pamāṇabaddha). Defilements (kilesa) here refer to those that exist as latent tendencies (anusaya). Obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) are defilements that have reached the stage of active occurrence (samudācāra). Volitional formations leading to rebirth (ponobbhavika-saṅkhāra) are those formations that have the nature of repeatedly producing birth.
207:
"Dependent" (āyatta) means that defilements and so on are called "bound by measure." Defilements are those existing as latent tendencies (anusaya); obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) are defilements that have reached active occurrence (samudācāra). "Volitional formations leading to rebirth" (saṅkhārā ponobbhavikā): renewed existence is called "punabhava" because it produces birth again and again; because those formations have that renewed existence as their habit, they are called "ponobbhavika"; "ponobbhavika" is the same as "ponobbhavika." These are the formations known as wholesome and unwholesome kamma. "Immeasurable" (appamāṇa) means immeasurable because of the absence of the aforementioned "measure" (pamāṇa). Since the paths and fruits are also immeasurable, the terms "by way of the sense of being unshakable" and "by way of the sense of being unconditioned" are stated to distinguish it from them. It is "unshakable" (acala) because of the absence of dissolution (bhaṅga); it is "unconditioned" (asaṅkhata) because of the absence of conditions. That which is unshakable and unconditioned is exceedingly devoid of measure.

In the sentence "How is it well-undertaken?", the word "enlightenment factor" (bojjhaṅga) should be connected according to the method mentioned previously. "Uneven" (visama) means uneven because it is itself disharmonious and because it is the cause of a disharmonious state. "Even state" (samadhamma) means a state that is even because of the sense of being peaceful and the sense of being sublime. It is peaceful because of the absence of measure (pamāṇa). In accordance with the word, "Bhikkhus, whatever states there are, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (Nibbāna) is said to be the foremost of those states," it is sublime because it is superior to all states. Because it is undertaken in that very even Nibbāna, called the "even state," it is called "well-undertaken" (susumāraddha). "Because of adverting" (āvajjitattā) is said with reference to the time of occurrence of the attainment of fruition. It means because mind-door adverting has arisen in Nibbāna, which is described as "non-arising" and so on. "Remains" (tiṭṭhati) means it occurs. The terms "arising" (uppāda) and so on have the meanings stated below. The same method applies to the sections based on the remaining enlightenment factors.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Enlightenment Factors is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Discourse on Loving-kindness

Now, I shall explain the meanings not yet mentioned in the Discourse on Loving-kindness, which was taught immediately after the Discourse on the Enlightenment Factors, follows the same course as the Discourse on the Enlightenment Factors, and is preceded by a Sutta. In that Sutta, "practiced" (āsevitāya) means cultivated with respect. "Developed" (bhāvitāya) means increased. "Frequently practiced" (bahulīkatāya) means done again and again. "Made into a vehicle" (yānikatāya) means made like a well-yoked vehicle. "Made into a foundation" (vatthukatāya) means made like a foundation in the sense of being a support. "Well-established" (anuṭṭhitāya) means made manifest before one. "Consolidated" (paricitāya) means accumulated and developed from all sides. "Well-undertaken" (susumāraddhāya) means thoroughly well-undertaken.
208:
"Sukata" means due to a well-done action. "Ānisaṃsa" means benefits. "Pāṭikaṅkhā" means things that should be expected or desired. "Sukhaṃ supati" (sleeps happily) means sleeping happily without tossing and turning or snoring, unlike others who sleep miserably; it means sleeping happily without such occurrences. Even when asleep, it is like being in an attainment (samāpatti).

"Sukhaṃ paṭibujjhati" (wakes happily) means waking happily without change, like a blooming lotus, unlike others who wake miserably, groaning, stretching, and tossing. "Na pāpakaṃ supinaṃ passati" (does not see evil dreams) means even if one dreams, one sees only good dreams. It is like worshipping a cetiya, making an offering, or listening to the Dhamma. Unlike others who dream of being surrounded by thieves, attacked by wild beasts, or falling into a chasm, the practitioner of loving-kindness does not see such evil dreams.

"Manussānaṃ piyo hoti" (dear to humans) means being dear and pleasing to humans like a pearl necklace worn on the chest or a flower worn on the head. "Amanussānaṃ piyo hoti" (dear to non-humans) means being dear to non-humans just as to humans. "Devatā rakkhanti" (deities protect) means deities protect him as parents protect their child. "Nāssa aggi vā visaṃ vā satthaṃ vā kamati" (fire, poison, or weapons do not affect him) means fire, poison, or weapons do not strike, penetrate, or harm the body of one who dwells in loving-kindness.

"Tuvaṭaṃ cittaṃ samādhiyati" (the mind concentrates quickly) means the mind of one who dwells in loving-kindness concentrates quickly without sluggishness. "Mukhavaṇṇo vippasīdati" (the complexion of the face becomes clear) means the face has a clear complexion like a ripe palm fruit fallen from its stalk. "Asammūḷho kālaṃ karoti" (dies unconfused) means for one who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no dying in confusion; one dies unconfused as if falling asleep. "Uttariṃ appaṭivijjhanto" (if not penetrating higher) means if one cannot yet attain Arahantship, which is higher than the metta-attainment, upon passing away from this life, one reaches the Brahma world like one waking from sleep.

In the description of loving-kindness (metta), "anodhiso pharaṇā": a limit (mariyādā) is called "odhi"; "anodhi" means no limit. Therefore, it means all-pervading without limit (anodhiso). "Odhiso" means having limits by way of parts. "Disāpharaṇā" means pervasion in the directions. "Sabba" means including all without exception. The meaning of the word "satta" (beings) was explained in the commentary on the Ñāṇakathā Mātikā. However, by conventional usage (ruḷhī), this term "satta" is also used for those free from passion, just as a specific fan made of bamboo strips is still called a "palm-leaf fan" (tālavaṇṭa). "Avera" means free from enmity. "Abyāpajja" means free from ill-will (byāpāda). "Anīgha" means free from suffering. There is also a reading "aniggha". "Sukhī attānaṃ" (being happy, [may they maintain] themselves...)
209:
"Pariharantu" means being happy, may they be able to maintain their individual existence (attabhāva). By the term "avera", the absence of enmity is shown in one's own continuity (santāna) in relation to others, and in others' continuity in relation to the person dwelling in loving-kindness. In "abyāpajja" etc., the absence of ill-will (byāpāda) rooted in enmity is shown due to the absence of enmity. By "anīgha", the absence of suffering rooted in ill-will is shown due to the absence of ill-will. By "sukhī attānaṃ pariharantu", the happy maintenance of individual existence is shown due to the absence of suffering. Thus, the connection of words here should be understood. Among these four phrases like "avera hontu", whichever phrase becomes clear, one should pervade with loving-kindness by way of that clear phrase.

In the words "pāṇa" etc., they are called "pāṇa" because they have breath (pāṇana); it means their existence is dependent on inhalation and exhalation. They are called "bhūta" because they have become manifest (bhūtattha); it means they have been born. Hell is called "pu"; because they go (galanti) to that hell, they are called "puggala". The body is called "attabhāva", or the group of five aggregates itself is called "attabhāva". Because it is a mere designation (paññatti) based on those five aggregates, they are called "attabhāvapariyāpanna" because they are included, delimited, and contained within that individual existence. Just as the word "satta" is understood metaphorically, so too the remaining words like "pāṇa" should be understood as synonyms for all beings, applied by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī). Although there are other synonyms for all beings like "sabba jantū" and "sabba jīvā", only these five starting with "satta" and "pāṇa" are taken to be called "the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness pervading without limit in five ways" because they are well-known. If some teachers desire a difference not only in words but also in meaning for "satta", "pāṇa", etc., then for them, unspecified pervasion (anodhiso pharaṇā) would be contradicted. Therefore, without taking such differences in meaning, one should pervade with loving-kindness without limit by way of any one of these five ways.

In specified pervasion (odhiso pharaṇā), it is stated by way of gender as "women, men"; by way of Noble Ones and ordinary people as "ariyā, anariyā"; and by way of rebirth as "deities, humans, those in states of deprivation (vinipātikā)". In the pervasion of directions (disāpharaṇā), pervasion in all directions without distinguishing directions using the method "all beings" etc. is unspecified pervasion (anodhiso pharaṇā). Pervasion in all directions using the method "all women" etc. is specified pervasion (odhiso pharaṇā).

Since these three types of loving-kindness pervasion are stated by way of a mind that has reached absorption (appanā), absorption should be taken in the three sections: the section on unspecified pervasion, the section on specified pervasion, and the section on pervasion of directions. In unspecified pervasion...
210:
Firstly, the absorption (appanā) of "May all beings be free from enmity" is one; the absorption of "May they be free from mental suffering" is one; the absorption of "May they be free from physical suffering" is one; and the absorption of "May they maintain themselves in happiness" is one. These four types (starting from "free from enmity," etc.) are also spoken of solely by way of bringing about welfare. This is because loving-kindness (mettā) has the characteristic of bringing about welfare. Thus, by way of the four absorptions in each of the five modes such as "beings," there are 20 absorptions. In the specified pervasion (odhisa-pharaṇa), by way of the four absorptions in each of the seven modes such as "all women," there are 28 absorptions. In the directional pervasion (disā-pharaṇa), however, by the method of "all beings in the eastern direction," etc., there are 20 for each direction, making 200; by the method of "all women in the eastern direction," etc., there are 28 for each direction, making 280; totaling 480 absorptions. Thus, all the absorptions mentioned in this text are 528. Just as the pervasion in three ways is spoken of regarding loving-kindness, it should be understood that it is spoken of in the same way for compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā).

## 1. Indriyavāra-vaṇṇanā

Then, to show the manner of bringing about welfare through loving-kindness and the cultivation of the faculties (indriya), etc., the text says "avoiding the oppression of all beings," and so on. In that Pāḷi, "oppression" (pīḷana) means internal physical oppression. "Harm" (upaghāta) means external physical injury. "Distress" (santāpa) means mental distress from any source. "Exhaustion" (pariyādāna) means the natural depletion of life, etc. "Harassment" (vihesā) means the harming of life in another way. "Avoiding" (vajjetvā) means removing any one of these oppressions, etc., with one's own mind. These five terms, "oppression," etc., are spoken of by way of avoiding the opposites of loving-kindness. The terms "for non-oppression" (apīḷanāya), etc., are spoken of by way of bringing about welfare through loving-kindness. "For non-oppression" means one loves all beings with the manner of non-oppression; this is how it should be connected. The same applies to the remaining terms. "May they not be inimical, may they not be suffering, may they not be troubled in soul"—these three terms are also words that reject the opposites of bringing about welfare through loving-kindness. The word "mā" (not) has the meaning "may they not be." "Free from enmity, happy, happy in soul"—these three terms are words that bring about welfare through loving-kindness. It should be understood that the two terms "free from mental suffering" (abyāpajjā) and "free from physical suffering" (anīghā) are included in the word "happy" (sukhinā). "Happy in soul" (sukhitattā) is a term showing the constant occurrence of that happiness. The term "sukhitattā" and the term "sukhī attānaṃ pariharantu" are one in meaning. Alternatively, the words "free from mental suffering" and "free from physical suffering" are included by the terms "for non-oppression," etc. "By eight modes" refers to "for non-oppression," etc.
211: (Loving-kindness should be developed) by these eight modes: the five modes of bringing welfare of loving-kindness starting with 'May they be free from enmity' and the three modes of bringing welfare of loving-kindness starting with 'May they be free from enmity.' 'Mettāyati' means one loves or cherishes. It means one thinks of, produces, or causes to occur the state of bringing welfare to others. It is said, 'He is liberated from all obsessions of ill-will (byāpāda),' because he is liberated through suppression (vikkhambhana) from all occurrences of ill-will which are the opposite of loving-kindness. Loving-kindness (mettā), mind (ceto), and liberation (vimutti)—thus a single loving-kindness is described in three ways. These three terms, 'free from enmity, safe, happy,' are stated by summarizing the modes mentioned earlier. The five faculties (indriya) stated by the method beginning with 'resolves with faith' are indeed associated with loving-kindness. In the six cycles (vāra) starting with 'cultivation' (āsevanā), it is called 'āsevanā' because loving-kindness is cultivated by these associated faculties. Similarly, it is called 'development' (bhāvanā) and 'frequent practice' (bahulīkamma). 'Alaṅkāra' means ornamentation. 'Svālaṅkatā' means they are well-ornamented. 'Parikkhāra' means equipment or causal factors. 'Suparikkhata' means they are well-prepared by causal factors. 'Parivāra' is called retinue in the sense of protecting. Again, twenty-eight terms starting with 'āsevanā' are stated for the purpose of praising the qualities of loving-kindness. Among those twenty-eight terms, 'pāripūrī' is so called because of the state of being fulfilled. 'Sahagatā' means they are concomitant with loving-kindness. The terms 'sahajāta' and so on are the same. 'Pakkhandanā' means the initial entering into the object of beings in loving-kindness. Or, it is called 'pakkhandanā' because loving-kindness enters the object of beings through those faculties like faith. The two terms 'saṃsīdanā' and so on are the same. 'Touching this as peaceful' (etaṃ santanti phassanā) means there is touching through development that 'this loving-kindness is peaceful' by means of those faculties like faith; thus it is called 'etaṃ santanti phassanā.' It is used in the neuter gender like the term 'etadaggaṃ.' 'Svādhiṭဋ္ဌိtā' means well-established. 'Susammuggatā' means well-raised. 'Suvimuttā' means well-liberated from their respective opposites. 'Nibbattenti' means the faculties like faith, being associated with loving-kindness, produce loving-kindness. 'Jotenti' means they make it manifest. 'Patāpenti' means they make it brilliant. ## 2-4. Commentary on the Three Cycles of Powers, etc. 24-27. The cycle of powers (bala-vāra) should be understood in the same way as stated in the cycle of faculties (indriya-vāra). The cycles of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and path factors (maggaṅga) are stated figuratively (pariyāyena), not according to their individual characteristics. In the cycle of path factors, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are stated in terms of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) preceding loving-kindness, not in terms of absorption (appanā). This is because these—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—cannot occur together with loving-kindness (in absorption). In the passage 'Of all beings' and so on...
212:
The meaning of the remaining cycles should also be understood in the same manner as stated in the cycle of beings beginning with "May all beings be free from enmity." As for the procedure for developing the meditation on loving-kindness, it should be taken and understood from the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga, 1, 240 etc.).

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Loving-kindness is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Discussion on Dispassion

Now, I shall explain the meanings not yet mentioned in the Discussion on Dispassion (Virāgakathā), which is preceded by the Noble Path called Dispassion and is taught immediately after the Discussion on Loving-kindness, which culminates in the benefit of the Noble Path. In that Discussion on Dispassion, first, wishing to show the meaning of the two Sutta terms taught as "When one is weary [of suffering], one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated," the thesis (uddesa) is established: "Dispassion is the Path, Liberation is the Fruit."

In that thesis, first, wishing to show the meaning of the terms, it is said: "How is dispassion the Path?" and so on. In that text, "virajjati" means one becomes dispassionate (viratta). The meanings of the remaining terms are just as stated in the Description of Path-Knowledge (Maggañāṇaniddesa). "Virāga" (Dispassion) means that because Right View is free from wrong view, it is called Virāga. Furthermore, that Virāga is called Virāga because it has Virāga (Nibbāna) as its object... [pe]... it stands in Virāga. Thus, the connection of the five expressions beginning with "virāgārammaṇa" should be understood.

Among those expressions, "virāgārammaṇa" means having Nibbāna as its object. "Virāgagocara" means having Nibbāna as its range (object). "Virāge samudāgata" means arising in Nibbāna. "Virāge ṭhita" means standing in Nibbāna by way of occurrence. "Virāge patiṭṭhita" means being well-established in Nibbāna by way of non-regression.

Nibbāna is also called Virāga because it is the cause of the absence of passion (rāga). "Nibbānārammaṇatājāta" means those [states] born in the object that is Nibbāna, or born by way of having Nibbāna as an object. All those states such as contact (phassa) associated with the Path are called Virāga in the sense of being free from passion. "Sahajāta" (co-nascent) refers to the seven path-factors such as Right Intention that arise together with Right View. "They go to Virāga; Virāga is the Path" means they are called Virāga because they have Virāga, which is Nibbāna, as their object and go towards it; they are called "Path" (magga) in the sense of seeking.

Each individual path-factor also receives the name "Path". Thus, when the path-nature of each factor is stated, the path-nature of Right View is also already stated. For that very reason, it is said "by this path," taking the eight path-factors together. By the term "Buddhas," Paccekabuddhas are also included. For those Paccekabuddhas are also [Buddhas], as it is taught: "Monks, these two are Buddhas: the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Paccekabuddha."
214:
In the same manner as stated in the Exposition on Dispassion (Virāga-niddesa), the meaning in the Exposition on Liberation (Vimutti-niddesa) should also be understood. In this Exposition on Liberation, the Fruition (phala) is called 'liberation' because it is liberation through tranquility (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and Nibbāna is called 'liberation' because it is liberation through escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti). Statements such as 'the seven factors of the path that arise together' and so forth are not mentioned here because they are not applicable in this Exposition on Liberation. Only this much is stated: that it is liberation in the sense of relinquishment, because it is itself the liberation of Fruition. The remaining passages are just as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Discussion on Dispassion is finished.

## 6. Paṭisambhidākathā (Discussion on Analytical Knowledges)

## 1. Dhammacakkappavattana-vāra-vaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Section on Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion)

Now, desiring to show the divisions of analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) accomplished by the power of the path known as 'dispassion' (virāga), I shall explain the meanings not yet mentioned in the Discussion on Analytical Knowledges, preceded by the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Firstly, in the Sutta, regarding 'Bārāṇasiyaṃ': there is a river named Bārāṇasā; the city situated not far from that Bārāṇasā river is called Bārāṇasī. In that city of Bārāṇasī. Regarding 'Isipatane Migadāye': in the monastery known as Migadāya (Deer Park) because it is a place where safety is given to deer, and which received its name [Isipatana] due to the descending and ascending of seers (isis). For in that place, all the Omniscient Seers (Buddhas) who have arisen descend; it means they reside there for the purpose of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. Furthermore, after seven days, having emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) in the Nandamūlaka cave and having performed the duty of washing their faces at Lake Anotatta, the Paccekabuddha-seers also descend there by way of gathering; they assemble for the purpose of the Uposatha or for non-Uposatha matters, and when returning to Mount Gandhamādana, they ascend from there. Thus, because of this descending and ascending of seers, it is called 'Isipatana'. There is also a variant reading 'Isipadana'. Regarding 'Pañcavaggiye':

'Koṇḍañña, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahānāma, and Assaji—
these five great elders are called the Group of Five (Pañcavaggiya).'

The group of these five monks thus mentioned is called 'Pañcavagga'. Those who belong to that group of five, or are included within it, are called 'Pañcavaggiya'; to those five monks. 'Addressed the monks' means that from the time of making the initial aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs)...
215:
...fulfilling the perfections in due order through successive births and reaching the final existence, and in that final existence, having made the Great Renunciation and reaching the Bodhi-maṇḍa in due order, sitting there on the Unconquered Seat (aparājita-pallaṅka), defeating the army of Māra, recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati) in the first watch, purifying the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) in the middle watch, and at the end of the last watch, causing the ten-thousandfold world system to echo and tremble while attaining Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), passing seven weeks at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, being requested by Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, and out of compassion for the world, going to Bārāṇasī and informing the five monks, He addressed them, desiring to set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.

'Monks, these two extremes' means 'Monks, these two portions'. Upon the utterance of these words, the sound of the teaching reached the Avīci hell below and the peak of existence (Bhavagga) above, spreading throughout the ten-thousandfold world system; at that very moment, eighteen crores of Brahmas assembled.
