In the western direction, the sun was about to set, and in the eastern direction, the full moon rose in conjunction with the constellation Uttarāsāḷha. At that time, the Blessed One, beginning the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, said: 'Monks, these two extremes,' and so forth.

In that passage, 'pabbajitena' (by one who has gone forth) means by one who has cut the bond of the laity and the objects of sensual desire (vatthu-kāma) and has gone forth. 'Na sevitabbā' (should not be pursued) means should not be indulged in. Because monks are specifically the proper vessels for the practice, it was said, 'should not be pursued by one who has gone forth.' 'Yo cāyaṃ kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogo' means the repeated devotion to the pleasure of defilement-sensuality (kilesa-kāma) in the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma), or to the basis of that pleasure. 'Hīno' (low) means base. 'Gammo' (vulgar) means belonging to the village-dwellers. 'Pothujjaniko' (of the worldlings) means practiced by worldlings who are blind and foolish. 'Anariyo' (ignoble) means not noble; or rather, not belonging to the pure and supreme Noble Ones. 'Anatthasaṃhito' (unprofitable) means not connected with the goal; it means not relying on the cause that brings happiness.

'Attakilamathānuyogo' means the devotion to self-mortification, meaning the act of causing suffering to oneself. 'Dukkho' (painful) means bringing suffering through self-mortifying practices such as sleeping on a bed of thorns and so forth. Because ascetics (tapasīs) held this to be the 'supreme austerity,' the word 'hīno' (low) was not used here out of regard for their feelings. Because it is a practice of those who have gone forth, the word 'gammo' (vulgar) was not used, and because it is not common to householders, the word 'pothujjaniko' (of the worldlings) was not used. However, regarding that devotion to sensual pleasure, some who claimed to be monks and held the view of Nibbāna in this very life (diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna-vāda) said, 'Friends, indeed, when...'
216: "Friends, this self is fully provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure and enjoys itself; to this extent, friends, this self has attained Nibbāna in the present life" (as held in the Dīgha Nikāya). Because of holding this view, and for the sake of protecting their minds, and because the undertaking of that Dhamma is pleasant in the present, it was not called "suffering." The devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) should not be pursued because it is a pleasure defiled by craving and wrong view in the present, because it has suffering as its result in the future, and because those devoted to it are bound by the fetters of craving and wrong view. The devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) also should not be pursued because it is suffering defiled by wrong view in the present, because it has suffering as its result in the future, and because those devoted to it are bound by the fetters of wrong view. "Ete kho" refers to those two extremes. "Anupagamma" means without approaching (those two extremes). "Majjhimā" is called the middle way because it exists in the middle, being free from defiled pleasure and pain. It is called "paṭipadā" (way/practice) because it leads to Nibbāna through that very practice. It is called "abhisambuddhā" because it is fully and perfectly realized. Among the terms beginning with "cakkhukaraṇī," it is called "cakkhukaraṇī" because it gives rise to the eye of wisdom. "Ñāṇakaraṇī" is just a synonym for that "cakkhukaraṇī." It is said: "upasumāya" for the subsiding of defilements; "abhiññāya" for the direct knowledge of the Four Noble Truths; "sambodhāya" for the full awakening to those same truths; "nibbānāya" for the realization of Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is called "cakkhukaraṇī" because it produces the knowledge of the path of seeing (dassanamagga-ñāṇa), and "ñāṇakaraṇī" because it produces the knowledge of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmagga-ñāṇa). It is for the subsiding of all defilements, for the direct knowledge of all dhammas, for the awakening to the fruit of arahantship, and for the extinguishing (Nibbāna) of defilements and the aggregates. The discourse concerning the truths has already been taught in the Abhiññeyyaniddesa. Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the truths and having heard the sequence of realization of those five (monks) who held him in great esteem, established them in the practice by instilling esteem for the practice. Seeing their realization of the truths, he showed his own sequence of realization of the truths, starting with: "Bhikkhus, this is the noble truth of suffering." In that Pali text, "ananussutesu" means in things not heard from others (known by oneself). The meaning of the terms beginning with "cakkhu" will be made clear later. The seeing and realization of the four truths as "This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, this is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering" occurs in the stage of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi). The realization through cultivation of the four truths as "It should be fully understood, it should be abandoned, it should be realized, it should be developed" also occurs in the stage of the trainee. The reviewing of the four truths as "It has been fully understood, it has been abandoned, it has been realized, it has been developed" occurs in the stage of the beyond-trainee (asekkhabhūmi). "Tiparivaṭṭaṃ" means having three rounds, because there are three rounds in that knowledge by way of the three rounds called knowledge of the truth (sacca-ñāṇa), knowledge of the task (kicca-ñāṇa), and knowledge of what has been done (kata-ñāṇa). Herein (among the four noble truths), "This is suffering, this is..."
217:
“This is the noble truth of suffering, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, this is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering”—thus, the knowledge that knows these Four Noble Truths as they really are is called Sacca-ñāṇa (knowledge of the truth). Within those same Four Noble Truths, the knowledge of knowing the tasks to be performed as “should be fully understood, should be abandoned, should be realized, should be developed” is called Kicca-ñāṇa (knowledge of the task). The knowledge of knowing the completion of those tasks as “has been fully understood, has been abandoned, has been realized, has been developed” is called Kata-ñāṇa (knowledge of completion). “Dvādasākāraṃ” (twelvefold aspect) means having twelve aspects based on the three aspects (Sacca-ñāṇa, Kicca-ñāṇa, Kata-ñāṇa) for each of the Four Noble Truths. “Ñāṇadassanaṃ” (knowledge and vision) is the vision known as knowledge that arises by way of these three rounds (parivaṭṭa) and twelve aspects.

“Attamanā” means they were delighted in their own minds. Since beings desire happiness and loathe suffering, a mind associated with rapture and joy is called “one's own mind” (sakamana). It means “Attamanā” because the mind is seized by rapture and joy, or because they pervade the mind. “Abhinandu” means they rejoiced, being face-to-face [with the teaching]. “Veyyākaraṇe” means in the Sutta. A Sutta without verses is called a Veyyākaraṇa (exposition) because it purely explains the meaning. “Bhaññamāne” means while being preached. The present tense (the suffix māna) is used to denote the immediate past, thus it means “after it had been preached.” “Virajaṃ” means being free from the dust of passion and so forth. “Vītamalaṃ” means being free from the stain of passion and so forth. Passions and the like are called “dust” (raja) in the sense of overwhelming, and “stain” (mala) in the sense of corrupting. “Dhamma-cakkhu” (the Dhamma-eye) refers in some places to the knowledge of the first path, in some places to the first three path-knowledges, and in some places even to the fourth path-knowledge. However, here it refers only to the knowledge of the first path (Sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa). The meaning is that the Dhamma-eye arose through the power of insight (vipassanā) in this manner: “Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.”

“Dhamma-cakke” refers to both the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). For the Blessed One seated at the throne of enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka), the twelvefold knowledge of penetration into the Four Noble Truths is the Dhamma-cakka. For the Blessed One seated at Isipatana, the knowledge of teaching that sets in motion the twelvefold teaching of the truths is also the Dhamma-cakka. Both of these are simply the knowledge that arose in the Possessor of the Ten Powers (Dasabala). By the Blessed One manifesting that knowledge through this discourse, it is said that the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion. Furthermore, as long as the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña, along with eighteen crores of Brahmas, had not yet become established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), the Blessed One is said to be “setting it in motion” (pavatteti). Only after they were established [in the fruit] is it said to be “set in motion” (pavattitaṃ). Referring to that establishment, it was said: “When the Wheel of Dhamma had been set in motion by the Blessed One.”

“Bhummā devā” refers to the earth-dwelling deities. “Saddamanussāvesuṃ” means that they raised a cry, giving a shout of approval (sādhu) all at once, saying, “This [Wheel of Dhamma] by the Blessed One...” and so forth.
218:
Appaṭivattiya means having the sense of being impossible to oppose or reverse by saying, “This Dhamma is not so.” The deities and Brahmas who had assembled for this teaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta uttered a cry of “Sādhu” (well done) all at once at the conclusion of the discourse. It should be understood that the deities such as the Bhummadevas (earth-dwelling deities) who did not attend the assembly also uttered “Sādhu” upon hearing the voices of those deities and Brahmas.

Among those deities, those who arise in mountains, trees, and so forth are called Bhummadevas. Although these deities are included within the class of the Cātumahārājika deities, they are mentioned separately in this Sutta. Cātumahārājika refers to the attendants of the four Great Kings known as Dhataraṭṭha, Virūḷhaka, Virūpakkha, and Kuvera. They reside in the middle of Mount Sineru. Among those deities, there are those who dwell on mountains and those who dwell in the sky. Their lineage extends as far as the Cakkavāḷa (world-system) mountains. The Khiḍḍāpadosika deities, Manopadosika deities, Sītavalāhaka deities, Uṇhavalāhaka deities, the young deity Candima, and the young deity Suriya—all of these are also residents of the Cātumahārājika deva world.

They are called Tāvatiṃsa because thirty-three individuals were reborn in that place. Alternatively, it is said that Tāvatiṃsa is simply the name of those deities. Among them, too, there are mountain-dwelling and sky-dwelling deities, and their lineage extends as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountains. The same applies to the Yāma deities and others. Indeed, even in a single deva world, there is no instance where the lineage of deities does not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountains. They are called Yāma because they have reached (yāta) divine happiness. They are called Tusita because they are exceedingly joyful and delighted. They are called Nimmānarati because, when they wish to enjoy themselves with objects superior to natural ones, they create (nimminitvā) their desired pleasures again and again and delight in them. They are called Paranimmitavasavatti because, knowing the intentions of others, they exercise control (vasaṃ vattenti) over the pleasures created by others. They are called Brahmakāyika because they are included in the Brahma group (Brahmakāya). Here, all Brahmas of the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra) are included.

To distinguish the phrase “tena khaṇena” (at that moment), it is said “tena muhuttena.” This refers to the moment known as a muhutta (an instant), not the ultimate moment (paramattha-khaṇa, consisting of arising, presence, and dissolution). “Yāva brahmalokā” means including the Brahma world (up to the Brahma world). “Saddo” refers to the sound of the “Sādhu” acclamation. “Dasasahassī” refers to the area encompassing ten thousand world-systems. “Saṅkampi” means shaking violently by rising upwards. “Sampakampi” means shaking violently by rising upwards and descending downwards. “Sampavedhi” means shaking violently in the four directions. 

When the Bodhisatta descended into his mother’s womb to attain Buddhahood, and when he emerged from that womb (was born), the great earth shook due to the power of his merit (puñña-teja). At the time of attaining Buddhahood, it shook due to the power of his penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). At the time of the Dhammacakkappavattana (the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma), the earth shook by the power of the deities, as if wanting to give a “Sādhu” acclamation due to the power of the Buddha’s knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). At the time of renouncing the life-force and at the Great Parinibbāna, it shook by the power of the deities, as if unable to endure the agitation of the mind due to compassion (karuṇā).

“Appamāṇo” means being immeasurable, like the measure of the Buddha. Regarding the word “uḷāra”—in contexts such as “uḷārāni khādanti,” uḷāra refers to an excellent taste. In contexts such as “uḷārāya vatthabhogāya namanti,” uḷāra refers to noble requisites. In the context where the Brahmin Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with “noble praise,” uḷāra refers to the highest quality. In this context, however, uḷāra means extensive (vipula). “Obhāso” refers to the radiance produced by the power of the teaching-knowledge or by the power of the deities. “Loke” means in the ten thousand world-systems. “Atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ” means surpassing the divine power of the deities. The divine power of the deities refers to the radiance of their garments, their physical aura, the radiance of their ornaments, and the radiance of their mansions, which extends for twelve leagues. It means that this radiance appeared only by surpassing that divine power of the deities. “Udānaṃ” refers to an utterance inspired by joyful knowledge (somanassa-ñāṇa). “Udānesi” means he uttered. This inspired utterance, “Aññāsi vata bho Koṇḍañño,” also spread throughout the ten thousand world-elements. “Aññāsikoṇḍañño” means Koṇḍañña who has understood perfectly.

In the explanation of “cakkhu” and so forth, it should be understood as “in the sense of seeing” (dassanaṭṭhena) and so on. A single knowledge is called “cakkhu” (eye) because it performs the function of seeing the Truths that are to be known, like a physical eye. It is called “ñāṇa” (knowledge) because it performs the function of knowing. It is called “paññā” (wisdom) because it performs the function of knowing in various ways. It is called “vijjā” (true knowledge) because it performs the function of absolute penetration.
219:
The earth shook by the power of the deities, as if unable to endure the agitation of the mind caused by the task of compassion. 'Appamāṇa' means having the measure of great activity. Regarding the term 'uḷāra', in passages such as 'uḷārāni uḷārāni khādanīyāni khādanti', 'uḷāra' means a delicious taste. In passages such as 'uḷārāya vatthabhogāya cittaṃ na namati', 'uḷāra' means excellent requisites. In passages such as 'uḷārāya khalu bhavaṃ vacchāyano samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pasaṃsāya pasaṃsati', 'uḷāra' means the best. In this context, however, 'uḷāra' means pervasive. 'Obhāsa' is the radiance that arises due to the power of the knowledge of teaching and the power of the deities. 'Loka' refers only to the ten thousand world systems. 'Surpassing the power of the deities' means that while the radiance of the deities' clothing, bodies, ornaments, and mansions spreads up to twelve yojanas, this [radiance] surpasses even that power of the deities. 'Udāna' (inspired utterance) is the sound uttered with knowledge accompanied by joy (somanassa). 'He uttered an inspired utterance' means he spoke it out. The sound of this inspired utterance, 'Friends, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood,' spread throughout the ten thousand world systems. 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña' means Koṇḍañña who has understood thoroughly.

In explaining 'eye' (cakkhu) and so on, in the sense of 'seeing' and so forth, a single knowledge is called 'eye' (cakkhu) because it performs the function of seeing the truth to be known, just like the physical eye. It is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) because it performs the function of knowing; 'wisdom' (paññā) because it performs the function of knowing in various ways; 'true knowledge' (vijjā) because it performs the function of penetrating without remainder; and 'light' (āloka) because it performs the function of illuminating in every way. In 'cakkhu dhammo' and so on, the single knowledge is described in five ways due to the difference in functions. 'Ārammaṇa' is in the sense of supporting. 'Gocara' is in the sense of the objective field (visaya). The function of knowledge is stated in five ways, starting with 'in the sense of seeing'. In this way, in each of the three turns (vāra), there are five each, making 15 dhammas, 15 meanings (attha), and 30 linguistic expressions (nirutti) (in the 15 dhammas and 15 atthas), totaling 60 knowledges to be understood. The same method applies to the remaining Noble Truths. Among the four Noble Truths, by way of 15 dhammas and 15 atthas for each, there are 60 dhammas and 60 atthas. In those 60 dhammas and 60 atthas, there are 120 niruttis, making a total of 240 knowledges to be understood.
220:
## 2-3. Satipaṭṭhānavārādivaṇṇanā
31-32. In the explanation of analytical knowledge (Paṭisambhidāniddesa) preceded by the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, and in the Paṭisambhidāniddesa preceded by the Iddhipāda Sutta, the meaning (attha) and the count (gaṇanā) should be understood in this same way.

## 4-8. Sattabodhisattavārādivaṇṇanā
33-37. In the Mahāpadāna Suttas of the seven Bodhisattas such as Vipassī, in each [case], there are five dhammas such as the eye in the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) and five in the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca), making ten dhammas. There are five meanings (attha) such as the sense of seeing in the Truth of the Origin and five in the Truth of Cessation, making ten meanings. By way of those ten dhammas and ten meanings, there are twenty linguistic expressions (nirutti) and forty knowledges of analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa). The count stated by combining the seven Buddhas is easily understood.

In the Paṭisambhidāniddesa taught by the power of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), in the section with each root such as things to be known by higher knowledge (abhiññeyyaṭṭha), among these five statements: "It is known by wisdom, seen, understood, realized, and touched," in each one, by way of the five groups of five dhammas such as the eye and five meanings such as the sense of seeing, there are 25 dhammas, 25 meanings, 50 niruttis (double the number), and 100 knowledges (double that number) to be understood.

In the section taught by combining the five terms: abhiññeyya, pariññeyya, pahānāya, bhāvanāya, and sacchikiriya, by doing it five times, there are 125 dhammas, 125 meanings, 250 niruttis (double the number), and 500 knowledges (double that number) to be understood. Here, 'aḍḍhateyyāni' means two hundred and fifty. The same method applies to the aggregates (khandha) and so on. In this way, the counting of dhammas and so forth in the Saccavāra and Paṭisambhidāvāra should be understood.

## 9. Chabuddhadhammavāravaṇṇanā
In the section on the Buddha-dhammas, 'diyaḍḍhasataṃ' means one hundred and fifty, obtained by taking twenty-five six times. There are 300 niruttis (double that) and 600 knowledges (double that). 'Paṭisambhidādhikaraṇe' means in the context where analytical knowledge is the primary focus. 'Aḍḍhanavadhammasatāni' (eight hundred and fifty) means: 60 dhammas in the four Truths taught first, 60 in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), 60 in the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), 70 in the explanations (veyyākaraṇa) of the seven Buddhas, 125 in the five categories such as the sense of higher knowledge (abhiññaṭṭha), 125 in the five categories such as the sense of aggregates (khandhaṭṭha), then 100 in the four Noble Truths, 100 in the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and 150 in the six Buddha-dhammas; thus there are 850 dhammas. Similarly, there are also 850 meanings (attha).

In this same way, in the three categories of Truths, Satipaṭṭhāna, and Sammappadhāna, there are 120 niruttis each; in the seven veyyākaraṇas, there are 140 niruttis; and in the categories such as abhiññaṭṭha and khandhaṭṭha...
221:
There are two hundred and fifty linguistic analyses (nirutti) each [in two categories]; in the Noble Truths and in the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), there are two hundred linguistic analyses each; and in the Buddha-dhammas, there are three hundred linguistic analyses. Thus, there are one thousand and seven hundred (1,700) linguistic analyses. Similarly, in the three bases such as the Truths, there are two hundred and forty knowledges (ñāṇa) each; in the seven expositions (veyyākaraṇa), there are two hundred and eighty knowledges; in the bases of direct knowledge (abhiññā) and the bases of the aggregates (khandha), there are five hundred knowledges each; in the Truths and in the analytical knowledges, there are four hundred knowledges each; and in the Buddha-dhammas, there are six hundred knowledges. Thus, there are three thousand and four hundred (3,400) knowledges.

## The Explanation of the Patisambhidākathā is finished.

## 7. Dhammacakkakathā

## 1. Saccavāravaṇṇanā

Once again, I shall explain the meanings not yet discussed in the Dhammacakkakathā, which is taught by taking the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta as the precursor. In that Dhammacakkakathā, 'dukkhavatthukā' means that for those five states and five meanings, the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) is the basis by virtue of simultaneous penetration (ekābhisamaya). Distinguishing that very truth of suffering by the power of the four truths, [the Teacher] said 'saccavatthukā' and so on. Among those terms such as 'saccavatthukā', they are called 'saccārammaṇā' because truth is the supporting object for those states. They are called 'saccagocarā' because truth is the range or domain for those states. 'Saccasaṅgahitā' means they are included within the truth of the path (magga-sacca). 'Saccapariyāpannā' means they are contained within the truth of the path. 'Sacce samudāgatā' means they have well-arisen in the truth of suffering through the full understanding of suffering. Likewise, they are established and firmly established in that very truth of suffering.

Now, wishing to point out the Wheel of Dhamma mentioned as 'when the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion by the Blessed One,' [the Teacher] said 'dhammacakkanti' and so on. That Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the Wheel of Dhamma as realization (paṭivedhadhammacakka) and the Wheel of Dhamma as teaching (desanādhammacakka). The Wheel of Dhamma as realization occurs at the seat of enlightenment (bodhi-pallaṅka); the Wheel of Dhamma as teaching occurs at Isipatana. By the Pali 'He sets in motion the Dhamma and the Wheel,' the Wheel of Dhamma as realization is intended. By the Pali 'He sets in motion the Wheel and the Dhamma,' the Wheel of Dhamma as teaching is intended. How? For the Blessed One, seated at the seat of enlightenment, at the moment of the path, sets in motion the Dhamma which is divided into faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), path factors (maggaṅga), and so on. That very Dhamma is like a striking-wheel (paharaṇacakka) because it proceeds for the purpose of destroying the enemy of defilements (kilesa) in one's own continuity; therefore, it is called a 'wheel.' The Blessed One, who brings about the path-dhamma, is said to set that wheel in motion. By this first Pali, the meaning of the Kammadhāraya compound is taught, signifying that the Dhamma itself is the wheel. For the Blessed One seated at Isipatana, at the moment of teaching the Dhamma, He sets in motion the wheel of teaching (desanācakka) which is like a striking-wheel because it proceeds for the purpose of destroying the enemy of defilements in the continuity of those to be led (veneyya). In the continuity of those to be led...
222:
...likewise, [He sets in motion] the wheel. Only when the Blessed One brings about the Dhamma is He said to set that wheel in motion. By this, the status of a Kammadhāraya compound is stated, meaning the Dhamma itself is the wheel. The Blessed One, dwelling at Isipatana, at the moment of teaching the Dhamma, sets in motion the wheel of teaching which is like a striking-wheel because it proceeds for the purpose of destroying the enemy of defilements in the continuity of those to be led; and He sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma which is divided into faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, and so on, in the continuity of those to be led. By this, the status of a Dvanda compound is stated, meaning 'the Dhamma and the wheel are the Dhammacakka.' However, since 'setting in motion' can only occur when there is a person who sets it in motion, it is said in all instances that 'He sets it in motion'; and it should be understood that it is called 'wheel' (cakka) in the sense of being set in motion. It should be understood that terms such as 'Dhammacakka' in the sense of 'setting in motion by means of the Dhamma' are spoken with reference only to the Wheel of Dhamma as teaching.

Among those terms, 'setting in motion by means of the Dhamma' means it is called 'Dhammacakka' because it is a wheel set in motion by the Dhamma in accordance with its true nature. 'Setting in motion by the practice of Dhamma' means it is called 'Dhammacakka' because it is a wheel set in motion for the benefit of the Dhamma in the continuity of those to be led. By terms such as 'He is established in the Dhamma,' the Blessed One's state of having become Dhamma (dhamma-bhūta) and His being the Lord of Dhamma (dhamma-ssāmī) are stated. Thus it was said: 'Friends, that Blessed One knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen; He has become vision, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma; He is the sayer, the proclaimer, the bringer out of meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata.' Therefore, by those terms, it is called 'Dhammacakka' because it is the wheel of the Lord of Dhamma. 'Established' (ṭhito) means established by way of being an object. 'Firmly established' (patiṭṭhito) means established in an unshakeable manner. 'Vasippatto' means having attained mastery. 'Pāramippatto' means having reached the summit. 'Vesārajjappatto' means having attained fearlessness. By the words spoken with regard to the continuity of those to be led, such as 'He establishes them in the Dhamma,' it means the wheel exists because of His being the Lord of Dhamma and for the benefit of the Dhamma. By terms such as 'He honors the Dhamma,' it means the wheel exists for the benefit of the Dhamma. Whoever sets the Dhamma in motion by way of honoring it and so on, is said to bring about the benefit of the Dhamma. 'He honors the Dhamma' means He acts so that the Dhamma is well-performed. 'He respects the Dhamma' means He treats it as weighty because of the arising of reverence for that Dhamma. 'He reveres the Dhamma' means He dwells making the Dhamma dear and venerable. 'He worships the Dhamma' means He performs worship by way of teaching and practice with reference to that Dhamma. 'He venerates the Dhamma' means He acts with humility through honoring and respecting that very Dhamma. 'He has the Dhamma as His banner, the Dhamma as His standard' means He has the Dhamma as His banner because He proceeds by placing the Dhamma in front like a banner and raising it up like a standard.
223:
It means having the Dhamma as its banner. He is called Dhammādhipateyya (one who has the Dhamma as his sovereign) because he acts with the Dhamma as the supreme authority, and because he performs all actions solely through the power of the Dhamma of mental development (bhāvanā-dhamma). That Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) is said to be of unobstructed progress because no one can turn it back. Therefore, it is called a 'Wheel' (cakka) in the sense of setting the Dhamma in motion.

The faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is a Dhamma; 'he sets that Dhamma in motion' means that by giving rise to the faculty of faith associated with the Path in the mental continuities of those to be guided (veneyya), he sets that faculty of faith in motion. The same method applies to the remaining factors. 'Truths' (sacca) refer to the knowledges of the truths (sacca-ñāṇa). Insight (vipassanā) and clear vision (vijjā) are indeed Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). 'Knowledge of non-arising' (anuppāda-ñāṇa) is the knowledge in the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). He also sets that knowledge in motion in the mental continuities of those to be guided; indeed, by causing the realization of Nibbāna, he is said to set it in motion.

In the sections on the Origin (Samudaya-vāra) and so forth, the text is abbreviated by showing specific terms such as the object of origin (samudaya-vatthu), the object of cessation (nirodha-vatthu), and the object of the path (magga-vatthu). Here too, it should be understood according to the method previously mentioned.

## 2-3. Explanation of the Section on the Foundations of Mindfulness, etc.

41-42. The sections beginning with the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna) and the Bases of Power (Iddhipāda) are also taught by way of the Path-moment. These sections are also abbreviated by showing specific terms in their respective places.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Wheel of Dhamma is Finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Discourse on the Supramundane

Now, I shall explain the meanings not yet discussed in the Discourse on the Supramundane (Lokuttara-kathā), which was taught immediately after the Discourse on the Wheel of Dhamma containing supramundane states. Therein, the meaning of the term 'supramundane' (lokuttara) will become clear in the Section of Exposition (Niddesa-vāra). The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), such as the four foundations of mindfulness, are associated with the Path and Fruition as appropriate. They are called 'factors of enlightenment' (bodhipakkhiya) because they belong to the side (pakkha) of the Noble Path, which is named 'enlightenment' (bodhi) in the sense of knowing. 'Belonging to the side' means existing in a state of being helpful. It is called 'establishment' (upaṭṭhāna) because of entering into and plunging into those objects such as the body; mindfulness itself is the establishment, thus it is 'foundation of mindfulness' (satipaṭṭhāna). It is divided into four types because of the mode of grasping the body, feelings, mind, and mental objects as unattractive, suffering, impermanent, and non-self, and because of accomplishing the task of abandoning the perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. Therefore, they are called the 'four foundations of mindfulness' (cattāro satipaṭṭhānā).
224:
It is called 'effort' (padhāna) because one strives by means of this energy. It is 'right effort' (sammappadhāna) because it is a beautiful striving. Alternatively, it is 'right effort' because one strives well by means of this energy. That energy is beautiful and called 'right effort' because it is free from the distorted modes of defilements, because it brings about the state of excellence by way of producing welfare and happiness, or because it creates the state of being foremost. This is a designation for energy (viriya). It is of four types because it accomplishes the tasks of abandoning and preventing the arising of arisen and unarisen unwholesome states, and the tasks of arising and maintaining unarisen and arisen wholesome states. Therefore, they are called the 'four right efforts' (cattāro sammappadhānā).

It is called 'success' (iddhi) in the sense of being accomplished through the manner of completion, or by the figurative sense that 'by this, beings succeed, prosper, and reach excellence.' It is called the 'base of success' (iddhipāda) because it is associated with that success, because it acts as the precursor to the success which is the fruit, and because it is the cause in the preliminary stage. That base of success is of four types by way of desire (chanda), energy (viriya), consciousness (citta), and investigation (vīmaṃsā). Therefore, they are called the 'four bases of power' (cattāro iddhipādā).

They are called 'faculties' (indriya) in the sense of sovereignty, known as overcoming, because they overcome lack of faith, laziness, negligence, distraction, and delusion. They are called 'powers' (bala) in the sense of being unshakable because they cannot be overcome by lack of faith and so forth. Both of these are of five types by way of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, they are called the 'five faculties' (pañcindriyāni) and the 'five powers' (pañca balāni). The seven factors beginning with mindfulness are 'factors of enlightenment' (bojjhaṅga) because they are the components of a being who is awakening. The eight factors beginning with right view are 'path factors' (maggaṅga) in the sense of leading out [from saṃsāra]. Therefore, it is said: 'the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path.'

Thus, when these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment occur in mundane insight (lokiya-vipassanā) in the preliminary stage: for one who grasps the body in fourteen ways, there is the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna); for one who grasps feelings in nine ways, there is the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna); for one who grasps the mind in sixteen ways, there is the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna); for one who grasps mental objects in five ways, there is the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of mental objects (dhammānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna).

Thus, when one sees an unwholesome state that has arisen in another, which has never arisen in this individual existence (attabhāva), and strives so that it will not arise, thinking: 'That unwholesome state arose because that person practiced in such a way; I will not practice in that way; thus, this will not arise in me,' that is the first right effort. When one sees an unwholesome state that frequently occurs in one's own continuity and strives to abandon it, that is the second right effort. For one who strives to give rise to jhāna or insight that has never arisen before in this individual existence, that is the third right effort. For one who repeatedly gives rise to arisen jhāna or insight so that they do not decline, that is the fourth right effort. When one gives rise to wholesome states by making desire the leader, it is the base of power of desire (chandiddhipāda). When one gives rise to wholesome states by making energy, consciousness, or investigation the leader, it is the base of power of investigation (vīmaṃsiddhipāda). When one abstains from wrong speech...
225:
When abstaining from wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood, Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are obtained in various consciousnesses. However, at the moment of the four paths, they are obtained in a single consciousness. At the moment of fruition, the remaining thirty-three factors of enlightenment are obtained, excluding the four right efforts.

Among these factors obtained in a single consciousness, mindfulness (sati) alone, which takes Nibbāna as its object, is called the "four foundations of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna) because it accomplishes the task of abandoning the perception of beauty (subhasaññā) and so forth in the body and other objects. Similarly, energy (viriya) alone is called the "four right efforts" (sammappadhāna) because it accomplishes tasks such as preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states. In the remaining five groups (bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and path factors), there is no decrease or increase in name.

Alternatively, among those factors:
Nine factors are of a single kind,
One factor is of two kinds, one is of four, one is of five,
One is of eight, and one is of nine kinds;
Thus, they exist in six ways.

"Nine factors are of a single kind" means that these nine—desire (chanda), consciousness (citta), joy (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), equanimity (upekkhā), thought (saṅkappa), speech (vācā), action (kammanta), and livelihood (ājīva)—exist only in one way by way of the bases of power (iddhipāda) and so forth, and do not belong to other groups. "One factor is of two kinds" means that faith (saddhā) exists in two ways by way of faculty (indriya) and power (bala). "One factor is of four kinds, one is of five kinds" means another single factor exists in four ways, and another in five ways. Therein, the single mental factor of concentration (samādhi) exists in four ways by way of faculty, power, factor of awakening, and path factor. Wisdom (paññā) exists in five ways by way of those four and the group of bases of power. "One factor is of eight kinds, one is of nine kinds" means another single factor exists in eight ways, and another in nine ways. Mindfulness (sati) exists in eight ways by way of the four foundations of mindfulness, faculty, power, factor of awakening, and path factor; and energy (viriya) exists in nine ways by way of the four right efforts, bases of power, faculty, power, factor of awakening, and path factor. Thus:

The factors of enlightenment are only fourteen in terms of distinct ultimate realities,
Seven by way of groups, and thirty-seven by way of classification.
Because they accomplish their respective tasks and exist as ultimate realities,
All these factors of enlightenment arise when the Noble Path arises.

After showing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment associated with the paths and fruits in this way, they are again summarized within the paths and fruits as the four Noble Paths and the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). The state of a recluse is called "sāmañña," which is a name for the four Noble Paths. The fruits of those "sāmañña" (paths) are called "sāmaññaphala." Nibbāna, however, is entirely unmixed with all other states. Thus, by way of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna in detail...
226:
There are forty-six supramundane states (by way of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna). Briefly, there are nine supramundane states by way of the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna. Even more briefly, there are three supramundane states by way of path, fruit, and Nibbāna. When the supramundane nature of the foundations of mindfulness and the paths and fruits is mentioned, the supramundane nature of associated factors such as contact (phassa) is also implicitly stated. However, only the foundations of mindfulness and so forth are mentioned by way of being the predominant states. In the Abhidhamma's description of supramundane states (Lokuttaradhamma-niddesa), the supramundane nature of contact and other factors associated with the paths and fruits is also stated.

"They cross the world" (lokam taranti) means they transcend the world. All such present-tense terms here are spoken with reference to the four Noble Paths. Indeed, the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) crosses the world of woeful states (apāya-loka); the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga) crosses a portion of the sense-sphere world (kāmāvacara-loka); the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) crosses the sense-sphere world; and the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga) crosses the fine-material and immaterial worlds (rūpārūpāvacara-loka). "They emerge from the world" (lokā uttarantī) means they rise above the world. The terms "lokato" and "lokamhā" are shown as variations of the same ablative case (nissakka-vacana) for the word "lokā." "They completely transcend the world" (lokam samatikkamanti) has the same meaning as previously stated. In the first term, it was stated without considering the meaning of the prefix "sam-"; here, it is stated together with the meaning of the prefix. "Those who have completely transcended the world" (lokam samatikkantā) means those who have properly transcended the aforementioned world. All such past-tense terms here are spoken with reference to the fruits and Nibbāna. This is because the fruit of stream-entry and so forth stand having transcended the aforementioned world, and Nibbāna always stands having transcended the entire world. "They are superior to the world" (lokena atirekā) means they have become greater than the world. This is spoken with reference to all supramundane states. "They depart" (nissaranti) means they go out. "Departed" (nissaṭā) means those who have gone out. The eighteen expressions such as "they do not stay in the world" apply to all supramundane states. "They do not stay" is said because they are unincluded (apariyāpanna) in the world. "They are not smeared in the world" means that even while occurring in the continuum of the aggregates, they are not smeared in that world. "They are not smeared by the world" means they are not smeared by any mind of those who have not realized the truths, nor by any unwholesome or even slight mind of those who have realized the truths. "Asaṃlittā" and "anupalittā" are distinguished by prefixes. 

"Vippamuttā" (fully released) is the same as the state of being unsmeared, but distinguished by different syllables (words). Indeed, whatever states are unsmeared in or by anything, they are fully released in or by that. The three terms beginning with "lokā vippamuttā" are stated by way of the ablative case (nissakka-vasa). "Visaññuttā" (disconnected) is a qualification of the state of being fully released. Indeed, whatever states are fully released in, with, or from any world, those states...
227:
In that world, they are called 'disconnected' (visaññutta) by that and from that. "They are purified from the world" means they are purified from the world by washing away the stain of the world. "They are distinctly purified" (visujjhanti) is the same purification distinguished by the prefix 'vi-'. "They emerge" (vuṭṭhahanti) means they have arisen. "They turn away" (vivaṭṭanti) means they revolve back. "They do not cling" means they do not adhere. "They are not grasped" means they are not taken up with attachment. "They are not bound" means they are not obstructed. "They completely cut off" means they bring about non-occurrence. Just as it is said "because of completely cutting off the world," so too it is said "because of being purified from the world," and so on. "They tranquilize" (paṭippassambhenti) means they cause to cease. The four terms starting with 'apatha' are applicable to all supramundane states. "Apatha" means they are not a path. "Agati" means they have no standing place. "Avisaya" means they are not within the domain. "Asādhāraṇa" means they are not common (unequal). "They vomit" means they eject. "They do not vomit back" is said by way of the opposite of the aforementioned; the meaning is that they do not eat again what has been vomited. By this, the state of having well-vomited the world is stated. The same method applies to the next three dyads. "Visīnenti" means they scatter or release; the meaning is that they do not bind. "Na ussīnenti" means they do not scatter or release. The reading "visinenti" and "na ussinenti" with short vowels is good. "Vidhūpenti" means they extinguish. "Na saṃdhūpenti" means they do not burn. "Transcending the world, they stand overcoming it" means all supramundane states (lokuttara dhammā) are called 'supramundane' because they stand having well transcended and overcome the world. By all these aforementioned ways, the state of supramundane states being beyond the world and superior to the world is stated.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Supramundane is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Discourse on Powers (Balakathā-vaṇṇanā)

Now, following the Discourse on the Supramundane, I shall explain the meaning not yet mentioned in the Discourse on Powers, which contains supramundane talk and is preceded by the Suttanta. In that Discourse on Powers, having first shown the five powers by way of the Suttanta, the Teacher said "Furthermore, there are sixty-eight powers," etc., wishing to show other powers as well. All these sixty-eight are called 'powers' (bala) because they are unshakable by their respective opposites. In the passage starting with 'hiri-bala' (the power of shame), 'hiri' is that by which one is ashamed of evil; this is a name for shame (lajjā). 'Ottappa' is that by which one is afraid of evil; this is a name for the dread of evil. Shame (hiri) is a state arising from within; dread (ottappa) is a state arising from without. Shame (hiri) has oneself as the dominant factor; dread (ottappa) has the world as the dominant factor...
228:
Ottappa is so called because it is the state of being terrified of faults. The state established in the nature of shame is hiri, and the state established in the nature of fear is ottappa. Hiri has the characteristic of respect and humility, while ottappa has the characteristic of seeing danger in faults. That same hiri is called the power of shame (hiri-bala) because it is unshakable by shamelessness (ahirika). That same ottappa is called the power of moral dread (ottappa-bala) because it is unshakable by fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa). It is called the power of reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna-bala) because it is unshakable by non-reflection (appaṭisaṅkhāna); this is a name for investigative wisdom (upaparikkhana-paññā). The strength that arises for one who develops the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) led by energy (vīriya) is called the power of development (bhāvanā-bala); it is also a name for the four mental aggregates (nāma-kkhandha) occurring in that manner. Pure virtue and so forth are called the power of blamelessness (anavajja-bala). The four bases of sympathy are called the power of sympathy (saṅgaha-bala). There is also a variant reading, 'saṅgahe balaṃ'. Enduring suffering is called the power of patience (khanti-bala). Pleasing others with Dhamma talk is called the power of designation (paññatti-bala). Causing the attainment of the learned meaning is called the power of conviction (nijjhatti-bala). Abundance in wholesome states is called the power of sovereignty (issariya-bala). Establishing oneself as desired in wholesome states is called the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-bala). The meanings of the power of shame and so forth are taught by selecting what is particularly appropriate according to the syllables in the mātikā terms. The power of serenity (samatha-bala) and the power of insight (vipassanā-bala) are simply serenity and insight that have reached the state of power.

In the Mātikā-niddesa, after stating the meaning of the primary power as the power of faith (saddhā-bala) because it is unshakable by lack of faith (assaddhiya), the Buddha further demonstrated that same power of faith by distinguishing it through nine other ways. When a certain state is unshakable and has reached the state of power, it supports conascent (sahajāta) states; it exhausts the defilements (kilesa) that are its opposites; it purifies virtue (sīla) and view (diṭṭhi), which are the beginning of penetration (paṭivedha); it establishes the mind on the object (ārammaṇa); it makes the mind radiant and pure; it leads to mastery (vasi) and causes the attainment of distinction; it leads to higher states and causes penetration by the higher path; it leads sequentially to the Noble Path (ariya-magga) and causes the realization of the Four Truths; and by reaching fruition (phala), it establishes one in cessation (nirodha [Nibbāna]). Therefore, the meaning of 'power' is distinguished in nine ways. This method also applies to the four powers such as the power of energy (vīriya-bala).

"Being ashamed of sensual desire (kāmacchanda)" means that a practitioner (yogī) endowed with renunciation (nekkhamma [jhana]) is ashamed of sensual desire through renunciation. The same method applies to moral dread (ottappa). By these terms, hiri and ottappa, being ashamed of and dreading all unwholesome states is intended. The meaning of terms such as ill-will (byāpāda) should also be understood in this way. 'Paṭisaṅkhāti' means investigating in terms of danger without delusion. 'Bhāveti' means to increase or develop. 'Vajja' refers to faults such as lust (rāga). 'Saṅgaṇhāti' means to bind or collect. 'Khamati' means it is pleasing or agreeable to that practitioner. 'Paññāpeti' means to please. 'Nijjhāpeti' means to make one reflect. 'Vasaṃ vatteti' means being a master over the mind and making the mind follow one's will. 'Vidahati' means to arrange and establish. All powers such as the power of development are indeed renunciation and so forth. In the commentary on the mātikā, it was taught by the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, through reasons other than the meaning taught in the Niddesa. However, it should be understood that in the Niddesa, since the meaning of the mātikā terms was already clear through the syllables, Venerable Sāriputta did not teach them separately but taught only the jhanas. After explaining the power of serenity and the power of insight in detail, finally, the passage beginning with "unshakable by defilements associated with restlessness (uddhacca)" was taught to show the characteristics of the power of serenity and the power of insight.

Regarding the power of the trainee (sekha-bala) and the power of the non-trainee (asekha-bala), the phrase "sammā-diṭṭhiṃ sikkhatīti sekhabalaṃ" means that a trainee is called 'sekha' because he trains in Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi), and that Right View is called the power of the trainee because it is the strength of that trainee. The phrase "tattha sikkhitattā asekhabalaṃ" means that an Arahant is called 'asekha' because he has already trained in that Right View and does not need to train further; that same Right View associated with the fruition of Arahantship is called the power of the non-trainee because it is the strength of that Arahant. The same method applies to Right Thought (sammā-saṅkappa) and so forth. Right Knowledge (sammā-ñāṇa) refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). That reviewing knowledge can also be mundane; it is taught that if it arises in a trainee, it is called the power of the trainee, and if it arises in an Arahant, it is called the power of the non-trainee. Right Liberation (sammā-vimutti) refers to the remaining eight path factors...
229:
He makes it occur according to his own will. 'Adhiṭṭhāti' means he establishes (arranges). All powers such as the power of development (bhāvanā-bala) and so forth are indeed renunciation (nekkhamma) and so forth. In the explanation of the Matika, it is taught by other means; however, it should be understood that because the meaning is clear through the phrasing itself, it is not taught separately in this exposition (niddesa). Having explained the power of serenity (samatha-bala) and the power of insight (vipassanā-bala) in detail, at the end, it is taught to show the characteristics of the power of serenity and the power of insight by such phrases as 'he is not shaken by the defilements associated with restlessness (uddhacca) and the aggregates,' and 'he is not shaken by the defilements associated with ignorance (avijjā) and the aggregates.'

Regarding the power of a trainee (sekha-bala) and the power of one beyond training (asekha-bala), the phrase 'he trains in Right View' refers to the power of a trainee. A trainee (sekha) is so called because he trains in Right View; that Right View is the power of that trainee, thus it is called 'sekha-bala.' It is called the power of one beyond training because he has already trained in that Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). An Arahant is called 'asekha' (one beyond training) because, having already trained in Right View in that Path of Arahantship, he does not need to train further; that same Right View is the power of that Arahant, thus it is called 'asekha-bala.' The same method applies to Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa) and the others. 'Right Knowledge' (sammā-ñāṇa) refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). Even though that reviewing knowledge is mundane (lokiya), it is called 'sekha-bala' when it occurs in a trainee and 'asekha-bala' when it occurs in an Arahant. 'Right Liberation' (sammā-vimutti) refers to the remaining states associated with fruition (phala), excluding the eight path factors. However, some teachers say, 'Excluding supramundane liberation (lokuttara-vimutti), the remaining liberations are called Right Liberation.' The way it becomes the power of a trainee or one beyond training is the same as previously mentioned.

Regarding the powers of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava-bala), all the powers of knowledge are indeed powers of knowledge. In the phrase 'khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno,' the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; it means 'by the monk whose taints are destroyed.' 'As impermanent' (aniccato) means being impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. 'As it really is' (yathābhūta) means according to its true nature. 'By wisdom' (paññāya) means by the path-wisdom (magga-paññā) together with insight. When things are well seen as impermanent, they are also well seen as suffering (dukkha) and non-self (anatta) because they are rooted in that impermanence. The word 'yaṃ' is a neuter term used as an adverb, or it means 'for which reason.' 'Agamma' means depending on (paticca). 'Paṭijānāti' means he acknowledges or makes a claim. 'Aṅgārakāsūpamā' means they are compared to a pit of glowing coals because of the sense of intense burning. 'Sensual pleasures' (kāmā) refers to both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma).

'Inclines towards seclusion' means inclining towards Nibbāna, known as seclusion from the bases of existence (upadhi-viveka), by the power of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). There are three kinds of seclusion: physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from the bases of existence (upadhi-viveka). Physical seclusion occurs for those who are secluded from the group and delight in renunciation. Mental seclusion occurs for those devoted to the higher mind (concentration). Seclusion from the bases of existence occurs for those persons who have reached Nibbāna, where the bases of defilement are stilled. Alternatively, it means inclining towards Nibbāna, known as seclusion as escape (nissaraṇa-viveka). There are five kinds of seclusion: seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka), seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-viveka), seclusion by eradication (samuccheda-viveka), seclusion by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-viveka), and seclusion as escape (nissaraṇa-viveka). The next two terms, 'leans towards seclusion' and 'slopes towards seclusion,' are synonyms of the first term. 'Stands in seclusion' means he is secluded from defilements, or it means he is far from defilements. 'Delights in renunciation' means he greatly delights in Nibbāna, or it means he delights in the life of a monk. 'Being detached in part' means being liberated and not associating, without clinging even with a single thought. 'Entirely' means being detached from the defilements that are the causes of taints by the power of connection (saṃyoga). Alternatively, it means being detached from base craving, thus being free from craving. How could he not be detached from all states that are the basis of taints, and from all states belonging to the three realms? (He is indeed detached). By the ten powers of one whose taints are destroyed, the mundane and supramundane paths of the Arahant are taught. Some teachers also say: the power 'all formations are impermanent' is the power of the full understanding of suffering (dukkha-pariññā-bala); the power 'sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals' is the power of abandoning the origin (samudaya-pahāna-bala); the power 'the mind inclines towards seclusion' is the power of the realization of cessation (nirodha-sacchikiriyā-bala); and the seven powers shown by 'the four foundations of mindfulness' and so forth are the powers of the development of the path (magga-bhāvanā-bala). The ten powers of psychic potency (iddhi-bala) will be clarified in the Iddhikathā. In the exposition of the powers of a Tathāgata (tathāgata-bala-niddesa), the powers of a Tathāgata are those powers unique to the Buddhas, not shared with other Paccekabuddhas or disciples. Or, they come just as the powers of previous Buddhas came through the fulfillment of the store of merit.
230:
There are five types of seclusion (viveka): tadaṅgaviveka (seclusion by substitution of opposites), samucchedaviveka (seclusion by destruction), paṭippassaddhiviveka (seclusion by tranquilization), and nissaraṇaviveka (seclusion by deliverance). 'Vivekaninna' means the mind's inclination toward seclusion (either upadhiviveka or nissaraṇaviveka). 'Vivekapoṇa' means leaning toward or being associated with seclusion. 'Vivekapabbhāra' means being established in seclusion as if it were one's head. These latter two terms are also synonyms of the first term. 'Vivekaṭṭha' means the sense of being excluded from or distant from the defilements (kilesas). 'Nekkhammābhirata' means taking great delight in Nibbāna or taking great delight in renunciation (ordination). 'Byantībhūta' means being purified in part, not being attached to even a single thought (among the stages of arising and passing away), being liberated, and being unassociated. 'Sabbaso' means in every way. 'Asavaṭṭāniyehi dhammehi' means from the defilements that are the causes of the taints (āsavas) through the power of association. Alternatively, 'byantībhūta' means being free from base craving. Why? Because how could one not be free from all the things of the three planes (tebhūmaka) which are the causes of all taints? In this context, the mundane and supramundane paths of the Arahant are shown through the ten powers of an Arahant. They say that the power of full understanding of suffering (dukkhapariññābala) is shown by the text "All conditioned things are impermanent"; the power of abandoning the origin (samudayapahānabala) by "Sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals"; the power of realizing cessation (nirodhasacchikiriyābala) by "The mind inclines toward seclusion"; and the seven powers of path-development (maggabhāvanābala) by "The four foundations of mindfulness," and so on. The ten powers of psychic potency (iddhibala) will be clearly explained in the Iddhikathā.

In the explanation of the Tathāgata's powers (Tathāgatabalaniddesa), 'Tathāgatabalāni' refers to the powers unique to the Buddha, not shared with others. Alternatively, it means powers that have arisen due to the fulfillment of the accumulation of merit, just as the powers of previous Buddhas arose. There are two types of Tathāgata's powers: physical power (kāyabala) and knowledge power (ñāṇabala). Among these, physical power should be understood according to the ten lineages of elephants. The ancient teachers said:
"Kāḷāvaka elephant, Gaṅgeyya elephant, Paṇḍara elephant, Tamba elephant, Piṅgala elephant, Gandha elephant, Maṅgala elephant, Hema elephant, Uposatha elephant, and Chaddanta elephant—these are the ten lineages of elephants."

These are the ten lineages of elephants. Among them, 'Kāḷāvaka' refers to the ordinary lineage of elephants. The strength of ten men is equal to the strength of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The strength of ten Kāḷāvaka elephants is equal to the strength of one Gaṅgeyya elephant. The strength of ten Gaṅgeyya elephants is equal to the strength of one Paṇḍara elephant. The strength of ten Paṇḍara elephants is equal to the strength of one Tamba elephant. The strength of ten Tamba elephants is equal to the strength of one Piṅgala elephant. The strength of ten Piṅgala elephants is equal to the strength of one Gandha elephant. The strength of ten Gandha elephants is equal to the strength of one Maṅgala elephant. The strength of ten Maṅgala elephants is equal to the strength of one Hemavata elephant. ...
231:
The strength of ten Hemavata elephants is equal to the strength of one Uposatha elephant. The strength of ten Uposatha elephants is equal to the strength of one Chaddanta elephant. The strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is equal to the strength of one Tathāgata. This very strength is also called Nārāyanasaṅghātabala. In terms of ordinary elephants, this strength is equal to ten billion (koṭisahassa) elephants; in terms of men, it is equal to one hundred billion (dasakoṭisahassa) men. This is the physical power (kāyabala) of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the knowledge power (ñāṇabala), there are the ten powers of knowledge (dasabalañāṇa) mentioned here and in other Pali texts, the four intrepidities (catuvesārajjañāṇa) mentioned in the Majjhima Nikāya, the knowledge of being unshakable in the eight assemblies, the knowledge of distinguishing the four modes of birth, the knowledge of distinguishing the five destinations (gati), the seventy-three kinds of knowledge and seventy-seven kinds of knowledge mentioned in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, and many other thousands of knowledges. This is called knowledge power (ñāṇabala). Here too, knowledge power is intended. Knowledge is called 'power' (bala) because of its sense of being unshakable and its sense of providing support.

'Ṧhānañca ṭṭānato' means knowing what is a cause as a cause. A cause is called 'ṭṭāna' (possibility/ground) because the effect depends on that cause to arise and persist. The Blessed One knows as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, knowing: "These certain things are the causes and conditions for the arising of those certain things—that is ṭṭāna (possibility)"; and "These certain things are not the causes and conditions for the arising of those certain things—that is aṭṭāna (impossibility)." 'Yampi' means "by which knowledge." 'Idampi' means "this knowledge of the possible and impossible is also called the Tathāgata's power (Tathāgatabala)." The connection of the remaining terms should be understood in this same way.

'Āsabhaṁ ṭṭānaṁ' means the noble position, the supreme position (Omniscience). Alternatively, 'Āsabha' refers to the previous Buddhas; it means the position of those previous Buddhas. Furthermore, a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows is called 'usabha'. A bull that is the leader of a thousand cows is called 'vasabha'. Or, the leader of a hundred cow-pens is an 'usabha', and the leader of a thousand cow-pens is a 'vasabha'. A bull that is superior to all cattle, able to endure all dangers, white and inspiring confidence, capable of bearing great burdens, and undaunted even by the sound of a hundred thunderclaps is called 'nisabha'. Here, that nisabha is intended by the term 'usabha'. Indeed, this is a synonymous term for it. Because it belongs to the usabha, it is called 'āsabha'. 'Ṧhāna' means standing firmly by pressing the ground with four feet. This (Omniscience) is called 'āsabha' because it is like the āsabha bull. How so? Just as the bull known as nisabha, being endowed with the strength of an usabha, stands unshakably pressing the ground with its four feet, so too the Blessed One, being endowed with the ten powers, [stands in] the ground of the eight assemblies with the four feet of the knowledge of intrepidity...
232:
Just as a noble bull, endowed with its own strength, stands firm and unshakable by pressing the ground with its four legs, so too the Blessed One, endowed with the ten Tathāgata powers and the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja) as his four legs, stands firm and unshakable in the world with its devas, pressing the ground of the eight assemblies, unable to be moved by any enemy or adversary. Standing thus, he recognizes, claims, approaches, and does not renounce but takes upon himself that noble bull-like position. Therefore, it is said: "He claims the noble bull-like position."

"In the assemblies" refers to the eight assemblies: the assembly of nobles (khattiya), the assembly of brahmins (brāhmaṇa), the assembly of householders (gahapati), the assembly of ascetics (samaṇa), the assembly of the Four Great Kings (cātumahārājika), the assembly of the Thirty-three (tāvatiṃsa), the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmās. "Roars the lion's roar" means making a noble sound, a fearless sound, or a sound like that of a lion king. This meaning should be understood through the Sīhanāda Sutta. Alternatively, just as a lion is called 'sīha' because of its endurance (sahana) and its killing (hanana), so too the Blessed One is called 'sīha' because of his endurance of worldly conditions and his destruction of the doctrines of others. The roar of such a lion is called the 'lion's roar' (sīhanāda). In this regard, just as a lion king, endowed with lion-strength, roars the lion's roar, being confident and without horripilation in all places, so too the lion-like Tathāgata, endowed with the Tathāgata powers, roars the lion's roar, being confident and without horripilation in the eight assemblies, through various modes of teaching such as "Thus is form," etc. Therefore, it is said: "He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies."

In the phrase "He sets in motion the supreme wheel (brahmacakka)," 'brahma' means noble, supreme, or pure. The word 'cakka' (wheel) is seen in the sense of:

Prosperity (sampatti), marks (lakkhaṇa), chariot parts (rathaṅga), postures (iriyāpatha), giving (dāna), gems (ratana), Dhamma, and weapons (cakka), etc. Here, it should be understood as the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka), which is explained in two ways.

In passages such as "Monks, there are these four wheels, endowed with which devas and humans [attain prosperity]," the word 'cakka' is evident in the sense of prosperity (sampatti). In "On the soles of his feet, there are marks of wheels," it is in the sense of marks (lakkhaṇa). In "The wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the cart," it is in the sense of a chariot part (rathaṅga). In "Four wheels (postures), nine doors," it is in the sense of postures (iriyāpatha). In "Give and enjoy, do not be negligent, set the wheel (giving) in motion," it is in the sense of giving (dāna).
233:
In the Jātaka Pali "Pamādo cakkaṃ vattaya kosalādhipa," the word 'cakka' is in the sense of giving (dāna). In the Dīgha Nikāya Pali "Dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosi," it is in the sense of the wheel-gem (ratanacakka). In the Sutta Nipāta Pali "Mayā pavattitaṃ cakkaṃ," it is in the sense of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka). In the Jātaka Pali "Icchāhatassa posassa cakkaṃ bhamati matthake," it is in the sense of a razor-wheel (uracakka). In the Dīgha Nikāya Pali "Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena," it is in the sense of a wheel-weapon (paharaṇacakka). In the Pali "Asanivicakkaṃ," it is in the sense of a thunderbolt-circle (asanimaṇḍala). In this context, however, this word 'cakka' should be understood in the sense of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka). That Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). Among these, the path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) which is infused with wisdom and brings the noble fruit (ariya-phala) for oneself is called the knowledge of penetration. The knowledge which is infused with great compassion and brings the noble fruit for disciples is called the knowledge of teaching. Among these, the knowledge of penetration is of two types: arising (uppajjamāna) and arisen (uppanna). That knowledge of penetration is called 'arising' from the time of the Great Renunciation until the Path of Arahatship, and 'arisen' at the moment of the Fruit. Or, it is called 'arising' from the Tusita heaven until the Path of Arahatship on the Bodhi-seat, and 'arisen' at the moment of the Fruit. Or, it is called 'arising' from the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Path of Arahatship, and 'arisen' at the moment of the Fruit. The knowledge of teaching is also of two types: being set in motion (pavattāmāna) and set in motion (pavatta). That knowledge of teaching is called 'being set in motion' until the Path of Arahatship of the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña, and 'set in motion' at the moment of the Fruit. Among these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane (lokuttara), and the knowledge of teaching is mundane (lokiya). Both these knowledges are the unique personal knowledge (orasa-ñāṇa) of the Buddhas, not shared with others. Therefore, it is said: "He sets in motion the supreme wheel (brahmacakka)."

"Kamma-samādānānaṃ" refers to the wholesome and unwholesome kamma that are undertaken and performed. Or, the wholesome and unwholesome kamma themselves are called 'kamma-samādāna'. "Ṭhānaso hetuso" means by way of supporting cause (paccaya) and by way of generating cause (hetu). Among these, destination (gati), physical excellence (upadhi), time (kāla), and effort (payoga) are called the supporting causes (ṭhāna) for the result. Kamma is the generating cause (hetu). "Sabbatthagāminiṃ" means leading to all destinations (gati) and also leading to the non-destination (leading to Nibbāna). "Paṭipadaṃ" means the path (magga). "Yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti" means that even though many people kill the same single being, he knows correctly and without distortion the nature of the practices known as wholesome and unwholesome intentions, in the manner: "This person's intention will lead to hell; this person's intention will lead to the animal realm."
234:
"Anekadhātu" means many elements, such as the eye element and so forth, or the sense-desire element and so forth. "Nānādhātu" means various kinds of elements because of the difference in their characteristics. "Loka" (the world) means the world of the aggregates, bases, and elements. "Knows as it really is" means penetrating the nature of those various elements without distortion.

"Nānādhimuttikatā" means the state of having various dispositions, such as low or superior.

"Parasattānaṃ" means of superior beings. "Parapuggalānaṃ" means of other inferior beings. Alternatively, although these two terms have the same meaning, the Blessed One taught them in two ways according to the needs of those to be guided (veneyya). In this Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali as well, the Blessed One taught in that very same manner. "Indriyaparopariyatta" refers to the superiority and inferiority, the growth and decline of the faculties such as faith (saddhā) and so forth.

"Of jhānas, vimokkhas, samādhis, and samāpattis" refers to the four jhānas such as the first jhāna, the eight liberations such as "Possessing form, one sees forms," the three concentrations such as those with initial and sustained thought, and the nine successive attainments such as the attainment of the first jhāna. "Saṅkilesa" (defilement) means the factors belonging to decline (hānabhāgiya-dhamma). "Vodāna" (purification) means the factors belonging to distinction (visesabhāgiya-dhamma). "Vuṭṭhāna" (emergence) means the cause by which one emerges from jhāna and so forth. Specifically, regarding this emergence, it is stated: "Vodāna is also emergence; emerging from various concentrations is also emergence." This refers to practiced jhāna, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). A lower practiced jhāna is the proximate cause for a higher jhāna; therefore, it is said, "Vodāna is also emergence." Emergence from all jhānas occurs through the life-continuum, and emergence from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) occurs through the attainment of fruition. With reference to such emergence, it is said, "Emerging from various concentrations is also emergence."

The knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints have already been explained below.

In the passage concerning the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, "āsavānaṃ khayā" means by the destruction of all defilements through the Path of Arahatship. "Anāsava" means that which is free from taints. In the phrase "cetovimutti paññāvimutti," the word "ceto" refers to the concentration associated with the fruition of Arahatship, and the word "paññā" refers to the wisdom associated with that fruition. Among these two, concentration is called "deliverance of mind" (cetovimutti) because it is liberated from lust (rāga), and wisdom is called "deliverance by wisdom" (paññāvimutti) because it is liberated from ignorance (avijjā). This matter was taught by the Blessed One: "Monks, whatever concentration he has, that is his faculty of concentration. Monks, whatever wisdom he has, that is his faculty of wisdom. Thus, monks, deliverance of mind is through the fading away of lust."
235:
'Due to the fading of ignorance, there is liberation by wisdom,' as taught in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. Alternatively, it should be understood that the power of serenity (samatha) is the cause for liberation of mind, and the power of insight (vipassanā) is the cause for liberation by wisdom. 'Diṭṭhe va dhamme' means in this very life, in this present existence. 'Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā' means having realized by oneself through superior wisdom, knowing directly without relying on others. 'Upasampajja' means having attained or accomplished. The details of these ten powers of knowledge (dasa-balañāṇa) should be understood according to the method taught in the Abhidhamma (Vibhaṅga).

Regarding the ten powers, there is a view of the proponents of other doctrines (paravādī): 'There is no separate knowledge called the Ten Powers; this is merely a division of Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa).' This should not be viewed that way. Because the Ten Powers are one thing, and Omniscience is another. The Ten Powers know only their respective functions, whereas Omniscience knows those functions and everything else besides. Among the Ten Powers: the first knows only cause and non-cause; the second knows only the diversity of kamma and its results; the third knows only the classification of kamma; the fourth knows only the cause of the diversity of elements; the fifth knows only the dispositions and inclinations of beings; the sixth knows only the sharpness or dullness of faculties; the seventh knows the defilement, etc., of jhānas and so on; the eighth knows only the continuity of aggregates lived in the past; the ninth knows only the death and rebirth of beings; the tenth knows only the classification of the Four Truths. Omniscience knows what is to be known by these powers and also knows beyond that. However, Omniscience does not perform all the functions of those powers. For Omniscience cannot become a jhāna to attain absorption, it cannot become a psychic power to perform transformations, and it cannot become the Path to exhaust defilements.

Furthermore, the opponent should be asked: 'Are these Ten Powers with thought and examination (savitakka-savicāra), with examination only (avitakka-vicāramatta), or without thought and examination (avitakka-avicāra)? Are they of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), mundane (lokiya), or supramundane (lokuttara)?' The knowledgeable opponent will reply: 'The first seven knowledges in sequence are with thought and examination. The next two are without thought and examination. The knowledge of the destruction of taints may be with thought and examination, with examination only, or without thought and examination.' Similarly, he will reply: 'The first seven knowledges in sequence are of the sense sphere. The next two are of the fine-material sphere. The final one (destruction of taints) is supramundane.' But he will reply: 'Omniscience is only with thought and examination, only of the sense sphere, and only mundane.'
236:
Thus, having understood the explanation of the meaning not previously mentioned in these Ten Powers (Dasa Bala), now, the Blessed One first of all, through the Knowledge of Possibility and Impossibility (Thānāthāna-ñāṇa), sees the absence of the hindrance of defilements, which is the cause (thāna) and non-cause (athāna) for the attainment or non-attainment of the destruction of the taints (the Path of Arahatship) by beings to be tamed (veneyya). This is because He sees the cause of the Path, which is mundane right view, and He sees the non-cause of the Path, which is fixed wrong view. After that, through the Knowledge of the Result of Kamma (Kamma-vipāka-ñāṇa), He sees the absence of the hindrance of result (vipākāvaraṇa) because He sees their triple-rooted rebirth (tihetu-paṭisandhi). Through the Knowledge of the Way Leading to All Destinations (Sabbatthagāminī-paṭipadā-ñāṇa), He sees the absence of the hindrance of kamma (kammāvaraṇa) because He sees the absence of heinous crimes (anantariya-kamma). Thus, for the sake of teaching the Dhamma appropriately to those who are free from hindrances, He sees the specific temperaments through the Knowledge of Many and Various Elements (Anekadhātu-nānādhātu-ñāṇa), because He sees the diversity of elements.

After that, through the Knowledge of Various Dispositions (Nānādhimuttikatā-ñāṇa), He sees the disposition (adhimutti) of those beings in order to teach the Dhamma by the power of their disposition, without taking into account their effort (payoga/temperament). After that, in order to teach the Dhamma according to the capacity and strength of those persons whose dispositions have been thus seen, He sees the inferiority and superiority of the faculties through the Knowledge of the Superiority and Inferiority of Faculties (Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa), because He sees the sharpness or dullness of faith and so on. If these beings, whose faculties have been thus distinguished, are in a distant place, He quickly approaches them by means of special psychic power, as He has attained mastery in jhāna and so on. Having approached them, He discerns the conditions of their past lives through the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives (Pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa), and through the Knowledge of Discerning the Minds of Others (Cetopariya-ñāṇa) obtained by the power of the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu), He sees their current specific state of mind. Then, being free from delusion regarding the practice leading to the Path of Arahatship by the power of the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints (Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), He teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints. Therefore, it should be understood that these Ten Powers are taught in this stated order.

Now, wishing to point out all the Powers (Bala) by their characteristics, He asks a question in the manner of "In what sense is it the Power of Faith (Saddhā-bala)?" and gives the answer in the manner of "In the sense of being unshakable by faithlessness." In that answer, the phrase "is ashamed (hirīyati)" and so on is a teaching based on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna).
