In the terms starting from the Power of Development (Bhāvanā-bala) up to the Power of Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-bala), it should be understood that the words "therein (tattha)," "by that (tena)," and "that (taṃ)" refer only to renunciation (jhāna) and so on. The phrase "by that, the mind is one-pointed" means that by that concentration (samādhi), the mind becomes one-pointed. "Arisen therein" means those states arisen by way of association in that serenity (samatha), or those states arisen having become the object of insight (vipassanā) in that serenity. "Trains therein" means that the trainee (sekha) trains in that Power of the Trainee, thus it is called the Power of the Trainee (Sekha-bala). "Because of having trained therein" means the Power of the Beyond-training (Asekha-bala) because the Arahat has already trained in that Power of the Beyond-training. "By that, the taints are destroyed" means that the taints are destroyed by that mundane and supramundane knowledge; thus, that knowledge (is called the Power of the Destruction of Taints).
237:
The Power of the Destruction of Taints (Khīṇāsava-bala). Indeed, the taints are said to be destroyed even by mundane knowledge when, in the absence of insight (vipassanā), the supramundane path is absent. Thus, it is the Power of the Destruction of Taints because it is the power of the Arahat whose taints are destroyed. It is called the Power of Psychic Potency (Iddhi-bala) because it succeeds for that person who possesses psychic power; the psychic potency (iddhi) itself is the power (bala), hence it is called Iddhi-bala. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of being immeasurable (appameyya)," since the disciples (sāvakas) know the Knowledge of Possibility and Impossibility and so on only partially, the phrase "knows as it really is" is spoken referring only to the knowing in every aspect. Although it is not explicitly said "knows as it really is" in the three knowledges (tevijjā), because it is stated elsewhere, it is considered as already stated in those three knowledges as well. "Elsewhere" refers to the remaining seven powers of knowledge and also to the ten powers in the commentary on the Ñāṇavibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma. However, the Knowledge of the Superiority and Inferiority of Faculties (Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) is entirely unshared (asādhāraṇa) with the disciples. Therefore, all ten powers are unshared with the disciples. They are called immeasurable (appameyya) in the sense of being pre-eminent and incomparable; for that very reason, it is said, "The Tathāgata's Power in the sense of being immeasurable."

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Powers is Finished.
## 10. Suññakathā
## Explanation of the Discourse on Emptiness

Now, following the Discourse on Powers which ends with the supramundane powers, the explanation of the meaning not previously mentioned in the Discourse on Emptiness (Suññatākathā), which ends with supramundane emptiness and is preceded by the Sutta, will be stated. In the Sutta, the word "atha" is a particle (nipāta) used in the sense of introducing another statement. By this particle "atha," the introduction of the words "the venerable (āyasmā)" and so on is made. "Kho" is a particle used in the sense of a verse-filler (padapūrana). "Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī" (where the Blessed One was, there he approached) uses the instrumental case in the sense of the locative (ādhāra). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "In which place the Blessed One was, to that place he approached." Alternatively, it should be understood as: "For whatever reason the Blessed One should be approached by devas and humans, for that very reason he approached." For what reason should the Blessed One be approached? Just as flocks of birds approach a great tree that is always fruiting with the desire to enjoy sweet fruit, he approached with the desire to attain various specific qualities and virtues; thus the meaning should be understood. "Upasaṅkamī" means "he went." "Upasaṅkamitvā" indicates the completion of the act of approaching. Alternatively, it means that having gone in this way, he then went to a very close place, which is called the presence of the Blessed One.
238:
"Abhivādetvā" means bowing by touching the ground with the five points: the two knees, the two hands, and the forehead. Now, the Venerable Ānanda, wishing to ask the reason for which he had come to attend upon the Buddha, the supreme person in the world, placed his joined palms—shining with the assembly of ten fingernails—upon his head and sat down to one side. The word "ekamantaṃ" is an expression of the nature of the action (adverbial neuter), as in "The moon and sun move unevenly" (visamaṃ candimasūriyā pariharanti), etc. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: he sat in such a way that his sitting was "to one side." Alternatively, this word "ekamantaṃ" is the use of the accusative case in the sense of location (ādhāra). "Nisīdi" means he took a seat. Indeed, wise devas and humans, having approached those worthy of respect, sit to one side due to their skill in seating; and this Elder was one among those wise ones, therefore he sat to one side.

How is one sitting when it is said he sits "to one side"? It is by sitting while avoiding the six faults of sitting. They are: too far, too near, upwind, a high place, directly in front, and directly behind. For if one sits too far, if he wishes to speak, he must speak with a loud voice. If he sits too near, it causes physical contact. If he sits upwind, he disturbs with his body odor. If he sits in a high place, it shows a lack of respect. If he sits directly in front, if he wishes to look, he must look eye-to-eye. If he sits directly behind, if he wishes to look, he must look by stretching his neck. Therefore, this Venerable Ānanda also sat avoiding these six faults of sitting. With reference to such sitting, it is said, "ekamantaṃ nisīdi" (he sat to one side). "Etadavoca" means he spoke these words.

"Venerable Sir, it is said, 'The world is empty, the world is empty'"—the meaning is that various monks practicing in this Dispensation (Sāsana) are saying, "The world is empty, the world is empty." Because such words are frequent in various discourses, the repetition (āmeḍita) is made to encompass all of them. By saying it twice in this way, all those statements are included. "Kittāvatā" means "to what extent?" The word "nu" is a particle in the sense of doubt. "Empty of self or of what belongs to self" means it is empty of a "self" as conceived by the world as "a doer, an experiencer, or one with self-mastery," and because of the absence of self, it is also empty of the requisites (parikkhāra) which are the belongings of a self. All mundane phenomena such as the eye, etc., are called "the world" (loka) in the sense of disintegrating and crumbling (lujjana-palujjana). And because there is no self in them, nor anything belonging to a self, it is said, "The world is empty." Even supramundane...
239:
...Dhamma is indeed empty of self and what belongs to self; however, in accordance with the question, only mundane Dhamma is spoken of here. When it is said "it is empty," it does not mean that the Dhamma does not exist; it means the absence of the essence of self and what belongs to self in that Dhamma. In the world, when it is said, "an empty house" or "an empty pot," it does not mean the house or the pot does not exist, but rather that there is an absence of other things like people or water in that house or pot. The Blessed One also spoke of this very meaning: "Thus, whatever is not there, one regards that as empty of it. But whatever remains there, one knows that existing thing as 'this exists'." This same meaning is also stated in the treatises of Logic (Nyāya) and Grammar (Sadda). Thus, in this sutta, only the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) is discussed.

In the Suttanta-niddesa, twenty-five mātikā terms such as suñña-suñña, etc., are pointed out in connection with "empty," and then their explanation is given. In that mātikā, first, the emptiness called "empty" is called "suñña-suñña" because it is not distinguished by other qualifying terms such as saṅkhāra, etc. In this Pali, because a specific thing is not pointed out, or because it regards only the state of being empty, the neuter gender is used. The same applies to the remaining terms. A formation (saṅkhāra) itself is called "saṅkhāra-suñña" because it is empty of other formations. Transformation (vipariṇāma) is the change of aging and disintegration; it is called "vipariṇāma-suñña" because it is empty of that transformation. The foremost Nibbāna is called "agga-suñña" because it is empty of self and what belongs to self, or of all formations. A characteristic itself is called "lakkhaṇa-suñña" because it is empty of other characteristics. It is called "vikkhambhana-suñña" because it is empty through the suppression (vikkhambhana) by means of renunciation (nekkhamma), etc. The same method applies to the four beginning with tadaṅga-suñña. Internal phenomena are called "ajjhatta-suñña" because they are empty of self and what belongs to self, etc. External phenomena are called "bahiddhā-suñña" because they are empty of self and what belongs to self, etc. Both are called "dubhato-suñña" because they are empty of self and what belongs to self, etc. That which has a similar part is called "sabhāga"; it is called "sabhāga-suñña" because it is empty of self and what belongs to self, etc.; the meaning is "empty while being similar." That which lacks a similar part is called "visabhāga"; it is called "visabhāga-suñña" because it is empty of self and what belongs to self, etc.; the meaning is "empty while being dissimilar." In some books, sabhāga-suñña and visabhāga-suñña are written after nissaraṇa-suñña. Seeking (esanā) such as renunciation is called "esanā-suñña" because it is empty of sensual desire (kāmacchanda), etc. The same method applies to the three beginning with pariggaha-suñña. Because of being established in a single object and thus having no distraction toward various objects, it is called "ekatta" (oneness); it is called "ekatta-suñña" because it is empty of nānatta (diversity). Conversely...
240:
That state is both diversity (nānatta, having various objects) and empty of unity (ekatta, a single object); therefore, it is called 'emptiness of diversity' (nānattasuñña). The virtue of patience (khanti) beginning with renunciation (nekkhamma) is called 'emptiness of patience' (khantisuñña) because it is empty of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth. The same method applies to 'emptiness of resolution' (adhiṭṭhānasuñña) and 'emptiness of penetration' (pariyogāhanasuñña). There is also a reading as 'pariyogahanasuñña'. The term 'sampajānassa' refers to an Arahant who, endowed with clear comprehension (sampajañña), attains final passing away (parinibbāna). 'Pavattapariyādāna' refers to final passing away without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna). 'Sabbasuññatānaṃ' means the sense of all types of emptiness. 'Paramatthasuñña' (ultimate emptiness) is the emptiness that is the highest meaning because of the absence of all conditioned formations (saṅkhāra).

In the 'Description of the Matrix' (mātikāniddesa), the phrase 'niccena vā' (or by way of permanence) means emptiness of the nature of permanence because there is no permanent thing that exists beyond dissolution (bhaṅga). 'Dhuvena vā' (or by way of stability) means emptiness of the nature of stability because even during the time of existence, there is no stable thing as it depends on conditions. 'Sassatena vā' (or by way of eternity) means emptiness of the nature of eternity because there is no thing that exists continuously at all times. 'Avipariṇāmadhammena vā' (or by way of unchangeability) means emptiness of the nature of unchangeability because there is no thing that has an unchangeable nature due to aging and dissolution. Although only emptiness of self (attasuññatā) is taught in the Suttas, here 'niccena vā' and so forth are taught to show emptiness of permanence (niccasuññatā) and emptiness of happiness (sukhasuññatā). Since only the impermanent is suffering due to its connection with oppression, when emptiness of permanence is taught, emptiness of happiness is also taught. In this context, the six objects such as visible forms, the six consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness, the six contacts such as eye-contact, and the six feelings born of eye-contact should be understood in brief.

Regarding 'meritorious volitional formations' (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth: it is called 'merit' (puñña) because it purifies its doer, fulfills their aspirations, and produces a worthy existence. It is called 'formation' (abhisaṅkhāra) because it conditions the resultant (vipāka) and the kamma-born materiality (kaṭattārūpa). A meritorious formation is 'puññābhisaṅkhāra'. An formation that is the opposite of merit is 'apuññābhisaṅkhāra' (demeritorious formation). It is called 'āneñjābhisaṅkhāra' (imperturbable formation) because it conditions an imperturbable existence. Meritorious formations consist of thirteen volitions: eight wholesome volitions of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-kusala) occurring by way of giving, virtue, and meditation, and five wholesome volitions of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-kusala) occurring only by way of meditation. Demeritorious formations consist of twelve unwholesome volitions occurring by way of killing and so forth. Imperturbable formations consist of four immaterial-sphere volitions (arūpāvacara-cetanā) occurring only by way of meditation. All these three formations total twenty-nine volitions. In 'bodily formation' (kāyasaṅkhāra) and so forth, a formation that occurs from the body or conditions the body is called 'kāyasaṅkhāra'. The same method applies to 'vocal formation' (vacīsaṅkhāra) and 'mental formation' (cittasaṅkhāra). This...
241:
This triad of bodily formations is taught to show the occurrence of meritorious formations and so forth through the doors of body and speech at the moment of accumulating kamma. Indeed, the twenty-one volitions—namely, the eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions, the twelve unwholesome volitions, and the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā)—which originate bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) and occur through the bodily door, are called 'bodily formations' (kāyasaṅkhāra). These same twenty-one volitions, when they originate vocal intimation (vacīviññatti) and occur through the vocal door, are called 'vocal formations' (vacīsaṅkhāra). However, all twenty-nine volitions occurring in the mind door are called 'mental formations' (cittasaṅkhāra). In 'past formations' (atīta saṅkhāra) and so forth, all conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) that have reached their own moment and ceased are 'past formations'. All conditioned things that have not yet reached their own moment are 'future formations'. All conditioned things that are currently reaching their own moment are 'present formations'.

In 'emptiness of change' (vipariṇāmasuñña), present things are shown first because the change of those specific present things can be easily stated. Therein, 'arisen materiality' (jātaṃ rūpaṃ) refers to present materiality (rūpakkhandha). In the phrase 'empty of inherent nature' (sabhāvena suññaṃ), 'sabhāva' means arising by itself without conditions; the meaning is arising solely by itself. Alternatively, 'sabhāva' means arising as a self (atta) without being mixed with other elements. Since materiality exists in dependence on conditions, there is no arising by itself apart from conditions; therefore, it is said to be 'empty of inherent nature' (sabhāvena suññaṃ), meaning it is empty of arising by itself or empty of arising as a self.

Alternatively, 'sabhāva' means the nature (bhāva) of one's own (saka). For instance, among the many material and immaterial things such as the earth element, each thing is called 'own' (saka) in relation to another. The word 'bhāva' is a synonym for 'dhamma'. For a single thing, there is no other thing called 'bhāva' apart from that thing itself. Therefore, it is empty of any other 'bhāva' in what is called 'own'; the 'own' is empty of any other 'nature'. By this, the state of having a single individual nature for a single thing is stated. Alternatively, 'empty of inherent nature' means it is empty only of the nature of emptiness (suñña-sabhāva). What is meant? It means it is empty only by way of 'emptiness of emptiness' (suññasuññatā), and not empty by other figurative types of emptiness.

If some teachers should say: 'One's own thing is sabhāva, and it is empty of that sabhāva.' What would that mean? 'Bhāva' means a thing (dhamma); that thing, when specified by the prefix 'sa-' in relation to another, is called 'sabhāva'. Because no thing exists [in their view], the phrase 'arisen materiality is empty of inherent nature' would mean the non-existence of materiality. If this were so, it would contradict the phrase 'arisen materiality' (jātaṃ rūpaṃ). Indeed, that which is devoid of the arising phase (uppāda) cannot be called 'arisen' (jāta). Nibbāna is devoid of the arising phase, and it is not called 'arisen'. Furthermore, birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa), though devoid of the arising phase [of a conditioned entity], are called 'arisen' [in a different sense]. For this reason, in the description of this 'emptiness of change', it is not taught by extracting them as 'arisen birth is empty of inherent nature, arisen aging and death are empty of inherent nature', but is shown ending only with materiality. If it were proper to call something devoid of arising 'arisen', then He should have taught 'arisen birth, arisen aging and death'. Since the word 'arisen' is not used for birth, aging, and death which are devoid of the arising phase, the statement of some teachers that 'it is empty of inherent nature and does not exist' contradicts the word 'arisen', because anything that does not exist must always be devoid of the arising phase. Moreover, saying that non-existent materiality is 'empty' contradicts worldly usage, the Buddha's words, and the words found in logic and grammar texts. It also contradicts many logical reasonings. Therefore, the words of those teachers should be discarded like rubbish. It is concluded here that things do indeed exist in their own characteristics (sabalakkhaṇa), according to many authoritative Buddha-words such as 'Monks, I will teach...' and according to many logical reasonings.
242:
That which is called 'arisen' (jāta) does not occur; birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa), being devoid of the moment of arising (uppāda), are not called 'arisen'. For this very reason, in this Exposition on the Voidness of Change (Vipariṇāmasuñña Niddesa), it is presented by ending with 'existence' (bhava) only, without bringing forth the statement: 'Birth is arisen and void by nature; aging and death are arisen and void by nature.' If it were appropriate to use the word 'arisen' for that which is devoid of the moment of arising, then it should have been stated: 'Birth is arisen; aging and death are arisen.' Since the word 'arisen' was not used for birth, aging, and death which are devoid of the moment of arising, the statement made by some teachers that 'it is void by nature and non-existent' contradicts the word 'arisen', because that which is non-existent is devoid of the moment of arising. Furthermore, calling that which is non-existent 'void' (suñña) contradicts the worldly usage mentioned below, the words of the Blessed One, and the statements found in the treatises of logic (Nyāya) and grammar (Sadda); it also contradicts many logical reasonings. Therefore, that statement should be discarded like rubbish.

'Bhikkhus, whatever is agreed upon as existing by the wise in the world, I too say that it exists. Bhikkhus, whatever is agreed upon as not existing by the wise in the world, I too say that it does not exist. And what, bhikkhus, is agreed upon as existing by the wise in the world, which I too say exists? Bhikkhus, material form (rūpa) that is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is agreed upon as existing by the wise in the world; I too say that it exists,' etc. By such numerous authoritative words of the Buddha and by many logical reasonings, it should be concluded here that phenomena (dhammas) truly exist in their own characteristics.

'Vanished form' (vigata-rūpa) refers to past material form that has arisen, reached the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga), and ceased. 'Both changed and void' means it has reached a state of altered appearance by way of aging and dissolution; it also means it is void of that change because only the presently occurring material form possesses the nature of change, while past material form does not possess change. The same method applies to 'arisen feeling' (jātā vedanā), etc. However, birth, aging, and death are inappropriate here because they are non-produced (anipphanna) and cannot be obtained by their own nature. Therefore, discarding the two methods such as 'birth is arisen, aging and death are arisen', the method beginning with 'existence' (bhava) is established as the conclusion.

'Agga' means being at the top or foremost. 'Seṭṭha' means highly praiseworthy. 'Visiṭṭha' means distinguished or superior. There is also a reading 'viseṭṭha'. Nibbāna, which is praised by these three terms, is called 'pada' (state/path) because it is to be attained through the right practice. 'Yadidaṃ' means 'yaṃ idaṃ' (that which is this). Now, it points to the Nibbāna that is to be spoken of. Since, depending on Nibbāna, there is the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra), the relinquishing of the acquisitions (upadhi) known as the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesūpadhi), the acquisition of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārūpadhi), and the acquisition of the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇūpadhi), and there is the destruction, fading away, and cessation of craving, therefore it is the stilling of all formations...
243:
...it is called the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, the fading away of lust, and cessation. The term 'Nibbāna' is concluded by its individual essence (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa).

Regarding the Voidness of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇasuñña): "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool, signs of a fool, conduct of a fool. What three? Here, bhikkhus, a fool is one who thinks bad thoughts, speaks bad words, and does bad deeds. Bhikkhus, these are the three characteristics of a fool, signs of a fool, conduct of a fool." This has been taught. Because the wise recognize a fool as a fool by these, the three types (bad thoughts, etc.) are called the characteristics of a fool. "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a wise man, signs of a wise man, conduct of a wise man. What three? Here, bhikkhus, a wise man is one who thinks good thoughts, speaks good words, and does good deeds. Bhikkhus, these are the three characteristics of a wise man, signs of a wise man, conduct of a wise man." This has been taught. Because the wise recognize a wise man as a wise man by these, the three types (good thoughts, etc.) are called the characteristics of a wise man.

"Bhikkhus, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. What three? Arising (uppāda) is manifest, vanishing (vaya) is manifest, and change while standing (ṭhitassa aññathatta) is manifest. Bhikkhus, these are the three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned." This has been taught. Arising itself is the characteristic for recognizing the conditioned, thus it is called a conditioned characteristic. The meaning of the other two terms (vanishing and change while standing) should be understood in the same way. By this, it is shown that at the moment of arising, the other two (presence and dissolution) are absent; at the moment of presence (ṭhiti), the other two are absent; and at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga), the other two are absent. As for the characteristics of arising, etc., of birth, aging, and death mentioned here by way of abbreviation (peyyāla), this contradicts the method in the Exposition on the Voidness of Change where birth, aging, and death are excluded and the method ends with 'existence', and it also contradicts the view that does not describe arising, etc., as arising, etc. However, it should be understood that they are written here because they fall within the stream of the discourse (desanā-sota) on characteristics. Just as in the Summary Chapter (Saṅgahavāra) of the Abhidhamma, the factors of jhāna that are obtainable in the rootless resultant mind-element and mind-consciousness-element are not extracted because they fall within the stream of the discourse on the fivefold consciousness, so too here, it should be understood as falling within the stream of the discourse. Alternatively, the arising, etc., of formations that possess birth, aging, and death are taught as if they were the arising, etc., of those birth, aging, and death themselves, as in the passages: "Birth, aging, and death are impermanent."
244:
"By renunciation, sensual desire is both suppressed and empty" means that sensual desire is suppressed by renunciation, and because renunciation is absent in that sensual desire, it is also empty of that renunciation which is called suppression. The same application should be made to the remaining terms. Here, in the cases of abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna) and abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), it is called suppression (vikkhambhana) because of the sense of making distant the states that have been abandoned by the power of substitution and eradication.

"By renunciation, sensual desire is empty by substitution of opposites" means that sensual desire, which has been abandoned by renunciation, is empty of that factor called renunciation. Alternatively, any sensual desire is empty of that factor called renunciation because renunciation is absent in it. The same application should be made to the remaining terms. Here, the emptiness by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-suññatā) is shown by the power of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), attainment concentration (appanā-jhāna), and insight (vipassanā), merely by the absence of each respective factor in each respective place. Because there is no word indicating abandonment, insight is shown ending only with the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā); the four paths (magga) are not shown. In the passages such as "By renunciation, sensual desire is both eradicated and empty," the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on suppression. Here, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) that have been abandoned by the power of substitution and suppression are also called eradicated (samuccinna) because they no longer occur; in this sense, eradication (samuccheda) is spoken of. Alternatively, it should be understood as being spoken of by the power of renunciation, etc., associated with the path that accomplishes the respective task of eradication. The meaning in the emptiness of tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-suñña) and the emptiness of escape (nissaraṇa-suñña) should also be understood in the same way as stated here. However, in these cases of abandonment by substitution, suppression, and eradication, it is spoken of by taking the mere state of being calmed and the mere state of being escaped. In all these five types of emptiness, renunciation and so on are themselves called by the names suppression, substitution, eradication, tranquillization, and escape.

"Ajjhatta" means that which is internal. "Bahiddhā" means that which is external. "Dubhatosuñña" means emptiness of both. Indeed, it is called emptiness of both. In terms like paccatta, etc., the word "to" (suffix) is certainly present.

The six internal bases (ajjhattikāyatana), etc., are similar (sabhāga) in their nature as the six internal bases. They are dissimilar (visabhāga) from others. In terms such as "viññāṇakāya" (group of consciousness), the word "kāya" refers to consciousness and so on. In "nekkhammesanā" (seeking renunciation), etc., it is called seeking (esanā) because renunciation and so on are sought by wise persons who desire those states. Alternatively, it means that in the preceding stage, the seeking of renunciation, etc., is also empty of sensual desire, etc.; how much more so renunciation itself? In the emptiness of possession (pariggaha-suñña), etc., renunciation and so on are sought in the preceding stage, and in the subsequent stage...
245:
Because of grasping (the jhānas) by bringing them into one's own continuity, it is called 'possession' (pariggaha). Because of obtaining the grasped jhānas through the power of attainment, it is called 'attainment' (paṭilābha). Because of penetrating and seeing the obtained jhānas with wisdom, it is called 'penetration' (paṭivedha). After asking about the emptiness of oneness (ekatta-suñña) and the emptiness of manifoldness (nānatta-suñña) at the same time, only the emptiness of oneness is answered, and without answering the emptiness of manifoldness, the conclusion is made together. If it is asked why it is not answered, it should be understood that it is not answered because the application here can be known by the same method already taught. The application here is as follows: renunciation is oneness (ekatta), sensual desire is manifoldness (nānatta); the manifoldness called sensual desire is empty of the oneness called renunciation. In this way, the application should be understood for the remaining states.

In the cases of emptiness such as patience (khanti), renunciation and so on are called 'patience' (khanti) because they are liked; they are called 'determination' (adhiṭṭhāna) because they remain established after being liked; and they are called 'plunging into' (pariyogāhana) because one associates with the established jhānas as much as one likes. Here, the explanation of ultimate emptiness (paramattha-suñña-niddesa) beginning with 'sampajāna' (clearly comprehending) has already been described in the explanation of the knowledge of parinibbāna (parinibbāna-ñāṇa-niddesa).

Among all these types of emptiness, the emptiness of formations (saṅkhāra-suñña), the emptiness of change (vipariṇāma-suñña), and the emptiness of characteristics (lakkhaṇa-suñña) are taught to show the non-mixture of the aforementioned states with one another. Where the emptiness of unwholesome states from wholesome states is taught, it is for the purpose of showing the danger (ādīnava) in the unwholesome. Where the emptiness of wholesome states from unwholesome states is taught, it is for the purpose of showing the benefit (ānisaṃsa) in the wholesome. Where emptiness from self (atta) and what belongs to self (attaniya), etc., is taught, it is for the purpose of generating disenchantment (nibbidā) with all formations. Foremost emptiness (agga-suñña) and ultimate emptiness (paramattha-suñña) are taught to generate effort (ussāha) toward Nibbāna.

Among those, the two types of emptiness—foremost emptiness and ultimate emptiness—refer to the single Nibbāna in terms of meaning, taught in two ways by the power of 'foremost' and 'ultimate', and by the power of Nibbāna with residue (saupādisesa) and without residue (anupādisesa). Those two are similar in nature to emptiness from self and what belongs to self, and to the emptiness of formations. These six types of emptiness—'emptiness of emptiness (suññasuñña), internal emptiness, external emptiness, emptiness of both, similar emptiness, and dissimilar emptiness'—are indeed emptiness of emptiness. However, they are taught in six ways according to the divisions of internal and so on. These six are also similar in nature to emptiness from self and what belongs to self. The seventeen types of emptiness—namely, the three: emptiness of formations, change, and characteristics; the five: emptiness of suppression, substitution, eradication, tranquillization, and escape; the four: emptiness of seeking, possession, attainment, and penetration; the two: emptiness of oneness and manifoldness; and the three: emptiness of patience, determination, and plunging into—are taught separately according to the power of non-existent states, because they are empty of those respective states that do not exist in them. The emptiness of formations, change, and characteristics are...
246:
Furthermore, they are similar by way of being unmixed with other types of voidness. The five types, such as vikkhambhana-suñña (voidness by suppression), are similar because they are void of factors belonging to the wholesome side. The four types, such as esanā-suñña (voidness of seeking), and the three types, such as khanti-suñña (voidness of patience), are also similar because they are void of factors belonging to the unwholesome side. Ekattasuñña (voidness of unity) and nānattasuñña (voidness of diversity) are similar by way of being mutual opposites.

All phenomena, in brief,
In three ways, in two ways, and likewise in one way,
Are void; thus the wise who know the meaning of voidness,
Explain in this Dispensation.

How? First, all mundane phenomena are called dhuvasubhasukha-attasuñña (void of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self) because they are devoid of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. The phenomena of the Path and Fruition are called dhuvasukhattasuñña (void of permanence, happiness, and self) because they are devoid of permanence, happiness, and self. They are void of happiness only because they are impermanent. They are not void of beauty because they are free from taints (anāsava). The phenomenon of Nibbāna is called attasuñña (void of self) because of the absence of self. All conditioned (saṅkhata) phenomena, whether mundane or supramundane, are called sattasuñña (void of a being) because of the absence of any being. The unconditioned (asaṅkhata) phenomenon of Nibbāna is called saṅkhārasuñña (void of formations) because of the absence of those formations. All phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned, are called attasuñña (void of self) because of the absence of a person called self.

## In the Saddhammappakāsinī, the Commentary on the Paṭisambhidāmagga,
## The Explanation of the Discourse on Voidness (Suññakathā-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
## The Explanation of the Chapter on Yoking (Yuganaddhavagga-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
## The Explanation of the Meanings Not Previously Mentioned in the Middle Group (Majjhimavagga) is also finished.
247:
## (3) Paññāvagga
## 1. Mahāpaññākathā-vaṇṇanā
Now, I shall explain the meanings not previously mentioned in the Discourse on Wisdom (Paññākathā), which was spoken immediately after the Discourse on Voidness (Suññakathā), the latter being specifically the proximate cause of wisdom. In that Discourse on Wisdom, first, among the seven contemplations (anupassanā), seven types of wisdom, each having one contemplation as its root, are shown preceded by questions. Again, three types of wisdom, having the seven contemplations as their root and each having a progressively higher root, are shown without questions. Thus, from the beginning, the ten complete types of wisdom are shown.

Among those ten types of wisdom, first, aniccānupassanā (contemplation of impermanence) occurs swiftly in formations seen as impermanent, as 'what is impermanent is suffering' (by way of suffering) and 'what is suffering is non-self' (by way of non-self). Therefore, when that contemplation of impermanence is developed and frequently practiced, it fulfills javanapaññā (swift wisdom). Indeed, it is called javana (swift) because it runs swiftly in its own objects; being both swift and wisdom, it is called javanapaññā.

Dukkhānupassanā (contemplation of suffering), being based on the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) and thus becoming powerful, breaks through and shatters longing (craving). Therefore, it fulfills nibbedhikapaññā (penetrative wisdom). Indeed, it is called nibbedhika because it penetrates; being both penetrative and wisdom, it is called nibbedhikapaññā.

Anattānupassanā (contemplation of non-self) fulfills mahāpaññā (great wisdom) because it reaches greatness by attaining growth through the vision of voidness. Indeed, it is called mahāpaññā because it reaches growth and is great; being both great and wisdom, it is called mahāpaññā.

Nibbidānupassanā (contemplation of disenchantment) is sharp because it is capable of being disenchanted with all formations, having reached a powerful state through the repeated practice of the three contemplations (impermanence, suffering, and non-self) even more than before. Therefore, it fulfills tikkhapaññā (sharp wisdom).

Virāgānupassanā (contemplation of fading away) is extensive because it is capable of being dispassionate towards all formations, having reached a more developed state through the power of repeated practice of the three contemplations even more than before. Therefore, it fulfills vipulapaññā (extensive wisdom).

Nirodhānupassanā (contemplation of cessation) is profound because it is capable of seeing the cessation of all formations by way of the characteristic of passing away, having reached a more developed state through the power of repeated practice of the three contemplations even more than before. Therefore, it fulfills gambhīrapaññā (profound wisdom). Indeed, the cessation (nirodha) of formations is profound because its basis cannot be obtained by those with shallow wisdom. Wisdom that has gained a footing in that profound cessation is also profound.

Paṭinissaggānupassanā (contemplation of relinquishment) is 'not near' (dissimilar) because it is capable of relinquishing all formations by way of the characteristic of passing away, having reached a more developed state through the power of repeated practice of the three contemplations even more than before. It means it is far from the six types of wisdom mentioned previously because it has reached the culmination of growth.
248:
Therefore, (relinquishment-contemplation) fulfills the uncommon wisdom (asāmanta-paññā) because it is unlike other wisdoms. That uncommon wisdom is called asāmanta-paññā because it is far from lower wisdoms, or it is called asāmanta-paññā because it is a wisdom that is not near (to them). "Paṇḍiccaṃ paripūrenti" means fulfilling the state of being a wise person (erudition). Because a person who has fully developed the aforementioned seven wisdoms and has reached the characteristic of a wise person, becomes a wise person and is endowed with erudition through the knowledges of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa), conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), which are called the culminating insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā); therefore, it is said, "Paṇḍiccaṃ paripūrenti."

"Aṭṭha paññā" (eight wisdoms) refers to all eight wisdoms together with the wisdom called erudition (paṇḍicca). "Puthu-paññံ paripūrenti" means that a wise person endowed with that erudition, immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), takes Nibbāna as the object and, due to attaining the supramundane state and being distinct and separate from mundane wisdom, reaches the wisdom of the Path and Fruit called abundant wisdom (puthu-paññā). Therefore, it is said, "The eight wisdoms fulfill the abundant wisdom."

In the words beginning with "Imā nava paññā" (these nine wisdoms), for that noble person (ariya-puggala) who has attained the Path and Fruit in due order, five types of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) occur: reviewing the Path, and then after descending into and emerging from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) immediately after the Fruit, reviewing the Fruit; in this same manner, reviewing the defilements abandoned, reviewing the remaining defilements, and reviewing Nibbāna. These occur because of the noble person's association with the sublime supramundane Dhamma and because the mental continuum exists in a state of joy. Among those reviewings, the wisdom reviewing the Path and the wisdom reviewing the Fruit constitute the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). How? It is stated in the Commentary, following the Abhidhamma Pali: "These five things—resultant (effect) produced by a cause, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, the resultant (vipāka), and the functional (kiriya)—are called 'attha' (meaning/result)." Since Nibbāna is an 'attha', the Path and Fruit knowledges that take Nibbāna as their object are the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), according to the statement: "Knowledge regarding meanings is attha-paṭisambhidā." The knowledge that reviews that Path and Fruit knowledge (which is attha-paṭisambhidā) is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā), according to the statement: "Knowledge regarding knowledges is paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā." That reviewing wisdom is called joyous wisdom (hāsa-paññā) for a person whose mental continuum exists in a state of joy. Therefore, it is said, "The nine wisdoms fulfill the joyous wisdom," and "Joyous wisdom is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity." Wisdom of all kinds is called 'paññā' because of its sense of making known (paññāpana), which is the making clear of various meanings, or it is called 'paññā' because it knows things in various ways.
249:
"Tassa" means of that noble person (ariya-puggala) who has the aforementioned qualities. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa). "Attha-vavatthānato" means by way of determining the fivefold meaning (attha) as previously mentioned. Regarding this, it is stated in the Samaṇakaraṇīyakathā: "Among the five types of meaning—cause-result, Nibbāna, the meaning of the word, and then resultant and functional—it is the knowledge that has reached the first type of division." "Adhigatā hoti" means it is attained. That very analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) is realized through the realization of attainment. It is touched by wisdom through the touch of attainment. "Dhamma-vavatthānato" means by way of determining the five things called 'dhamma' as stated in the Abhidhamma according to the Pali: "These five things—the cause that produces the result, the Noble Path, the spoken word (bhāsita), the wholesome (kusala), and the unwholesome (akusala)—are called 'dhamma'." Regarding this also, it is stated in the Samaṇakaraṇīyakathā: "Among the five types of dhamma—cause, the Noble Path, the word, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—it is the knowledge that has reached the second type of division." "Nirutti-vavatthānato" means by way of determining the expressions (nirutti) that are appropriate to those respective meanings (attha) and laws (dhamma). "Paṭibhāna-vavatthānato" means by way of determining the three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) referred to as perspicuity (paṭibhāna). The words "Tassimā" are a concluding statement.

Having thus shown the distinction of the contemplations (anupassanā) by way of all-inclusiveness, the Teacher now says "Rūpe aniccānupassanā" etc., showing them by way of the division of objects (vatthu). That statement has the same meaning as explained below. Again, wishing to show swift wisdom (javana-paññā) by way of the past, future, and present in the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) and so on, the Teacher posed questions by way of the pure form aggregate etc., and by way of the past, future, and present form aggregate etc., and gave the answers according to the order of the questions. In those answers, the wisdom first pointed out in the answers regarding the pure form aggregate etc., is pointed out as swift wisdom (javana-paññā) by way of being swift in those past etc. (objects) in all the answers that have the past, future, and present as their basis.

Furthermore, wishing to show the divisions of wisdom preceded by many Suttas, the Teacher first summarized the Suttas. In those many Suttas, "sappurisa-saṃsevo" means associating with good people (sappurisa) of the kind mentioned below. "Saddhamma-savanaṃ" means hearing the words of the true Dhamma, which explain the practice of virtue (sīla) and so on, in the presence of those good people. "Yoniso-manasikāro" means attending (to the Dhamma) by proper means, by way of investigating the meaning of the teachings heard. "Dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti" means practicing the practice of virtue etc., which follows the supramundane Dhamma.
250:
The four terms—*paññāpaṭilābhāya* (for the acquisition of wisdom), *paññāvuddhiyā* (for the growth of wisdom), *paññāvepullāya* (for the expansion of wisdom), and *paññābāhullāya* (for the abundance of wisdom)—are expressions describing the state [of wisdom] by way of wisdom itself (such as its acquisition, etc.). The remaining twelve terms are expressions describing the state [of wisdom] by way of the person (such as the greatness of their wisdom, etc.).

## 1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixteen Kinds of Wisdom (Soḷasapaññāniddesavaṇṇanā)

In the Suttanta Exposition, the phrase "of the six direct-knowledge insights" (*channaṃ abhiññāñāṇānaṃ*) refers to the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*), the divine ear (*dibbasota-ñāṇa*), penetration of the minds of others (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), and the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*). "Of the seventy-three kinds of knowledge" (*tesattatīnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ*) refers to the knowledges common to disciples that have been explained in the *Ñāṇakathā*. Regarding "of the seventy-seven kinds of knowledge" (*sattasattatīnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ*):

"Monks, I will teach you the seventy-seven bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*). Listen well and pay close attention; I will speak." (He said:) "Monks, what are the seventy-seven bases of knowledge? The knowledge that 'with birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be'; the knowledge that 'when birth is absent, aging-and-death does not come to be'; the knowledge that in the past, 'with birth as condition, aging-and-death came to be'; the knowledge that 'when birth was absent, aging-and-death did not come to be'; the knowledge that in the future, 'with birth as condition, aging-and-death will come to be'; the knowledge that 'when birth is absent, aging-and-death will not come to be.' And whatever knowledge he has regarding the stability of the Dhamma (*dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa*), he also has the knowledge that 'this knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma is of a nature to decay, to vanish, to fade away, and to cease.' The knowledge that 'with existence as condition, birth comes to be' ... (and so on) ... the knowledge that 'with clinging as condition, existence comes to be' ... the knowledge that 'with craving as condition, clinging comes to be' ... the knowledge that 'with feeling as condition, craving comes to be' ... the knowledge that 'with contact as condition, feeling comes to be' ... the knowledge that 'with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact comes to be' ... the knowledge that 'with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold sense base comes to be' ... the knowledge that 'with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be' ... the knowledge that 'with volitional formations as condition, consciousness comes to be' ... the knowledge that 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be'; the knowledge that 'when ignorance is absent, volitional formations do not come to be'; the knowledge that in the past, 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations came to be'; the knowledge that 'when ignorance was absent, volitional formations did not come to be'; the knowledge that in the future, 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations will come to be'; the knowledge that 'when ignorance is absent, volitional formations will not come to be.' And whatever knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma he has, he also has the knowledge that 'this knowledge is of a nature to decay, to vanish, to fade away, and to cease.' Monks, these are called the seventy-seven bases of knowledge."
251:
Thus, the Blessed One taught the seventy-seven kinds of knowledge in the *Nidānavagga*. However, the forty-four bases of knowledge taught by way of four kinds for each of the eleven factors—namely, "knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death, knowledge of the cessation of aging-and-death, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of aging-and-death"—are not included here in the *Paññā* section of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*. In both cases, these knowledges are called "bases of knowledge" (*ñāṇavatthu*) because they are the bases for welfare and happiness. In the words beginning with *lābha* (gain), the word *lābha* itself is distinguished by a prefix and called *paṭilābha* (acquisition). Again, by way of explaining its meaning, it is called *patti* (attainment) and *sampatti* (achievement). *Phassanā* (touching) means touching by way of attainment (*adhigama*). *Sacchikiriyā* (realization) means realization by way of acquisition. *Upasampadā* (attainment/entering upon) means accomplishment.

"And of the seven trainees" (*sattannañca sekkhānaṃ*) refers to the [knowledge] of the seven types of persons, such as those standing on the path of stream-entry, who are called "trainees" (*sekkhā*) because they are training in the three trainings. "And of the noble worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇakassa ca*) refers to the [knowledge] of a worldling who is called "noble" (*kalyāṇa*) in the sense of being good, because they are engaged in the practice leading to Nibbāna. It is called *vaḍḍhitavaḍḍhanā* (growth of what has grown) because there is the increasing of the wisdom that has been developed by this wisdom. It occurs for the growth of wisdom by way of the path-wisdom and fruition-wisdom of the aforementioned eight persons, and especially by way of the wisdom of the Arahant. Likewise, it occurs for the expansion of wisdom (*paññāvepullāya*). In the words beginning with "he grasps great meanings" (*mahante atthe pariggaṇhāti*), the noble disciple who has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) grasps meanings and so forth by making them objects. All "great wisdom" (*mahāpaññā*) occurs only for noble disciples. The objects of that wisdom are only the meanings mentioned below.

In the words beginning with "in the many various aggregates" (*puthunānākhandhesu*), the word *nānā* (various) expresses the meaning of the word *puthu* (many). Knowledge proceeds; therefore, it is called "many-sided wisdom" (*puthupaññā*). The meaning is that because knowledge proceeds in those aforementioned aggregates and so forth, that knowledge is called *puthupaññā*. "In various [modes of] dependent origination" (*nānāpaṭiccasamuppādesu*) is stated in the plural because of the multiplicity of conditions by way of dependently arisen phenomena. "In various voidnesses and non-apprehensions" (*nānāsuññatamanupalabbhesu*): "Apprehension" (*upalabbha*) means obtaining; it has the meaning of grasping (by way of self or what belongs to self). That which is not to be grasped is "non-apprehension" (*anupalabbha*). Because these non-apprehensions are many, it is stated in the plural as *anupalabbhā*. Alternatively, *nānāsuññatānupalabbha* means the non-obtaining of self, what belongs to self, etc., in the many voidnesses by way of the twenty-five kinds of voidness; [knowledge occurs] in those things. Instead of saying *nānāsuññatānupalabbhesu*, the letter 'm' is inserted by way of euphonic junction (*padasandhi*), as in *adukkhamasukhā* and so forth. These five kinds of wisdom are common (*sādhāraṇa*) to noble worldlings. The wisdoms occurring in various meanings and so forth are common only to the noble ones. "In states common to worldlings" (*puthujjanasādhāraṇe dhamme*) refers to mundane states. By this concluding teaching on what is common to worldlings, it is a distinct wisdom because it is separate from mundane states and takes Nibbāna as its object; therefore, it is called *puthupaññā*.

"Extensive wisdom" (*vipulapaññā*) should be understood by the method of "great wisdom" (*mahāpaññā*). Because there are many benefits for the person who grasps the aforementioned states, the abundance of the wisdom that grasps those [states such as] language (*nirutti*) and Dhamma should be understood. Because those states are naturally abundant and extensive, the extensiveness of both the states and the wisdom should be understood. "Profound wisdom" (*gambhīrapaññā*) should be understood by the method taught in the exposition of "many-sided wisdom" (*puthupaññā*). Those states such as the aggregates, and those non-apprehensible states called the fifteen kinds of voidness, and the wisdom that knows those states such as the aggregates, which ordinary people...
252:
By the sequence of teaching starting from the common worldling to the end, wisdom that is distinct from the mundane and takes Nibbāna as its object, being separate and distinct, is called varied wisdom (puthupaññā).

Extensive wisdom (vipulapaññā) should be understood in the same way as great wisdom (mahāpaññā). For one who grasps the aforementioned dhammas, the greatness of the wisdom that grasps those dhammas should be understood because of the greatness of their qualities; and the extensiveness of the dhammas and the wisdom should be understood because those dhammas themselves are great and sublime. Profound wisdom (gambhīrapaññā) should be understood in the same way as varied wisdom (puthupaññā). Those dhammas, those unattainable dhammas, and that wisdom are profound because their basis cannot be attained by ordinary people.

"Of which person" refers only to a noble person (ariya). "Any other person" refers to a worldling (puthujjana). "To attain" means to reach. "Unattainable" means unable to reach. "Other persons" refers only to worldlings. "The eighth person" refers to one standing in the path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimaggaṭṭha), who is the eighth when counting from the state of the fruit of Arahantship. "Distant" means far from being near. "Particularly distant" means especially far. "Extremely distant" means very especially far. "Not near" means not close. "Not in the vicinity" means not in the nearby area. These two statements with negation are words that emphasize only the state of being distant. "Depending on" means because of. "Of a Stream-enterer" refers to one standing in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphalaṭṭha). By this statement starting with "the eighth person," it is said that the wisdom of each respective path is distant from the wisdom of each respective fruit. The word "Paccekasambuddha" is distinguished by a prefix (upasagga). However, the other two words, "Tathāgata" and "Arahaṃ," appear purely without prefixes.

"The wisdom of a Paccekabuddha and of the world with its devas is distant from the wisdom of a Tathāgata," and so on; wishing to show that same meaning of being distant in various ways, he said "skilled in the divisions of wisdom" (paññāpabhedakusala) and so on.

In that context, "skilled in the divisions of wisdom" means being expert in the infinite varieties of one's own divisions of wisdom. "Possessing divided knowledge" (pabhinnañāṇa) means having knowledge that has reached infinite divisions. By this word "pabhinnañāṇa," even though one is skilled in the divisions of wisdom, it shows the state of those types of wisdom having infinite divisions. "Attained analytical insights" (adhigatapaṭisambhidā) means having attained the four supreme analytical insights. "Attained the four kinds of intrepidity" (catuvesārajjappatta) means having reached the four kinds of knowledge known as intrepidity (vesārajja).

As it is said (Yathāha):

"To you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, 'These things are not fully understood [by you]'—that a recluse, a brahmin, or a deva..."
253:
Or that Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else in the world will, in accordance with the Dhamma, accuse me—O bhikkhus, I do not see any such ground. O bhikkhus, not seeing any such ground for accusation, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence. [Regarding the claim:] 'While you claim to be one whose taints are exhausted, these taints are not fully exhausted'; [or regarding the claim:] 'Those sexual practices which are said to be obstructive are not able to be an obstruction to one who indulges in them'; [or regarding the claim:] 'The Dhamma you have taught for a certain purpose does not lead one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering'—O bhikkhus, I do not see any ground on which a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could, in accordance with the Dhamma, accuse me in such matters. O bhikkhus, not seeing any such ground for accusation, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence (AN 4.8, MN 1.150).

'Dasabalabaladhārī' means: these Buddhas possess the ten powers, therefore they are called 'Dasabala'. The powers of the Dasabala are called 'Dasabalabala'. Because He bears these 'Dasabalabala', He is called 'Dasabalabaladhārī'. It means He bears the powers of the Tenfold Knowledge. By these three expressions, only the beginning of the various infinite things to be known is shown. That very Blessed One is called 'Purisāsabha' (Bull among men) because He is regarded as the most auspicious through the power of wisdom. He is 'Purisasīha' (Lion among men) because of His fearlessness. He is 'Purisanāga' (Elephant among men) because of His greatness. He is 'Purisājañña' (Noble steed among men) because He knows things in detail. He is 'Purisadhōrayha' (Leader among men) because He bears the burden of worldly affairs.

Then, wishing to show the special qualities such as radiance (teja) obtained from infinite wisdom, and showing that those qualities like radiance have infinite wisdom as their root, He said 'Anantañāṇo' and then 'Anantatejo' and so on. Therein, 'Anantañāṇo' means having wisdom that is without end in terms of number and efficacy. 'Anantatejo' means having infinite radiance of wisdom by dispelling the darkness of delusion in the continuities of those to be tamed. 'Anantayasa' means having an infinite sound of fame spread throughout the three worlds solely through the qualities of wisdom. 'Aḍḍho' means being prosperous with the wealth of wisdom. 'Mahaddhano' means having great wealth of wisdom due to its great efficacy even though it is an increase of the wealth of wisdom. There is also a variant reading 'Mahādhano'. 'Dhanavā' means one who possesses the wealth of wisdom that is praiseworthy, constant, and superlative. Experts in grammar accept this word in all three of these meanings.
254:
In this way, having shown the accomplishment of the Blessed One's personal attainment (attasampatti) through the quality of wisdom, the author now speaks the words beginning with "Netā" to show the accomplishment of the welfare of the world (lokahitasampatti) through that same quality of wisdom. In that passage, he is called "Netā" (the Leader) because he leads beings (veneyya) from the place of danger called Saṃsāra to the place of safety (peace) called Nibbāna. Even at the time of leading them, he is called "Vinetā" (the Discipliner) because he disciplines beings through the power of restraint-discipline (saṃvara-vinaya) and abandonment-discipline (pahāna-vinaya). At the time of teaching the Dhamma, he is called "Anunetā" (the Conciliator) because he leads them appropriately by cutting off their doubts. He is called "Paññāpetā" (the Declarer) because, having cut off doubts, he makes known the various meanings that should be known. He is called "Nijjhāpetā" (the Insight-inducer) because he causes them to see by making them reach a decision regarding those meanings. He is called "Pekkhetā" (the Observer) because he makes them see specifically through the power of applying themselves to the meaning thus perceived. He is called "Pasādetā" (the Gladdener) because he gladdens those practicing beings with the fruit of their practice (paṭipatti-phala).

In the phrase "So hi Bhagavā", the word "hi" is a particle used to indicate the reason for the meaning just mentioned. Regarding "Anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā" (the producer of the unarisen path): he is called "Uppādetā" because, for the sake of the world's welfare, he produced in his own continuity at the foot of the Bodhi tree the Noble Path, which had never arisen before in his continuity and which is the cause of the six uncommon knowledges (cha-asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa). Regarding "Asañjātassa maggassa sañjanetā" (the generator of the ungenerated path): he is called "Sañjanetā" because, from the time of turning the Wheel of Dhamma until the present day, he has generated in the continuities of beings the Noble Path, which had never been generated before and which has the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa) as its cause. Indeed, because the Noble Path arises in the continuities of the disciples to be guided only through the words spoken by the Blessed One, the Blessed One is called "Sañjanetā". Regarding "Anakkhātassa maggassa akkhātā" (the declarer of the undeclared path): he is called "Akkhātā" because, after giving the prophecy (byākaraṇa) for Buddhahood to Bodhisattas who are endowed with the eight qualities and have made the resolution (abhinīhāra), he declares the path of perfections (pāramī-magga) which had not been declared before. Alternatively, he is called "Akkhātā" because he declares the Noble Path that is to arise at the foot of the Bodhi tree, or simply by giving the prophecy, "You will become a Buddha." This method is also applicable in the case of giving prophecies to Paccekabodhisattas.

"Maggaññū" (knower of the path) means he knows the Noble Path he himself produced through the power of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa). "Maggavidū" (knower of the path) means he is skilled in the Noble Path that is to be generated in the continuities of beings. "Maggakovido" (expert in the path) means he is especially skilled in the path to be declared to Bodhisattas. Alternatively, he is "Maggaññū" because he knows the path of practice for Supreme Enlightenment (abhisambodhi); "Maggavidū" because he knows the path of practice for Individual Enlightenment (paccekabodhi); and "Maggakovido" because he is expert in the path of practice for Disciple Enlightenment (sāvakabodhi). Or again, according to the words, "By this path they have crossed in the past, they will cross, and they are crossing the flood," the meanings are applied respectively according to the path of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the past, future, and present; or according to the paths of voidness (suññata), signless (animitta), and effortless (appaṇihita); or according to the paths of individuals of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū), those who understand through expansion (vipañcitaññū), and those to be led (neyya). "Maggānugāmī ca pana" refers to those who follow the path traveled by the Blessed One (meaning the disciples).
255:
...having become. In this context, the word "ca" is a particle in the sense of "reason". By this word "ca", the reason for the Blessed One's attainment of qualities such as producing the path is meant. The word "pana" is a particle in the sense of "action". By that word "pana", the Blessed One's performance of the path-making is meant. "Pacchā samannāgatā" (endowed afterwards) means being endowed with qualities such as virtue (sīla) that arise after the Blessed One, who traveled first. Thus, the Elder Sāriputta, through words such as "the producer of the unarisen path," spoke of the Blessed One's qualities by relying only on the Path of Arahantship, because all the Blessed One's qualities, such as virtue, arise only by relying on the Path of Arahantship.

"Knowing, he knows" means he knows what should be known. Because he possesses omniscience (sabbaññutā-ñāṇa), it means he knows with wisdom all things that should be known, including all five categories of things to be known (neyyapatha). "Seeing, he sees" means he sees what should be seen. Because he is all-seeing (sabbadassāvitā), it means he sees with the eye of wisdom those very categories of things to be known, as if seeing them with the physical eye. Alternatively, unlike some people who, while perceiving wrongly, do not know even though they think they know, and do not see even though they think they see, the Blessed One is not like that. The Blessed One, perceiving according to reality, truly knows when he knows, and truly sees when he sees. This Blessed One is "become the eye" (cakkhubhūta) because he is the leader in seeing the Four Noble Truths. He is "become knowledge" (ñāṇabhūta) because of the sense of knowing clearly. He is "become Dhamma" (dhammabhūta) either because his nature is unerring, or because he brings about the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma), being composed of the Dhamma thought by the mind and uttered by the voice. He is "become Brahma" (brahmabhūta) because he is the most excellent. Alternatively, he is cakkhubhūta because he is like an eye, ñāṇabhūta because he is like knowledge, dhammabhūta because he is like the Dhamma, and brahmabhūta because he is like Brahma. That Blessed One is the "Speaker" (vattā) because he teaches or brings about the Dhamma. He is the "Proclaimer" (pavattā) because he teaches or brings it about in various ways. He is the "Bringer of Meaning" (atthassa ninnetā) because he draws out and shows the meanings. He is the "Giver of the Deathless" (amatassa dātā) because he teaches the practice for attaining Nibbāna, or because he causes the attainment of Nibbāna through the Dhamma teaching that reveals Nibbāna. He is the "Lord of Dhamma" (dhammassāmī) because he produced the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), because he grants the supramundane Dhamma to beings as appropriate and at ease, and because he is the master of all dhammas. The meaning of the term "Tathāgata" is as stated below.

Now, wishing to distinguish the quality mentioned by the words "Knowing, he knows," etc., through omniscience, the author speaks the words beginning with "Natthi" (there is not) to establish omniscience. For the Blessed One, who is such, there is nothing that is not realized, because delusion (moha) along with its latent tendencies (vāsanā) has been destroyed in all dhammas by the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship, which is accomplished through the power of the merit of his perfections. Because all dhammas are known without delusion, there is nothing that is unknown.
256:
In the same way, because all phenomena are seen by the eye of knowledge just as they would be seen by the physical eye, there is nothing that is unseen. Because they are attained and reached by knowledge, there is nothing that is unknown. Because they are realized through the realization of non-delusion, there is nothing that is not realized. Because they are touched by the wisdom of non-delusion, there is nothing that is not touched by wisdom.

'Present' (paccuppanna) refers to either the present time or a present phenomenon. 'Taking up' (upādāya) means having taken or having included within. By the word 'taking up' itself, Nibbāna, which is free from time, is also included. Words such as 'past' (atīta) and so on are connected either with the word 'does not exist' (natthi) or with the word 'all' (sabba). 'All phenomena' (sabbe dhammā) means the exhaustive inclusion of all conditioned (saṅkhata) and unconditioned (asaṅkhata) phenomena. 'In every way' (sabbākārena) means the exhaustive inclusion of every single phenomenon through all its aspects, such as the aspect of impermanence (anicca). 'In the presence of knowledge' (ñāṇamukhe) means in the presence of knowledge. 'They come into range' (āpāthaṃ āgacchanti) means they reach the point of convergence. The word 'to be known' (jānitabba) is stated to explain the meaning of the word 'knowable' (neyya).

In the words 'benefit for oneself' (attattho vā) and so on, the word 'vā' has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya). 'Benefit for oneself' (attattho) means one's own benefit. 'Benefit for others' (parattho) means the benefit of others in the three worlds of beings. 'Benefit for both' (ubhayattho) means the benefit of both oneself and others simultaneously. 'Pertaining to the present life' (diṭṭhadhammiko) means an interest connected with the present life or a benefit in the present life. An interest connected with the future life or a benefit in the future life is called 'pertaining to the future life' (samparāyiko). In the words 'evident' (uttāno) and so on, that which is expressed through conventional usage and is easily established in knowledge is called 'evident' (uttāna). That which is expressed beyond conventional usage, is connected with emptiness (suññatā), and is difficult to establish in knowledge is called 'profound' (gambhīra). Supramundane (lokuttara) phenomena are called 'hidden' (gūḷha) because they are extremely concealed. Aspects such as impermanence are called 'concealed' (paṭicchanna) because they are covered by compactness (ghana) and so on. That which is expressed through obscure conventional usage and must be understood by drawing out the intention rather than taking it literally is called 'to be inferred' (neyya). That which is expressed through clear conventional usage and whose intention is understood by the words alone is called 'explicit' (nīta). The meaning of perfectly pure virtue, concentration, and insight is called 'blameless' (anavajja) because it is free from fault through the power of abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna) and abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna). The meaning of the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is called 'free from defilements' (nikkilesa) because it completely cuts off defilements. The meaning of the Noble Fruit (ariyaphala) is called 'purified' (vodāna) because of the subsiding of defilements. Nibbāna is called the 'ultimate meaning' (paramattha) because it is the supreme phenomenon among conditioned and unconditioned things. 'Revolves' (parivattati) means that because it is the object of the Buddha's knowledge, it does not exist outside of it, but occurs by pervading, encompassing, embracing, or specifically existing within the Buddha's knowledge.

By the words 'all bodily action' (sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ) and so on, he shows the state of the Blessed One as being composed of knowledge. 'Follows knowledge' (ñāṇānuparivattati) means it follows knowledge; the meaning is that it is never devoid of knowledge. 'Unobstructed' (appaṭihata) shows the state of being without hindrances (nirāvaraṇa). Again, illustrating omniscience with a simile...
257:
Desiring to complete the explanation of omniscience with a simile, he said 'as far as' (yāvatakaṃ) and so on. In that text, because it is to be known, it is called 'knowable' (neyya). Because this knowledge has the limit of the knowable phenomena, it is called 'having the knowable as its limit' (neyyapariyantika). For those who are not omniscient, such as Paccekabuddhas, there is no limit to the knowable. In the term 'having knowledge as its limit' (ñāṇapariyantika), the same method should be understood. He shows the meaning already stated in the first pair (yamaka) with distinction by this second pair; and by the third pair, he shows it by defining it through the power of negation (paṭisedha). Here also, the knowable is called the 'path of the knowable' (neyyapatha) because it is the path of knowledge. 'Standing at each other's limits' (aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyino) means that by knowing the knowable and the knowing knowledge exhaustively, they have the nature of standing at each other's limits. 'Dependent on advertence' (āvajjanappaṭibaddha) means it is dependent on mind-door advertence; the meaning is that he knows immediately after advertence. 'Dependent on wish' (ākaṅkhappaṭibaddha) means it is dependent on his wish; the meaning is that he knows with the knowledge in the impulsion (javana) immediately after advertence. The other two terms are stated to clarify the meaning of these two terms, 'advertence' and 'wish', respectively. The terms 'The Buddha knows the inclinations' (Buddho āsayaṃ jānāti) and so on have been explained in the 'Discourse on Knowledge' (Ñāṇakathā). In the Mahāniddesa, however, it appears as 'The Blessed One knows the inclinations' (Bhagavā āsayaṃ jānāti). Where 'of the Buddha, the Blessed One' (Buddhassa Bhagavato) appears in that Mahāniddesa, in some places in this text, it appears as 'of the Buddha' (Buddhassa).

'Even' (antamaso) means by way of the upper limit (at the very least). In the phrase 'the timi and timingala fish' (timitimingalaṃ), there is one species of fish named timi; there is one species of fish named timingala, larger than that, which is able to swallow the timi fish; and there is one species of fish named timitimingala, five hundred leagues in size, which is able to swallow even the timingala fish. Here, it should be understood that the singular number is used by taking the species (jāti). In 'the garuḷa venateyya', the name garuḷa is by way of species, and venateyya is by way of lineage (gotta). 'In a portion' (padese) means in one part. 'Equal to Sāriputta' (Sāriputtasamā) should be understood as referring to the Elders who were the Generals of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) of all Buddhas. Indeed, there are no other disciples besides Venerable Sāriputta who are equal to the General of the Dhamma in wisdom. Therefore, he said: 'Bhikkhus, foremost among my bhikkhu disciples of great wisdom is Sāriputta.' And it is said in the Commentary:
'Setting aside the Buddha, the Lord of the World, whatever other living beings there are, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of Sāriputta's wisdom.'

'Having pervaded' (pharitvā) means that the Buddha's knowledge reaches the wisdom of all devas and humans, and stands pervading and encompassing their wisdom. 'Having surpassed' (atighaṃsitvā) means that the Buddha's knowledge transcends the wisdom of all devas and humans, and encompasses all knowable phenomena (neyyadhamma) that are not within their range...
258:
Among my disciples, the monks of great wisdom, the Venerable Sāriputta is the foremost. In the Visuddhimagga Commentary, it is also stated: "Setting aside the Buddha, the Lord of the World, the wisdom of all other beings in the entire universe cannot match even a sixteenth part (or one part in two hundred and fifty-six) of the wisdom of the Venerable Sāriputta."

The Buddha's Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa) stands pervading and overwhelming the wisdom of all devas and humans. It stands surpassing and destroying all the things that should be known (neyyadhamma) which are not the objects of those devas and humans. In the Mahāniddesa, however, there is the reading 'abhibhavitvā'; it also has the meaning 'madditvā' (crushing). Through the Pali passages beginning with 'yepi te', he shows the evident reason for standing thus by pervading and surpassing. In that Pali, 'paṇḍita' refers to those endowed with wisdom. 'Nipuṇa' refers to those who possess subtle and fine intellect and are capable of penetrating subtle and profound meanings. 'Kataparappavādā' refers to those who know the doctrines of others and have practiced debating with others. 'Vālavedhirūpā' refers to those who are like archers capable of hitting the tip of a hair.

'Vobhindantā maññe caranti paññāgatena diṭṭhigatānīti' means that just as a hair-splitting archer pierces the tip of a hair, they go about breaking and destroying the subtle views (diṭṭhi) of others with their own wisdom. Alternatively, as in phrases like 'gūthagataṃ muttagataṃ', wisdom itself is called 'paññāgata', and views themselves are called 'diṭṭhigata'.

'Pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā' means having prepared questions consisting of two parts, three parts, or four parts. Because those questions are so numerous, the word 'abhisaṅkharitvā' is mentioned twice to include them all. The phrase 'gūḷhāni ca paṭicchannāni atthajātāni' should be understood as the remaining text. Seeing that those people are fit to be disciplined, the Buddha, desiring that 'they may ask the questions they have prepared,' allows them to ask. However, to others who are not fit to be disciplined, he does not give the opportunity to ask questions but preaches the Dhamma to those who approach him.

He taught this matter thus: "Those people prepare questions, thinking, 'We will approach the recluse Gotama and ask this question; if the recluse Gotama, being thus asked, answers in this way, we will refute him in this manner. If, being thus asked, he answers in that way, we will also refute him in that manner.' When they approach the recluse Gotama, the Buddha instructs, urges, rouses, and gladdens them with a Dhamma talk. Then, having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the recluse Gotama's Dhamma talk, they do not even dare to ask the question, let alone refute him; on the contrary, they simply become disciples of the recluse Gotama."

If it is asked why they do not ask the questions, it is because the Buddha, while preaching the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly, observes the inclination of the assembly. Then he sees, 'These wise men have come having prepared secret and profound questions like a treasure carried in a waistband.' Even before they ask, the Buddha sees the potential faults in the questions, in the answers, and in the meaning, phrasing, and syllables. He incorporates the explanation into his Dhamma talk, showing, 'One who wishes to ask should ask thus; one who wishes to answer should answer thus,' regarding the questions they brought like treasures in their waistbands. Then those wise men are satisfied, thinking, 'It is indeed great that we did not ask these questions we devised; if we had asked, the recluse Gotama would have placed us in an untenable position and brought us to shame.'
259: Even though they have not yet asked, the Buddha, seeing that 'There are such faults in asking questions, such faults in answering, and such faults in the meaning, words, and syllables; one who wishes to ask these questions should ask thus, and one who wishes to answer should answer thus,' brings forth questions like treasures kept in a waistband and inserts them into the middle of his Dhamma discourse to demonstrate them. At that time, the wise think, 'It is truly great that we did not ask these questions. If we had asked, the Ascetic Gotama would have placed us in an unstable position and defeated us,' and they become delighted. Furthermore, when the Buddhas preach the Dhamma, they pervade the assembly with loving-kindness (mettā). Because of this pervading loving-kindness, the minds of the multitude become clear and confident in the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala). The Buddhas have reached the pinnacle of physical form (rūpaggappatta); they are endowed with a sight that one never tires of looking at, a sweet voice, a soft tongue, and well-aligned teeth. They preach the Dhamma as if pouring the nectar of immortality (amata) into the heart. Then, those whose minds are clear due to his pervading loving-kindness think, 'We are unable to hold a contrary view against the Blessed One who speaks such unambiguous speech, speech that is not in vain, and speech that leads to liberation (niyyānika).' Thus, due to their own state of devotion, they no longer ask questions. 'They are preached and answered' means that by uttering the questions that should be asked, saying 'You should ask thus,' those questions are already preached by the Blessed One.
