And just as they should be answered, they are already answered. 'Having shown the reasons' means that by answering with the reasons, saying 'It is thus because of this reason,' those questions have their reasons shown by the Blessed One. 'They fall at the feet of the Blessed One' means that those wise kshatriyas and others, due to the Blessed One's answering of questions, become those who have fallen near the Blessed One, lying at his feet; the meaning is that they become disciples (sāvaka) or lay followers (upāsaka). It means they attain the achievement of being a disciple or a lay follower. 'Then' refers to the time immediately after they have attained that state. 'In that place' means in that context or in the matter of that incomparable wisdom (asāmanta-pañña). 'Shines intensely' means it illuminates and makes clear exceedingly. 'By wisdom' means that by whatever wisdom the Blessed One possesses, the Blessed One alone shines intensely. This word 'iti' indicates the cause. For this reason, the one of incomparable wisdom (asāmanta-pañña) is supreme. ## Bhūripaññā means overcoming lust (rāga). It is called Bhūripaññā because the respective path-wisdom (magga-paññā) overcomes, conquers, and crushes the lust (rāga) that is to be abandoned by it. 'Bhūri' has the meaning of 'extensive' and 'consuming poison'. The wisdom that is extensive overcomes the opposing defilements. Wisdom that is not extensive cannot overcome them. Therefore, the meaning of overcoming is stated for Bhūripaññā. According to the reading 'one who overcomes,' the respective fruition-wisdom (phala-paññā) has the nature of having already overcome the respective lust; therefore, it is called Bhūripaññā. There is also a reading 'abhibhavatā'. In the remaining terms, it should be understood in this same way. The meaning of lust (rāga) and so on should be understood thus: the state that has the characteristic of attachment is called lust. Alternatively, lust is attachment...
260:
The meaning is very clear. That wisdom which spreads (over objects) is the one that overcomes the opposing defilements; wisdom that does not spread cannot overcome them. Therefore, the sense of 'overcoming' is stated in Bhūripaññā. 'Abhibhavitā' means that the respective wisdom of the fruit (phala-paññā) has the nature of overcoming and crushing the respective lust (rāga); thus it is called Bhūripaññā. There is also a variant reading 'Abhibhavatā'. The same method should be understood for the remaining terms. Among lust and others, the state characterized by attachment is Rāga (lust). The state characterized by corruption is Dosa (hatred). The state characterized by delusion is Moha (delusion). The state characterized by anger is Kodha (anger). The state characterized by malice is Upanāha (enmity). Anger occurring in the earlier period is called Kodha, and in the later period, it is called Upanāha. The state characterized by denigrating others' virtues is Makkha (denigration). The state characterized by domineering is Paḷāsa. The state characterized by envying others' prosperity is Issā (envy). The state characterized by concealing one's own prosperity is Macchariya (avarice). The state characterized by hiding one's own wrongdoings is Māyā (deceit). The state characterized by displaying virtues one does not possess is Sāṭheyya (hypocrisy). The state characterized by the mind's stiffness is Thambha (obstinacy). The state characterized by overbearing action is Sārambha (impetuosity). The state characterized by haughtiness is Māna (conceit). The state characterized by excessive haughtiness is Atimāna (arrogance). The state characterized by intoxication is Mada. The state characterized by letting the mind loose in the five cords of sensual pleasure is Pamāda (negligence).

What is meant by 'Lust is the enemy, and the wisdom that crushes that enemy,' and so forth? Defilements such as lust are enemies (ari) that have arisen (bhūta) in the mental continuum; thus, it would be 'Bhū-ari'. By eliding the letter 'a' according to the rules of euphonic combination (sandhi), it is called 'Bhūri'. In the expression 'Bhūrimaddanipaññā', meaning the wisdom that crushes the enemy (bhūri) in the mental continuum, it should be known that the word 'maddani' is elided, resulting in 'Bhūripaññā'. In the phrase 'crushing that enemy', it should be understood by breaking the words as 'the wisdom that crushes those enemies'. 'Because it is like the earth' means it is like the earth only in the sense of being extensive and vast. 'Extensive' refers to wisdom that spreads and knows the objects to be known, not wisdom that exists only in one part. 'Vast' refers to wisdom that is grand and extensive. In the Mahāniddesa Pali, it appears as 'vast and extensive'. 'Endowed with' refers to the person. The word 'iti' is used in the sense of cause; because a person is endowed with Bhūripaññā for this reason, that person's wisdom is called Bhūripaññā. It also means Bhūripaññā because it delights (ramati) in the true (bhūta) meaning (attha). In the expression 'the wisdom of a person who has Bhūripaññā', one word 'paññā' is elided, and it is called 'Bhūripaññā'. Alternatively, it is Bhūripaññā because it is wisdom equal to the earth (bhūri). The word 'api ca' is stated to show another method. 'Paññāyametaṃ' should be broken as 'paññāya etaṃ'. 'Adhivacanaṃ' means an extraordinary designation. 'Bhūri' is so called because it delights in the true meaning. 'Medhā' is so called because it destroys (medhati) defilements just as a thunderbolt destroys a stone mountain. Or, it is called Medhā in the sense of quickly grasping and retaining. 'Pariṇāyikā' is so called because for whichever being that wisdom arises, it leads (pariṇeti) that being in the practice of benefit, and in the penetration of the true characteristics of associated states. These terms themselves are synonyms for other...
261:
...or it is called Medhā. For whichever person wisdom arises, it is called Pariṇāyikā because it leads that person in the practice of welfare, in associated states, and in the penetration of the true characteristics. By these terms, other synonyms of wisdom are also stated. Paññābāhulla (abundance of wisdom) means a person is called Paññābahula because he has much wisdom; the state of being Paññābahula is Paññābāhulla. That wisdom which occurs abundantly is itself Paññābāhulla. In sentences such as 'In this world, a certain person...', it refers to either a virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) or a noble one (ariya). One who treats wisdom as paramount is Paññāgaruka. One who has the habit of practicing with wisdom is Paññācarita. One who has wisdom as his resort is Paññāsaya. One who is resolved on wisdom is Paññādhimutta. One who has wisdom as his banner is Paññādhaja. One who has wisdom as his standard is Paññāketu. Wisdom itself is the dominant factor, thus Paññādhipati; because one comes toward Nibbāna through the dominance of wisdom, it is called Paññādhipateyya. One who frequently investigates the nature of phenomena (dhamma) is Vicayabahula. One who frequently investigates the nature of phenomena in various ways is Pavicayabahula. Entering into various phenomena with wisdom and making them clear is Okkhāyana; one who frequently makes them clear is Okkhāyanabahula. Rightly observing various phenomena with wisdom is Sampekkha; the occurrence of such right observation is Sampekkha-yana; one who has the nature of such right observation is Sampekkha-yanadhamma. One who dwells making various phenomena manifest and clear is Vibhūtavihārī; or, one who has a manifest dwelling is Vibhūtavihārī. Because he practices with that wisdom, treats it as paramount, and has it abundantly, he is called Taccarita, Taggaruka, and Tabbahula. Because he is inclined, sloped, slanted, and resolved toward that wisdom, he is called Tanninna, Tappoṇa, Tappabbhāra, and Tadadhimutta. That wisdom is the dominant factor, thus Tadadhipati; coming from that, it is Tadadhipateyya. Terms such as 'Paññāgaruka' are stated starting from previous births, as in the passage: 'One knows a person who indeed pursues sensual pleasures as one who treats sensual pleasures as paramount.' Terms such as 'Taccarita' are stated regarding this current birth.

Sīghapaññā (swift wisdom), Lahupaññā (quick wisdom), Hāsapaññā (joyous wisdom), and Javanapaññā (fleet wisdom) are wisdoms that mix the mundane and the supramundane. It is Sīghapaññā in the sense of being fast. It is Lahupaññā in the sense of being light. It is Hāsapaññā in the sense of having much joy. It is Javanapaññā in the sense of occurring fleetly in the formations (saṅkhāra) that lead to insight and in the unconditioned (visaṅkhāra), which is Nibbāna. Saying 'swiftly, swiftly' (sīghaṃ sīghaṃ) twice is for the purpose of encompassing and counting many virtues (sīla) and so forth. Virtues (sīla) refers to the Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla (virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha) prescribed by way of performance (cāritta) and avoidance (vāritta).
262:
Restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) means preventing the entry of passion and aversion into the six sense faculties, such as the eye, by blocking or closing them with the door-leaf of mindfulness. Moderation in eating (bhojane mattaññutā) means the state of knowing the proper measure in food by way of reflective consumption. Devotion to wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga) means practicing only the Dhamma of a recluse while remaining awake without sleeping during the three parts of the day and during the first and last watches of the night. One who remains awake without sleeping is called 'jāgara'. The state or act of such a person is called 'jāgariya'. Devotion to that wakefulness is called 'jāgariyānuyoga'. The aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) refers to the aggregate of virtue of a trainee (sekha) or a non-trainee (asekha). The remaining aggregates should be understood in the same way. The aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) refers to path-wisdom and the mundane wisdom of trainees and non-trainees. The aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha) refers to liberation known as fruition (phala). The aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha) refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa).

'Hāsabahulo' (abounding in joy) is the root term. 'Vedabahulo' (abounding in feeling) is the elaborative term for the pleasant feeling (somanassavedanā) associated with that rapture (pīti) shown by the root term. 'Tuṭṭhibahulo' (abounding in satisfaction) is due to the aspect of being satisfied with rapture that is not very strong. 'Pāmojjabahulo' (abounding in gladness) is due to the state of being glad with strong rapture.

The phrase 'Whatever kind of form' (yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ) and so forth has the meaning already stated in the description of the knowledge of comprehension (sammasanañāṇa). 'Having weighed' (tulayitvā) means having weighed by way of group comprehension (kalāpasammasana). 'Having judged' (tīrayitvā) means having judged by way of contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā). 'Having clarified' (vibhāvayitvā) means having made clear by way of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) and so forth. 'Having made distinct' (vibhūtaṃ katvā) means having made it distinct and tangible in knowledge by way of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa) and conformity knowledge (anulomañāṇa). Sharp wisdom (tikkha-paññā) is only supramundane wisdom. 'Arisen' (uppanna) refers to defilements that, although abandoned by way of serenity and insight or by way of suppression (vikkhambhana) and substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), are called 'arisen but not yet uprooted' (asamūhatuppanna) because they have not been completely eradicated by the Noble Path and thus have not yet transcended the nature of arising; it is this 'asamūhatuppanna' that is intended here. 'Does not tolerate' (nādhivāseti) means not allowing it to remain by taking it into the mental continuum. 'Abandons' (pajahati) means abandoning by way of eradication (samuccheda). 'Dispels' (vinodeti) means throwing away. 'Makes an end' (byantīkaroti) means making it come to an end. 'Leads to non-existence' (anabhāvaṃ gameti) means reaching the Noble Path through the sequence of insight and leading to non-existence solely by way of eradication. Herein, thought associated with sensual objects or sensual defilements is called sensual thought (kāmavitakka). Thought associated with the death of others, such as 'May these beings die,' is called ill-will thought (byāpādavitakka). Thought associated with the harming of others, such as 'May these beings be harmed,' is called cruelty thought (vihiṃsāvitakka). 'Evil' (pāpaka) has the meaning of being low or vile. 'Unwholesome states' (akusalā dhammā) are states that arise from unskillful delusion (moha).

Penetrative wisdom (nibbedhikapaññā) is the path-wisdom that arises in a person who abounds in revulsion (nibbidā). 'Abounding in agitation' (ubbegabahulo) refers to a person who abounds in fear by way of the knowledge that views things as fearful. 'Abounding in terror' (uttāsabahulo) means...
263:
A person who abounds in very strong fear; this is an explanation of the meaning of the previous term 'ubbegabahulo'. 'Abounding in weariness' (ukkaṇṭhanabahulo) refers to a person who abounds in weariness towards formations (saṅkhāra) because of facing Nibbāna, which is above formations. 'Abounding in non-delight' (anabhiratibahulo) shows the absence of delight in formations solely through the power of weariness. Now, that meaning is further explained with two words. Among them, 'outward-facing' (bahimukho) refers to a person facing Nibbāna, which exists outside of formations. 'Does not delight' (na ramati) means simply not taking delight. 'Not previously pierced' (anibbiddhapubbaṃ) refers to the Dhamma that has not been previously pierced by reaching the end of abandonment in the beginningless cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra). 'Not previously shattered' (appadālitapubbaṃ) is a word expressing the same meaning as 'anibbiddhapubbaṃ', meaning not having shattered defilements by making an end of them. 'Mass of greed' (lobhakkhandhaṃ) refers to a heap of greed or a portion of greed. A person endowed with these sixteen kinds of wisdom refers, in the highest sense, only to an Arahant. However, because it was stated above that 'a trainee (sekha) attains the analytical knowledges,' Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners are also included.

## 2. Description of the Specification of Persons (Puggalavisesaniddesavaṇṇanā)

With the words 'Two persons' (dwe puggalā) and so forth, the sequence of special persons who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) is shown. In those words, 'former devotion' (pubbayoga) refers to the meritorious effort which is the cause for attaining the analytical knowledges in past lives. 'By that' (tena) means because of that cause of meritorious effort in past lives. The remaining terms should be understood in this same way. 'Is superior' (atireko hoti) means he is excessive, or he is called 'atireka' because of having excessive devotion. 'Is pre-eminent' (adhiko hoti) means he is foremost. 'Is distinguished' (viseso hoti) means he is excellent, or he is called 'viseso' because of having distinguished devotion. 'Knowledge is differentiated' (ñāṇaṃ pabhijjati) means attaining the various divisions of the analytical knowledges.

'Learned' (bahussuto) means having much hearing and learning of the Buddha's word. 'Abounding in teaching' (desanābahulo) means frequent teaching of the Dhamma. 'Depending on teachers' (garūpanissito) means depending on a noble teacher who is superior in wisdom. 'Abounding in dwelling' (vihārabahulo) means dwelling much in the dwelling of insight (vipassanā) or dwelling much in the dwelling of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). 'Abounding in reviewing' (paccavekkhaṇābahulo) means frequent reviewing of insight when dwelling in insight, or frequent reviewing of the attainment of fruition when dwelling in the attainment of fruition. 'One who has attained analytical knowledges as a trainee' (sekhapaṭisambhidappatto) means attaining the analytical knowledges while being a trainee. 'One who has attained analytical knowledges as a non-trainee' (asekhapaṭisambhidappatto) is to be understood in the same way. In the phrase 'attained the perfection of a disciple' (သာဝကပါရမိပ္ပတ္တော), 'perfection' (pāramī) means reaching the end of the sixty-seven disciple-knowledges of a Great Disciple (Mahāsāvaka) who is foremost among those of great wisdom. The perfection of a disciple is 'sāvakapāramī'. One who has reached that perfection of a disciple is called 'sāvakapāramippatto'. There is also a variant reading 'sāvakapāramitāppatto'.
264:
That Great Disciple who is engaged in guarding and fulfilling the sixty-seven types of disciple's knowledge is supreme. The occurrence of the sixty-seven types of knowledge (ñāṇakiriya) of that supreme Great Disciple is called pāramī (perfection). The state of being that supreme Great Disciple, or the knowledge, or the energy produced by that knowledge, is also called pāramī. Because he has reached the perfection of a disciple, he is called 'Sāvaka-pāramippatta'. The term 'Sāvaka-pāramippatta' can refer to any disciple such as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and others. It is said that he is not a Paccekabuddha because there is no other disciple superior to a disciple who has reached the perfection of a disciple. Furthermore, the meaning already stated is summarized and shown by words such as 'skilled in the classification of wisdom' (paññāpabhedakusala). In the Ñāṇakathā (Discourse on Knowledge), many knowledges are generally referred to. In the Paññākathā (Discourse on Wisdom), however, generally a single wisdom is spoken of by making it various through different aspects; this is the distinction between the Ñāṇakathā and the Paññākathā.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Great Discourse on Wisdom.

## 2. Commentary on the Discourse on Psychic Power

Now, I shall explain the meanings not yet mentioned in the Iddhikathā (Discourse on Psychic Power), which is spoken for the purpose of showing the power of wisdom immediately following the Paññākathā. Among the questions in that Iddhikathā, the question 'What is psychic power?' is a question regarding the nature (sabhāvapucchā). 'How many psychic powers are there?' is a question regarding classification (pabhedapucchā). 'How many planes are there?' is a question regarding the requisites (sambhārapucchā). 'How many bases are there?' is a question regarding the foundation (patiṭṭhapucchā). 'How many basic factors are there?' is a question regarding the proximate cause (āsannakāraṇapucchā). 'How many roots are there?' is a question regarding the initial cause (ādikāraṇapucchā).

In the answers, it is called 'iddhi' (psychic power/success) because of the meanings of 'fulfillment, perfection, and attainment'. Whatever thing is fulfilled or attained, that thing is said to be successful (ijjhanti). It is as said: "If that sense-pleasure is fulfilled for that person who desires the desired sense-pleasure." In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is stated: "Renunciation is called iddhi because it succeeds; it is called pāṭihāriya (miracle) because it discards opposing states," and so on. Another way: it is called iddhi because of the perfection of means (upāyasampadā). Indeed, the perfection of means succeeds because it produces the desired result. As it was said to Citta the Householder: "This Citta the Householder is virtuous and of good character; if he should aspire, 'In the future, may I become a Wheel-turning Monarch,' the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous will succeed because of its purity." Another way: it is called iddhi because beings succeed (prosper) by means of this quality. To succeed means to prosper, to increase, and to reach a state of excellence.

Among the ten psychic powers, it is called 'adhiṭṭhānā iddhi' (power of determination) because it is accomplished by the power of determination. It is called 'vikubbanā iddhi' (power of transformation) because it proceeds by way of transformation, discarding the natural appearance. It is called 'manomayā iddhi' (mind-made power) because it is the power of creating another mind-made body within the body. The distinction that arises through the power of path-knowledge, whether before, after, or at that moment, is called 'ñāṇavipphārā iddhi' (power of knowledge-pervasion). The distinction that arises through the power of concentration, whether before, after, or at that moment, is called 'samādhivipphārā iddhi' (power of concentration-pervasion). It is called 'ariyā iddhi' (noble power) because it occurs only to the Noble Ones who have attained mastery over the mind. The distinction that arises by the power of kamma-result is called 'kammavipākajā iddhi' (power born of kamma-result). The distinction that arises for one who has performed merit in the past is called 'puññavato iddhi' (power of the meritorious). The fulfillment of various tasks through various right efforts is called iddhi because of the sense of succeeding due to the cause of those various right efforts. Although the four planes of iddhi are mentioned without specification, they are only the planes of adhiṭṭhānā iddhi, vikubbanā iddhi, and manomayā iddhi as applicable; they are not the planes of the remaining seven. The state that arises due to being secluded from the hindrances etc. is called 'vivekajabhūmi' (the plane born of seclusion) (it is the second jhana). Along with tatramajjhattūpekkhā and...
265:
It is called 'manomayā iddhi' (mind-made power) because it occurs by way of producing another mind-made body within the body. The distinction produced by the power of knowledge, whether before, after, or at the moment of the occurrence of knowledge, is called 'ñāṇavipphārā iddhi' (power of knowledge-pervasion). The distinction produced by the power of serenity (samatha), whether before, after, or at the moment of concentration (appana-samādhi), is called 'samādhivipphārā iddhi' (power of concentration-pervasion). It is called 'ariyā iddhi' (noble power) because it arises only for the Noble Ones who have attained mastery over the mind. The distinction that arises by way of kamma-result is called 'kammavipākajā iddhi' (power born of kamma-result). The distinction that arises for one who has performed merit in the past is called 'puññavato iddhi' (power of the meritorious). The distinction that arises through science/magical arts is called 'vijjāmayā iddhi' (power of science). The fulfillment of various tasks through various right efforts is called iddhi in the sense of succeeding because it has those various right efforts as its cause.

Although the "four planes of iddhi" are spoken of without specification, they are, according to what is attainable, the planes only of adhiṭṭhānā iddhi, vikubbanā iddhi, and manomayā iddhi; they are not the planes of the remaining seven types of iddhi. "Vivekajabhūmi" (plane born of seclusion) is so called because it arises from seclusion from the hindrances etc., or because it arises in a secluded state. "Pītisukhabhūmi" (plane of rapture and happiness) is the plane associated with rapture and happiness. "Upekkhāsukhabhūmi" (plane of equanimity and happiness) is the plane associated with equanimity (tatramajjhattūpekkhā) and the feeling of happiness. "Adukkhamasukhabhūmi" (plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure) is the plane associated with the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Among those jhanas, the first and second jhanas are called the pervasion of rapture (pītipharaṇatā). The three jhanas are called the pervasion of happiness (sukha-pharaṇatā). The fourth jhana is called the pervasion of mind (cetopharaṇatā). Among these planes, the preceding three jhanas should be known as preparatory planes (sambhārabhūmi) because, through the pervasion of rapture and the pervasion of happiness, one enters into the perception of happiness and the perception of lightness, and having a body that is light, soft, and wieldy, one reaches psychic power; thus, in this manner, they lead to the gain of psychic power. The fourth jhana, however, is the natural plane (pakatibhūmi) for the gain of psychic power. "Iddhilābhāya" (for the gain of psychic power) means for the gain of psychic powers by way of their manifestation in one's own continuity. "Iddhipaṭilābhāya" (for the regaining of psychic power) means for the regaining of psychic powers that have been lost, through the exertion of energy; or, the word "lābha" is expanded by the power of the prefix "paṭi". "Iddhivikubbanatāya" (for the transformation of psychic power) means for the state of performing various transformations with psychic power. "Iddhivisavitāya" (for the diversity of psychic power) means 'visavī' because it produces or manifests various distinctions; or, 'visavī' means one who has various manifestations; the state of that visavī is 'visavitā'. It means for that visavitā, that is, for the state of being able to manifest various distinctions with psychic power. "Iddhivasībhāvāya" (for mastery over psychic power) means for the state of lordship over psychic power. "Iddhivesārajjāya" (for intrepidity in psychic power) means for the state of being bold in psychic power. The meaning of the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) has already been stated in the Ñāṇakathā.
266:
If a monk, relying on desire (chanda) and making desire the predominant factor, attains or produces absorption concentration (appanā samādhi), it is said: "If a monk, relying on desire..." The same method applies to the remaining terms: energy (vīriya), consciousness (citta), and investigation (vīmaṃsā). In analyzing these eight terms, there are the four terms called desire, energy, consciousness, and investigation, and the four types of concentration associated with them, making eight terms in total. Furthermore, it should be understood that these eight terms were taught because just as the desire to produce psychic power, being united with concentration, arises for the attainment of psychic power, so too do energy and the others arise in the same way.

Desiring to show the method of practice to be performed by a yogi who wishes to produce the higher knowledges (abhiññā), the Blessed One taught the imperturbability of the mind, saying: "When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability." Desiring to show this imperturbability in sixteen ways, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, taught "the sixteen roots" (soḷasa mūlāni) and so forth. In those passages, "not bent down" (anonataṃ) means the meaning of not shrinking or leaning down by the power of sloth (kosajja). "Not lifted up" (anunnataṃ) means the meaning of not rising upwards by the power of restlessness (uddhacca), or being without restlessness. "Not bent towards" (anabhinataṃ) means the meaning of not leaning forward by the power of greed (lobha), or being without attachment. Leaning towards an object due to desire is called "bent towards" (abhinata); it means this mind does not have the nature of leaning towards the object in such a way. "Lust" (rāga) occurs because of greed that has formations (saṅkhāra) as its object. "Not bent away" (anapanataṃ) means the meaning of being free from leaning away by the power of hatred (dosa), or being without resentment. The terms "bent" (nata) and "bending" (nati) are the same in meaning. Because it is free from leaning away, it is called "bent away" (apanata). It means this mind does not have such a nature of leaning away or anger.

"Unattached" (anissitaṃ) means, because of having seen things as non-self (anatta), there is no relying on anything as "self" (attā) or "belonging to self" (attaniya) by the power of wrong view (diṭṭhi). "Unfettered" (appaṭibaddhaṃ) means not being bound by the desire that expects a return favor. "Lustful desire" (chandarāga) occurs because of greed that has beings (satta) as its object. "Liberated" (vippamuttaṃ) means liberation from sensual lust (kāmarāga) by the power of liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti). Or else, it is liberation from various opposing defilements by the power of the five kinds of liberation. This term "liberated" (vippamutta) is taught with specific distinction for worldlings (puthujjana), trainees (sekha), and non-trainees (asekha) as well, due to the arising of higher knowledge, according to the method stated in the knowledge of the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti-ñāṇa) as "by the sixteen modes of knowledge-conduct" (ñāṇacariya). However, it should be taken according to whatever level is attained. "Sensual lust" (kāmarāga) occurs because of sexual lust (methuna-rāga). "Disconnected" (visaññuttaṃ) means being disconnected from the remaining defilements by way of abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). Or else, it is being absolutely disconnected from defilements by way of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), which is the highest method. "Defilement" (kilesa) occurs because of the remaining defilements. "Made borderless" (vimariyādikataṃ) means the mind is made free from the boundary (mariyāda) of defilements that are abandoned by suppression. Or else, it is the mind made free from the boundary of defilements already abandoned by the respective paths (magga).

It is also because of the boundary of those various abandoned defilements. In this term "mariyāda," it should be known that the feminine gender has been changed to the masculine gender. "Gone to oneness" (ekattagataṃ) means occurring in a single object. Because of defilements that occur in various objects, this term "oneness" (ekattagata) is taught with reference to the object. However, terms such as "not bent down" (anonataṃ) and so forth are taught only with reference to defilements such as sloth (kosajja) and so forth. "Gone to illumination" (obhāsagataṃ) means the mind has reached the light of wisdom by the power of the pure arising of wisdom. "Darkness of ignorance" (avijjandhakāra) occurs because of powerful ignorance (avijjā). It should be understood that the four planes (bhūmi) and the sixteen roots (mūla) are taught by way of occurring in the preliminary stage of psychic power (iddhi). The four bases (pāda) and the eight terms (pada) are taught by way of occurring in the preliminary stage of psychic power as well as by way of association with psychic power.

## 10. Having thus shown the dhammas that are the planes, bases, terms, and roots of psychic power, and desiring to show those psychic powers, the Teacher taught "What is the psychic power of determination?" (katamā adhiṭဋ္ဌānā iddhi) and so forth. In that passage "What is the psychic power of determination?" and so forth, the meaning of the summary terms (uddesa-pada) has already been taught in the Exposition of the Knowledge of the Modes of Psychic Power (Iddhividha-ñāṇa-niddesa). "Monk" (bhikkhu) means a monk in this Dispensation. By that Pali word "here" (idha), in every way...
267:
By means of that path, the boundary of defilements to be abandoned is removed, or it is made free from the boundary of defilements. 'Kilesamariyāde' refers to the boundary of those respective abandoned defilements. In this context, the change of gender (from feminine to masculine) should be understood. 'Ekattagataṃ' means reaching a single object. 'Nānattakilesehi' refers to defilements occurring in various objects. This statement is made with regard to the object; however, the statement beginning with 'anonataṃ' is made with regard only to the defilements. 'Obhāsagataṃ' means reaching the light of wisdom through the clear occurrence of wisdom. 'Avijjāndhakāre' refers to powerful ignorance. The four bases (bhūmi) and sixteen roots (mūla) are spoken of in terms of the preliminary stage of psychic power. The four feet (pāda) and eight steps (pada) are spoken of in terms of the preliminary stage and in terms of association.

## Having thus shown the factors that are the bases, feet, steps, and roots of psychic power, he now says 'Katamā adhiṭṭhānā iddhi' etc., wishing to show those psychic powers.

In that context, the meaning of the terms in the summary (uddesa) has already been stated in the description of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (Iddhividhañāṇaniddesa). 'Idha bhikkhu' means a monk in this Dispensation (Sāsana). By the word 'idha', he shows that one who can perform psychic feats in every way does not exist elsewhere (outside the Sāsana). The explanation of these two words has the meaning stated below. Through these words, it means being endowed with the factors that are the bases, feet, steps, and roots of psychic power; having a mind disciplined by the fourteen or fifteen modes stated in the Visuddhimagga; and having a mind that is soft and wieldy through the mastery of attaining individual predominant factors (adhipati) such as desire (chanda), and through the mastery of adverting (āvajjana) etc. A monk who, being endowed with strong previous practice (pubbayoga), attains qualities such as higher knowledge (abhiññā) simultaneously with the attainment of Arahantship due to the perfection of previous practice, is also meant here, as he is endowed with the bases etc.

'Bahukaṃ āvajjati' means: having entered and emerged from the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge and has the earth kasiṇa as its object, if he desires a hundred, he adverts by way of preliminary work (parikamma), thinking 'May I be a hundred, may I be a hundred'. 'Āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti' means: having thus performed the preliminary work, he determines with the knowledge of higher knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa). Here, re-entering the basis-jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) after the preliminary work is not mentioned. Although not mentioned, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) it is said: 'Āvajjati is said only by way of preliminary work; Āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti is said by way of the knowledge of higher knowledge. Therefore, he adverts to many; then, at the end of those preliminary thoughts, he attains (samāpajjati); having emerged from the attainment, again...'
268:
"...adverting 'May I be many,' and then, immediately after the three or four preliminary (upacāra) thoughts that occur, he determines with a single higher knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa) named 'determination' (adhiṭṭhāna) by way of completion. This is how the meaning should be understood here; thus it should be regarded. For example, when it is said 'He sleeps after eating,' it does not mean he sleeps immediately after eating without drinking water or washing hands; even though there are other tasks in between, it is said 'He sleeps after eating.' Similarly, in this matter of higher knowledge, it should be understood in the same way. For, the initial entry into the basis-jhāna is also not explicitly stated in the Pāḷi text. Simultaneously with that knowledge of determination, a hundred (created forms) appear. The same method applies to a thousand or a hundred thousand. If it is not successful in that way, he should perform the preliminary work again, enter (the basis-jhāna) a second time, emerge, and then determine. In the Saṃyutta Nikāya Commentary, it is said: 'It is proper to attain once or twice.' Among those thoughts, the basis-jhāna thought has the (counterpart) sign as its object; the preliminary thoughts have a hundred objects or a thousand objects. And those are by way of color (vaṇṇa), not by way of concept (paññatti). The determination-thought likewise has a hundred or a thousand objects. That higher knowledge thought, like the absorption (appanā) thought mentioned before, is a single Rūpāvacara fourth jhāna thought that arises immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū).

The statement 'Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, being one, becomes many' is said to show the personal realization of the state of being many. The use of the present tense (hoti) here should be understood as being due to the Elder's nature of doing so, and because it was the time when the Elder was still living. The same method applies to the section 'He becomes one'.

The story here is as follows: Those two brothers, it is said, received the name 'Panthaka' because they were born on the road. Among them, the elder, Mahāpanthaka, went forth and attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Having become an Arahant, he ordained his younger brother Cūḷapanthaka and (gave him this verse):
'Look at the Angīrasa (the Buddha) shining like the sun glowing in the sky, like a fragrant Kokanada lotus that blooms in the morning with its scent lingering.' The Elder Cūḷapanthaka could not master this verse even after studying it for four months. Then the elder brother..."
269:
He gave this verse. Although Cūḷapanthaka studied and memorized this verse for four months, he was unable to master it. Then, his elder brother, the Elder, said, "You are not worthy of attaining the special Dhamma in this Dispensation; leave from here." At that time, the Elder was the monk who allocated meals (bhattuddesaka). Jīvaka Komārabhacca took many flowers, perfumes, and scented ointments, went to his Mango Grove, made offerings to the Buddha, and after listening to the Dhamma and paying homage to the Dasabala Buddha, he approached the Elder and said, "Venerable Sir, tomorrow, please accept alms at our house together with five hundred monks headed by the Buddha." The Elder replied, "I accept for the rest of the monks, excluding Cūḷapanthaka." Hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka became exceedingly distressed. Early the next morning, he left the monastery, but out of longing for the Dispensation, he stood weeping at the monastery gatehouse.

The Blessed One, seeing his supporting condition (for the path and fruit), approached him and asked, "Why are you weeping?" He reported the matter. The Blessed One said, "One is not called unworthy in my Dispensation merely because he cannot recite a verse. Do not grieve, Panthaka." He stroked Panthaka's head with His golden hand, the palm of which was adorned with the wheel-marks, took him by the arm, entered the monastery, and seated him near the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī). He gave him a clean piece of cloth created by psychic power and said, "Dear Panthaka, sit here rubbing this piece of cloth with your hand, reflecting, 'It removes impurity, it removes impurity' (rajoharaṇaṃ)." When the time for the meal was announced, the Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, went to Jīvaka's house and sat on the prepared seat. As the Elder rubbed that piece of cloth, it became soiled and gradually turned black in color. He gained the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) and impermanence (anicca-saññā), thinking, "This piece of cloth was clean; there was no fault in this cloth. Indeed, this fault of impurity has arisen because of my own body (attabhāva)." He then applied insight-knowledge to the five aggregates and developed Vipassanā. Then, the Blessed One emitted a radiance and, appearing as if sitting right in front of him, spoke these verses of radiance:

"Lust (rāga) is called dust, but physical dust is not called dust in this Dispensation. This name 'dust' is a synonym for lust. Having abandoned this dust of lust, the monks dwell in the Dispensation of the Buddha, who is free from dust."

"Hatred (dosa)... [as above] ...in the Dispensation."

"Delusion (moha)... [as above] ...in the Dispensation."

For the Arahant who is of noble mind, who is diligent, who has trained in the paths of sagehood (monapatha), who is endowed with the quality of equanimity (tādi), who is peaceful, and who is always mindful, sorrows do not arise.

At the end of the verses, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka attained Arahatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Having attained the meditative absorption of mind-made psychic power (manomayiddhi), he became many from being one, and from being many, he could become one again. Along with the Path of Arahatship, the three Pitakas and the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) came to him. Jīvaka offered the water of donation to the Buddha. The Blessed One covered the bowl with His hand and said, "Jīvaka, there is still one monk left in the monastery." Jīvaka instructed a man, saying, "Go, invite the venerable one who remains in the monastery and return quickly." Before that man arrived, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, wishing to let his elder brother know of the special Dhamma he had attained, created a thousand monks, making each one different from the others. One created monk was performing the duties of a monk, such as preparing robes.
270: Delusion (moha) is called dust (raja), but physical dust is not called dust. This name 'dust' is a synonym for delusion. Having abandoned this dust of delusion, the monks dwell in the Dispensation of the Buddha, who is free from dust. For the Arahant who is of noble mind, who is diligent, who has trained in the paths of sagehood (monapatha), who is endowed with the quality of equanimity (tādi), who is peaceful, and who is always mindful, sorrows do not arise. At the end of the verses, the Elder attained Arahatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Having attained the meditative absorption of mind-made psychic power (manomayiddhi), he became many from being one, and from being many, he became capable of being one again. By the Path of Arahatship itself, the three Pitakas and the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) came to that Elder. Jīvaka also offered the water of donation to the Blessed One. The Blessed One covered the bowl with His hand, and when asked, "What is it, Bhante?", He said, "Jīvaka, there is still one monk in the monastery." Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Go, invite the venerable one who remains in this monastery and return quickly." Before that person arrived, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, wishing to let his elder brother know of the special Dhamma he had attained, created a thousand monks. He made the created monks different from one another, and also made their monastic duties, such as preparing robes, different from one another. That man went to the monastery, saw many monks, and returned, saying to Jīvaka, "Venerable Sir, there are many monks in the monastery; I do not see the venerable one who is to be invited." Jīvaka asked the Blessed One, and having learned the Elder's name, sent the man again. He went and asked, "Venerable Sirs, which one is named Cūḷapanthaka?" A thousand mouths spoke at once, "I am Cūḷapanthaka, I am Cūḷapanthaka." He returned again and said, "It seems everyone is Cūḷapanthaka; I do not know whom to invite." Jīvaka, being one who had realized the Truths, understood by way of inference, "He is a monk of great psychic power." The Blessed One said, "Go, whoever you see first, take him by the hem of his robe and say, 'The Teacher calls you,' and bring him." He went and did as instructed. At that very moment, all the created monks vanished. The Elder sent the man ahead, finished his bodily duties such as washing his face, and arriving first, sat on the prepared seat. At that moment, the Blessed One accepted the water of donation and performed the meal-service, and then had the Elder Cūḷapanthaka himself deliver the sermon of appreciation (anumodanā). The Elder delivered a discourse as extensive as the Dīgha Nikāya and Majjhima Nikāya. This is the story of Cūḷapanthaka. Other monks, through their supernormal knowledge, can create only three or four mind-made forms. Many (mind-made forms)...
271:
(The Elder) sat in the prepared seat. At that moment, the Blessed One, having received the water of donation and finished his meal, had Elder Cūḷapanthaka alone deliver the Dhamma discourse of appreciation. The Elder delivered a Dhamma discourse equivalent in length to the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas.

Other monks, through resolution, create mind-made bodies, creating three or four; they create many identical forms performing the same single action. However, Elder Cūḷapanthaka, with just a single advertence, created a thousand monks. He did not make even two of them identical, nor were they performing the same action. Therefore, he became the foremost among those who create mind-made bodies. When other possessors of psychic power create many without specific determination, those created forms are identical to the possessor of power. Whatever the possessor of power does—such as standing, sitting, speaking, or remaining silent—the created forms do the same.

If one wishes to create various appearances—some in the first stage of life, some in the middle stage, some in the last stage; likewise, those with long hair, those with half-shaven heads, those with shaven heads, those with mixed hair; those with half-dyed robes, those with pale-red robes; those reciting by syllables, preaching the Dhamma, chanting melodiously, asking questions, answering questions, dyeing, cooking, sewing robes, washing robes, and so forth—if one wishes to create such various forms, that possessor of power must emerge from the foundation jhāna, perform the preliminary work in the manner of "Let this many monks be in the first stage of life," and so on, then enter the attainment again, emerge, and make the resolution. Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, they become exactly as desired. This same method applies to the Pali passages such as "Having been many, he becomes one," and so forth.

This is the distinction: "Being many by nature" means being many through the nature of the created forms within the duration of the creation. After creating such a multitude, if this monk thinks, "I will become one again and practice walking meditation, recite, or ask questions," or if, out of fewness of wishes, he thinks, "This monastery has few monks; if people come and see so many identical monks, they will know me, thinking, 'Where did these many identical monks come from? Surely this is the Elder's power,'" and thus wishes to become one in the interim, he should enter the foundation jhāna, emerge, perform the preliminary work saying "Let me be one," enter the attainment again, emerge, and resolve "Let me be one." Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, he becomes one. If he does not do so, he becomes one naturally according to the predetermined time.
272: It should be understood that only the desired varieties arise along with the mind of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā). This same method applies to the phrases such as "having been one, he becomes many" and so on. The distinction is that the multiplicity of the created form within the created time is called "natural multiplicity" (pakaṭi-bahuka). A monk who has attained this supernormal knowledge, having created such multiplicity, may then wish to become one again, thinking, "I shall walk to and fro, I shall recite, I shall ask a question." Or, out of a desire for fewness of wishes, wanting others to know him as a powerful monk, he might think, "This monastery is always sparsely populated with monks; if some guests arrive, where will they find so many monks? This multiplicity must be the psychic power of the elder residing in this monastery." Before the determined time arrives, the monk who wishes to become one enters the foundation jhāna (pādaka-jhāna), emerges, performs the preliminary work (parikamma) thinking "Let me be one," enters the attainment again, emerges, and resolves (adhiṭṭhāna) "Let me be one." Simultaneously with the abhiññā mind, he becomes one. A monk who does not do this becomes one naturally by the power of the determined time. 11. Regarding the term "āvibhāva" (manifestation), it is said to be "not obstructed by anything," thus the evident meaning of "āvibhāva" is expressed by the phrase "not obstructed by anything." By the word "hoti" (is), the remaining text "karoti" (makes) is intended. When manifestation is made, becoming evident occurs. "Kenasici anāvaṭaṃ" means not obstructed by anything such as a wall, meaning free from obstruction. "Appaṭicchannaṃ" means not covered from above by grass or such. That very object in view is called "vivaṭa" (open) because it is unobstructed, and "pākaṭa" (evident) because it is not covered. "Tirobhāvaṃ" (concealment) means making the state of being hidden. An object that is blocked by an obstruction like a wall is called "āvaṭa" (obstructed). An object covered from above by grass, leaves, etc., is called "paṭicchanna" (covered). "Ākāsakasiṇasamāpattiyā" refers to the attainment of the fourth jhāna produced in the space kasina of limited space. "Lābhi" (possessor) means one who possesses that fourth jhāna attained through abhiññā. "Apparikkhitte" refers to a place not surrounded on all sides by anything. Since only the space kasina is mentioned here, it should be understood that only the jhāna developed in that space kasina is the cause for creating space, not any other. In the case of the water kasina etc. mentioned above, only the jhāna taking that as an object should be understood, not any other. "Pathaviṃ āvajjati, udakaṃ āvajjati, ākāsaṃ āvajjati" refers to reflecting on natural earth, water, and space. "Antalikkhe" (in the air) is intended to show the state of the created space being far from the natural ground. 12. In the stroking of the moon and sun, since it is stated generally as "one with psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind" without specifying a kasina, it should be understood that there is no restriction of kasina attainment here. "Nisinnako vā nipannako vā" means either sitting or lying down. By these two, the other two postures are also implied. "Hatthapāse hotu" means "let it be near the hand." There is also a variant reading "hatthapasse hotu." This is said according to the wish of the person who wants to do so. In fact, this powerful monk either goes to that place or stretches out his hand and touches it. "Āmasati" means touching lightly. "Pāraမsati" means touching firmly. "Parimajjati" means stroking all around. "Rūpagataṃ" refers only to the form situated near the hand. "Dūrepi santike adhiṭṭhāti" means that after emerging from the foundation jhāna, he reflects on a distant deva world or Brahma world, thinking "let it be near." Having reflected and performed the preliminary work, he enters the attainment again, emerges, and resolves with knowledge, "let it be near." Then it becomes near. This same method applies to the remaining terms.
273: For the possessor of psychic power who wishes to go to the Brahma world, after explaining the making of the distant Brahma world near, the phrase beginning with "santikepi" is said to show the excellence of the fulfillment of this power, even if it does not directly assist in going to the Brahma world. In that text, it is not merely making the few many or the many few; whatever is desired, such as making a non-sweet object sweet, all is fulfilled for the one with psychic power. Another method: he resolves for the distant Brahma world to be near the human world. He resolves for the near human world to be in the distant Brahma world. If many Brahmas are assembled, because they have large bodies, they give up the range of vision and the range of hearing. Compressing that range of vision and range of hearing into one, he resolves for the many to be few. If he wishes to go with a large retinue, he resolves for his single self to be many and goes with a large retinue. Thus the meaning should be understood. In this way, these four modes assist in going to the Brahma world. While staying in this human world, having expanded the light, if he wishes to see the form of a certain Brahma, he sees that Brahma's form with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). While staying right here, he hears the voice of that Brahma speaking with the divine ear element (dibba-sota-dhātu). He knows that Brahma's mind with the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa). "Dissamānena" means by way of being seen with the eye. He directs the mind by the power of the material body. Taking the foundation jhāna mind and applying it to the body, he makes a slow movement following the body. This is because traveling with the body is slow. "Adhiṭṭhāti" is a synonym for that "pariṇāmeti"; it means establishing well. "Having entered the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness" means having entered, touched, and reached the perception of bliss and perception of lightness that arise together with the psychic power mind which has the foundation jhāna as its object. "Sukha-saññā" (perception of bliss) is the perception associated with equanimity (upekkhā). This is because equanimity is called "peaceful bliss." That very perception should also be known as "laghu-saññā" (perception of lightness) because it is liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and from opposing states such as initial thought (vitakka). For one who has entered that, even the physical body (karaja-kāya) becomes as light as a tuft of cotton. He goes to the Brahma world with a visible body that is as light as a tuft of cotton tossed by the wind. While going thus, if he wishes, he creates a path in the sky by the power of the earth kasina and goes on foot. If he wishes, in the sky...
274:
By the power of the earth kasina itself, he creates a lotus at every step and walks on foot, placing his foot on each lotus. If he wishes, by the power of the air kasina, he resolves on the air and travels by the air like a tuft of cotton. Indeed, in this context, the desire to go is the measure (the primary factor). If there is a desire to go, having such a mental resolution, he travels like an arrow shot from a bowstring, propelled by the momentum of the resolution, with a visible body.

"He transforms the body by the power of the mind" means taking the physical body (karaja-kāya) and mounting it upon the mind of the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna), making the rapid movement follow the mind. For the movement of the mind is swift. "Having entered the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness" refers to the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness that arise together with the supernormal knowledge (iddhi-citta) mind which has the material body as its object. The remaining meaning should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. This is indeed the movement of the mind. When asked, "Does this person traveling with an invisible body go during the moment of arising (uppāda), the moment of presence (ṭhiti), or the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga) of that resolutive mind?", the Elder replied, "He goes in all three moments." Does he go himself, or does he send a created form? He does as he pleases. Here, however, it refers to going himself.

"Mind-made" (manomaya) means it is called mind-made because it is created by the resolutive mind. "With all limbs and parts" means being complete with all major and minor limbs. The phrase "with faculties not lacking" is said in terms of the shape of the eyes, ears, etc.; however, in a created form, there is no sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa). If that possessor of psychic power walks to and fro, the created form also walks to and fro there—all such statements are made with reference to forms created by disciples. As for forms created by the Buddha, they perform whatever the Blessed One performs, and by the power of the Blessed One's mind, they also perform other actions. "It smokes, it blazes" is by the power of the fire kasina. The three terms such as "He preaches the Dhamma" are stated without limiting the kasina. "He stands together" means he stands in company. "He talks together" means he speaks in company. "He engages in discussion" means he converses by way of giving answers and counter-answers to one another.

In this context, that possessor of psychic power, while staying right here, sees forms with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), hears sounds with the divine ear element (dibba-sota-dhātu), and knows the minds of others with the knowledge of encompassing the mind (cetopariya-ñāṇa). While staying right here, he stands, talks, and engages in discussion with that Brahma. There is also the kind of resolution such as "He resolves on a distant place as if it were near." He goes to the Brahma world with either a visible or an invisible body. By this much, he does not yet "exercise mastery with the body" (kāyena vasaṃ vatteti). However, when he arrives at the procedure described in the manner of "He creates a material form in front of that Brahma," etc., only by this much...
275:
...is it called "exercising mastery with the body." The remaining text should be understood as being stated to show the preliminary stage of exercising mastery with the body. This is the power of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi).

In the explanation of the power of transformation (vikubbana-iddhi), the pointing out of the disciple of Sikhi Buddha (the Elder Abhibhū) is stated to show the person who is a personal witness (kāyasakkhi) of the power of transformation. Wishing to show that matter, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) first showed the power of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi) which makes the sound heard in a thousandfold world system while staying in the Brahma world—an exceedingly wonderful and marvelous thing.

Now, to explain that story, this is said: Thirty-one aeons ago from this present aeon, the Blessed One Sikhi, having passed away from the Tusita heaven in his immediately preceding life, was conceived in the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the chief consort of King Aruṇavā in the city of Aruṇavatī. Having reached mature wisdom, he went forth in the Great Renunciation, realized the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) at the terrace of enlightenment (Bodhimanda), and set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka). While dwelling in dependence on the city of Aruṇavatī, one day early in the morning, after attending to his bodily needs and being surrounded by a large community of monks, he thought, "I will enter Aruṇavatī for alms." Standing near the gatehouse of the monastery, he addressed the chief disciple named Abhibhū: "Monk, it is still too early to enter Aruṇavatī for alms. Let us go to a certain Brahma world until it is time for the meal." As it is said:

"Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, addressed the bhikkhu Abhibhū: 'Come, brahmin, let us go to a certain Brahma world until it is time for the meal.' 'Yes, Bhante,' the bhikkhu Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhi and the bhikkhu Abhibhū went to a certain Brahma world" (as stated in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).

In that Brahma world, the Great Brahma (Mahābrahmā), upon seeing the Fully Enlightened One, joyfully went out to meet him, prepared a seat for the Brahma, and offered it. They also prepared a suitable seat for the Elder. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat, and the Elder also sat on the seat provided for him. The Great Brahma also paid homage to the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) and sat down at one side. Therefore, it is said: "Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One Sikhi, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, to the bhikkhu Abhibhū..."
276:
(The Blessed One Sikhī) addressed (the monk Abhibhū): 'Brahmin, let a Dhamma talk be clear to your intellect for the Great Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' the monk Abhibhū replied to the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, and then delivered a Dhamma talk to the Great Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā. While the elder was delivering the Dhamma talk, the Brahmās complained: 'It is only after a long time that we have obtained the coming of the Teacher to the Brahmā world, yet this monk, setting aside the Teacher, starts a Dhamma talk himself.' The Blessed One, knowing the dissatisfaction of those Brahmās, said to the monk Abhibhū: 'Brahmin, the Great Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā are complaining. Therefore, Brahmin, stir up those Brahmās even more excessively.' The elder, having accepted the word of the Blessed One, performed various kinds of supernormal transformations and, wishing to make the thousandfold world system understand by his voice, recited these two verses:

'Exert yourselves, go forth,
Apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching;
Scatter the army of Death,
As an elephant crushes a hut of reeds.

Whoever shall dwell heedfully
In this Dhamma and Vinaya,
Having abandoned the round of births,
Shall make an end of suffering.'

How did the elder make the thousandfold world system understand by his voice? First, having entered the blue kasina and emerged from it, he pervaded the entire thousandfold world system with darkness through the power of direct knowledge. Then, when the thought 'What is this darkness?' arose in the beings, he entered the light kasina and, having emerged, displayed light. To the beings who were searching, 'Whose light is this?', he showed himself. The devas and humans in the thousandfold world system stood with hands joined in salutation, paying homage only to the elder. The elder made a determination, 'Let the great multitude hear the sound of my Dhamma teaching,' and recited these verses. All the beings heard the sound as if he were sitting and preaching in the midst of an assembly of radiant light. The meaning of the Dhamma also became clear to them. With reference to making them understand in this way, it is said, 'He made them understand by voice.' With reference to the various supernormal transformations performed by the elder, it is said again, 'Even while he was visible,' and so forth. Therein, 'preached the Dhamma' means first...
277:
It should be understood that he preached the Dhamma while displaying the aforementioned various supernormal transformations, and thereafter made them understand by voice while reciting the two verses in the stated order. In the phrase 'diissamānena pi kāyena' (even with a visible body) and so forth, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic of being in such a state (itthaṃbhūta-lakkhaṇa), meaning 'having such a body.' Now, having shown that story, and wishing to show the method of performing the power of transformation (vikubbana-iddhi) for another possessor of supernormal power, the text says, 'so pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā' (he, having abandoned his natural appearance) and so forth. In that passage, 'so' (he) refers to that monk with supernormal power whose mind has been made soft and wieldy by the aforementioned method. If he wishes to perform the power of transformation, he abandons his natural appearance and natural form and displays, for instance, the appearance of a youth. How does he display it? Having emerged from the fourth jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge and has the earth kasina as its object, he should reflect on the appearance of the youth to be created, thinking, 'Let me become a youth of such a form.' At the end of the preliminary work (parikamma), having entered the jhāna again and emerged, he determines with the knowledge of direct knowledge, 'Let me become a youth of such a name and form.' Simultaneously with the determination, he becomes a youth. In the Kasina-niddesa of the Visuddhimagga, it is said: 'By the power of the earth kasina, being one, he becomes many,' and so forth; thus the foundation jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) with the earth kasina as its object is appropriate here. However, in the Abhiññā-niddesa of that same Visuddhimagga, regarding the power of transformation, it is said: 'Having emerged from the foundation jhāna for direct knowledge from any one of the objects such as the earth kasina,' and it is also said there: 'One should reflect on one's own appearance as a youth.' This seems inappropriate for the creation of Nagas and so forth. The same method applies to the creation of the appearance of a Naga and so forth. 

In that passage, 'nāga-vaṇṇa' means the form of a serpent. 'Supaṇṇa-vaṇṇa' means the form of a garuda. 'Inda-vaṇṇa' means the form of Sakka. 'Deva-vaṇṇa' means the form of the remaining devas. The appearance of the ocean, however, is accomplished by the power of the water kasina. 'Patti' means infantry. 'Vividham pi senābyūhaṃ' means various arrays of armies consisting of elephants and so forth. In the Visuddhimagga, however, it is said: 'He displays an elephant also,' and so forth, in the sense of displaying elephants etc. external to oneself. In such a display, one should not determine 'Let me be an elephant,' but should determine 'Let there be an elephant.' The same method applies to horses and so forth. That statement (in the Visuddhimagga) contradicts the root words 'having abandoned his natural appearance' and the nature of the power of transformation (vikubbana-iddhi). According to the order stated in the Pali, displaying another form to others without abandoning one's natural appearance is called the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi). Displaying oneself as another form by abandoning one's natural appearance through the power of determination is called the power of transformation (vikubbana-iddhi).
278: In the explanation of the knowledge of mind-made psychic power (manomayiddhī-ñāṇa), regarding the words 'He creates another body from this body' and so on, a monk who wishes to perform the mind-made psychic power arises from the basic jhāna (pādakajjhāna) which has the space-kasiṇa (ākāsa-kasiṇa) as its object. First, he adverts to his own physical body (rūpakāya) and, in the manner already described, determines, 'Let it be hollow.' Then it becomes hollow. After that, he adverts to another body inside himself by the power of the earth-kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa), performs the preliminary work (parikamma), and determines in the manner already described. Another body then appears inside him. He pulls that created body out from his mouth and places it outside. Now, wishing to clarify this meaning with similes, the Buddha said 'Seyyathāpi' and so on. In that text, 'muñjamhā' means from the muñja grass. 'Isikaṃ pavāheyya' means one should pull out the reed. 'Kosiyā' means from the scabbard. 'Karaṇ္ဍā' means from the basket; it means from the slough which is the old skin. In that simile, 'should pull out' should be understood as pulling out by the mind alone. In reality, this creature called a snake, while remaining in its own kind, depending on the space between logs or trees, by the power called the effort of extracting the body from the old skin, as if biting its own body, loathing the old skin, abandons the slough (skin) by itself due to these four reasons. In this context, just as the reed and others are similar to the muñja grass and others, so too this mind-made form (nimmita-rūpa) produced by the supernormal mind is similar in all aspects to the monk who possesses psychic power; these similes are spoken to demonstrate this. In the passage 'He approached with the mind-made body by psychic power,' the body made by the supernormal mind (abhiññā-mana) is called the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya). In the passage 'He is reborn in a certain mind-made body,' the body produced by the jhāna-mind is called the mind-made body because it is made by that mind. But here, the body produced by the supernormal mind is called the mind-made body because it is made by that mind. If so, can a body made by the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāniddhī) and the power of transformation (vikubbaniddhī) also be called a mind-made body? Yes, it can. However, because in this text (Paṭisambhidāmagga), the power of determination and the power of transformation are explained separately and specifically, only the creation from within is called mind-made psychic power (manomayiddhī). In the explanation of the power pervaded by knowledge (ñāṇavipphāriddhī), it is called 'ñāṇavipphāra' (power of pervading knowledge) because it has the momentum of the pervading knowledge. Here too, the power is shown only by the power of the seven contemplations (anupassanā), and it should be understood that the remaining states up to the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga) are summarized.
279:
In the passages such as "The Power of Knowledge Diffusion of the Venerable Bākula" and so forth (the meaning should be understood as follows): The Elder Bākula received this name because he was raised in two families (kula). He was an elder who had made aspirations under previous Buddhas and was endowed with the fulfillment of merit. To elaborate, while experiencing great prosperity and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was born in the family of a treasurer (seṭṭhi) in the city of Kosambī, even before the birth of our Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala). When the child was born, for the sake of an auspicious ceremony, he was taken to the Yamunā River with a large retinue. Nurses, along with the retinue, bathed him while letting him play by submerging and emerging in the water.

A large fish, thinking "This is my food," opened its mouth and approached. The nurses abandoned the child and fled. The large fish swallowed the child. The meritorious being, as if entering a bedroom and lying down, did not experience any suffering. Due to the child's power, the large fish felt as if it had swallowed a red-hot plowshare; burning intensely, it swam with great speed for thirty leagues (yojana) and entered the net of a fisherman living in Bārāṇasī. Due to the child's power, the fish died as soon as it was taken out of the net. The fishermen, carrying the whole fish on a pole and wandering through the city saying "We will sell it for a thousand [kahāpaṇas]," reached the door of a treasurer who possessed eighty crores of wealth but was childless. They sold it to the treasurer's wife for only one kahāpaṇa.

The treasurer's wife herself placed the fish on a board and split it from the back. Seeing the golden-colored child inside the fish's belly, she cried out joyfully, "I have obtained a son from the belly of a fish!" and taking the child, she went to her husband, the treasurer. The treasurer immediately had the drums beaten, took the child to the King, and reported the matter. The King said, "This child is a meritorious one; raise him." The other treasurer's family (from Kosambī), having heard the news, went to Bārāṇasī and disputed to take the child, saying "This is our son." Both families went to the royal palace. The King decided, "I cannot make both families childless; let him be the heir to both."

From then on, both treasurer families attained the highest gain and the highest fame. Because he was raised by two families, they named him "Bākula Kumāra" (the youth Bākula). When he reached the age of discretion, they had three palaces built for him in each of the two cities and provided him with dancers. He lived for four months in each city. After staying for four months in one city, they would build a pavilion on joined boats, place him there with the dancers, and while he enjoyed great prosperity, they would escort him halfway to the other city over a period of two months. The dancers of the other city, thinking "He will arrive at the halfway point in two months"...
280:
In the same manner, they welcomed him and after two months, they would take him to their own city. The other dancers would turn back halfway and return to their own city. Having stayed in that city for four months, he would go again to the other city in the same way. Thus, enjoying such prosperity, eighty years of his life were completed.

At that time, our Bodhisatta, having attained omniscience and having set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, arrived at Kosambī while wandering in stages. (The Majjhima-bhāṇakas [reciters of the Middle Length Discourses], however, say it was the city of Bārāṇasī.) The merchant Bākula, hearing that "the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) has arrived," took many perfumes and flowers, went to the Teacher, and after listening to the Dhamma talk, gained faith and went forth as a monk. He remained a worldling (puthujjana) for only seven days, and at dawn on the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Then, the women of the two cities who were familiar with him, staying in their own family homes, made robes and sent them to him. For half a month, the Elder used the robes sent by the people of Kosambī, and for the other half-month, those sent by the people of Bārāṇasī. In this manner, whatever excellent things were available in the two cities, they were brought only to the Elder. Eighty years passed comfortably for the Elder even after his ordination. In both his lay life and monkhood, not even for a moment did any illness, however slight, ever arise in him. In his final days, he passed away into Parinibbāna after preaching the Bākula Sutta. Thus, the state of being free from illness within the belly of the fish, which arose for the Venerable Bākula—a pacchimabhavika (one in his last birth)—through the power of the knowledge of Arahantship to be attained in that very life, is called "ñāṇavipphārā iddhi" (the power of the diffusion of knowledge). Some also say it is through the power of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa) attained as a result of well-performed deeds.

The Elder Saṅkicca also had merit performed in previous lives and was reborn in the womb of a daughter of a wealthy family in Sāvatthī, who was a supporter of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta). While the child was in her womb, that woman died suddenly of a certain disease. When her body was being cremated, the fire consumed the rest of the flesh except for the flesh of the womb. Then, they removed the womb-flesh from the funeral pyre and pierced it with stakes in two or three places. The tip of a stake touched the corner of the child's eye. Having thus pierced the womb-flesh, they threw it into a heap of embers, covered it with coals, and left. Although the womb-flesh was burnt, the child remained atop the embers like a golden image, as if lying in the hollow of a lotus. Indeed, for a being in his last birth, even if he were crushed by Mount Sineru, there is no such thing as the end of life until he has attained Arahantship.
281:
For beings in their last birth, there is no such thing as the end of life as long as they have not yet reached Arahantship. The next day, people who came saying, "We shall extinguish the funeral pyre," saw the child lying there in that manner. Filled with wonder and amazement, they took the child to the city and consulted the soothsayers. The soothsayers said, "If this child lives the household life, his relatives will be poor for seven generations. If he goes forth as a monk, he will wander surrounded by five hundred ascetics." His grandmother raised the child. When he grew up, his relatives raised him with the intention, "We shall have him ordained in the presence of our master, the Elder Sāriputta."

When the child reached the age of seven, he heard the words of his friends saying, "While you were in your mother's womb, your mother died; even when her body was cremated, you were not burnt." Hearing this, he thought, "Since I have been delivered from such danger, what is the use of living the household life? I shall go forth." He informed his relatives. The relatives said, "Very well, dear son," and took him to the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, and handed him over, saying, "Venerable Sir, please ordain this child." The Great Elder gave him the meditation subject of the fivefold skin-group (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. Even before the shaving of his hair was finished, at the very tip of the razor, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. When he reached the full age for higher ordination, he received it, and upon reaching ten years of seniority, he wandered with a retinue of five hundred monks. As stated, the state of being healthy and unharmed in the wooden funeral pyre is the ñāṇavipphārā iddhi of the Venerable Saṅkicca.

The Elder Bhūtapāla was also endowed with previous causes of merit. His father was a poor man in the city of Rājagaha. He took the boy and went to the forest with a cart for wood. Having gathered a load of wood, he arrived near the city gate in the evening. Then, his pair of oxen broke free from the yoke and entered the city. He sat his young son down near the cart and, following the tracks of the oxen, entered the city himself. Before he could come back out, the gate was closed. The boy lay down under the cart and fell asleep for the whole night. Rājagaha is naturally a place full of non-human beings (amanussa), and this spot was also near a cemetery. However, no yakkha was able to cause harm to that child who was in his last birth. Later, he went forth, attained Arahantship, and became known as the Elder Bhūtapāla. Thus, the state of being healthy and unharmed even in a place frequented by fierce yakkhas is the ñāṇavipphārā iddhi of the Venerable Bhūtapāla.
282:
In the section explaining the power of diffusion of concentration (samādhivipphāra-iddhi), it is taught starting with the power of the Venerable Sāriputta due to concentration. While the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Kapotakandarā with the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, on a moonlit night, sitting in the open air with a freshly shaved head, a wicked yakkha struck him on the head despite being warned by his companion yakkha. The sound of that blow was as loud as a thunderclap. At the time the yakkha struck, the Elder was sitting in a meditative attainment (samāpatti). Consequently, he suffered no injury or illness from that blow. This is the Elder's power of diffusion of concentration.

Regarding this, the Blessed One taught as follows: "Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were staying at Kapotakandarā. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting in the open air on a moonlit night with a freshly shaved head, having entered a certain meditative attainment.

At that time, two yakkhas who were companions were traveling from the north to the south on some business. Those yakkhas saw the Venerable Sāriputta sitting in the open air on a moonlit night with a freshly shaved head. Having seen him, one yakkha said to the second yakkha: 'Friend, it occurs to me to give this recluse (samaṇa) a blow on the head.' When this was said, the other yakkha said to that yakkha: 'Enough, friend! Do not strike the recluse. Friend, that recluse is excellent, of great power and great majesty.'

A second time... [as before]... A third time, that yakkha said to the other: 'Friend, it occurs to me to give this recluse a blow on the head.' For the third time, the other yakkha warned him: 'Enough, friend! Do not strike the recluse. Friend, that recluse is excellent, of great power and great majesty.'"
283:
Then that yakkha, disregarding the words of the (warning) yakkha, struck the Venerable Sāriputta on the head with all his might. That blow was so powerful that it could have sunk a great elephant seven or seven and a half cubits tall into the ground, or split a great mountain peak. After striking, that yakkha cried out, "I am burning! I am burning!" and fell into the great hell right there.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, with the purified divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) surpassing that of humans, saw the yakkha giving the blow to the Venerable Sāriputta's head. Having seen this, he approached the Venerable Sāriputta and asked: "Friend Sāriputta, are you comfortable? Are you keeping well? Are you free from any pain?" "Friend Moggallāna, I am comfortable; I am keeping well. However, my head is slightly aching," he replied.
