"Friend Sāriputta, it is wonderful! Friend Sāriputta, it is marvelous! How great is the power and majesty of the Venerable Sāriputta! Friend Sāriputta, just now a certain yakkha gave you a blow on the head. That blow was so powerful that it could have sunk a great elephant seven or seven and a half cubits tall into the ground, or split a great mountain peak. Yet, the Venerable Sāriputta says: 'Friend Moggallāna, I am comfortable; I am keeping well. However, my head is slightly aching.'"

"Friend Moggallāna, it is wonderful! Friend Moggallāna, it is marvelous! How great is the power and majesty of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, in that he could even see a yakkha! As for me, Sāriputta, I do not even see a mud-sprite (paṃsupisāca) at this time," he said.
284:
The Blessed One heard the conversation of those two great Nagas with his divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses that of humans.

Then, the Blessed One, having understood the matter, uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) at that time:

Whose mind is like a rock, steady and unshakable,
Detached from things that incite lust, and not provoked by things that incite anger,
For one whose mind is thus developed, from where can suffering come?

In this verse, the words spoken by the Blessed One, "from where can suffering come?" align perfectly with the commentary's statement that "due to that blow, there was no ailment whatsoever." Therefore, the statement "Indeed, my head hurts a little" does not mean that painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) occurred; rather, it was said as "suffering" (dukkha) in reference to the head's temporary state of being unresponsive (unfit for work). In the world, one who can carry out tasks without difficulty is called "sukha-sīla" (of ease), and one who carries out tasks with difficulty is called "dukkha-sīla" (of difficulty). It should be understood that such unresponsiveness occurred because it was the time of emerging from the meditative attainment. While absorbed in the attainment, even that would not occur. The statement "Now, we do not even see a ground-dwelling demon (pamsu-pisāca)" was not said because of an inability to see, but because of a lack of exertion in the higher knowledges (abhiññā).

The Elder, out of compassion for future generations, thinking "May future generations of worldlings not perceive the essence in the psychic powers of worldlings," generally did not use psychic powers. And in the Elder's verses:

I have no longing for the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa),
Nor for the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), nor for the knowledge of discerning others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), nor for psychic powers (iddhi),
Nor for the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cuti-upapatti), nor for the purification of the ear element (dibba-sota-ñāṇa) — I have no longing for these.

Thus, the Elder himself stated his lack of desire for the higher knowledges. However, the Elder had reached the far shore of the sixty-seven types of knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa).

As for the Elder Sañjīva, the second chief disciple of the Blessed One Kakusandha, while he was in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), cowherds and others, thinking "He is dead," gathered grass, wood, and so on, and set them on fire. Not even a single thread of the Elder's robe was burnt. This was the psychic power of the diffusion of concentration (samādhi-vipphāra-iddhi), which arose from the power of serenity (samatha) practiced through the successive meditative attainments of that venerable one. As it is said:
285:
"O Evil One, at that time, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, had appeared in the world. O Evil One, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, had a pair of disciples named Vidhura and Sañjīva, an excellent and auspicious pair. O Evil One, among all the disciples of the Blessed One Kakusandha, there was no one equal to the Venerable Vidhura in terms of teaching the Dhamma. O Evil One, for this reason, the name 'Vidhura' became famous for the Venerable Vidhura. O Evil One, the Venerable Sañjīva, whether he went to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, would enter the cessation of perception and feeling (saññā-vedayita-nirodha) easily and without difficulty.

"O Evil One, it happened in the past that the Venerable Sañjīva was sitting at the foot of a certain tree, having entered the cessation of perception and feeling. O Evil One, cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Venerable Sañjīva sitting at the foot of that tree in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen him, the thought occurred to them: 'How wonderful, sirs! How marvelous, sirs! This recluse has died while sitting. Come, let us cremate him.'

"Then, O Evil One, those cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers gathered grass, wood, and cow dung, piled them on the body of the Venerable Sañjīva, set them on fire, and departed. Then, O Evil One, at the end of that night, the Venerable Sañjīva emerged from that attainment, shook his robes, and in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, entered the village for alms. O Evil One, those cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Venerable Sañjīva walking for alms. Having seen him, the thought occurred to them: 'How wonderful, sirs! How marvelous, sirs! This recluse died while sitting, and now he has come back to life!' O Evil One, for this reason, the name 'Sañjīva' became famous for the Venerable Sañjīva."
286:
The Elder Khāṇukoṇḍañña, by nature, frequently entered meditative attainments (samāpatti). That Elder was sitting in a certain forest at night, having attained a meditative state. Five hundred thieves, coming along after stealing goods, thought, "There is no one following us now," and wishing to rest, they lowered their bundles. Mistaking the Elder for a "tree stump" (khāṇu), they placed all their goods right on top of the Elder. When they were about to leave after resting, at the time of picking up the first bundle placed, the Elder emerged from the attainment according to the predetermined time limit. Seeing the movement of the Elder, the thieves cried out in terror. The Elder said, "Do not be afraid, lay devotees, I am a monk." They came and paid homage, and being inspired by the Elder, they ordained and reached the state of Arahatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). From that time on, the Elder became known as Khāṇukoṇḍañña Thera. In this story, the fact that the Venerable One suffered no affliction despite being pressed down by five hundred bundles is the power of the diffusion of concentration (samādhivipphāra-iddhi).

The laywoman Uttarā was the daughter of the wealthy treasurer Punna in the city of Rājagaha. Even as a young girl, she attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) along with her parents. When she reached of age, due to the great persistence of the treasurer of Rājagaha, she was given in marriage to his son, who held wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi). She felt oppressed because she had no opportunity to see the Buddha, hear the Dhamma, or give alms to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Therefore, she sent for a courtesan named Sirimā in that city and, giving her fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas brought from her father's house for the purpose of creating an opportunity, she entrusted her to her husband, saying, "Take these coins and attend to the treasurer's son for this fortnight." She herself undertook the Uposatha precepts and, with a joyful heart thinking, "During this fortnight, I shall have the chance to see the Buddha and so forth," she invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha until the day of Pavāraṇā and gave great offerings for the fortnight. After the meal, she would supervise the preparation of food and snacks in the kitchen. Her husband, thinking "Tomorrow is Pavāraṇā," stood at the window with Sirimā and, looking outside, saw Uttarā moving about in that manner, drenched in sweat and covered with ash and charcoal soot. He laughed, thinking, "This foolish woman does not enjoy her own wealth but instead performs what she calls merit." Uttarā also looked at him and laughed, thinking, "This fool does not perform merit for the hereafter."
287:
Sirimā, seeing the expressions of those two laughing, thought, "I am the mistress of the house." Overcome by jealousy and angry with Uttarā, she thought, "I will cause her suffering," and descended from the palace. Realizing Sirimā's intention, Uttarā sat on a bench and suffused Sirimā with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (mettā). Sirimā descended from the palace, entered the kitchen, took a ladleful of boiling ghee from the frying pan, and poured it over Uttarā's head. That ghee rolled off her like cool water falling on a lotus leaf. The maidservants struck Sirimā with their hands and feet and threw her to the ground. Uttarā, emerging from her meditative absorption of loving-kindness (mettā-jhāna), stopped the maidservants who were striking her. Sirimā begged Uttarā for forgiveness. Uttarā said, "Ask for forgiveness in the presence of the Blessed One tomorrow." When Sirimā asked to perform personal service for her, Uttarā told her to prepare the dishes. Sirimā prepared the dishes and, together with her retinue of five hundred courtesans, served the Buddha and the Saṅgha. She said, "Please be my companions in asking for forgiveness." The next day, as planned, after the Buddha had finished his meal, she paid homage to the Buddha along with those courtesans and said, "Venerable Sir, I have wronged Uttarā; may Uttarā forgive me." When the Buddha said, "Uttarā, forgive her," and she replied, "Venerable Sir, I forgive her," the Buddha preached the Dhamma, beginning with: "Conquer anger with non-anger" (Dhammapada 223). Even before the meal, Uttarā had brought her husband and her parents-in-law to the presence of the Buddha. At the end of the discourse, those three people and all the courtesans were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Thus, the fact that the laywoman Uttarā was not harmed by the boiling ghee is called samādhivipphāra-iddhi.

The laywoman named Sāmāvatī was the chief queen of King Udena in the city of Kosambī. That king had three chief queens, each with a retinue of five hundred women. Among them, Sāmāvatī was the daughter of the treasurer Bhaddiya in the city of Bhaddiya. When her father died, the King saw Sāmāvatī, who had grown up with a retinue of five hundred women in the house of the treasurer Ghosita in Kosambī (a friend of her father). Having reached marriageable age, the King felt affection for her, took her to his palace along with her retinue, consecrated her, and gave her the position of chief queen. There was also another queen named Vāsuladattā, the daughter of King Caṇḍappajjota. When the daughter of the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya was offered by her father to serve at the feet of the Blessed One, the Buddha said:

"Having seen Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, I had no desire for sexual intercourse. What is this body filled with urine and excrement? I would not want to touch it even with my foot." (Sutta Nipāta 841).
288:
Having heard the verse spoken by the Blessed One, she bore a grudge against the Blessed One. Her parents, at the conclusion of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta discourse, attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmī) and, having ordained, attained Arahantship. Her uncle, the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, took her to the city of Kosambī and presented her to King Udena. She became one of the King's chief queens.

At that time, three bankers named Ghosita, Kukkuṭa, and Pāvārika, having heard that a Buddha had arisen in the world, went to the Blessed One at Jetavana. Having heard the Dhamma, they attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). After offering great alms for half a month to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, they requested the Blessed One to visit the city of Kosambī. Returning to Kosambī, they built three monasteries named Ghositārāma, Kukkuṭārāma, and Pāvārikārāma. When the Teacher arrived at Kosambī in due course, they took turns hosting the Teacher at one monastery each day, and each banker offered great alms to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha.

Then one day, a florist named Sumana, who served those three bankers, asked for their permission and invited the Teacher along with the Saṅgha to his house for a meal. At that moment, a slave-woman named Khujjuttarā, who was a servant of Sāmāvatī, took eight kahāpaṇas and went to Sumana the florist’s house. Sumana said, "Please assist in serving the Teacher and the Saṅgha." Khujjuttarā did so, and at the conclusion of the Teacher’s meal, she heard the Dhamma discourse and became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). On other days, she used to take four kahāpaṇas for herself, but now, being incapable of taking what was not given, she bought flowers with all eight kahāpaṇas and presented them to Sāmāvatī.

When Sāmāvatī asked why there were so many flowers, Khujjuttarā, being incapable of telling a lie, told the truth. When asked, "Why did you not take the money today?" she replied, "Having heard the Dhamma of the Fully Enlightened One, I have realized the Deathless (Nibbāna)." Sāmāvatī said, "Dear Uttarā, please preach that Dhamma to us as well." Khujjuttarā replied, "If so, let me bathe, give me a pair of clean clothes, seat me on a high seat, and all of you sit on lower seats."

All those women did as she requested. Khujjuttarā, an Ariyan disciple who had attained the analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) accessible to those in higher training (sekha), dressed in one cloth and draped another over her shoulder. Holding a fan, she preached the Dhamma to those women. Sāmāvatī and the five hundred women attained the fruit of Stream-entry. All those women bowed to Khujjuttarā and said, "Mother, from today onwards, do not perform any more menial tasks. Remain in the position of our mother and teacher; listen to all the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One and then preach it to us."

As Khujjuttarā did so, she later became one who was learned in the Tipiṭaka. The Blessed One placed her in the highest position among the laywomen who were of great learning, and she received the title of Etadagga. The women, led by Sāmāvatī, also desired to see the Blessed One. When the Blessed One walked along the main road, they made holes in the wall and gazed upon the Blessed One. They also performed acts of reverence and offerings.

Māgaṇḍiyā, when she arrived at that place and saw those holes, inquired about the reason. Learning that the Blessed One was passing by, and because of her existing grudge against the Blessed One, she became angry with those women as well. She reported to the King, saying, "Great King, the women led by Sāmāvatī have external longings. They have made holes in the wall to look at the ascetic Gotama. Within a few days, they will kill you." Although the King saw the holes, he did not believe Māgaṇḍiyā’s words; instead, he had air-vents (windows) constructed high up. Again, Māgaṇḍiyā, wishing to cause a rift between the King and those queens, had eight live chickens brought and said, "Great King, to test those queens, send these chickens and tell them to kill and cook them for me." When Sāmāvatī and the others said, "We do not dare to take the life of another," she said again, "Then have them cooked and sent for the ascetic Gotama."
289: "Please listen to all the Dhamma taught by the Teacher and then preach it back to us," they requested. Khujjuttarā did as requested and later became a disciple capable of bearing the Tipitaka. The Teacher appointed her to the foremost position (etadagga) among the laywomen who are very learned (bahussuta). The women, led by Sāmāvatī, desired to see the Buddha. When the Buddha walked along the main street, as the air vents were insufficient, they made holes in the walls to behold the Teacher and performed acts of worship and reverence. Māgaṇḍiyā arrived there, saw those holes, and upon inquiring about the reason, learned of the Teacher's arrival. Out of malice toward the Blessed One, she also became angry with those women and told the King, "Great King, the women led by Sāmāvatī have external desires; they have pierced the walls to look at the ascetic Gotama. Within a few days, they will kill you." Although the King saw the holes, he did not believe her words and instead had ventilation windows constructed in the upper parts of the walls. Again, Māgaṇḍiyā, wishing to create a rift between the King and those women, had eight live chickens brought and said, "Great King, to test those women, send these chickens to them saying, 'Kill these and cook them for me.'" The King sent them as suggested, but Sāmāvatī and the others said, "We do not take life." Then she said, "Tell them to cook and send them for the ascetic Gotama." When the King sent them accordingly, Māgaṇḍiyā sent eight already-killed chickens with the same instruction. Sāmāvatī cooked them and sent them to the Buddha. Even by this means, Māgaṇḍiyā was unable to make the King angry. King Udena used to stay for seven days at a time in the residences of each of his three chief queens. Wherever the King went, he would take with him the lute called Hatthikantavīṇā. When the King was about to go to Sāmāvatī's palace, Māgaṇḍiyā had a young cobra brought, rubbed its fangs with medicine, placed it inside the lute, and blocked the opening with a flower garland. When the King arrived there, Māgaṇḍiyā, pretending to walk here and there, removed the flower garland from the lute's opening. The snake came out, spread its hood, and lay coiled on the royal bed. Then Māgaṇḍiyā cried out loudly, "Oh, what a terrifying snake!" Seeing the snake, the King became enraged. Sāmāvatī, knowing the King's anger, instructed the five hundred women, "Today, radiate loving-kindness toward the King, pervading him thoroughly with mettā." She herself did the same. The King took up a bow with the strength of a thousand viss, strung it, and...
290: Placing Sāmāvatī at the front and making all those women stand in a row, he fitted a poison-tipped arrow, aimed the bow, and stood there. The King was unable to shoot the arrow, nor was he able to lower it. Sweat poured from his body, his body trembled, saliva (or foam) fell from his mouth, and he could not maintain control. Then Sāmāvatī asked the King, "Great King, why are you exhausted?" The King replied, "Yes, Queen, I am very exhausted; be my refuge." Sāmāvatī said, "Very well, Great King, point the arrow toward the ground." The King did so. Sāmāvatī made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), "May the arrow be released from the King's hand." At that moment, the arrow was released. At that very moment, the King, as if submerged in water, with wet clothes and wet hair, prostrated at Sāmāvatī's feet and said, "Queen, forgive me," and spoke: "I am greatly confused, utterly bewildered; All directions are unclear to me. Sāmāvatī, protect me, And you be my refuge." Sāmāvatī said: "Great King, do not take me as your refuge. Take refuge only in that Blessed One in whom I have taken refuge. Take refuge only in that Buddha, And you, Great King, be my protector." The King said, "In that case, I take refuge in both you and the Blessed One, and I grant you a boon." Sāmāvatī replied, "Great King, I accept the boon." The King approached the Blessed One, established himself in the refuges, and after inviting and offering a great almsgiving (mahādāna) for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he said, "Sāmāvatī, take your boon." Sāmāvatī requested, "Very well, Great King, grant me this boon: let the Blessed One come to this palace with five hundred monks so that I may listen to the Dhamma." The King paid homage to the Blessed One and requested, "Venerable Sir, please come to this palace regularly with five hundred monks; the women led by Sāmāvatī wish to hear the Dhamma." The Blessed One replied, "Great King, it is not proper for Buddhas to go regularly to a single place; many people also look forward to the Buddha's arrival." "Venerable Sir, if that is so, please send monks." The Blessed One then instructed the Elder Ānanda. The Elder took five hundred monks and went regularly to the palace. Those women, led by Queen Sāmāvatī, offered alms-food to the Elder and listened to the Dhamma. The Blessed One appointed Sāmāvatī to the foremost position among the laywomen who dwell in loving-kindness (mettā-vihārī). Thus, it should be understood that the King's inability to release the arrow was due to the expansion of concentration (samādhi-vipphāra) of the laywoman Sāmāvatī. In this context, she is called an 'upāsikā' because she attends upon the Triple Gem. 17. In the Ariyiddhi-niddesa, it should be understood as 'ariyiddhi' (noble psychic power) because it occurs only to the noble ones (arahants) who have mastered their minds. In this Dispensation, a monk is one whose defilements are exhausted...
291:
In this term 'Iddhi', she is called an 'Upāsikā' because she attends to the Triple Gem through unwavering faith (aveccappasāda), or through conviction (okappanappasāda), or by taking refuge in the Triple Gem.

In the explanation of Noble Power (ariya iddhi), it is called 'Noble Power' because it can only occur to Noble Ones who are Arahants (khīṇāsava) who have attained mastery over the mind. 'A monk in this Dispensation' refers to an Arahant monk in this Dispensation whose taints are exhausted. (The following explains the mode of attention) towards a disagreeable object, whether it be a being or a formation (saṅkhāra). If it is a being, he pervades it with the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā). If it is a formation, he applies the attention to elements, thinking, 'It is merely an element.' Applying the attention to elements is also appropriate regarding beings. If it is a being, he pervades it with the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā). If it is a formation, he applies the attention to impermanence, thinking, 'It is impermanent.' 'Both of them' refers to both of those types. 'One who is equanimous' means one who is equanimous through six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā). 'One who is mindful' means because of having reached the fullness of mindfulness. 'One who is clearly comprehending' means because of acting with clear comprehension through wisdom.

'Having seen a form with the eye' means having seen a form with the eye-consciousness which is capable of seeing forms and which has received the conventional name 'eye' by way of its cause. However, the ancient teachers said: 'The eye does not see because it is without mind; the mind does not see because it is without the eye; but when there is a collision between the door and the object, one sees with the mind based on the sensitive material quality (pasāda).' This kind of statement is a 'discourse with its constituents,' like saying 'one shoots with a bow.' Therefore, 'having seen a form with the eye-consciousness' is the meaning here. Alternatively, it means having seen a form with the eye as the instrument.

'He is neither glad' refers to the rejection of household-based joy (somanassa), and not the rejection of functional joy-feeling. 'Nor is he sad' refers to the rejection of all grief (domanassa). 'He dwells equanimous' means he dwells equanimous with equanimity-of-the-middle (tatramajjhattupekkhā), which is named 'six-factored equanimity' because it occurs at the six doors in a manner that does not abandon its pure natural state when desirable and undesirable objects come into range. The same method applies to 'having heard a sound with the ear,' and so on.

In the explanation of power born of kamma-result (kammavipākaja iddhi), 'of all birds' refers to the flight of all kinds of birds through the sky even without jhāna or direct knowledge (abhiññā). Likewise, it includes the flight through the sky and the vision, etc., of all devas. 'Of some humans' refers to the power of humans at the beginning of the aeon. 'Of some fallen beings (vinipātika)' refers to Piyaṅkaramātā, Punabbasumātā...
292:
The female yakkhas (vinipātika) such as Phussamittā and Dhammaguttā, because they have fallen away from the body which is the cause of happiness, their ability to travel through the sky and so on, as well as the travel through the sky of other hungry ghosts (petas), nagas, and garudas, is called power born of kamma-result (kammavipākaja iddhi).

In showing the power of the meritorious (puññavanta): He is called 'King' (rājā) because he delights others righteously. He is called a 'Wheel-turner' (cakkavatti) because he causes the jewel-wheel to turn. 'Goes through the sky' (vehāsaṃ gacchati) is a usage in the sense of continuous connection. 'With the fourfold army' (caturaṅginī) means the army possessing the four factors known as elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. 'Army' (senā) refers merely to the collection of those four. 'Even to the lowest' (antamaso) means by way of the lowest limit. 'Horse-binders' (assabandhā) are horse-keepers. 'Cow-men' (gopurisā) are cow-herds. 'Taking along' (upādāya) means without leaving behind. Thus, the ability of these people to travel through the sky is the power of the meritorious.

The power of the meritorious Jotika the Treasurer is as follows: Jotika was a treasurer in the city of Rājagaha who had performed meritorious deeds under previous Paccekabuddhas. It is said that on the day of his birth, all the weapons in the entire city glowed, and the ornaments worn on the bodies of all people emitted light as if they were burning; the whole city became a single blaze of light. Therefore, on the day of his naming, they gave him the name 'Jotika' (The Luminous One) because the entire city had become a single light. Later, when he reached the age of maturity and the ground was being cleared to build a house, Sakka, the king of devas, came and, breaking the earth in a place about sixteen karīsas in size, brought forth a seven-storied palace made of the seven gems. Surrounding the palace, he brought forth seven walls made of the seven gems, provided with seven gate-towers. At the edge of the walls, he brought forth sixty-four wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha). At the four corners of the palace, he brought forth four large golden treasure pots measuring one league, three-quarters of a league, half a league, and a quarter league respectively. At the four corners of the palace, four golden sugarcane stalks the size of young palmyra trunks appeared. Their leaves were made of emeralds and their joints were made of gold. At the seven gate-towers, seven Yakkhas, with retinues of one, two, three, four, five, six, and seven thousand Yakkhas respectively, took up guard.

King Bimbisāra, hearing of the appearance of the palace and so on, sent the treasurer's parasol. That treasurer became famous throughout the whole of Jambudīpa as Jotika the Treasurer. He lived in that palace enjoying great prosperity together with his wife, who had been brought from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) by deities and placed in the auspicious chamber, and who had come bringing a single nāḷi (pint) of rice and three flame-stones (joti-pāsāṇa). For them, that single nāḷi of rice was sufficient for their meals for as long as they lived. Indeed, if they wished to fill a hundred carts with rice, they could do so; and even after filling them, the original nāḷi of rice remained just as it was. When cooking rice, they would put the rice in a pot and place it on top of those three flame-stones. At that moment, flames would emerge from the three stones, and when the rice was just cooked, they would extinguish by themselves. By seeing the fire extinguished, they knew the rice was cooked. The same method applied when cooking curry. Thus, for them, by means of the flame-stones...
293: For that couple, even a single measure (nāḷi) of rice was sufficient for their entire lives. If they wished to fill a hundred carts with rice, that rice would fill a hundred carts and yet remain as the original single measure. When cooking rice, they would put the rice in a pot and place it on top of those three joti stones. At that moment, the stones would burst into flames and burn, and as soon as the rice was cooked, they would go out. By that sign of the fire extinguishing, they knew the rice was cooked. The same method applied when cooking curry and other dishes. Thus, they cooked their food with the joti stones and lived by the light of gems. They did not even know the light of fire or the light of lamps. The fame of Jotika the Treasurer's such prosperity spread throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. Many people came by carts and other vehicles to see it. Jotika the Treasurer fed all who came with rice cooked from the rice obtained from Uttarakuru. He commanded, "Take clothes and ornaments from the wishing trees (kalpavriksha)." He also commanded, "Open the mouth of the treasure pot that is a gāvuta in size and take as much wealth as is sufficient for your livelihood." Even though all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa took wealth, the treasure pot did not decrease even by a finger's breadth; such was the power of that meritorious treasurer. Regarding the power of Jaṭila the Treasurer: The treasurer named Jaṭila was a treasurer from Takkasilā who had performed meritorious deeds at the relic stupa of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha. His mother was the daughter of a treasurer in Bārāṇasī, who was exceedingly beautiful. When she reached the age of fifteen or sixteen, they made her live on the top floor of a seven-storied mansion for her protection. One day, a Vijjādhara (sorcerer) traveling through the sky saw her looking out of the window; he fell in love, entered through the window, and had relations with her. She became pregnant. Then a maidservant saw it and asked, "Mistress, what is this?" She replied, "Let it be, do not tell anyone," and the maid remained silent out of fear. When ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son. She had a new pot brought, placed the child inside, closed the pot, and placed flower garlands on top. She commanded the maid, "Carry this on your head and set it adrift in the Ganges River. If anyone asks, 'What is this?', say, 'It is my mistress's offering to the gods.'" The maid did as she was told. Two women bathing downstream in the Ganges saw the pot floating in the water. One said, "Let this pot be mine." The other said, "Let whatever is inside the pot be mine." When the pot reached them, they took it and placed it on the bank.
294: Upon opening the pot and seeing the child, the woman who had said "My pot" now said, "Let the child be mine alone." The other woman, who had said "Whatever is inside the pot is mine," said, "He is my son." As the two women were quarreling, they went to the court of justice, but the ministers could not decide, so they went before the King. When the King heard their words, he decreed, "You take the child, and you take the pot." The woman who received the child was a lay follower (upāsikā) of the Elder Mahā Kaccāyana. She raised him, thinking, "I will have this child ordained as a novice under the Elder." On the day of the child's birth, although the birth impurities were washed, they were not completely removed, and his hair remained matted. Therefore, they named the child "Jaṭila" (the matted-haired one). When the child was able to walk, the Elder entered that house for alms. The lay follower invited the Elder to sit and offered him almsfood. Seeing the child, the Elder asked, "Lay follower, did you obtain a child?" "Yes, Bhante, I am raising this child to be ordained under you," she replied. The Elder said, "Very well," and while taking the child away, he reflected, "Does this child have the merit to enjoy worldly prosperity?" He realized, "He is a person of great merit and will enjoy great prosperity, but he is still young and his wisdom is not yet mature." Thinking thus, he took the child and went to the house of a supporter (upaṭṭhāka) in Takkasilā. That donor prostrated before the Elder and, seeing the child, asked, "Bhante, did you obtain a child?" "Yes, donor, he will be ordained in the future, but for now, since he is young, let him stay with you," he said. The donor agreed, saying, "Very well, Bhante," and raised him as his own son. In that man's house, there was a large quantity of goods that had remained unsold for twelve years. When he was about to go to another village, he brought all those goods to the shop, told him the price of each item, and instructed, "Sell this item for this much," and then departed. On that day, the guardian deities of the city caused even those who wanted only a little cumin or pepper to come only to that boy's shop. The boy sold all the goods that had been piled up for twelve years in a single day. When the merchant returned and found nothing in the shop, he asked, "Dear son, have you destroyed all the goods?" "I have not destroyed them, father. I have sold them all as you instructed. This is the money for those goods, and this is..."
295:
“This price is the price for such and such goods,” he said, and handed over all the money to that householder. The householder, being pleased, thought, “This man is priceless; he is capable of making a living anywhere.” He gave his grown daughter to Jaṭila and ordered men, “Build a house for him.” When the house was finished, he said, “Go, live in your own house.” Then, at the moment Jaṭila entered the house and merely stepped on the threshold with one foot, a mountain of gold eighty cubits high rose up from the ground at the back of the house. The King of Takkasilā, hearing that a mountain of gold had risen from the ground in Jaṭila’s house, granted him the parasol of a Treasurer (Seṭṭhi). He became known as Jaṭila the Treasurer. This was the psychic power (iddhi) of that meritorious person (puññavanta).

The psychic power of the meritorious Meṇḍaka the Treasurer: Meṇḍaka was a treasurer in the city of Bhaddiya in the kingdom of Magadha, who had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under the Buddha Vipassī. It is said that in a place about eight karīsas in size behind his house, golden rams the size of elephants, horses, and bulls rose up, breaking through the earth and standing back to back. In their mouths were placed balls of thread of five colors. When there was a need for ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and such, or for clothing, silver, gold, and so on, they would pull a ball of thread from their mouths. From the mouth of even a single ram, enough ghee, oil, honey, molasses, clothing, silver, and gold would emerge to suffice for all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. From then on, he was known as Meṇḍaka the Treasurer. This was the psychic power of that meritorious person.

The psychic power of the meritorious Ghosita the Householder: Ghosita was a treasurer in Kosambī in the kingdom of the Sakkas, who had performed meritorious deeds under a Paccekabuddha. Having passed away from the deva world, he was conceived in the womb of a courtesan in the city of Kosambī. On the day he was born, she placed him in a basket and had him abandoned on a rubbish heap. Crows and dogs surrounded the child and sat there. A man, seeing him, felt a fatherly affection and thinking, “I have gained a son,” took him home. At that time, the Treasurer of Kosambī saw the chaplain (purohita) and asked, “Teacher, have you observed the lunar day and the constellations today?” When he replied, “Yes, Great Treasurer,” he asked again, “What will happen to the country?” “The child born today in this city will become the Chief Treasurer,” the chaplain said. At that time, the Treasurer’s wife
296:
was heavily pregnant. Therefore, he quickly sent a message to his house, “Go, find out whether she has given birth or not.” Hearing “She has not given birth,” he went home, called a maidservant named Kāḷi, gave her a thousand [pieces of money], and said, “Go, search in this city and buy the child born today and bring him here.” While searching, she went to that laborer's house, and knowing that the child was born on that very day, she gave a thousand, brought him, and showed him to the Treasurer. The Treasurer thought, “If a daughter is born to me, I will have him live with her and make him the master of the treasurer’s position. But if a son is born, I will kill him,” and he had the child brought up in the house.

After a few days, his wife gave birth to a son. The Treasurer thought, “Only if this child is gone will my son obtain the position of Treasurer. It is proper to kill him right now.” He called Kāḷi and said, “Hey girl, go; when the cows are coming out of the pen, lay this child across the middle of the gate. The cows will trample him to death. Come back after finding out whether he was trampled or not.” Kāḷi went and, just as the cowherd opened the gate, she laid the child down as instructed. The lead bull, the largest of the herd, which usually came out last at other times, came out first that day and stood over the child, keeping him between his four legs. Hundreds of cows went out, brushing against both sides of the bull. The cowherd thought, “This bull usually comes out last, but today he came out first and stands motionless in the middle of the gate. What could this be?” He went to look and, seeing the child lying under the bull, felt a fatherly love and said, “I have gained a son,” and took him home.

When Kāḷi went back and was questioned by the Treasurer, she reported the matter. He said, “Go again, give this thousand and bring the child back.” She brought him back and gave him to him. Then the Treasurer said, “Mother Kāḷi, in this city, five hundred carts rise at dawn and set out for trade. Take this child and lay him in the cart track. Either the oxen will trample him or a wheel will cut him. Come back after knowing what happens to him.” She went and laid him in the cart track. The leader of the caravan was at the front. Then his oxen, reaching that spot, threw off their yokes. Even though the yokes were put on again and again and the oxen were driven, they would not go forward. While he was struggling with the oxen in this way, dawn broke. The caravan leader, looking at the road to see what the oxen were doing, saw the child and said, “What a heavy burden...”
297:
Thinking, 'Alas, what a heavy deed I have done!' and with a joyful heart, thinking, 'I have gained a son,' he took the child to his home.

Kāḷī also went, and when questioned by the treasurer, she told him what had happened. He said, 'Go, give another thousand coins and bring him back,' and she did as she was told. Then the treasurer said, 'Now, take this child to the Āmakasusāna cemetery and lay him down in the midst of the bushes. There, he will die, either eaten by dogs and such, or struck by a non-human. Go and find out whether he is dead or alive, and then return.' Kāḷī took the child, laid him down in that cemetery, and stood at a distance. Neither the dogs nor the non-humans dared to approach the child.

At that time, a goatherd was driving his goats to their pasture and passed by the side of the cemetery. A she-goat, while eating leaves, entered the bushes, saw the child, and kneeling down, gave him her milk. Even when the goatherd shouted, 'Hey! Hey!', she did not come out. Thinking, 'I will drive her out by striking her with my staff,' he entered the bushes and saw the she-goat kneeling and suckling the child. Feeling a fatherly love for the child, he thought, 'I have gained a son,' and took him away.

Kāḷī returned home and told the treasurer what had happened. The treasurer said, 'Go, give another thousand coins and bring him back,' and she did so. Then the treasurer said, 'Lady Kāḷī, take this child, climb the mountain with the precipice where thieves are thrown, and cast him into the abyss. He will strike the mountain slope, be broken into pieces, and fall to the ground. Go and find out whether he is dead or alive, and then return.' Kāḷī did as the treasurer said and threw the child from the mountain top. However, supported by that mountain slope, a large bamboo thicket grew along the mountain, and its top was covered by a dense growth of jin̄juka bushes. When the child fell, he landed on the bushes as if falling onto a woolen rug.

On that very day, it was time for the chief of the basket-makers to pay his bamboo tax. He went with his son and began to cut that bamboo thicket. When the thicket shook, the child cried out. Hearing the child's voice, the basket-maker climbed up from one side, saw him, and with a joyful heart, saying, 'I have gained a son,' he took him away. Kāḷī told the treasurer what had happened, and the treasurer said, 'Go, give another thousand coins and bring him back,' and she did so.

While the treasurer was performing various such deeds, the child grew up. Because he used to speak with a loud voice, he came to be known only by the name 'Ghosita.' He appeared like a thorn in the treasurer's eye. The treasurer did not even dare to look at him directly. Then, plotting his death, he went to his potter and asked, 'When will you fire the kiln?' The potter replied, 'I will fire it tomorrow.' The treasurer said, 'If so, take these thousand coins and do a task for me.' The potter asked, 'Lord, what task?' The treasurer said, 'I have a base-born son. I will send him to you. When he arrives, take him into a room, cut him into pieces with a sharp knife, put him in a jar, and place it in the kiln.' He added, 'These thousand coins are just a down payment; later, I will give you more wealth appropriate for the task.' The potter agreed, saying, 'Very well.'

The next day, the treasurer called Ghosita and sent him, saying, 'Yesterday, I assigned a task to the potter. Go to that potter and say, "Complete the task my father ordered yesterday."' Ghosita said, 'Very well,' and went. While going, he saw the treasurer's own son playing marbles with his friends, who asked, 'Where are you going?'...
298:
He appeared like a thorn in the treasurer's eye; he did not even dare to look at him directly. Then, plotting the child's death, he went to his potter and asked him, 'When will you fire the kiln?' When the potter said, 'I will fire it tomorrow,' the treasurer said, 'If so, take these thousand coins and do a task for me.' 'Lord, what task?' he asked. 'I have an ill-born (avajāta) son. I will send him to you. When he arrives, take him inside, cut him into pieces with a sharp cleaver, put him in a jar, and place it in the kiln. These thousand coins are like a down payment for you; later, I will also give you wealth worthy of this deed.' The potter accepted, saying, 'Very well.'

The next day, the treasurer called Ghosita and sent him, saying, 'Dear son, come. Yesterday, I assigned a task to the potter. Go to that potter and say, "Complete the task my father assigned yesterday."' Ghosita said, 'Very well,' and went. While Ghosita was going, the treasurer's own son saw him while playing marbles with his friends, called him, and asked, 'Where are you going?' When Ghosita told him his father's message and said, 'I am going to the potter,' the son said, 'I will go there. These boys have won about a hundred thousand coins from me. Win back that lost money for me.' Ghosita said, 'I am very afraid of my father.' The son replied, 'Brother, do not be afraid of father. I will go and deliver that message. Until I return, win back the hundred thousand coins I lost.' It is said that Ghosita was very skilled at playing marbles; that is why the treasurer's son urged him so. Ghosita then sent him, saying, 'If you wish to go, go to the potter and say, "Complete the task my father assigned yesterday."' That treasurer's son went to the potter and spoke as his father had instructed. Then the potter killed the treasurer's son as instructed by the treasurer and threw him into the kiln.

Ghosita, after playing all day, returned home in the evening. When the treasurer asked, 'Dear son, why did you not go?', he explained the reason why he did not go and that his younger brother had gone instead. The treasurer cried out loudly, 'Woe! Woe!', feeling as if his whole body were filled with boiling blood. Crying out, 'O potter, do not destroy me! Do not destroy me!', he ran to the potter with his arms raised. When the potter saw the treasurer coming in such a state, he said, 'Lord, do not make a sound; the task you ordered is finished.' The treasurer, overwhelmed by a great grief as if crushed by a huge mountain, experienced immeasurable sorrow.
299:
Even though his plans had failed in this way, the Treasurer could not look Ghosita directly in the eye. Thinking, "How can I kill him?" he devised a plan, considering, "I will send him to the manager of my hundred villages and have him killed." He wrote a letter to that manager: "This man is my degenerate son. Kill him and throw him into a cesspool. Only when this is done will I know what is proper to be done for the uncle." Then he said, "Dear Ghosita, there is a manager in our hundred villages; take this letter and give it to him." He tied the letter to the hem of Ghosita’s garment. Ghosita, however, was illiterate. Since the Treasurer had been trying to kill him since he was a child, why would he have him taught to read? Carrying his own death warrant tied to the hem of his garment, Ghosita departed, saying, "Father, I have no provisions for the journey." The Treasurer replied, "There is no need for provisions. In such-and-such a village along the way, there is a merchant who is a friend of mine. Have breakfast at his house and then proceed."

Ghosita said, "Very well," paid respects to his father, and departed. Upon reaching that village, he inquired about the merchant’s house, went there, and met the merchant’s wife. When she asked, "Where have you come from?" he replied, "From the city." When she asked, "Whose son are you?" he said, "I am the son of the Great Treasurer, your friend." When she asked, "Is your name Ghosita?" he replied, "Yes, mother." As soon as she saw him, a motherly love for him arose in her. Now, that merchant had a daughter about fifteen or sixteen years old, who was exceedingly beautiful and graceful. To guard her, they had given her only one maidservant and made her live in the auspicious chamber on the top floor of a seven-storied mansion. At that moment, the merchant’s daughter had sent that maid to the market. Seeing the maid, the merchant’s wife asked, "Where are you going?" and when told, "I am going on an errand for the lady’s daughter," she said, "Come here for a moment. Let the errand wait. First, prepare a seat for my son, bring water and wash his feet, rub them with oil, and prepare a bed for him. Afterwards, you may do your errand." The maid did as she was told.

Later, when the maid returned after a long time, the merchant’s daughter rebuked her. The maid said, "Do not be angry with me. The Treasurer’s son Ghosita has arrived, and I was delayed because I had to attend to his needs." Upon hearing the name "the Treasurer’s son Ghosita," the daughter—due to their association in a previous life—felt a love that pierced through her skin and reached her very bone marrow. She then asked, "Mother, where is he?" "He is asleep on the bed," the maid replied. She asked again, "Is there anything in his hand?" and the maid said, "There is a letter tied to the hem of his garment." Then the merchant’s daughter wondered, "What kind of letter is this?" While Ghosita was asleep and her parents were busy with other matters and not watching, she descended from the mansion, went to Ghosita, and untied the letter. Returning to her room, she sealed the door, opened the window, and being literate, she read the letter. "Oh, how foolish!" she thought. "He is traveling with his own death warrant tied to the hem of his garment. If I had not seen this, this Treasurer’s son would no longer be alive." She then tore up and destroyed the letter. Afterwards, she wrote a new letter in the name of the Treasurer: "This youth is my son Ghosita. Have the gifts from the hundred villages brought, and celebrate his marriage with the daughter of this provincial merchant. Build him a two-storied house in the middle of the village where he resides, and provide it well with a surrounding wall and guards. I, the Treasurer, order this to be done."
300:
"He is sleeping," (I said). "Is there anything in his hand?" (the merchant's daughter asked). "There is a letter at the hem of his garment," (I replied). Thinking, "What kind of letter is this?", while Ghosita was sleeping and her parents were busy with other matters and not looking, she descended from the mansion, went near Ghosita, and untied the letter. Entering her room, she closed the door, opened the casement window, and being skilled in reading and writing, she read the letter. "Oh, how foolish! He travels about with his own death warrant tied to the hem of his garment. If I had not seen it, he would have no chance of living," (she thought). She tore up and destroyed that letter and wrote another letter in the merchant's words as follows: "This youth is my son named Ghosita. Having brought gifts from a hundred villages, celebrate his marriage with the daughter of this country merchant. Have a two-story house built in the middle of the village where he resides, and provide well-arranged protection with a surrounding wall and male guards. Send a message to me saying, 'I have performed such and such tasks.' When this is done, I will know what is appropriate to do for the uncle." Having written this, she rolled up the letter and tied it back to the hem of Ghosita's garment. 

After sleeping for about half a day, Ghosita woke up, ate, and departed. Early the next morning, he arrived at that village and saw the village headman managing the taxes. Seeing him, the headman asked, "Dear boy, what is the matter?" "My father has sent a letter to you, Uncle," he said and gave the letter. After taking and reading the letter, the headman was very delighted and said, "Look, friends, my master, out of love for me, has sent his eldest son to me, saying, 'Perform the marriage ceremony for my son.'" He ordered the householders, "Bring timber and other materials quickly." He had the house built in the middle of the village as described, brought gifts from a hundred villages, brought the country merchant's daughter, and performed the marriage. Then he sent a message to the merchant, "I have performed such and such tasks."

Upon hearing this news, the merchant felt great distress, thinking, "What I ordered did not happen; only what I did not order has come to pass." That sorrow, combined with the grief for his [deceased] son and the failure of his plans, caused a burning sensation in his stomach and produced dysentery. The merchant's daughter also gave an order: "If anyone comes from the merchant, do not tell the merchant's son before telling me." The merchant, thinking, "Now I will not let this wicked son be the owner of my property," called a workman and said, "Uncle, I wish to see my son. Send someone who stays near me with a letter to call my son." The man agreed, took the letter, and sent a person. 

The merchant's daughter took the youth Ghosita and went only when the merchant was severely ill. The merchant passed away. After the father's death, the King gave the wealth enjoyed by the father to Ghosita and appointed him to the position of merchant (Seṭṭhi) with a retinue of a hundred each of elephants, horses, and so on. Ghosita, established in great wealth, came to know from the words of the merchant's daughter and the slave woman Kālī how he had escaped death in seven places from the beginning, and he performed almsgiving by spending one hundred thousand daily. This is the story of Ghosita. Thus, Ghosita's freedom from danger in seven places is called the "power of a meritorious person."

In the Pali phrase "Ghositassa gahapatissa," "gaha" means house. Because he is the master of the house, he is called "gahapati." This name "gahapati" is the title of the head of a Gahapati-mahāsāla family. In some books, the Pali describing the power of the merchant Meṇḍaka is written immediately after Ghosita. In the phrase "Pañcannaṃ mahāpuññānaṃ puññavato iddhi," the meaning is that the power called the "power of a meritorious person" should be understood regarding five great meritorious ones. The five great meritorious ones are the merchant Meṇḍaka, his wife...
301:
...sent [him] and wrote a letter saying, "Call my son." That man said, "Very well," took the letter, and sent a man. The merchant's daughter took the youth Ghosita and went when the merchant was critically ill. The merchant passed away. After the father's death, the King granted the wealth and property enjoyed by the father and appointed him to the position of merchant (Seṭṭhi) along with a full retinue of elephants and horses. Having become the merchant named Ghosita and established in great wealth, he learned from the words of the merchant's daughter and the slave woman Kālī how he had escaped death in seven places from the beginning. Consequently, he established almsgiving by spending one hundred thousand daily. Thus, the merchant's freedom from danger in seven places is the "power of a meritorious person" (puññavato iddhi).

In that Pali phrase "Ghositassa gahapatissa," "gaha" refers to a house. Because he is the master of the house, he is called "gahapati" (householder). This name is the title for the head of a Gahapati-mahāsāla family. In some books, the account of the merchant Meṇḍaka is written immediately after Ghosita.

In the phrase "Pañcannaṃ mahāpuññānaṃ puññavato iddhi," the power of a meritorious person should be understood as the power of five great meritorious ones. Those five great meritorious ones are the merchant Meṇḍaka, his wife Candapadumā, his son the merchant Dhanañjaya, his daughter-in-law Sumanadevī, and his slave named Puṇṇa. These five people had performed meritorious deeds toward Paccekabuddhas. Among them, the merchant Meṇḍaka had one thousand two hundred and fifty granaries cleaned, performed the head-washing ceremony, and sat at the door of the granary looking up. Then, streams of red Sāli rice fell from the sky and filled all the granaries. 

His wife took about one measure (nāḷi) of rice, had it cooked, and made a curry in one vessel. Adorned with all ornaments, she sat on a prepared seat at the gatehouse and had it proclaimed, "Let all who need food come!" She called them, took a golden ladle, and filled the vessels brought by those who came. Even though she gave all day, it seemed as if only the amount taken by the ladle once was diminished. His son also performed the head-washing ceremony, took a bag containing a thousand coins (kahāpaṇas), and had it proclaimed, "Let those who need coins come!" He filled the vessels brought by those who came. There were always exactly one thousand coins in the bag. His daughter-in-law, adorned with all ornaments, took a basket of paddy holding one basket (four doṇas), sat on a seat, and had it proclaimed, "Let those who need seed-grain and food come!" She filled [the vessels of] those who came. The basket remained as full as it was. His slave, adorned with all ornaments...
302:
The treasurer's servant, having harnessed oxen with golden ropes to a golden yoke, holding a golden goad, gave the oxen perfumes taken with five fingers, fitted golden casings on their horns, went to the field and drove them. Seven furrows were broken: "three on this side, three on that side, and one in the middle." The inhabitants of Jambudīpa took whatever they desired—rice, seeds, gold, silver, etc.—only from the treasurer's house. In due course, when the Blessed One arrived at the city of Bhaddiya, through the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma, the five great meritorious ones and Visākhā, the daughter of Dhanañjaya the treasurer, attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). This is the "power of the meritorious" (puññavato iddhi) of those five meritorious ones. In brief, the special success that is fulfilled when the accumulation of merit has matured is called the "power of the meritorious."

In the explanation of the power consisting of knowledge (vijjāmayiddhi), they are called "knowledge-bearers" (vijjādhara) because they possess the Gāndhārī knowledge which has the nature of fulfillment, or knowledge accomplished through medicinal preparation, or knowledge accomplished by mere wishing, or other such knowledge. The phrase "vijjaṃ parijappetvā" means reciting the knowledge (spell) verbally according to the prescribed procedure. The rest is as previously explained.

In the explanation of the power of right effort (sammāpayogiddhi), since only the manner of fulfillment is asked and there is no other distinction, the question was asked as "how?" (kathaṃ) instead of "what?" (katamā), desiring to ask only about the manner. Likewise, it concluded with "thus" (evaṃ). Here, because of the desire to show right effort, which is called practice (paṭipatti), the text appears similar to the previous Pali. In the Commentary, however, it is stated that "iddhi" in the sense of fulfillment due to right effort in various places refers to the special result achieved by performing various tasks, starting from arranging a wagon-array, etc., any management, any craft, any medical work, learning the three Vedas, learning the three Piṭakas, and even down to plowing and sowing.

## ဣဒ္ဓိကထာဝဏ္ဏနာ နိဋ္ဌိတာ။

## ၃။ အဘိသမယကထာဝဏ္ဏနာ

Now, following the discourse on power, I shall explain the as-yet-unmentioned meaning of the discourse on realization (abhisamayakathā), which is taught to show realization (magga-phala), the supreme power. In that discourse on realization, "realization" (abhisamaya) means the meeting face-to-face with the Truths; the meaning is "penetration" (paṭivedha).
303:
## ၃-အဘိသမယကထာဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the phrase "By what does one realize?", what is the meaning? In the Sutta passages such as "Monks, thus the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) is of great benefit" (Saṃyutta Nikāya), that which is called "realization"—when that realization is occurring, by what state (dhamma) does the person who realizes face the Four Truths, meet them, and penetrate them? This is first the question (pucchā) of the objector (codaka).

"One realizes by the mind" (cittena abhisameti) is given because there can be no realization apart from the mind. The phrase beginning with "hañci" is a further objection. "Hañci" means "if". Since it was said "by the mind", he asks, "If so, does one without wisdom (aññāṇī) realize?" "One without wisdom does not realize" is a rejection because realization cannot occur by mere mind alone. "One realizes by wisdom" (ñāṇena abhisameti) is the admission (paṭiññā). Again, because it was said "by wisdom", the objection "hañci..." is made: "Does one who has wisdom but is without mind (acittaka) realize?" "One without mind does not realize" is a rejection because realization cannot occur for one without mind. "By mind and (by wisdom)..." is the admission. Again, the objection "hañci..." is made by way of commonality with all minds and wisdoms. The same method applies to the remaining objections and answers.

Later, in the phrase "by the mind of ownership of kamma and by wisdom" (kammassakata-cittena ca ñāṇena ca), it means realizing by the mind and wisdom that occur as the ownership of kamma, in the sense that "beings have kamma as their own property." In the phrase "by the mind conforming to the truths and by wisdom" (saccānulomika-cittena ca ñāṇena ca), it means realizing by the mind associated with insight (vipassanā) and by insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), which are called "conforming to the truths" because they are favorable to the penetration of the Four Truths. The question "How?" (kathaṃ) is a question (pucchā) asked with the desire to explain how realization occurs.

"Predominance in arising" (uppādādhipateyya) is because if there is no arising of the mind, there is no arising of mental factors (cetasika). The mind takes the object; how could the mental factors arising with it arise if the object is not taken? In the Abhidhamma, too, mental factors are analyzed only by the arising of the mind. Therefore, the meaning is: the mind is the predominant factor in the arising of path-wisdom (magga-ñāṇa). "Ñāṇassa" means of path-wisdom. "Hetu paccayo ca" means both the producer (janaka) and the supporter (upatthambhaka). "Taṃsampayuttaṃ" means the mind associated with that wisdom. "Nirodhagocaraṃ" means having Nibbāna as its object. "Predominance in seeing" (dassanādhipateyya) means, since there is no function of seeing in the remaining states, it is the predominant factor in seeing Nibbāna. "Cittassa" means of the mind associated with the path. "Taṃsampayuttaṃ" means the wisdom associated with that mind.

Because this reason is also a figurative explanation (pariyāya), it is not that realization occurs only by mind and wisdom; rather, all mental states (cittacetasika) associated with the path...
304:
They are called realization (abhisamaya) by virtue of accomplishing the task of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, desiring to show that method as well, the author asks, "Is this much alone realization?" and rejecting that statement with "Not so," he says, "At the moment of the supramundane path," and so forth. Realization through vision (dassanābhisamaya) means realization that is vision (dassana). This same method applies to the remaining types of realization. Truths (sacca) refers to the knowledges of the truths (sacca-ñāṇa). Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) itself is called insight (vipassanā) because of its nature of repeatedly contemplating Nibbāna. Liberation (vimokkha) refers to the liberation of the path. Knowledge (vijjā) refers to path-knowledge itself. Deliverance (vimutti) refers to deliverance by cutting off (samuccheda-vimutti). It is called realization (abhisamaya) because Nibbāna is penetrated (abhisamīyati); the remaining states are called realizations because [beings] penetrate [the truths] by means of them.

Again, desiring to show realization by dividing it according to path and fruition, he says, "How is it?" and so forth. However, at the moment of fruition, because knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇa) in the sense of cutting off cannot be obtained, it is called knowledge of non-arising (anuppāde ñāṇa) in the sense of tranquility. The remaining points should be understood accordingly. Now, since realization occurs when there is the abandoning of defilements, and the abandoning of defilements occurs when there is realization, he says, "This noble person standing in the path," and so forth, desiring to show the abandoning of defilements preceded by a challenge. Therein, "yvāyaṃ" (yo ayaṃ) means this noble person standing in the path. These four such statements are the questions of the challenger. Again, the statement "He abandons past defilements" is an answer given to provide an opportunity for the challenge. "Khīṇaṃ" (destroyed) means defilements already destroyed by virtue of the moment of dissolution. "Niruddhaṃ" (ceased) means defilements that have ceased by virtue of the continuum, not arising again and again. "Vigataṃ" (departed) means defilements that have departed from the present moment. "Does he make them depart?" (vigameti). "Atthaṅgataṃ" (gone to non-existence) means defilements that have reached non-existence. "Does he make them go to non-existence?" (atthaṅgameti). Having shown the fault in that past [defilement], it is rejected with, "He does not abandon past defilements."

In challenging regarding the future, "ajātaṃ" (unborn) means defilements that have not yet reached birth. "Anibbattaṃ" (unproduced) means defilements that have not yet reached their nature. "Anuppannaṃ" (unarisen) means defilements that have not proceeded upwards starting from arising. "Apātubhūtaṃ" (unmanifested) means not being manifest in the mind as a present state. For one who abandons the past and the future, since there are no states to be abandoned, the effort would be fruitless. Therefore, both are rejected. "One who is lustful abandons lust" means one who is lustful with present lust abandons that very present lust. This same method applies to present defilements. "Thāmagato" means one who has reached a firm nature. "Kaṇhasukkā" (dark and bright) means that unwholesome and wholesome dhammas occur together in yoked-alignment; this is the meaning of what would follow. "Saṅkilesikā" (defiled) means that if there is such a state of association with defilements, the development of the path would be joined with defilements; this is the meaning of what would follow. Thus, for one who abandons the present, along with the effort...
305:
...because the defilements to be abandoned exist, the development of the path would also be defiled, and the effort would be fruitless. This is because there is no such thing as present defilements being dissociated from the mind.

The words "Na hi" (Not so) are a rejection of the statement made by the challenger in four ways. The word "Atthi" (There is) is the admission of the person answering. The phrase "Yathā kathaṃ viya" (Just how is it?) is a question asked to show an example of that existence. The meaning is: In what way does it exist? In what manner does that nature exist? Like what does it exist? "Seyyathāpi" means "just as if."

"Taruṇarukkho" (a young tree): the word "young" is used to illustrate the capacity to bear fruit. "Ajātaphalo" (one whose fruits are unborn) refers to the time before the fruits are born, even though the tree is capable of bearing fruit. "Tamenam" refers to that tree. "Enam" is merely a particle; the meaning is "that very tree." "Mūlaṃ chindeyya" means one should cut it from the root. "Ajātaphala" refers to the fruits that have not yet arisen.

"Evamevaṃ" means "even so." By these four terms—arising (uppāda), occurrence (pavatta), sign (nimitta), and accumulation (āyūhana)—only the present aggregate-continuum is meant. For in whichever aggregate-continuum a particular path-knowledge arises, by that particular path-knowledge, the aggregate-continuum becomes seedless (not a ground for seeds) for the defilements to be abandoned. Because that aggregate-continuum has become seedless, due to that cause, those various defilements, being truly unarisen, do not arise again.

"Ādīnavaṃ disvā" means having seen the danger through impermanence and so forth. By the four terms beginning with "anuppāda" (non-arising), only Nibbāna is meant. "Cittaṃ pakkhandati" means the mind associated with the path leaps forward into Nibbāna. "Hetu-nirodhā dukkha-nirodho" (through the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of suffering) means that because of the cessation of the aggregate-continuum—which is the seed of defilements—by way of non-arising, there is the cessation of the defilements—which are the causes of suffering in the form of future aggregates—by way of non-arising. Thus, because of the cessation of the defilements which are the causes of suffering by way of non-arising, there is the cessation of suffering by way of non-arising.

Because there is thus logical reasoning in the abandoning of defilements, he says, "Atthi maggabhavanā" (There is the development of the path), and so forth. In the Visuddhimagga Commentary, however, it is said: "What is shown by this? The abandoning of defilements that have gained a footing (bhūmiladdha) is shown. Are the defilements that have gained a footing past, future, or present? They are only those that have arisen having gained a footing (bhūmiladdhuppanna)." The detailed explanation of the abandoning of defilements as taught there should be understood in the same manner as stated in the explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of the Path in the Discussion on Knowledge Consisting in What is Heard (Sutamaya-ñāṇa-kathā). In this Discussion on Realization, however, only the defilements to be abandoned by path-knowledge are intended.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Realization is finished.
306:
## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Seclusion (Vivekakathā)

Now, after explaining the meaning of the Discourse on Realization (Abhisamayakathā), which is the end of the abandonment of defilements, the Elder Mahākassapa will explain the meanings not yet mentioned in the Discourse on Seclusion (Vivekakathā), which is preceded by the Suttanta, as he wishes to show the manner of abandonment. In that Vivekakathā, in the Sutta, the phrase 'ye keci' (whosoever) is an all-inclusive term without exception. 'Balakaraṇīyā' (to be done by strength) refers to activities to be performed by the strength of the thighs and the strength of the arms. 'Kammantā' (activities) refers to tasks such as running, jumping, plowing, and planting. 'Karīyanti' (are performed) means they are performed by those who possess strength. 'Sīlaṃ nissāya' (depending on virtue) means taking the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) as a support. 'Bhāveti' (develops) means the development of the mundane and supramundane path, because development is not possible for one whose virtue is broken.

'Vivekanissitaṃ' (depending on seclusion) means depending on seclusion by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgaviveka), seclusion by eradication (samucchedaviveka), and seclusion by deliverance (nissaraṇaviveka). 'Viveka' means the state of being secluded. Indeed, a yogi devoted to the development of the Ariyan path develops it by depending on tadaṅgaviveka by way of function at the moment of insight (vipassanā), by depending on nissaraṇaviveka by way of inclination, by depending on samucchedaviveka by way of function at the moment of the path (magga), and by depending on nissaraṇaviveka by way of object. This same method applies to 'virāganissita' (depending on dispassion) and so on. For seclusion (viveka) itself is called 'virāga' (dispassion) in the sense of fading away, 'nirodha' (cessation) in the sense of ceasing, and 'vossagga' (relinquishment) in the sense of letting go. Alternatively, it is viveka because it is secluded from defilements, virāga because it is detached from defilements, nirodha because defilements have ceased, and vossagga because defilements have been relinquished and given up, and because the mind is released into Nibbāna.

Relinquishment (vossagga) is of two kinds: relinquishment as giving up (pariccāgavossagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandanavossagga). Therein, pariccāgavossagga is the abandonment of defilements by way of substitution of opposites at the moment of insight, and by way of eradication at the moment of the path. Pakkhandanavossagga is the entering into Nibbāna by way of inclining towards it at the moment of insight, and by way of making it the object at the moment of the path. In this method of explanation which mixes the mundane and supramundane, both kinds are appropriate. Therefore, each factor of the path, such as Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) and so on, relinquishes defilements and enters into Nibbāna in the manner already described. By the full phrase 'vossaggapariṇāmiṃ', it means 'inclined toward, matured for, and ripened for the sake of relinquishment'. A monk devoted to the development of the Ariyan path develops each factor of the path, such as sammādiṭṭhi, so that it ripens for the sake of relinquishment as giving up defilements and for the sake of relinquishment as entering into Nibbāna, and so that it becomes fully matured.
307:
In the phrase 'bījagāmabhūtagāma', there are five kinds of seeds: root-seed (mūlabīja), trunk-seed (khandhabīja), bud-seed (aggabīja), cutting-seed (phaḷubīja), and seed-seed (bījabīja). 'Bījagāma' means a collection of seeds. That same bījagāma is called 'bhūtagāma' from the time the lush green sprouts appear. It means a collection of 'bhūta', which are the arisen and produced green sprouts. Some also say it is 'bhūtagāma' because from the time the green sprouts appear, they are taken possession of by deities (devatā); thus it is a 'gāma' (abode) of those 'bhūta' known as deities. 'Vuddhi' (growth) means increase by way of sprouts and so on. 'Virūḷhi' (expansion) means stature by way of trunks and so on. 'Vepulla' (abundance) means fullness by way of flowers and so on.

Regarding the Dhamma, however, 'vuddhi' means growth by way of the occurrence of new states. 'Virūḷhi' means expansion by way of accomplishing one's own task. 'Vepulla' means the state of abundance by way of the completion of the task. There is also a variant reading 'vipulattaṃ'. Alternatively, these three terms are also connected with virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā).

## Commentary on the Exposition of Path Factors (Magganganiddesavaṇṇanā)

In the Suttanta exposition, 'sammādiṭṭhiyā' is in the genitive case. It refers to Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) which occurs in jhāna, insight (vipassanā), path (magga), fruit (phala), and Nibbāna, as well as in the mind associated with mundane abstinence (virati), as appropriate by way of association and by way of object, and which is unified by way of its general characteristic. 'Vikkhambhanaviveka' (seclusion by suppression) means seclusion by way of suppression, by way of making distant. Distancing what? The hindrances (nīvaraṇa). In the passage 'tassa paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ bhāvayato' (for him developing the first jhāna) etc., only the first jhāna is mentioned by way of suppression. When that is mentioned, the remaining jhānas are also considered mentioned. Since Right View exists even in the jhānas, it is called the seclusion of Right View.

'Tadaṅgaviveka' (seclusion by substitution of opposites) means seclusion by means of the respective factors of insight knowledge. In the phrase 'diṭṭhigatānaṃ' (of views), only seclusion from views is mentioned because it is difficult to achieve and is primary. When that seclusion from views is mentioned, seclusion from the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) and so on is also considered mentioned. 'Nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ samādhiṃ' means concentration associated with insight. 'Samucchedaviveka' (seclusion by eradication) means seclusion by the total cutting off of defilements. 'Lokuttaraṃ khayagāmimaggaṃ' means the supramundane path leading to the destruction [of defilements], which is Nibbāna. 'Paṭippassaddhiviveka' (seclusion by tranquilization) means seclusion by the tranquilization of defilements. 'Nissaraṇaviveka' (seclusion by deliverance) means seclusion from conditioned things (saṅkhāraviveka), which is the deliverance from all that is conditioned. 'Chandajāto hoti' means that the desire for Dhamma (dhammachanda) has arisen in the preliminary stage. 'Saddhādhimutto' means he is one resolved through faith even in the preliminary stage. 'Cittañcassa svādhiṭṭhitaṃ' means that even in the preliminary stage, the mind of that yogi is well-established, firmly placed. Thus, desire...
308:
Desire (chanda), faith (saddhā), and consciousness (citta)—these three states are called supports (nissaya) because they serve as natural decisive supports (pakatūpanissaya) for those in whom seclusion (viveka) has arisen in the preliminary stage. Some teachers, however, say that concentration (samādhi) is referred to by the passage, "and his mind is well-established." The same method applies to detachment (virāga) and so forth.

In the section on cessation (nirodha-vāra), the term "deathless element" (amata-dhātu) is used to show a synonym other than "cessation" (nirodha). In the remaining sections, it is stated that "cessation is Nibbāna," thus in both cases, only Nibbāna is intended. By applying the three factors—desire, faith, and consciousness—to each of the four states such as seclusion, there are "twelve supports (nissaya)."

The explanation of the meaning of Right Intention, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration should be understood in this same way. Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood do not exist at the moment of jhāna or the moment of insight (vipassanā); therefore, it should be understood that the abstinences (virati) occurring by way of the preliminary and subsequent stages of jhāna and insight are spoken of as being dependent on jhāna and insight. The seclusion, detachment, cessation, and relinquishment of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and views (diṭṭhigata) should be understood as the "seclusion etc." of those abstinences occurring in that manner. Just as in the Book of Eights (Aṭṭhakanipāta) of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, it is said: "Therefore, bhikkhu, you should develop this concentration with initial and sustained application, develop it with sustained application only without initial application, develop it without initial or sustained application, develop it with rapture, develop it without rapture, develop it with happiness, and develop it with equanimity," where states like loving-kindness and the foundations of mindfulness are spoken of as if they were associated with the fourfold and fivefold jhānas by way of the original concentration within oneself; so too in this Pāḷi text, it should be understood that the abstinences are spoken of by way of the preliminary and subsequent stages. The Blessed One should not be misrepresented by merely grasping the shadow of the words. For the word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) is profound; it should be grasped according to its intention after attending upon teachers.

26-27. The meaning in the sections on the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga-vāra), the powers (bala-vāra), and the faculties (indriya-vāra) should also be understood in this same way.

## The Explanation of the Talk on Seclusion is Finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Talk on Conduct

28-29. Now, following the Talk on Seclusion, the Talk on Conduct (Cariyākathā) is taught again—even though it was explained in the Talk on the Faculties—in order to show the means of realizing Nibbāna, which is the supreme seclusion known as the seclusion of escape (nissaraṇa-viveka) and which ought to be realized;
309:
likewise, it is taught to show the nature of the conduct that performs the welfare and happiness of the world of beings by a person who has realized the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). The explanation of the meaning of that Talk on Conduct should be understood as having already been taught in the Talk on the Faculties. ## The Explanation of the Talk on Conduct is Finished. ## 6. Explanation of the Talk on Miracles. Now, following the Talk on Conduct which ends with conduct for the welfare of the world, the following is the explanation of the unprecedented meanings in the Talk on Miracles (Pāṭihāriyakathā), which is preceded by the Suttanta and taught to show the miracle (pāṭihāriya) that ends with instruction for the welfare of the world. In that Suttanta, first, 'pāṭihāriyāni' means miracles in the sense of warding off (patiharaṇa) opposing states. 'Iddhipāṭihāriya' means: 'iddhi' in the sense of succeeding (ijjhana), and 'pāṭihāriya' in the sense of warding off; the miracle itself is the iddhi, thus it is 'iddhipāṭihāriya'. In the other miracles, however, it is 'ādesanā' (mind-reading) by way of pointing out (ādissana), and 'anusāsanī' (instruction) by way of instructing (anusāsana). The rest is as previously explained.

'Idha' means in this world. 'Ekacco' means a certain person. The description of the miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya) has the same meaning as stated below. 'He points out by a sign' (nimittena ādisati) means he speaks by way of a sign of coming, a sign of going, or a sign of standing. 'Thus also is your mind' (evampi te mano) means 'In this way also your mind is either accompanied by joy (somanassa), accompanied by grief (domanassa), or associated with sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) and so forth.' The word 'api' has the sense of inclusion.
