'In this way too is your mind' (itthampi te mano) is a demonstration of the various types even within a single kind of mind, such as those accompanied by joy. 'So too is your mind' (itipipi te cittaṃ) means 'In this way also your mind occurs thinking of this and that matter.' 'Even if he points out much' (bahuṃ cepi ādisati) means he speaks of many things other than the mind, such as 'this and that matter has been, is, or will be.' 'It is just so and not otherwise' (tatheva taṃ hoti, no aññathā) means all that is spoken happens exactly as it was said and does not happen in any other way.

'He does not point out merely by a sign' (na heva kho nimittena ādisati) means that even though he knows the sign, he does not speak based on the sign alone. 'Moreover' (apica) is a word showing another method. 'Of humans' (manussānaṃ) means of humans who know the minds of others. 'Of non-humans' (amanussānaṃ) means of yakkhas, petas, and so forth, whether they have possessed a person or not. 'Of deities' (devatānaṃ) means of those such as the Four Great Kings. 'Having heard the sound' (saddaṃ sutvā) means...
310:
They know by hearing the voices of those who speak after knowing the minds of others. The word "pana" is a particle used in the sense of further effort. "Vitakkayato" refers to a person who is thinking or reflecting on this or that matter with thought (vitakka). "Vicārayato" refers to a person who is investigating or examining with only the examination (vicāra) that is associated with thought. "Vitakkavipphārasaddaṃ sutvā" means knowing by hearing the sound of muttering or groaning from those who are asleep or negligent, which arises by the power of the momentum of thought. For a person who is reflecting on a certain object, that (muttering) sound arises; by the power of that object, one points out, "Your mind is also like this," and so on.

"Avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhiṃ" (concentration without thought and examination) is stated to show the ability to know the mind of a person who has a peaceful mind free from the disturbance of thought and examination; as for knowing other types of minds, it goes without saying. "Knowing the mind of another by encompassing it with one's own mind" refers to a person who has attained the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa). "Bhoto" means "of the venerable one". "Manosaṅkhārā paṇihitā" means mental formations have been placed. "He will think of such and such a thought" means knowing that he will think of or produce a thought associated with the wholesome, etc. The person who knows, knows by way of coming (āgamana), by way of the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), or by looking at the mind within an attainment (samāpatti).

Knowing by way of coming means knowing even during the preparatory work for a kasiṇa (kasiṇa-parikamma): "This person practices the kasiṇa meditation in such a manner; by that manner, he will produce the first jhāna, or the second jhāna, etc., or the eight attainments (samāpatti)." Knowing by way of the preliminary stage means knowing when the initial insight (vipassanā) has been undertaken: "This person practices insight in such a manner; by that manner, he will produce the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) ... pe ... or the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga)."

Knowing by looking at the mind within an attainment means knowing: "The mental formations of this person have been placed in such a manner; immediately after this mind, he will think of such and such a thought; for this person who has emerged from this attainment, there will be concentration partaking of diminution (hānabhāgiya), or concentration partaking of stability (ṭhitibhāgiya), or concentration partaking of distinction (visesabhāgiya), or concentration partaking of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya); he will also produce the higher powers (abhiññā)." "Points out much" means that because the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others takes only the mind and mental factors as its object, it speaks much only by way of the sixteen-fold divisions such as the mind with lust (sarāga), and it should be understood that it does not speak by any other way. "It is just so" means this (known matter) is exactly as stated. There is no such thing as a change into another way for what is known by the power of the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others.

"Think thus" means think while producing thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) and so on. "Do not think thus" means do not think while producing sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) and so on...
311:
...think. "Reflect thus" means to reflect either on the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) itself or on one of the others such as the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā). "Do not reflect thus" means do not reflect in the manner of "permanence" (nicca) and so on. "Abandon this" means to abandon lust (rāga) and so on for the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Dwell having attained and accomplished this" means to dwell having attained and accomplished only the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma) categorized into the four paths and four fruits.

Now, wishing to show specifically another sequence of teaching regarding the miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya), he said: "Renunciation succeeds, therefore it is psychic power (iddhi)," and so on. In that text, "it removes sensual desire" means that because it is capable of abandoning sensual desire (kāmacchanda) which is its opposite, that renunciation (nekkhamma) itself is called a miracle (pāṭihāriya). "Those who are endowed with that renunciation" refers to persons who are endowed by way of attainment with that renunciation which removes sensual desire. "Those with pure minds" means those who have pure minds due to the absence of sensual desire. "Those with unclouded intentions" means those who have intentions of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) that are not disturbed by sensual intentions (kāma-saṅkappa). "Thus is the miracle of manifestation" means that a person skilled in knowing the minds of others, or another Fully Enlightened Buddha, or the disciples of the Buddha, thus point out the miracle of manifestation (ādesanā-pāṭihāriya). Alternatively, "such pointing out is the miracle of manifestation"—the word ādesanā should be applied to the rest of the text. "Thus it should be cultivated" means it should be cultivated from the beginning in this and that manner. The same method applies to the remaining three terms. "Mindfulness in accordance with that Dhamma should be established" means mindfulness that is favorable to that renunciation should be firmly established. In this text, "Thus is the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya)", the interpretation should be made just as in the explanation of the miracle of manifestation. The same method applies to non-ill will (avyāpāda) and so on. In the Pali text, however, the jhānas and so on are summarized, and it is written showing only the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga) at the end. In those four paths, the Pali "Thus it should be cultivated" and so on should be understood as being spoken by way of the mundane path (lokiya-magga) in the preliminary stage, because the path (magga) lasts only for a single mind-moment. For when cultivation (āsevanā) and so on are performed for the arising of the path through insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā), which is called the mundane path and is the preliminary stage of the path, the path that arises because of that insight is also said to be cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently. The teachers of the Sabbatthivāda (Sarvāstivāda) school, however, say: "Each path has sixteen moments." The establishing of mindfulness in accordance with that path is indeed appropriate in the preliminary stage.

Again, the words "Renunciation succeeds, therefore it is psychic power" and so on are spoken to show that "iddhipāṭihāriya" is a kammadhāraya compound. Among the three miracles taught in the Suttas, when the compound nature of the miracle of psychic power is explained, it is already explained for the other two as well. Therefore, it should be understood that in this section on miracles (pāṭihāriya-vāra), only the compound meaning of the first one, the miracle of psychic power, is taught.

The explanation of the Discourse on Miracles (Pāṭihāriya-kathā) is finished.
312:
In this way, it should be understood that only the compound meaning of the original miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya) is taught.

## Conclusion of the Explanation of the Discourse on Miracles.

## 7. Explanation of the Discourse on the Equal-Headed One

Now, following the Discourse on Miracles, although the state of the equal-headed one (samasīsī)—who is the primary miracle and is included within the miracle of psychic power—has already been explained in the Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā), it is taught again here in connection with the miracle of psychic power to demonstrate its nature as a miracle of psychic power. The explanation of its meaning is exactly as taught in that Discourse on Knowledge.

## Conclusion of the Explanation of the Discourse on the Equal-Headed One.

## 8. Explanation of the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness

Now, following the Discourse on the Equal-Headed One, wishing to show the seven specific types of insight (vipassanā) that accomplish the miracle of psychic power which was taught, I shall explain the meaning not yet mentioned in the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānakathā), which is preceded by the Suttanta. In that Suttanta of the Satipaṭṭhānakathā, first, the word "four" (cattāro) is a delimitation of number. By this word, the limit of the foundations of mindfulness is shown, indicating that they are neither fewer than four nor more than four. The word "these" (ime) is a term used to point out what is being indicated. The word "monks" (bhikkhave) is a form of address for those receiving the Dhamma.

Regarding "foundations of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhānā), there are three types: the object of mindfulness, the Teacher’s state of having transcended resentment and attraction towards disciples who practice in three different ways, and mindfulness itself. In passages such as, "Monks, I will teach the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness," the object of mindfulness is called "satipaṭṭhāna." Its meaning is: it is called "paṭṭhāna" because mindfulness is established (patiṭṭhāti) upon that object. What is established? Mindfulness is established. Because it is the place where mindfulness is established, it is called "satipaṭṭhāna."

In the passage, "There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One frequents, frequenting which the Teacher is worthy of instructing a group of disciples," the Teacher’s state of having transcended resentment and attraction towards disciples who practice in three different ways is called "satipaṭṭhāna." Its meaning is:
313:
It is called "paṭṭhāna" because it should be set up (paṭṭhapetabba); the meaning is that it should be set in motion. By what is it set up? It is set up by mindfulness. The setting up of mindfulness is called "satipaṭṭhāna." However, in passages such as, "The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment," mindfulness itself is called "satipaṭṭhāna." Its meaning is: it is called "paṭṭhāna" because it stands firmly (patiṭṭhāti); the meaning is that it proceeds by entering into and plunging into the object. Mindfulness itself is the foundation, thus it is "satipaṭṭhāna." Alternatively, it is "sati" in the sense of remembering, and "upaṭṭhāna" in the sense of standing near. Thus, that which is both mindfulness and standing near is "satipaṭṭhāna." This is the meaning intended here. If so, why is the plural form "satipaṭṭhānā" used? It is because of the multiplicity of mindfulness. Indeed, those instances of mindfulness are many due to the diversity of their objects.

The question "Which four?" is a question asked with the desire to explain. "Here" (idha) means in this Dispensation (sāsana). "Bhikkhu" means one who sees danger (bhaya) in the cycle of rebirths (saṃsāra). The explanation of the remaining terms has already been given in the explanation of the Section on the Truth of the Path (Maggasaccaniddesa) in the Discourse on Knowledge Consisting of What is Heard (Sutamayañāṇakathā) of this work.

Why did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more? It is because it serves the welfare of those to be led (veneyya). Among those of craving temperament (taṇhācarita), view temperament (diṭṭhicarita), those who have calm as their vehicle (samathayānika), and those who have insight as their vehicle (vipassanāyānika), each exists in two ways: with dull faculties or sharp faculties. For the one of dull craving temperament, the gross foundation of mindfulness of body (kāyānupassanā) is the path to purification. For the one of sharp craving temperament, the subtle foundation of mindfulness of feeling (vedanānupassanā) is the path to purification. For the one of dull view temperament, the foundation of mindfulness of mind (cittānupassanā), which is not highly differentiated, is the path to purification. For the one of sharp view temperament, the foundation of mindfulness of dhammas (dhammānupassanā), which is highly differentiated, is the path to purification. Also, for the one of dull calm-vehicle temperament, the first foundation of mindfulness, which has a sign (nimitta) to be obtained without difficulty, is the path to purification. For the one of sharp calm-vehicle temperament, because they do not settle on gross objects, the second foundation of mindfulness is the path to purification. For the one of dull insight-vehicle temperament, the third foundation of mindfulness, which has an object that is not highly differentiated, is the path to purification. For the one of sharp insight-vehicle temperament, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, which has a highly differentiated object, is the path to purification. Thus, exactly four are taught, neither fewer nor more.

Alternatively, they are taught as four to abandon the four perversions (vipallāsa) of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self. Indeed, the body is foul (asubha), yet beings are perverted by the perversion of beauty (subha-vipallāsa) regarding it. To abandon that perversion by showing the nature of foulness in that body, the first foundation of mindfulness is taught. Regarding feelings and so on, which are grasped as pleasant, permanent, and self: feelings are suffering (dukkha), the mind is impermanent (anicca), and dhammas are non-self (anatta). Yet beings are perverted by the perversions of pleasure, permanence, and self regarding them. To abandon those perversions by showing the nature of suffering and so on in those things, the remaining three foundations of mindfulness are taught.
314:
The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are taught for the purpose of abandoning the four perversions (vipallāsa) of beauty (subha), happiness (sukha), permanence (nicca), and self (atta). It should be understood that the four foundations of mindfulness are taught not only for abandoning the perversions but also for abandoning the four floods (ogha), bonds (yoga), taints (āsava), ties (gantha), clingings (upādāna), and wrong courses (agati), as well as for the full understanding of the four nutriments (āhāra).

(a) In the Suttanta description, "earth-body" (pathavīkāya) refers to the earth element within this physical body. Because the earth elements are numerous throughout the entire body, the term "body" (kāya) is used in the sense of a collection or group to include all earth elements. The same method applies to the "water-body" (āpokāya) and so forth. The terms "hair-body" (kesakāya) and so forth are also used because they are numerous. However, it should be understood that terms like "kidney" (vakka) and so forth are not suitable to be called a "body" because they are distinct and limited, and thus they are not referred to as such.

(b) In the passage beginning with "pleasant feeling" (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ), pleasant feeling refers to either bodily or mental pleasant feeling. The same applies to painful feeling (dukkha vedanā). However, "neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" (adukkhamasukha vedanā) refers only to mental equanimity (upekkhā vedanā). "Worldly pleasant feeling" (sāmisa sukha vedanā) refers to the six kinds of joy (somanassa) based on the household life (sensual pleasures). "Unworldly pleasant feeling" (nirāmisa sukha vedanā) refers to the six kinds of joy based on renunciation (nekkhamma). "Worldly painful feeling" (sāmisa dukkha vedanā) refers to the six kinds of grief (domanassa) based on the household life. "Unworldly painful feeling" (nirāmisa dukkha vedanā) refers to the six kinds of grief based on renunciation. "Worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" (sāmisa adukkhamasukha vedanā) refers to the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life. "Unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" (nirāmisa adukkhamasukha vedanā) refers to the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation.

(c) The meanings of "mind with lust" (sarāgaṃ cittaṃ) and so forth are as already stated in the Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathā).

(d) "The remaining phenomena" (tadavesese dhamme) refers to the phenomena belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka) that remain after excluding the body, feelings, and mind. In every instance, one should contemplate with that sevenfold knowledge of contemplation (anupassanā-ñāṇa). Any meanings not explained here and there in this Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness are the same as those already explained in the respective discourses below.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Discourse on Insight (Vipassanākathāvaṇṇanā)

Now, following the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness which is connected with insight, I shall explain in order the meanings not yet stated in the Discourse on Insight, which is preceded by the Suttanta, as I wish to show the different types of insight. In that Discourse on Insight, since the word "he" (so) in the Suttanta is a pronoun...
315:
Whoever it may be, everyone is included. The word "vata" is an indeclinable used in the sense of "certainly." "Any formation" (kañci saṅkhāraṃ) means even a slight formation. Regarding "conformity-tolerance" (anulomika-khanti), insight knowledge itself is called "conformity" (anulomika) because it conforms to the supramundane path; it is called "conformity-tolerance" because it regards that same tolerance. It is called "tolerance" (khanti) because all formations are tolerated (accepted) as impermanent, painful, and non-self by that yogi. This tolerance, which is called insight, is of three kinds: mild, medium, and sharp. Insight beginning from the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa) and ending with the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) is called mild conformity-tolerance. Insight beginning from the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa) and ending with the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) is called medium conformity-tolerance. Conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) is called sharp conformity-tolerance. "Endowed with" (samannāgata) means possessed of. "This case does not exist" means that the aforementioned case or cause is impossible. Regarding "the certainty of rightness" (sammatta-niyāma), it is called "rightness" (sammatta) because it occurs just as desired, thinking "it will bring me benefit and happiness," and because it has an undistorted nature as "impure" (asubha) and so forth in things that are impure. It is called "certainty" (niyāma) because it gives fruit immediately and because it is the constant cause for the arising of Arahantship; it means "determination." What is this certainty of rightness? It is the supramundane path, specifically the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). Because one is certain by that path-certainty, it is said, "He is certain, bound for enlightenment." The statement that one will enter that certainty of rightness immediately after conformity-tolerance is made without taking into account the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), because gotrabhū stands in the position of adverting to the path. Alternatively, among the eighteen principal insights (mahā-vipassanā), gotrabhū is called "insight that turns away" (vivaṭṭanānupassanā), and thus it is already included within conformity-tolerance. The meaning should be understood in this same way in all four Suttantas. These four Suttantas were taught in the Book of the Sixes (Chakka Nipāta) of the Aṅguttara Nikāya by way of the six things: conformity-tolerance, the certainty of rightness, and the four noble fruits. Indeed, there are only four Suttantas by way of the two sides: the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) and the bright side (sukkapakkha).

In the Suttanta description preceded by the question "In how many ways?" (katihaākārehi), when contemplating the five aggregates through modes such as impermanence, the yogi who has begun insight by comprehending mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) and their causes through the method of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana), contemplates each of the five aggregates as impermanent (anicca) because they are subject to destruction and because they have a beginning and an end. He contemplates them as painful (dukkha) because they are oppressed by arising and falling and because they are the basis of suffering. He contemplates them as a disease (roga) because they must be sustained by conditions and because they are the root of illness. He contemplates them as a boil (gaṇḍa) because they are like a thorn, because the impurities of defilements flow from them, and because they swell and burst through arising, presence, and dissolution. He contemplates them as a dart (salla) because they oppress, because they pierce within, and because they are difficult to extract. He contemplates them as a calamity (agha) because they are blameworthy, because they bring harm, and because they are the cause of suffering. He contemplates them as an affliction (ābādha) because they cannot be made to go according to one's will and because they are the proximate cause of illness. He contemplates them as alien (para) because they do not follow one's will and because they cannot be controlled. He contemplates them as disintegrating (paloka) because they are destroyed by aging, sickness, and death. He contemplates them as a plague (īti) because they bring many destructions. He contemplates them as a menace (upaddava) because they bring harm and because they are the cause of misfortunes. He contemplates them as a fear (bhaya) because they are the basis of all fears and because they are the cessation of suffering...
316: One contemplates (the five aggregates). One contemplates them as suffering (dukkha) because they are oppressed by arising and passing away, and because they are the basis of suffering. One contemplates them as a disease (roga) because they must be maintained by appropriate conditions and because they are the cause of ailment. One contemplates them as a boil (gaṇḍa) because they are associated with the thorns of suffering, because they ooze the impurities of defilements, and because they are swollen, ripened, and burst by birth, aging, and dissolution. One contemplates them as a dart (salla) because they cause affliction, because they pierce from within, and because they are difficult to extract. One contemplates them as misery (agha) because they are blameworthy, because they bring about lack of growth, and because they are the basis of misery. One contemplates them as an affliction (ābādha) because they do not occur according to one's will and because they are the proximate cause of illness. One contemplates them as a stranger (para) because they do not follow one's wishes and because they cannot be controlled according to one's will. One contemplates them as disintegrating (paloka) because they reach momentary and total destruction through illness, aging, and death. One contemplates them as a calamity (īti) because they bring about many kinds of ruin. One contemplates them as a misfortune (upaddava) because they bring about many unknown harms and because they are the basis of all dangers. One contemplates them as a danger (bhaya) because they are the source of all fears and because they are the opposite of the supreme relief known as the cessation of suffering (Nibbāna). One contemplates them as an adversity (upasagga) because many harms follow them, because they are beset with faults, and because they are unbearable like a plague. One contemplates them as unstable (cala) because they are shaken by illness, aging, and death, as well as by worldly conditions such as greed. One contemplates them as perishable (pabhaṅgu) because they have the nature of reaching destruction through effort or by their own nature. One contemplates them as impermanent (adhuva) because they fall away at every moment and because they lack stability. One contemplates them as protectionless (atāṇa) because they provide no protection and because safety cannot be obtained from them. One contemplates them as shelterless (aleṇa) because they are not fit for shelter and because they cannot perform the function of a shelter for those who seek refuge in them. One contemplates them as refugeless (asaraṇa) because they cannot destroy the dangers of those who rely on them. One contemplates them as empty (ritta) because they are devoid of the imagined states of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. One contemplates them as vain (tuccha) because they are empty and because they are insignificant. Indeed, in the world, even a small thing is called vain. One contemplates them as void (suñña) because they are devoid of an owner, a permanent resident, an enjoyer, a doer, or a director. One contemplates them as non-self (anatta) because they themselves lack ownership and so on. One contemplates them as a danger (ādīnava) because of the suffering of their occurrence and because they are a disadvantage of suffering. Alternatively, it is called ādīnava because it leads to or occurs in great misery. This term ādīnava is a designation for a wretched person; since the aggregates are also very wretched, they are contemplated as a danger (ādīnava) due to their similarity to a wretched person. One contemplates them as subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma) because they have the nature of being transformed by the two modes of aging and death. One contemplates them as coreless (asāraka) because they are weak and because they destroy happiness like pithless wood. One contemplates them as the root of misery (aghamūla) because they are the cause of misery. One contemplates them as a murderer (vadhaka) because they kill the one who is intimate with them, like an enemy disguised as a friend. One contemplates them as non-existence (vibhava) because they are devoid of prosperity and because they lead to ruin. One contemplates them as subject to taints (sāsava) because they are the basis for the taints (āsavas).
317:
One views it as conditioned (saṅkhata) because it is constructed by causes. One views it as the bait of Māra (mārāmisa) because it is the bait for the Māra of Death (maccu-māra) and the Māra of Defilements (kilesa-māra). One views it as having the nature of birth, aging, sickness, and death (jāti-jarā-byādhi-maraṇa-dhamma) because it is subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death. One views it as having the nature of sorrow, lamentation, and despair (soka-parideva-upāyāsa-dhamma) because it is the cause of sorrow, lamentation, and despair. One views it as a defiling state (saṅkilesika-dhamma) because it is the object of the defilements of craving, wrong view, and misconduct. In all these aforementioned phrases, the remaining verb "one views" (passati) should be understood as included.

38. Although it is stated as a collective group, "in the five aggregates" (pañcakkhandhe), it should be understood that this is done because the explanation of the meaning is given separately for each aggregate in the description of the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpa-sammasana-ñāṇa); because at the end, the contemplations are counted separately by way of the five aggregates; and because words used for a collective can also apply to its parts. Alternatively, it should be understood that it is called "in the five aggregates" because the separate acts of comprehension (sammasana) are preached collectively in brief. Or, since there is a statement in the Commentary, "One emerges from the five aggregates all at once," the comprehension of the five aggregates as a whole is also appropriate. One who views "The cessation of the five aggregates is the permanent Nibbāna," views "Nibbāna is permanent" by the power of the knowledge of the peaceful state (santipada-ñāṇa) during the time of developing insight, according to the method stated in the description of the knowledge of the contemplation of danger (ādīnava-ñāṇa). Regarding the phrase "enters the right path of assurance" (sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati), the entering occurs at the moment of the Path (magga), while at the moment of Fruition (phala), one is called "one who has entered." This same method applies to all other ways of describing the entry into the path of assurance. "Health" (ārogya) means the state of being free from illness. "Free from darts" (visalla) means being free from the darts (of lust, etc.). In such terms, it should be understood in this way. "Afflictionless" (anābādha) means the absence of affliction or being the opposite of affliction. In such terms, this is also the method. "Not dependent on others" (aparappaccaya) means being free from other causes. Some teachers read it with a conjunct 'sa', as "upassaggato" or "anupassaggaṃ". "Supreme void" (parama-suñña) is so called because it is void of all formations and because it is excellent. "Supreme goal" (paramattha) is so called because it is the highest among conditioned and unconditioned states. It is used in the neuter gender by way of gender transformation (liṅga-vipallāsa). Because Nibbāna is void and non-self, the reverse method (paṭiloma-pariyāya) is not stated for these two terms, "voidness" (suññata) and "non-self" (anatta). "Taintless" (anāsava) means being free from taints (āsava). "Unworldly" (nirāmisa) means being free from the bait (of defilements). "Unborn" (ajata) means not having arisen because of being free from birth. "Deathless" (amata) means free from death because there is no dissolution (bhaṅga). Death is also called "mata" by way of the neuter gender.

39. Thus, among the forty contemplations stated in this order and distinguished by their various aspects, the Elder, wishing to present them collectively in only three contemplations by way of grouping similar natures, said the words beginning with "as impermanent" (aniccato). In those insights, the application to the states of impermanence, suffering, and non-self should be made as appropriate. But at the end, they are shown as "twenty-five," etc., by way of counting those contemplations separately. In the counting, according to the numerical order, the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) is counted first. In those final counts, there are twenty-five contemplations of non-self among the five aggregates. "Fifty" means that by applying the ten terms from "as impermanent" (aniccato) to "as having the nature of death" (maraṇa-dhammato) to each aggregate, there are fifty contemplations of impermanence in the five aggregates. "Together with twenty-five" means that by applying the remaining twenty-five terms such as "as suffering" (dukkhato), "as a disease" (rogato), etc., to each aggregate, in the five aggregates...
318:
The Elder, wishing to group similar items, stated "as impermanent" and so on, referring to the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and others. In these contemplations, one should apply them as impermanent, suffering, and non-self as appropriate. At the end, these contemplations are shown separately by count. Among the counts, the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) is counted first according to the numerical order. In that counting, "twenty-five" means: "as another, as empty, as vain, as void, as non-self"—applying these five to each of the five aggregates (khandhas) results in twenty-five contemplations of non-self. "Fifty" means: "as impermanent, as disintegrating, as fickle, as perishable, as unenduring, as subject to change, as coreless, as disappearing, as conditioned, as subject to death"—applying these ten to each of the five aggregates results in fifty contemplations of impermanence. "One hundred and twenty-five" means: the remaining aspects such as "as suffering, as a disease," etc.—applying these twenty-five to each of the five aggregates results in one hundred and twenty-five contemplations of suffering. "The contemplations spoken of in suffering" means the contemplations spoken of by count regarding the five aggregates which are suffering; it should be understood that they are indeed one hundred and twenty-five. In this verse, the gender transposition (liṅgavipallāsa) in the word "yāni" should be noted.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Insight (Vipassanākathāvaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Discourse on the Matrix (Mātikākathāvaṇṇanā)

Now, the Great Elder, the General of the Dhamma, wishing to praise the qualities of calm (samatha), insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), the fruit (phala), and Nibbāna—which are explained throughout the entire Paṭisambhidāmagga following the Discourse on Insight—through various methods and by way of distinct modes, briefly stated nineteen matrix terms (mātikāpada) starting with "nicchāto" and then spoke the Discourse on the Matrix by way of detailed explanation of those terms. The explanation of the meanings not previously mentioned in that Discourse on the Matrix is as follows:

In the matrix, first, "nicchāto" means "unfaded" (amilāto). Indeed, all defilements (kilesa) are "faded" (withered) because they are associated with oppression. Even lust (rāga), occurring continuously, burns the body; what then need be said of other coarse defilements? "Monks, there are these three fires: the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion"—thus, only the three primary defilements are called "fires" because of their burning nature. However, the unwholesome states associated with those defilements also certainly burn. Thus, because of the absence of the "hunger" of defilements, one is "nicchāta" (without hunger). What is that? It should be understood as "liberation" (vimokkha) due to its connection with the term vimokkha. It is called "mokkha" because it releases. It is called "vimokkha" because it releases specially. This is the meaning. This term "vimokkha" is one matrix term. "Jhānavimokkho" means the jhana itself is the liberation. This is also one matrix term. It should be understood that the remaining terms are also individual matrix terms. Thus, there are nineteen matrix terms.

"Nicchāto from sensual desire through renunciation" means the yogi who is free from sensual desire through jhana is liberated. The renunciation (nekkhamma) attained by that yogi is also called "nicchāta vimokkha" (unfaded liberation) because it is free from sensual desire. The same method applies to the remaining terms. By the Pali "It is called liberation because one is liberated from sensual desire through renunciation," it is shown that the yogi is liberated from sensual desire by means of jhana; therefore, that renunciation is called liberation—this is the sense of the instrumental means (karaṇasādhana). The same applies to the remaining terms.

"Vijjātīti vijjā" means it is called "vijjā" (knowledge) because it clearly exists by its own nature. Or, it is called "vijjā" because the nature of renunciation is known by yogis who practice to know it. Or, it is called "vijjā" because it is attained by yogis who practice to attain the path and fruit. Or, it is called "vijjā" because it (the jhana) itself attains the object that is to be attained. Or, it is called "vijjā" because it causes the nature of things to be manifest, being the cause for seeing the nature of renunciation. One who has knowledge is liberated; one who is liberated...
319:
Vimokkha means liberation. This term 'Vimokkha' is a single matrix term (mātikāpada). Vijjāvimutti means knowledge itself is liberation. This term 'Vijjāvimutti' is a single matrix term. Jhānavimokkha means Jhana itself is liberation. This term 'Jhānavimokkha' is a single matrix term. The remaining terms are individual matrices. Thus, there are nineteen matrix terms.

'Free from craving' (nicchāta) from sensual desire through renunciation means a yogi who is separated from sensual desire by renunciation and is thus free from the defilement of sensual desire. The renunciation attained by that yogi is also called 'free from craving' liberation because it is separated from sensual desire. The same principle applies to the remaining states. 'Vimokkha' because of being liberated from sensual desire through renunciation means the yogi is liberated from sensual desire through renunciation; therefore, that renunciation is meant by the term 'Vimokkha'. The same principle applies to the remaining states. 'Vijjā' because it is known means it is clearly present by nature; it is meant as 'Vijjā' because it is attainable. Alternatively, it is called 'Vijjā' because the nature is known by yogis practicing to know the nature of renunciation. Alternatively, it is called 'Vijjā' because it is attained by yogis practicing to gain special benefits. Alternatively, it is called 'Vijjā' because one attains the ground that should be attained by oneself. Alternatively, it is called 'Vijjā' because it makes the nature clear as it is the cause for seeing the nature. 'Being present, one is liberated; being liberated, it is present' means the aforementioned state such as renunciation, being present through the five aforementioned meanings of 'Vijjā', is liberated from the aforementioned sensual desire and so on; being liberated from the aforementioned sensual desire and so on, it is present through the five aforementioned meanings of 'Vijjā'. Therefore, it is meant by the term 'Vijjāvimutti'.

'In the sense of restraining sensual desire' means that renunciation is called 'Purification of Virtue' (sīlavisuddhi) because it prevents sensual desire. That same renunciation is 'Purification of Mind' (cittavisuddhi) in the sense of non-distraction because it is the cause of non-distraction. It is 'Purification of View' (diṭṭhivisuddhi) in the sense of seeing because it is the cause of the knowledge that sees. The same principle applies to the remaining states. 'It calms' means the practitioner (yogāvacara) calms sensual desire and so on through renunciation and so on; therefore, the state of renunciation and so on is meant by the term 'Tranquility' (passaddhi). 'Because it is abandoned' means because it is abandoned by various types of abandonment. 'Knowledge in the sense of being known' means the knowledge that takes as its object the states such as renunciation, because it takes as its object what is known through the power of reviewing Jhana, through the power of insight (vipassanā), and through the power of reviewing the Path (magga). 'Vision because it is seen' follows the same principle here. 'It is purified' refers to the yogi; 'renunciation and so on' refers to purification (visuddhi).
320:
In the Nekkhamma-niddesa (Exposition of Renunciation), renunciation is called nissaraṇa (escape) because, being non-greed (alobha), it is liberated from sensual lust (kāmarāga). It is called nekkhamma because it has departed from that [sensual lust]. When it is said, "This renunciation is the escape from forms (rūpa)," the specific immaterial attainment (āruppa) as renunciation is not seen; therefore, to show that distinction, following the sequence of the text taught elsewhere, it is said, "This is the immaterial attainment." That immaterial attainment is also called nekkhamma by virtue of the name nekkhamma, because it has departed from form.

The term 'bhūta' (become) indicates the conjunction of states at the moment of arising (uppāda). The term 'saṅkhata' (conditioned) shows the specific power of conditions (paccaya). The term 'paṭiccasamuppanna' (dependently arisen) shows the absence of agency (avyāpāra) of conditions even when there is a conjunction of conditions. "Cessation is the renunciation of that conditioned" means Nibbāna is called the renunciation of that conditioned state because it has departed from that conditioned state. The inclusion of the immaterial attainment and cessation is done according to the sequence taught in other passages. If it were said, "The renunciation of sensual desire is renunciation," it would be redundant. Since the nature of renunciation is established by the word nekkhamma itself, that is not mentioned, and only the remaining types of renunciation are taught. That teaching is quite straightforward.

In the Nissaraṇa-niddesa (Exposition of Escape) as well, the meaning should be understood in this same way. However, in this Nissaraṇa-niddesa, the elements of escape (nissaraṇīyā dhātuyo) are directly called nekkhamma. 'Paviveka' (seclusion) is the state of being secluded, such as renunciation and so on. 'Vossajjati' (relinquishes) means the practitioner (yogī) gives up. Renunciation and so on are called 'vossagga' (relinquishment). A practitioner who brings about renunciation is said to "walk with renunciation" (nekkhammena carati). That renunciation itself is called 'cariyā' (conduct). This method applies to the remaining states as well. What should be said in the Jhāna-vimokkha-niddesa (Exposition of Jhāna-liberation) has already been stated in the Vimokkha-kathā. However, the distinction is that in the Vimokkha-kathā it was taught as "Because he knows, it is jhāna-liberation," whereas here the teaching is given by way of personal attribution (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), saying "He knows, he meditates."

In the expositions of Bhāvanā (Development), Adhiṭṭhāna (Foundation), and Jīvita (Livelihood), the teaching is also given by way of personal attribution. In terms of ultimate reality (dhammato), what is called bhāvanā is just renunciation and so on. What is called adhiṭṭhāna is the mind established by way of renunciation and so on. What is called jīvita is the right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) of a person whose mind is established by way of renunciation and so on. What is this right livelihood? It is the abstinence from wrong livelihood and the effort to seek requisites righteously and fairly. In that exposition, "lives evenly" (samaṃ jīvati) means he lives by way of an even livelihood. Or, it is an adverbial use, meaning he lives righteously according to the Dhamma. "Not unevenly" is an affirmation of the meaning "lives evenly" by way of negation (paṭisedha). "Lives rightly" shows the mode, and "not wrongly" is a restriction of that. "Lives purely" means he lives with a livelihood that is naturally pure. "Not impurely" is a restriction of that purity. With the words "Whatever..." (yaññadeva)...
321:
The benefits of the three accomplishments (sampadā) mentioned earlier (meditation, resolution, and life) are shown. In that context (the passage beginning with 'Yaññadeva'), 'Yaññadeva' means whatever nature it may be. 'Khattiyaparisā' refers to the assembly or gathering place of the nobles (khattiyas). This is because those without training or wisdom often sink (falter) from all sides in such an assembly or place; hence it is called 'parisā' (assembly). The same method should be understood for the remaining three assemblies (Brāhmaṇa, Gahapati, Samaṇa). Only these four assemblies are taken because the nobles and others are endowed with the accomplishment of learning and the accomplishment of wisdom; the Sudda (laborer) assembly is not included. 'Visārada' means one who is free from embarrassment and fearless, being endowed with the three accomplishments. 'Amaṅkubhūta' means not shrinking, not being one who lacks power or splendor. 'Taṃ kissa hetu' means 'For what reason or cause does such confidence arise?'. Now, with the words 'tathā hi', the reason for that confidence is stated. Because one is thus endowed with the three accomplishments, therefore 'he becomes confident'; thus, showing the cause of confidence, the teaching is concluded.

## In the Saddhammappakāsinī, the Patisambhidamagga Commentary,
## The explanation of the Mātikākathā is finished.
## The explanation of the Paññāvagga is finished.
## The explanation of the new meanings of the Cūḷavagga is finished.
## Hereby, the explanation of the meaning of the Patisambhidamagga, comprised of three divisions and adorned with thirty discourses, is finished.
322:
## Concluding Remarks

In this Patisambhidamagga Pali, the three divisions named Mahāvagga, Majjhimavagga, and Cūḷavagga are taught in sequence. In each division, ten discourses (kathā) are taught; these are the summary verses of those taught discourses in their respective order.

The ten in the Mahāvagga are: Ñāṇakathā, Diṭṭhikathā, Ānāpānakathā, Indriyakathā, and the fifth, Vimokkhakathā, Gatikathā, Kammakathā, Vipallāsakathā, Maggakathā, and Maṇḍakathā.

The ten in the Majjhimavagga are: Yuganaddhakathā, Saccakathā, Bojjhaṅgakathā, Mettākathā, and the fifth, Virāgakathā, Paṭisambhidākathā, Dhammacakkakathā, Lokuttarabalakathā, and Suññatakathā.

The ten in the Cūḷavagga are: Paññākathā, Iddhikathā, Abhisamayakathā, Vivekakathā, and the fifth, Cariyākathā, Pāṭihīrakathā, Samasīsakathā, Satipaṭṭhānakathā, Vipassanākathā, and Mātikākathā.

The Elder Dhammasenāpati, who is the chief among the sons of the Buddha, who delights in the welfare of beings, and who is endowed with stable virtues, taught this Patisambhidamagga Pali. Relying on the method and logic of the ancient commentaries, I (Elder Mahānāma) began this commentary on that Patisambhidamagga Pali, and it has now reached completion.

The minister Uttaramantī, who was endowed with the virtue of wisdom and possessed faith, built and donated the parivena (monastic cell) endowed with many noble qualities at the Mahāvihāra monastery. The Elder named Mahānāma, residing in that parivena, successfully completed this commentary in the third year after the death of King Moggallāna.

Just as this commentary, which is in accordance with the views of the Elders who preserve the Theravāda and which generates welfare for the world of beings, has reached completion, may the heart's desires of all beings also reach fulfillment in accordance with the Dhamma, accomplishing their own benefit and the benefit of others.

In this Saddhammappakāsinī Commentary, it should be understood that there are fifty-eight bhāṇavāras (recital sections) as counted by those skilled in counting.
323:
When counted by the Anuṭṭhubha meter consisting of eight syllables, this commentary has a count of fourteen thousand and five hundred verses.

For the long-lasting endurance of the Sasana and for the welfare of the world, I have respectfully composed this commentary, and thereby have attained extensive and vast merit.

Through that merit, may the world of beings, having enjoyed the pure elixir of the True Dhamma of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha), reach the bliss of Nibbāna through the easy practice.

## The Commentary on the Patisambhidamagga Treatise,
## named Saddhammappakāsinī, is finished.
